The authors offer curiosity rewards as a route to agents that learn who they are talking to while they talk.
arxiv-2504-03806:
A. V. Minkevich reviews a gauge theory of gravity built on a spacetime with torsion in a 2025 theoretical physics study. In Riemann-Cartan geometry, spacetime can twist as well as curve, and a gauge approach treats gravity like the other fundamental forces. The author sets out the theory's place among gauge approaches and builds cosmology from a general gravitational Lagrangian with free parameters.

Consequences include a possible ceiling on energy density, gravitational repulsion under extreme conditions, and a vacuum repulsion effect. Such features could remove the initial singularity and mimic cosmic acceleration. The review weighs which of those claims survive physical scrutiny.
arxiv-2504-04506:
Labeling data costs money, so active learning picks the examples most worth labeling by hand. It struggles when the budget allows few labels, and wobbles further when the labeler errs. Netta Shafir, Guy Hacohen and Daphna Weinshall propose Noise-Aware Active Sampling, a framework that adapts coverage-based selection to noisy labeling. Coverage methods spread chosen examples across the dataset. When a noisy example becomes a region's representative, that region ends up falsely covered.

Their framework spots those falsely covered regions and samples from them again. A simple noise filter from the same mechanism cleans labels before training. On standard image benchmarks, including a hundred-class dataset and subsets of a large photo collection, the method lifted the performance of standard active learning across noise types and noise rates. The authors present it as a practical patch for learning when labels are few and imperfect.
arxiv-2504-04606:
Deformed algebras tweak the usual rules of algebra and have been proposed as tools for quantum physics. Julio Cesar Jaramillo Quiceno and Plamen Neytchev Nechev examine those proposals with strict methods in a 2025 paper. They rebuild a special kind of integral, the Jackson integral, inside a carefully equipped space framework, using point measures where the construction allows.

Along the way, they correct mistakes and loose claims they found in earlier works they cite. Their closing analysis is cautious: real obstacles remain before deformed algebras can be applied soundly to quantum mechanics and field theory. The paper serves as both a repair job and a warning.
arxiv-2504-05506:
Ahmed Masry and a team of co-authors release ChartQAPro, a harder test for systems that answer questions about charts. Their paper from twenty twenty-five notes that charts fill reports and dashboards everywhere. Reading them well takes sharp eyes and hard thought. The older ChartQA test has grown too easy for top vision-language models.

The new set gathers charts from many sources and types, from plain plots to dashboards. Its questions span choice tasks, chat-style turns, what-if cases, and traps with no answer. The team ran a wide set of models on it. Scores fell hard versus the old test. One top model dropped from above ninety percent to the mid-fifties. Error studies map where models fail. The set aims to push chart reading toward real-world skill.
arxiv-2504-05706:
Fida Mohammad Thoker and co-authors stress-test how well self-taught video models travel beyond their training pond, in this 2025 paper. Video models that learn without labels shine on standard action tests, but those tests use near-identical training and scoring sets. The team broadens an earlier sensitivity study to modern transformer models, both video-only and video-text, plus older convolutional rivals. Over eleven hundred runs span eight datasets and seven tasks.

Four pressures are applied: new domains, fewer training samples, finer action classes, and new task types. No method held up across all four. Video-only transformers coped best with domain shift, plain convolutional nets won on fine-grained actions, and video-text models often lagged despite giant pretraining. Newer transformers did not reliably beat older ones.
arxiv-2504-06206:
Some quantum models let particles hop one way around a loop more easily than the other, breaking the usual rules of Hermitian physics. Eduard Naichuk and co-authors built a two-dimensional version of such a model and added electron repulsion. They asked whether magnetic order survives in a system that can gain and lose energy.

Antiferromagnetism, with neighboring spins opposed, does form. The model keeps a combined symmetry that splits its behavior in two: a region with real energies and a broken region with complex ones. The border between them coincides with the switch from metal to insulator, tuned by the repulsion strength. Spin waves come in paired diffusive modes, one tied to gain, one to loss.
arxiv-2504-06506:
Christoph Fischbacher, Fritz Gesztesy, and Lance Littlejohn review product rules for defect numbers in a 2025 paper. The paper is largely a teaching piece. Defect numbers measure how far a closed operator sits from being fully well behaved, and they matter when operators are multiplied together. The authors gather known facts on how defect numbers behave for products.

Their tools come from the theory of semi-Fredholm operators, a class with well mapped behavior. They apply the product facts to whole-number powers of symmetric operators. They then turn to minimal Sturm-Liouville operators and to higher even-order operators, in both ordinary and partial differential form. Along the way, they flag chances that past research groups missed when similar work was compared side by side.
arxiv-2504-07306:
Carolina Benedetti and three co-authors study an order on matroids in twenty twenty-five. Matroid quotients connect to deep questions about flag variety geometry. For lattice path matroids, earlier work characterized quotients by a simple combinatorial condition. The resulting quotient order is a graded poset whose rank polynomial refines the Catalan numbers.

The authors show this poset admits an EL-labeling. That labeling implies the order complex is shellable, a strong structural property. Shellability brings several combinatorial and topological benefits with it. They also bound the poset's Möbius function through falling chains in the labeling. Those chains are read through properties of the underlying permutations. The labeling turns out to be a Whitney labeling as well.
arxiv-2504-07406:
Yu-Hua Chen and five co-authors work on automatically transcribing amplified electric guitar recordings into notes. Amps, cabinets, and pedals reshape tone so much that models trained on narrow data fail on new rigs. Diverse training data were the first bottleneck.

They built EGDB-PG, a dataset spanning many amplifier and cabinet combinations to capture that tonal variety. Their Tone-informed Transformer adds a learned tone embedding so the model can adapt to each setup's character. Trained on the new dataset, it beat existing baselines across amplifier types. Ablation studies separated the contributions of tone and content augmentation, normalization, and the tone embedding itself.
arxiv-2504-08006:
Petri nets are a classic tool for modeling systems that reason and act step by step, but plain nets know nothing about the meanings of the things they move. Krzysztof Pancerz blends them with ontologies, structured webs of concepts and relations drawn from the OWL 2 web language. In these nets the tokens and places carry that meaning with them.

The paper lays out the basic theory of such nets and then presents a working Python toolkit for them. Users can define both the structure of a net and how it runs, while the ontology supplies semantic links in the background. The aim is richer models for reasoning and control processes. Domain knowledge, once locked in documents, becomes part of the machine that thinks with it.
arxiv-2504-09606:
Lexington Whalen and five co-authors, including Yingyan Lin, look for sparse subnetworks inside diffusion models that appear early in training and still generate well. Training these models is expensive because every step runs many timesteps. Pruning to an early-bird ticket could cut that cost sharply.

The team first confirms that ordinary early-bird tickets exist in diffusion models. They then refine the idea: timesteps matter unequally, so sparsity should be aggressive in unimportant ranges and gentle in critical ones. Their training scheme derives such timestep-aware tickets, trains them in parallel, and merges them for generation. Experiments support the efficiency gains, and the method combines with other acceleration techniques.
arxiv-2504-09806:
Albert Schwarz asks whether quantum theory can be forced on an observer who lives inside a classical world near equilibrium. He considers Hamiltonian systems with a non-degenerate minimum at zero momentum and position, where the sum of squares of momenta and coordinates is conserved. Near that point the quadratic part of the Hamiltonian dominates everything.

Suppose a classical observer can only measure quantities tied to quadratic Hamiltonians. Schwarz argues such an observer must describe his world with the laws of quantum theory. The catalog entry buries the author inside affiliation and email text; the head byline names Albert Schwarz of the University of California, Davis.
arxiv-2504-10006:
Valentin Charvet and co-authors recast robot control problems in dimensionless form so learned controllers travel better to new settings, in a 2025 paper. Controllers trained by reinforcement learning often fail when the test setup differs from training. The team's fix trains both the world model and the policy in scaled, unit-free variables, using a classic physics scaling theorem.

Their framework extends contextual decision processes with that scaling step, which makes policies respond evenly to context changes. A model-based search method with Gaussian process models carries the approach. On simulated pendulum and cartpole systems, policies trained in one setting held up when the setting's distribution shifted.
arxiv-2504-10606:
Milica Banic and co-authors present an exact way to simulate a prized quantum resource in a 2025 paper. The resource is the GKP state, a pattern of light that can correct its own errors, and its cluster form links many such states for quantum computing. Real versions are imperfect, and the standard simulation basis is too slow to cover the cases that matter.

Their method writes each resource state as a sum of Gaussian humps in phase space, which computers can handle exactly and fast. They use it to study making single GKP states by breeding cat states, and building multi-mode clusters with optical circuits and measurements. Scores from stabilizer measures match the slow standard simulations. They also test a popular noise shortcut against the exact answers and find gaps, a warning for designers who trust the shortcut.
arxiv-2504-11006:
Mingshuo Han, Shiwei Hu, Tianbai Xiao, and Yonghao Zhang present a hybrid method for simulating fast flows that break solid materials. Their 2025 paper joins two solvers at a fine scale. One handles compressible gas flow with a method rooted in molecular theory, and the other handles damage in solids without a mesh.

The two fields update together at each time step, swapping boundary data through a ghost-cell technique. Tests include a cracking plate, flow around a wing profile, supersonic flow past a cylinder, and a shock wave hitting an elastic panel. Results matched the hybrid method's aims across those varied cases. Such coupling matters in aerospace work, where high-speed flow and breaking parts meet in real failures.
arxiv-2504-11606:
Ruoqi Zhao, Hengyuan Shen, Allen LaCour, Joseph Heindel, Martin Head-Gordon, and Teresa Head-Gordon test a romantic idea about why oil droplets in water repel: maybe electrons themselves leak from water into oil. Emulsion droplets carry negative surface charge, and its molecular origin is contested. Ions gathering at the interface are the conventional suspect. Charge transfer across weak carbon-hydrogen to oxygen contacts is the challenger.

Energy decomposition analysis delivers the verdict. Forward and backward charge flows through those weak contacts nearly cancel, leaving a negligible net transfer. Droplets charged only that way would coalesce, contradicting experiment. The same analysis explains a spectroscopic blue shift as Pauli repulsion from interfacial confinement. Neither transfer nor polarization yields the conductivity that electrophoretic mobility requires. Ions keep their crown.
arxiv-2504-13206:
Aniket Roy and co-authors present DuoLoRA, a method to personalize image models for content and style at once, in a research paper from 2025. Users may want a subject from a few photos rendered in a style from a few others. Training split adapters for content and style, then merging them, is a promising route, but past merges treat the two as independent.

Content and style in fact intertwine. DuoLoRA merges inside the rank dimension of the adapters, cutting learnable parameters. Layer priors from the base model guide how much rank each layer gives to content or style. A cycle-consistency loss refines the merge. Tests show cleaner joint personalization from few examples.
arxiv-2504-14006: Zoé Chatzidakis and Nicholas Ramsey work in mathematical logic. In this 2025 arXiv paper they describe a way to build Keisler measures on bounded perfect PAC fields. As a payoff, they prove a broad amenability result. Every group that can be defined inside such a field is definably amenable. The same holds in a wider class of fields, the unbounded perfect Frobenius fields. The construction grows out of their earlier work on e-free PAC fields. It also builds on a related construction by Will Johnson.
arxiv-2504-14106:
Bulat Gafarov, Matthias Meier, and José Luis Montiel Olea wrote a paper in 2025 on projection inference for structural vector autoregressions. In these models the parameters of interest are set-identified rather than point-identified. Such models trace how economic shocks, such as shifts in labor supply or demand, move through an economy. In some, the values are pinned to a set of possible values, not a point.

The paper studies the classical projection method, which builds confidence regions covering both the structural impulse-response coefficients and their identified set. The authors show that, as the sample size grows, projection inference achieves at least the nominal level in two senses at once: frequentist coverage and robust Bayesian credibility. They calibrate the region's radius so that the robust Bayesian credibility is exact for a posterior. A demand and supply model of the United States labor market illustrates the method.
arxiv-2504-14706:
Shin-nosuke Ishikawa and Atsushi Yoshino test in 2025 whether large language models can act out set emotions. Public hopes for AI with feelings are rising as these models match human skill on many tasks. The team asked several leading models to answer questions while playing a given emotional state.

They set each state with a classic map of emotion that uses two scales: how pleasant it feels, and how stirred up it is. A separate sentiment tool, trained on a public set of labeled feelings, then scored the replies. The replies matched the states they were asked to play. The authors say this skill could support AI advisors that respond with a more personal touch.
arxiv-2504-14806:
Xiongwei Zhao and colleagues published a computer science paper in 2025 on robot navigation in bad weather. Self-driving systems use laser scans to recognize places they have visited. Rain, snow, and fog corrupt those scans with noise. Recognition then fails exactly when driving is hardest.

Their framework pairs a cleanup module with the recognition module. The two train together in alternating rounds. Cleaned scans help recognition stay accurate in storms. Recognition feedback, in turn, teaches cleanup what matters. Special blocks mix frequency and spatial features for the cleanup step. A semantic-aware generator rebuilds the damaged point clouds. The authors report stronger place recognition under harsh weather than earlier methods.
arxiv-2504-16006:
Wenlin Li, Xingli Li, Yan Li, Francesco Marzioni, Paolo Piergentili, Francesco Rasponi, and David Vitali wrote a 2025 paper on a light-and-motion device. Two thin membranes sit inside a mirrored cavity, and light bouncing inside pushes on them as they vibrate. Most studies use a simple model in which the push grows in a straight line with each membrane's shift.

The team instead worked out the full behavior, keeping the exact curved link between the light and the membranes. They compared the full model with the simple one and found where the two part ways. In some settings the simple model gives plainly wrong predictions, for linked vibration and for quantum links between the membranes. The work tells experimenters when the shortcut is safe and when it misleads.
arxiv-2504-17006:
Jalal Arabneydi and a large team set out a plan for deep learning rigs that learn with a human in the loop. Trial-and-error AI can steer hard tasks, yet real rigs gain when a human feeds hints mid-run. Their 2025 plan stacks three learning modes: self trial, copying a guide, and carry-over from past tasks. Human input comes in three forms too: score marks, set acts, and shown runs.

A drone duel tests the plan: guard drones must stop foe drones from a barred zone. The rig runs on an award-grade open tool for loop work. Loop runs trained faster and scored higher than lone runs. Hints steered the learning path and cut its shake. Too much or too little hint hurt the end grade, so dose counts. Twin stress tests, a flood and a decoy rush, also passed.
arxiv-2504-18406:
Yusen Zhang and co-authors published a 2025 paper testing how well AI vision models handle very large images. Some images hold over a million pixels: tissue scans, farm fields seen from the air, telescope views. Models that mix vision and language claim to cope with such pictures. Yet no test measured that claim across many kinds of scenes.

The team's benchmark, HRScene, gathers twenty-five datasets plus two made-up test sets. Image sizes run from about a thousand pixels square to more than thirty-five thousand on a side. Ten annotators collected and re-labeled the material. The scenes range from microscope views to street photos and scanned documents. The made-up sets hide a target image among distractors to probe how models use each region. Testing twenty-eight models showed how far current models fall short.
arxiv-2504-19206:
Ahmed Zahari Abdou, Kol Beatrice Gamou, and Ibrahima Bakayoko classify Leibniz algebras and their Rota-type operators in a two thousand twenty-five math paper. A Leibniz algebra is a variant of a Lie algebra. In the nilpotent kind, repeated products vanish. A compatible kind has two multiplication rules that interact in a set way.

The team gives computer based methods for these structures in four dimensions. It gives full lists of the compatible nilpotent ones with size below four. They also list the matching operators, which are linear maps that meet a weighted form of a classic identity. Other researchers can use these lists to test ideas and find examples.
arxiv-2504-19306:
Jixuan Liu, Long Feng, Liuhua Peng, and Zhaojun Wang build a test for sudden shifts in large data sets. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, works when data has many parts at once. A shift point is a spot where the pattern changes. Old tests based on means can fail when data has heavy tails.

The new test uses spatial signs and medians, which resist odd values. It checks both the largest shift in one part and the sum across parts. The authors prove how the test acts when no shift is present. Tests on made-up data show strong power for both sparse and dense shifts.
arxiv-2504-19406:
Good quiz questions from a lecture video must land on the right moment and the right answer. Mengxia Yu and co-authors build a system for that job in a 2025 paper, working from real classroom recordings rather than tidy textbook text.

They first gathered a data set of questions tied to actual lectures, speech and slides together. Current generators stumbled there, picking weak context and drifting from target answers. Their framework uses a language model to select context from both the transcript and key video frames, favoring passages near the target time and relevant to the answer. The chosen pieces are then rewritten into answer-bearing knowledge statements before questions are drafted. Question quality and relevance rose clearly.
arxiv-2504-20106:
Liang and eight co-authors split help and harm aims into shift codes for model tuning in this twenty twenty-five paper. A model tuned too strict says no too much, while a loose one may do harm. Past drills bake both aims in one pot, which blurs fine control at use time.

Inside, one model is drilled per aim, and its shift from base is kept as a code. At test time those codes merge in shares the user sets by hand. New aims join the mix with no fresh drill of the whole base. Tests show help gains with no wild rise in no-said calls. Smooth knobs let a user slide the help-harm mix live as needs shift.
arxiv-2504-21206:
Zihan Chen, Xingbo Fu, Yushun Dong, Jundong Li, and Cong Shen present FedHERO, a federated method for labeling nodes in graphs whose neighbors tend to differ. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Federated graph learning trains shared models across private data holders. Most methods assume neighbors resemble each other, as friends often share tastes.

Real graphs often break that rule: fraudsters link to honest users, and unlike nodes connect. When clients hold graphs with different mixing patterns, their local lessons clash. Merging them can wreck the global model. FedHERO's two-channel network learns the structure of each local graph as it goes. It separates the patterns that travel across graphs from those that stay local. Client models gain from both their own and the shared structural insight. The authors claim a new standard for heterophilic federated learning.
arxiv-2504-21506:
Nasipuri and Chatterjee study how exotic waves meet and merge in a coupled Boussinesq system, a model of shallow water waves. They use the Hirota bilinear method to build exact wave forms. Lump waves come first, derived from a quadratic form in the method. Then come meetings between lumps and kink waves, which yield double lump patterns. Breather waves add a further family of shapes.

Breathers were seen to spread in a diffusion-like way as they interact. They can meet periodic waves, kinks, and bright solitons for the right settings. Pairs of double breathers also interact in chains. Symbolic math and plots together reveal the behavior. The work reports patterns not seen before in this system.
arxiv-2505-00106:
Yuma Watanabe and four co-authors present a physics study from 2025 on a model of bosons on a ladder-like lattice. An past study had claimed a strange phase in which flow-like order and string-like order occur at once. The team tests that claim with two strong computer methods for such systems.

One method, used on finite chains, gave results that fit the claimed phase. The second method, built for endless chains, gave sharper phase lines and left no room for that phase. The work shows why the choice of method matters when teams map phases that are hard to pin down in low-dimension systems.  Their phase map is offered as a firmer guide for later theory and lab work on such ladders.
arxiv-2505-02406:
Zichen Liu, Xu Zou, Gang Hua, and Jiahuan Zhou present a new part for vision models in two thousand twenty-five. Such models are often tuned with a small set of learned prompts shared by all image tokens. The shared setup treats each token the same, though tokens play quite distinct roles.

Their part, called Token Coordinated Prompt Attention, splits prompts into two kinds. One kind works only with the class token, which sums up the whole image. The other kind works with patch tokens, and a matching rule gives each patch its own prompt. Tests on many standard sets show clear gains over the shared-prompt approach.
arxiv-2505-03006:
Chen studies random motions of many bosons that pull on each other at a single point, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The work is the third part in a series on this gas in two dimensions. The gas model is used to test hard ideas in quantum physics. Chen aims to link the random motions to path-sum formulas.

He uses motions built in the prior part of the series as the base paths. He shows the path-sum formulas hold for any count of three or more bosons. The weights on the paths take a new form here. They come from exact solutions found in an earlier paper in the series. For two bosons, the formula is a small tweak of a known one.
arxiv-2505-04406:
Valeev and co-authors launch YABLoCo, a bench for long-tale code birth in vast shops. Word tools can write code, yet tests use short tales in the main. Real shops span up to scores of 1,000s of code lines. Their bench holds 215 tasks picked from four big shops. Each task is a lone task form in a big shop set. Shop facts join task past, tale tiers, tales, and call webs.

Tasks aim at task body birth in C and C-plus tongues. Those tongues lacked past bench care in long-tale work. Shops span 200K to 2,000K lines of code in the set. A scale score pipe grades the made code at low cost. A sight tool lets hands view the made code in depth. The bench thus tests tools as real shops would strain them.
arxiv-2505-04806:
Chetan Pathade weighs in a set way how with ease top language models can be broke out of their guards. As these models spread into goods for home and work use, prompt tricks and jail breaks threat the guards meant to hold them in. The work sorts more than 1,400 prompts made to hit them. It tests them next to four models, GPT-4 and Claude 2 in that set.

The read checks rates of hits by such prompts, how plans spread through models, and the build sense in back of prompts that work. Pathade then sets out shield plans in tiers. His tip joins red team work that does not stop with sand box walls for firm guard. The text is a guard check. It maps the hit face of models in use and says guards must be built in form, not in looks.
arxiv-2505-06206:
Alexander Clow, Alfie Davies, and Neil Anderson McKay extend a game result in a 2025 combinatorics paper. A placement game on directed graphs was lately proved able to mirror any normal-play game. Games are classed by the day their values first appear, and past work built all day-two values on at most four graph points.

The team combined exhaustive and random computer searches to build all one thousand four hundred seventy-four day-three values. Each needed at most eight points, and the authors prove eight is sometimes required. They also improve bounds for day-four and day-five values. The work tightens the link between abstract game values and concrete graph constructions.
arxiv-2505-06306:
Yikun Li and co-authors describe a smart radio surface in a 2025 engineering letter. Such surfaces bounce wireless signals in chosen directions to boost coverage, and the best ones stay thin, work over a wide band, and steer smoothly. Their design adds a middle patch layer, with no extra air gap, to keep the panel slim.

A built array of ten by ten units steered beams cleanly across a wide slice of spectrum. The surface shifted signal phase smoothly over a broad range while keeping reflections strong. Tests showed stable behavior across the full band. The authors present the design as a fit for next-generation wireless systems that need flat, tunable panels on walls or towers.
arxiv-2505-06606:
Ernandes and co-authors read the life story of a swallowed galaxy in its stars' chemistry in a 2025 paper. The Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus merger was the Milky Way's last big one, roughly a Large Magellanic Cloud's worth of stars, and its debris records how a dwarf galaxy lived before it fell in. Heavy elements made by different kinds of stellar explosions act as dated receipts.

Using abundances gathered in the SAGA database, the team compared ratios of europium, barium, and magnesium against those in surviving dwarf satellites. The patterns say the lost galaxy formed stars slowly for more than two billion years before the merger shut it down. Such element fingerprints can date other eaten galaxies too.
arxiv-2505-08706:
Ningzi Li, Shiyang Lai, and James Evans review how big data and machine learning are reshaping the study of entrepreneurship and innovation, in a book chapter from 2025. Huge streams of text, network, image, and video data now record business life as it happens. That flood brings both fresh questions and fresh traps, such as spotting true novelty.

The authors describe two uses. First, models fed on large data can build precise measures that act as observatories, watching innovation across whole societies. Second, AI models can form digital doubles of technologies and firms, giving labs for virtual tests of ideas and policies. The chapter argues that pairing big data with big models can advance how theory in this field is built and checked.
arxiv-2505-09206:
Zhenyu Du and colleagues set out a randomized measurement protocol to gauge non-linear traits of quantum states. Quantum mechanics is linear at its base. That makes it hard to learn non-linear traits of a state. Single-copy randomized protocols had hit best sample counts for set tasks such as purity gauges. They had not done so for broader classes of traits.

Their protocol gauges the trace of an observable times the squared density matrix. That value sits at the core of quantum computing and many-body physics. They prove a bound on its sample count and show it is best for observables with large trace norm. That set includes Pauli and local observables. For those, the protocol runs well with Clifford circuits. Tests show it needs far fewer samples than classical shadows for the same precision.
arxiv-2505-09606:
Steve Cabrel Teguia Kouam, Jean-Pierre Tchapet Njafa, and others benchmark fast, rough quantum chemistry methods on semiconductor molecules in a 2025 study. The GFN family of semiempirical methods promises geometries at a fraction of the cost of density functional theory, the standard workhorse. Four variants, from tight-binding flavors to a force-field version, face that standard on small organic semiconductor molecules.

Optimized shapes and electronic traits are compared method by method. The systematic scorecard of accuracy against cost helps chemists choose the cheapest tool that stays sound for screening new electronic materials.
arxiv-2505-10006:
Diptarka Chakraborty and co-authors merge rankings fairly with better guarantees in a 2025 paper. Rank aggregation blends many orderings into one consensus, for hiring, admissions, and search. A consensus can quietly stack the top spots against a group. Fair variants demand balanced representation near the top, but the best known algorithm only promised a factor-three closeness to optimal.

The authors first give an algorithm within a hair above factor two of optimal. A second method reaches a factor just under two point nine, whatever fairness rule is chosen, as long as a closest fair ranking can be found. Tests on real data sets backed the theory against state-of-the-art rivals. The paper sharpens a young field's core tool. Fairness in aggregation, it shows, need not cost as much accuracy as feared.
arxiv-2505-10206:
Kendall Shepherd and co-authors published this study in 2025. It asks how stronger winds change the lives of very massive stars. Such stars, hundreds of times the Sun's mass, forge heavy elements and seed the largest black holes. Near a brightness limit, their winds may blow far harder than standard recipes say. The team put wind rules tied to that limit into a star evolution code. They modeled single stars and pairs, then checked against a real star cluster.

The stronger-wind tracks matched observed stars better. The cluster's brightest star still strains single-star origins, though mergers of pairs could explain it. In pairs, hard winds blocked mergers while stars still burned hydrogen. Leftover black holes shifted heavier in some ranges and vanished in others. Wind strength, the authors show, steers both star fates and black hole censuses.
arxiv-2505-10606:
Hector Pasten and co-authors prove two limits that hold back all Transformer models, in work from 2025. The first, isolation, says a learnable sequence must sit apart from other learnable ones, so some sets cannot be learned by one model at once. The second, continuity, says a learned sequence pulls near neighbors toward itself like a basin.

Both effects are proven for all models that use compact position codes. Careful tests show the same blocks arise at real scale, not just on paper. The authors frame the pair as basic facts about how these models store patterns, with weight for both theory and practice.
arxiv-2505-11606:
Alfaro, Rodriguez, and Ruiz wrote in twenty twenty-five about galaxies living inside cosmic voids. Voids are vast regions with very few galaxies in them. A halo occupation count shows how many galaxies sit in each dark matter halo. In voids that count runs low, but how it changed over time was less clear. The team used a large simulated galaxy catalog to find round voids at many past times.

Void counts stayed below the overall average at every time they checked. Galaxies found in voids today had also lived below average in the past. Small void halos formed late and sit deep inside voids. Large ones formed early and sit near void edges. The results show place shapes galaxy growth over long spans.
arxiv-2505-12506:
Yotam Norman and Ron Meir extend invariant risk minimization, a method that learns traits that hold across settings, to data with no labels. Classic forms need labels to find traits that shrug off distribution shifts. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The new frame redefines steadiness as match of trait spreads across settings. Two methods sit inside it, a linear one that pulls steady directions under bell curve premises, and a deep generative one that splits steady from setting bound traits. Both rest on a new cause model for unlabeled data and allow made samples per setting. Tests on made data, digit sets, and face photos show the traits hold.
arxiv-2505-13706:
Jose and Greenstadt tested whether large language models are good at detecting propaganda in twenty twenty-five. Propaganda uses fallacies and emotional appeals to push an agenda. Spotting its techniques helps readers make informed choices, and automated detection is an active research goal.

The team compared several large models with transformer-based systems on news articles. GPT-4 scored best among the large models but still far below a RoBERTa-based baseline. All three large models beat another baseline at spotting name-calling, one of six techniques tested. Two also beat it on appeals to fear and flag-waving. The authors conclude that large models, despite their fame, lag a smaller specialized model at this task overall.
arxiv-2505-14506:
Heat in a solid rides on tiny vibration packets, and how far each packet travels before it scatters sets how well the solid conducts. Katharina Dudde and co-authors show in a 2025 paper that a common light-based heat probe can map those travel lengths in silicon. They change the size of the laser spot and the depth the light reaches, then read how the measured conduction shifts.

With a wide spot, the readings settle at the known bulk value for silicon. As the spot shrinks, the reading climbs several-fold, a sign that some packets fly straight across the probed zone without scattering. Matching the trend to deep theory lets the team read off the travel-length spread. A second trick, swapping the laser color to change depth, shows the same effect in steps.
arxiv-2505-14706:
Eric Habjan, Richard Dube, James McIntyre, Mezmur Edo, and Richard Jones wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five, per its text, though the catalog names Jones alone. It uses machine learning to name the particles seen in the GlueX detector at Jefferson Lab.

The standing method sets hard cuts on track and shower traits. The team trains multi-layer perceptrons and boosted decision trees on the same rebuilt traits, from simulated GlueX data. Both learners name charged and neutral particles far more truly than the cuts. The gain comes with no new detector data, just a smarter read of what is already logged. The study makes the case for learned sorting in the GlueX pipeline.
arxiv-2505-15306:
Yiwen Song and four co-authors combine weak agents into a strong one in twenty twenty-five. Training a good reinforcement learning agent is touchy work. The choice of algorithm, settings, and even random seed can swing results. Ensembles help by merging several agents, but fixed rules like majority voting do not understand the task at hand.

Their method, LLM-Ens, uses a large language model to guide the merger. The model brings task-specific semantic understanding to how agents are combined. That makes the ensemble adapt to the task instead of following a frozen rule. The authors frame the result as many weak agents beating a single strong one. Readers get a smarter way to pool agents that were each trained cheaply.
arxiv-2505-15606:
Marino Romero and Joshua Jeishing Wen published a 2025 paper on a family of special polynomials used in modern algebra. Wreath Macdonald polynomials blend symmetry with extra structure drawn from a wreath, a ring-like group action. Their formulas are rich but hard to compute by hand.

The pair prove a set of five-term links between operators that act on these polynomials. The links echo a known set for a plainer branch of the same family. From them, the authors draw table-like rules for key values called Pieri coefficients. Those rules turn slow expansions into quick counts over filled diagrams. Fast formulas like these help both hand work and computer algebra in the field.
arxiv-2505-15906:
Ming Zhang, Cui-Qun Chen, Dao-Xin Yao, and Fan Yang work out where superconductivity lives inside a layered nickel oxide under pressure. Their paper appeared in 2025. The material stacks double and single nickel-oxygen layers, and it superconducts up to about 64 kelvin when squeezed, with a dome-shaped response to pressure. Computer band calculations show the two layer types form nearly separate electronic worlds.

Fluctuation analysis then finds the pairing in the double layers, with the same sign-changing wave pattern as its famous cousin compound. The single layers barely pair at all; instead they act as a bridge, locking the double layers into phase through Josephson coupling. The authors say the division of labor explains the dome.
arxiv-2505-16106:
Xiaoshan Chen, Chen Yang, and Zhou Yang build a pricing model for data assets in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Data assets are data goods that have been processed, priced, and traded to meet demand. Most past work prices data from the seller's side, based on traits and collection cost. These authors take the buyer's side. For a buyer, data pays off by giving an edge in choices, not by earning cash at once.

Their model grows out of two robust investment and spending problems set in markets with ambiguity. The fair price falls out of an equation tied to the buyer's value functions. In effect, data is worth what it adds to the buyer's decisions. The paper speaks to economists and to firms building data markets.
arxiv-2505-16206:
Lucas Lima and colleagues studied magnetism on unusual three-dimensional lattices in 2025. They use the Hubbard model, a basic model of electrons that hop between sites and repel when they share one. Their lattices extend the Lieb design, known for flat energy bands where electrons barely move and effects grow strong.

Heavy computer sampling, backed by simpler theories, maps when magnetic order survives at real temperatures. One lattice orders with spins aligned, the other with spins opposed, and each peak ordering temperature traces a hump as repulsion grows. Flat bands build local moments fast, yet weak links between orbitals cap the ordering heat. Rich connections help the second lattice order even without flat bands.
arxiv-2505-17506:
Seokmin Ko, Ambuj Tewari, and Kihyuk Hong study how to learn a safe policy from logged data when the logs cover only part of the state space, in a 2025 paper. In offline reinforcement learning the agent cannot test actions live, so it must reason from records. Adding safety limits makes the task harder, and many past methods need full coverage or knowledge of how the data were gathered.

Their algorithm, PDOCRL, treats the policy itself as a variable in a reshaped math program and runs a back-and-forth search for the best safe point. They show the usual form of this search can settle on false answers, and they name a stronger condition that rules those out. Under that condition, with coverage of just one good policy, the method returns a near-best, near-safe policy with a stated sample bound.
arxiv-2505-18406:
M. Kanafani and a large team measured how electrons bounce off a crystal detector in 2025. Simulation codes that track electrons through matter underpin dose estimates in medicine and detector design, but lab data at a few million electron volts are scarce for checking them. The team fired electrons across a wide energy range at a scintillator crystal and counted how many bounced back.

A near-full-angle catcher captured electrons even at steep entry angles. Compared with the Geant4 toolkit under its best physics settings, the counts agreed within a few percent. That close match raises trust in the simulations for nearby uses. New benchmark data at these energies had been a clear gap in the field.
arxiv-2505-18606:
Zhu-yao Jin and Jun Jing steer quantum systems with Hamiltonians that are not Hermitian, treating geometry as a first-class citizen. Standard control engineers the Hamiltonian and lets manifold geometry and constraints follow. Inspired by a classical principle that weighs active, constraint, and inertial forces evenly, the authors do the same here. The arena is a finite system driven in time.

Under a biorthogonal basis, the Hamiltonian can be triangularized in a constraint picture. That condition suffices to build a universal nonadiabatic passage in both halves of the state description. The target state arrives already normalized, with no artificial fix-ups. The passage resists parameter errors when its phase's real part varies fast. Perfect transfer in two levels and chiral transfer in three verify the scheme. The work extends universal control into biorthogonal quantum mechanics.
arxiv-2505-18706:
Viacheslav Sinii and co-authors show, in a 2025 paper, that a handful of steering vectors can teach a language model to reason as well as a full fine-tune. Their method trains one small vector per layer with reinforcement learning while every base weight stays frozen. On an eight billion parameter model, the added parts amount to a tiny sliver of extra size.

Across several base models and math reasoning tests, the light method matched fully tuned models. The savings are practical: less memory for the optimizer and less traffic between processors, which cuts the cost of training. A look inside the model shows the vectors amplify word directions that hang together, which sharpens the chain of thought. The authors argue that high-level reasoning needs far fewer trained numbers than assumed.
arxiv-2505-19706:
Pala and four co-authors improve the models that grade each step of a language model's math reasoning. Outcome-only grading checks just the final answer, which hides where reasoning goes wrong. Their system, PathFinder-PRM, first labels the kind of error in each step, then judges the step itself.

Training used a new dataset of 400,000 steps with three kinds of step-level labels. The model reached the best score yet on a standard benchmark while using three times less data. In guided search tests it also beat the strongest rival. The authors argue that naming errors before scoring them makes step grading both sharper and cheaper.
arxiv-2505-20006:
Raphaël Bagat, Irina Illina, and Emmanuel Vincent improved speech recognition for non-native accents in two thousand twenty-five. Systems often fail on accented speech, and data for many accents are scarce. Their method fine-tunes a model with a mixture of small adapter experts, each tuned to one accent.

The method works whether the accent is known at use time or not, with no need to retrain. Tests used the Whisper model on a corpus of second-language English speech. Word error fell clearly versus standard adapters and full fine-tuning when the accent was unknown, and fell further when it was known. The mixture also forgot less of its prior skill than rival methods.
arxiv-2505-20706:
Shaohua Zhang, Yuchong Luo, and five colleagues catalog dust absorbers that live in the same homes as their quasars, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. The absorbers carry the famous twenty-one seventy-five angstrom bump, a fingerprint of carbon-rich dust. Finding them at the quasar's own redshift ties them to its nucleus, host galaxy, or surroundings.

The team mined spectra and photometry for over five hundred fifty thousand quasars from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey's sixteenth data release. They identified eight hundred forty-three absorbers tied to their quasars. The bumps are weak and narrow on average, while their peak positions wander over a broad range. The average extinction curve resembles the Large Magellanic Cloud's, with a shallower rise. In quasars with broad absorption lines, the bumps shift systematically. A systematic census like this turns anecdotal dust sightings into population statistics.
arxiv-2505-21206:
The CMS Collaboration searches in 2025 for charge-parity violation in events with top quarks and Z bosons at the Large Hadron Collider. The catalog creator field is blank, so the byline in the text governs here. Data came from proton collisions at two energies, collected over several years.

For the first time in this channel, they use observables that are odd under the charge-parity transform. Machine learning informed by physics helps build those observables. Standard model processes predict symmetric distributions, while new effects would skew them. Results agree with the standard model within two standard deviations, and limits are set on two effective operators.
arxiv-2505-21706:
Gonzalo Travieso, Joao Merenda, and Odemir Bruno wrote a 2025 paper on telling networks apart by their shape. Networks model many systems, from friendships to roads to brain links. Given only the web of links, can a program guess what kind of system it came from? That task needs features that capture what makes each kind distinct.

The team proposes features drawn from random walks, where a walker hops from node to node and the path is measured. Walks reveal how tight or spread out a network is. They compared their walk-based features with leading rival methods on several data sets. The new method often won, though it lagged on some sets. The work adds a cheap, clear tool to the network analysis kit.
arxiv-2505-21806:
Brian Bue and co-authors present a 2025 computing paper on spotting greenhouse gas plumes with automated tools. Imaging spectrometers on planes and satellites can map methane leaks at fine scale. Turning that flood of data into reliable alerts still needs full automation.

The team tackles three blocks: poor data and label quality, biases in time and place, and mismatched training goals. With cleaned multi-campaign data from airborne and space instruments, their neural networks reach performance fit for operations. One multitask model finds plumes and outlines them pixel by pixel at the same time. The authors test detection across source types and regions to set deployment thresholds. They release data, models, and code, and propose shared validation standards for the field.
arxiv-2505-22606:
Dominic Briseno-Colunga and a team of co-authors study qubits driven by two microwave tones at once. Their twenty twenty-five paper deals with quantum bits in superconducting and semiconductor chips. Each drive that tunes a qubit also lets in low-frequency noise, which can cut its coherence time hard.

Sweet spots are drive settings where that noise bites least, and sour spots are where it bites most. With two drives of matched periods, the team maps both kinds of region using Floquet theory. They find whole manifolds of doubly sweet spots, along which settings can slide with no loss of coherence. That eases a trade-off seen with a single drive.
arxiv-2505-22706:
Fabio Rigamonti, Lorenzo Bertassi, Riccardo Buscicchio, and five colleagues re-examine a claimed pair of supermassive black holes in this two thousand twenty-five astronomy paper. Merged galaxies should often host two central black holes, among the loudest expected low-frequency gravitational wave sources. The galaxy SDSS J2320+0024 was proposed as a candidate because its light curve seemed periodic and its magnesium emission line varied. The authors reanalyzed the optical light curves in three bands with Bayesian model selection.

When periodicity competed against red noise, the g-band showed a broad posterior bump near two hundred ninety days, too broad to favor periodic models, and the other bands showed no matching peak. A periodic-only model picked a different, roughly eleven-hundred-day period but was statistically disfavored. The verdict: no significant evidence for true periodicity over ordinary red-noise variability. The binary interpretation is challenged but not ruled out.
arxiv-2505-23906:
Yu-Jen Chiu, Eric Weiner, and Ahmad Omar rebuild transport theory without assuming local equilibrium in a paper from 2025. The classic linear laws of transport rest on that assumption. Yet linear behavior shows up in many systems where local equilibrium is doubtful. The authors derive a mechanical theory for mixtures with several components. Their transport tensor reveals where the famous reciprocal relations break down.

The Einstein relations can fail too when equilibrium is absent. The framework is applied to passive mixtures, electrolytes in electric fields, and active matter. It also guides numerical methods for computing transport coefficients in driven systems. A worked example with nonreciprocal interactions shows the approach in action.
arxiv-2505-24006:
Agnideep Aich and seven co-authors build a spatial prediction model that respects extreme events, not just averages. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Maps of rainfall, pollution, or risk often bend toward Gaussian assumptions. Real fields can spike together in ways those assumptions miss. The team wants typical patterns and rare joint extremes in one model.

Their A2-SBNN network seeds its starting weights with a new copula, called A2. Copulas encode how values move together. Training blends a Wasserstein loss with moment matching and correlation penalties. Simulations across many dependence strengths show steady accuracy. The design manages uncertainty while mapping coordinates to continuous fields. Spatial modelers gain a route beyond Gaussian habits.
arxiv-2505-24106:
Dhruv Shah and Jorge Cortes designed controllers for neural feedback loops in a 2025 paper. Machine learning now models systems whose response to input bends in complex ways. Wrap a neural net inside a control loop and the pair form a bilinear system, whose stability is hard to vouch for.

Their frame recasts the loop with linear fractional tools and borrows from parameter-varying control. The controller comes from solving matrix inequalities offline, so it runs cheap online. Local stability of the target state is guaranteed by the math. The method gives learning-based control a safety proof it often lacks.
arxiv-2505-24306:
Kechen Li and seven co-authors build a bench that tests how well language models plan routes on a grid, alone and with classic algorithms at their side. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Models can reason about paths in words, yet most studies grade them in isolation. The gains from teaming them with proven pathfinders stay unmeasured.

Their grids vary in size, and moves run in the four compass directions. Six models, from small to large, were scored on correctness, best-ness, and speed. A new prompting style feeds the steps of a classic algorithm into the chat. That style lifted every model, most of all on big, tangled maps. The authors share the code in public. The bench gives a fair way to judge hybrid planning.
arxiv-2506-00406:
Huahui Yi and co-authors present a 2025 paper on iDPA, a method that teaches medical image detectors new object types step by step. Prompt-based continual learning works well for photo classification, but medical detection is different: foreground and background blur together, and prompts tangle with image tokens. The gap between medical and everyday images widens the problem.

The framework first builds prompts from single detected instances, keeping fine detail that dense predictions need. A second part decouples how prompts attend to the image, letting knowledge transfer more directly. The authors argue the design lets a detector grow with new findings and diseases without forgetting the old ones.
arxiv-2506-02006:
Zhaoyuan Su and co-authors present MorphServe, a system that reshapes a running language model to match the workload arriving at each moment. Serving these models is hard because demand arrives in bursts. Running full precision through a burst breaks response-time promises, while shrinking the model permanently costs accuracy even in quiet times.

MorphServe adapts on two fronts at once. During heavy load it swaps some layers of the model for smaller, quantized versions, choosing the layers whose loss hurts least. It also grows or shrinks the memory cache that holds conversation context, following the pressure of the moment. In tests on two model families with realistic traffic, broken response promises fell by over ninety percent. Reply speed at the slow tail improved two to four times over. Output quality held steady, which the authors offer as proof that elastic serving can be practical.
arxiv-2506-03306:
Santosh Harish and a large team of co-authors present the MIRI results of COSMOS-Web in a two thousand twenty-five astronomy paper. COSMOS-Web is the largest JWST Cycle 1 observing program, and MIRI is its mid-infrared camera.

The paper describes the MIRI observations, the data reduction, and the first public photometric catalog covering the full survey area. Custom background subtraction handled strong instrumental features in the images. The team reached depths better than expected and compared fluxes with earlier Spitzer measurements, finding good agreement. Their galaxy number counts at 7.7 micrometers span five orders of magnitude in brightness.
arxiv-2506-04206:
Reza Ramezanpour and four co-authors estimate the hidden template behind large networks by matching a handful of counted patterns, in this 2025 paper. The template, called a graphon, summarizes how connection probability varies across a network's latent space. Older estimators were slow or needed costly distance computations between graphs.

Their method trains a small neural network that maps coordinates to connection probabilities, adjusting it until the small subgraph counts it implies match those counted in real graphs. A theorem bounds the error when the counted motifs represent the truth well. A companion trick mixes training graphs in pattern space to sharpen learning. Across benchmarks the estimator won on accuracy for small graphs and on speed for large ones, and the mixing trick lifted graph classification in most tests.
arxiv-2506-05006:
Willem Meyer and Herbert Weigel show that quantum effects can destabilize solitons that look perfectly stable classically, in a 2025 paper. Their models pair two scalar fields in one space dimension. Solitons there are built from special BPS equations. Classical energy is fixed by the fields' behavior far away. The models have several flat ground states. Some solitons spend long stretches in a secondary ground state. Classically, those stretches cost nothing.

The team computes the one-loop quantum correction to the energy. In every case the correction falls without bound. The longer the secondary stretch, the more negative it gets. So quantum physics penalizes exactly what classical physics allowed free. The result backs an older conjecture from a famous example. The authors constructed some of these solitons fresh for the test. The moral reaches beyond these models. Apparent classical stability can hide quantum decay channels.
arxiv-2506-05306:
Thomas Connolly and a large team of co-authors study unwanted state changes in a superconducting qubit in this 2025 paper. Reading a qubit quickly needs a strong readout tone. Too strong a tone can flip the qubit state, which breaks quantum error correction. A newer readout uses a tone far above the qubit frequency.

The team mapped the ways flips occur in that high frequency regime. In the main path, the qubit absorbs part of a readout photon and returns the rest at lower frequency. Other paths involve package modes, material defects, and stray resonances. Knowing each path tells builders what to fix. The goal is fast readout that leaves the qubit state untouched.
arxiv-2506-05906:
Vira Dhaliwal, Jingbang Liu, and Andreas Carlson model how a wavy elastic membrane settles onto a sticky surface through a thin fluid film, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Sticky molecules on the membrane bind and unbind across the gap. Heat-driven ripples make first contact a rare, slow event.

Rare-event theory predicts the wait grows steeply with the starting gap. Simulations then show bound and unbound zones splitting apart and coarsening, much like ripening droplets. Fluid flow changes the growth law, and a new slower regime ruled by bending appears. The work speaks to cell adhesion and soft engineering contacts.
arxiv-2506-06006:
Yifu Qiu and co-authors teach vision-language models to predict future frames by first learning the reverse task, in this 2025 paper. Asked to imagine the next image from a current one plus a written action, such models produce physically implausible changes. The reverse job, naming the action that links two frames, turns out far easier to learn. That asymmetry drives their whole approach.

The reverse model labels actions for raw video frame pairs, growing training data for the forward task without human work. At run time it also scores several forward guesses, guiding search toward the best. On an action-based image editing benchmark, the bootstrapped model matched or beat specialist editors. Human judges rated it best on average across all test subsets.
arxiv-2506-07106:
Samir Abdaljalil, Hasan Kurban, Khalid Qaraqe, and Erchin Serpedin split machine reasoning among three agents in a 2025 computing paper. Language models reason in brittle, hard-to-check ways, and chain-of-thought prompting adds steps without enforcing logic. Their framework, Theorem-of-Thought, runs three agents side by side: one guesses explanations, one deduces, one generalizes from cases. Each output becomes a formal graph of steps.

A scoring pass then grades every step for how well the steps agree with each other. The most consistent graph supplies the final answer. On logic and math benchmarks the method beat chain-of-thought and self-consistency baselines. Splitting thought into three styles makes errors easier to spot.
arxiv-2506-07606:
Peyman Rostami and co-authors (2025) release PolitiSky24, a data set of political stances from the social platform Bluesky. Stance detection asks which side a text takes toward a target. Most older sets label single posts on older platforms. This one labels whole users, using their full posting history, which gives a fuller picture. The set covers the 2024 United States presidential election. It holds more than sixteen thousand user-target pairs.

Each entry carries engagement data, the interaction graph, and the user's posts. Labels came from a pipeline mixing search methods with large language models. That pipeline reached about 81 percent accuracy and records its reasons for each label. The authors stress transparency: researchers can audit why a user was tagged. They present the set as open infrastructure for studying political talk on a new platform, at the level of people rather than posts.
arxiv-2506-08606:
Radoslaw Klimek wrote this 2025 paper proposing a plan that carries early design models from sketches to checked code outlines. Requirements engineering decides software quality early, yet its models are usually checked by eye. The plan pairs large language models with formal logic at each step of preliminary design, focused on chosen UML diagrams.

Models drafted with that help are translated into formal logical specifications. Deductive checks then test the requirements and the links between parts for clashes that a by-eye check can miss. Pictures at each stage let the team follow each change as it happens. At the end, it builds program skeletons from the checked models. The pitch is a line where AI speed drafts and logic checks the drafts, each side making up for the weak point of the other.
arxiv-2506-09106:
Generative image models can bake in bias, but bias in unconditional generation, where no prompt steers the output, is poorly understood. The five authors define attribute bias as the gap between an attribute's share in generated images and its share in an ideal reference. They train unconditional models and run a standard bias evaluation to watch how attribute shares shift from training data to output.

The detected shifts were small. More importantly, the shifts proved sensitive to the classifier used to label the generated images, above all when its decision boundary crosses dense regions. Spectrum-like attributes, which vary by degree rather than kind, showed the worst sensitivity. The authors urge better labeling practice, harder scrutiny of evaluation frameworks, and respect for the social complexity of attributes when judging bias.
arxiv-2506-09406:
Minji Kang, Chanwoo Baek, and Yoonsang Lee teach a four-legged robot to scoop up objects and toss them onto its own back, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Legged robots already open doors and press buttons with their legs, but such tasks are mostly slow and still. A simple scoop fixed to one leg does the lifting here.

Two expert policies handle approach and scoop-and-toss, each trained apart. A meta-policy then switches between them for smooth multi-object rounds. The robot collects items with no extra arm or gripper. The work stretches what robot legs can do beyond walking, the authors note.
arxiv-2506-09506:
Jäckl, Kloda, Keim, and Lokoč present a study from twenty twenty-five on searching look-alike image sets by sub-region. In uniform domains like underwater scenes, users can name only broad labels. Whole-image text search then misses many apt matches. Their work adds position hints to text queries. Dynamic splitting carves candidate images into meaningful regions on the fly. Users point to regions they recognize rather than whole scenes. Position rules then blend with a multimodal model's semantic skill.

Dynamic splitting doubles retrieval scores versus fixed splitting in their tests. That gain is fragile, though, since small shifts in marked positions hurt it. Static splitting proves sturdier but weaker overall. The authors map both the promise and the limits of region search.
arxiv-2506-10206:
Hakimoglu-Brown proves new identities for the dilogarithm, a classic special function, in twenty twenty-five. The function shows up across number theory and physics. Many of its neat closed forms were only guessed, not proven. His method builds the identities from a beta integral trick.

The proofs settle open guesses by two earlier authors. New ladder style identities with fourth and sixth power bases are built and proved. Two term identities reach into number fields with square roots of small primes. Single term values are also derived. The paper adds firm ground to a web of special function lore.
arxiv-2506-11006:
At a big telecom firm, engineers tried letting language models write test code from plain English steps. Sai Krishna and nine co-authors report in 2025 what it took to make the drafts real. Plain prompts failed: the model dreamed up functions that the code base does not hold. The team fed the prompt with facts pulled by static code scans, plus sample outputs drawn from the base itself.

Tuning the model on that rich prompt style lifted the drafts further. Scores grade how well the made code's calls match the calls in tests folk wrote by hand. The tuned mid-size model gained about eight points over its base form. It matched a model near three times its size. (The catalog title is padded with venue and book data; the head title is clean.)
arxiv-2506-11506:
Komal Kumar, Bivas Mallick, Tapaswini Patro, and Nirman Ganguly study how two gauges of quantum entanglement relate in two thousand twenty-five. Entanglement links two systems so that each alone looks random. One gauge, fidelity, tells how close a state sits to a fully entangled one, while entropy gauges tell how mixed each part is.

States with high fidelity serve many quantum tasks, and states with a rare negative entropy trait help others. The authors sort the channels that cut fidelity past a set limit and coin a name for the harshest kind. They then set those channel families beside the ones that flip the entropy trait, using a noise channel as the test case.
arxiv-2506-13106:
Fen Liu, Shenghai Yuan, Thien-Minh Nguyen, and Rong Su design guardian drones that hunt hostile drones in this 2025 paper. Rogue commercial drones can carry dangerous loads or disrupt air traffic. Ground-guided defenses fail when sight lines break, satellite signals are denied, or radar is jammed.

Their plan uses only two noisy distance readings taken in real time. From these, guardian drones estimate where the target sits, then circle it in three dimensions using a patterned flight motion. The circle can shift from guarding a friendly craft to watching a hostile one. If the target crosses a warning line, a guardian may ram it. Real drone flights and computer tests both supported the approach.
arxiv-2506-13306:
Salah Ghamizi, Georgia Kanli, Yu Deng, Magali Perquin, and Olivier Keunen review, in a 2025 preprint, whether foundation models have truly arrived for brain imaging. These large pre-trained networks promise strong results from little labeled data. Brain imaging, central to neurology, has been oddly skipped by earlier surveys. The field's data is scattered, mixed in type, and split across hospitals. The authors gather that record. They catalog over one hundred sixty datasets and eighty-six model designs aimed at the brain.

For each design they note the training style and the tricks that drive its gains. Leading models for main tasks are named, with their novel points. The review also lists blind spots: narrow task coverage, weak handling of mixed scan types, and thin clinical testing. Closing directions aim the field at those gaps, for lab and clinic work alike.
arxiv-2506-13406:
Kunda Yan and co-authors present CALM, a method for merging several fine-tuned AI models into one that keeps each model's skills, in a 2025 paper. Merging is cheap compared with training a joint model, but naive merges let the models' settings fight each other. Local methods protect task details yet can lose what the tasks agree on.

CALM merges in stages, a few tasks at a time, and builds masks that mark which settings belong to which task. Those masks are tuned to match the shared direction all tasks agree on, so the merged parts do not clash. It also draws unlabeled data with a sampling rule that keeps classes balanced. In tests, CALM beat earlier merging methods and came close to full multi-task training.
arxiv-2506-14306:
Ata Yalcin and six co-authors present a 2025 study of fairness in machine learning when data are doubly imbalanced: skewed both in the outcome label and in the sensitive group attribute. Many debiasing methods quietly fail in that corner. The authors first run an exploratory analysis showing exactly how standard fixes disappoint on such data. Then they propose a multi-criteria search over sampling schemes.

The method hunts for the resampling and distribution of label and group that best balances fairness against classification accuracy. The authors frame the two goals as a genuine trade-off to optimize, not a single score to maximize. The work targets decision systems, like lending or hiring, where both skews are common and fairness failures hit minorities twice.
arxiv-2506-14506:
Yuva Himanshu Pallam and Shantanu Desai wrote a 2025 paper that rechecks a claim about neutrinos from Jupiter. Neutrinos are faint particles that pass through almost all matter. A past study said the BOREXINO detector's data held a small Jupiter signal, about 6 percent of the total flux.

The pair reworked the same data on their own. They found the same signal, at the same strength and weight. But the same method also produced fake signals from Venus and Saturn, where none should exist. That warning led them to a stricter test that weighs rival models. Their caution shows why odd claims need extra checks before belief.
arxiv-2506-14606:
Ahmed Heakl and four co-authors translate low level code between chip architectures with language models in a 2025 paper. Moving programs from complex instruction chips to simpler reduced instruction chips is hard because the two families differ deeply in instructions, memory, and execution style. Their pipeline asks a large language model for candidate translations, then wraps them in a software testing framework to build measurable confidence.

Across two datasets, tests with over ninety eight percent code coverage passed at ninety nine percent on one benchmark and about half on a harder one. Against Apple's Rosetta 2 on the same tasks, their translated code ran faster, used less energy, and took less memory. Code, data, and models are to be released openly.
arxiv-2506-14906:
Robert Czupryniak and co-authors (2025) used a neural network to measure radar distances finer than the usual limit. A radar's range sharpness is normally capped by its bandwidth. The team asked a denoising autoencoder to estimate the gap between two equal reflectors closer than that cap. The network squeezed each returning waveform into a tiny bottleneck code. That code tracked the true gap closely across training runs.

Pulse shape decided how well the trick worked. A pulse built from spherical Bessel functions performed best. A triangle-style pulse came second, and the standard sinc pulse trailed. The bottleneck stayed stable when noise was added, which matters for field use. The authors present the work as a demonstration rather than a finished sensor. It shows that learning the right compression, on the right waveform, can beat the classic resolution limit in tests. Signal design, they stress, is half the method.
arxiv-2506-15006:
Jesmin Jahan Tithi, Hanjiang Wu, Avishaii Abuhatzera, and Fabrizio Petrini design data centers for next-generation language models, in a research paper from 2025. Models with trillions of parameters strain every part of a data center, from compute to memory to networking. A joint design study can show which choices lift throughput per cost before hardware is built.

Their framework explores compute power, memory bandwidth and size, network shapes, and parallel strategies together. A flat optical network that links all nodes evenly shows strong gains in speed and scale. Sensitivity tests weigh overlap of compute and communication, hardware collectives, and wider scale-out domains. Both sparse and dense model types are covered with an analytic performance tool.
arxiv-2506-15206:
Saak Gabriyelyan and Evgenii Reznichenko give new tests for when a topological space is controlled by its compact pieces or its convergent sequences, in a 2025 paper. The two classes have names, k_R-spaces and s_R-spaces, and they matter because properties of function spaces hinge on them. The authors characterize both classes and aim the results at spaces of continuous real functions with the pointwise topology, written C_p(X).

They prove that this function space is a k_R-space whenever the underlying space has one non-isolated point. If the space is also large in a stated sense, the function space is an s_R-space. Under an extra set-theoretic assumption, they build a separable, metrizable space whose function space is Ascoli yet fails to be a k_R-space. The paper sharpens the map of a corner of general topology.
arxiv-2506-16206:
James Carr tests if classic theorems hold in many-valued logic, in this two thousand twenty-five paper on logic. Many-valued models stretch classic model theory, letting truth values live in an algebra, not just true and false. Models over varieties of residuated lattices give the meanings for first-order substructural logics. Carr asks how far the Hanf and Gaifman locality theorems, workhorses of model theory, stretch in this place.

The reply hangs on how locality is read and how the truth algebra acts. Hanf's theorem fails on the plain read of local neighborhoods but comes back for well-connected residuated lattices on a next read. For Gaifman's theorem, Carr proves the lemma, that models that agree on local sentences are elementarily equivalent. He proves it on several reads of locality, for a well-behaved algebra. A connective that reads the algebra's order proves to be the key link.
arxiv-2506-17806:
Arsalan Hojjat Ansari and Olaoluwa Jeremiah Omidire widen the Banach fixed point idea with C-class enriched Hardy-Rogers contractions. Their paper from twenty twenty-five joins a long line of extensions to the classic contraction principle. That principle guarantees a unique fixed point for shrinking maps and powers many solvers. Enriched contractions relax the shrink demand; Hardy-Rogers forms mix several distance terms.

C-class functions supply the new general frame. Within it, the authors prove convergence to a unique fixed point for their map class. Common fixed points for pairs of maps are covered as well. Set iterative schemes drive the proofs. Past results in the literature fall out as special cases. The work is pure fixed point theory, aimed at the analysts who stock the solver toolbox.
arxiv-2506-19006:
The CHIME/FRB Collaboration and co-authors report an exceptionally bright, nearby fast radio burst, in a 2025 paper. Fast radio bursts are millisecond flashes of unknown origin. This one, caught in March 2025, was pinned to a spot within thirteen parsecs of precision thanks to a web of telescopes across radio, optical, and X-ray bands.

A nearby, one-off burst is a rare gift: its home galaxy can be studied in detail, and the burst's path through space can be mapped. The team combines data from many facilities to fix the position and describe the surroundings. Such pinpointing is the bottleneck in the field, since most bursts are too fleeting for slow follow-up. Bright local cases like this one anchor theories of what makes the flashes.
arxiv-2506-19406:
Chen Yi and Shan LianLei present GLCANet, a neural network that labels every pixel in ultra high resolution satellite images, in this 2025 paper. Such images are huge, so methods must be both accurate and light on memory. The hard part is joining the big picture with fine detail: roads and fields need context, while edges need precision.

The design runs two streams in parallel, one for global meaning and one for local detail. A self attention step strengthens long range links in the global stream. A masked cross attention step then blends the streams, boosting fine detail where it helps and leaning on context elsewhere. In tests the network beat leading methods on accuracy while using less memory, which suits real mapping work on very large scenes.
arxiv-2506-19606:
Priyank Vasu, Rahul Kumar Singh, and Subham Paul construct a timelike minimal surface that ends in as many arms as one wishes. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Minimal surfaces are the math form of a soap film at rest. The timelike kind lives in a space where one direction acts like time.

The team shows such a surface exists with any chosen number of ends. Each end is weak and complete, in the technical senses of the field. They then study how the simple ends behave far out. The shape of the singularity set, where the surface fails to be smooth, is also mapped. Results like this test how far classic surface theory stretches into Lorentzian settings. They may inform models where membranes move through spacetime.
arxiv-2506-21406:
Tommaso Bonato and co-authors propose a routing scheme for supercomputer networks that adapts paths without scrambling packet order, in a 2025 paper. Network delay is a top limit on supercomputer work. Adaptive routing spreads packets across paths to cut delay. But packets from one flow can then arrive out of order. Several transport protocols suffer badly from that. Reordering can slash throughput or burn processor time.

Flowlet switching, the usual fix, assumes bursty traffic. It can still reorder packets in some cases. The new scheme, flowcut switching, guarantees in-order delivery under any conditions. It also works for steady, non-bursty traffic. That covers remote memory access patterns common in big machines. The authors present the design and its reasoning. They position it against existing adaptive schemes. Network builders for high-performance systems are the audience. The guarantee, not just speed, is the selling point.
arxiv-2506-21906:
Lachlan Barnes and co-authors build math scores that describe the shape of radio galaxies, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. New telescopes will flood astronomers with images, so automatic shape tools are in high demand. Their scores capture traits such as asymmetry, blur, focus, disorder, and stretch.

The scores were tried on two sets, one from a pilot sky survey and one of well-studied bright sources. They held up when image sharpness changed and each measured a distinct trait. Blended together, the scores recovered the classic two-type sorting of radio galaxies. The work suits the huge surveys now starting.
arxiv-2506-22506:
Momin Ahmad Khan, Yasra Chandio, and Fatima Muhammad Anwar wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It mounts the first study of backdoor attacks on federated prompt learning, and builds a guard against them.

In this setup many clients tune the prompts of a big vision-language model like CLIP, and no raw data moves. A rogue client can slip a faint learned noise mark into images, so the shared prompt trips on marked inputs while clean ones still score high. The guard, SABRE-FL, screens prompt updates with an anomaly detector that works in embedding space. It needs no client data or labels, and trains offline on odd data. Across five sets and four rival guards it cuts the backdoor's hit rate most while keeping clean scores.
arxiv-2506-22706:
Arun Ramamurthy and Neil Dhir work, in a 2025 paper, on cyber defense agents that stay competent when the network itself keeps changing shape.
