Experiments cover synthetic data and a real application to geomagnetic storms, where the method finds minimal yet highly informative feature sets without losing predictive performance. Interpretable reduction matters wherever model inputs must be explained, not just used.
arxiv-2509-08006:
Nikoleta E. Glynatsi and 2 co-authors derive exact conditions for stable cooperation through reputation in a 2025 paper on social evolution. Indirect reciprocity means helping others partly to earn a good name, which pays off when others check reputations before helping. Social norms spell out how to act and how reputations should be updated after each action.

Earlier work found several norms that sustain cooperation, but a complete analytical account of all evolutionarily stable norms was missing, especially when actions or assessments are noisy. The authors supply that characterisation for the noisy case. Knowing exactly which norms survive evolution helps explain human cooperation at large scales and could guide the design of reputation systems online.
arxiv-2509-08106:
Martín A. Quijada and 2 co-authors follow how two kinds of plasma waves trade energy with protons in a 2025 space physics paper. In simple linear theory, Alfvén-cyclotron waves and ion-acoustic waves travelling along a magnetic field ignore each other. Real plasmas break that separation through resonant interactions, so proton heating evolves differently than linear theory predicts.

Moment-based quasilinear equations track the coupled evolution for protons and electrons, keeping the full kinetic response of both species instead of assuming cold electrons. Transverse proton heating relaxes under the combined wave activity. Plasmas like the solar wind are heated this way in reality, so getting the wave coupling right matters for explaining temperatures spacecraft actually measure near the Sun.
arxiv-2509-08306:
Generative AI is changing academic writing, but the rewards of using it are not shared evenly. Farhan Kamrul Khan and 4 co-authors analyze that imbalance in a 2025 research paper. They examined a very large set of Scopus-indexed computer science articles published between 2021 and 2025. A zero-shot detector estimated how AI-like each article's style had become.

Authors in the Global East adopted AI writing tools more aggressively. Western authors, though, gained more visibility per unit of adoption, because human-sounding writing had previously been penalized unevenly. Prestigious journals still favored human-sounding texts. Network analysis showed Eastern visibility rising modestly, with tighter regional clusters but little real integration. The study warns that AI may widen recognition gaps in scholarship even as it lowers the cost of writing.
arxiv-2509-08406:
Timing detectors used at particle colliders drift with temperature, and Weiyi Sun with 3 co-authors build a compact theory of that drift in a 2025 instrumentation paper. Low-gain avalanche diodes give modest internal gain and time resolution of a few tens of picoseconds, prized for ultrafast timing. Both gain and timing shift strongly with bias voltage and temperature.

The non-uniform multiplication region is replaced by an equivalent rectangular gain layer, yielding an analytical framework across temperatures. A first-order rule then says how to adjust bias to hold gain constant as temperature changes. Collider detectors cannot control their thermal environment perfectly, so a compensation formula turns a wandering instrument back into a predictable one.
arxiv-2509-08706:
G. Ciliberto and 3 co-authors study quantum backreaction in an analog black hole in a 2025 paper. An analog black hole is a flowing condensate where sound cannot escape a region, mimicking a real horizon. Quantum fluctuations may change that flow itself.

An extended Gross-Pitaevskii equation adds fluctuation effects to the condensate motion. Applied to a quasi-one-dimensional transonic flow, it predicts steady density and velocity ripples in the supersonic region. Those ripples act like the black hole interior. The authors also compute how Hawking radiation shifts flow speeds upstream and downstream. The work links quantum effects and analog gravity in cold gases.
arxiv-2509-09306:
Finding a picture from a spoken request is harder when several people are talking at once. Wenhao Yang and 4 co-authors define that task and a system for it in a 2025 research paper. Their target speaker speech-image retrieval must pick out one designated voice from a mix. The command hidden in that voice then has to match the right image.

The framework extracts the target speaker's speech first, then aligns it with images through contrastive learning. Pre-trained audio encoders and vision models supply the raw representations. On two mixed-speaker benchmarks, the system beat existing methods clearly in two-speaker and three-speaker settings. Recall at the top rank improved substantially over single-speaker baselines. Assistive robots and smart devices live in multi-speaker rooms. A retrieval system that knows whose voice to obey is a basic requirement for deploying them safely.
arxiv-2509-09406: Vinícius V. Fávaro and 3 co-authors settle a question posed by F. Bayart in 2024 about epsilon-hypercyclic operators. Their 2025 paper constructs a weighted backward shift on a nested sequence space with an exact threshold property. For every smaller positive delta below one, the operator counts as delta-hypercyclic precisely when delta reaches at least the fixed epsilon value.
arxiv-2509-09806:
Vasanth Kumar Babu and 1 co-author use a neural network to calm deadly spiral waves in simulated heart tissue in a 2025 paper. Ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation, the rhythms behind most sudden cardiac deaths, appear in tissue models as spiralling or broken electrical waves. Wiping those spirals out with gentle applied currents would mimic a kinder form of defibrillation, if the right currents could be chosen quickly.

Their U-Net method reads the tissue state and directs control currents that erase the turbulence in two models, one simple and one ionically detailed. Patterns with shorter correlation lengths proved easier to clear. The work points toward learned, low-energy strategies for ending arrhythmias inside computational test beds before any clinical step is considered.
arxiv-2509-10106:
Cong Li and 13 co-authors report a hidden pattern on the surface of a topological material in this 2025 paper. In such materials, states on the surface are supposed to mirror the order inside the bulk. On low-symmetry faces that mirror breaks down, because the surface and bulk patterns cannot line up. The team studied the (103) face of the Weyl semimetal NdAlSi.

Photoemission measurements revealed closed Fermi-arc loops and a moiré-like modulation in momentum space, neither expected from standard theory. The authors show both come from partial bulk projection and interference across several unit cells, governed by a least-common-multiple rule. Computer models using that rule matched the measured spectra closely, suggesting a general law for complex surfaces.
arxiv-2509-10406:
Rupert Mitchell and Kristian Kersting speed up the attention mechanism inside transformer models in this 2025 machine learning paper. Attention lets a model weigh which earlier tokens matter, but its cost grows quadratically with sequence length, choking pretraining on very long inputs like whole code repositories.

Their method, Multipole Semantic Attention, clusters the attention queries and keys separately in representation space, building a tailored summary for each query. That beats carving the sequence into spatial blocks at the same sparsity, and it drops into existing pretrained models with no architectural change. They validate it on Llama models without retraining and pretrain models up to a billion parameters at sixty-four thousand tokens of context on code and scientific text. Training ran about a third faster while matching the baseline's loss.
arxiv-2509-10506:
Retail demand is noisy and fast-changing, and Yadi Liu with eight co-authors build AttnBoost to forecast it in this 2025 study of supply chain analytics. Gradient boosting decision trees already perform strongly on structured sales data, but they cannot shift their focus as conditions change. AttnBoost adds a lightweight attention mechanism that reweights features during every boosting round.

Promotions, prices, and seasonal signals get emphasis exactly when they matter most. On a large retail sales dataset, the model beat standard machine learning methods and deep tabular rivals, while staying interpretable enough to hand managers usable insights. An ablation study, removing parts one by one, confirmed the attention module itself curbs overfitting and sharpens explanations. The authors pitch attention-guided boosting as a scalable, explainable direction for real forecasting work.
arxiv-2509-10906:
Tawfiq Ammari, writing alone, follows two years of argument over CDC COVID-19 guidance on Twitter in this 2025 paper. The data set holds more than 275,000 tweets that mentioned or addressed the agency's account. Ammari combined topic modeling, sentiment scoring, source credibility checks, and change point detection to trace how the conversation moved.

Three phases emerge: early hoax claims and testing fights, then lockdown and mask disputes, then post-vaccine variant worries. Old agency statements kept resurfacing as receipts in later fights, a pattern the author names crisis messaging journeys. Skeptical, trust-questioning talk kept people engaged longest, while supportive posts predicted quick drop-off. Design advice for health agencies closes the paper.
arxiv-2509-11006:
Enterprise blockchains need scale without giving up control. M. Z. Haider, M. Dias de Assuncao, and Kaiwen Zhang propose a sharding protocol for them in this 2025 paper. Sharding splits the ledger across parallel groups. Earlier designs faced three problems. Coordinating shards is hard. Fault tolerance with few nodes is hard. Heavyweight consensus is expensive.

Their Range-Based Sharding protocol is implemented on Quorum. It allocates shards through a commit-reveal scheme. Validator distribution stays secure and unbiased that way. Delays on transactions that cross shards fall. Load balancing, lighter consensus, and parallel execution do the rest. In evaluations, throughput was significantly higher than in existing enterprise frameworks. Latency was lower, too. For banks and supply chains that want blockchain guarantees at business speed, the design argues one point. Sharding can be both controlled and fast.
arxiv-2509-11106:
Valentin Hofmann and nine co-authors wrote this 2025 paper on grading language models. Fixed test sets are costly to run. They often measure the wrong skill. They also lose value as models master them. Labeling errors creep in as well.

The team borrows from psychometrics, the field that designs exams for people. Their method is called Fluid Benchmarking. It fits a statistical model to past results from many models. The fit estimates each item's difficulty and each model's ability. A new model can then be graded with items matched to its level. The idea mirrors adaptive school tests. On the MMLU benchmark, the method matched standard grading quality. It used about fifty times fewer questions to do so. It also improved consistency and resisted saturation.
arxiv-2509-11206:
Tae Soo Kim and four co-authors address a trust problem in this 2025 human-computer interaction paper. Researchers often ask large language models to grade AI outputs. The single score that comes back hides key details. Nobody can see which parts of the output drove the grade.

Their approach is called functional fragmentation. It cuts each output into key fragments. Each fragment gets a label for the job it does. The labels relate to the grading criteria. A system named Evalet displays the fragments across many outputs. Users can inspect, rate, and compare judgments there. Ten practitioners joined a study of the system. They spotted nearly half again as many grading mistakes. That helped them calibrate trust in the automated scores.
arxiv-2509-11306:
Carl Bettosi and 7 co-authors connect a social robot to a patient's intentions in this 2025 paper. Exercise instructors who are robots need rapport to keep patients engaged over months of therapy. People build rapport by copying each other's movements, a trick long used when patients mirror a physiotherapist.

Their brain-robot interface lets a robot instructor copy a patient's exercise in real time, driven by mental commands read from the patient's intention rather than by cameras alone. Fourteen people took part in an exploratory study, three physiotherapists and eleven patients recovering from stroke or other injuries. The system pulled off mimicry in most sessions, with varied accuracy. Patients trusted and accepted the robot well, and adding the interface did not dent that goodwill.
arxiv-2509-11406:
Missing scans are the daily reality behind this 2025 medical imaging paper. Christoph Fürböck and five co-authors wrote it. Models trained on multi-modal patient data usually demand every mode for every patient. Clinics then drop incomplete cases or patch the holes.

Their answer is a hypernetwork. It builds a bespoke classifier for the modes a patient has. One system can then train and run on every sample. The team tested on data with modes removed on purpose. Rivals were complete-data training, channel dropout, and hole patching. The built models adapted best. Gains reached eight points of accuracy when just a quarter of training data were complete.
arxiv-2509-11606:
Milan Marocchi and three co-authors listen for heart disease with help from synthetic signals. This 2025 biomedical engineering paper uses heart sounds and heart electric signals. Such signals can flag heart disease cheaply. Matched recordings and multi-microphone sets are scarce, though. Modern models crave exactly those.

The team mixed classic signal processing with denoising diffusion generators. The mix enlarged the data on hand. A Wav2Vec 2.0-based classifier was fine-tuned on the enriched set. It hit state-of-the-art scores on the standard single-channel heart sound set. It did so again on matched sound-plus-ECG records. A wearable vest set with many channels scored lower but still showed promise. Transformer models can serve heart screening once data gaps are filled.
arxiv-2509-12206:
Maximum likelihood estimation can misbehave when a model folds or mixes. A solo 2025 paper by Koustav Mallik works out the fine print for two such cases. One is the folded normal distribution. The other is finite mixtures of Gaussians. The goal is consistency. That is, proof that the estimator settles on the truth as data grows. Every constant is tracked along the way.

For the folded normal, one result stands out. A sixth-order expansion gives an odd convergence rate for the location at the kink. The rate is a one-fourth power, not the usual square root. The scale keeps the standard rate. For mixtures, identifiability is shown up to relabeling. Spikes from collapsing variance are bounded. A penalty term then restores consistency on growing search spaces.
arxiv-2509-12706:
A Josephson junction, two superconductors weakly linked, usually behaves like a single cosine energy well for the phase between them. Ádám Bácsi and two co-authors re-derive that behavior in 2025 with the Schrieffer-Wolff transformation, starting from single-electron tunneling, and then push past it systematically.

The phase bias becomes an operator in their treatment, a door to richer physics. A stray Bogoliubov quasiparticle couples its motion to the Cooper pairs and reshapes the junction's spectrum. Higher-order terms generate extra Josephson harmonics whose sizes trace back to microscopic details of the leads and the junction, offering knobs to tune the harmonic mix.
arxiv-2509-13006:
Shermin Khosravi and David Bremner shrink the linear programs built from algorithms in 2025. Compilers can turn fast algorithms into programs, but the output is often huge. Huge programs strain solvers in practice.

A layered pipe method splits nested code into synced zones. Each zone holds its own vars and rules. That split cuts size while the program stays valid for all inputs. Tests on span scheduling and lightest tree tasks cut size up to twenty-five fold. Solver speed rose on both paid and free solvers. The path aims at compact forms for hard integer tasks too.
arxiv-2509-13206:
A. Kopyev, V. Sirota and two co-authors fix in 2025 a clash between dynamo theory and simulations at low Prandtl numbers. Near threshold, theory foresaw slow power decay below the line. Simulations showed fast exponential decay instead.

The fast decay is brief and stems from flattening of the speed correlator at large scales. That flattening acts like a long-lived virtual level in a wave equation. Growth and decay rates plus the critical Reynolds count are given via correlator traits. Theory and diverse simulations can now be compared on shared terms. Concord is restored without discarding either side.
arxiv-2509-13406:
Shreya Vardhan and Jinzhao Wang introduce free mutual information in a 2025 quantum physics paper, a new measure of quantum chaos borrowed from free probability theory. Chaos here means how fast a quantum operator spreads out. The known tools track spreading through physical space, but operators actually live in a far larger space of all possible operators.

The pair prove two results that hold in any physical system. First, they give an explicit formula for the new measure based on the eigenvalues of a product of two observables. Second, they show it equals a weighted sum of all higher-point out-of-time-ordered correlators, giving those quantities a clear meaning. Tests on chaotic circuits and spin chains support the picture.
arxiv-2509-13806:
Petri Laarne studies rare jumps in a noisy wave system in a solo 2025 probability paper. The model is a stochastic heat equation on a one-dimensional ring with a sine-Gordon nonlinearity, a sine term that creates several potential wells. Random noise occasionally kicks the system from one well to another, and such metastable transitions are the paper's subject.

Laarne proves an Eyring-Kramers law for the jump rate in the small-noise limit, meaning the average waiting time follows the classic exponential formula set by the barrier height and the noise strength. He also shows the transition state itself bifurcates at a sharp parameter threshold where the product of two model constants equals one. The argument follows the potential-theoretic approach of Berglund and Gentz.
arxiv-2509-13906:
Afrin Dange and Sunita Sarawagi teach forecasting foundation models to use covariates in a 2025 time series paper. Time series foundation models forecast new series from a short history alone. That is a genuine breakthrough. But they ignore covariates, the outside variables known in advance. Holidays or planned prices often drive the future.

Their TFMAdapter is a small add-on. It learns at prediction time, for the single series at hand. It blends covariate information with the base model's univariate forecasts. No fine-tuning is needed. Training it naively would need forecasts at every historical step. So they bootstrap with pseudo-forecasts from simple regression. A Gaussian process then refines the predictions. Across real datasets, the adapter beat both foundation models and supervised baselines by clear margins.
arxiv-2509-14206:
Marco Mirabile and twenty-two co-authors study four very spread out, faint galaxies in the Hydra I cluster in 2025, as part of the LEWIS survey. Old star clusters around a galaxy, called globular clusters, keep traces of how that galaxy formed and met others in the past.

Working with MUSE spectra and new infrared images, the team confirmed a handful of bright clusters by their speeds and found many more faint candidates from their colours and shapes. Counts suggest three of the four galaxies hold many clusters for their size. Estimates from cluster counts and star mass also indicate that all four are dominated by dark matter, with far more total mass than their stars alone would suggest.
arxiv-2509-14306:
Davood Momeni, writing alone in 2025, reviews inflation in modified gravity in plain pedagogical form. Inflation is a burst of fast expansion in the very early universe. Modified gravity theories change the rules for gravity using curvature, torsion or other geometric ideas.

Momeni walks through how scalar fields interact with each geometric quantity and steer expansion. Background growth, reheating after inflation and numbers observers can measure are covered for each family. Exotic cases from string theory, extra dimensions and nonlocal models also appear. The review aims to connect model building with data from current and future missions. Readers new to the field get a map of how geometry choices change what inflation predicts.
arxiv-2509-14806:
Alba María Mármol-Romero leads a team of six authors describing the SINAI entry to the eRisk lab at CLEF 2022, written up in 2025. The lab runs shared tasks on finding mental health risks early in online writing. The team entered two tasks: early detection of pathological gambling signs, and measuring the severity of eating disorder signs.

For gambling detection, the system used Transformer sentence embeddings plus features for text volume, word variety, complexity, and emotion. For eating disorder severity, it compared texts with contextual word embeddings. The gambling entry placed second among forty-one submissions, and the severity entry also placed second in its smaller field. Together the results show language models can flag risky writing early and grade its severity.
arxiv-2509-14906:
Xiaodan Liu leads a team of eleven authors describing multi-color X-ray pulses for filming ultrafast processes, in a 2025 accelerator physics paper. X-ray free-electron lasers are bright enough to image single molecules at atomic resolution. To capture motion, researchers want several X-ray snapshots at different colors and times within one shot.

Their method uses a single electron beam to generate four-color pulses with adjustable wavelength separation and time delay. An optical klystron scheme boosts intensity and shortens the undulator line, while a magnetic chicane between undulators sets the delay. Start-to-end simulations using parameters of the SHINE facility show delays of hundreds of femtoseconds and four colors spanning a nanometer-scale range. Recording several diffraction frames in one exposure would give a new view of fast molecular change.
arxiv-2509-15106:
Chengkai Zhu, Hongyu Mao, Kun Fang, and Xin Wang set tighter bounds on quantum links with the help of geometry, in a 2025 paper. Two key values are at stake: how much quantum data a channel can carry, and how much shared entanglement can be drawn from a state. A quirk called superadditivity makes both values hard to pin down.

Their method searches over extensions of states and channels that pull known upper bounds down. All extensions are laid out as a Stiefel manifold, which turns guesswork into a full search. A sharper bound on quantum conditional entropy feeds the search. The joint tools give new best upper bounds on channel capacity, firm caps for the design of future quantum networks.
arxiv-2509-15206:
Irina Proskurina, Guillaume Metzler, and Julien Velcin make model shrinking fairness-aware in a 2025 paper. Shrinking, called quantization, stores a model's weights as low-grade whole numbers to cut its heavy memory needs. Past studies show the savings can come with more biased text and weaker fairness scores.

Fair-GPTQ is presented as the first shrinking method built to cut unfairness head-on. Fairness rules for groups enter the goal the method optimizes. That steers how weights get rounded, toward text that is less biased for groups the law protects. Tests focus on stereotype output about jobs and on slurs tied to sex, race, and faith. The cost to plain skill is small. The authors argue skill and fairness must be tuned as one.
arxiv-2509-15306:
Nicholas Borsato and five co-authors detect calcium in the air of an ultra-hot Jupiter with an Australian scope, in a 2025 paper. High-grade transit spectra read starlight that passed through a planet's air, which reveals its atoms and ions. The target, WASP-189b, is baked by its star and orbits a bright host, a fine test case.

One transit watched with the Veloce spectrograph on the Anglo-Australian Telescope is that tool's first exoplanet air result. Cross-matching with standard templates gives a firm catch of ionized calcium. Signs of hydrogen, sodium, magnesium, and metals such as iron and titanium also show, in both plain and ionized forms. The strongest catch sits in the scope's red arm, as hoped, which backs Veloce for future air surveys.
arxiv-2509-15506:
Jian-hao Kang, Zhun Gou, and Nan-jing Huang solve a planning problem for an insurer. The insurer buys reinsurance and invests funds, while its view of risk shifts at random. Its aims also change over time, which makes the plan time inconsistent: a plan made now may not suit its later self. Past wealth feeds in with a delay as well.

They model the surplus with a drifting random walk and the market with a model whose spread shifts with price. A game view treats each future self as a player. They prove a check for the best balanced plan and derive that plan in near closed form for two gain styles. Number tests then show how the balanced plan behaves.
arxiv-2509-16006:
Robots in farms and plants must do long jobs made of many small tasks, and the mix of tasks can shift on the fly. Francesco Argenziano and three co-authors set out an architecture that pairs large language models with symbolic planning. People state a high-level job in plain words, and the system turns that into steps a robot can follow.

Staff can also ask the robot what it has done, what it is doing, and what comes next. The team built the system with current tools and tested it in a real precision farming case. Measured results show the approach can track complex work in the field.
arxiv-2509-16206:
Slow, factor-based investing could gain from learning agents, but the stock pool shifts as firms enter and leave. Junlin Liu compresses stock returns into a small set of hidden factors, shaped by ninety-four traits of each firm. A learning agent then sets long and short weights for a portfolio based on those factors.

On twenty years of United States stock data, the method beat equal-weight, classic, and rival learning portfolios out of sample. It posted a strong yearly return and a solid risk-adjusted score. A feature study showed the factors line up with sound economic sense, which aids trust in the system.
arxiv-2509-16306:
When a massive star's core collapses, almost all the energy of the blast escapes as neutrinos, ghostly particles that barely interact. Georg G. Raffelt, Hans-Thomas Janka, and Damiano F. G. Fiorillo review what these supernova neutrinos teach us. The one such burst ever caught, from a 1987 supernova, came with sparse counts, yet many large detectors now stand ready for a galactic event.

Neutrinos drive the delayed blast itself and swirl in dense packs that can swap flavors in joint patterns. A future nearby supernova, though rare, would yield rich data on both stars and particle physics.
arxiv-2509-16506:
Fillable forms hide in billions of web documents, but no large open data set existed for teaching machines to find their fields. Joe Barrow builds CommonForms by filtering a giant web crawl for PDFs with fillable parts, ending with tens of thousands of documents and hundreds of thousands of pages. Fields come in three types: text inputs, choice buttons, and signatures.

A third of the pages are not in English, and no single topic dominates. Two detector models trained cheaply reach high precision, and they beat a popular commercial reader, adding checkbox detection it lacks. Data, models, and code are released openly.
arxiv-2509-16606:
Wei Duan, Jie Lu, and Junyu Xuan study teams of learning agents linked by a network, in a 2025 paper. Each agent sees only its local area and can talk to a few neighbors. Fixed neighbor lists, though, fit poorly when conditions change or agents differ. The team let each agent infer its own view of who it interacts with.

Their method builds a personal graph for each agent from data. That graph is learned jointly with the agent's strategy. Tests used traffic control with well over a hundred agents. The method beat strong rivals on scale, cost, and score. Flexible links could help fleets and grids where ties shift over time.
arxiv-2509-16806:
Kacper Marzol and co-authors rebuild body interiors in three dimensions in a 2025 medical paper. Doctors use scope cameras inside the gut, airways, and urinary tract to find disease. Turning those views into a 3D scene could aid diagnosis. Their method, MedGS, uses a splatting technique that spreads soft blobs to form the scene.

MedGS merges several scan types into one model. Unlike prior tools, it lets users edit tissue in the scene. Light still behaves in a physically sound way after edits. That mix brings the tool closer to real clinic use. Code is shared in a public repository for others to build on.
arxiv-2509-17106:
Hendry M. Lim writes a note on star products and their Hilbert space mirrors in a 2025 math paper. Quantization turns products of phase-space functions into operators. Once quantized, a product of two such functions can be recast through a mapping that commutes. That mapping links the quantized forms of the two factors. Lim discusses that mapping inside a classic parameterized correspondence frame, named for Cahill and Glauber.

The note offers a heuristic derivation of the mapping's bidifferential form. Heuristic here means guided by intuition rather than full rigor, which can make the result easier to grasp. Such mirrors between classical products and operator products sit at the heart of quantum mechanics' link to classical physics.
arxiv-2509-17306:
Kai Fukami, Yuta Iwatani, Soju Maejima, Hiroyuki Asada, and Soshi Kawai study violent shaking in air flow over a wing in a 2025 arXiv paper. At transonic speeds, shock waves and turbulent boundary layers interact to produce buffet, a pulsing load that can damage an aircraft. The flow is strongly nonlinear, yet a single dominant rhythm runs through each buffet cycle.

The team ran large-eddy simulations of a standard supercritical airfoil at two speeds, one calm and one in buffet, to build their data. A lift-augmented autoencoder then squeezed the flow into just three numbers that still track the shock's motion. Those numbers also catch the moment flow splits near the trailing edge. The team shows sensors can rebuild the flow from this compact code, and they map how sensitive the code is to flight conditions. The result gives engineers a small handle on a wild flow.
arxiv-2509-17406:
Jonathan Wuntu, Muhamad Dwisnanto Putro, and Rendy Syahputra test a tiny vision model for spotting fish at sea. Their 2025 arXiv paper works in Indonesian waters, part of the Coral Triangle, a region famed for rich marine life. Counting fish by hand is slow and needs expert eyes, so conservation teams need automated tools that run in real time.

The team chose YOLOv10-nano, a light detector with only a few million parameters. Test footage came from Bunaken National Marine Park, and training drew on the DeepFish and OpenImages fish data sets. The model scored high detection accuracy while staying cheap to run. It processed video at real-time speed even on a plain CPU. One data set alone gave weaker results, but joining the two made the detector sturdier. The authors present it as a practical monitor for busy reef ecosystems.
arxiv-2509-17606:
Luca Negri and Anuradha Samajdar speed up gravitational wave analysis with a neural likelihood tool. Their 2025 arXiv paper applies a Neural Likelihood Estimator to real detector data for the first time. Standard Bayesian analysis of a wave signal is sound but slow, since it must call the likelihood vast numbers of times.

The trained network stands in for the likelihood and returns posterior distributions at modest cost. The authors map where in parameter space the estimator stays robust. The same network can also yield the evidence for a hypothesis, which makes it a complete inference tool rather than a shortcut for one step. On a binary black hole signal, it needed about a hundred times fewer likelihood calls than standard methods. The network is simple to train and accepts any waveform, noise model, or prior, so it can be spun up on the fly.
arxiv-2509-18006:
Jorge Olmos Trigo, Cristina Sanz-Fernandez, and Ivan Fernandez-Corbaton present a new light test for the twist of round objects. Their 2025 letter deals with chirality, where an object and its mirror form differ. The standard test reads how much light each twist of a beam loses, which can be noisy.

Their test reads a set of light traits at any off-forward angle. The new score wipes out noise from non-twisted parts. It does not shift with how much stuff is in the beam or how long the path is. In a mix of both mirror forms, it can tell which form leads.
arxiv-2509-18106:
Elisa Tomassini, Enrique Garcia-Macias, and Filippo Ubertini move a damage model from one bridge to a second. Their 2025 study deals with bridge networks, where sensors now stream data from many spans. A model per bridge does not scale, while like bridges share damage modes.

Neural stand-in models hold that shared behaviour. A model trained on one bridge is tuned to a like bridge with far less new data. Paired with a stats frame, it scans for damage from live modal traits. On real data from two bridges, it was sharp on where damage sits and how bad it is.
arxiv-2509-18406:
Regression models often improve when the analyst adds sensible limits on their coefficients. Pierre Masselot, Devon Nenon, Jacopo Vanoli, Zaid Chalabi, and Antonio Gasparrini present a general frame for such constrained models in this 2025 paper. Their focus is generalized linear models, a wide family used across health and social research. Barriers in fitting and inference have kept constrained versions rare.

Their method, called CIRLS, fits the model with a reweighted least squares routine that respects linear limits. It adds inference tools that account for the limits, based on a clipped normal distribution and corrected degrees of freedom. Wide simulations showed good behavior, even when models were slightly over-limited. The tools ship as an R library with plain syntax inside standard routines. Case studies cover dose-response curves and composition data. The frame unifies many constrained problems in one workflow.
arxiv-2509-19006:
Sampling the states of a two-dimensional spin glass is a notorious bottleneck in computational physics. Tao Chen and four co-authors speed up a newer sampling method called tensor network Monte Carlo. Spin glasses pair random, frustrated couplings with frozen disorder, so chain-based samplers slow down badly on large lattices. The tensor network method helps, but its first version ran one sample at a time.

Their version, BatchTNMC, rewrites the method to run in parallel on graphics processors. It draws samples for many disorder cases at once. On a single graphics card it produced a thousand clean samples for each of a thousand cases on very large lattices in a few hours. Speed gains reach up to five orders of magnitude over the original serial code, with a healthy share of samples accepted.
arxiv-2509-19106:
Borophene is a sheet just one atom thick, made only of boron, and it comes in many atomic patterns called polymorphs. Alam Osorio and two co-authors compare the electronic structure of seven representative patterns. A tidy idea, called the rigid model, says all these patterns share one electronic skeleton and differ only in how many electrons fill it. That extra or missing filling is known as self-doping.

The comparison mostly supports the shared skeleton, but with clear limits. Some patterns sprout defect-like states that the parent skeleton does not predict, and a two-layer pattern shows its own bonding states. Bending, or buckling, in two patterns turns out to be a tuning knob: it can open Dirac cones, where electrons act massless, and create semimetal behavior. The authors hope the map encourages work on larger borophene structures.
arxiv-2509-19506:
Making new molecules in a computer means placing atoms in three-dimensional space with the right symmetry. Mohan Guo, Cong Liu, and Patrick Forré propose a diffusion method built on frames, which are fixed views that set each molecule's pose. Their design keeps exact symmetry while freeing the main model from symmetry chores. They test three frame styles: one shared frame, one frame per atom, and frames set before the run.

On the QM9 test set, the shared-frame version with an edge-aware transformer scored best. Its molecules stayed intact at high rates, and sampling ran near twice as fast as a key rival method. The authors argue that frames give a flexible, physics-based route to molecule design. The work may help chemists search for new compounds in software first.
arxiv-2509-19706:
Sound waves on a chip can stir magnetic waves in a thin metal film, and the two can sing together. Yunyoung Hwang and eight co-authors watched that duet with a focused light-scattering microscope. Their device traps surface sound in a resonator that holds a cobalt-iron-boron film. Rotating an in-plane magnetic field tunes the coupling from weak to strong in the same device.

Under weak coupling, only the base tone appeared. Under strong coupling, extra tones emerged at one and a half, two, and three times the base rate. An analytic model matched those extra tones well. The result shows sound can be used to create and steer nonlinear magnetic waves. Such control could serve future magnonic circuits, which process signals with spin waves instead of electric current.
arxiv-2509-19906:
Sending speech to cloud models exposes both what was said and who said it. Kohei Tanaka, Hitoshi Kiya, and Sayaka Shiota strengthen an encryption scheme that hides both. The base method scrambles speech with a secret random orthogonal key, letting cloud models work on the scrambled signal. Its weakness was limited resistance to attack and a narrow range of usable models.

Using several random orthogonal keys at once hardens the scheme. The authors also relax the constraints on which models can accept the encrypted input. Attack resistance is analyzed directly. Privacy-preserving inference would let hospitals and firms use cloud speech tools without leaking voices. Each relaxation of model limits widens where the method can actually be deployed.
arxiv-2509-20206:
Herbert Susmann, Alec McClean, and Ivan Diaz wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on causal inference. The average treatment effect compares outcomes under treatment and control for a whole population. Estimating it normally requires overlap: every subject must have some chance of either status. When overlap fails, researchers usually retreat to a smaller trimmed population.

The authors show that retreat is needless when the outcome is bounded. They derive bounds on the full effect that work without overlap. The bounds widen in proportion to the size of the non-overlap group, so they stay informative when violations are limited. Because the bounds are not smooth, they build smooth approximations and an efficient targeted estimator. A bootstrap method gives confidence sets that stay valid across all settings. Simulations and real data illustrate the method.
arxiv-2509-20506:
Knowing an average effect hides who was helped and who was harmed. Zach Shahn and David Madigan target the full joint distribution of potential outcomes in a 2025 arXiv paper. That distribution answers questions like the probability that a treatment caused an outcome. Recent work identified it by pooling several studies. This paper brings the trick inside a single study.

The key is a baseline covariate tied to untreated outcomes that does not modify the treatment effect once those outcomes are given. Identification and estimation theory are developed for that setting. A Neyman-orthogonal estimator handles cases where independence holds only after adjustment. The authors warn that exact assumptions are rare in practice, making sensitivity analysis essential. Simulations and a voter turnout mailing experiment illustrate the method.
arxiv-2509-20606:
A polynomial tied to a cone turns out to match a known geometric count, as Guanxi Li proves in a 2025 arXiv paper. Each polyhedral cone, a wedge with flat sides, has an adjoint polynomial set by algebra. Li shows it equals the multidegree polynomial of the cone's toric ideal, graded by the rays at the cone's edges. The two sides of the match come from unlike fields.

The match settles a conjecture of Aluffi. For cones that sit in the positive orthant, the adjoint polynomial is a covolume polynomial, just as the conjecture said. Such identities pay off twice: each side can now be worked out with the other side's tools. The paper is short and dense. Its readers are experts in algebraic geometry and kindred fields.
arxiv-2509-20706:
Speech emotion recognition often fails when a model trained in one setting meets voices from another. Hsiao-Ying Huang, Yi-Cheng Lin, and Hung-yi Lee address that mismatch in a 2025 paper on unsupervised domain adaptation. Their method, MI-Fuse, works even when the strong teacher model is closed and reachable only through an API.

Only unlabeled audio from the new domain is available. MI-Fuse draws repeated predictions from two teachers: a large audio-language model and a classifier trained on the source domain. It weights their averaged outputs by a mutual-information measure of uncertainty. This denoised label fusion then trains a student model. The authors report that the student can beat the large model itself in the target domain.
arxiv-2509-20806:
A dormant black hole in our galaxy, Gaia BH3, has a companion star on a strikingly stretched orbit. Qingru Hu, Bin Liu, and Wei Zhu propose an explanation in a 2025 paper accepted by the Astrophysical Journal Letters. They suggest the dark object is not one black hole but a hidden tight binary of two.

As the inner black hole pair slowly spirals inward, its precession rate can match that of the outer star's orbit. That resonance pumps the star's orbit to extreme eccentricity, matching what is observed. The authors compute the starting sizes and shapes the inner binary would need. The leftover binary would leave two observable imprints, which future observations could check to confirm or rule out the idea.
arxiv-2509-21606:
Clients in federated learning meet tasks in sequence and must not forget old ones. Seohyeon Cha and 2 co-authors propose a replay free continual method in a 2025 paper. Past approaches suffer catastrophic forgetting or store replay data that can violate privacy. Task identities are often assumed known at inference, which real deployments cannot promise. Their framework predicts task identity as part of the model.

Each client extracts low rank core bases from intermediate activations with randomized singular value decomposition. Those bases capture dominant feature directions for the current task. The server aggregates bases into global task subspaces shared across clients, without data sharing. Gradient projection then protects earlier subspaces during new training. The method is task agnostic and replay free by design.
arxiv-2509-22006:
Alan A. Dzhioev and N. V. Antonenko describe how a superheavy atomic nucleus splits, under three different rules for heat and energy. Their 2025 paper studies induced fission of the nucleus Lv-296 within nuclear energy-density functional theory. The calculations use a self-consistent method at finite temperature, with a standard Skyrme-type energy model. The fission path is traced as the nucleus stretches, measured by its quadrupole deformation.

The three rules hold temperature, entropy, or total energy fixed along the path, and each gives a different effective potential hill the nucleus must climb. At the same excitation energy, the fixed-energy rule predicts the highest barrier and the strongest damping. They also note a shift in the level-density parameter: it depends on shape at low excitation, then flattens at high excitation, as simple gas models expect.
arxiv-2509-22106:
Miguel-Angel Sanchis-Lozano, writing alone, asks whether the afterglow of the Big Bang can reveal the shape of the early universe. The cosmic microwave background, measured today in temperature and polarization, may carry marks of the universe's topology before inflation stretched it. His 2025 paper studies one specific possibility: a Kaluza-Klein model with an extra spatial dimension that curled up at the grand unification epoch, with mixed boundary conditions at its fixed points.

That setup leaves natural low-end cutoffs in both the scalar and tensor spectra of the early universe. Those cutoffs should show up in the microwave sky. The paper examines the expected signatures in detail, especially a lopsidedness between even and odd patterns at the largest scales, already reported by three satellite missions. It also looks ahead to the high-precision polarization measurements expected from the future LiteBIRD mission.
arxiv-2509-22306:
Muhammad Yarahmadi, Amin Salehi, and Ameneh Tohidi test a cosmological model that couples dark energy to neutrinos, against the mismatch known as the Hubble tension. Different measurements of the universe's expansion rate disagree, and exotic models try to reconcile them. Their 2025 paper uses a coupled quintom model, where a non-canonical scalar field interacts with neutrinos. They fit it against several major data sets at once: the microwave background, supernova records, cosmic clocks, sound-wave scale measurements, and lensing.

In the combined fits, the model eased the Hubble tension to a mild level of disagreement with both reference values of the expansion rate. It also sharpened the bound on the total neutrino mass, an important open quantity. The effective dark energy behavior crossed into the phantom regime, where expansion accelerates harder than a cosmological constant allows.
arxiv-2509-22706:
Kevin Momanyi estimates whether telecare shortens hospital stays, and questions how such effects should be measured. Telecare delivers care remotely, which may let patients leave hospital sooner. He builds a theoretical model linking demand for telecare to length of stay. Three statistical models follow, each with a different assumption about the distribution of the outcome. All are fit to data with controls for confounding factors and unobserved traits.

He compares the results with propensity score matching, a quasi-experimental method, keeping the same covariates throughout. His models gave treatment effects he judges better than the experimental-style estimate. In his analysis, the matching approach misses systematic differences in how individuals produce health within each study arm.
arxiv-2509-23006:
Goal-driven AI agents are hard to grade beyond whether they pick the right tools. Hassen Dhrif proposes Creative Adversarial Testing, or CAT, to judge goal-task fit. Current tests check agent, tool, and parameter choices, but not whether tasks serve the system's aims. CAT is built to map that link between tasks and goals. Dhrif tests the framework on synthetic data modeled after Alexa+ audio services.

Synthetic data let him probe edge cases and failure modes without risking user privacy. Results gave new insight into where tasks drift from goals. Dhrif argues such insight can guide better tuning of agentic systems. The paper is a single-author framework proposal with simulation support.
arxiv-2509-23106:
The Muon optimizer trains language models fast, but its high-precision states eat memory. Aman Gupta and 9 co-authors quantize those states to eight bits. Blockwise quantization keeps the scheme simple. Muon's update style turns out to fit plain linear quantization well. AdamW, by contrast, needs complex dynamic scaling when quantized.

Pretraining tests ran up to two point seven billion parameters, at Chinchilla-optimal scale. The eight-bit version matched full Muon on validation loss and downstream scores. Optimizer memory fell by up to sixty-two percent. Instruction fine-tuning results held up too. Theory on robustness to quantization noise backs the findings.
arxiv-2509-23206:
Function calling across a long chat needs memory of what is done and what comes next. Huacan Chai and 13 co-authors built PARL-MT to train that progress awareness. Single-turn training samples ignore task-level planning. End-to-end reinforcement learning suffers redundancy instead. Their pipeline auto-builds data that pairs chat summaries with future plans.

A guided reinforcement algorithm then trains with progress in the loop. Context redundancy drops as local calls align with global goals. Two public benchmarks show clear wins over prior methods. The team credit explicit progress signals for the robustness. Multi-stage tasks like travel planning are the target use.
arxiv-2509-23406:
A warm Jupiter around a cool M dwarf star offers a clean test of cloud physics in alien skies. Nishil Mehta and 16 co-authors study WASP-80b with fresh JWST spectra. Emission and transmission data cover the planet broadly. A global circulation model with a live cloud module makes the predictions. Radiatively active tracer clouds feed back on the air itself.

Only two stories fit the data. The air may be effectively cloudless. Or its clouds may be made of large particles that settle deep and hide. Small particles are ruled out by their strong feedback on the air structure. Particle size, the team stress, decides whether clouds matter at all.
arxiv-2509-23606:
Coloring a huge graph fast enough for live use, with colors counted in minutes, is a different game from exact theory. Chenghao Zhu and Yi Zhou built RECOL, an algorithm that shrinks the graph before coloring it. Reduction rules cut the problem down while keeping the best answer intact. Three rules, covering domination, complement crowns, and independent sets, are used on large instances for the first time here.

RECOL alternates between quick bound estimates, reductions, and heuristic coloring. On benchmark sets from SNAP, DIMACS, and other repositories, it beat leading methods on very large sparse graphs within one minute. Extra tests single out the reductions as the key to that speed.
arxiv-2509-24006:
Attention in video diffusion transformers eats most of the compute, because every token looks at every other. Jintao Zhang and 12 co-authors split attention weights into a small high-rank set of large weights and a low-rank remainder. Their method, SLA, treats the two parts differently: sparse attention for the critical weights, linear attention for the marginal ones, and nothing for the negligible. All of it runs in one GPU kernel, forward and backward.

A few fine-tuning steps adapt a model to the scheme. Attention compute fell by about ninety-five percent with no loss in generation quality, and end-to-end video generation sped up more than twofold on their test model.
arxiv-2509-24306:
Soil carbon supports healthy soil and climate resilience, but its movement through depth and time is hard to forecast. Satyanarayana Raju G V and 4 co-authors test a scientific machine-learning frame built on universal differential equations. The method blends known transport physics with neural networks that learn microbial production and respiration.

On synthetic data, six cases ran from clean benchmarks to stress tests with heavy, spatially linked noise. In clean and mild-noise cases the model rebuilt carbon dynamics with near-perfect fidelity. Heavy noise at the start caused overfitting, and heavy noise at the end collapsed the profile toward a smooth mean. The authors call for noise-aware training before field use.
arxiv-2509-24406:
The Muon optimizer is gaining ground as a rival to AdamW for training transformers, and its fans claim unusual efficiency. Sushant Mehta and 3 co-authors give it a full theoretical and empirical study on small to medium decoders. They prove convergence rates, show spectral rules that stop gradients from exploding, and link Muon to natural gradient descent on a curved space.

In tests, Muon reached target loss with about half the training of AdamW at equal or better quality. Paired with latent attention and mixture-of-experts designs, gains multiplied: far less memory, faster inference, and better perplexity. The study adds procedures for many components and checks across over a hundred runs.
arxiv-2509-24906:
Max Pellert, Clemens Lechner, Indira Sen, and Markus Strohmaier wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five about whether language model embeddings can recover human value dimensions. Psychometric surveys map values such as tradition or self-direction through long questionnaires. The team asked whether the meaning of the questions alone, as read by a neural network, holds the same structure.

Their method, called SQuID, compares embeddings of survey items to extract dimension relations. It recovered value dimensions on par with human rater data, without task-specific training. Its maps aligned with pooled human data from forty-nine countries. Tests on three personality inventories also improved, which hints the method may serve social science more broadly at lower cost.
arxiv-2509-25006: Prerna Dhankhar, Rebecca Field, Arjun Nigam, Quigley, and Albert Yang computed several K-theory variants for the cyclic group of order two in two thousand twenty-five. K-theory is an algebraic tool that classifies vector-like structures over spaces and rings. The group in question is the simplest non-trivial symmetry, with two elements.
arxiv-2509-26406:
Gili Goldin, Shira Wigderson, Ella Rabinovich, and Shuly Wintner wrote a 2025 paper on an annotation scheme for a slippery trait of speech: factuality, how fact-bound an utterance is. An utterance can state a fact, a possibility, or an imaginary world. Fact checking lives on that distinction. The trait is read from linguistic cues of many kinds.

The scheme combines concepts from a wide range of past work into one set of labels. It was built for Hebrew, one language of the Middle East, but the team trusts it can be adapted to more. Nearly five thousand sentences of parliamentary speech were annotated by hand under the scheme. The labels of two annotators were set side by side for their agreement rate. Automated tools were then tried at the calls of the scheme, to extend the annotation to a larger corpus.
arxiv-2509-26506:
Yutong Dai and a team of collaborators introduce a benchmark for AI agents doing office work in this two thousand twenty-five paper. SCUBA tests computer-use agents on customer relationship management workflows inside Salesforce, a platform where agents must click, type, and navigate real enterprise software. Its three hundred tasks come from interviews with real users and cover three personas: platform administrators, sales representatives, and service agents. Skills tested include interface navigation, data manipulation, workflow automation, information retrieval, and troubleshooting.

Tasks run in Salesforce sandbox environments with parallel execution and milestone-level scoring. Results exposed large gaps: open-source agents that shine on related benchmarks scored under five percent success zero-shot, while closed-source based agents reached up to thirty-nine percent. Adding demonstrations lifted success to fifty percent while cutting time and cost. The authors offer SCUBA as a realistic yardstick for enterprise agent automation.
arxiv-2510-00206:
Zhanda Zhu and five colleagues published this 2025 systems paper on LoRAFusion, a faster way to fine-tune language models. LoRA tuning trains small adapter weights instead of the whole model, saving memory. Existing systems borrow designs from full-model training and waste LoRA's special structure. The authors pinpoint redundant memory traffic and a missed chance to run many adapters together.

At the kernel level, their graph-splitting fusion cuts memory access in LoRA modules substantially. At the scheduling level, an adaptive batching scheme staggers and packs concurrent adapter jobs. Together the changes raised GPU use from about two-thirds to nearly ninety percent in their tests. End-to-end speed beat the Megatron-LM system by up to nearly twofold across models and datasets. The work matters because fine-tuning many adapters at once is now a routine cloud workload.
arxiv-2510-00606:
Xueze Kang and a large team of co-authors published this 2025 paper on keeping giant AI training runs alive when hardware fails. Pretraining now spans hundreds of thousands of accelerators, so breakdowns are routine events. An elastic system must reshuffle work without corrupting parameters or wasting throughput. Their system, ElasWave, builds elasticity in from the start rather than bolting it on.

Per-step fault tolerance comes from scheduling across the compute graph, data flow, chip clocks, and random number streams. Micro-batches reshape on the fly while the global batch and gradient scale stay fixed. Communication groups rebuild in place, with recovery finishing inside one second in tests. Throughput beat strong baselines by up to about sixty percent on their ninety-six-chip testbed. Migration downtime dropped by as much as half against blocking approaches. Training results stayed consistent through the churn, the authors report.
arxiv-2510-00706:
Ibrahimov and four co-authors present AttentionDep in this 2025 arXiv paper, a model that estimates depression severity from social media posts and explains its judgements. Questionnaires and interviews detect depression reliably but scale poorly, while millions of people describe their mental state in posts. Attention mechanisms over word and phrase features can flag clinically relevant wording, yet text alone misses medical context. The authors fuse both sources.

Posts are encoded hierarchically from unigrams and bigrams, with attention highlighting the tokens that matter clinically. A cross-attention step enriches those features with a mental health knowledge graph built from Wikipedia material. An ordinal regression head predicts severity, respecting the ordering of clinical levels. Across three datasets the model beat baselines by over five percent in graded F1 score, reaching ninety-two percent on the binary task. Its attention maps show reviewers which words drove each call.
arxiv-2510-00806:
Yang and four co-authors make videos obey physics by predicting motion first, in this 2025 arXiv paper presenting TrajVLM-Gen. Video diffusion models render textures and lighting, yet objects in their output drift, slide, and collide in impossible ways. Control-based fixes need external inputs, and language-only trajectory predictors ignore what the scene actually looks like. The authors give a vision-language model both jobs in a two-stage design.

Given a starting image and a text description, the model first forecasts object trajectories that respect real-world dynamics. Attention mechanisms then guide the video generator to refine motion along those tracks. The team built a trajectory dataset from video tracking data with motion patterns. On UCF-101 and MSR-VTT the system beat methods, posting Fréchet video distance scores. The authors argue trajectory-first design is the missing link between seeing and physically plausible generation.
arxiv-2510-00906:
Lemmel and five co-authors at TU Wien introduce TubeDAgger in this 2025 arXiv paper on interactive imitation learning. Imitation learning trains a novice policy from expert demonstrations, and DAgger-style methods retrain it on its own rollouts while an expert corrects mistakes. Handing control back too often is expensive and sometimes safety-critical, so variants gate the expert behind a learned doubt model. Those extra classifiers need per-environment threshold tuning and can be fragile.

TubeDAgger instead estimates when help is needed with stochastic reach-tubes, a tool borrowed from dynamical systems verification. The tube describes where the system could plausibly travel next, and the expert intervenes only when the novice risks leaving the safe region. In the authors' comparisons, the method cut expert interventions substantially versus doubt-classifier approaches. It also avoided the fragile threshold fine-tuning those approaches require.
arxiv-2510-01006:
Venkatachalam, at Wayne State University, describes a forecasting system for a manufacturer's after-sales parts business in this 2025 arXiv paper on operations analytics. The system forecasts demand across more than ninety countries and roughly six thousand parts. Its ensemble blends statistical, machine learning, and deep learning models, weighted by revenue and horizon, and it feeds signals such as installed base, pricing, and macroeconomic indicators. COVID-19 is treated as a regime, and forecasts carry intervals.

High-revenue parts are modelled individually under a Pareto-aware segmentation, while long-tail parts are pooled into clusters. Above the forecasts sits an analytics layer with performance scorecards and trend diagnostics. Scorecards decompose bias, find geographic and product hotspots, and rank root causes for the costliest misses. Trend views flag improving and deteriorating parts and detect change points. Language models embedded in that layer write role-aware summaries and enforce reporting contracts.
arxiv-2510-01206:
Le and co-authors speed up molecular dynamics by treating atomic motion as a time series to forecast instead of a physics problem to integrate. Standard quantum-based simulation is accurate but so slow that long processes stay out of reach. Forecasting displacements, step by step, lets modern sequence models do the heavy lifting.

A physics-informed penalty, built from standard pair potentials, forbids atoms from crowding unphysically. Forecast trajectories stayed stable for thousands of steps and finished in minutes. Accuracy beat standard baselines across several different materials. Physical guardrails, not bigger networks, supplied the reliability that pure forecasting lacks. Predicting displacements rather than positions keeps errors from compounding as fast. Five hundred atom pairs per step feed the physics penalty during training. Early stopping and adaptive rates keep the training stable. Minutes replace days for long trajectories in practice.
arxiv-2510-01506:
Wu, Linton, Karpitschka, and Pandey turn creases in a soft gel surface into gates that steer droplets without touching them. Microfluidics usually needs patterned substrates, external fields, and feedback loops to move droplets. A crease instead repels droplets at long range through elastocapillary forces, acting as an energy barrier.

Droplets below a critical size are barred; larger ones pass, enabling size filtration. Surface tension differences allow a second, active filtering mode. The team built path guidance, pulse modulators, and elementary logic like adders from the same mechanism. Droplet circuits gain computation without electronics at the gate. A multi-scale force-distance law describes the drop-crease interaction quantitatively. Tunable hysterons give the surface a primitive memory. Strain and ridge height tune the gate's threshold in practice. Contact-free gating avoids contamination and wear at once. Information flows as droplets through the device.
arxiv-2510-01606:
Ma and co-authors wire classic collaborative filtering into a language-model recommender without retraining the big model. Adapter links let the language model borrow filtering knowledge cheaply, but static snapshots age fast as tastes move. Many items also carry images and audio that plain text prompts ignore.

Their framework adapts online, folding fresh interactions into light modules instead of full retrains. Multimodal fusion brings visual and audio evidence into the same representation. Explanations cite concrete collaborative evidence rather than inventing plausible stories. Fresher, richer, and more honest recommendations are the combined goal. Frozen base models keep deployment costs sane while adapters do the learning. Preferences drift within weeks, so a snapshot recommender quietly goes stale. Evidence-grounded wording lets users audit why an item appeared. Text, image, and sound finally vote together. Trust follows receipts, not adjectives. Shops gain a recommender that explains itself.
arxiv-2510-01706:
Shah and Khosla propose a new way to compare representations in this 2025 paper on neural networks and brains. Standard methods match each layer of one network to its best partner in another network. That layer-by-layer matching gives uneven results and no single global score. It also struggles when two networks have different depths.

Their method, Hierarchical Optimal Transport, aligns whole networks at once instead. Source neurons can spread their mass across several target layers, subject to clear marginal limits. The method yields one alignment score plus a soft transport plan for interpretation. Tests covered vision models, large language models, and human visual cortex recordings. The method matched or beat standard matching, and it revealed smooth layer patterns. Early layers mapped to early layers without that order being imposed in advance.
arxiv-2510-02306:
Tang and co-authors rethink what a draw means when two chatbots face off. Their 2025 evaluation paper studies arena style contests. In an arena, a user reads two answers and picks a winner. The user may also call the battle a draw. Rating systems borrowed from chess then pull both scores together. The authors doubt that a draw proves equal skill. They suspect draws mostly mark easy questions. On easy questions, both models succeed and look tied.

They tested the idea on three real arena datasets. Ignoring rating updates for draws improved outcome prediction. The gain ran about one to three percent across four rating systems. Draws made up thirty to forty percent of all battles. Draws also clustered on very easy and highly objective questions. Future rating systems should model question traits directly.
arxiv-2510-02606:
Habel and co-authors take infrared spectra of young stars forming in a metal poor galaxy region. Their 2025 astronomy paper uses the JWST observatory. The target region, NGC 346, sits in the Small Magellanic Cloud. Its metal content is about one fifth of the Sun's share. That poverty mimics cosmic noon, when star formation peaked. Five young stellar objects got full mid-infrared spectra. Three more likely young stars got partial coverage. The instrument split their light across four wavelength channels. Spectral features revealed dust, ices, accretion, and outflows together.

Fitting the energy distributions gave stellar masses for all eight. The five main stars ranged from about seven to eighteen solar masses. Hydrogen lines signaled active accretion onto the stars. Molecular hydrogen and fine structure lines traced outflows and gas. Metal poor star birth can now be compared directly with local cases. JWST spectroscopy reaches nurseries once blurred beyond study.
arxiv-2510-02706:
Elamvazhuthi extends flow matching from moving data clouds to steering controlled systems. His 2025 control theory paper treats probability measures as the cargo. Control-affine systems mix drift with chosen inputs. A balance equation describes how the measure evolves. Exact and approximate matching build paths between measures. An output variant matches only what sensors observe. Classic control tools plug straight into the framework. Feedback design, oscillatory inputs, and trajectory steering all transfer. Regression based controllers come out sample efficient.

A second viewpoint flips the direction entirely. Adding noise destabilizes, so reversing time stabilizes. That reads stabilization as a denoising task. Two recipes build the noising process. Four algorithms emerge with existence and smoothness proofs. Numerical examples test each variant. Generative modeling ideas now serve feedback control. The bridge may enrich both fields.
arxiv-2510-03006:
Mobsite and co-authors test land cover mapping under cloudy skies. Deep models label each pixel of satellite images by land type. Training sets, though, are mostly cloud-free scenes. The tropics, where maps matter most, sit under frequent cloud. The team built a tool that injects fake clouds into clear images. Models can then be graded on cloudy versions of known scenes. Radar data from Sentinel-1 offers a way to see through cloud.

A second trick guards fine detail inside the networks. Spectral index maps are fed into the late decoding layers. That kept spatial detail that downsampling usually erases. On clear images, the trick lifted two standard models by clear margins. Under injected cloud, adding radar data helped every model a lot. Optical-only models also improved when trained with fake clouds. They learned to guess hidden ground from clear edges nearby.
arxiv-2510-03106:
Bugueño and co-authors trace disks of stars that spin backward inside their galaxies. Two stellar disks can share one plane yet rotate in opposite ways. The team searched the IllustrisTNG simulation for Milky Way-mass galaxies. Two hundred sixty late-type systems passed their cuts. Stars with strongly negative circularity marked the backward parts. Mass share, size, and birth history were then measured.

Only twenty-six galaxies held a sizable backward disk. That rarity matches what telescopes report in the real sky. Most backward disks were compact in extent. Most of their stars were born inside the galaxy itself. Their birth histories spiked in bursts tied to outside disturbances. Backward gas, it seems, can spark local star birth. Smooth inflow and mergers both fed that gas in cases found. Backward disks thus serve as sensitive fossils of accretion.
arxiv-2510-03206:
Zhou and co-authors merge continuous and discrete diffusion into one language model that reasons latently. Diffusion language models generate text by gradual denoising. Discrete versions lead in practice, but continuous ones promise more. The authors prove continuous diffusion is the more expressive family. It can even simulate looped transformers, a rival design. Training, though, sabotages that theoretical edge. Decoding tokens back out of continuous states is the hard part.

Their CCDD process denoises in both spaces at once. One model serves the joint space of tokens and representations. Explicit tokens keep sample quality and trainability high. Rich continuous states keep semantics and reasoning depth. New architectures and sampling tricks support the scheme. Language modeling tests on two real corpora followed. Validation perplexity fell well below the baselines. The work reframes latent reasoning for diffusion models. Latent chains of thought need not live in token space.
arxiv-2510-03506:
Nguyen and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper on OneFlow, a model that writes text and pictures at the same time. Standard models generate word by word in a fixed order, which forces text and images into a line. OneFlow instead inserts text tokens where confidence is highest and paints image content in parallel through flow matching. Content lands before grammar polish, much like a person sketching ideas first. The model handles mixed output of any length in one pass.

Across sizes from one to eight billion parameters, OneFlow beat word by word baselines on generation and understanding tasks in the study. It used up to half the training compute of those rivals. It also topped diffusion based image models in the reported comparisons. Insert first generation unlocks revision, since any span can be reopened and refined. Such mixed media drafting could change how assistants compose reports, lessons, and stories.
arxiv-2510-03606:
Scardecchia presents a 2025 arXiv survey of unsupervised pre-training for image transformers, centered on the DINO family of methods. These methods teach a network by self-distillation: a student model learns to match a teacher that is a moving average of itself. Random crops supply views of each image, and the model learns features that stay stable across them. The survey traces how ideas developed and how DINOv2 added a masked modeling objective.

DINOv2 was the first self-supervised method whose general purpose features rivaled supervised systems like CLIP on benchmarks. Its features work on tasks with no fine tuning. They show an emergent grasp of object boundaries and scene layout that nobody trained. One limitation stands out: the recipe leans on hand crafted image augmentations, which ports poorly to data types. The survey maps where the approach shines and where successors like joint embedding methods may take it.
arxiv-2510-03806:
Behnamian and Fogh present this 2025 arXiv paper in pure mathematics, on a new family called twisted triangular Banach algebras. Banach algebras are systems whose elements can be added, multiplied, and measured. The authors build their structures from two such algebras, a linking module, and a pair of twisting maps. The twist changes how the parts interact compared with the classical construction.

The paper gives a complete rule for when two of these twisted algebras are really the same structure in disguise. For group algebras, the rule detects classes of symmetry maps that the untwisted theory cannot see. The authors also bound a measure of complexity called cohomological dimension. They prove the twisted algebra can be amenable, a strong regularity property, only when the linking module is zero. The results show twisting enriches the classical theory while keeping its tools usable.
arxiv-2510-03906:
Aryashad and colleagues at the University of Southern California wrote this 2025 arXiv paper testing whether clearing fog from road images helps self-driving cars. Fog scatters light and hides pedestrians, vehicles, and signs from a car's cameras. Many defogging methods exist, but prettier images do not always mean better detection. The team built a benchmark judging methods by driving tasks, not looks.

They compared classical filters, modern learned restorers, chained combinations, and prompt-driven editing models from vision-language systems. Tests used the Foggy Cityscapes dataset and scored detection plus segmentation quality. Methods trained on synthetic fog often gained on paper but failed to transfer to real fog. Chaining a filter with a model helped or hurt depending on the order used. Scores from a vision-language judge tracked the detection metric surprisingly well. The study gives developers a clear way to tell when defogging truly helps perception.
arxiv-2510-04106:
Ilee, Walsh, and Calahan present this 2025 arXiv paper reporting new ALMA observations of methanol in the TW Hya planet-forming disk. Methanol ice is a feedstock for complex, possibly prebiotic molecules, yet its gas form had been seen in only one disk around a Sun-like star. The team observed four methanol transitions with high sensitivity. They aimed to locate the gas and test how it escapes the ice.

The emission sits in a lukewarm molecular layer of the disk, at roughly thirty-six kelvin. Chemical models confirm that ultraviolet photodesorption releases the methanol from grain surfaces. Still, no static model matched both the observed quantity and its radial distribution. The authors argue that dynamic processes like vertical mixing and radial dust drift must also operate. The findings tie the seeds of complex chemistry to how dust evolves in young disks.
arxiv-2510-04306:
Longo, Magrone, and Walchek present this 2025 arXiv paper connecting big Heegner points to p-adic L-functions for quaternionic modular forms. Heegner points are special points on modular curves whose heights encode values of L-functions, and Howard's big Heegner points package them across a Hida family. Castella had shhow points specialize at weights in the classical GL2 setting. The quaternionic setting, based on quaternion algebras, needed its own version.

The authors extend Castella's interpolation and specialization results to quaternionic families. Their main theorem is an reciprocity law tying the big Heegner points to the big p-adic L-function built in their companion work. The proof strategy uses families of p-adic L-functions as a bridge and leans on the density of weight-two specializations. Reciprocity laws of this kind are the engine behind Euler system arguments toward Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer type results in families.
arxiv-2510-04606:
Alexandre Galashov and four coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on a shortcut for training neural networks. Training usually nudges every layer with gradient steps, last layer included. Under a squared loss, though, the best last layer for any fixed backbone has a known closed form. The team treats the final layer as a function of the backbone and optimizes the backbone alone. Each step pairs a gradient move on the backbone with an exact reset of the last layer.

The stochastic version must balance the current batch against all batches seen before. Their update blends fresh data with accumulated statistics so the last layer does not overfit one batch. In the neural tangent kernel regime, they prove the method reaches an optimal solution. Tests covered regression and classification, plus operator learning and instrumental variable problems. The method beat standard gradient training on those tasks under squared loss.
arxiv-2510-04706:
Foivos Paraperas Papantoniou and Stefanos Zafeiriou wrote this 2025 paper on giving generated faces any expression on demand. Storytelling tools need the same character to smile, frown, or raise an eyebrow across scenes. Face generators keep identity well but steer expressions crudely. Their diffusion framework starts from a face model built for identity consistency. An added module reads expression controls from a standard three dimensional face model.

Those controls, called blendshape parameters, spell out muscle level movements in numbers. Cross attention lets the parameters steer generation while the identity path stays intact. Training mixed images and videos rich in expressive range. The system handled subtle micro expressions and smooth transitions, not just the basic emotion set. A plug in adapter can also borrow appearance from a reference photo to edit real images. In their tests the model beat rivals on tailored, identity true expression generation. The code and models are public.
arxiv-2510-05306:
Chris Godsil and four co-authors map when quantum information can hop perfectly through a network in this 2025 arXiv paper. A continuous quantum walk spreads a state across a graph's vertices. Perfect state transfer delivers the state intact to a target vertex or pair. Sparse networks matter, because every physical link costs money to build.

The authors prove a key result about equitable partitions of bounded weighted graphs with twin subgraphs. With it they construct infinite families of graphs admitting pair or plus state transfer. For every maximum degree at least three, such connected graphs exist in endless supply. Almost all finite planar graphs and trees admit pair transfer at special times. One negative edge weight can likewise unlock plus-state transfer on most planar graphs.
arxiv-2510-05706:
