Walker and colleagues replace random sampling inside a popular control optimizer. Cross-entropy method control plans actions by sampling candidate sequences and keeping the best. Random samples cluster and leave gaps, which wastes effort and jerks the controls. Their 2025 variant draws deterministic samples from localized distributions instead.

Modular schemes generate and adapt the deterministic sample sets over time. Temporal correlations in the samples keep control trajectories smooth. The method drops into existing cross-entropy controllers as a sampling replacement. Tests cover mountain car and cart-pole swing-up tasks. Deterministic variants beat the state-of-the-art iCEM on cumulative cost and smoothness. Low-discrepancy coverage explains why deterministic sets explore more evenly. The fully deterministic variant produced the smoothest trajectories of all. The advantage is largest exactly when samples are scarce. Smooth controls matter for real actuators that hate jerky commands.
arxiv-2510-05806:
Deligkas and colleagues map when temporal connected components are computable. Temporal graphs change over time, edge by edge. A temporal component requires time-respecting paths between every pair of vertices. Their 2025 paper studies open and closed variants under structural parameters.

Treewidth alone does not tame either problem's complexity. Both variants stay NP-hard even at treewidth nine. Closed components are also hard at temporal path number six. Open components, however, admit an XP algorithm by path number. Combining treewidth with path number restores fixed-parameter tractability. So do treewidth paired with lifetime or maximum temporal degree. The open question is whether open components by path number are FPT or W-hard. Enumerating all maximal open components cannot be improved for the XP algorithm. Small local gadgets defeat the parameters in the hardness constructions.
arxiv-2510-06106:
Favero's 2025 doctoral thesis asks why deep networks can learn high-dimensional tasks at all. Statistics says such tasks should be intractable through the curse of dimensionality. Their success implies learnable data hides latent structure, and the thesis investigates it.

The work centers on locality and compositionality. Locality means outputs depend on limited, nearby input pieces, not everything at once. Compositionality means tasks are built by combining simpler functions into hierarchies. Favero studies how these properties appear in data and tasks, and how networks encode and exploit them. A recurring quantitative question is how generalization improves as training examples grow. The answers connect data structure to sample complexity, showing when learning is cheap or hard. The thesis gives deep learning theory a concrete account of why real-world tasks are learnable.
arxiv-2510-06206:
De Ro proves equivariant Eilenberg–Watts theorems for locally compact quantum groups in a 2025 operator algebras paper. Rieffel's theorem says correspondences between two von Neumann algebras match functors between their representation categories. It lets operator algebraists translate between bimodules and functors freely.

De Ro equips both algebras with actions of one locally compact quantum group. Using module categories, he establishes several equivariant forms of the theorem. The symmetry is built into the correspondence–functor dictionary from the start. He also proves that unitary representations of the Drinfeld double form a category isomorphic to the Drinfeld center of the representation category. That generalizes a Neshveyev–Yamashita theorem from compact to locally compact quantum groups. The extension matters because many physically interesting quantum groups are not compact. Equivariant Morita theory for them now rests on firmer foundations.
arxiv-2510-06306:
Solyst and four co-authors study critical AI literacy through fashion design with Black Muslim teen girls in a 2025 human–computer interaction paper. Drawing on culturally responsive computing, they designed learning around intersectional identity. Fashion offered a culturally rich domain for using generative AI and then questioning it.

The case study follows a three-day voluntary informal program. Participants used generative tools to depict their dream fashion collections. The tools repeatedly failed them in revealing ways. Biased models and malfunctioning safety systems blocked outputs reflecting their ideas, bodies, and cultures; the title quotes one such clash. Guided discussion turned frustration into analysis. Talking through impossible creative realization helped them articulate how identity-affirming technology should behave. Linking creativity and identity, the study suggests, grows critical AI literacy better than abstract bias warnings.
arxiv-2510-06706:
Phuong Tuan Dat and Tran Huy Dat work on catching fake speech before it fools speaker verification systems. Their 2025 paper improves a detection model called XLSR-Conformer. Voice synthesis and conversion tools now produce convincing imitations. Verification systems that unlock accounts by voice need strong defenses against such spoofing.

The authors swap one standard component of the model for a Kolmogorov-Arnold Network. That network type is built on a classic theorem about representing complex functions. The redesigned model is named XLSR-Kanformer. On the ASVspoof 2021 benchmark, the change cut error rates sharply. Equal error rates improved by about sixty percent in relative terms on two test sets. One test set reached an error rate as low as zero point seven percent. The swap also stayed robust across different self-supervised backbones. The results suggest this network type deserves wider use in audio forensics.
arxiv-2510-07006:
Jinho Cha and four co-authors model when firms adopt smart contracts, and what that adoption is worth. Their 2025 paper builds an optimization model for derivative markets under bounded risk. Smart contracts automate settlement and promise lower costs and better transparency. Whether firms adopt them depends on fixed costs and readiness.

Simulations and comparative statics reveal a split personality in the results. The adoption level itself is stubbornly stable. It sits pinned at a boundary value, unmoved by variance shocks or differences between firms. Cross a fixed-cost threshold, though, and adoption collapses all at once. Profitability tells the opposite story. Profits and service outcomes erode under volatility and heavy-tailed demand. Moderate adoption improves profit and service performance, a co-benefit the authors confirm. The duality mirrors options theory, where decisions wait for thresholds but cash flows stay fragile. Firms should expect stable uptake and unstable earnings.
arxiv-2510-07106:
Liu, Hickling, and MacArt train software to tame the air flow over a wing. Their 2025 study uses computer simulations of a standard wing shape in rough, turbulent air. A small jet on the upper surface blows or sucks air to steer the flow. The goal is more lift for the drag the wing creates. Poor flow control lets the air peel away and lift falls.

A neural network reads pressure sensors on the wing and sets the jet strength moment by moment. Training used exact math that traces how each network change alters the flow. The trained controllers raised the lift-to-drag balance and shrank the zone where flow breaks away. Controllers trained on flat wing models also worked on full 3D wings. That transfer hints at cheaper training for real aircraft design. Smarter flow control could cut fuel use on future planes.
arxiv-2510-07206:
Shoushtari, Wang, Shi, and Kamilov present EigenScore, a way to spot inputs that a model was never trained on. Their 2025 paper uses diffusion models, which clean noise from data step by step. The authors argue that the model's own uncertainty carries that warning. They read it from the spread of plausible clean versions of an input.

Unusual inputs inflate that spread in a measurable way. The largest eigenvalues of the spread grow, forming a clear spectral signature. Theory links the inflation directly to how far the input sits from the training distribution. On benchmarks, EigenScore beat the best rival methods by a solid margin. It stayed strong on hard near-miss cases, where a photo set of one hundred classes masquerades as a ten-class set.
arxiv-2510-07306:
Bal and co-authors use machine learning to enlarge the sample of gamma-ray bursts with known distances. Their 2025 paper studies how the properties of long bursts changed across cosmic time. Distance, or redshift, is usually measured with follow-up spectroscopy. About four fifths of bursts lack it, shrinking every study. The team instead trained models on prompt and afterglow traits to predict distances without those assumptions.

With the augmented sample, they tested three stories about how bursts evolve. Evolution in the beaming of burst jets, or in all properties at once, can match burst rates at middling distances. None of the three stories fits the rates at low and high distances together. The mismatch hints that burst evolution is not a simple power law. Machine-estimated distances have become a crucial ingredient in burst cosmology.
arxiv-2510-07406:
Torres Luna and co-authors chart the fundamental trade-offs in building Majorana-based quantum bits. Their 2025 paper compares two platforms: semiconductor nanowires coated with a superconductor, and chains of quantum dots. Majorana bound states promise qubits protected by topology. Two quality measures rule their usefulness. A large topological gap guards coherence, while a short localization length keeps devices compact and faithful. Multi-objective optimization maps what each platform can achieve when both measures compete for the same tuning knobs.

The two measures cannot be maximized together in realistic models, the team proves. Their best compromises form Pareto frontiers that bound the achievable space. Quantum dot chains matched nanowire quality overall. They also reached a regime with much shorter localization length. That regime matters because real devices are short and dirty, exactly where long localization hurts most.
arxiv-2510-07706:
Li and nine coauthors wrote this 2025 survey on large language models for virtual cell research. A virtual cell is a computer system that represents and predicts how real cells behave. Language models promise to power such systems by learning from vast biological data. The survey organizes a fast-growing literature for biologists and model builders. It also names the benchmarks and datasets that the field relies on.

The authors sort existing methods into two paradigms. In one, the model acts as an oracle that models the cell directly. In the other, it acts as an agent that runs complex scientific tasks and tools. They review three core tasks: representing cells, predicting responses to perturbations, and inferring gene regulation. They close with open challenges in scaling, generalization to new cell types, and interpretability. The survey gives newcomers a map of a young and crowded field.
arxiv-2510-08306:
A. A. Farafontova, M. S. Kirsanova, and S. V. Salii present MOLLId in a 2025 arXiv paper, a program that names molecules from telescope spectra. Young stars emit and absorb light at lines set by the molecules around them. Matching hundreds of lines by hand is slow and error-prone. MOLLId fits each line with a Gaussian curve and compares its center with database rest frequencies.

The team tested the program on spectra of two young stellar objects in the RCW 120 region. For the first source, it identified one hundred lines from forty-one molecules above set signal levels. For the second, it found four hundred seven lines from seventy-nine molecules. A standard desktop processor finished each range in about six to eight minutes. From methanol and related molecules, they also derived a two-component structure for the second source.
arxiv-2510-09106:
Wang and co-authors review retrieval-augmented generation and ask where it still earns its keep, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The technique bolts a search step onto a language model, so answers can draw on fresh or specialized documents instead of frozen training memory alone. It spread quickly as a cure for stale knowledge and invented facts. Since then the models themselves have grown far stronger, which has quietly eroded the margin the technique adds.

The review first lays out the goals and moving parts of a retrieval system, then dissects its weak points in detail. Retrieval can fetch the wrong passages, and the model can ignore or mangle the right ones. The authors then showcase the settings where models alone still fall short and retrieval clearly helps, such as fast-moving facts and narrow domains. They close hoping the field will design a sharper next generation.
arxiv-2510-09206:
Fu and Li prove a reversed version of one of information theory's classic inequalities for a well-behaved family of random variables, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Shannon's entropy power inequality says the uncertainty of a sum of independent variables is at least the sum of their separate uncertainty powers, with the Gaussian distribution as the extreme case. Reversals, where the inequality flips direction, need extra structure. The authors work with log-concave variables, whose densities have a convex-shaped logarithm.

They use the Rényi entropy of infinite order, a worst-case measure of uncertainty. Their theorem bounds a sum of two independent log-concave variables by the sum of exponential variables with matched entropy values. Exponentials are the extreme case in this reversed world. The proof leans on rearrangement, majorization, and a change of measure. Companion results cover integer-valued monotone variables, extending the reversal to discrete data.
arxiv-2510-09506:
Bob Holdom, the sole author, explores an unusual possibility in the study of the universe in a 2025 arXiv paper. He studies static, uneven, spatially closed solutions of Einstein's equations of gravity. Inside some of them sit one or two singularities with negative mass, points where the usual rules break down in an unexpected direction.

These singularities produce a positive Komar mass, a global measure of a spacetime's mass, and they shrink the real size of the cosmological constant compared with normal matter. The fluid's energy density vanishes at the singularities and stays finite elsewhere. Holdom gives worked examples whose stability resembles the classic Einstein static universe. As the universe expands, the singularities make expansion speed up more, much as dark energy would. He closes by reviewing how benign such a naked singularity really is, given the field's wish to avoid them.
arxiv-2510-09606:
Peiwen Sun and ten co-authors introduce SpaceVista in a 2025 arXiv paper, a push toward spatial reasoning at every scale. Vision-language models have learned indoor scenes well, but robotics and driving demand reasoning from millimetres to kilometres. Two obstacles stand out: training data leans on costly indoor scans, and models overfit single scenes instead of learning scale.

The team answers with a structured knowledge system, scale-aware modelling, and a progressive training plan. A specialist-driven pipeline curates over thirty-eight thousand video scenes across five scales, forming SpaceVista-1M with about one million question-answer pairs over nineteen task types. A separate benchmark carries precise manual annotations, since specialist models cannot be trusted as judges. Naive training on the new data falters from knowledge conflicts, so the staged training plan and the resulting SpaceVista-7B model are designed to absorb the specialists' knowledge cleanly.
arxiv-2510-09706:
Md Habibur Rahman, Md Sharif Hossen, Nathan Stephenson, Vijay Shah, and Aloizio Da Silva demonstrate a self-defending radio network in a 2025 arXiv paper. Open radio access networks, or O-RAN, make 5G infrastructure modular and programmable through open interfaces and virtualised functions. That openness invites jamming attacks, where an adversary floods frequencies to degrade the network.

Their framework, SAJD, detects jamming without human intervention. It forms a closed loop: a machine learning application running near real time infers jamming from radio signals, while companion applications monitor performance and retrain the detector continuously. The demonstration runs on an O-RAN-compliant testbed under varied and previously unseen interference. The authors report that SAJD beats a state-of-the-art detection application that was trained offline with manual labels, both in accuracy and in adaptability to changing conditions.
arxiv-2510-10106:
Sioulas and co-authors analyze Alfvénic fluctuations in the solar wind in this 2025 arXiv paper in space physics. These fluctuations are waves that travel along magnetic field lines, named for Hannes Alfvén. The team uses observations from Parker Solar Probe and Solar Orbiter to track them from the outer corona out to Earth's orbit.

Conservation of wave-action flux gives the baseline for how wave amplitudes should scale as the wind speeds up, measured by the Alfvén Mach number. Comparing the data with that baseline shows where the waves lose energy along the way. How this energy dissipates helps heat the solar wind, a long-standing puzzle in heliophysics that close-up spacecraft data can now test.
arxiv-2510-10606:
Yuqi Liu and six co-authors merge two standard ways of training large vision and language models into one, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Supervised fine tuning teaches new knowledge from labeled examples, but often lands at suboptimal performance. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards sharpens reasoning, yet stalls on tasks beyond the model's own knowledge. Their framework, ViSurf, combines both inside a single training stage instead of running them in sequence.

The core trick is to inject ground truth labels directly into the reinforcement learning rollouts, so external supervision and internal reinforcement act at once. The team derives a single objective that unifies the two paradigms and adds three reward control strategies to keep training stable. Across several benchmarks, ViSurf outperformed supervised fine tuning alone, reinforcement learning alone, and the usual two stage pipeline. Follow up analysis supported both the derivation and the design choices.
arxiv-2510-10706:
Mamoona Ghafoor and Tatsuya Akutsu design neural networks that generate every tree within a set distance of a given tree, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Tree edit distance measures how many edits turn one labeled tree into another. Generating all trees within a fixed distance matters for biology and structured data analysis. The open question was how large a generative network must be. The authors answer it theoretically for ReLU based networks.

For a rooted, ordered, labeled tree, they prove that all trees within edit distance d can be generated by a network of cubic size in the tree's size, with constant depth. They implemented the networks and tested generation for trees up to 21 nodes. The deterministic design produced every valid tree. Rival graph generators, GraphRNN and GraphGDP, reached validation rates of only up to 35 and 48 percent in the same comparisons. The work grounds exact, valid generation of tree structured data.
arxiv-2510-11006:
Hai-Bo Yu argues that one kind of dark matter halo explains three separate astronomical puzzles, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The halos are core collapsed self interacting dark matter clumps of about a million solar masses. Self interacting dark matter particles collide with each other, and in some halos the core contracts into an unusually dense state. Such a halo was first simulated to explain a dense perturber inferred in the GD-1 stellar stream, a ribbon of stars in the Milky Way.

Yu shows the same simulated halos also reproduce the structure inferred for the dense perturber in JVAS B1938+666, a strong lensing system seen through radio observations. And the halos are compact and dense enough to gravitationally capture passing field stars inside Milky Way satellite galaxies. That offers a natural origin for Fornax 6, a puzzling star cluster in the Fornax dwarf galaxy.
arxiv-2510-11206:
Knowing when a map covers its whole target space, and when paths in the target can be lifted back, is a classical question with modern uses in robot motion planning. Yacine Chitour and co-authors prove new global surjectivity theorems in this 2025 arXiv analysis paper. Their results build on second-order information rather than the first-derivative invertibility that the classical Hadamard-Lévy theory requires.

For a smooth map from a Hilbert space into a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, such bounds hold. Uniform upper and lower bounds on the second differential yield global path-lifting, even with singularities present. The proof uses the homotopy continuation method, which deforms a known problem into the target problem. They apply the theory to nonlinear motion planning, establishing that the continuation method stays well-posed despite critical values of the endpoint maps.
arxiv-2510-11806:
Georgios Papas opens a series on the values of G-functions in this 2025 arXiv paper. G-functions are power series introduced by Siegel in the nineteen twenties and tied to geometry by Bombieri and André. Each family of abelian varieties, higher-dimensional cousins of elliptic curves, carries such a family of functions. Their values at special points encode deep arithmetic information.

This first installment lays the theoretical foundations uniformly, covering both the ordinary archimedean setting and the non-archimedean p-adic one. Papas then studies values attached to splittings in the moduli space A-two, where an abelian surface breaks into simpler pieces. Those values matter for the Zilber-Pink conjecture, a sweeping statement about unlikely intersections in arithmetic geometry. Daw and Orr first used G-function values to win unconditional cases of that conjecture. Papas's program extends their paradigm; a companion paper applies it to elliptic curve families.
arxiv-2510-11906:
Andrea Visonà and four co-authors model how tiny magnetic discs wiggle inside living tissue. Vortex microdiscs, steered by magnetic fields, are promising tools for prodding cells. How they move inside soft, springy, and sticky living material was only partly understood. The team's 2025 arXiv paper builds a simplified two-dimensional model of the discs in a viscoelastic medium, part solid and part fluid.

Combining a Maxwell model of the medium with simple elasticity, they derive formulas and check them in computer runs. Under rotating fields the discs usually settle into swaying motion. Past a critical frequency, set by the medium's viscosity and stiffness, the motion falls out of sync. When the medium's resistance dominates the magnetic drive, the motion is strongly damped. At the few tens of hertz explored, the discs generate no heat, unlike magnetic hyperthermia treatments. The elastic energy delivered could still perturb major cellular processes.
arxiv-2510-12006:
Riku Yamamoto and eight colleagues probe the magnetism of an exotic metal where electrons behave as if enormously heavy. The compound CeRh6Ge4 is a heavy-fermion ferromagnet sitting near a quantum critical point. Their 2025 arXiv paper uses germanium-73 nuclear magnetic resonance and quadrupole resonance, listening to atomic nuclei at the material's two distinct germanium sites.

The spectra reveal the local electric field gradients and their orientations. Relaxation measurements show clear critical slowing down as the ferromagnetic transition approaches, driven mainly by fluctuating local moments on cerium. The ordered moment turns out small, about a quarter of a Bohr magneton per cerium, and confined to the crystal's basal plane. Within that plane it points every which way equally, the signature of XY-type magnetism with strong easy-plane anisotropy. A shift anomaly below about twenty-five kelvin hints at crystal-field effects mixing with Kondo screening.
arxiv-2510-12206:
Chen and co-authors tackle the controlled generation of collision scenarios for testing self driving cars, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Crashes are the most important test cases, yet they are rare on real roads and dangerous to stage. Simulations can create them, but steering a generated crash toward a chosen type and a chosen time to accident has been hard.

The team defines this controllable generation task and builds COLLIDE, a large dataset made by transforming real driving logs into varied collisions. The dataset balances five collision types across different time to accident intervals. Their framework first predicts a collision pattern, a compact description of where the ego car and the attacking car sit at impact, then rolls out full trajectories. The method beat strong baselines in collision rate and controllability, and its scenarios exposed more planner failures.
arxiv-2510-12406:
Mobini and colleagues split users between two precoding styles to respect the limited fronthaul links of a cell free wireless system, in a 2025 arXiv telecommunications paper. In cell free massive antenna systems, many access points serve users jointly, but the fronthaul links feeding them have finite capacity. Centralized precoding performs best yet loads the fronthaul, while distributed precoding is lighter but weaker.

Their hybrid strategy assigns one group of users to centralized precoding and the rest to distributed precoding. They set up an optimization problem covering user grouping and power control. It maximizes total spectral efficiency under fronthaul and per access point power limits. After transforming the problem into a tractable form, they give efficient solution algorithms. Numerical results show the hybrid scheme beat fully centralized and fully distributed approaches across diverse configurations, confirming its versatility.
arxiv-2510-13706:
Zhou, Yu, Wang, and Lu analyse the strong interaction vertices of several hadronic molecules with three-point QCD sum rules. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies bound pairs such as a D meson with a kaon, plus their bottom-quark analogs. Whether such loose two-hadron states explain certain exotic resonances hinges on their coupling strengths. Those couplings also fix how fast the states decay.

On one side of the sum rule, the authors model how currents couple to low-spin particles. On the other side, they include vacuum condensates, the background fields of the QCD vacuum, up to high order. From the matched calculation they extract strong coupling constants for each molecule. Feeding those into decay formulas gives partial widths for the candidate states. Two charm-sector widths agree with measured data for the known resonances Ds0(2317) and Ds1(2460). The bottom analogs come out far broader, near one hundred MeV.
arxiv-2510-14006:
Tanmay Khale studies how large a disc in an imaginary quadratic field can be while containing no prime elements, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Imaginary quadratic fields extend ordinary number systems with the square root of a negative number, and their rings of integers have their notion of primes. A prime-free disc is a region, measured using the field's norm, that avoids every prime.

Khale defines a function capturing the largest radius of a prime-free disc. Its center must not be too large, in a precise norm sense. He proves a lower bound for how fast this radius grows. The bound is expressed through layered logarithms of the center's size bound, with the field setting the constant. The result extends the classical question of gaps between primes into the richer geometry of quadratic number fields. The paper is dedicated to the memory of Zachary Polansky.
arxiv-2510-14906:
Liu and co-authors demonstrate, in a 2025 arXiv paper, an attack that slips malicious network traffic past machine learning detectors while learning almost nothing about them. Such detectors beat rule-based systems, but their robustness is largely unexplored. Earlier evasion attacks assumed unrealistic advantages, like knowing the model or its training data, or worked only on setups such as encrypted tunnels.

Their attack, NetMasquerade, needs only the detector's final verdict on each flow, dropped or not, the hard-label setting. A pre-trained model called Traffic-BERT learns what benign traffic looks like, using a network-specific tokenizer and attention. Reinforcement learning then reshapes attack traffic to imitate those benign patterns with minimal changes. In experiments, both brute-force and stealthy attacks evaded six detection methods across eighty scenarios, with a success rate above 96.65 percent reported overall, even against methods considered robust. The attack generates its traffic with low latency.
arxiv-2510-15006:
Tandon, Vamplew, and Foale modify, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a leading algorithm that teaches agents from the distribution of rewards, not just the average. Distributional reinforcement learning promises richer information about uncertainty, and C51 is its popular workhorse. But C51 learns its distribution with a greedy update that trusts only the best next action. When several actions promise similar average rewards with different spreads, that greed destabilizes the distribution.

Their variant, ES-C51, swaps in an Expected Sarsa update. A softmax calculation blends information from all actions at each state, weighted by their likelihood, instead of betting everything on one. The change reduces instability in the similar-reward situations and lets the agent learn higher-performing policies. The authors evaluate on classic control environments from Gym and on the Atari-10 game suite. For fairness, the comparison version of C51 also gets softmax exploration, so the difference isolates the update rule.
arxiv-2510-15106:
Issam Seddik and three colleagues propose a way to catch hidden backdoors planted inside large language models during training. Their 2025 arXiv paper starts from a simple trust problem: an outside auditor cannot easily verify that a developer followed the declared training recipe. Earlier verification schemes demanded full retraining, which is far too costly for today's giant models.

Their protocol, called Proof-of-Training-Steps, checks the training process step by step instead of after the fact. It probes how the model's language modeling head reacts to small input changes, a sensitivity that reveals tampering in data batches or settings. Even when triggers hid in up to a tenth of the training data, the checks sharply cut the attacker's success rate. Verification also ran about three times faster than a training step, allowing problems to surface early.
arxiv-2510-15206:
David Lima, J. M. Viana Parente Lopes, José Matos, and Joao Penedones test a theory of vibrating strings against a classic model from statistical physics. Their 2025 arXiv paper treats the domain wall inside the three-dimensional Ising model, the boundary between regions of opposite magnetization, as a string whose ripples follow effective string theory. The setup folds both the wall and its surrounding space into donut shapes called tori.

The authors compute the wall's free energy as a series in shrinking area, reaching the second order that depends on unknown details of the specific system. They then simulate the Ising model with flipped boundary conditions, using a two-step Monte Carlo method designed for high precision. The string theory prediction matched the simulation using only two fitted numbers, the string tension and one coefficient. Their measured value for that coefficient agreed with earlier estimates from other groups.
arxiv-2510-15306:
Kuang-Da Wang and four colleagues build a benchmark for AI systems that generate whole webpages from written instructions. Their 2025 arXiv paper, WebGen-V, notes that older benchmarks rely on full-page screenshots and long raw HTML files. That format limits both how well models learn visual design and how precisely judges can score the results.

WebGen-V instead stores each page section by section, pairing metadata, local screenshots of each interface block, and structured text and image assets in JSON form. An agentic crawling framework keeps collecting real pages, so the data can keep growing. Scoring also happens per section, aligning text, layout, and visuals at a fine grain. Experiments with leading language models, plus ablation studies, confirmed that the structured data and section-level scoring each improve results. The team presents WebGen-V as a unified pipeline from data collection to evaluation.
arxiv-2510-15706:
Judging whether a research idea is truly new takes wide knowledge of prior work. Italo Luis da Silva, Hanqi Yan, Lin Gui, and Yulan He built a tool for this in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their system, GraphMind, is an interactive web tool combining Semantic Scholar data with language models. Users capture a paper's structure, explore related ideas from several angles, and annotate connections. Novelty judgments then come with verifiable context instead of a bare model opinion.

The tool classifies papers and maps how an idea relates to existing literature. Structured views show a contribution's core and its links to earlier work. GraphMind is publicly available online, with source code released for others to extend.
arxiv-2510-15806:
Dibyendu Mondal, Debaarjun Mukherjee, and Rahul Maitra propose a method in a 2025 paper. It builds compact quantum circuits for chemistry. Today's quantum hardware is noisy. The target method is the variational quantum eigensolver. It needs a trial state called an ansatz. The ansatz must capture electron correlation well. It must also stay small enough to optimise reliably. Hand design often fails on one side or the other.

Their strategy screens candidate operator blocks first. It checks whether the blocks commute with each other. The chosen blocks are then reordered step by step. The ansatz is built dynamically this way. Starting from the dominant blocks keeps the circuit compact. Flexibility for accurate molecular energies is retained.
arxiv-2510-15906:
Yunsheng Bai leads four co-authors in automating the hunt for why a hardware property failed formal checks. Such debugging is one of the slowest steps in chip design. Engineers trace counterexamples over many cycles. They read waveforms and cross-check design specs by hand. One bug can take hours or days to find.

Their system, FVDebug, joins waveforms, design code, and specs in one analysis. A causal graph first structures the failure trace. A scanner then uses batched language model checks, with for-and-against prompts, to flag suspect nodes. A rover agent explores the graph and writes a plain causal story. A fix tool proposes concrete code repairs. On open benchmarks, the system scores high on hypothesis quality and fix rates. The team also reports results on two production-scale cases from industry.
arxiv-2510-16006: D. K. Kozyreva and V. V. Ryzhikov prove a recurrence claim about generic extensions of aperiodic maps of a probability space. Such a map preserves measure. Aperiodic means its points do not return in short cycles. An extension enlarges the system while still projecting back to the first one. Generic means the trait holds for the typical extension, not for each one. The pair show those generic extensions are recurrent. Typical enlarged systems thus return near their start states over time.
arxiv-2510-16106:
Andreas L Faisst leads a team of fifty-six co-authors studying how fast early galaxies gained heavy elements, which astronomers call metals. Their sample holds eighteen massive galaxies. They appear as they were about a billion years after the Big Bang. All come from a joint survey using the Webb space telescope. The team measures how metal content links with galaxy mass and star birth rate.

They find these young galaxies were already rich in metals. Their metal share rose from about forty to sixty percent of the Sun's level by cosmic noon. The link between mass, metals, and star birth is far messier here than in today's galaxies. That is a sign of bursty star birth and fresh gas inflows. The results match most computer models of galaxy growth and show that chemical build-up began very early.
arxiv-2510-16306:
Xin Wang and four co-authors improve virtual screening, the computational sieve drug hunters pour chemical libraries through. Screening struggles with three problems at once: active compounds are rare, a few molecular scaffolds dominate the actives, and finding structurally fresh hits matters most for new drugs.

Their framework, ScaffAug, generates synthetic training compounds with a graph diffusion model conditioned on real hit scaffolds, sampling extra data for underrepresented scaffolds to rebalance both class and structure. A self-training module then folds the synthetic data in safely, and a reranking step promotes scaffold diversity among the top recommendations. Experiments across five target classes, with ablations of each module, show gains over existing baselines in both accuracy and diversity of suggested molecules.
arxiv-2510-16906:
Iryna Dubovets'ka and Mykhailo Moklyachuk survey estimation for repeating random patterns in a 2025 paper. The patterns are periodically correlated processes, signals whose statistics repeat in cycles. The goal is estimating weighted sums of their unknown values. Observations mix the signal itself with added noise.

The survey covers two settings for the signal's spectrum. A spectrum describes how energy spreads across frequencies. Under spectral certainty, the spectrum is known exactly. Formulas then give the best linear estimate and its error. Under spectral uncertainty, only allowed sets of spectra are known. The authors present worst-case spectra and robust estimates for that case. Together the results organize a scattered literature on cyclic-signal estimation.
arxiv-2510-17006:
Masahiro Kaneko, Zeerak Talat, and Timothy Baldwin defend chatbots against persistent attackers in a 2025 paper. Iterative jailbreaks rewrite harmful prompts again and again. Each attempt learns from the model's previous replies. Existing defenses react passively and miss this trial-and-error cycle.

Their defense updates itself online as each new prompt arrives. It learns the difference between attack prompts and harmless ones. A reinforcement learning method tunes prompts toward safe behavior. Harmful requests get refused while harmless tasks proceed normally. A damping trick stops the defense overfitting to narrow attack styles. Tests covered three models, five defenses, and five attack methods. The new approach outperformed every existing defense tested. Results suggest active learning beats static filters against adaptive attackers.
arxiv-2510-17206:
Michael Hersche and three co-authors soften the mask step in diffusion language models in this 2025 paper. Such models build text by filling masked words step by step. Each step keeps the mask or swaps in a guessed word. Kept masks throw away the guess, which wastes useful hints.

Their soft-masking blends the mask with top guessed words for each kept slot. The blend gives the next step a richer hint than a bare mask. Training can add the trick to fresh or pre-trained models alike. A small fresh model beat bare-mask peers on text scores. Two large code models also gained, most where speed counts most.
arxiv-2510-17306:
Checking whether groups of agents can force a desired outcome is the problem Sofia Garcia de Blas Garcia-Alcalde and Francesco Belardinelli address. They work with ATL star, a logic for stating what coalitions of agents can achieve over time in a multi-agent system. Their paper gives two new symbolic methods for checking such statements automatically.

One method handles endless traces by reducing the check to a contest known as a parity game, and the other handles finite traces. Both are built into a tool called ATL star AS. On test problems and a security case, the symbolic methods beat step by step state checks, and the finite trace version ran much faster.
arxiv-2510-17506:
Neural network training often uses step sizes so large that the loss bounces instead of falling smoothly, a regime nicknamed the edge of stability. Lachlan Ewen MacDonald and five co-authors quantify that behaviour for the simpler case of overparametrised least squares, where many settings fit the data perfectly. In that setting, the set of perfect solutions forms a curved surface, and the training path can be split into motion along that surface and motion across it.

Motion along the surface amounts to a search for flatter solutions, while the crosswise motion forms a system that can split into two branches. MacDonald and his co-authors derive convergence rates for three step size regimes. Small steps settle after a brief unstable spell, medium steps creep toward the flattest solution by a power law, and large steps end in a two step cycle around it.
arxiv-2510-17606:
Layered oxide films can gain new electronic and magnetic behaviour when their atomic layers are stacked in a designed order. Claudio Bellani, leading a team with fifteen co-authors, grows superlattice films of chromium vanadium oxide one atomic layer at a time. By alternating single layers of chromium oxide and vanadium oxide in stacks of one, two, or three, the team controls the pattern below the scale of one unit cell.

Bellani and his co-authors confirm that fine control with X-ray diffraction, electron microscopy, and Raman spectroscopy. They also stabilise, for the first time, the ilmenite crystal phase of this compound, and compare the film properties with density functional theory calculations. The approach opens a route to new ordered oxides whose properties are set by the stacking recipe.
arxiv-2510-17806:
Vasily E. Tarasov lays out general fractional dynamics, a field for systems with memory. Such systems are nonlocal, meaning past states keep shaping present behavior. The field uses general fractional calculus, with integrals and derivatives of general form. Tarasov stresses studying the general kernels, not just special cases.

He proposes general nonlocal maps as exact solutions at discrete time points. Those maps link to equations with periodic kicks, meaning repeated sudden pushes. The kernels tie back to Sonin and Luchko kernels from fractional calculus. The paper frames a research program for nonlocal systems. It spans linear and nonlinear dynamics across many sciences.
arxiv-2510-18106:
Tomasz Kania, as sole author, asks when changing the drift of a noisy system leaves the law of its path unchanged. The systems are Ornstein-Uhlenbeck dynamics driven by Lévy noise, a setting tied to filtering, control, and simulation. Earlier answers covered only bounded drift changes, and this work extends them to a wide class of generator drifts.

The proof splits the problem into a Gaussian path and a jump path, each with its own closeness condition. Under those conditions the path laws stay equivalent. For pure jump noise a rigidity effect appears. Probability readers get sharper rules for when two noisy models are truly the same.
arxiv-2510-18206:
Hanyu Meng and four co-authors make the front end of an audio system adapt while it listens, instead of freezing after training. Learnable front ends beat fixed ones on many tasks, but their settings cannot react when the acoustic scene changes. The new design adds a neural controller in a closed loop around a simplified energy normalization stage.

The controller reads current and buffered past band energies and retunes the representation on the fly. Across several audio classification tasks it beat fixed and learnable front ends. Audio engineers get a front end that treats changing noise as a signal to adapt, not a surprise.
arxiv-2510-18306:
Hongkun Gao, with Tianjun Li and two co-authors, builds high-quality axion models in a 2025 particle physics paper. Axions are hypothetical light particles proposed to solve a puzzle in the strong nuclear force. Poor axion quality, meaning unwanted symmetry breaking, would spoil that solution.

Their models use an anomalous gauge symmetry, meaning a symmetry whose quantum effects would normally break consistency. A Green-Schwarz mechanism cancels those effects, keeping the theory sound. Unwanted symmetry-breaking terms then appear only at very high dimension, so quality stays high. Only two pairs of extra vector-like particles are needed, and one model unifies the force couplings neatly.
arxiv-2510-18706:
P. Laskos-Patkos, with S. Papadopoulos and Ch. C. Moustakidis, hunts for a universal rule linking two properties of compact stars, the dense remnants of massive stars. Researchers prize such rules because they let one property be inferred from another without knowing the exact behavior of matter inside the star. Both binding energy and the frequency of the star's non-radial wobbling might one day be measured from the same supernova event.

Assuming ordinary hadronic matter, the authors found an empirical relation connecting oscillation frequency to binding energy, holding for both the fundamental mode and the first pressure mode of the star's ringing. Adding hybrid recipes for the interior, where matter changes phase sharply, broke the pattern and caused deviations. The result adds a candidate to the family of near-universal relations and shows exactly where that family stops applying.
arxiv-2510-18806:
Annapurna Vadaparty and her seven co-authors describe and evaluate a redesigned introductory computer science course that treats large language models as a learning tool rather than a contraband. Coding-capable models now ace the classic assignments of such courses, forcing a rethink of what skills to teach and how to assess them. The new course was built at a large research university around stated design principles and revised objectives.

Measured by exams and surveys, student outcomes, including gaps between demographic groups, looked largely similar to historical results from courses without such tools. Large open-ended projects seemed especially valuable in this setting, where models help less mechanically. Students mostly found the tools helpful, though some worried about leaning on them too much. The authors present their course design and evidence as a reference point for computing educators facing the same transition.
arxiv-2510-19006:
Hamed Jelodar and three co-authors present XGen-Q. It is a language model built for software security work. General models read code well. But malware checks need more. A good tool must face hidden or new threats. It must also explain its verdicts.

XGen-Q starts from a code-focused model. It trains on more than one million malware samples. The samples come in source and assembly form. Staged prompts plus search of stored material guide its work. It aims for sound finds and full forensic reports. Analysts get results they can check, not just a label.
arxiv-2510-19106:
Ethan Abraham, Martin Z Bazant, and Troy Van Voorhis build first-principles free energy surfaces for coupled ion-electron transfer, the process behind many electrochemical reactions. The framework explains reaction rates well, but it lacked a fully microscopic description of how ion motion and electron motion couple at an electrode surface.

Extending Marcus theory, the authors condition nuclear configurations on a variable describing surface direction, then build the energy surface from constrained quantum simulations. Applied to carbon dioxide reactions on gold, the method yields a two-dimensional barrier picture and a direct route from atoms to current-voltage behavior.
arxiv-2510-19306:
Pattravadee de Favereau de Jeneret and Ioannis Diamantis test a new lens on currency data. They ask if topological data analysis adds insight. Currency moves are nonlinear and high-dimensional. Classic statistics may miss their structure. Topology studies shape, so it may catch more.

The data are monthly returns for thirteen major exchange rates. All are measured against the euro. The authors cluster with topology-based features and with classic features. Two standard algorithms do the clustering. Standard indices score the quality. The contrast shows where topology helps, and where the extra machinery earns its place.
arxiv-2510-19606:
Washington R. Carvalho and Lech Wiktor Piotrowski revisit how radio signals from cosmic-ray air showers spread across the ground. They show the strength of the radio lateral distribution depends strongly on Xmax, the atmospheric depth where the shower reaches its maximum, even after accounting for shower energy. Because Xmax tracks the mass of the incoming particle, the signal amplitude itself carries composition information.

Two competing effects explain the pattern: one tied to air density at Xmax, the other to the distance from Xmax to the ground. At steep angles, magnetic deflections further scramble the emission's coherence. The overlooked amplitude dependence could let detectors infer each cosmic ray's composition directly, without first reconstructing Xmax.
arxiv-2510-19806:
David Mora and five co-authors argue that the prompts used to make synthetic training data are an overlooked lever for multilingual language models. The usual pipeline translates English prompts. That imports English framing and style, and it neglects cultural context. Their framework instead reshapes translated prompts along three axes: naturalness, cultural adaptation, and added difficulty.

Applied across twelve languages from seven families, with the data otherwise identical, the reshaped prompts improved downstream results across the board. Scores rose on a global knowledge test and on translation quality. Human preference wins on a hard arena benchmark jumped sharply. The authors present prompt-space optimization as a cheap, general way to build models that serve many languages and cultures better.
arxiv-2510-19906:
Antoine Petitjean and six co-authors present a machine learning method for unfolding particle jets. Unfolding reverses the warps a detector imposes on collision data. The results can then be published in detector-independent form. Doing this for hundreds of quantities at once, the full inner structure of jets included, had defeated earlier learned approaches. Their framework unfolds in three stages.

The method handles jet-level kinematics and the substructure of both light-flavor jets and top jets. The authors describe it as the first generative unfolding study to reach great detail on high-dimensional jet substructure. For Large Hadron Collider physics, such unfolding turns raw detector output into results that other experiments and theorists can use directly.
arxiv-2510-20306:
Sayantika Bhowal and Arnab Bose review spin splits of non-relativistic root in magnets with no net moment. In these solids, bands split by spin with no net pull and no need for spin-orbit force. The split hides, since it shows most off the high-symmetry lines in momentum space. That is why many known solids were seen as such only in the past few years.

The review sorts solids by spin layout: in-line, in-plane, and off-plane forms. It states the symmetry rules that let the split occur. It also lists the band marks to look for and gives steps to spot new cases. New uses and open paths for the field close the work.
arxiv-2510-20406:
Xiaogang Jia and fourteen co-authors introduce PointMapPolicy, a robot learning approach that conditions diffusion policies on structured grids of three-dimensional points without downsampling. Point clouds capture detailed geometry while color images carry rich semantic context, and each modality alone misses what the other provides. Their structured point maps preserve fine detail and make shape and spatial relations easier to extract.

Because the points sit on a regular grid, established computer vision techniques apply directly to the 3D data, and the maps transform cleanly between reference frames. An xLSTM backbone fuses the point maps with image data for multimodal perception. Experiments on the RoboCasa and CALVIN benchmarks plus real robot trials show leading performance across diverse manipulation tasks.
arxiv-2510-20506:
Panagiotis Giannakopoulos and four co-authors build light round-trip time gauges to aid load choice for spread apps. Low trip lag counts at the edge and in the cloud, where apps share thin stock. Stock load plans react late and use stale or coarse marks. Their gauges train on time logs from a Kubernetes GPU group, with a small set of top tied checks.

Truth tops near 95 in 100, while gauge lag stays in a tenth of the app trip time. The team also finds the least truth a gauge needs and the host facts that count for live use. Sim tests show gauge-led load choice cuts app trip time by a lot and trims stock waste.
arxiv-2510-20606:
L Elisa Celis, Lingxiao Huang, Milind Sohoni, and Nisheeth K Vishnoi model fair selection as a game where candidates choose how much effort to spend before being judged on merit alone. Groups differ in how much they believe a win is worth, a view shaped by social context and by new AI career advice tools.

In the large group limit the team finds a single stable outcome and clear formulas linking belief gaps and strictness to effort, representation, welfare, and gain. When one group expects less reward, its members rationally try less, so gaps in belief turn into gaps in results even under merit only rules. A cost aware plan shows how tuning strictness or perceived value can narrow gaps without hurting shared goals.
arxiv-2510-20806:
Paulina Alejandra Roco-Avilez and six co-authors build a generic light profile for Seyfert one galaxies to test the unified view of active galaxy centers. That view holds that type one and type two centers are the same objects seen at different angles through a ring of gas and dust.

The sample holds nearly thirty nine hundred nearby type one systems split into four groups by narrow lines and wind signs. A profile fitting code finds one shared profile that fits ninety percent of the sample, with a clumpy dust ring seen nearly face on. Findings back the ring picture and add a cycle in which a burst of infall triggers a wind, and wind matter then rebuilds the ring over time.
arxiv-2510-21306:
Yarik Menchaca Resendiz and Roman Klinger test whether large language models can act as agents in reinforcement learning tasks, where learning happens by trial, error, and reward rather than from labeled answers. Most past tests used tasks written in words, not structured spatial problems with numbers.

Their method, PARL, puts actions, states, and rewards into a prompt and lets the model learn through interaction, with no fine-tuning at all. On three standard tasks, including a grid world where positions must be read from coordinates, the model matches or beats classic reinforcement learning agents in simple settings. It falls short where heavy arithmetic or complex decoding of states and actions is required, marking a clear limit of prompting alone.
arxiv-2510-21706:
Tobias Schmidt, Steffen Schneider, and Matthias Bethge teach a neural encoder to respect symmetry without building the symmetry in. Many data sets transform under groups, rotations, shifts, flips. Models that internalize those actions generalize better, yet standard designs hard-wire one chosen group and cannot discover the symmetry structure from raw observation pairs.

Their method, Equivariance by Contrast, learns the embedding and the group's action together from pairs of an observation and its transformed twin. In the learned space, each group element acts as an invertible linear map, with no group-specific assumptions baked into the architecture. On shape data with combined rotations and cyclic shifts, the embeddings reproduce group operations faithfully, and synthetic tests cover non-abelian groups too. A proof guarantees the structure is identifiable, the first such general encoder-only result.
arxiv-2510-22006:
Dalen Dockery and Marie Jameson work in partition theory. That branch of number theory counts the ways a whole number splits into parts. Two restricted families are in focus. In PED partitions, even parts are distinct. In POD partitions, odd parts are distinct.

Both families satisfy neat divisibility patterns for infinitely many inputs. Such patterns are called congruences. Recent work by Garvan, Sellers, Smoot, and others linked pattern families across counting schemes. Dockery and Jameson follow that line. The PED and POD congruences link naturally to families for overpartitions. Overpartitions allow a mark on the first use of each part size. Links of this kind let results for one family inform the others.
arxiv-2510-22106:
Di Wang, Xiaoyu Zhang, Guodong Li, and Wenyang Zhang fit regression models where each person's predictor is a whole matrix and the shared structure across people is only partly shared. Treating everyone as identical wastes real differences. Fitting each person alone wastes the strength that pooling provides, especially when the matrices are large and the true pattern lives in a low-dimensional corner.

Their framework writes every coefficient matrix as shared low-rank subspaces combined with personal low-rank loadings, a tensor-style factorization that keeps both levels visible. Estimation runs on scaled gradient descent, with theory bounding the error and showing faster convergence from the shared information. A thresholding extension recovers sparse hidden structure, and the guarantees cover both plain and generalized linear models. The result is a principled middle ground between pooling everyone and splitting everyone.
arxiv-2510-22406:
Anargyros Michaloliakos and three co-authors present a data driven way to find the vibration modes of a mechanical system when two modes sit very close together. Fourier methods often blur such modes or miss how they interact. Their approach uses the continuous wavelet transform, which tracks frequency over time more sharply, to isolate each mode and rebuild its motion.

From the rebuilt motions they extract phases and build a modal matrix that stays robust under noise and interference. The found parameters rebuild the system response and support a smaller reduced model. The method aims to stay accurate in a stated frequency range.
arxiv-2510-22606:
Fast electrons passing through tiny metal particles can excite confined bulk plasmons, collective electron oscillations that local models cannot reach. Mattin Urbieta, Eduardo Ogando, Alberto Rivacoba, Javier Aizpurua, and Nerea Zabala study that excitation in 2025 for spherical particles smaller than five nanometers.

Using a linear hydrodynamic model with nonlocal effects, they derive a formula for electron energy loss probability. Several new peaks appear above the plasma frequency, and the peak pattern shifts blue as particles shrink. Excitation depends strongly on beam path, energy, and particle size, with a threshold path length for some modes. Selection rules explain which modes appear.
arxiv-2510-22706:
Humans read a scene's geometry and its objects together, while most computer systems treat them apart. Hao Li, with ten co-authors, proposes IGGT in 2025, a unified transformer that reconstructs three dimensional scenes while also grounding individual object instances in them.

A contrastive learning strategy, which pulls matching views together, teaches one representation holding both structure and instance grouping. Training uses only two dimensional visual inputs, yet the model lifts them into a coherent three dimensional scene with distinct objects. Earlier systems either rebuilt geometry alone or borrowed a fixed language model's limits. IGGT aims for better generalization across downstream three dimensional understanding tasks.
arxiv-2510-22906:
Pedro Bairrao wrote a dissertation that teaches string theory by walking toward one of its best known ideas, the AdS/CFT link. That link says a gravity theory in a curved space can match a gauge theory on its edge. He starts with the large N expansion of Yang-Mills theory, which first hinted that gauge theories might need a string language.

The thesis covers the bosonic string, D-branes, and duality checks from brane interactions. It then moves to type II superstrings and their match with ten-dimensional supergravity. Students get a careful, step-by-step path from basic strings to a deep claim about space and fields.
arxiv-2510-23006:
Shenran Wang, Timothy Tin-Long Tse, and Jian Zhu compare how different model designs learn from examples placed in the prompt. In-context learning lets a model do a new task from a few shown cases. Transformers are the usual design, but state-space and hybrid models are now strong rivals.

Across knowledge-based tasks, models with different internals scored alike yet worked differently inside. The team found function vectors, the carriers of the prompted task, mainly in attention and Mamba layers. They suggest Mamba2 may use a distinct route. The study warns that equal scores can hide unlike mechanisms.
arxiv-2510-23406:
Hengxing Pan leads a team of nine astronomers measuring how neutral hydrogen gas mass relates to stellar mass in massive galaxies seen when the universe was younger. That relation shows how galaxies turn their gas reservoir into stars. Using MIGHTEE-HI spectral data, they study a stellar-mass selected sample between redshifts of about zero point two five and zero point five.

With a Bayesian stacking technique, they measure for the first time the full joint distribution of hydrogen and stellar mass for galaxies above a high mass threshold. The distribution shape reveals how unevenly gas is spread among similar galaxies.
arxiv-2510-23606:
Yichi Zhang, Alex Schwing, and Zhizhen Zhao improve masked diffusion models, a flexible family of generators for discrete data such as text. These models reveal tokens step by step, but tokens predicted in the same step are treated as independent. When the data has strong links between tokens, that shortcut hurts the quality of what gets generated.

Their fix, Variational Masked Diffusion, adds latent variables to the process so the model can represent links among tokens revealed together. On synthetic datasets, the new model learned links that the standard one missed entirely. Tests on Sudoku puzzles and text data told the same story: global consistency and generation quality both improved. The results argue that bringing variational inference into masked diffusion is a practical way to make discrete generators aware of token links.
arxiv-2510-23906:
Wasim Ahmad and two co-authors introduce gCDMI, a causal discovery method that works on groups of variables rather than single pairs. Most causal tools test one variable against another, yet real systems — brain networks, climate subsystems — act in interacting groups whose collective influence is the real story. Finding those group-level links in nonlinear time series is the target here.

The method has three steps. First, a deep network learns the joint structure among all variable groups. Second, the trained network is intervened on, group by group, mimicking an experiment. Third, invariance testing checks which causal links survive those interventions. On simulated data the method beat existing approaches at recovering group-level structure. It was then validated on real brain network and climate ecosystem data. The authors argue that intervening on trained networks, paired with invariance tests, is a practical route to complex causal maps.
arxiv-2510-24006:
Ming-Hui Yu and a co-author apply the island paradigm to the information paradox in Kerr-Newman black holes — the rotating, charged case, the most general stationary black hole. Near the horizon, the four-dimensional quantum field reduces to a two-dimensional theory, so the standard formula for entanglement entropy carries over. With that machinery, the entropy of escaping radiation behaves as unitarity demands once entanglement islands appear.

The authors then vary spin and charge. Page time and scrambling time both grow with angular momentum and shrink with charge. For near-extremal holes, the Kerr/CFT correspondence replaces the geometry with a warped anti-de Sitter throat governed by a Schwarzian mode. One-loop corrections follow, and the recalculated times come out delayed — information leaks more slowly under strong quantum fluctuations. The authors read this as further support for information conservation, extending the island picture to the hardest background.
arxiv-2510-24106:
Junhong Zou and six co-authors propose UniField, a neural model for surface pressure on objects across several fields at once. Pressure on a surface is central to designing cars, trains, and aircraft, but full fluid simulations are slow and costly. Neural models are faster, yet they often lack data and fail outside the field they were trained on.

UniField trains jointly on data from cars, trains, and aircraft. A shared encoder reads the shape from surface points, while a special layer adds flow details for each domain. By pooling datasets across fields, the model learns broader patterns. The authors report better generalization than models trained on a single domain alone.
arxiv-2510-24206:
Rob van Glabbeek shows that a guarded set of self referring rules has just one solution, working alone. Process algebras are math tools that describe systems step by step. In these tools, a process can refer to itself. A rule is guarded when each self call sits behind an action. That guard keeps the rules well behaved and stops loose ends.

He proves there is one solution up to a strong match of behavior. The proof holds for any such tool whose rules fit a known format. The same holds for weaker matches and for their order forms. So these match tests stay sound when guarded self calls are added. The result also gives a full, sound set of laws for the strong match in finite cases.
arxiv-2510-24506:
Tamanna Chatterjee writes alone on graded Lie algebras and sheaves. A Lie algebra is a space where a bracket rule mimics rotation twists. Grading splits the algebra into layers indexed by whole numbers. The work sits in positive characteristic, where arithmetic wraps around a prime. Chatterjee builds a theory of primitive pairs for this graded world.

Primitive pairs play the role that cuspidal pairs play in Springer theory. She fixes a symmetry subgroup and watches it act on each layer. Parity sheaves are geometric objects stacked over the algebra's points. She shows each such sheaf comes from primitive data on a subgroup. Primitivity survives the Fourier-Sato transform, a key duality tool. The results ground a graded form of the Springer correspondence.
arxiv-2510-24606:
Siheng Xiong, Joe Zou, Faramarz Fekri, and Yae Jee Cho tackle slow, costly long reads for large language models. When a model reads a very long text, its focus step grows fast and eats memory. Their fix, called DHSA, picks which parts of the text to focus on as it goes.

DHSA first ranks big chunks, then passes that rank down to single words. Tests on long search and quiz sets kept scores close to full focus while using far less of it. On one small chip setup it ran a text of 100,000 words where the full method failed.
arxiv-2510-24906:
Mikolaj Czarnecki, Michal Korniak, Oskar Skibski, and Piotr Skowron split a pool of whole, uncut goods in a fair way among players in a group game. The pool size is a whole count: seats in a house, swap slots for organs, or top traits in a model call. A fair split of such goods can not just cut a share in half.

The team names a whole good form of the known Shapley worth, a classic fair share rule. They study its traits and show it in three case works. In one case, it picks the key zones of a shot that drive a class call. The rule gives a fair way to hand out what can not be split.
arxiv-2510-25006:
Christopher R Schwarze, Anthony D Manni, David S Simon, and Alexander V Sergienko do small math tasks with weak shifts in the phase of plain light. In their rig, glass paths are set in a tweaked line form. A task is done not in a fixed state, but by a move from one state to the next.

That move taps the odd phase map of the rig, so plain linear glass can yield bent math such as splits and powers. In and out are both phase shifts off a set base point, and the out shift is read as a shift in light power. The math is near, not exact, and gets more true as the in shifts shrink. Small inputs buy more true outs.
arxiv-2510-25506:
Florian Angermeir led eight co-authors on reproducibility of language models. Maximilian Amougou, Mark Kreitz, and Andreas Bauer helped. Matthias Linhuber, Davide Fucci, and Fabiola Moyon C joined. Daniel Mendez and Tony Gorschek complete the team. Their 2025 paper studies empirical software engineering studies. Commercial language model results may not reproduce reliably.

Many publications now perform tests with language models. Reproducible results remain challenging for scholars and practitioners. They studied reproducibility across eighty-five articles total. Those articles appeared at ICSE and ASE in 2024. Eighteen supplied artifacts and used OpenAI models. The team attempted replication of those eighteen studies. Only five were sufficiently complete and executable. None of the five reproduced fully in results. Two studies seemed partially reproducible on inspection. Three studies did not seem reproducible at all. Stricter artifact testing is needed, they argue. More robust study designs would ensure publication value.
arxiv-2510-25706:
Andres N Salcedo led nine co-authors constraining cosmology with clusters. Eduardo Rozo, Hao-Yi Wu, and David H Weinberg helped. Pranav Chiploonkar, Chun-Hao To, and Shulei Cao joined. Eli S Rykoff, Nicole Marcelina Gountanis, and Conghao Zhou joined. Their 2025 paper forward-models Dark Energy Survey clusters. Run-based inference extracts cosmology from optical samples.

Abundance and weak-lensing signals of redMaPPer clusters are used. The model embeds cosmology-dependent optical choice realistically. Counts-in-cylinders method handles that choice effect. Cluster miscentering and baryonic feedback are accounted for. Lensing signals include those systematic corrections too. Assuming flat Lambda CDM cosmology, settings are obtained. Matter density and form amplitude are constrained tightly. Results agree with low-redshift form readings. Planck results differ at about two point six sigma. Run-based forward modeling proves promising for precision cosmology. Stage IV survey data will benefit from approach.
arxiv-2510-25806:
Mustafa F. Abdelwahed, Ahmed Shafee, and Joan Espasa describe a system that automates part of cyber threat hunting. Threat hunting means forming a guess about an attack and then searching a network for signs that the guess is right. Doing that by hand is slow, and the guesses can carry the bias of the analyst who made them.

Their system, APThreatHunter, uses automated planning to form hunting goals with little human input. It weighs risks from the current state of a system and checks indicators that show whether a risk is actually present. Tests with real Android malware samples showed that planning can support practical, goal based hunting.
arxiv-2510-25906:
Yiren Tong and Panagiotis Tsoutsanis present a faster way to simulate compressible flow, such as air over a wing with shock waves, on irregular grids. High order methods are accurate in smooth regions but costly and unstable near sharp jumps. Their hybrid framework switches method by region, using cheap linear reconstruction where flow is smooth and stronger non oscillatory methods only where needed.

A new detector sorts each cell in one pass as smooth, mildly rough, or discontinuous. Smooth zones keep high order accuracy, rough zones use a weighted method, and jumps fall back to a safe second order scheme. Tests in two and three dimensions, run in an open source solver, confirm the design accuracy and better stability near shocks at lower cost.
arxiv-2510-26006:
Rishika Bhagwatkar, Syrielle Montariol, Angelika Romanou, Beatriz Borges, Irina Rish, and Antoine Bosselut introduce a benchmark for spotting and explaining odd things in real images. People easily notice, reason about, and explain anomalies in a scene. Computer vision work has mostly used factory defects or synthetic fakes, which miss the range and surprise of real world anomalies.

Their benchmark, CAVE, supports three open ended tasks: describing an anomaly, explaining it, and justifying why it counts as one. Detailed annotations mark where the anomaly sits and rate its complexity, severity, and commonness, drawing on cognitive science. Top vision language models still struggle with both perception and commonsense reasoning on the tasks, even with advanced prompting.
arxiv-2510-26306:
Sophie Rosu, Luca Sciarini, Sylvia Ekstrom, and Raphael Hirschi use the slow drift of an eccentric binary orbit to probe the insides of massive stars. In a close eccentric pair, tidal interactions make the orbit orientation rotate, a motion called apsidal motion, at a rate set by a constant that reflects the star inner density profile. Standard models predict too high a value, the famous discrepancy: real stars are more centrally concentrated than models suggest.

Rosu and the team build bespoke rotating binary models with the GENEC evolution code, including tidal mixing, for the twin massive binary HD 152248. Advective diffusive mixing models match the observed constant better than magnetic ones. Large core overshooting is necessary but not sufficient, and a larger initial helium share also helps.
arxiv-2510-26606:
Kentaro Ozeki, with five co-authors, benchmarks how well large language models reason about duties and permissions. Normative reasoning deals with what ought to be done, using modals such as must and may. These models do well on many reasoning tasks, but this corner has been little tested.

Ozeki and the team build a data set of formal reasoning patterns in both the normative domain and the epistemic domain, which deals with knowledge and shares the same formal shape. Human-style cognitive factors are mixed in. Models mostly followed valid patterns, yet they slipped on specific kinds of normative steps. They also showed biases much like those seen in human reasoning studies. All data and code are public, and the authors aim the findings at making model reasoning more reliable.
arxiv-2510-26806:
Apoorva Mathur, with four co-authors, studies how molecular glues hold proteins together, water included. Molecular glues stabilise weak, fleeting protein-protein contacts, which opens drug targets once thought undruggable. Two known glues, rapamycin and WDB002, both bind the protein FKBP12 and pair it with different partners.

Mathur and the team run molecular dynamics simulations to watch what the glues change. The glues shifted how flexible each protein is, stiffening some regions. They also changed the pattern and stability of hydrogen bonds that are mediated by water molecules sitting between the proteins. The authors argue that these water-mediated bonds deserve a central place in the rational design of new glues, not an afterthought.
arxiv-2510-26906:
Kieran Loehr and Bryan K Clark improve a neural method for describing strongly correlated quantum matter. Neural Network Backflow enhances a mean-field wavefunction by letting a network adjust single-particle orbitals for each configuration. In theory it is universal for large networks, but the pair find practical gains saturate as networks grow.

Loehr and Clark instead expand the ansatz to several determinants, generated without adding variational parameters. They test a single Lanczos step and symmetry projection, benchmarked against diffusion Monte Carlo on a doped square Hubbard model near optimal doping. A Lanczos step, diffusion Monte Carlo, and symmetry projection gave similar gains at minimal cost. Optimising the projected states directly gave significantly lower energies, which they report as the lowest variational energies for that Hamiltonian on two lattice sizes.
arxiv-2510-27106:
Rajarshi Haldar and Julia Hockenmaier test whether language models give consistent grades when used as judges. Model-as-judge scoring has grown popular for rating generated text because it tracks human preference better than word-overlap metrics. The catch is reliability: the same judge may score the same answer differently across runs.

Across several generation tasks and benchmarks, the pair find low intra-rater reliability, meaning a judge often disagrees with itself. In the worst cases the ratings look almost arbitrary, which clouds any claim about how good the judgments are. The study quantifies the inconsistency and asks whether careful guidelines can still make such judges useful. For evaluation teams, it is a warning to measure judge stability before trusting judge scores.
arxiv-2510-27406:
A. S. Barabash, L. Bergé, and thirty-seven other co-authors describe a shield for a rare-event hunt in this 2025 paper. The hunt, called CROSS, sits in the Canfranc laboratory deep under Spain. It seeks neutrinoless double-beta decay, a decay that would rewrite what we know about neutrinos, ghostly light particles. The detectors are cold crystals that read heat and light together.

Cosmic muons, fast particles from space, still reach the hall and fake the signal. The shield, a muon veto, wraps the setup in panels on the sides, top, and bottom. When a muon crosses, the panels flag it so the event can be cut. Simulations matched the panel rates seen in real runs. Two trigger rules, with cuts on the heat detectors, would reject over ninety-nine percent of muon fakes.
arxiv-2510-27506:
Ke He, Thang X. Vu, and four other co-authors route data packets through a crowded satellite sky in this 2025 paper. Low Earth orbit constellations now hold thousands of fast-moving satellites. Links form and break as the fleet wheels overhead, and delays run long. Each satellite must choose paths alone, on its own clock, while guarding against bad tail outcomes.

Their framework, PRIMAL, lets each satellite act on local events rather than a shared tick. Agents learn the full spread of costs for quality goals like delay and load. A primal-dual method then keeps worst-case slips in check. In a simulated fleet of 1584 satellites, PRIMAL cut queuing delay by over seventy percent versus a recent risk-blind rival. End-to-end delay fell by nearly twelve milliseconds under load.
arxiv-2510-27606:
Yuhong Liu and eight co-authors present Spatial-SSRL in 2025, a way to teach vision-language models about space without costly labels. Such models join sight and text, yet they often judge position and depth poorly. Past training leans on hand labels, special tools, or narrow settings that limit scale.

Five auto-built tasks draw clear, checkable answers from plain color or depth photos. They ask a model to reorder shuffled patches, spot flipped patches, fill a cut patch, rank depth by region, and judge 3D position. Training on these tasks lifts scores on seven space tests for two model sizes. General sight skill stays intact, which shows self-guided drills can teach space sense.
arxiv-2511-00706:
Marcos Vinicius Cruz, Pragya Verma, and Grischa Liebel give voice to dyslexic software engineers, a group never studied in its own right. Dyslexia mainly impairs reading and writing, core acts in programming, yet early hints suggested dyslexic engineers perform on par with colleagues and may bring strengths in design.
