Conflict between student practice and instructor norms varied sharply by task. Generating writing and solving quiz problems clashed clearly with norms, while revising text and checking quiz answers drew broad agreement. Project work fell in between. The authors note that instructors are shifting from bans toward recording model use as part of grading. They close with design guidelines for campus AI tools, such as guardrails that keep students engaged and comprehension checks that turn low-conflict uses into chances to learn.
arxiv-2602-06106:
Whether people wipe down shared gym gear or shared work tools is a cooperation puzzle, studied by Alexander Feigel and Alexandre V Morozov. Each user can clean before or after use, pay a cost, and lower the risk for the next person. Some users free-ride on the cleaning of others.

The pair built an evolution-style model tuned with real-world values. Cleaning spread when its cost fell, when social rewards for cleaning rose, and when rule-breaking was watched. Surprisingly, raising infection costs through punishment mattered less for keeping a fully cooperative group stable. The model shows sudden flips between clean and dirty norms, matching patterns seen in shared facilities.
arxiv-2602-06306:
Special curved spaces called Fano manifolds admit highly symmetric metrics, and Satoshi Nakamura studies a weighted version of the constant scalar curvature condition on them. The weighted metrics, introduced by Lahdili, depend on two weight functions. Nakamura builds a third weight from the pair and links the two kinds of special metric.

Under positivity and curvature conditions on the weights, he proves that a weighted constant scalar curvature metric exists exactly when a matching soliton metric exists. He also explains how the soliton arises naturally from Sasaki geometry, through a circle bundle over the manifold. There, the soliton on the base gives rise to a transverse Mabuchi soliton tied to the bundle's Reeb field.
arxiv-2602-06806:
Silpa Vadakkeeveetil Sreelatha, Dan Wang, Serge Belongie, Muhammad Awais, and Anjan Dutta introduce RAIGen, a tool for finding rare traits that text-to-image models seldom show. Earlier bias work either fixed fairness groups in advance or looked for traits that dominate outputs. Both miss minority traits that are still stored in the model but rarely drawn. RAIGen needs no preset minority groups.

It uses a sparse autoencoder with a nested shape and a new score that mixes how rarely a neuron fires with how distinct in meaning it is. Neurons flagged this way reveal seldom-shown traits in their most strongly firing images. The tool found traits beyond standard fairness groups in Stable Diffusion, scaled to a larger model, and enabled boosting of rare traits during generation, supporting checks across model types.
arxiv-2602-07006:
Alokesh Manna, Neil Spencer, and Dipak K. Dey develop a statistical model for forensic footwear evidence. Shoe prints from crime scenes can identify a shoe's make and model, but thousands of identical shoes exist, so investigators look for accidentals, the cuts and scrapes a sole accumulates through wear. Some accidental patterns are common, others highly distinctive, and quantifying a pattern's rarity measures the strength of the evidence.

The authors build a hierarchical Bayesian model framed as a latent Gaussian model, which scales efficiently to large collections of annotated prints through integrated nested Laplace approximations. Spatially varying coefficients capture how tread patterns relate to where accidentals appear. On held-out data the model beat existing methods, improving accuracy and reliability in forensic shoe print analysis and giving courts a better-grounded measure of how distinctive a print really is.
arxiv-2602-07306:
Serving large language models across many GPUs is throttled by synchronization: tensor parallelism splits matrices but forces devices to coordinate constantly.  Chong Wang and ten co-authors restructure the computation with the Parallel Track Transformer, which minimizes cross-device dependencies.

The design cuts synchronization operations up to sixteenfold against standard tensor parallelism while keeping model quality competitive. Integration into TensorRT-LLM and vLLM brings faster first tokens and faster per-token times.  Inference builders get an architectural change rather than another tuning trick, aimed at the communication bottleneck that limits multi-GPU scaling.  The gains hold across both serving stacks tested, suggesting the restructuring generalizes rather than tuning one system.
arxiv-2602-07606:
A classic theorem says large twin-free graphs must contain a large matching, co-matching, or half-graph as a semi-induced subgraph. Those three patterns define eight graph classes by which indices stay bounded.  Jan Dreier and two co-authors completely classify the parameterized complexity of Independent Set, Clique, and Dominating Set across all eight classes.

Drawing tractability and hardness results from the literature and filling the remaining gaps, they show Independent Set is fixed-parameter tractable whenever the half-graph and co-matching indices are bounded. They also construct classes that separate other cases.  Parameterized complexity teams get a finished map for three canonical problems across a natural family of graph classes.
arxiv-2602-07706:
Medical AI models often squeeze patient data into a few narrow patterns, which hurts reuse on new tasks. Yuanyun Zhang and six co-authors propose dense feature learning, a training approach that shapes the geometry of medical embeddings directly instead of chasing one prediction target.

The method rewards balanced, well-spread, and mutually distinct features using only linear-algebra rules, with no labels and no attempt to rebuild the input. Tests on hospital records over time, clinical text, and combined patient data show steadier features and better results on later tasks. The paper suits readers building reusable representations for health data rather than one-off predictors.
arxiv-2602-08406:
Designing solar absorbers from MXene metasurfaces means predicting light spectra that are expensive to compute with full-wave solvers. Shujaat Khan and two co-authors offer a deep-learning shortcut that predicts 102-point absorption spectra from small metasurface patterns. Their arXiv paper combines transfer learning with multi-channel refinement and smoothing.

A pretrained MobileNetV2 backbone is fine-tuned for the task, while parallel convolutional channels sharpen features and Savitzky-Golay smoothing trims high-frequency noise. The model beats standard and deformable convolutional baselines, reaching an average error of 0.0227 and an R-squared of 0.9563. Readers get a fast, accurate tool for nanophotonic design iteration.
arxiv-2602-08806:
Kelvin-Helmholtz instability ripples the edges between flowing plasmas in space, from solar-wind interfaces to jets and disks. Shishir Biswas and four co-authors analyze its rare-gas version, where uneven pressures arise and the Chew-Goldberger-Low rules replace MHD. Their arXiv paper mixes math and sims.

Growth rates and magnet effects peak in the MHD limit. In the large slow-down rare-gas limit, energy sent into tilt leaves less for bending field lines, so currents, magnetic islands, and gusts all weaken. Readers get a side-by-side look across regimes, with lessons for churn and merging in the heliosheath.
arxiv-2602-09106:
William B. Johnson and one co-author introduce a quantitative version of Steinhaus' property (S) for Banach spaces, called uniform property (S). A space has the property when, for any two distinct unit vectors and any perturbation size, the largest gap in perturbed norms stays above a positive function. That function depends on perturbation size and vector separation. The modulus is computed exactly for atomless L-one spaces.

The class proves stable under ultrapowers and Bochner L-one constructions, and includes all Gurariĭ spaces and Banach lattices of almost universal disposition. Each Banach space fits isometrically inside a non-strictly convex space of the same density with uniform property (S). An explicit renorming of l-one spaces is given, settling several open questions in ZFC about property (S) geometry.
arxiv-2602-09306:
Shared step-by-step suggesting keeps user data on devices, but split, noisy, same-like local logs cap model quality. Thi Minh Chau Nguyen and five co-authors bring LUMOS, a setting-split build that uses an on-device language model as a local meaning maker, instead of sharing slopes or helper settings. From each user past, the model builds three matching forms: future-leaning runs, meaning-same rewordings, and taste-clashing what-ifs as telling negatives.

Those built runs enter a three-view rival tuning inside the shared spine, deepening picture learning without baring private facts. Across three public tests, LUMOS always beats rival hub-run and shared baselines on hit-rate and ranking quality at cutoff 20. The design shows how local making can cure shared data thinness privately.
arxiv-2602-09606:
Automated traffic now exceeds human traffic on the web, and a growing share is explicitly malicious, with evasive bots faking users, solving captchas, and mimicking human patterns. Ghalia Jarad and Kemal Bicakci explore a gentler protocol-level defense in their 2026 paper: telling bots from users by TLS fingerprints using the JA4 technique, which encodes handshake parameters.

Two gradient-boosted classifiers were trained and tested on a dataset of real JA4 fingerprints after feature extraction. The CatBoost model performed best, with near-perfect discrimination, F1, and accuracy scores, while XGBoost ran nearly as well. Feature analysis flagged specific JA4 components, including handshake bytes and counts of ciphers and extensions, as most influential. Future work aims at newer protocols and added device features to resist advanced evasion.
arxiv-2602-09906:
Some equations change character as their solutions change, turning singular in one range and degenerate in another. A 2026 paper led by Simone Ciani, with four co-authors, studies nonnegative solutions to doubly nonlinear equations in exactly that mixed regime. The goal is local Hölder continuity, a precise way of saying solutions cannot jump or spike wildly on small scales.

The authors introduce a new technique that handles both the singular and degenerate cases up to certain Barenblatt numbers. Their proof rests on a new integral Harnack estimate linking two averaged norms, a result they note stands on its own. The work gives analysts a single route through a regime that previously had to be split apart.
arxiv-2602-10306:
A 2026 paper by S. S. Podkorytov, sole author, describes how homotopy similarity relations and finite-order invariants behave under composition. The setting is the function from maps of X into Y to maps of X into Z, induced by a map from Y to Z. That inducing map is strongly r-similar to the constant map.

The paper traces both structures through the induced function, recording how composition with a nearly constant map reshapes similarity relations and finite-order invariants alike. The composition viewpoint unifies the two behaviors in one setting, giving a compact account of maps, invariants, and induced functions under homotopy similarity.
arxiv-2602-10506:
Wei Chen and nine co-authors model graph domain adaptation as a steady process in a 2026 paper. Recent methods chop adaptation into discrete steps, building intermediate graphs or aligning in stages. Real graph structures, however, evolve continuously and nonlinearly, so fixed-step approximations miss the actual transformation.

Their method, DiffGDA, treats the journey from source to target graphs as a spread process governed by random differential rules. Structure and semantics evolve jointly along steady paths rather than jumping between checkpoints. The paper argues this steady framing captures the true motion of domain shift better than stepwise alignment. It reports stronger transfer results for graph tasks where the shift itself is gradual and intertwined.
arxiv-2602-11206:
Spiking networks promise energy-fast, brain-like computing, but spikes do not differentiate. Jose Marie Antonio Miñoza, writing alone, offers UltraLIF, a frame that replaces surrogate gradients with ultradiscretization from tropical shape. A soft maximum converges to hard thresholding as a learnable heat falls.

Two neuron models follow: UltraLIF from leaky integrate-and-fire motion, and UltraDLIF from diffusion building gap-junction coupling. Both train by standard backpropagation with no forward-backward mismatch, and theory gives convergence to classic motion with bounded, non-vanishing gradients. Tests on six benchmarks beat surrogate-gradient rivals, most clearly in single-timestep settings on neuromorphic and time data.
arxiv-2602-11906:
Proving that one logical theory conservatively extends another often hinges on largeness notions that measure how much combinatorial structure a set contains. Quentin Le Houérou and one co-author introduce a variant of parameterized largeness and obtain polynomial bounds, using a tree partition theorem based on Milliken tree theorem. Through forcing interpretation, any proof of a universal statement in the stronger theory can be translated into a proof in the weaker theory. The cost is only a polynomial increase in size.

The result concerns Ramsey theory for pairs and weak König lemma, theories whose relationship has been studied through conservation results. The polynomial size bound turns a qualitative conservation claim into a quantitative one: translations exist and they do not blow up proofs uncontrollably. For reverse mathematics, that precision matters, since the cost of moving between theories is itself informative.
arxiv-2602-12006:
Optimal control of mean-field random systems needs a maximum principle, and Peng's version for McKean-Vlasov equations lacked a clean proof. Johan Benedikt Spille and one co-author present a novel approach whose main step adds a third adjoint equation, a conditional McKean-Vlasov backward stochastic differential equation. That equation handles the pairing of squared terms containing two independent copies of the first-order variational process.

The construction extends Peng's principle from standard random equations in full, giving a proof the authors describe as conceptually consistent. Beyond its own clarity, the approach should prove useful for extensions to common-noise cases and endless cases, where mean-field control theory continues to expand.
arxiv-2602-12206:
Citation graphs map how research links together, but the OpenAIRE graph is huge: over 200 million works and over 2 billion citations, about 2.5 terabytes uncompressed. Joakim Skarding led this work with one co-author, Pavel Sanda, shrinking that graph so ordinary computers can use it. The processed version fits in 16 gigabytes of memory while keeping the full link structure.

The data also come in a simple format for easy handling, plus a Python pipeline to process future OpenAIRE releases. A larger version adds more fields, such as titles and author lists. For researchers without cluster access, the work turns a daunting dump into a usable map of scholarly citation.
arxiv-2602-12406:
Selecting many objects at once in extended reality starts with two steps: switching into multi-selection mode, then picking each intended object. Mohammad Raihanul Bashar led this work with three co-authors, testing how eyes, hands, and voice serve each step. Four mode-switching methods were compared, from pinch variants to voice, and three subselection methods, all combining gaze with dwell, pinch, or voice.

DoublePinch paired with Gaze plus Pinch performed best overall, while SemiPinch performed worst. Voice mode-switching helped, but Gaze plus Voice subselection was less favoured, since repeated vocal commands felt tedious. The findings give empirical guidance for designing multi-selection in XR, where speed must be balanced against fatigue and the feel of repeated commands.
arxiv-2602-12506:
Reinforcement learning fine-tuning has boosted vision-language models on reasoning tests, yet those models still suffer weak visual grounding, hallucinations, and over-reliance on text cues. Rosie Zhao led this work with seven co-authors. They show that simple, set textual changes, such as misleading captions or wrong chain-of-thought traces, cause large drops in robustness and confidence.

Effects grow stronger when chain-of-thought consistency is counted, across open-source multimodal reasoning models. Closed models show similar failure modes but keep markedly greater robustness and reasoning consistency. That gap suggests open-source fine-tuning practice, not an inherent task limit, is at fault. Analysis reveals an accuracy-faithfulness trade-off. Fine-tuning raises benchmark accuracy while eroding the reliability of accompanying reasoning. Adversarial augmentation helps robustness but does not alone prevent faithfulness drift. Faithfulness-aware rewards can restore alignment, though pairing them with augmentation risks shortcut strategies.
arxiv-2602-12606:
Relational deep learning learns directly on relational stores, modelling items and links across linked tables. Justin Gu led this work with ten co-authors, giving RelBench v2, a major growth of the RelBench benchmark. Four large relational data sets are added, spanning scholarly publications, business resource planning, buyer sites, and medical files. That grows the benchmark to 11 data sets with over 22 million rows across 29 tables.

New auto-complete jobs require models to guess missing field values within tables while following time limits, growing beyond forecast jobs built from SQL queries. External tests are also added, including Temporal Graph test event streams, ReDeLEx access to over 70 real-world stores, and 4DBInfer data sets and jobs. Tests show relational models steadily beating single rivals on auto-complete, forecast, and suggestion, showing the value of modelling relational structure directly.
arxiv-2602-12806:
Text fed to language models is usually scrubbed of names and other identifiers, but scrubbing specific items does not guarantee that a person cannot be re-identified. Nataša Krčo and three co-authors introduce RAT-Bench, a benchmark that judges anonymisation tools by re-identification risk rather than by item removal alone. Using United States demographic statistics, they generate synthetic texts carrying varied direct and indirect identifiers, spanning several domains, tongues, and difficulty levels.

An attacker model then tries to infer attributes from the scrubbed text, and the risk is reported for the United States population, accounting for how identifiers differ in power. Even the best tools fall far short of perfect, especially with non-standard direct identifiers and indirect clues. Language-model-based anonymisers trade better privacy for higher compute, and work well across languages, pointing to concrete design lessons.
arxiv-2602-12906:
Rings and gaps in protoplanetary discs are thought to trace dust traps and forming planets, but many extended discs had never been resolved sharply enough to check. Quincy Bosschaart and three co-authors present high-resolution ALMA observations of 26 previously unresolved extended discs within 200 parsecs, completing the sharp sample for nearby star-forming regions. Seventeen discs show clear substructures, while nine look smooth, compact, or ambiguous.

Combined with literature data across 730 discs, the team finds nearly all extended discs carry substructures: about 91% overall, rising to about 98% after correcting for highly inclined systems where structures hide. Substructures appear more often in larger, massive discs around higher-mass stars, and structured discs hold onto their dust over time. The result supports dust traps, possibly carved by giant planets, as a near-universal disc feature.
arxiv-2602-13006:
Quantum thermal averages are hard to compute straight, but an strong standard likely can mimic them as an ordinary ensemble average. Vijay Ganesh Sadhasivam and two co-authors build such a likely next Feynman and Hibbs, with a twist: quantum fluctuations are treated around where the path starts rather than around its centre. Instead of fully tuning the likely variationally, they explore approximate functional forms chosen for number toughness.

The closed-form likely that results is exact in both the standard and harmonic limits. Tests against exact position distributions for quartic, Morse, and double-well potentials in one dimension show good agreement where harmonic support holds. For practitioners, the method offers a practical shortcut: quantum thermal expectations from standard-style sampling, without the full machinery of path-integral mock run.
arxiv-2602-13206:
Large AI models collaborating at the mobile edge promise better services under tight resources, but model complexity clashes with limited compute, memory, and communication. Peichun Li and four co-authors survey joint AI in mobile edge networks, covering system design and uses in transportation and healthcare. They organise recent resource-lean techniques into spatial and time groups.

Spatial techniques cover mixture of experts, federated tuning, hierarchical diffusion, and patch-based diffusion. Time techniques cover routing fitting, split learning, speculative decoding, and cascading fitting. Building on that survey, the authors propose a multi-stage diffusion system that elastically distributes large making models across mixed edge resources. Tests show gains in leanness and adaptability for making data, supporting joint AI as a practical edge paradigm.
arxiv-2602-13806:
Rebuilding dynamic scenes from casual videos matters for scalable robot learning, yet four-dimensional rebuilding from a single camera remains highly ill-posed. The key insight is that real-world motion shows multi-scale order from object level down to particle level. A multi-scale dynamics mechanism splits complex motion fields, and Gaussian sequences with multi-scale dynamics represent dynamic 3D Gaussians through layers of multi-level motion.

That layered structure greatly reduces ambiguity and promotes physically plausible dynamics. Multi-modal priors from vision foundation models add complementary guidance, limiting the solution space and improving rebuilding fidelity. The approach enables accurate, globally consistent 4D rebuilding from monocular casual videos, with large improvements on dynamic novel-view synthesis benchmarks and real-world manipulation data. Can Li leads the work with four co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14206:
Mona Azadkia and one co-author study a 2026 arXiv estimator for Chatterjee's dependence coefficient. The coefficient runs from 0 to 1, hits 0 exactly under independence, and hits 1 when Y is a measurable function of X. It matches an earlier coefficient of Dette, Siburg, and Stoimenov for continuous marginals.

The paper analyzes the kernel-type estimator's asymptotics and local power. Under independence, a non-degenerate central limit theorem holds after centering, at rate root n over h1. Under Gaussian-copula alternatives with correlation tending to zero, second-order expansions trace how power behaves. The work sharpens the statistical footing for a widely used dependence measure.
arxiv-2602-14306:
Sylwia Zielińska-Raczyńska and one co-author study a 2026 arXiv problem in pulse propagation through Rydberg exciton media. Short pulses travel through a Cu2O crystal holding Rydberg excitons, modeled with density matrix formalism and finite-difference time-domain methods. Saturation effects under Rydberg blockade take center stage.

The paper explores not only absorption bleaching but also power-dependent shifts in the medium's dispersive properties. Exciton lifetime and coherent population oscillations shape the dynamics in key ways. A two-pulse pump-probe setup is also examined, with results matching recent experiments well. The work clarifies how blockade physics governs fast light pulses in exciton media.
arxiv-2602-14406:
Fathima Ameen and three co-authors introduce a 2026 arXiv dataset of conversations on Truth Social. Argument mining and stance detection help explain how opinions form and clash online, but most public resources cover Twitter and Reddit, leaving alt-tech platforms understudied. TruthStance fills that gap with threads from 2023 to 2025.

The dataset holds 24,378 posts and 523,360 comments with reply-tree structure preserved. A human-annotated benchmark of 1,500 instances covers argument mining and claim-based stance detection, with inter-annotator agreement reported, and evaluates language-model prompting strategies. Using the best configuration, the team released model-generated labels for 24,352 posts and 107,873 comments, enabling analysis of stance patterns across depth, topics, and users.
arxiv-2602-14506:
Kutay Tire and three co-authors probe a 2026 arXiv use of transformers for quadratic programs and choice-making. Linear focus can provably crack free quadratic programs by chopping matrix values row by row and mimicking gradient descent rounds. Adding multilayer perceptrons widens the trick: one transformer block can crack l1-penalized quadratic programs via loop soft-thresholding, and l1-capped quadratic programs with an added feedback loop.

That theory spurs Time2Decide, a method that boosts a time series base model by feeding it plainly the co-move matrix between variates. For portfolio tuning, framed as an l1-capped square plan, Time2Decide uniformly beat the base base model. It also beat the old forecast-then-tune plan, showing co-move-aware transformers can lift choice-making past forecasting alone.
arxiv-2602-14706:
Zihan Li and coauthors tackle popularity bias in diffusion recommender systems, where strong accuracy often leaves less popular items unseen. Their system, A2G-DiffRec, uses adaptive autoguidance: the main model learns from a less-trained version of itself, with the balance between the two learned during training rather than fixed in advance.

A fairness-aware regulariser steers that balance toward even exposure across items of different popularity. Tests on three public datasets show fairness gains at only a marginal cost in accuracy, the authors report. The paper offers recommenders a way to spread attention without giving up much precision.
arxiv-2602-14906:
Chao-Qiang Geng, Xiang-Nan Jin, Chia-Wei Liu, and Bin Wu introduce an anomaly-based framework probing quark electric dipole moments in exclusive hadronic final states from electron-positron annihilation. Chern-Simons-induced anomalous couplings yield a clean T-odd asymmetry from interference between Standard Model and dipole-moment amplitudes.

Applied to gamma-star to K+ K- pi0, the method directly senses the strange-quark dipole moment in the chiral limit. Claimed precision reaches ten to the minus sixteenth electron-centimetres from existing CMD-3 data and ten to the minus eighteenth from BESIII J/psi samples, improving direct hyperon constraints by two to three orders. A tiny asymmetry becomes a powerful probe.
arxiv-2602-15006:
Gandhi and Kontoudis propose distributed quantum Gaussian processes for teams of agents. Gaussian processes model uncertain functions well, but classical kernels limit their reach in complex, large-scale domains. Quantum computing may widen that reach by embedding data into vast Hilbert spaces that capture correlations classical methods miss. Their Distributed Quantum Gaussian Process method spreads modeling across agents and merges local models into one global model.

Merging poses a hard non-Euclidean optimization problem, solved here with a distributed consensus Riemannian ADMM algorithm. Tests run on a quantum simulator in classical hardware, using NASA Shuttle Radar Topography Mission elevation data and synthetic quantum process data. Beyond modeling gains, the paper points to speedups that real quantum hardware may one day offer for Gaussian processes and distributed optimization.
arxiv-2602-15106:
Guerci and colleagues show that a superconducting state coexisting with the fractional quantum anomalous Hall effect in twisted semiconductors is topological. That pairing was recently seen in twisted MoTe. It was also modeled for repulsively interacting electrons under a magnetic field that emerges from the layer pseudospin texture in a moire superlattice.

The team shows the state is a chiral superconductor hosting an array of vortices induced by the field, with flux quanta per moire unit cell. The vortex lattice state is of that kind and yields a half-integer thermal Hall conductance. Their theory offers one shared mechanism and a unified account of Hall physics and superconductivity, with a rich phase diagram steered by spatial modulation of the field.
arxiv-2602-15306:
Kanamori and colleagues introduce thin adding-model trimming for order-based learning. Cause finding gauges cause links between factors as a loop-free map from observed data. The order-based method first gauges an order of the DAG, then trims false edges from the DAG it induces. Work often focuses on the order step because it can shrink the DAG search space.

In use, trimming is equally key for speed and scores. Most tools use CAM-trimming, based on broad adding models and checks. That method can slow work by fitting models for variables, and may harm quality through repeat checks. The team introduces thin adding-model trimming, straight trimming extra edges without checks. They propose a fast routine training thin adding models, combining random tree coding with group fitting. Tests on fake and real sets show their method is much faster than trimming tools with similar scores.
arxiv-2602-15506:
Rehlinger works alone to present LuxMT, a translation system for Luxembourgish built by fine-tuning Gemma 3 27B. It handles Luxembourgish into French and English, and it is judged on a new benchmark drawn from human translations in Luci, a tourist magazine about Luxembourg. Training draws on LuxAlign, a parallel set of multilingual Luxembourgish news texts, plus parliament transcripts topped up with machine translation.

A filter based on LuxEmbedder, Luxembourgish sentence embeddings, drops segment pairs that match poorly. Results beat the Gemma 3 base by a wide margin, even for Luxembourgish to German, though no German sat in the training data. The author also tests LuxEmbedder as a quality gauge, finds strong links to reference-based scores, and still urges care in its use.
arxiv-2602-15806:
Greenberg and colleagues demonstrate tunable microwave tone synthesis with optical spectral purity. Microwave sources serve tests across radio, radar, spectra, and time standards. But top sources trade tone tunability against spectral purity. Electro-optic frequency division, or eOFD, splits optical purity to microwaves. Yet prior sources suffer limited tunability from feedback locking.

Their feed-forward design preserves microwave tunability while splitting optical purity through feed-forward cancel, with no downstream synthesis. Cutting source phase noise without feedback removes loop bandwidth and noise limits of prior designs. They achieve octave-spanning tunability, including the X-band, with phase noise below minus 140 dBc per Hz at kHz offsets. The noise floor sits between minus 155 and minus 145 dBc per Hz for carriers 8 to 16 GHz, matching single-fs timing jitter.
arxiv-2602-15906:
Dehaghani and colleagues study quantum-inspired tensor networks for flow maps of hydrodynamic partial differential equations. Tensorising discretised transport and diffusion dynamics yields a low-rank form. PDE states are coded as matrix product states, and the evolution operator becomes a low-rank matrix product operator in tensor-train form.

That form comes from finite-difference schemes built as operators. The operator acts straight on the state form, and rank growth is curbed by canonicalisation plus SVD truncation after each step. Theory gives exact bounds on states, the locally best choice for SVD truncation, and a Lipschitz-type estimate of multi-step error. Tests on linear advection-diffusion and nonlinear viscous Burgers flows, in one and two dimensions, show accurate short-horizon forecasts, good scaling in smooth diffusive cases, and error growth in nonlinear multi-step forecasts.
arxiv-2602-16006:
Heras Rivera and colleagues tackle a gap in brain tumour radiology: few open paired image and report data sets exist for neuro oncology, so report generation there has lagged. Their framework, BTReport, builds natural language reports from quantitative imaging features pulled out by fixed, deterministic rules rather than by a model guessing at the scan.

Large language models enter only at the end, to shape wording and narrative, which keeps reports interpretable and less prone to invention. The extracted features predict survival and IDH mutation status, and BTReport text matches reference clinical reports more closely than existing baselines. A companion data set pairs BraTS imaging with synthetic reports from the same pipeline, and the code is open.
arxiv-2602-16206:
Self-driving vehicles on nonplanar terrain, such as hills and uneven surfaces, need control that adapts to changing shape in real time. Ahmad Amine and coauthors propose a nonplanar model predictive control design for self-driving vehicles on such terrain. A shape-aware modeling approach learns a residual Gaussian process to approximate complex vehicle dynamics. A recursive sparse Gaussian process enables real-time adaptation to varying terrain shape.

Effectiveness is shown in a reference-tracking task using a model predictive path integral controller. Validation in a custom Isaac Sim environment confirms high tracking accuracy on challenging three-dimensional surfaces. The design thus pairs a learned dynamics model that updates as terrain changes with a controller designed for nonplanar motion. For self-driving off flat ground, it offers a tested route to staying on path where fixed models would drift.
arxiv-2602-16306:
Sujoy Bhore and coauthors study dynamic and streaming algorithms for union volume estimation. The problem asks for an approximation to the volume of the union of many given objects. Karp, Luby, and Madras solved it in 1989 in an oracle model. There each object supports three queries: volume, random sampling, and containment testing. That running time was recently shown optimal.

Later work designed one-pass algorithms with polylogarithmic time per object and space. The paper studies algorithms supporting both insertions and deletions in the oracle model. It obtains three results. First, an algorithm for insertions and deletions in polylogarithmic update and query time and linear space, the first such dynamic algorithm even for two-dimensional triangles. Second, an algorithm for insertions and suffix queries in polylogarithmic update, query time, and space. Third, an algorithm for insertions and deletions of convex bodies of constant dimension in polylogarithmic update, query time, and space.
arxiv-2602-16406:
Zuo Ye leads three coauthors extending the theory of codes for ordered DNA sequences. The paper builds on foundational work by Dollma and coauthors, moving from the binary case to a general alphabet size and resolution. It investigates error-correcting codes for substitution and deletion errors under several channel models.

The authors first establish equivalences among groups of composite-error and composite-deletion codes, reducing the sets needing separate study. They then derive novel, general upper bounds on composite-error code sizes through sphere-packing arguments and random methods, covering all values. For deletion codes they generalize a known upper bound and give a cleaner asymptotic bound. They also propose codes with near-optimal redundancies for any alphabet size. For substitution errors they design the first explicit encoding and decoding algorithms for the binary code of Dollma and coauthors and extend the approach to general alphabets.
arxiv-2602-16606:
Chak Fung Choi, Yin Tang, and Bing Li sharpen the convergence rate of Generalized Sliced Inverse Regression for nonlinear sufficient dimension reduction. That method is prized because its rate does not depend on predictor dimension, dodging the curse of dimensionality. Under added mild eigenvalue decay and smoothness conditions, the authors prove a faster rate than the earlier result of Li and Song.

The new rate can be pushed arbitrarily close to a cube-root rate under suitable decay and smoothness, against the earlier fourth-root rate at best. That gap matters in semiparametric problems, where nuisance estimation often must beat the fourth-root rate for efficiency guarantees. The sharpened rate also extends to functional dimension reduction, giving statisticians a stronger tool with wider reach.
arxiv-2602-16706:
Massimo Stiavelli and Massimo Ricotti test how bursty star formation explains early galaxies seen by JWST. They use a simple parametric model. It asks if bursty formation with a standard mass function, no steady formation, no mergers, and no dust can fit galaxies above redshift five. The fit is judged in the ultraviolet brightness versus stellar mass plane.

The simplest fitting model has quiet gaps near one hundred million years between bursts. Stellar mass grows roughly linearly in time from redshift twelve to five. Burst masses across galaxies follow a power law with slope near minus two. Above redshift nine or ten, galaxies typically had only one or two bursts. Their observed masses thus roughly trace single-burst masses.
arxiv-2602-16806:
Sutapa Dey Tithi and co-authors test interactive worked examples in a logic tutoring system. Tutoring systems lift learning through tailored help such as worked examples. Yet they often show an aptitude-treatment snag: low prior knowledge learners gain more than others. The team used ICAP learning theory to design two new example types with varied cognitive demand.

Buggy examples ask students to fix bugs, while Guided examples ask them to fill in missing rules. In a controlled trial with over one hundred fifty undergraduates, both groups beat passive worked examples on the posttest. Buggy problems aided high prior knowledge learners, while Guided problems aided low prior knowledge learners. Behavior study found Buggy spurred explore-revise cycles, while Guided spurred help-seeking with fewer errors.
arxiv-2602-16906:
Giovanni Alberti, Wadim Gerner, and Matteo Santacesaria study inverse problems for quasi-linear elliptic systems that model electrolysers. Processes in an electrolyser cell are modeled by a coupled system of second-order quasi-linear elliptic equations. The inverse problem aims to rebuild both the nonlinear diffusion values and the link defining the electric potential.

Boundary measures alone cannot rebuild those nonlinear quantities. Yet a mix of boundary and interior measures allows unique rebuild. To achieve it, the authors generalize a linearization result for the scalar quasi-linear Calderón problem to systems with nonlocal nonlinearities. Unlike the Calderón case, the generalized linear version does not freeze values. Interior data are what enable that freezing and thus unique rebuild.
arxiv-2602-17106:
Xiaoran Cai led a six-author team tackling a credibility problem in sustainability ratings. Agencies score firms on environmental, social, and governance performance from disclosures and outside data, yet different agencies rate the same company very differently, which weakens comparability and trust. The paper proposes a shared human-AI collaboration framework for building benchmark datasets against which rating methods can be judged.

The framework has two parts: STRIDE, a principled scoring system that guides construction of firm-level benchmarks with large language models, and SR-Delta, a discrepancy-analysis procedure that surfaces where adjustments may be needed. Together they promise scalable, comparable evaluation of rating methods. The authors urge the wider AI community to adopt such approaches to strengthen ratings that back urgent sustainability goals.
arxiv-2602-17206:
Ron Shapira Weber led a two-author paper releasing an open-source PyTorch library for Soft Dynamic Time Warping on graphics processors. Existing GPU versions of the method suffer three limits. First, a hard cap on sequence length. Second, unstable backward passes for small smoothing values. Third, huge memory use from storing pairwise distance tensors. The new library, softdtw-cuda-torch, attacks all three.

Tiled anti-diagonal kernels remove the length cap. A log-space backward pass stops floating-point overflow. A fused distance mode drops the large intermediate tensor, cutting memory use by up to nearly all of the prior amount. The library handles arbitrary lengths, plugs into PyTorch autograd, and supports Soft-DTW barycenter computation, giving time-series researchers a faster, leaner alignment tool.
arxiv-2602-17306:
Ravi Kamal Pandey led a four-author team on teleporting quantum information between discrete and continuous encodings. Teleportation from a polarized single-photon qubit to a phase-opposite coherent-state qubit uses a hybrid entangled resource and entangled coherent states. While continuous-to-discrete teleportation can reach near-unit success probability, the reverse direction usually caps at one half.

The paper shows that cross-Kerr nonlinearity plus passive linear optical components, including polarizing beam splitters, beam splitters, and phase shifters, lifts the discrete-to-continuous direction to almost perfect teleportation as well. The result closes a directional gap in hybrid teleportation, giving quantum networks a near-complete bridge between single-photon and coherent-state encodings.
arxiv-2602-17606:
C. A. Gonzalez and team analyze compressible fluctuations in the solar wind. Such fluctuations shape how the wind speeds up and heats, yet their origin across balanced and imbalanced turbulence regimes stays poorly understood. The team drew on in-situ measures from Wind, Solar Orbiter and Parker Solar Probe.

They tracked how density and magnetic field fluctuations vary with scale, plasma beta and distance from the Sun. Non-Alfvenic wind is ruled by anti-correlated fluctuations. Alfvenic wind mixes correlated and anti-correlated types, with the latter still ahead. The dominant slow-mode component explains the beta dependence and the strong density fluctuations near the Sun, pointing to slow modes as a major source of compressible energy and heating there.
arxiv-2602-17706:
Rongyao Cai and team propose PaCoDi, a frequency-native diffusion frame for time series making. Diffusion models learn distributions through denoising, yet strong time links force the noise estimator to untangle cross-time ties, a curse of entanglement. The discrete Fourier transform splits time links into spectral modes, diagonalizing second-order structure and aligning the data manifold with isotropic Gaussian noise.

Frequency-native diffusion paths face a barrier from complex-valued dynamics, so PaCoDi swaps the complex estimator for parallel real-valued estimators for real and imaginary parts. Theory proves statistical orthogonality of spectral Gaussian noise and extends the design to continuous-time spectral stochastic equations. A mean field take with an interactive correction branch handles marginal coupling, and Hermitian symmetry halves focus compute with no information loss. Tests beat five leading baselines on five benchmarks.
arxiv-2602-18106:
Bin Yi studies a strange quantum effect in which waves pile up at one edge of a chain. His 2026 paper asks what happens over time, not just in still snapshots, when hopping in the chain favors one direction. To track cause and effect, he uses a tool that measures which way influence flows between parts of the system.

The tool shows a scissors pattern: the one-way bias grows in a straight line with a small push, then peaks at a middle level of edge pile-up. Flow against the pile-up direction gets blocked, and time splits into three stages: early spread, settling, and steady swings. The paper links still edge pile-up to moving signals for the first time in numbers, a step toward guiding signals in one-way quantum devices.
arxiv-2602-18306:
Dongming Jin and six co-authors built ReqElicitGym, a testbed for how well language models interview users about software needs. Their 2026 paper notes the bottleneck in automated software building has moved from writing code to drawing out requirements, yet interview skill in requirements chats remains barely studied. Existing tests lean on few scenarios, live users, and subjective scoring.

ReqElicitGym supplies a dataset of one hundred one website requirements scenarios across ten application types. A simulated oracle user and a task evaluator agree well with real users and expert judges. Any conversational elicitation approach can then be scored reproducibly. A study of seven leading models finds limited interview skill. Models uncover less than half of users' hidden requirements, ask their best questions late, and handle interaction and content needs better than style needs.
arxiv-2602-18406:
Minh Dinh and one co-author test latent equivariant operators for recognizing transformed objects. Their 2026 paper notes deep learning still struggles with objects seen in odd poses, scales, positions, or mixes rarely present in training. Equivariant networks generalize across symmetric transformations but demand those transformations be known in advance.

An alternative family learns such operators in latent space from examples of symmetric transformations. On simple sets of rotated and translated noisy MNIST digits, the team shows such architectures succeed at out-of-distribution classification, beating limits of both standard and equivariant networks. The paper is candid about scaling challenges to more complex datasets, and code is public for others to build on.
arxiv-2602-18606:
Rwik Rana and seven co-authors plan robot routes from satellite images and language. Their 2026 paper notes aerial imagery gives global context for navigation beyond onboard sensing. The team addresses generating global costmaps for long-range planning from satellite imagery when entities and rules are expressed in natural language.

Mission requirements vary, entities may be unknown, and prompts often encode compositional logic, which fixed mappings cannot handle. While foundation models excel at language reading and sensing, no single model can parse directives, locate entities in imagery, and synthesize an executable cost function. OVerSeeC, a zero-shot framework, splits the problem into Interpret-Locate-Synthesize. A language model extracts entities and ranked preferences, an open-vocabulary pipeline locates them in imagery, and the language model synthesizes costmap code. Tests show it handles new entities, respects ranked and compositional preferences, producing human-like routes.
arxiv-2602-18706:
Magnetic reconnection in the Sun's corona can run far faster than simple theory predicts, and blobs of plasma called plasmoids are suspects in that speedup. Zehao Tang, writing alone in 2026, traces a full coronal plasma sheet with Solar Dynamics Observatory data, from its birth through tearing to decay.

The sheet first rose fast, stretched, and tore only rarely, then rose more slowly, shortened, and tore more often. Heating came both from tearing itself and from plasmoids merging with magnetic cusps. The key claim is that plasmoids carry magnetic flux across the sheet so effectively that their birth and ejection drive the fast reconnection itself, not merely accompany it.
arxiv-2602-18806:
Language models can reason well yet still fail to notice, diagnose, and fix their own mistakes. That gap matters when a wrong answer looks confident. Abraham Paul Elenjical, with two co-authors, presents Think 2 in 2026. It is a metacognitive frame grounded in Ann Brown's cycle of planning, monitoring, and evaluation. A light dual-process MetaController runs it and allocates effort as needed.

Explicit structuring triples successful self-correction in the reported tests. It also improves error diagnosis across reasoning and diagnostic benchmarks, using Llama-3 and Qwen-3 models. Blinded human judges over hundreds of query pairs strongly prefer the frame's answers for trust and self-awareness. They prefer it over plain and chain-of-thought baselines. Grounding reasoning in cognitive theory, the authors argue, is a principled route to more transparent AI.
arxiv-2602-18906:
Recovering camera poses and scene geometry from many views is a core 3D vision task. Monocular depth estimation can now give dense depth from a single image. Yet integrating those depth maps into structure-from-motion is hard, because their errors vary greatly. Shengjie Zhu, with four co-authors, proposes Marginalized Bundle Adjustment in 2026 to meet that challenge.

The method mitigates depth error variance by leveraging density, inspired by modern RANSAC estimators. With it, monocular depth maps prove accurate enough for leading or competitive results in structure-from-motion and camera relocalisation. Tests span few-frame setups to systems with thousands of images. Performance stays robust across scales. The work shows monocular depth has significant potential for multi-view 3D vision.
arxiv-2602-19006:
How well do language models actually solve quantum mechanics problems? S. K. Rithvik, writing alone in 2026, presents a systematic evaluation of fifteen models from five providers, spanning three capability tiers, on twenty tasks covering derivations, creative problems, non-standard concepts, and numerical computation.

Results show clear tier stratification. Flagship models average about four-fifths correct, ahead of mid-tier and fast models. Derivations prove easiest, with flagship models reaching perfect average performance. Numerical computation proves hardest, at well under half correct on average. Tool augmentation on numerical tasks gives modest overall improvement at triple token cost, masking wide heterogeneity from large gains to notable degradation. Reproducibility analysis shows average variance across runs, with flagship models exceptionally stable. Tasks, verifiers, and results are publicly released.
arxiv-2602-19406:
Long-range forecasts of geophysical systems run into chaos and numerical error. Phillip Si and Peng Chen propose LEVDA, a latent ensemble variational data assimilation method that works inside a pretrained, differentiable neural dynamics model's low-dimensional latent space. Classical variational smoothers need costly tangent-linear and adjoint models, while recent latent filters impose weak trajectory constraints and fixed observation grids.

LEVDA runs four-dimensional ensemble-variational fitting inside an ensemble subspace, jointly taking in states and unknown parameters with no adjoint code and no extra observation-to-latent encoders. Because the surrogate is fully differentiable and continuous in time and space, it handles highly irregular sampling at arbitrary spots. Tests on three hard geophysical benchmarks show the approach bridging the gap between accuracy and efficiency.
arxiv-2602-19706:
Turning one ordinary photo into a high dynamic range image is hardest where bright areas have lost all detail. A 2026 arXiv paper by Yo-Tin Lin and four co-authors presents a training-free way to boost existing reconstruction methods, using diffusion models to fill in over-exposed regions.

The approach pairs text-guided diffusion with a refinement step, generating plausible content for blown-out areas while keeping brightness consistent across several exposures. Because it needs no new training, it plugs into current pipelines through an iterative compensation step. Tests on standard sets and on real-world captures show clear gains in perceived quality and in measured scores, with natural detail restored where older methods failed.
arxiv-2602-20106:
The time tunneling takes is still hotly debated. Its strangest feature may be tunneling faster than light. A 2026 arXiv paper by Ossama Kullie and Igor A. Ivanov asks whether tunnel-ionization of hydrogen-like atoms can show that effect.

An earlier time-delay model from the authors matches attoclock measurements in two field calibrations, adiabatic and nonadiabatic. That match also yields the barrier time-delay. Now the authors show atoms with large nuclear charge can tunnel superluminally. In principle, attoclock experiments could probe the effect. The paper examines the regimes of tunnel-ionization in detail and concludes faster-than-light tunneling is possible, though only under somewhat extreme conditions.
arxiv-2602-20206:
Vibe coding lets novices put semantic intent first, over syntactic code. Without teaching guardrails, that habit may clash with how thinking skills form. A 2026 arXiv paper by Sreecharan Sankaranarayanan, working alone, argues open AI pushes novices to hand off intrinsic cognitive load needed for schema building, rather than just shedding extra load. That argument draws on Kirschner's split between shedding and outsourcing.

That buildup of knowledge debt creates fragile experts. These are coders whose strong day-to-day usefulness hides badly low fixing skill. To measure and ease the debt, the paper reports a study with seventy-eight people chosen to stand for AI-native learners. The tool was a Cursor IDE plugin built for the study and backed by Claude 3.5 Sonnet. Three groups are compared: manual work as control, unrestricted AI as outsourcing, and supported AI as shedding. The study tests whether support keeps learning while keeping AI help.
arxiv-2602-20306:
Davide Carrara and five co-authors build shape-aware surrogates for heart mechanics that work when training data are scarce. Detailed heart models show how the heart works but cost too much compute for routine clinical use, and surrogates often fail across different anatomies. This 2026 paper splits the problem in two: first learn a compact shape code for left ventricular shapes, then learn the physics response conditioned on that code.

The shape model turns anatomies into codes and can generate synthetic geometries for data augmentation. A neural-field surrogate then predicts how the ventricle moves under load, using universal ventricular coordinates to aid generalization across shapes. Two ways of encoding shape are compared: a PCA approach for point clouds, and a DeepSDF neural representation learned directly from point clouds. Tests on idealized and patient-specific data show accurate results for unseen shapes and steady results with noisy or sparse inputs.
arxiv-2602-20406:
Silicon-organic hybrid platforms offer fast, low-energy, compact electro-optic devices, but poling methods for polymers do not scale, and liquid crystals switch slowly. Iman Taghavi and six co-authors build a poling-free, CMOS-compatible microring modulator on silicon, coating the ring with ferroelectric nematic liquid crystal. Both the radio-frequency signal and the direct-current bias share the same electrodes, using the dual phase shift unique to this liquid crystal.

The device reaches an electro-optic bandwidth of about eight gigahertz, the highest reported for such a modulator. As a proof of concept, it shows a nearly linear resonance shift across the full width at half maximum. Static power is low, the footprint tiny, and on-chip insertion loss under one decibel. The team also shows selective patterning of the liquid crystal on phase shifters and optical links made with free-form photonic wire bonds.
arxiv-2602-20706:
Julien Dallot and four co-authors introduce online algorithms with unreliable guidance, a model for ML-aided online decision-making that keeps predictive and algorithmic parts separate. Framed through request-answer games, the model offers a single, well-defined analysis setup depending only on the problem at hand.

The model brings concepts such as guesses from the answer space, guide, and anytime competitiveness. That lets ML-aided methods be judged apart from model-specific choices like guess semantics, error functions, or probing strategies. The first generic compiler in this line, the drop-or-trust-blindly method, turns almost any standard, prediction-free online method into an ML-aided one. Though simple, it yields new ML-aided methods with strong consistency-robustness guarantees for bipartite matching with adversarial arrivals, caching, and uniform metrical task systems.
arxiv-2602-21206:
Doped Mott insulators challenge the quasiparticle picture of metals. Can Cui, Jing-Yu Zhao, and Zheng-Yu Weng study loop currents in that setting in this 2026 arXiv paper, for the t-J model. Variational wave functions built on antiferromagnetism at half filling plus an exact phase-string sign structure yield sharply different single-hole and two-hole states.

The single-hole state resonates equally between a quasiparticle component and a local loop-current component, breaking Landau's one-to-one correspondence with an incoherent part carrying magnetization from a minimal loop current. The two-hole state fuses into a tightly bound pair resonating between incoherent and coherent pairing channels, small enough to survive as a minimal superconducting building block even at dilute doping.
arxiv-2602-21406:
Asim Unmesh and four co-authors explore open-vocabulary, zero-shot action splitting for video. The task is to split videos into action segments without a fixed label set. Existing methods stay within closed vocabularies. Yet the sheer range of activities and ways to break them down makes full datasets infeasible to collect.

Their training-free pipeline pairs two parts. Frame-Action Embedding Similarity matches frames to candidate action labels. Similarity-Matrix Temporal Segmentation then enforces consistency over time. A broad study across 14 vision-language models gives the first wide read on which models suit open-vocabulary splitting. On standard benchmarks the pipeline scores well with no task-specific supervision, showing the promise of vision-language models for structured temporal understanding.
arxiv-2602-21606:
Kart-Leong Lim and two co-authors show inverse prediction of capacitor multiphysics dynamic settings with a deep making model. Finite element runs help package design builders model design shapes, but the process is one-way: every tiny shape tweak demands a fresh input-setting run. Inverse prediction models changing small design shapes through varying input settings.

The team shows inverse prediction on the static charge field of an air-filled capacitor dataset, where shape change follows a dynamic setting of the edge rule. Using a recent deep making model, they beat the best baseline on inverse prediction both by eye and by numeric measure. It shows making models can invert run workflows that normally run only forward.
arxiv-2602-21906:
Davide Batic and two co-authors build an exact spinning Morris-Thorne traversable wormhole, held up by an anisotropic fluid. Using the Teo wormhole ansatz, unit lapse, and the Morris-Thorne shape function, they solve in closed form for the frame-dragging function. That yields two-parameter asymptotically flat solutions, keyed to throat radius and total angular momentum. Curvature scalars and stress-energy parts come out in closed form, showing a smooth throat, equatorial mirror symmetry, and breaks of every standard energy condition, as required.

They probe causal structure. With an ergoregion at high spin, coordinate time gives a global temporal function. The spacetime is therefore stably causal, without closed timelike curves. They trace photon paths to study how it looks. Its shadows run smaller than Kerr's and shift with shape. Last, Geroch-Hansen multipoles show a massless yet spinning setup whose distinctive higher moments carry the throat scale.
arxiv-2602-22206:
Dwarf galaxies are the small building blocks of the cosmos, but why they look so different from one another is poorly understood. Chi-Hong Lin and three co-authors run high-resolution zoom-in simulations of eight dwarf galaxies with halos near a billion solar masses, following them until most of their gas is expelled. Their samples scatter widely in halo mass at the reionization epoch.

The stellar-to-halo mass ratios expected today scatter across nearly two orders of magnitude, and the compactness of stellar distributions varies too. The spread shows that similar starting halos can end with very different stellar contents and shapes, linking dwarf diversity to distinct formation histories.
arxiv-2602-22306:
Galaxy shapes encode their history, but measuring shapes for tens of thousands of distant galaxies takes uniform, careful fitting. Elizabeth J. McGrath and forty-four co-authors fit nearly fifty-four thousand galaxies in CEERS infrared imaging across six broadband filters, publishing a catalog of shape, size, brightness, and orientation per galaxy per filter. Uncertainties come from simulated galaxies matched in noise and background.

Cross-checks against earlier Hubble measurements in the same field agree closely on sizes and Sérsic indices. The catalog traces the size-mass relation's evolution out to redshift nine, consistent with lower-redshift results, and maps color gradients for galaxies in the middle cosmic ages. Astronomers gain a public, uniform shape catalog spanning cosmic dawn to the present era's youth.
arxiv-2602-22606:
Masahiro Yoshida and six co-authors built CoLyricist, an AI lyric-writing tool shaped around how experienced songwriters actually work. Tools that ignore that workflow frustrate creators, and past research understood the stages poorly. Interviews with ten experienced lyricists surfaced four stages: theme setting, ideation, drafting lyrics, and melody fitting.

CoLyricist gives tailored AI support at each stage, aiming for a smoother, faster process. A study with sixteen writers, novices and veterans mixed, found the workflow-aligned design helped across skill levels. Newcomers prized the melody-fitting help most, while veterans valued ideation support, suggesting stage-aware design beats one-size-fits-all assistance.
arxiv-2602-23006:
Arsalan Jawaid and two co-authors propose regular Fourier features for shifting Gaussian processes. Simulating a Gaussian process means drawing from a high-dimensional Gaussian spread, which scales cubically with sample spots. Spectral methods ease this by treating the spectral density as a chance spread for Monte Carlo use, but this reading fails for shifting processes, where densities are mostly not chance measures.

The new method slices the spectral form directly for harmony-type processes with one-dimensional inputs, keeping link structure among spectral weights without chance guesses. With finite spectral support it gives a fast low-rank estimate, valid by design and steady under mild smoothness rules. The setup also extends to kernel learning from data, matching strong baselines on real and synthetic tests.
arxiv-2602-23406:
Nicolas Andorno and three co-authors give a careful math and computer study of Beggar-My-Neighbour, the fixed-rule card game. A formal state-space framework frames the central split: matches that end versus matches that run forever. Long runs show finite match lengths roughly follow an exponential decay, with notable gaps, hinting at emergent memory-less dynamics.

Ultra-long matches reveal distinct wave-like patterns and disorder states. On the theory side, the authors define reverse determinism, showing the trick rule can send two states to one, even among reachable states. Crucially, they add to the recent settling of the long-standing question of infinite games. An automated 'Infinite Loop Factory' method, using smart deck-building steps, finds endless loops from balanced starting decks. That confirms infinite play in standard and wider versions of the game.
arxiv-2602-23606:
Noel D. Richardson and 10 co-authors ask whether dust eclipses in WR 104 can constrain the binary's orbital inclination. When two massive stars orbit each other, their winds form a shock cone. In WR 104, the carbon-rich Wolf-Rayet star's wind collides with an OB companion's wind, condensing into dust seen as large spiral structures drifting into the interstellar medium.

Keck aperture masking revealed an evolving face-on dust spiral with multiple rungs, yet recent spectroscopy implied a quite different orbital inclination. The authors examine ASAS and ASAS-SN photometry, phase-binning the light curve. The recent g-band curve peaks when the OB star sits in front of the Wolf-Rayet star, with lowest flux at the opposite conjunction. A scattering-eclipse model fit yields forty-one point eight degrees, plus thirteen point zero, minus fourteen point nine, agreeing with the spectroscopic orbit and challenging prior image readings.
arxiv-2602-23906:
Bora Kargi and two co-authors show that similarity-based image-text retrieval breaks under half-truths, descriptions extended with a plausible but wrong detail. The 2026 paper argues that adding a wrong detail should lower similarity, yet CLIP-style encoders often score the longer, partly false description higher.

On a standard caption set, CLIP picks the correct shorter description only a minority of the time, and it fares worse when the added detail is a relation rather than an object. The authors trace the flaw to contrastive training, which aligns whole sentences without forcing each entity and relation to be grounded. Their fix, CS-CLIP, splits captions into entity and relation units, builds a minimally edited foil for each, and fine-tunes the model to prefer the true unit. Half-truth accuracy rises sharply, with gains on compositional benchmarks too.
arxiv-2602-24006:
Yuhan Lu and two co-authors study Fulde-Ferrell superfluids in an asymmetric three-component Fermi gas. The 2026 paper considers a gas where Raman-induced spin-orbit coupling links the first two components, while contact interaction acts only between the first and third. The gas joins two mechanisms known to stabilize Fulde-Ferrell pairing. The mechanisms are spin-orbit coupling and population imbalance.

Working in two dimensions at zero temperature and minimizing the thermodynamic potential, the authors reveal a new class of composite Fulde-Ferrell superfluids. They emerge when strong spin-orbit coupling creates a double-well structure in momentum space within the lower spin-orbit-coupled band, letting pairing draw on both wells. The paper identifies the key features of these composite states, extending the known landscape of exotic superfluids in multi-component Fermi gases.
arxiv-2603-00106: Zheng and colleagues present DRFF-R2, a real-world multi-scenario dataset of drone radio-frequency signals gathered on a dedicated platform. Its recordings span 26 drone units across 8 distinct models, covering varied flight states, heights, speeds, days and receiver setups. Files sit in seven subsets by scenario and signal mix, under one naming scheme for easy indexing and repeatable analysis. The set supports drone fingerprinting, model recognition, flight-state study, time-varying fingerprint work and interference-aware processing.
arxiv-2603-00206: Medeiros introduces TACIT, a programmatic visual reasoning benchmark with 10 tasks across 6 reasoning domains, from spatial navigation and pattern completion to causal simulation, logic constraints, graph theory and topology. It offers two tracks: a generative track where models produce solution images checked by vision pipelines, and a discriminative track with five-way multiple choice using near-miss distractors. Each distractor breaks exactly one structural constraint, forcing fine-grained reasoning over surface cues. The first release ships 6,000 puzzles with 108,000 PNG images across three resolutions, under the Apache 2 licence.
arxiv-2603-00306: Wang, Dong, and Lei ask when step-by-step chain-of-thought prompting improves reasoning, modelling each reasoning path as a Markov chain of intermediate steps. Their theory singles out transition alignment, whether instances share the same step-to-step transition pattern, as the deciding factor. When transitions stay identical across steps, chain-of-thought needs fewer example trajectories to recover the final decision; when they vary, the benefit can vanish. Noise in intermediate steps further shapes the gain, and synthetic benchmarks built to isolate these factors support the predictions.
arxiv-2603-00406: Bagherian builds an axiomatic base for quantum distance measures on projective Hilbert spaces, bringing scattered measures in quantum information under one roof. From five axioms on invariance, covariance, superposition, entanglement, and measurement context, she shows any valid distance depends only on state overlap. That forces the Fubini-Study metric as the unique canonical geodesic distance. Her frame also orders related distances, adds a complementarity rule, and ties them to telling states apart and to metrology.
arxiv-2603-00806: Blank and three colleagues study condensation in random lattice gases with size-linked steady weights and a math tweak that fades as the system grows. Above a key density, the system splits into an even bulk and a dense phase, forming either one large cluster or many separate clusters at smaller scale. They prove the shift via ensemble math and derive the cluster size spread through size-biased sampling, building on earlier zero-range and inclusion work. Zero-range tests show the results on dense phase scale and spread.
arxiv-2603-01006: Zhang and three colleagues improve REPA training for audio flow matching by picking supervised layers with cause, not depth habit. They find layers richest in semantic content are not always those driving the flow speed, a gap they call Store-Contribute Dissociation. A forward-only gate test scores each layer's causal role, giving sparse picks and tuned weights that beat standard REPA rivals on speech and general audio.
arxiv-2603-01106: Gao and nine colleagues fix two flaws of group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) for multimodal reasoning: thin rewards on hard problems and fading gains when group rewards agree too closely. DIVA-GRPO judges problem hardness from a global view. It samples variants at fitting hardness and works out gains across local and global groups with hardness-weighted scaling. The result eases thin rewards and gain loss with steadier training, beating rival methods on six test sets for speed and scores.
arxiv-2603-01506:
Jianqiang Ren, Lin Liu, and Steven Hoi build a way to turn one photo into a moving 3D head in this 2026 work. Fast, detailed head avatars matter for games, film, meetings, and virtual worlds. A single model should also serve both weak and strong hardware without losing key detail.

Their method, OMG-Avatar, stores the head as Gaussian blobs at several levels of detail. A transformer reads broad face traits, while sampled points add local detail, joined with depth cues to keep overlaps sane. Head and shoulders are built apart, then merged, which fixes a weak spot of older face models. The build takes a fraction of a second, and tests beat prior tools on rebuild quality, acting control, and speed.
arxiv-2603-01806:
Xiong Zhang, Hong Peng, Zhenli He, and colleagues spot anomalous nodes in networks without any labeled examples. Their 2026 work targets bad actors in social and review graphs, such as fake accounts and banned users. A recent method boosts links among normal nodes while cutting links of odd nodes, yet its fixed cutoff misfires.

Their model, GCTAM, splits the cutoff step into contextual and global parts that work together. Contextual truncation lowers the affinity of likely anomalous nodes based on local cues. Global truncation raises affinity among normal nodes, using high-order links the old method ignored. Wide tests on large real graphs show wins over peer methods on most tasks. Gains stand out on two famous review data sets, and the method still finishes on the largest sets where rivals fail.
arxiv-2603-02306:
Adrian Fraser simulates a mixing process inside stars in this 2026 paper. Fingering convection stirs chemicals in star zones where heavy material sits above light material. It matters in red giants and possibly in polluted white dwarfs. Past three-dimensional simulations could not reach the extreme settings found in real stars.

The gap is set by one ratio, comparing viscosity with heat spread, which is tiny in stars. Fraser runs simulations spanning old settings down to true stellar values. A standard mixing model stays consistent with simulations across that whole range. So clashes between that model and observations cannot be blamed on the old gap. Extra physics, not simulation limits, must explain the mismatch.
arxiv-2603-02806:
Jonas von Berg, Adalbert Fono, Massimiliano Datres, and colleagues prove that steady classifiers need to be much bigger than their data. Their 2026 paper defines stability as the average distance from a data point to the model's decision boundary. A larger margin means small input changes rarely flip the answer.

Their bound improves as stability grows, and it needs no smoothness assumptions, covering jagged classifiers too. A direct consequence follows: a model that merely fits its training points with about as many parameters as points must be unstable. Real robustness therefore demands heavy overparameterization. Experiments back the theory, with stability rising alongside model size and tracking test accuracy, while older norm-based measures said little.
arxiv-2603-03206:
Cullen Anderson, Narmeen Oozeer, Foad Namjoo, and colleagues test how poisoned examples can hijack an AI model's steering. Contrastive steering finds a trait direction by comparing the model's inner signals on paired examples. It then shifts those signals along that line at runtime. Safety teams use it a lot, yet nobody had checked how it holds up when the example set is rigged.

A modest share of rigged examples leaves steering mostly intact. Past a clear threshold, though, attackers can plant strong unwanted side effects on purpose. A look at the shapes of distinct attack types points to guards. The weak step is a plain average over many signals. Swapping in a robust form of that average cancels most of the harm.
arxiv-2603-03506:
A M Guzman and M C McDonald hunt for a pattern in detector noise that should exist across columns if it exists at all. Their hunt appears in an instrument report for Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. Read noise in bias frames already grows with row number, because dark current builds during readout. Their report checks the column direction for the Wide Field Channel's four amplifiers, across different maintenance periods called anneal cycles.

No column dependence appears. Read noise in the physical prescan regions sits about half an electron lower than in the science arrays, exactly where no readout dark accumulates. Three follow-ups round out the study. Read noise shows no visible trend across an anneal period. Two amplifiers show a brief linear decline across their first science columns. And masking unstable hot pixels lowers the noise of their columns.
arxiv-2603-03606:
Satabdi Das and four colleagues ask blind and visually impaired people what would make photo sharing feel safe. A shared image can accidentally expose sensitive or embarrassing content its owner cannot see, risking privacy and relationships. Their 2026 study tests image obfuscation filters as a pre-sharing shield, with twenty blind and visually impaired participants judging filtered images of varying sensitivity.

Pixelation was the least preferred filter. Other preferences shifted with image type and with the audience, family, friends, or strangers, so no single filter wins everywhere. Across audiences, participants felt more comfortable sharing filtered images than unfiltered ones. The authors turn those patterns into design guidelines for sharing tools that warn and protect without taking control away from the person sharing.
arxiv-2603-03806:
Hanpeng Liu and four colleagues teach a vision model to read many images as one long book, with separators between chapters. Mamba, a state-space architecture, processes sequences causally and efficiently, which suits autoregressive pretraining, but vision versions were stuck with short sequences. Their 2026 method, STAR, inserts an identical separator token before each image, marking where one picture ends and the next begins.

That simple device quadruples the usable input sequence length while keeping every dataset image at its original size. Pretrained the long way, their STAR-B model scores competitively on the standard ImageNet classification benchmark, at the top of the Vision Mamba class. The authors argue the gain comes from finally exploiting the architecture's strength, long-range dependence across a genuinely long visual sequence, rather than from any added parameters.
arxiv-2603-04006: Ariola and others study structural corecursion with standard thought, proving the infinite pigeonhole principle and choice. The authors examine coiteration plus corecursion with the standard callcc operator, giving a computational reading of standard thought. As a use they prove the Infinite Pigeonhole Principle with corecursive control methods. They also build the Axiom of Countable Choice, showing termination by coiteration alone.
arxiv-2603-04106: Hapka and others present optimally tuned multiconfigurational short-range DFT for linear response. Multiconfigurational short-range DFT joins wavefunction theory and DFT, yet unlike single-reference hybrids it lacked grounded rules for setting the range-separation setting. Their tuning scheme enforces exponential density decay, fixing the setting via ionization possible from the smallest eigenvalue of an Extended Koopmans' Theorem matrix. Validation covers static and dynamic polarizabilities for ground-state molecules in full linear response and a random phase variant. Optimal tuning aids polarizabilities over the commonly used universal setting.
arxiv-2603-04206: Gauvain and others present a global high-resolution hydrological model to simulate surface liquid reservoir motion. Surface runoff shapes planetary landscapes, yet global hydrological models often miss the resolution and flexibility for simulating dynamic surface water bodies beyond Earth. Outputs give surface water body extent and depth and spot main drainage pathways via overflow fluxes as runoff indicators.
arxiv-2603-04306: Sun and Kejriwal automate choosing specifications for exponential random graph models of social networks. Such models test tie formation ideas, but researchers now propose, fit, check, and revise models by hand. Forge, their agentic system, takes a network and domain description, proposes hypotheses, builds candidates, and refines the best by goodness of fit. It returns a readable interpretation of the final model, beating the best baseline on 13 of 16 benchmarks and tying the rest. Median goodness of fit improves by 24.8 percent over that baseline.
arxiv-2603-04406: Tan and colleagues train retrieval models to stay faithful to context with CTRL-RAG. Old reinforcement rewards judge faithfulness poorly and miss similar answers. No self reward exists, and self judgment without objective feedback breeds hallucinations and collapse. Contrastive Likelihood Reward optimizes the likelihood gap between answers with and without evidence.
