Big schemas make picking the right columns the hard part. Separate retrievers train on fixed gold columns that may not suit the current generator.

ACE-SQL instead trains both parts together with reinforcement learning from execution feedback. Rollouts build an online pool of candidate column sets. The column set behind the most correct executions becomes the retriever's moving target. Each side adapts to the other as training proceeds. Only about three thousand synthetic question-database pairs fed the training. On the BIRD development benchmark the system reached about sixty-five percent greedy execution accuracy. It did so while emitting under a thousand output tokens per query. Co-adaptation, the authors argue, beats static supervision for schema linking.
arxiv-2606-06006:
Yadav, Fantuzzi, Mason, and Antony ask how much a modeling choice bends electron collision predictions for nitric oxide in a 2026 arXiv paper in Nuclear Instruments and Methods B. Nitric oxide matters in biology, the atmosphere, plasmas, and space, and its properties are well known. That makes it a clean test target. Four density functionals, from B3LYP to a range-separated option, built target models across basis sets up to quadruple-zeta.

Bond length, dipole moment, ionization potential, and polarizability were checked against experiment. R-matrix scattering runs covered a low-energy range with the largest basis. Cross sections showed resonance features whose strength depended most on the functional near one electron-volt. A structure below two electron-volts shifted measurably with the functional choice. Angular distributions differed at higher energies. The authors recommend a protocol pairing one functional's geometry with the big-basis property calculation.
arxiv-2606-06106:
Gjorgjevska, Mirceva, and Mirchev build an open-source workbench for testing internal link changes before a site ships them in a 2026 arXiv paper. Internal links redistribute weight and steer readers, yet SEO teams still choose them by habit or template. WebKnoGraph models a crawled site as a directed graph with page embeddings. A GraphSAGE network scores candidate links.

Candidate strategies are then embedded into larger host environments for evaluation. One host graph derives from the FineWeb corpus; another is a synthetic scale-free network. A production crawl of a real marketing site supplied the test case. Automatic picking generally redistributed weight more strongly, with higher measured yield, but cost more semantic coherence. Expert-assisted selection preserved coherence better. Targeting low-PageRank pages with expert help gave the top yield, though with the least favorable loss-gain balance. The practical workflow evaluates intervention sets jointly across several metrics before deployment.
arxiv-2606-06206:
Marie-Françoise Bidaut-Véron studies solutions of a nonlinear elliptic equation in this 2026 arXiv paper on partial differential equations. The equation mixes a diffusion term, a gradient term raised to a power q, and an exponential reaction term. Such equations model steady states where growth feeds on itself, so solutions can blow up at a point or behave strangely far away. The paper asks what solutions look like near an isolated singularity and at large distances.

Working in punctured and exterior domains, the analysis sorts solutions by how the exponent q compares with the threshold value two. Behavior changes drastically across that line, with different blow up rates and far away shapes on each side. Much of the work converts the equation into dynamical systems and reads off their equilibria and stable manifolds. The paper also proves solutions exist that realize the behaviors it catalogs.
arxiv-2606-06306:
Victor De Marez, Luna De Bruyne, and Walter Daelemans dissect why language models cave to pressure in this 2026 arXiv paper. Factual sycophancy means a model drops a correct answer when a user pushes a false one. A flip needs two things: a weak baseline preference for the truth, and pressure strong enough to overcome it. Single flip rates mix those two channels together and hide which one changed.

The authors split sycophancy into a truth margin channel and a manipulation sensitivity channel. They measured both across fifty six open weight models, from zero point three to thirty two billion parameters, under thirteen manipulation styles. Size governed vulnerability most, but instruction tuning twisted its effect. Small tuned models could grow less robust, while large tuned models usually grew more robust. Tuning mainly bought truth margin, and its payoff depended on the manipulation type used.
arxiv-2606-06606:
Martin Bauer, Francesca Chadha Day, and Alexander Eberhart warn that axion hunters may be listening for the wrong choir in this 2026 arXiv paper. String theory and its cousins predict not one light axion like particle but many: an axiverse. Fifth force experiments look for tiny extra forces between matter. They usually model a single new particle. The authors compute the potentials for the general case of many axions, both spin dependent and spin independent.

The crowd changes the signal. For axion dark matter, the spin dependent potential can grow with the number of light states. The spin independent one can grow with its square. Fifth force searches may thus beat broadband halo searches in sensitivity. Just as important, the potential's shape can differ from anything one particle produces. The force's distance profile itself can then tell axiverse scenarios apart.
arxiv-2606-06706:
A neutron star packs more than the Sun's mass into a ball the size of a city, and its outer layers freeze into a crystal crust. Caplan and co-authors ask how that crust bends and breaks in this 2026 arXiv paper. They ran molecular dynamics simulations, computer models that track each particle, at strain rates far slower than earlier studies had managed.

Slowing down revealed a new regime: past the breaking point, the crust flows steadily like a plastic solid instead of shattering once. Many grained crystals shifted from elastic stretch to smooth flow at a shear strain of about five hundredths, while single crystals held on longer before breaking and then flowing too. The final flow barely depended on how the crystal started out. If broken crust can heal into large grains, the authors note, the breaking could repeat and help power magnetar flares.
arxiv-2606-06906:
Small language models often hold the answer inside a long document yet fail to use it. Yuan and co-authors tackle that failure in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their method is called EASE-TTT. It adapts the model at test time, while the question is being answered. The answer still comes from the full original context.

First the system locates the chunks that carry evidence. Then it turns those chunks into a soft attention target. That target teaches the model's query side where to look. Earlier retrieval tools stopped at showing the evidence. Earlier test time training never found the evidence at all. Tests covered six long document question tasks and three small models. EASE-TTT earned the strongest average score among all rivals. Ablations showed attention guidance beat simply training on the chosen chunks.
arxiv-2606-07006:
Imitating one expert solution can teach a model the script instead of the skill. Miao and co-authors make expert help adaptive in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their method, RASFT, first lets the model try each problem itself. Verified trial runs estimate how solvable the problem is for the current model.

Supervision then adjusts to that estimate. Where the model struggles, expert guidance tightens. Where it already reasons reliably, imitation relaxes. Correct self generated solutions join the training mix. A clipped ratio against a frozen reference model prevents wild drift. Tests covered six math benchmarks and two code benchmarks. RASFT beat standard fine tuning, its variants, and leading reinforcement learning methods. The core idea travels well: treat demonstrations as guidance that bends, not rails that bind.
arxiv-2606-07106:
If dark matter particles annihilate into neutrinos, the sky should carry a faint extra glow of them. Leng and Li ask how to confirm such a signal in this 2026 arXiv paper. Neutrino telescopes alone cannot prove where the particles came from. A recent Super-Kamiokande hint of extra electron antineutrinos makes the question timely.

The authors add two cosmic cross checks. Dark matter annihilating early would shift the effective number of neutrino species in the early universe. It would also distort the spectrum of the cosmic microwave background. Both effects are measurable by cosmology experiments. The paper maps where these probes overlap the reach of four detectors: Super-Kamiokande, JUNO, Hyper-Kamiokande, and DUNE. For dark matter masses from mega to giga electron volts, the joint windows line up. A detection in a telescope plus a matching cosmic signature would be far harder to explain away.
arxiv-2606-07206:
Sending secret keys through open air using quantum light is the goal of work by Nandan and co-authors in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their method is continuous-variable quantum key distribution, which encodes keys in the amplitude and phase of light waves. A simpler one-dimensional variant modulates only one of those two properties, easing the hardware demands. The team tested whether it still works when detector electronics are very noisy.

Their laboratory system sent polarized light pulses together with a reference beam through free space. Detector noise reached about one point four times the basic quantum noise level, a harsh regime for such systems. Under a trusted-detector assumption the setup produced secret keys, peaking near two hundred seventy kilobits per second at the best modulation setting. With untrusted detector noise no secure key emerged, and channels had to stay low-loss.
arxiv-2606-07306:
Dakir, Slaoui, and Ahl Laamara explore quantum effects harvested from empty space inside a stack of graphene sheets, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their system places triple-layer graphene, three atom-thin carbon layers, inside a planar microcavity that confines light. Even vacuum electromagnetic fluctuations in the cavity can link the layers and generate quantum resources. The authors solve the system's behavior with time-dependent perturbation theory, an approximation method for evolving quantum states.

They track three quantities: coherence, tripartite entanglement among the layers, and non-Markovianity, which measures memory effects where the environment feeds information back. All three resources proved tunable through practical knobs, including the layers' positions, a momentum parameter, and the number of cavity modes included. The sharpest sensitivity involved the rotation angle between layers, echoing the twistronics theme in graphene research. The authors propose cavity-confined graphene stacks as a controllable platform for photonic quantum devices.
arxiv-2606-07406:
Gössler, Hofer, and Goessler settle how chemists should design standard addition experiments for precision, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Standard addition measures a concentration by spiking a sample with known amounts of the substance and extrapolating the response to zero. The literature on design for this method is scattered and mathematically forbidding, so the authors translate optimality theory, c-optimality, into guidance chemists can use. The target is the smallest variance of the concentration.

For a linear response, the optimal design uses two spiking levels, regardless of whether measurement error stays constant or grows with concentration in the patterns. The best split of measurements between those levels, however, varies a lot with the setting and can deviate from an even split. The spike level matters. A practical bonus emerges: with a two-point design, weighted regression is unnecessary for results, simplifying the workflow. Bias effects are examined alongside precision.
arxiv-2606-07506:
Tuba Girgin and co-authors let a four-legged robot choose where to stand and where to push, on its own, in this 2026 arXiv paper on pedipulation, manipulation using a leg. Prior quadruped research learned low-level skills but relied on experts to script the approach. Their three-level hierarchy uses affordances, the interaction possibilities an object's pose offers. Navigation policy is guided by which poses afford good contact, while the pedipulation policy uses interaction-point affordances to align the robot with the object.

Training ran in the IsaacSim simulator, with tests in simulation and on real hardware across object tasks, forming a real-world dataset. The framework identified poses from their affordance scores and executed manipulation tasks without guidance in trials. Ablations across scenarios isolated how much the pose guidance contributed at each level. The authors present the hierarchy as removing the last hand-designed piece, the approach trajectory.
arxiv-2606-08106:
ZayxShawn identifies the weak point of self-improving AI agents: not the part that proposes changes, but the part that accepts them, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Self-evolving agents edit their own prompts and keep edits that score higher on a small development set. Applied hundreds of times to the same noisy estimate, the usual keep-if-better rule amounts to uncontrolled repeated testing: the agent p-hacks itself.

The proposed gate, PACE, recasts each commit as a hypothesis test. Candidate and incumbent are compared on identical instances. The change is committed only when a testing-by-betting e-process accumulates decisive evidence, with false-commit risk controlled at a user-set level. On Qwen agents evolving prompts across three reasoning benchmarks, greedy acceptance committed thirty to forty-two percent false and ten to thirty-three percent harmful modifications. PACE committed the genuine improvement while eliminating the false commits.
arxiv-2606-08206:
Wielgosz, Puliti, and Astrup present a tool for mapping individual trees in three-dimensional forest scans in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their system, SegmentAnyTreeV2, works on point clouds, the clouds of measured points produced by laser scanning from aircraft, drones, or ground sensors. It combines a transformer backbone, a neural network design good at weighing context, with a decoder that outlines one tree at a time. Semantic predictions, which label what each point is, first restrict the search to points belonging to trees.

The authors also release an expanded benchmark of four hundred twenty-seven scenes holding more than twenty-six thousand annotated trees across many forest types. On the standard test split the system reached precision near ninety percent and recall near eighty percent, ahead of earlier learning-based methods in the reported comparisons. Tests on entirely new sites, without retraining, still performed strongly.
arxiv-2606-08706:
Pérez Castillo teaches the statistical mechanics of random matrices in lecture notes posted as a 2026 arXiv paper. Random matrix theory studies large random matrices; their eigenvalues govern phenomena from nuclear levels to wireless channels. Expanded from lectures at the 2024 Spring College on the Physics of Complex Systems in Trieste, the notes take a physics route into sparse matrices, where most entries are zero.

The toolkit is statistical mechanics: cavity and replica methods, probing a system by removing or duplicating parts, resolvent techniques, and population dynamics for spectral densities. Later chapters cover eigenvalue-count fluctuations, large deviations, conditioned spectra, and non-Hermitian matrices, whose eigenvalues spread into the complex plane. The author is candid that the selection tilts toward his own work, and that the written version goes beyond the lectures, adding continuations that need the central methods in place. The notes are submitted to SciPost Physics Lecture Notes.
arxiv-2606-08906:
Zhou and colleagues present DifferSeg, a general framework for binary segmentation across many images, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Binary segmentation means labeling every pixel as target or background, separating objects such as tumors or camouflaged animals from their surroundings. Models often combine input types, such as color plus depth, by stacking their features, which ignores how the inputs disagree. Their decoders also lean on low-frequency content, the broad shapes, and blur fine edges.

DifferSeg attacks both weaknesses. Its fusion module uses learnable difference operators to align inputs and merge them through residual connections, cutting mismatch and waste. A frequency-guided decoder then mixes high- and low-frequency features along several upsampling paths, sharpening boundaries while suppressing noise. The payoff is breadth: with no task-specific tricks, DifferSeg surpassed 67 state-of-the-art methods across 29 public datasets covering 18 downstream tasks, in both natural and medical images.
arxiv-2606-09106:
Moca, Sticlet, and Dora borrow a law from growing surfaces to classify quantum transport of charge, spin, and energy, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Family-Vicsek scaling describes how interface roughness depends on size and time. They apply it to the one-dimensional Hubbard model, the standard model of interacting electrons on a chain, at infinite temperature. With a quantum generating function, they compute cumulants of transferred charge, spin, and energy.

Integrability, many conserved quantities, controlled everything. In the non-interacting limit, all three sectors move ballistically. In the interacting integrable chain, charge and spin cross over to KPZ scaling, the superdiffusive Kardar-Parisi-Zhang regime, while energy stays ballistic. Breaking integrability with a next-nearest-neighbor interaction made every sector diffusive. A short-time ballistic regime appeared first, universally. Surface-growth math can organize transport across quantum phases.
arxiv-2606-09506:
Rahul Biswas, Sunit Das, and Amit Agarwal work out what drives the planar Hall effect in electron gases with Rashba spin-orbit coupling in this 2026 arXiv paper. The planar Hall effect is a sideways voltage that appears when electric and magnetic fields lie in the same plane. Rashba coupling links an electron's spin to its motion where symmetry is broken.

The authors study single layers and bilayers, which are paired layers, of a two-dimensional electron gas. They find two routes to the effect. In the first, an in-plane field warps the band shape through Zeeman coupling, so carrier speeds differ by direction. In the second, electrons spread across an uneven bilayer create Berry curvature and orbital moments in the plane. The response grows with the square of the field. For the cases studied, the Zeeman route is the stronger of the two.
arxiv-2606-09806:
Lennart Bastian and his co-authors lift neural operators from points and edges to full cell complexes in this 2026 arXiv paper. A neural operator learns a map between function spaces, the engine for fast physics surrogates. Cell complexes add faces and volumes to the mesh, so data can live on parts of each size. Past operators stuck to points and links, and lost that spread.

Their Topological Neural Operators route data through discrete exterior calculus. Fixed gradient, curl, and divergence maps set where signals may flow. Learned parts then shape how each signal is changed on the way. The split keeps the physics' support and its balance laws in view. A stacked variant learns coarse complexes to ferry far-off news across the mesh. Plain point and graph operators fall out as trimmed cases. On equation tests, among them flows on odd shapes, the new models raised accuracy.
arxiv-2606-10106:
Macedo pins down what the term agent harness actually means, in a 2026 arXiv paper on software engineering concepts. The phrase now circulates widely for the layer that wraps a language model and turns it into a coding agent acting on a repository. Usage is loose: sometimes it names whole products, sometimes evaluation scaffolds, and it gets conflated with frameworks, SDKs, IDE plugins, and orchestrators.

Through conceptual analysis of documented works and primary grey literature, Macedo reconstructs the term's genealogy from horse tack to test harnesses to machine learning evaluation. He then proposes a constitutive definition stating necessary and sufficient conditions, operationalized as an inclusion and exclusion test. Applied to six real systems, including Claude Code, Codex CLI, and OpenHands, plus deliberate edge cases, the test classifies consistently. The paper closes with a research agenda organized by design tension axes for agent tooling.
arxiv-2606-10206:
Coquet and his team ask how much charm quark production happens before a heavy-ion collision reaches equilibrium, in a 2026 arXiv paper on nuclear physics. Hadrons containing charm quarks are key probes for deconfinement, heavy-quark diffusion, and hadronization in the quark-gluon plasma created by colliding heavy nuclei. Building on earlier work on dilepton production, the authors evaluate charm and anticharm output from the pre-equilibrium phase, the brief period before the plasma thermalizes.

They find a real share of overall charm production from this early phase, though large theory uncertainties currently limit how exact this can be. Their verdict is hedged but pointed: precise readings of total charm production, combined with improved calculations of the hard-scattering contribution, can be used to infer information about the early stage. The study lists what lab and theory progress is needed to make that reading sharp.
arxiv-2606-10306:
Lim and his team show a single optical platform that can switch between two quantum key distribution protocols, in a 2026 arXiv paper on quantum communication. Measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution removes detector side-channel holes but is demanding in the lab, needing two-photon interference between phase-randomized light states. Their platform supports both that protocol and the standard BB84 protocol on the same hardware over twenty-kilometer fiber channels. Two phase-randomized weak coherent states are made from one shared laser using electro-optic tuning and etalon filtering.

Channel indistinguishability is checked through Hong-Ou-Mandel interference readings, showing a degree of indistinguishability near the classical upper limit for such states. Sent states pass through partial Bell-state checks to run the measurement-device-independent protocol. Switching to BB84 requires only rotating a single half-wave plate by twenty-two and a half degrees in one arm.
arxiv-2606-10406:
Nguyen and co-authors argue in this 2026 arXiv paper that forgetting in neural networks is not only a problem of learning tasks in sequence. Even in ordinary training, the strongest batches push updates in directions that erase rarer but useful knowledge. Their optimizer, FOGO, orthogonalizes each update so no single direction dominates. It also keeps a compact codebook of past update directions, built by random projection, and corrects new updates that conflict with stored ones.

FOGO stores no raw training data, and its corrections add little overhead. It is tested on imbalanced image classification, continual visual learning under shifting domains and classes, fine-tuning of the LLaVA-7B vision-language model, and pretraining of GPT-2. In each setting it converges better and retains more knowledge than the widely used Adam optimizer and the recent Muon optimizer. The authors offer this as evidence that forgetting can be treated inside the optimizer.
arxiv-2606-10606:
Shapiro discusses a geometry problem posed by Agrachev in this 2026 arXiv paper in differential geometry. A closed curve is nondegenerate when its Frenet frame, the ladder of directions built from its derivatives, never collapses. Agrachev asked how many times a plane circle must be traversed before it admits tiny deformations into such curves in higher dimensions. The answer depends sharply on which topology measures smallness.

For the literal reading, the least turn counts are one in dimension two, two in dimension three, and one again from dimension four up. A simple spherical obstruction from Fenchel's theorem kills the naive control interpretation in dimensions four and above. To keep the question interesting, decorated turn data record turns in several planes at once. In even dimensions, every nonresonant choice of distinct positive counts is achievable by constant controls.
arxiv-2606-10706:
Schmidt and colleagues survey how to train large language models within resource limits in this 2026 arXiv paper. Efficiency research usually treats data, memory, and compute as separate problems. The survey organises it around three bottlenecks: data efficiency, what to train on; memory efficiency, how training fits hardware; and compute awareness, when to spend floating-point operations. On data, it reviews selection and pruning methods, from proxy signals and influence scoring to difficulty-aware curricula.

Two lessons emerge. Good data depends on the task and budget, so no universal subset exists. And in fine-tuning, GPU memory, not compute, is the binding constraint, so weights, optimiser states, and activations must shrink together. Optimising one axis alone shifts the bottleneck to the others. The survey flags a selection paradox, selection methods can cost more than they save at scale, and points to dynamic, hardware-aware co-design as the next step.
arxiv-2606-10806:
Chen and Jiang present Moonshine, an autonomous agent for mathematical research, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Rather than solving set problems, Moonshine mines classical questions for structure, distills new concepts, and states fresh conjectures worth testing. As a case study, it revisits the Jacobian conjecture, which asks whether local nondegeneracy forces a map to be globally one-to-one.

Moonshine transfers that logic to one-hidden-layer sigmoid networks and states a Neural Jacobian Conjecture: if such a network's Jacobian determinant stays strictly positive everywhere, the network must be globally injective. With help from large models, it proves the case where width exceeds input size by one. The general higher-width case stays open.
arxiv-2606-10906:
Eric Nalisnick and colleagues study human-AI teaming through calibration in this 2026 arXiv paper. A calibrated forecaster's stated confidence matches its hit rate. The authors assume both the human and the model are calibrated on their own slices of cases. They then ask what happens under two team designs: merging both predictions, or delegating each case to one of them.

Merging, they show, does not preserve the human's calibration, however the parts were combined. Delegation keeps the downstream predictors calibrated but loads the burden onto the rejector, the meta-model choosing who predicts. That rejector must be calibrated finely enough to spot where each member wins. The demand grows with the human's expertise and can become impossible when the human sees things the system cannot.
arxiv-2606-11606:
Raajitha Muthyala leads a nine-author warning about medical image AI in this 2026 arXiv paper. Hospitals increasingly reuse frozen foundation models, large pretrained networks kept unchanged, to read chest X-rays. The authors ask where tiny, faint lesion signals get lost inside these models. They probe five vision transformers plus a ResNet control across three X-ray collections totalling nearly half a million images.

The standard summary token, which pools the whole image into one vector, performs at chance level for small lesions, barely above a coin flip. Yet the signal is not gone. Pooling only the image patches inside a known lesion box recovers near-perfect detection from the very same model pass. On a detection dataset with 1,462 small-lesion boxes, local pooling scores high on every model and lesion type. The loss happens at the global pooling step, so pre-deployment checks must test small lesions directly.
arxiv-2606-11706:
Rohit Pokhrel reworks a deep area of number theory in this 2026 arXiv paper on p-adic Hodge theory. That theory classifies Galois representations, symmetry objects of number fields, using period rings: special rings where representations become simple enough to read off. The classical theory, built by Fontaine, handles one variable. Several-variable versions exist, but their foundations sit awkwardly with the classical picture.

Pokhrel presents a new approach to multivariate period rings that stays closer to the classical theory and describes their structure more clearly. The key step is defining an analogue of regular rings, the well-behaved rings at the centre of the classical classification. The definition is adapted to a setting where the usual requirement of being an integral domain fails. He then proves the category of admissible representations forms a Tannakian subcategory, the structured class the classical theory predicts.
arxiv-2606-11906:
Xuan Dong and four colleagues test robot models in ten languages in this 2026 arXiv paper. Vision-language-action models turn images plus spoken-style instructions into robot actions. The team translated the LIBERO manipulation benchmark into ten languages and found success rates fall by thirty to fifty percent under non-English instructions. Fine-grained analysis of executions shows language does not matter uniformly.

Failures concentrate at a few language-critical steps, while most steps proceed almost identically whatever the instruction language. Acting on this, the authors intervene only at sensitive steps, aligning internal representations there during inference. This step-wise fix substantially restores performance under linguistic variation, whereas step-blind fixes do not help. The same sensitivity map also guides selective fine-tuning, making training more data-efficient. The authors conclude that language robustness in embodied agents is a step-wise control problem, best studied over time.
arxiv-2606-12006:
Minh-Khoi Pham and five colleagues repurpose table-reading AI for predicting patient survival in this 2026 arXiv paper, accepted at AIiH 2026. Survival analysis predicts time-to-event outcomes like mortality, often with censored data where follow-up ends before the event. Tabular foundation models learn general representations of structured data, but had barely been tried on survival tasks.

The adaptation is lightweight: freeze the pretrained model and train a survival-aware prediction head on its representations. The head is a multi-task logistic regression designed for right-censored outcomes. Three architectures, TabPFN, TabDPT and TabICL, are tested on public benchmarks and two large intensive care cohorts. On the MIMIC-IV cohort the best variant reached a concordance index around zero point eight six, beating zero-shot use by about seven percent relative. On the eICU cohort gains were similar. The adapted models also produced cleaner risk groups for clinical stratification.
arxiv-2606-12206:
Bianchi and co-authors compute what stays fixed as braided systems grow without bound, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Complex braid groups generalize ordinary braids, the groups of intertwined strands, using reflections in complex space. Homology measures a group's shape by algebraic hole-counting; stable homology is the pattern emerging as strand count grows. The team tackles the two remaining infinite families.

They compute the quillenization, a cleaned-up classifying space, for both families explicitly. That finishes the stable homology of every infinite family of complex braid groups. A side result settles old unfinished business: the stable picture for Artin groups of type D, claimed by Fuchs in the 1970s without a full published proof. The claimed space, built from loop spaces of spheres and a degree-two map's fiber, is now proven. The uniform formulas cover all cases at once rather than family by family.
arxiv-2606-12306:
Lars Oerlemans and co-authors send drones scouting ahead of a ground robot, but only where scouting actually protects it, in this 2026 arXiv paper. An unmanned ground vehicle crossing threat-filled terrain faces hazards it cannot see in time. Drones can survey widely, yet generic mapping wastes effort on places the vehicle will never go. The team maintains a shared exposure belief: a live map of estimated danger, updated from aerial observations.

Drones prioritize route-relevant regions, and the ground vehicle replans around newly revealed threats. Spatial region assignment splits the area among drones to stop redundant sensing. In simulations, cumulative ground-vehicle exposure drops by thirty-eight percent versus a system ignoring hazard levels. Redundant aerial coverage falls from 38.8 percent to 3.7 percent under the coordination scheme. Coupling aerial reconnaissance to the ground mission's own risk map, rather than to coverage alone, is what buys the safety.
arxiv-2606-12506:
Thompson nearly closes a stubborn gap in operator theory, using the golden ratio, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A contraction is an operator that never stretches vectors. Dilation theory asks when contractions can be enlarged into nicer normal operators acting on a bigger space, losing as little norm as possible. The universal commuting dilation constant measures that unavoidable loss when several contractions must dilate to commuting normal operators. For pairs, the constant was trapped between about 1.5438 and 2, and whether it fell below 2 was open.

Thompson proves it does: the pair constant is at most two divided by the square root of the golden ratio, about 1.5724. That is nearly optimal, squeezing the gap to a sliver. The answer settles the asked question affirmatively. He also tightens both the upper and lower bounds for tuples of arbitrary length.
arxiv-2606-12606:
Yukalov untangles decades of confusion about what Bose-Einstein condensation implies, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A condensate forms when many bosons crowd into one quantum state. Around it swirl linked notions: Bogolubov's quasiaverages, gauge symmetry breaking, ergodic decomposition, and feared wild fluctuations dubbed the grand canonical catastrophe. Papers have asserted and denied links among them for decades.

Working in the grand canonical ensemble, Yukalov sorts the chain. The Bogolubov substitution, replacing the condensate's operator by a plain number that minimizes the free energy, is exact for large systems. Condensation without external fields guarantees it in the quasiaverage sense. That form equals gauge symmetry breaking. So plain condensation does imply breaking, by that route. The survey also gives the correct ergodic splitting of a symmetric state into broken-symmetry parts. And stability rules tame the condensate's wobbles, parting real physics from ensemble artifacts.
arxiv-2606-12706:
Nguyen and colleagues present VLADriveBench, a benchmark for checking whether a self-driving model's stated reasoning drives its actions, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Vision-language-action models produce chain-of-thought reasoning, a written explanation, alongside a driving path. Existing benchmarks grade only the trajectory, never whether the explanation is relevant, consistent, or causally connected to the action.

VLADriveBench joins observational metrics, spanning mentioning, hallucination, contradiction, and action alignment, with interventions that replace the reasoning text and watch whether the action changes. Applied to 3 models across 2 model designs, the two views diverge sharply. ORION scores highest on observational alignment, yet its reasoning proves epiphenomenal, a by-product with no causal grip on driving. Alpamayo v1.5 scores lower, but its reasoning is strongly causal, with visual salience gating how much influence the reasoning exerts.
arxiv-2606-12806:
Od and colleagues propose a quantum reservoir computing framework for short-term electricity load forecasting on resource-limited devices, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Reservoir computing feeds inputs through a fixed, untrained dynamic system and trains only a readout layer on its states. Here the reservoir is a quantum circuit, and the readout is a classical Elastic Net regression, keeping training cheap while the quantum system supplies temporal features.

The framework is tested on the Tetouan and Spain load data sets under exact simulation, 512-shot sampling, and noise models from IBM's FakeTorino and FakeMarrakesh backends. To cut running costs, the readout is shrunk with fixed-point quantisation from 8 down to 2 bits. Six-bit precision preserves full-precision scores while reducing readout memory by 81.2 percent. Below 6 bits, accuracy degrades unevenly by data set, with Tetouan more sensitive than Spain. The readout also transfers to noisy reservoir states without retraining.
arxiv-2606-13006:
Lin and colleagues propose Emo-LiPO, a listwise preference optimisation framework for fine-grained emotion intensity control in language-model-based text-to-speech, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Prompt-conditioned speech systems can select an emotion category such as happy or sad. But making distinguishable degrees of intensity is hard because of the semantic-acoustic gap between text wording and realised speech.

Emo-LiPO casts intensity control as a learning-to-rank problem. Within each emotion and fixed transcript, it models the ordering of utterances by intensity, matching prompt-conditioned generation to relative emotion strength stated in text. The authors construct ESD-plus, a multi-speaker dataset with emotion intensity changes, to support fine-grained modelling and evaluation. Tests on ESD-plus show Emo-LiPO lifts emotion accuracy and intensity controllability over supervised and DPO-based baselines, with clear gains at high intensity levels.
arxiv-2606-13306:
Garg presents EconCSLib in this 2026 arXiv paper, a library and workflow for formally verifying research in economics and computation. Formalisation means rewriting a paper's claims as precise statements in Lean, a proof assistant that checks every logical step. Most applied researchers cannot write Lean themselves. EconCSLib is built around a human-AI-Lean workflow: a language model drafts the Lean code and Lean verifies the statements and proofs. Humans plus judges check that the formal version faithfully matches the original paper.

The repository holds 20 fully formalised papers and 4 partial ones. Shared libraries cover probability, auctions, matching markets, social choice, and graph tools. The total comes to nearly a million lines of Lean code, a striking scale for modelling fields. Garg notes the team is among the first to formalise its publications while building the library. The aim is a community resource that makes verified research routine.
arxiv-2606-13406:
Vitkus, Draukšas, and Gajdosik compute how heavy particles decay in a Higgs model in this 2026 arXiv paper. The Grimus-Neufeld model adds a second Higgs doublet and a Majorana neutrino to the Standard Model. For parameter choices it resembles the Inert Doublet Model, which contains a scalar dark matter candidate, a particle that interacts through gravity. That resemblance motivates asking whether its scalars could contribute to dark matter. A candidate must live longer than the universe, so lifetimes are the decisive test.

The authors present the two-body decays of the model's scalars, the decay channels where one particle splits into two. They compute the lifetime of the pseudoscalar in the inert doublet limit. Comparing that lifetime against the age of the universe judges whether the candidate survives long enough. The calculations give model builders decay patterns to check against collider and cosmological constraints.
arxiv-2606-13506:
Iakovlev distinguishes two kinds of labour market mismatch and links them to earnings in this 2026 arXiv paper. Educational mismatch means a worker's schooling level does not match their job's requirements. Skill mismatch compares the worker's measured skills with what the job uses, and the two need not coincide. Using cross-sectional data for 26 countries from the Survey of Adult Skills, Iakovlev examines both kinds with a set of indicators. He explores how the patterns vary across worker characteristics.

A puzzle motivates the analysis: country-level correlations between mismatch and earnings conflict across studies. An error components model traces the conflict to unobserved country-level heterogeneity, which biases estimates, with the bias's direction and size varying by mismatch indicator. Separating education-based from skill-based measures matters for policy, since over-qualification on paper and skill under-use carry different earnings consequences.
arxiv-2606-13606:
Xiao and Ryu study how quantum magic spreads in random circuits in this 2026 arXiv paper. Nonstabilizerness, also called magic, is the resource that lets quantum computers outperform classical simulation, beside entanglement. Symmetries shape the motion of many quantities, but their effect on magic was unclear. The authors compute the stabiliser Rényi entropy, a measure of magic, in one-dimensional random circuits with a conserved charge symmetry. The disorder-averaged dynamics are captured by a four-replica tensor network, worked out in the large-system limit.

Together with a flow argument, the results identify a shared diffusive pattern for how magic nears its random-state value, with the remaining gap closing inversely with time. The same scaling checks out in an energy-conserving Ising chain that is not integrable, a Hamiltonian system. The framework gives a flow view of magic generation and informs work on approximate random states.
arxiv-2606-14006:
Dantas and colleagues predict where ships will go from a single radar snapshot, when their tracking beacons are silent. Ships normally broadcast positions through the Automatic Identification System, but signals vanish through failure, switch-off, or spoofing. Synthetic aperture radar sees ships day and night in any weather, yet only as still scenes at a moment. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents HARBOR, a pipeline turning one radar image into probabilistic motion forecasts with no extra data at run time.

The pipeline enhances the image, detects vessel candidates, groups them by size, and estimates heading from skeleton geometry and brightness patterns. Beacon data enter only in offline calibration, supplying motion parameters per vessel type. A case study on COSMO-SkyMed imagery from southern Brazil produced projection maps of likely future positions. A quantitative check against reference beacon tracks remains to be done. Currents, wind, and richer ship features are planned additions.
arxiv-2606-14106:
Choi and colleagues show that giving computer-using agents a visual memory can hurt as much as it helps. GUI agents automate tasks from screenshots, and memory of past screens is a popular reliability fix. Their 2026 arXiv paper builds a taxonomy of four failures: cognitive failure, visual state misunderstanding, hidden operation blindness, and grounding error. It then measures how full-image memory shifts that distribution. State-level failures fall, but action-level ones grow.

Their fix, Action-Grounded Visual Memory, stores tight image crops around successful actions instead of whole screenshots. On OSWorld it improved task success by thirty-three point three percent over full-image memory, and nine point one percentage points over the plain agent. Failure profiles vary by benchmark: with one model, OSWorld failures were dominated by cognitive failure at eighty-two point six percent, while a web benchmark was dominated by grounding error at seventy percent.
arxiv-2606-14206:
Kang, Sevior, and Usman extend the Fourier lens on quantum neural networks from angle to amplitude embedding, and from clean circuits to noisy ones. A circuit's output decomposes into frequencies set by its data encoding; the spread of Fourier coefficients measures expressivity and warns of barren plateaus. Their 2026 arXiv paper analyzes it, a compact encoding packing data into state amplitudes.

Assuming the circuit ensemble forms at least a two-design, a randomness benchmark, they derive via Weingarten calculus that Fourier coefficients have mean at zero, and variance decaying exponentially in frequency magnitude. A subtlety in the input domain changes the zero-frequency coefficient's expressivity. Noise hurts further: with a unitary-Kraus noise channel applied Q times, variance shrinks by an extra factor below one, the sum of squared outcome weights raised to Q. Simulations, noiseless and noisy, validated the formulas, giving trainability guarantees for real devices.
arxiv-2606-14506:
Ulichney and Coston study pre-deployment model checks in a 2026 arXiv paper. The question is how a prediction model will fare in a new setting. Two problems degrade models. The first is covariate shift, where the new group's inputs differ. The second is selective labels. There, outcomes were recorded only when past decisions allowed it. Lending and medicine both show this pattern.

The authors present a double machine learning procedure. It estimates the target risk of any black-box model under a general loss. It handles both problems at once. They prove the target can be identified under standard assumptions. They derive a bias-corrected estimator from the risk's influence function. Tests used electronic health records from the eICU database. Their estimator tracked the true target risk more closely than rival methods. Rivals handled only shift, or only selective labels.
arxiv-2606-14706:
Moradi and co-authors design data-driven upkeep policies with vanishing regret in a 2026 arXiv paper. Condition-based upkeep swaps worn parts based on their seen state. It cuts downtime and extends life. Their parts wear down through random steps. Hidden part-specific values govern the wear. The decision maker must learn those values from data.

The full problem is a hard, partly seen decision process. Their policy instead mimics the best acts of a make-believe oracle. The oracle knows the true values. In a scaling regime where lifetimes and costs grow next to decision gaps, regret fades to zero. That holds when the learner is steady. Tests on real and fake data show very low regret. Where the exact best policy can be worked out, the gap is tiny.
arxiv-2606-14806:
Fox, Karamchedu, and Mygdalas argue that classical gravity coupled to quantum matter would be an impossibly powerful computer in a 2026 arXiv paper. Semiclassical gravity treats the gravitational field as classical while matter follows quantum rules, joined by the semiclassical Einstein equations. The authors examine a massive, non-relativistic qubit evolving in the weak-field limit of that theory.

They show this setup could in principle solve an NP-complete problem, among the hardest standard problems in computing, in only polynomial time. They attribute the power to the nonlinear dynamics the semiclassical equations allow. Such power would violate the physical extended Church-Turing thesis, the claim that no physical process efficiently simulates beyond a Turing machine's reach. The authors therefore present the result as evidence that gravity itself must be quantized.
arxiv-2606-15006:
Enad and coauthors analyze symbol errors for linear receivers in terahertz wireless channels in a 2026 study. Terahertz links promise very high data rates, but hardware flaws couple the channel with the receiver noise. Most analyses ignore that dependence, which can misstate real performance. The authors study zero-forcing and minimum mean-square error detectors under three fading models.

The fading models cover Rayleigh fading plus indoor and outdoor terahertz settings with tailored distributions. The team derives semi-analytical, approximate, and asymptotic formulas for the symbol error rate. Channel-noise dependence enters through both plain statistics and copula models of the joint behavior. Simulations match the formulas closely across the tested range. Strong correlation costs several decibels of effective signal strength at a fixed error target. A mismatched MMSE detector loses a further decibel against zero-forcing, yet stays more stable when fading is severe.
arxiv-2606-15106:
Landgren and coauthors test whether homophily explains why Americans underestimate climate policy support in a 2026 study. Most climate policies hold majority backing, yet people across parties guess support is far lower. Homophily, the pull toward like-minded company, could skew what each side hears. The authors model opinion perception on social networks.

A stochastic block model and a preferential attachment model simulate how network structure shapes perceived support. Homophily alone explains opponents underestimating support more than supporters do. Supporters underestimate only when their own homophily is low enough to mix them with opponents. Adding Bayesian rescaling and faulty priors still demands strongly one-sided homophily to match the data. Media bias changes the picture: with it, even symmetric homophily reproduces realistic misperception. The authors note real-world evidence on media bias stays mixed, so the explanation remains open.
arxiv-2606-15306:
Mittal and coauthors introduce LatentGym in a 2026 machine learning paper, a testbed for studying whether AI agents learn from experience across related tasks. Each test environment is built around a hidden variable that shapes a whole family of tasks. Because that structure is known and adjustable, the suite can separate two skills: exploring to uncover the hidden pattern, and exploiting what was learned.

Three studies run inside the suite. Frontier models still fail to adapt across tasks in interpretable ways. Training on task sequences does build the ability, and it carries over to new hidden structures. Oddest of all, models trained with standard feedback between tasks generalize better than models given full feedback, because the full-feedback models break when the feedback format changes at test time. A cheap, controlled laboratory like this lets researchers prototype training methods before spending on realistic settings.
arxiv-2606-15506:
Wrathall, an independent researcher, presents a small geometric construction in 2026 that starts with two unit squares on the integer lattice sharing a single corner. At each step a new square is built outward on the hypotenuse of the right triangle formed by the outer edges near that corner. Repeating the step traces two interlocking spiral orbits of lattice points, one starting at the origin.

Both orbits follow recurrences driven by multiplication by the Gaussian integer one plus i, and the paired points stay symmetric about one fixed midpoint forever. Running the construction backward produces an iterated function system whose attractor resembles the Twindragon fractal, a classic self-affine tile. The squared lengths of the paired points also yield a new integer sequence, now catalogued in the OEIS. A construction found on graph paper thus ends up touching algebraic number theory and fractal geometry.
arxiv-2606-15906:
Zuo and colleagues present MAGE-RAG in 2026, a retrieval framework for answering questions over long multimodal documents, where evidence hides sparsely across text, tables, images, and charts. Fixed top-k retrieval forces a static trade-off: text chunks lose layout, while whole pages flood the reader with irrelevant regions. MAGE-RAG instead builds an evidence graph offline: page and element nodes linked by containment, reading order, layout, section hierarchy, and semantic neighbourhood.

At query time, a controller activates, opens, searches, and prunes evidence under explicit budgets, then renders the surviving subgraph as structured reader input. On LongDocURL it reaches about fifty-three percent overall accuracy; on MMLongBench-Doc, fifty-three percent accuracy with fifty-one F1. Budget curves and ablations show the gains come from organising evidence, not enlarging context. The framework leans on offline graph quality and extra controller calls, so short, single-hop documents may not repay it.
arxiv-2606-16306:
Chan and co-authors build a graph operator in 2026 that carries signals across directed networks by blending spread with directed flow. Graph signal processing studies data living on network nodes, but many real networks are directed: influence runs one way, as in brain networks. Pure diffusion operators ignore that direction, smearing signals symmetrically. The team defines a diffusion-advection operator for directed graphs, joining a heat-like diffusion part with a transport part that follows edge direction.

The construction gives directed graph signal processing a tool analogous to the advection-diffusion equations of fluid physics. Heat kernels handle the spread, while transport kernels move signal mass along the arrows. The authors come from a neuroimaging group mapping electrical brain network dynamics, with epilepsy as the driving application. Directed operators matter there because brain influence is not symmetric between regions.
arxiv-2606-16506:
Palai and Ray prove maximal ergodic theorems in a 2026 paper on operator theory. Ergodic theorems describe long-run averages of a system acted on repeatedly by an operator. Maximal versions bound the largest partial average, which is the key step toward pointwise convergence results. Their setting is noncommutative, using von Neumann algebras, the operator algebras behind quantum probability.

For positive contractions whose numerical range sits inside a polygon on the unit circle, they prove a maximal inequality for every exponent between one and infinity. The commutative version alone generalizes a classical theorem of Stein from the nineteen-sixties. They also prove a stronger variational inequality for operators whose peripheral spectrum is finite and satisfies a resolvent bound. These results extend work by Junge, Xu, Le Merdy and others, and they widen the class of operators with controlled long-run averages.
arxiv-2606-16806:
Yong and colleagues build a design copilot for aerospace engineers in a 2026 paper on visual programming with language models. Aerospace firms prize safety and explainability, so no major manufacturer yet uses a public language-model copilot for geometric design. Visual programming, where engineers wire components together, is a natural place to test one.

Their copilot applies a visual form of the ReAct method, which interleaves reasoning with actions, using a current large model. Alongside it, they release Wingbuilder, a plugin library of aerospace geometry components for the Grasshopper design tool. A companion dataset holds eighteen expert-designed tasks at graded difficulty, with reference solutions. Two experienced engineers from a large aircraft maker tried the copilot on real tasks. Its suggestions were judged helpful, and both engineers would use it again. Slow multi-step inference, though, limits the tool to complex tasks where waiting pays off.
arxiv-2606-17106:
Mehdizavareh and colleagues generate synthetic patient lab histories that keep the pattern of what is missing in a 2026 medical informatics paper. In electronic health records, lab tests arrive irregularly, and a test that was never ordered carries information: it reflects clinician judgment and patient state. Treating gaps as mere preprocessing noise throws that signal away.

Working on a public benchmark derived from the MIMIC-III intensive care database, the team aligns records into four-hour bins and seven-day windows. Each trajectory pairs lab values with indicators of whether each test was observed. Their model extends the TimeDiff diffusion framework with two complementary objectives, one for continuous lab values and one for the discrete missingness pattern, learned jointly. Generated data closely match real trajectories in single-lab distributions and in the joint value-missingness structure. The synthetic priors could seed clinical foundation models.
arxiv-2606-17306:
Tabeshnezhad and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on secure beamforming for sixth-generation networks that sense and communicate with the same hardware. Their setting is an uplink system using non-orthogonal multiple access, where a base station receives user data while sensing a possible eavesdropper whose location is uncertain. Sharing resources for sensing and communication can leak information, so the design must maximise user rates and sensing quality while keeping the eavesdropper at bay.

A robust sensing signal is designed to both detect and jam the eavesdropper at once, hardening the physical layer. The joint optimisation is non-convex, so an alternating algorithm splits it into two tractable subproblems solved in turn. One step fixes receive combiners in closed form through an eigenvalue method, the other tunes transmit beams and sensing power. Simulations show fast convergence and effective resource allocation for the scheme.
arxiv-2606-17706:
Kommalage and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper pulling apart curriculum learning into its two hidden choices: how examples are scored for difficulty, and how fast harder ones are fed in. Because the two are usually tested together, nobody can say which one deserves credit for any gain. Working inside the Transfer Teacher framework, where a pre-trained teacher ranks examples, they propose a confusion-aware score. It weighs not just confidence in the right class but how the remaining belief spreads over wrong ones.

Two protocols judge scoring on its own: staged test subsets, and a control run with the same pacing over random order. The new score ranked examples in ways matching human intuition on a standard image benchmark. At full data, though, no ordering beat plain training, an honest negative result. In the low-data regime the confusion-aware order won clearly, marking where curricula truly help.
arxiv-2606-17806:
Jun and colleagues present a 2026 speech technology paper on cleaning up noisy speech recordings. Their system, PhASE-Flow, works inside the representation space of self-supervised speech models rather than in the usual spectral domain. Those learned representations carry both sound detail and phonetic structure, and the authors model how clean acoustic features follow from phonetic ones.

Using flow matching, the framework generates the clean representation and then rebuilds the waveform with a neural vocoder. Experiments show better perceptual quality and intelligibility than strong existing baselines, along with higher speaker similarity. Notably, the method stays competitive with only four sampling steps, which makes inference fast. The work also reports fewer of the invented sounds that generative enhancers can add, and points toward real-time use.
arxiv-2606-17906:
Qian and colleagues teach robot world-action models to improve by practice rather than by imitation alone, in a 2026 paper from Peking University. Such models pair a world model, which predicts what happens next, with an actor that picks actions. Training usually needs expert demonstrations, which caps skill at what demonstrators showed and blocks learning from live trial and error.

Their framework, WAM-RL, trains both parts together through online interaction with the environment. Reconstruction-based rewards guide the actor, while the world model keeps learning from fresh interaction video through supervised fine-tuning. Experiments delivered a clear lesson: polishing the actor alone helps on short tasks, but long tasks fail when the world model's errors pile up. Joint training improved fine control and long-horizon performance, showing model quality is the real bottleneck.
arxiv-2606-18106:
Halley and Gruppi teach a reinforcement learning agent to seed a color spread through a network as cheaply as possible, in a 2026 paper. The puzzle is the minimum zero-forcing set. Color a few starting nodes, and a rule lets a colored node force its lone uncolored neighbor. The goal is the smallest seed set that eventually colors the whole graph. The problem is NP-hard, with uses in network control and circuit design.

Their framework, SD-ZFS, adapts a graph-aware deep Q-network built for combinatorial problems to the forcing rules. Trained models were tested across graph datasets of varied structure, and the authors probe how well they generalize, scale, and transfer to unseen network types. The learner proved effective against optimal values where those are known, and the study maps which network traits, like hubs or tree-like parts, make instances harder.
arxiv-2606-18206:
Movahedi and colleagues build a transformer that loops until its answer settles, then stops on its own, in a 2026 paper from the ELLIS Institute and Max Planck Institute in Tübingen. Looped architectures suit step-by-step reasoning, since effective depth grows with each pass. Deep looping, though, degrades the signal, and postponing the decision to halt makes it worse, just as in very deep ordinary networks.

Their Fixed-Point Reasoning Model applies pre-norm layers and residual scaling to keep signals healthy across loops. Halting is then end-to-end and principled: the model iterates until its internal state reaches a fixed point, spending compute in proportion to each problem's difficulty. On Sudoku, maze solving, state tracking, and ARC-AGI tasks it outperformed hierarchical baselines of similar size, and on the hardest Sudoku and state-tracking sets it visibly adapted its effort per instance.
arxiv-2606-18506:
Farahani and colleagues build an interpretable score for how well a person actually recovers during sleep, in a 2026 connected health paper from the University of California, Irvine. The standard clinical yardstick, the apnea-hypopnea index, counts breathing events but says little about the physiology behind how rested patients say they feel.

Working with overnight polysomnography from two large cohorts totaling more than two thousand participants, the team used causal graph learning to find candidate drivers of recovery. They then screened them with physiology-based constraints and a constrained language-model audit to remove confounders. Five domains recurred across both cohorts: respiratory burden, hypoxic burden, sleep fragmentation, sleep architecture, and autonomic regulation. Combined into a hierarchical Sleep Recovery Score, they aligned with perceived recovery up to two and a half times more strongly than the standard index. The authors frame the score as a bridge to wearable-based health monitoring.
arxiv-2606-18706:
Borysenko and the team study how acceleration reshapes the Josephson dynamics of two tunnel-coupled rings of atoms, in a 2026 cold-atom physics paper. Their junction is a Bose-Josephson junction, formed by coplanar Bose-Einstein condensate rings. In a symmetric trap, the imbalance between the rings oscillates at a single plasma frequency.

An in-plane linear push breaks the axial symmetry. It turns that single oscillation into a many-mode response with beating. Gross-Pitaevskii simulations and Bogoliubov-de Gennes analysis show where the spectral parts come from. They are collective modes that gain overlap with it when symmetry breaks. Modes switch on by their reflection symmetry about that direction. Antisymmetric modes stay silent. The authors propose a mode-resolved spectroscopy protocol, using a local periodic drive. And they give a theory with loss whose analytic response functions match the sim runs in quantity.
arxiv-2606-18806:
Bugajski, Pedersen, and Vera-Valdés ask where the acceleration of global warming first becomes detectable, in a 2026 climate science paper. Whether warming is speeding up remains contested. Internal natural swings and spatial heterogeneity obscure changes in the rate. Work on the global average can delay finding it, by blending regions where acceleration is established with regions where it is weak.

The authors fit a Bayesian hierarchical spatio-temporal model with spatial dependence, to estimate warming paths and speed-up. They then truncate the observations in time, to infer when the signal emerges. Detectable speed-up appears in patches. The earliest high-confidence signals sit in high-latitude regions. Across grid cells, the share passing a posterior threshold for acceleration rose from under fourteen percent for the window ending in 1990, to nearly forty percent for the window ending in 2026. That shows how spatial grouping hides emerging acceleration.
arxiv-2606-18906:
Park and the team fix the failures of image editing when several objects must change, in a 2026 computer vision paper. Editing images with diffusion models works well for one object. But multi-object edits produce blending, duplicated objects, or incomplete changes. The authors trace these to attention leakage, where signals leak across regions and text tokens.

They distinguish two forms. Edit-token leakage is where alignment between target tokens and regions blends objects. Source dominance leakage is where tokens naming the original objects starve their replacements of attention. BindEdit counters both, inside a diffusion trajectory, with three terms: binding guidance, source suppression, and a region fidelity term. Binding guidance ties target token groups to mask regions, while separating instances. Source suppression rebalances cross-attention within editable regions. The fidelity term keeps each concept coherent across its mask. On a multi-object benchmark, BindEdit beat approaches in metrics and human evaluation.
arxiv-2606-19006:
Spiridon studies monomial resonance in a 2026 mathematics note on Koszul modules and resonance varieties. These objects link algebra with geometry and first arose from geometric group theory. The note focuses on subspaces spanned by monomials, a special but revealing case. It asks when the Fitting scheme tied to such a subspace is reduced, meaning it carries no extra nilpotent structure beyond its support.

The first part fully sorts the cases where that reduced property holds for monomial subspaces. It also studies how the Fitting ideal breaks into primary parts, which exposes its finer algebraic build. The second part turns to non-monomial subspaces that still share the resonance of a monomial one. That contrast helps show which features come from the monomial form itself and which are more general.
arxiv-2606-19406:
Yao and colleagues present a scintillation study in 2026 of PSR B1257+12, the first-known pulsar planetary system, using the FAST radio telescope. Scintillation, the twinkling imposed by interstellar plasma, probes the medium along the line of sight. The team analyzed dozens of observations. For the longest ones, autocorrelation analyses yielded the scintillation timescale, bandwidth, and frequency-drift rate across twelve epochs.

Two observations show strong periodic modulation, likely from astronomical-unit-scale structures along the path, which blocks reliable measurement there. In three observations, secondary spectra reveal inner, middle, and outer arcs at once. Tracking the annual modulation of the inner arc's curvature indicates isotropic scattering. The analysis pins down the screen distance and its transverse velocity. Delay profiles for the inner and outer arcs give spectral exponents near or below the classic Kolmogorov value. Its scintillation now serves plasma physics, charting fine structure in the interstellar medium.
arxiv-2606-19806:
Ved Datar, Vamsi Pingali, and Harish Seshadri settle the top Yau-Yang conjecture for a class of Kähler manifolds in 2026. Kähler manifolds blend complex, symplectic, and Riemannian geometry in one structure. The setting is complete, non-compact manifolds with positive sectional curvature.

The trio prove the top wedge power of the Ricci form has finite integral. A result of Chen and Zhu then gives quasiprojectivity under bounded sectional curvature. Quasiprojective means the manifold embeds in projective space minus a closed subset. A fresh idea drives the proof: Bézout estimates paired with a Lipschitz weight. That weight carries finite Monge-Ampère mass, taming growth at infinity. The argument closes a named conjecture of Yau and Yang for this curvature class. Positive curvature Kähler geometry gains a firm algebraic foothold as a result.
arxiv-2606-19906:
Fa-Xin Yang, Feng-Lan Shao, Zhi-Long Han, and Honglei Li open new search channels for heavy neutral leptons at a muon collider in 2026. Heavy neutral leptons are hypothetical partners that could explain neutrino mass through seesaw models. A multi-TeV muon collider doubles as an electroweak boson collider.

Vector boson fusion grows dominant at such energies for many processes. In a gauged seesaw extension, a new Z-prime boson and heavy Higgs enrich the lepton's interactions. Fusion of two Z-primes can birth a heavy Higgs that decays to lepton pairs. Direct Z-prime fusion to lepton pairs works even when the heavy Higgs is too heavy to make. The new channel escapes the small mixing-angle suppression of the classic route. Lepton-number-violating signals with muons and a fat jet get a detailed analysis. Muon colliders thus gain fresh reach into seesaw physics.
arxiv-2606-20106:
Ming-Hsiang Hu and colleagues at National Taiwan Normal University tackle personalized keyword spotting, where a voice device must wake for a user-chosen phrase spoken by its owner, and nobody else. Their 2026 paper calls this the dual zero-shot setting, since both keyword and speaker are new to the system. Earlier spotters learn speaker-blind features, so an impostor saying the right phrase still gets in, a real security hole.

Their system, ZP-KWS, pairs a phoneme-guided audio encoder with a compact speaker encoder trained to tell voices apart. Multiplicative late fusion lets each branch veto the other, supporting modes from plain detection to strict speaker-gated access without retraining. On LibriPhrase, Google Speech Commands, and Qualcomm data, false rejects at a one percent false-alarm rate fell by up to sixty percent against the strongest baseline. The whole model fits a 1.55 million parameter budget for edge devices.
arxiv-2606-20306:
Borhan Ahmadi asks whether a quantum battery can power a parametric amplifier, and finds that stored energy alone is not enough. His 2026 paper studies quantum-limited amplifiers, whose pump tone is normally supplied as a continuous microwave drive. Replacing that drive with a finite, precharged bosonic battery would suit superconducting hardware. Quantizing the pump exposes a hidden distinction: pump energy can create signal-idler photon pairs, but only pump phase coherence creates a phase-locked field.

In a closed trilinear model, coherent and phase-randomized pumps with identical photon statistics produce comparable pair counts. Only the coherent pump yields the two-mode coherence and the EPR-squeezed interference dip marking real amplification. With leakage included, its dip reached 0.553 against 1.94 for the randomized pump, at nearly identical collected energy. Battery-powered amplification needs phase-coherent stored energy, not just stored energy.
arxiv-2606-20606:
Atit Pokharel, Shaba Shaon, Thomas Morris, and Dinh Nguyen analyze convergence and security for distributed quantum learning over near-term devices. Their 2026 paper studies a paradigm that interconnects multiple quantum devices to scale quantum-enhanced machine learning. Real deployment needs to know how training converges on noisy hardware, and how it stays secure.

The authors characterize convergence under practical scenarios, with the security design developed alongside rather than bolted on afterward. Distributed training spreads circuit depth across devices, but noise and adversarial risks spread too. Equal first authors Pokharel and Shaon anchor the work. The analysis gives near-term quantum networks a realistic performance and security baseline.
arxiv-2606-20706:
Savar Sinha presents algorithms in a solo 2026 paper for learning how open quantum systems evolve over time. Such dynamics matter for fault-tolerant quantum computing. Under Markovian assumptions, meaning the future depends only on the present state, evolution is described by a Lindbladian operator. Sinha uses Bell sampling to learn that operator without a fixed ansatz, or guessed form. Classical postprocessing runs in polynomial time.

A second protocol tackles state preparation and measurement noise, called SPAM noise. Such noise is common on near-term devices. The protocol is described as the first efficient SPAM-robust method of its kind. It learns the gauge-independent parts of sparse Lindbladians to chosen precision, even with constant SPAM error. Sinha also characterizes gauge freedom in noisy learning. That result identifies which parts can still be learned when preparation and measurement are imperfect, a key limit for real quantum hardware.
arxiv-2606-20906:
Trung Nguyen and Duc Nguyen introduce MMGNN in 2026, a graph neural network that predicts molecular properties by splitting a molecule into colored subgraphs. Standard message-passing networks send chemically diverse interactions through one graph. Signals can mix. Long-range effects may need deep propagation. MMGNN instead decomposes the graph into overlapping subgraphs based on atom-type pairs, while keeping atom-level detail.

One variant builds subgraphs from covalent bonds. A second uses spatial proximity in three dimensions. Its edges carry distance, angle, and torsion descriptors. A shared message-passing backbone processes each subgraph. Results are combined per atom and read out for the whole molecule. Tests span five classification and three regression benchmarks from MoleculeNet. The two-dimensional variant achieves the highest average score reported across classification sets. Separating interaction types could help models learn cleaner chemical signals.
arxiv-2606-21306:
Xiaoliang Wu and five colleagues propose Dys-XAI in 2026, an explanation method for automatic assessment of dysarthria, a motor speech disorder that makes speech hard to produce and judge. Clinicians rate severity by ear, which is slow and varies between raters, while deep learning models score well but cannot say why. Feature-importance charts, the usual explanation, are hard for clinicians and patients to read.

Dys-XAI instead explains each decision with real training utterances that support it and others that compete with it. Gradient-based influence scores rank which past cases shaped a given prediction. Deleting the most influential samples, from five to twenty percent, shifts predictions in a systematic way, which validates the explanations. Linking verdicts to audible reference cases gives clinics an auditable trail for each severity call.
arxiv-2606-21406:
Hanzhi Chen and seven colleagues ask in 2026 whether robots can improve themselves using what people do on video, not just copy it. Human videos are plentiful and can seed robot policies, but using them to judge and repair a robot's own failed attempts is harder. The team learns action, dynamics, and value models from human footage that ignore which body produced the motion, so they transfer across robot types.

Their Dynamics-Guided Action Correction treats each failure as a query: the learned models propose fixes and rank them, turning failures into training signal for the next policy round. Across seven real manipulation tasks on two different robots, success rates rose from 40 to 81 percent across several policy backbones. Human priors plus robot failures, they show, can drive autonomous improvement.
arxiv-2606-21706:
Minaya Allahverdiyeva computes the inner structure of the deuteron holographically in 2026. The deuteron, one proton bound to one neutron, is the simplest nucleus and a test bed for how QCD builds nuclei. Working in the hard-wall AdS/QCD model, which trades strong-interaction math for geometry in a curved extra dimension, she derives the deuteron's gravitational form factors and generalized parton distributions.

The form factors describe how energy, momentum, and pressure are distributed inside the nucleus. Their momentum dependence matches the earlier soft-wall model's results, and the gravitational mean-square radius agrees with experimental data. Parton distributions then follow from the form factors through exact sum rules, with shapes consistent with those extracted from electromagnetic form factors. The agreement between two different holographic walls strengthens confidence in both.
arxiv-2606-21806:
Chen, Ruan, and Zhang tackle confounded image generation in 2026. Generative models copy the statistical patterns in their training data, including spurious links planted by a hidden confounder that shapes two attributes at once. Older causal generators settle the ambiguity by assuming enough structure to force one answer, but image data rarely justify such strong assumptions, since many causal mechanisms fit the same observations.

Their system, CauVaDE, starts from a canonical model where the hidden confounder becomes a discrete cluster variable of bounded size, which they prove loses no generality. A mixture variational autoencoder then learns that cluster structure from data, and an entropy regularizer traces out a whole family of candidate causal effects. Each candidate fits the observations about equally well while spanning the feasible region. On image benchmarks, CauVaDE produced diverse interventional samples and improved image quality scores against an unconfounded reference.
arxiv-2606-22206:
Ambrosia and Mizrach track, in 2026, how transaction costs and speed evolved across the Ethereum ecosystem from January 2024 to March 2026. They compare the Ethereum mainnet and its layer-2 networks with Solana and Polygon. Upgrades that raised block size and blob counts doubled transactions per second on both the mainnet and the layer-2 networks over the period.

Mainnet median fees fell from over two dollars to under two cents. Layer-2 median fees fell more than ninety-five percent, from five cents to a fraction of a cent. The authors forecast mainnet median fees converging with Solana's in August 2027. Throughput, though, stays below one hundred transactions per second until 2034 on their projection. With continued blob expansion, layer-2 networks should surpass Solana's throughput in March 2029. They already project lower layer-2 median fees by October 2026.
arxiv-2606-22406:
Lan Truong studies the theory behind attention in this 2026 paper, asking why the mechanism finds the tokens that matter. Attention drives modern language models, yet its success in noisy data lacks a firm proof. Truong uses a simplified softmax-attention model where a query vector learns from a mix of useful and nuisance tokens.

Using the model's symmetry, Truong derives the population objective, the ideal goal that learning tracks on average. The work then pins down the differential equation that governs learning in the limit, and links the noisy algorithm to that limit with tools from stochastic approximation. The main result shows the learned query settles, with probability one, on the one-dimensional signal subspace spanned by the hidden useful direction. Only a sign ambiguity remains, which no method could remove. Attention, in this model, provably works as signal extraction in high-dimensional noise.
arxiv-2606-22506:
Yuyang Hua, Zhonghai Zhao, and Bin Qiao measure a hidden error source in plasma simulations in this 2026 paper.
