Simulations of magnetohydrodynamic turbulence, the chaotic flow of magnetized fluids, lose energy through numerical dissipation, a grid artifact rather than physics. Knowing its size and shape is essential for trusting results.

The team present a framework that estimates this loss directly from simulation output, with no prior assumptions, in their open-source package PyMHD. They apply it to Alfvénic flows, small-scale dynamos, and MRI-driven flows in accretion disks. It does remove energy mainly at small scales, as conventionally assumed. Its spectrum, though, differs from that of physical viscosity and resistivity, so simple effective coefficients cannot mimic it. It also inherits the turbulence's directionality and can even add energy in some circumstances. The framework identifies when physical dissipation dominates at every scale.
arxiv-2606-22606:
Despina Christou and Grigorios Tsoumakas ask how far small language models can go in relation extraction in this 2026 paper. Relation extraction pulls structured facts, such as who founded what, out of text. Frontier models do it well but demand heavy compute and proprietary access, which privacy-sensitive settings cannot allow.

The pair evaluate five models from 360 million to three billion parameters across nine benchmarks in two domains. The best sub-billion model, a fine-tuned Qwen with half a billion parameters, scored 0.83 on average in the general domain, ahead of GPT-5.4 at 0.69 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 at 0.66 under the same zero-shot protocol. A discriminative RoBERTa baseline also beat both frontier models, showing the advantage comes from task adaptation, not generation. On literary text the tuned small models led by about eight F1 points on one benchmark and far more on another. A pretraining case study added nothing meaningful.
arxiv-2606-22906:
Jiawei He and six colleagues help language models understand huge industrial codebases in this 2026 paper. Models perform well on software tasks, but a production repository is too large to read whole. Existing retrieval methods return only local fragments, missing the broader context a complex task needs.

Their method, DeepDiscovery, works in two stages: localization and inference. It first finds high-confidence task anchors, then recovers wider task-relevant context across the repository's multi-relational structure, under a budget constraint and with no offline preprocessing. On twenty-seven medium-scale tasks it achieved the best file recovery quality among five representative baselines. On internal industrial tasks it raised full recall by up to about nine points on large subprojects. In an end-to-end test on SWE-bench Verified, the system beat its baseline by 8.2 points, reaching a 78.6 percent solve rate.
arxiv-2606-23006:
Jaša Samec and colleagues navigate underwater robots with sonar in a 2026 robotics paper. Underwater, radio positioning fails and cameras see only a short way through cloudy water. Forward-looking sonar reaches much farther, so robots rely on it. Sonar pictures are noisy, full of artifacts, and poor in clear landmarks. Standard vision methods for spotting and matching landmarks therefore perform badly on them. The team names its odometry method ISOPoT, where odometry means estimating motion from sensor data.

Samec and colleagues build the method on modern point tracking, following many points across a run of sonar frames. Those tracks serve as the main matching evidence between views. Light extra optimization steps add robustness against noise. On a public dataset from 2017 and on the team's own real-world recordings, ISOPoT beat the best earlier methods. The wins held for sonar alone and for combined sensor setups.
arxiv-2606-23106:
Ananda Hota and colleagues report a citizen science discovery of an oddly shaped radio galaxy in a 2026 astronomy paper. Volunteers in the RAD@home project spotted the source in survey data from the LOFAR telescope. The galaxy's radio jets form a bow-and-arrow pattern spanning hundreds of thousands of light years in radio terms. On the west side, a narrow jet feeds a sector of emission that sweeps back into a long arc. On the east side, the jet bends into an S shape with a faint offset tail.

Hota and colleagues analyze the host galaxy's surroundings and find a crowded, multi-halo environment with cluster-scale systems at similar distances. That setting supports their reading of the shapes. The radio plasma appears shaped by its interaction with the surrounding medium. Large-scale gradients and bulk motions in that medium explain the strong one-sided asymmetry.
arxiv-2606-23206:
Zhangyuan Yu and colleagues teach vision-language models to ground their reasoning in the image in a 2026 paper. Large vision-language models reason impressively across pictures and text. Standard reinforcement learning for them lacks any counterfactual or causal pressure. Models therefore drift toward ignoring the picture and answering from language habits, or hallucinate during long reasoning chains. Their framework, CFPO, enforces causal consistency between seeing and reasoning. It compares the model's prediction with a counterfactual state where key visual cues are suppressed, and rewards a healthy gap between them.

Yu and colleagues plug CFPO into standard algorithms without external reward models or extra supervision. Across experiments, reasoning fidelity rose by several points over standard reinforcement learning baselines. Gains also topped a leading perception-aware method. The counterfactual pressure keeps long chains of thought anchored to visual evidence.
arxiv-2606-23306:
Ivan Novosad dissects why speech recognition candidate lists resist improvement from inside the recognizer in a 2026 paper. Connectionist Temporal Classification, or CTC, is a common training method for speech models. Its oracle gap is the distance between the best candidate in a list and what internal scores can actually pick. Novosad tests eleven CTC-internal and acoustic scoring strategies, from dropout sampling to a trained value head. None significantly beats plain greedy decoding on a standard test set. The internal ranking signal degrades steadily as candidate lists grow.

Novosad shows the bottleneck is linguistic, not acoustic. Feeding external language information into decoding through a language-model-based score breaks through the ceiling. That route cuts the word error rate meaningfully on held-out data. The external score also keeps its discriminating power exactly where the internal one fades.
arxiv-2606-23406:
Yuval Domb, Hadar Sackstein, and Tomer Solberg present HyperQuant, a compression pipeline for large models, in a 2026 paper. Quantization stores model weights in fewer bits, shrinking memory and speeding inference. HyperQuant targets both the weights and the key-value cache of language and diffusion transformers. It combines four known ideas into one construction. A randomized Hadamard transform per tile makes weight values nearly Gaussian. Values then snap to an optimal low-dimensional lattice. Lossless bit-stripping and Rice coding pack the indices near the entropy limit.

Domb and colleagues report gains across their test suite. HyperQuant beat a recent rival scheme at every tested precision for weights. It also beat two rivals on cache compression down to very low bit rates. End to end, it compressed weights and cache roughly fourfold at near-lossless quality.
arxiv-2606-23706:
Jean Jacques and colleagues test whether brain signal decoding can transfer to new people and new tasks with no calibration, in a 2026 paper on brain computer interfaces. Electroencephalography, or EEG, records electrical activity from the scalp, and decoders turn it into predictions about behavior or mental state. Models usually fail on unseen subjects because brain signals vary widely between people and drift over time. Per subject calibration is costly and blocks wide deployment in clinics and psychiatry.

On the large Healthy Brain Network dataset, the team benchmarks three models: a convolutional network, a hybrid recurrent model, and a transformer foundation model. Progressive unfreezing adapts the transformer to regression while protecting its pretrained knowledge. The plain baseline scores a normalized error just below one, no better than predicting the mean. The fine tuned transformer does better on unseen subjects, supporting calibration free decoding.
arxiv-2606-24006:
Lao and colleagues study a number puzzle built from the Fibonacci sequence. Any whole number can be written uniquely as a sum of non-consecutive Fibonacci numbers, a form called its Zeckendorf decomposition. A number earns the label Zeckendorf-Niven when it divides evenly by the count of summands in that decomposition, and a parallel definition uses Lucas numbers instead. The team's 2026 paper settles whether such rare numbers keep appearing along evenly spaced sequences.

Existence comes first: Lao and co-authors prove infinitely many Zeckendorf-Niven and Lucas-Niven numbers sit inside every arithmetic progression, meaning every sequence formed by adding a fixed step each time. Beyond existence, they bound how many such numbers can appear in a row within certain progressions. The work extends the older idea of Niven numbers, originally defined through ordinary decimal digit sums, into Fibonacci-based counting.
arxiv-2606-24806:
Thomas Hall, Iain Smears, Endre Süli, and Harry Wells explain a puzzling failure in software for optimal control equations. Policy iteration is the standard solver, with superlinear convergence promised by theory. Modern finite element libraries let users state equations directly and pick integration rules automatically. Users found their policy iteration runs failing to converge inside such libraries. The cause turns out to be quadrature, the rule used to integrate the terms.

Automatic selection can assign mismatched quadratures to the terms of one equation. That mismatch, the authors show, can destroy the convergence of policy iteration. Theory expects the method to converge at a fast rate, and it does, once the rules match. Enforcing one matching rule across all terms is the simple remedy. The restored behaviour matches the promised rate. Hall and colleagues warn users of Firedrake, NGSolve, and similar libraries: convenient automation can silently break a solver.
arxiv-2606-25006:
Rui Jiao and six colleagues introduce Meet, a memory efficient transformer for designing peptides atom by atom. Peptide design needs sequence and structure together, under full atom level constraints. Latent generative methods shrink atomic structures into block level codes. Their scaling, though, depends on the backbone doing the encoding, decoding, and denoising. Meet is an E(3) equivariant backbone keeping two coupled feature streams, scalar and vector.

Its core work is rebuilt around memory efficient attention. Vector features start from a global pooling of coordinates. Pairwise distances enter through augmented query and key products, and bond information through sparse bond adaptation. Plugged into an autoencoder and latent diffusion pipeline, Meet uses memory that grows linearly with atom count. Output quality improves over peptide design methods. On datasets derived from the AlphaFold database, the backbone supports scaling of model and data, giving better physical validity, binding affinity, and sample diversity.
arxiv-2606-25306:
Generated videos can look sharp while breaking basic physics, like a paper towel dissolving instead of soaking up liquid. Atin Pothiraj and colleagues introduce a checking pipeline in 2026 that grades physical plausibility in fine detail. A vision language model turns a prompt into a graph of linked questions about objects, actions, and physical interactions, where later questions depend on earlier answers. Scores then pinpoint exactly which category of realism failed and where.

Human ratings on a new dataset, covering videos from three leading generators, matched the pipeline's fine grained scores better than earlier evaluation methods did. Closed source models ranked above an open model on physical realism. Follow up tests found models can write human like checking questions but still answer them worse than people do.
arxiv-2606-25406:
The Tutte polynomial packs a graph's or matroid's structure into two variables, and its coefficients obey hidden linear relations first found by Brylawski. Houshan Fu extends those identities in 2026 to semimatroids, a looser structure that also captures arrangements of hyperplanes. Fu also introduces ranked central sets, a mild further generalisation, and proves the same relations hold there too. The proof turns on evaluating it along one special curve.

Along that curve, a subgraph expansion over central sets collapses to a simpler counting polynomial of the associated complex. Applications include explicit formulas for the Tutte polynomials of affine arrangements and for the balanced versions attached to biased graphs. The results recover the classical results for ranked sets, matroids, and graphs as special cases of one theorem.
arxiv-2606-25906:
Zijia Song and colleagues tackle a hard problem in Chinese cultural heritage: understanding oracle bone script, the earliest mature writing system in China, carved on bone and shell during the Shang dynasty. Most computer tools so far only recognize the characters. Song's team argues that real progress needs analysis, meaning reasoned interpretation of what an unknown character likely means.

Called OracleAnalyser, their framework fine-tunes a three-billion-parameter vision-language model through several post-training stages. A new preference method, Stable Focal Preference Optimization, is tuned to the quirks of oracle bone data. Alongside the model, the team releases a reasoning dataset, a preference dataset, and a fresh benchmark for analytical skill. In their tests the small model outperforms much larger systems on the analysis tasks.
arxiv-2606-26006:
Shuyi Zhang leads a large team improving how vision-language-action robot models learn from practice. Such models copy demonstrations, so flawed training data caps their skill. Reinforcement learning can push past that ceiling, but it learns slowly and unstably. Early training often unlearns good behaviour because the value function starts out unreliable. Exploration data can also be too poor to learn from.

FORCE answers with three stages. A value-calibrated warm-up uses on-policy rollouts to fix the value function's shift. During online learning, that calibrated function filters action proposals. It also filters expert data, so only high-value actions update the policy. Across simulated and real tasks, success rates jump by seventy-nine points. Prior reinforcement methods trail by ten points, and training runs about a third faster. No human intervention is needed, and the usual early success drop disappears.
arxiv-2606-26106:
Zhixing Sun, Shenghe Xu, and Tao Li test whether Nonviolent Communication can calm language model dialogue. Models increasingly face frustrated, distressed users in open conflict. Safety work mostly blocks toxic or banned content. Escalation is subtler: a reply can fan blame and harden a fight without breaking any rule. The team turns Nonviolent Communication principles into prompt-level guidelines. Blame attribution is discouraged. Attention goes to the user's feelings first, and clarification comes before advice.

Dual-agent simulations supply the evidence. Simulated users resist at several set levels, across multiple instruction-tuned models. NVC-constrained prompting cuts escalation consistently in the results. Interactions with the most resistant users stabilize as well. Gains come from wording constraints alone, with no retraining or special tooling. The authors argue that simple communication rules can make model dialogue more trustworthy in conflict-prone settings, where tone decides whether a conversation heals or hardens.
arxiv-2606-26206:
Hadi Salloum and colleagues compare two dialects of binary optimization for probability problems solved by tensor sampling. QUBO, the quadratic dialect, is the established standard with many solvers. HUBO, its higher-order cousin, can state multi-way interactions directly, without helper variables. Reductions from HUBO to QUBO are always possible, but they fatten the problem. Tensor samplers feel that fat directly as extra effective dimension.

Theory and experiments point the same way. Max-Cut instances, RSA factorization, and synthetic polynomial objectives supply the test beds. When a problem is born with high-order interactions, keeping them native in HUBO usually wins. The reduction overhead outweighs QUBO's simpler algebra there. Naturally quadratic problems flip the verdict: QUBO stays competitive, even preferable. The practical guidance is to match the dialect to the problem's native shape, weighing fidelity, dimension growth, and solver strength together.
arxiv-2606-26406:
Yu. N. Berdinsky and A. S. Ushakov argue that safe artificial general intelligence, meaning software meant to match broad human ability, cannot rest on today's feedforward networks, where signals flow one way with no loop back. They propose an architecture built on a closed reentry loop, a cycle in which the system's output feeds back into itself. The authors claim this loop guarantees a self-model and safer goal-directed behaviour.

Inside their design, the agent's goal sits in an architectural desire vector, a built-in direction the system pursues, rather than in text that could be reinterpreted or hijacked by a crafted prompt. The authors present formal proofs, machine-checked versions in the Lean 4 proof assistant, and Python code. They also sketch industrial scaling plans and future variants. These safety guarantees are the authors' claims, presented as proofs, not settled results.
arxiv-2606-26706:
Pengcheng Shi, Kaiyuan Yang, Houjing Huang, and six colleagues present a multi-task system for reading brain aneurysm scans. An intracranial aneurysm is a bulge in a brain blood vessel. It often causes no symptoms until rupture, which is frequently fatal. Treatment planning needs both the aneurysm's shape and its anatomical location. Earlier automated tools mostly detected aneurysms without that detail.

Their framework classifies and outlines aneurysms and vessels together across thirteen locations and four scan types. A fast two-dimensional step first finds regions of interest from three viewing axes. A three-dimensional network then performs the joint tasks. Separate decoders handle the huge size imbalance between aneurysms and vessels. Their two-model ensemble placed second in the RSNA 2025 challenge on this problem. Code, weights, and a viewer plugin are public.
arxiv-2606-27606:
Sai Peng studies a one-dimensional equation for an active line. The line is a thin-sheet reduction of Oldroyd–B dynamics. Oldroyd–B is a standard model for elastic fluids such as polymer solutions. The regime studied has a high Weissenberg number. The unknown is a positive periodic line density. Peng presents proofs about this reduced mechanism in 2026.

The results cover several properties. Positive-density solutions exist locally and are well-posed. A no-rupture principle holds, so the line cannot tear. Small oscillations are globally stable, and finite-band data relax over time. Any remaining obstruction must follow a one-tail pattern. Peng separates the scalar mechanism from the full problem. For finite-thickness versions, a residual-work inequality is proved. It rules out lifts whose pressure-free work is too large. The full compactness theorem remains an open problem.
arxiv-2606-27806:
World models help language agents plan, but they come in two flawed forms. Agent-based models reason flexibly through an API. Their errors take the form of hallucinated state changes, which resist scoring. Parameterised models are trained transition predictors with measurable errors, but weaker planning. Xinyuan Song and Zekun Cai compare the families in 2026 on four graph-structured planning benchmarks. Their hybrid, GILP, combines both.

GILP trains only a small parameterised backbone. The backbone supplies valid actions, predicted state changes, risk, and value. The language model drafts its own action and imagined change. A consistency gate compares the two drafts, and disagreement triggers revision. On real GPT-4o-mini calls, the hallucinated-state rate fell from about eighteen percent to about four percent. In simulator tests, success rose from about sixty-seven percent to about eighty-four percent. The gain cost only about twenty-two percent more model calls.
arxiv-2606-27906:
Phone-class chips can now run vision-language models on device. Developers lack phase-level guidance for mapping the pipeline across CPU and neural processing unit, though. Aryama Murthy and five colleagues characterise this inference in 2026. Their testbed is the Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite chip. FastVLM-0.5B serves as the end-to-end case study. Encoder measurements span four architecture families.

Phase matters, the results show. Neural-unit execution speeds the prefill phase by about one point six times. The decode phase gains only about one point one eight times. Vision encoders gain far more, running twenty to forty-five times faster than on CPU. Steady-state temperature drops by about ten and a half degrees, and energy use falls by about two and a half times, avoiding throttling. A four-step graph rewrite brings previously unsupported encoders to the neural path. One reaches speedups of up to twenty-two times.
arxiv-2606-28406:
Davie Chen, writing alone, asks whether image generators can draw science. Researchers increasingly ask text-to-image models for mechanism diagrams, experiment schematics, and graphical abstracts. Yet existing benchmarks grade natural photos for realism and object counting. They do not grade whether a figure's labels are right or its arrows mean anything.

Chen introduces SciDraw-Bench, thirty-two figure tasks across eight figure types and ten fields, each with machine-checkable rules for labels, relations, components, conventions, and forbidden elements. Scoring covers text fidelity, semantic correctness, structural quality, and fit with field conventions. In a pilot across all figure types, a system built for the domain beat general text-to-image models on every dimension, with the widest gaps in semantics and conventions. Text fidelity stayed hardest for all models.
arxiv-2606-28506:
Duncan B. Maclean, Poojan Agrawal, Katelyn Breivik, Alexandra G. Guerrero, Michael Zevin, Mathieu Renzo, and Carl L. Rodriguez model the masses of merging black hole pairs. Gravitational-wave catalogs show a peak in the primary-mass spectrum near ten suns. The team asks what stellar physics sculpts it, using a fresh grid of star models with varied winds and convective mixing.

Feeding those tracks through binary population synthesis, Maclean and colleagues find the peak usually splits into two sub-populations, near eight and thirteen solar masses. The heavier group is dominated by pairs whose stars swapped mass roles during their lives. Shifting the assumed wind and mixing physics can merge the two peaks into one near nine suns. Mixing choices also swing the predicted merger rate roughly sixfold, mostly through the common-envelope channel.
arxiv-2606-28606:
John M. Campbell, writing alone, settles a conjecture about antichains in the continuous cube. An antichain is a set no two of whose points are comparable; a k-antichain relaxes this, allowing at most k points on any chain. Pelekis and Vlasák had conjectured that a k-antichain in the unit cube can attain a certain sharp size, measured by Hausdorff measure, and proved only the two-dimensional case.

Campbell proves the conjecture in full generality, for every dimension and every k. The extremal size they predicted is exactly achievable, so their upper bound is sharp. The result sits downstream of a classical theorem of Erdős about antichains in the discrete cube, and it closes the continuous analogue cleanly. It completes a picture that partial results, for two dimensions and for the single-antichain case, had sketched.
arxiv-2606-28706:
Avanzi, Wong and Zhu study how regulators should close down a failing firm gradually instead of at one hard line. Modern rules increasingly wind up distressed firms through a state-dependent process, where the worse a firm's surplus gets, the more likely forced liquidation becomes. Their model splits the firm's life into three zones: free, where dividends may be paid; regulated, where payouts are banned; and distressed, where the liquidation risk is active.

Shareholder value is framed as a control problem: pay out as much as possible, in present value terms, before liquidation arrives. The authors prove a verification result and show that a barrier strategy, paying only above a set level, is optimal. They give workable formulas for value and expected survival time. Placing the distress zone only below or only above the classical ruin point did not reliably help both goals. Combining the two placements did.
arxiv-2606-28906:
Marino reviews his theory of high-temperature superconductivity in cuprates, materials that conduct electricity without resistance at unusually warm temperatures. The key physics sits in copper oxide planes, well described by a three-band Hubbard model that is too complex to solve directly. Two simplifications dominate the field. One ties doped holes to copper electrons, forming Zhang-Rice singlets, and yields the t-J model. The other keeps copper electrons as localised spins, while holes move on oxygen sites and interact magnetically with the spins.

Marino chose the second road, the spin-fermion-Hubbard model. This article explains why he believes that choice succeeded. He presents this as a successful account, built over decades of results that earlier theories described only partially. The model's picture: localised spins on a square lattice, mobile holes on oxygen sites, a Kondo-like magnetic coupling, plus electric repulsion among the holes.
arxiv-2606-29406:
Dixon asks how much decision authority an organization should hand to artificial intelligence systems, and how that share should change as evidence improves or worsens. Current governance frameworks stress transparency, documentation, and oversight. They give little numeric guidance on when a manager should let a model decide alone. Dixon frames the problem for large language models and agentic systems working in high consequence settings.

He models delegation as a Governance-Aware Partially Observable Markov Decision Process. In that model, Bayesian inference, a method that updates beliefs as evidence arrives, tracks what is known. Sequential optimization then picks the right level of delegated authority at each step. Synthetic stress tests probe robustness when reported model confidence is wrong. Benchmarks against five fixed governance strategies follow. Sequential Bayesian governance performs best overall across mixed quality regimes, while simpler heuristics win only when conditions stay steady.
arxiv-2606-29506:
Rashidi audits a headline promise of AI surveillance: flagging suspicious behaviour in video, with high scores reported on standard benchmarks. Those scores come from training and testing within one camera and scene. He asks what survives when the detector faces a new scene.

His normality model trains only on normal frames from one dataset, plus frozen off-the-shelf embeddings from CLIP, DINOv2, ResNet-50, and EfficientNet-B0. A nearest-neighbour distance then scores test frames from the same and other datasets. Across four datasets and four backbones, same-dataset AUC averages well above chance. Cross-dataset AUC averages about chance level, and some pairs fall below it. DINOv2, the strongest backbone at home, drops the most abroad. A second detector design reproduces the collapse almost exactly. Rashidi concludes that benchmark numbers greatly overstate deployable reliability, and even a favourable setting yields tens of thousands of false alarms per hour.
arxiv-2606-29606:
Sánchez Cuadrado examines how Model-Driven Engineering, or MDE, is actually used in real projects on GitHub. MDE builds domain-specific modelling environments meant to raise productivity and quality. In theory, chaining tools such as EMF, ATL, Epsilon, and Xtext should produce strong environments with modest effort. Empirical evidence about how that idea has fared in practice has been thin.

He mined more than seven thousand GitHub projects holding over three hundred twenty-five thousand MDE artefacts, covering a dozen Eclipse EMF-related technologies. Repository-level information from git and the GitHub API enriches the dataset. A recovery technique then extracts each project's mega-model, a map of relationships among its artefacts. Near-duplicate analysis across all artefacts builds one global mega-model linking the projects themselves, supporting further questions about dependencies between projects.
arxiv-2606-29706:
Fernando, Xiao, Xin, and Chen build ARMOR, a retriever optimizer for telecom question answering under low resources. Telecom evidence is fragmented across standards, papers, and web documents. Answers often hinge on tables, equations, and protocol language. Fine-tuning the generator in such subdomains can over-specialize and degrade general skill, so the authors adapt the retriever instead.

ARMOR, short for Adaptive Regularized Mixture Optimization for Retrievers, trains the query encoder while the generator stays fixed. Two goals combine: the latent-document RAG likelihood and the InfoNCE contrastive objective. Separate learned temperatures serve each goal, and a penalty keeps the adapted encoder near the base encoder. Across telecom retrieval and QA benchmarks, ARMOR improves evidence retrieval and answers in several in-domain settings. Code is released.
arxiv-2606-30006:
Mátyás Szücs solves the piston effect in supercritical fluids exactly. Close to the liquid-vapor critical point, fluids become extremely compressible. A thin hot layer near a heated wall then expands strongly. It acts like a piston, squeezing the whole bulk fluid. The bulk then warms far faster than conduction alone would allow.

Because sound crosses the setup much faster than the layer grows, Szücs uses a post-acoustic approximation. Pressure stays uniform in space, though it changes in time. The problem then reduces to a diffusion equation with a special source term. Exact closed-form solutions follow for flat and spherical geometries. Boundary conditions of the first and second kinds are both covered. Short-time behavior and thermal penetration depth are analyzed case by case. Adding the container's heat capacity enables comparison with the Spacelab D-2 space experiment. Its measurements match the predictions well.
arxiv-2606-30206:
Marcin Korecki and Cesare Carissimo argue, in a philosophical essay, that the data centre is the body of artificial intelligence. AI is often framed as disembodied software awaiting a robot body. The authors invert that picture completely. Data centres, they say, already embody AI in material form. They also form part of the labouring body of capital.

Seen through a biological lens, data centres show organismic qualities. They archive, serve, and compute on data born of human desires. Yet they act without desire of their own. That split is where the organic analogy starts to tear. Pricing, the authors argue, is where capital speaks plainly. Automata and human labour get priced much the same way. Through AI pricing, capital distils the value of intelligence itself. Comparisons across the organism and mechanism divide become possible.
arxiv-2606-30306:
Tianyu Ding, Aditya Nannapaneni, Bingfan Liu, and Ling Zhang survey AI agents that never switch off, focusing on the state they accumulate. Always-on agents remember across sessions, unlike one-shot systems. Their durable state includes far more than memories. Task ledgers, permissions, credentials, commitments, and audit records all count. The survey reads the literature through six axes.

Each state item is scored for authority, scope, and mutability. Provenance, recoverability, and actionability complete the six axes. A lifecycle follows state from writing through validation and retrieval. Forgetting, auditing, and rollback close the loop. The coded corpus spans four hundred thirty-five works. Most work focuses on storing and fetching state, the authors find. Governing, recovering, or giving up state gets much less attention. Their pilot evaluation protocol scores mutation and recovery duties directly.
arxiv-2606-30706:
Adina Feinstein and eleven colleagues propose an observing program for the Nautilus Space Observatory, a planned constellation of space telescopes. Their target is a nuisance in exoplanet science: starspots and bright faculae on a host star can fake or hide the atmospheric signals astronomers seek during a planet's transit. Correcting that contamination needs stellar models tested against real data, across star types and activity levels.

The white paper lays out a two-generation program. Generation 1 would watch transiting exoplanet systems over broad wavelengths, linking spot-crossing events and out-of-transit variability with local and whole-disk surface properties. Generation 2 would use the best diagnostics found to monitor large samples of G, K and M stars spectroscopically, tracking both surface and upper-atmosphere activity. Together the generations would supply the benchmark data needed to make stellar contamination a calibrated input for atmospheric retrievals.
arxiv-2606-30806:
V. Niarchos, C. Papageorgakis and A. Stratoudakis extract thermal data about paired operators in quantum field theory from hot correlation functions. In a conformal field theory at finite temperature, two-point functions can be expanded into contributions from double-twist operators, pairs built from the original field. The team show how integrals of thermal response functions, suitably regularised, yield the expansion coefficients of those double-twist terms directly.

They apply the method to four-dimensional holographic theories, whose dual description is gravity in a five-dimensional anti-de Sitter space with a black brane for the hot state. There the response function comes from solving a radial wave equation numerically. The extracted coefficients agree with earlier holographic and bootstrap studies, and some spin-resolved values are new.
arxiv-2606-30906:
Cor Steging, Ludi van Leeuwen and Tadeusz Zbiegień test whether teams of AI agents reason about law better than a single model talking to itself. Multi-agent deliberation lets several language-model agents argue a question from assigned roles. The authors add two frameworks of their own, inspired by courtroom procedure and legal argumentation, and run them on legal and non-legal benchmarks against a standard single-model baseline.

Overall scores were comparable to the baseline, but the answers differed significantly. Each side solved cases the other missed: the multi-agent frameworks cracked some problems the lone model failed, and lost some it won. Qualitative review suggested multi-agent setups suit questions that reward critical thinking from several perspectives. The authors present the approach as a promising direction for legal AI and for deliberation generally.
arxiv-2606-31006:
Tao Jiang, Jie Liu and Li-Chen Zhao find a way to switch the topological charge carried by a pumping soliton. Thouless pumping moves particles by slowly cycling a periodic potential. The distance moved per cycle is fixed by a topological number, the Chern number. Gap solitons, self-trapped wave packets living in a band gap, normally keep their pumping direction under gentle ramping. The team modulate nonlinear parameters and vary how fast the relative phase between periodic potentials is ramped, pushing the soliton toward instability.

Under near-adiabatic ramping, the soliton developed instabilities with finite Bogoliubov excitations, small ripples on top of its profile. Those excitations drained particles from the soliton. Its direction of motion reversed, the signature of Chern number switching. Tracking the soliton's chemical potential against the band structure confirmed the switch, giving a control strategy for topological transport.
arxiv-2606-31106:
Jeon and three colleagues probe what self-driving policies actually learn inside. A driving policy can score well in closed-loop simulation and still reason badly. Summary scores hide whether the policy predicts where nearby cars will move, or just follows brittle habits that work in calm scenes. The team studies prediction and planning as separate internal skills.

They use linear probing and targeted perturbations on policies trained by imitation learning and by reinforcement learning. Scale is the test variable: do bigger datasets and longer training build real prediction and planning, or only better habits? The policies often failed to form timely predictions of nearby vehicles during near-collision events. That gap limits the signals available for safe planning. When the researchers corrected the wrong predictions directly, the car's plans shifted toward safer trajectories.
arxiv-2606-31406:
Ren and two colleagues test the Kibble-Zurek mechanism in a damped spin-orbit-coupled Bose-Einstein condensate. The mechanism predicts how defects scale when a system is driven across a phase change. Their condensate crosses from a plane-wave phase to a stripe phase, and damping is added to mimic an open system.

Without damping, slow quenches trap the system in the plane-wave phase, a stagnation caused by the energy gap and critical slowing down. With weak damping, the expected Kibble-Zurek power laws for freeze-out time and defect density hold. Strong damping or long quench times break them clearly. The results mark where universal scaling survives in open quantum systems and where dissipation rewrites the story, a guide for cold-atom experiments.
arxiv-2606-31606:
Dastidar proves a sign law for the coefficients of rho, one of Ramanujan's third order mock theta functions, which are q-series resembling modular forms without quite being them. Writing the series coefficients as r of n, the observed pattern splits by n modulo three. One class stays positive, and the other two stay non-positive. Zeros occur only at five small values.

Watson's identity rewrites twice rho plus another mock theta function as an eta quotient, turning the sign question into a comparison between the two sides. Dastidar bounds the difference using estimates at roots of unity, where the leading contributions cancel or stay small and the first surviving term carries exactly the claimed sign pattern. Exact integer arithmetic then settles the remaining finite range of cases.
arxiv-2606-31706:
Liu and six colleagues present AdaTrans, a system that converts C code into Rust automatically. Rust enforces strict ownership and borrowing rules, and language models often break them or hide inside unsafe blocks. Compiler feedback could guide repairs, yet earlier tools use it weakly and rarely check that safety was truly kept.

AdaTrans maps compiler errors to repair strategies through retrieval, sorts diagnostics into semantic categories, and adjusts sampling per category while watching for stagnation. A validation pipeline then checks both compilation and functional equivalence. On 104 contest problems it reaches a mean compilation pass rate of 95.51 percent across runs, with a solve rate near 81 percent under fuzz testing. Unsafe code stays rare, at about 1.19 percent of files.
arxiv-2606-31806:
MacBride and colleagues report the first year of on-sky performance for the LSST Camera's CCD array at the Rubin Observatory. The focal plane holds 189 science CCDs in 21 raft modules, plus wavefront and guider sensors in corner rafts. Together they form the largest focal plane ever built, feeding the Legacy Survey of Space and Time.

Work covered the period from delivery in May 2024 through early operations. The team restored several CCDs hit by an electrical short and a faulty analog-to-digital converter. Readout timing was retuned as the survey strategy changed, and an active clearing mechanism added focal-plane safety. On-sky sensor features and global performance, they conclude, support a wide, fast, deep survey of the southern sky.
arxiv-2606-31906:
Ferrari and three others present GW, a Gödel modal logic evaluated over witnessed Kripke models. Gödel logics grade truth over the unit interval, suiting graded uncertainty and vagueness. In ordinary Gödel Kripke semantics, modal values come from infima and suprema over accessible worlds, and those bounds may never be attained by any concrete world.

Witnessed models require each modal value to be realized by an actual accessible world. That single demand removes the limit phenomena that blocked the finite model property, giving the semantics a constructive flavor. A sound and complete refutation calculus is given, along with a terminating backward proof search that generates countermodels. The finite model property for GW follows directly from the procedure.
arxiv-2608-00006:
Islam and co-authors study how retrieval can cut misinformation for small firms. Small and medium enterprises now use language models for questions and decisions. Hallucinated output can act as misinformation in that setting. It lowers user trust in the tools. Retrieval-augmented generation adds outside knowledge to the model's process.

They model two forms, VectorRAG and GraphRAG, for SME use. Tests spanned LLaMA, Mistral, and Qwen models. Scores covered useful replies, hallucination risk, and contextual fit. Human interpretation of outputs was also judged. Both RAG forms cut hallucinations and lifted reply quality, they report. The gains support more context-aware choices inside small firms.
arxiv-2608-00306:
Bossard, Bekri, and Destexhe review mean-field models that bridge receptors to whole-brain dynamics. Many drug and disease effects start at tiny scales. They are observed through population and whole-brain signals, though. Reductions across scales must keep key mechanisms while staying tractable. The review asks which mechanisms stay explicit and testable after reduction.

A receptor-aware adaptive mean field serves as the worked case. They trace it into conductance-based nodes coupled through the connectome. Rival strategies include neural masses, spiking models, and learned surrogates. Receptor kinetics and adaptation can stay manipulable across scales, they find. That rests on assumptions like Markovianity and population homogeneity. Node-local detail mainly shifts prefactors, while dense covariances change scaling class. Models should be judged by what they preserve, they argue.
arxiv-2608-00406:
Lei and co-authors present LOCUS-DT for indoor localization with digital twins. Indoor settings bring heavy blockage and multipath spread. Likelihood surfaces there turn multimodal, so one point estimate can mislead. Their framework treats snapshot localization as posterior inference over transmitter position. A ray-tracing digital twin of the known space anchors the method.

The twin generates synthetic multipath profiles for candidate spots. Those are compared with the measured channel profile. A learned scoring function compares a fixed set of dominant specular paths. It stays robust to twin model errors and channel estimation errors. Training spans an ensemble of environments for layout generalization. On a Sionna ray-tracing back end, LOCUS-DT captures sharp multimodal posteriors better than Gaussian benchmarks.
atkinson-thought-vibration-1906:
William Walker Atkinson was a Chicago lawyer turned New Thought writer who filled magazines and cheap manuals with his teaching. His Thought Vibration, published in 1906, explains the law of attraction in the mental world. It became New Thought's most circulated manual.

Atkinson teaches that thoughts are vibrations that draw like conditions toward the thinker, as a magnet draws iron filings. Fear attracts failure, he argues, while steady, cheerful expectation pulls success near. His plain chapters on focus, will, and habit read like a training course for the mind's hidden pull. His brisk, salesman-like tone helped the manual travel far beyond church circles.
barbara-blomberg-volume-06:
Court management takes over Volume 6 of Barbara Blomberg, the novel by Georg Ebers about a singer and an emperor. Ebers explains that the two men standing nearest to Emperor Charles now place no obstacle in Barbara's way. Even the Bishop of Arras shows a friendly spirit toward the affair, and often attends when she sings at the Golden Cross in Ratisbon.

Chapter XXV lays out the arrangement with care. Charles summons Barbara almost daily, but always at changing hours, so courtiers and citizens will believe her favor rests on her singing alone. Granvelle, his minister, loves music truly, yet also reckons how a woman close to the emperor might serve his own designs. Affection here is scheduled, disguised, and quietly used by everyone around it.
bennet-john-1806: Bennet, John, 1806. The Bennet entry. This book preserves that record. Its place in history is secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
bibliotheca-chemica-a-catalogue-of-the-a:
John Ferguson compiled this catalogue of the chemical library of James Young of Kelly and Durris, printed at Glasgow in 1906 for private distribution by Young's family, under his instructions. Young, a shale-oil millionaire and friend of Livingstone, had gathered the finest alchemical collection in Britain. Ferguson, Regius Professor of Chemistry at Glasgow, describes each book with a bibliographer's full apparatus.

Entries swell into biographies. Friedrich Roth-Scholtz, the Nürnberg bookseller, is followed from Halle in 1710 through service in shop after shop. In 1716 he became factor for the late Johann Daniel Tauber's business. Two years on he bought the Neuenhausen shop at Nordhausen and took Benjamin Wedel into partnership. Such lives of printers and collectors make the catalogue a history of the chemical book trade itself.
bibliotheca-chemica-vol-1-1906:
John Ferguson built the Bibliotheca Chemica as a list of one great store. James Young had amassed books on alchemy, chemistry, and drugs for years. Book One of the list came out in 1906. It runs from A to K in the names of the scribes.

Each head gives the full title, date, size, and notes on the book's worth. Rare tracts stand by the great names of the field in one run. Ferguson was a Glasgow chemist with a love of the old books. The list is still a chief tool for all who trace the old chemists.
blackwood-empty-house-1906:
Algernon Blackwood made his name with The Empty House and Other Ghost Stories in 1906. It was his first book of ghost tales. Two tales lead the set. One is The Empty House. The other is A Haunted Island.

Most tales turn on lone men in wild or lone places. Fear grows slow and quiet, from mood more than shock. The book set a high mark for ghost tales in its day. It also marked Blackwood as a key voice in weird prose. Blackwood knew woods, lakes, and lone camps from his own treks. That first hand feel for wild places gives each haunting real grit.
brood-of-the-witch-queen-pg19706:
Sax Rohmer's 1918 London print of his sorcery novel stands here in full, put out by C. Arthur Pearson. Thirty-one chapters line the contents page. Antony Ferrara heads the cast list of chapter names. Phantom hands, the Ring of Thoth, and rustling shadows crowd the early run.

Cairo pulls the tale east at its heart. The Mask of Set, a scorpion wind, and the Witch-Queen herself mark the mid-run. Dr. Cairn comes on the scene in chapter fourteen. Spiders' lair, bats, incense rites, and the Thug's cord fill the late run. High Priest Hortotef and the Book of Thoth close the list. A front note binds the tale to old records of sorcery in Egypt and in medieval Europe. Ferrara's powers, it holds, stay inside what those records claim for such arts.
bukhari-traditions-islamiques-houdas-mar:
Tome II of Les Traditions Islamiques, printed in 1906, continues Houdas and Marçais's French rendering of al-Bukhari's Sahih. The great hadith collection proceeds book by book through prayer, alms, pilgrimage, trade, and the daily rules of the faith. Each report carries its chain of transmitters, the isnad that guarantees it in Muslim scholarship.

The translators worked under the Imprimerie nationale, and their version stayed standard for French readers of Islam. Tome II holds the middle of the Prophet's example as the tradition preserves it: law, worship, and conduct in reported detail. The set's scale shows the weight Sunni Islam lays on this book.
cartier-memoir-baxter-1906:
James Phinney Baxter's Memoir of Jacques Cartier, from 1906, gathers the record of the French explorer who opened the St Lawrence river. Cartier sailed for France in 1534, 1535, and 1541, probing the great river and meeting the peoples of its shores. Baxter newly translated the voyage accounts and wrapped them in full commentary.

The documents here form the founding record of French Canada, from first landfalls to winter camps. Cartier's own words describe ice, scurvy, and wary trade with the river nations. Baxter's notes guide readers through names, places, and rival claims. The memoir stands as the standard English collection of Cartier's voyages, and the base text for study of Canada's beginnings.
cia-0000008006:
November 1950 brought a CIA survey of Indochina's current situation and its probable course. France's fight against the Viet Minh was in its fourth year, and communist China had just won its own civil war. That victory raised the stakes along Vietnam's northern border.

The paper takes stock of French forces, Viet Minh strength, and local politics across Vietnam, Laos, and Cambodia. It stands near the start of formal American analysis of the region. Later US policy grew from readings like this one, made when involvement was still mostly money and advice. The file marks an early page in that story.
cia-0000009706:
How non-American prisoners were treated in Viet Cong detention camps is studied in an August 1971 CIA paper. Most prisoners in the southern system were South Vietnamese soldiers and officials, not Americans. Their numbers ran into the thousands, and their stories were less often told.

A treatment study would weigh food, labor, punishment, and release chances as sources reported them. Such knowledge served both humane concern and hard planning about the enemy's system. The paper widens the captivity record beyond its American center. It preserves evidence that the prison war's largest group of victims was Vietnamese.
cia-0000009906:
Three United States Air Force pilots were imprisoned together, and another died, a September 1967 report covers. The heading joins the two facts in one breath, as the event likely joined them. Aircrews captured together often stayed together through the prison system.

Companions in captivity could confirm each other's survival across years of silence. When one of a group died, the others' accounts became his record. Officials therefore valued group reports for the cross-checks they allowed later. This file opens three prisoner cases and closes a fourth, all from a single reported incident in the autumn of 1967.
cia-0000012306:
An undated Helms memo to the Director of Central Intelligence, its year estimated as 1962, carries the Penkovsky correspondence into the crisis year. That year would define the colonel's legacy, when his reporting on Soviet missiles faced its supreme test over Cuba. The memo's missing date is itself a small clue to the hurried paperwork of those months.

The letter belongs to the prelude: the tense season before the world learned how close it had come. Its summit address shows the case still commanding the top. For readers, it is one of the floating pages that drift through the files, dated by context.
cia-0000012406:
Yoga was the cryptonym for the Penkovsky meetings' summer phase, and a record opens its second phase in London across July and August 1961. The colonel was back in the chair after weeks in Moscow. Summer sessions resumed the questioning where spring had left it, with new tasking answered and new material delivered from inside the Soviet military.

The summer phase proved as productive as the spring's, if less frantic. Its records run under the Yoga heading through the season. For readers, the page opens the operation's second act: the same source, the same city, and higher stakes.
cia-0000013606:
Panama's gathering crisis fills a CIA paper from October 1968, titled simply the situation in Panama. The isthmus was sliding toward a change of power that autumn. The National Guard's officers were biding their time as the elected government wobbled. Within days, the Guard seized power in a coup. It began the military rule that lasted two decades, under the commander the analysts were already marking in these pages.

The paper covers the storm as it gathered over the canal republic. It weighs the guard's ambitions against the politicians' weakness. For readers, it shows a coup being foreseen in outline, in the files of the power that owned the canal.
cia-0000013906: Official Viet Cong policy on prisoner treatment did not always match local feeling, and a CIA report dated November 3, 1967, takes up that gap. Orders from above could soften or harden as they reached a camp. The report weighs the clash between the written line and real views. That clash helps explain why camp life varied so much.
cia-0000015306: A letter to Donald Keyhoe from J. S. Harmon fills a CIA file dated March 5, 1958. Harmon thanks Keyhoe for his letter of March 1. Keyhoe kept up a steady stream of demands for the truth on saucers. Polite thanks and no new facts was the reply he most often got. The Harmon reply is held in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000022306: General Carter called a meeting to discuss Gary Powers' proposed writings, a CIA record dated May 5, 1962, reports. Marshall Carter was then the agency's deputy director. Powers, newly freed in a spy swap, had a book in mind, and his old employer cared what he wrote. The meeting shows the agency managing the story of its own pilot.
cia-0000039306:
Case number 12517 receives its photo comparison results in a CIA record dated November 5, 1970. An attached memo also mentions Thomas H. Pilkington in connection with the case. The record belongs to the MIA and POW identification work of the Vietnam War.

Inside are the findings for the numbered case, with the memo adding its own notes. Attached memos often carried the context that the bare result left out. Together they show how a single case file could hold two things at once. It held a laboratory judgment and the office discussion around it. Both were preserved on the same few pages for later readers.
cia-0000044506:
The archbishop supported the Jesuit position on the killing probe, in a CIA record dated April 6, 1990. By spring the probe had run for months without satisfying its critics. Church support gave the Jesuits' stance public and moral backing.

Inside, the archbishop's backing of the order's position is recorded. The Jesuits had pressed for a fuller and braver investigation. Standing with them cost the archbishop ease with the government. He accepted that cost in public, which his office rarely did without great cause. The file shows the church holding together under that strain, months after the murders, when public attention had moved on and steady pressure mattered most.
cia-0000044906:
Chile's FPMR issued a communique on the Haeberle kidnapping, in a CIA record dated July 2, 1986. The FPMR was an armed group fighting the Pinochet regime. A communique announcing a kidnapping was its claim of responsibility.

Inside, the group's statement on the seizure is preserved as issued. Urban guerrillas used such claims to prove they could still strike. Each one was read closely by the regime and by foreign watchers. A kidnapping claim announced reach, planning, and a safe house somewhere in the capital. The file holds the group's voice from 1986, in a long campaign of raids and seizures waged against a dictatorship that answered in kind.
cia-0000045206:
AFP reported that the mayor of Santo Domingo was asked to mediate in the Duarte kidnapping, in a CIA record dated September 2, 1985. Outside mediators were sought when direct talks stalled or burned. A mayor from the Dominican Republic was an unusual choice of broker.

Inside, the mediation appeal is recorded as the wire reported it. Bringing in a third party admits that the two sides cannot finish alone. It also widens the circle of people who know the talks' secrets. The file preserves the appeal at its making, a sign of how far the search for a trusted middleman had ranged that September.
cia-0000049006: The Salvadoran left planned burials for its six assassinated FDR leaders in 1980, and a CIA item from that year preserves the plans. The FDR was the political front allied with the guerrillas, and its leaders had been seized and murdered that November. In that war, funerals were demonstrations, and the plans show mourning being organized as protest.
cia-0000049206: A partly blacked-out CIA item from 1991 reports improvement in human rights abuses by the Salvadoran air force. Improvement was the word certification season ran on: each claimed step forward argued for continued American aid. The item survives in the Truth Commission files, where such claims were later checked against the dead.
cia-0000049306: The investigation of the Jesuit murders had stalled by 1990, and a CIA item from that year records the stall, kept with the Truth Commission records. A stalled case was not a dead one: pressure could restart it, and everyone in the file knew that too. The item preserves the pause that the case's friends refused to accept.
cia-0000049406: Election outlook in El Salvador is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000049406, dated February 2, 1984. The paper carries a Truth Commission note and looks ahead to a Salvadoran vote. Readers find a short declassified forecast item whose title states its purpose, part of the agency's regular political reporting on El Salvador during the war years.
cia-0000095206: A cable to Leopoldville about Congo covert action against an unidentified high official is declassified CIA document 0000095206, dated July 6, 1960. The target is described only as an unidentified high official. Readers get a short declassified cable record from the Congo's independence summer, its heading stating the action type while withholding the person's name.
cia-0000108006: Fifth Report to the President by the President's Board of Consultants on Foreig is the heading, cut off mid-word, on CIA document 0000108006, dated February 2, 1960. The title marks a series: this was the board's fifth report to the president. The board's full field breaks off at Foreig in the heading. The brief record preserves the break exactly as released.
cia-0000119206:
Also from November 1968, this CIA document lists locations of four camps holding American, Thai, and Philippine prisoners in Laos. The heading breaks off at the start of that word four, but a companion document from the same month covers the same ground. Together they map one corner of the Laos camp system.

Camp locations were working knowledge for anyone planning rescues or tracking the missing. In Laos, where the war was officially secret, even basic facts about prisoners were hard won. The document preserves the agency's map of those four sites as its sources described them. It was part of the long effort to account for allied men held beyond Vietnam's borders.
cia-0000119706:
A February 1953 CIA paper forecasts probable developments in Egypt. The 1952 revolution had ended the monarchy, and Generals Naguib and Nasser were circling each other for control of the new state. Within two years Nasser would push Naguib aside and rule alone.

The paper tries to read that contest and Egypt's likely course. Egypt was the Arab world's largest state, and its direction shaped the whole region's politics. For readers, the forecast is a snapshot of judgment at a hinge moment. It was made when the revolution's winner was not yet clear, and its long rule over Egypt still lay in the future.
cia-0000124306: A November 1950 CIA document reports on American prisoners of war at Mukden and Erhmienpa, holding sites in Manchuria. The Korean War was then five months old, and the prisoner question was only beginning. The paper records some of the earliest traces of captured men. Early traces were precious because the first winter of captivity was the deadliest, and any confirmed location gave the tracing effort a place to begin asking questions.
cia-0000132306: Jordan denying a breach of the United Nations arms embargo leads Situation Report 616. The report belongs to the CIA's Iraq-Kuwait series and is dated January 4, 1991. Its headline breaks off after the denial. Jordan sat caught between Iraq and the coalition and had to walk a careful line. The short report records the denial as part of the daily political watch on the crisis.
cia-0000132506:
Two weeks into Kennedy's presidency, on February 4, 1961, the CIA produced this briefing on Cuba. An exile invasion force was taking shape, and the agency was gathering the intelligence to support it. Cuba reporting was being written for men weighing an attack.

Papers like this one tracked the island's politics and defenses during the run-up to the Bay of Pigs. Several Cuba briefings carry the same February 4 date, a sign of how fast the reporting cycle had become. Preserved from the CIA Reading Room, the text lets readers sit inside that pre-invasion information stream.
cia-0000132606: Relations between Yugoslavia and Cuba fill item 1 of a CIA general series dated July 1, 1960. Tito's Yugoslavia followed its own course inside the communist world, apart from Moscow. Havana courted Belgrade as one more patron standing outside the Kremlin's shadow. The short item covers that relationship and what each side hoped to gain from it.
cia-0000135806: A cable asking for guidance fills a CIA record dated May 1, 1954. The cable went to a senior representative whose name was deleted before release. Requests of this kind form the paper trail of command in a covert campaign. The field was asking headquarters what to do next in Guatemala. The short record keeps the request as it was sent that spring.
cia-0000136006: From 6 February 1954 comes a CIA routing sheet, since declassified, on courier and pouch information, carried on a routing sheet with a cable from Lincoln attached. In these files Lincoln names the field station of PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA plan to topple President Arbenz of Guatemala. What survives is the working paper itself, plain proof of how the mission was run from day to day.
cia-0000136206: A CIA cable dated 6 May 1954 deals with the availability of F-47 planes, called critical to the operation in the cable's own heading, in files since declassified. Lincoln was the station cryptonym for PBSUCCESS, the CIA operation against President Arbenz in Guatemala that ended in June 1954. Read on its own terms, the record shows the operation at work in its own words, with some names still blacked out.
cia-0000136306: Cable from Lincoln for Cadick and Broadfrost an Order: re Strike Mission is a declassified CIA cable dated 1954. The catalog title is unusually informative for this series: a sender signing as Lincoln, two recipients named Cadick and Broadfrost, and a message that gives an order about a strike mission. Names of that style were the working code names used inside agency traffic. The catalog adds nothing about the mission or its outcome. The cable survives as a brief piece of operational traffic, released through the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000136706: Dated 6 February 1961, a Spanish document from the declassified files of Brigade 2506. The exile brigade was in final training, its April landing in Cuba about ten weeks off. The catalog gives this item no subject heading. It is held in the original Spanish through the CIA Reading Room, one of the brigade's February records from the operation's last stretch of preparation.
cia-06786606:
Intelligence information cable, classed Confidential, gives a chronology of the Saigon-Gia Dinh situation from 0800 on 3 February to 2130 on 6 February 1968. The cable states the chronology was posted at the Combined Security Committee as events were reported. Later reporting showed a few entries held some inaccuracies, it warns.

The cable presents the chronology anyway, as a good picture of how the Viet Cong attack on Saigon-Gia Dinh developed. The first entry lifts the curfew from 0800 to 1400 on 3 February in the Saigon area, by precinct. Vehicles and bicycles were still barred from the streets, it notes. Middle entries report fighting at a bridge in the 8th precinct and a police sub-station partly collapsed. A police jeep with a machine gun was seized by the Viet Cong at the Hiep An Bridge.
cia-06841006:
Intelligence Memorandum dated 9 August 1993, from the Office of African and Latin American Analysis, is titled Liberia: War and Peace Through Taylor's Eyes. A summary states rebel leader Charles Taylor agreed to the recent Cotonou peace accord for two reasons. Economic problems pressed him, and he believed he could still win an election.

The memorandum assesses that Taylor would not hesitate to manipulate or scuttle the agreement if he felt he was losing ground. He was confident, it says, that Nigeria's weakening commitment to the ECOMOG force and disarray among other Liberian factions would work for him. He meant to keep a military option as insurance, the summary states. At the same time he saw American and United Nations involvement as critical to peace and recovery. That gave Washington some limited leverage to press him to keep the accord, the memorandum concludes.
cleopatra-volume-06:
Volume 6 of Cleopatra, by Georg Ebers, tightens the court intrigue around Queen Cleopatra in Alexandria. Ebers centers this stretch on Iras, the queen's sharp and jealous attendant. Barine, the woman Iras hates, is now held under guard in Charmian's rooms, and every hour of royal sleep becomes a chance to plot.

Chapter XIII follows Iras as she uses her mistress's rest to meet the Syrian Alexas and plan against her rival. Her old hope of seeing Barine crushed has hardened into open hatred. She even turns part of that anger on Charmian, her own kin, for standing in the way. Palace service here means watching doors, timing visits, and striking before the queen wakes and the guard returns.
conrad-mirror-of-sea-1906:
The Mirror of the Sea, published in 1906, is Conrad's book of memoir-essays on the sailing life he had left behind. After twenty years in the merchant service, he wrote of ships and the sea as a man speaks of a lost home.

The essays take up anchors, storms, the character of famous ships, and the fellowship of crews. 'The Fine Art' praises seamanship as a craft of hand and judgment. There is no plot here, only memory refined into prose of great beauty. Sailors and landsmen alike have kept it in print as the classic elegy for the age of sail.
constitution-brunei-2006:
Brunei, a small state on the island of Borneo, works under a constitution first issued in 1959 and hosted here with changes through 2006. Early parts cover the state religion and custom. Islam is the official faith, and Malay is the official language. Executive power, by the text's own terms, sits with the Sultan, who is both head of state and head of government.

The Sultan rules with the help of a Privy Council and a Council of Ministers that he appoints. A Legislative Council exists on paper, but its members are appointed and it met rarely for much of this period. Later parts cover finance, the public service, and citizenship. Real power stays with the palace throughout.
constitution-serbia-2006:
Serbia adopted this constitution in 2006, months after Montenegro left their shared state, and it is the text hosted here. Early parts give the principles of the charter and then human and minority rights and freedoms in detail. The preamble declares Kosovo and Metohija part of Serbia with wide self-rule, a claim Kosovo's own leaders reject, which keeps the text at the heart of a live dispute.

A president heads the state, while a prime minister leads the government. The National Assembly is the single lawmaking chamber. Serbian, in the Cyrillic script, is the official language. Later parts cover the economy and public finance, the powers of the republic, the courts, a Constitutional Court, and the provinces and towns. At 206 articles it is thorough.
contra-l-alchimia-e-gli-alchimisti-palin:
Contra l'alchimia e gli alchimisti, by Angelo Ingegneri, printed at Naples in 1606, is a palinode: a formal taking-back of the author's own earlier poem, the Argonautica. The same volume prints that poem with it, declared by copious marginal notes in the author's own hand. The dedication addresses Monsignor Girolamo Fosco, apostolic protonotary and secret almoner to His Holiness.

The Argonautica sings the oldest voyage for gold: Jason, Medea, and the winning of the golden fleece. Marginal summaries walk beside the verse, naming each turn of the story, the fortunate ship, the distant harbor, and the dangers overcome. Read against those margins, the poem serves its own retraction, an alchemy of gold retold only to be renounced.
contro-l-alchimia-e-gli-alchimisti-palin:
Contro l'alchimia e gli alchimisti, by Angelo Ingegneri, is the 1606 palinode of his Argonautica, dedicated to Monsignor Girolamo Fosco. In the dedication Ingegneri declines the usual motives. He does not write to honor a patron already most honored. He does not write to win reputation for a work incapable of it. He does not write to pay old debts, or to make new ones. He sends the discourse, he says, only as a token of love and reverence.

He had accompanied it, he explains, with a little poem to which the discourse has a particular relation. Both, he warns, are more curious than learned, and perhaps more pleasant than true, except where friends are named. The poem follows: an invocation over a fragile, too-daring prow, and the rich fleece already sighted in thought.
crowley-equinox-vol-1-no-06:
Number six of The Equinox followed in September 1911, the autumn half of the journal's year. Crowley kept his twice-yearly vow, and the numbers grew in size and range. London's occult readers knew the fat white volumes well by sight.

More rites and holy texts make their first bow in print in this issue. Essays and reviews around them show the order at talk with its age. Each number is a season's harvest of the young movement at work. This one documents the movement in its rich middle growth. The harvest here is rite, song, and polemic in turn.
dampier-voyages-vol1-1906:
William Dampier, an English buccaneer with a naturalist's eye, circled the globe in the late seventeenth century. Volume One of John Masefield's 1906 edition centers on his A New Voyage Round the World of 1697. Dampier was the first Englishman to explore Australia's coast.

Sailing with pirates in the Pacific, he still found time to note winds, plants, animals, and peoples. His plain, exact style shaped English travel writing and fed Swift and Defoe. Masefield, himself a sailor-poet, edits with love. Dampier's double life, pirate and pioneer of science, makes the volume a lasting pleasure. His word lists for native tongues were among the first printed in English.
dampier-voyages-vol2-1906:
Volume Two of Masefield's edition of Dampier's Voyages continues the buccaneer-naturalist's writings. Dampier's later works include his discourse on trade winds and his voyage to New Holland in 1699. The Royal Navy had by then given the old pirate a ship of his own.

His wind charts served sailors for a century, and his account of Australia's west coast was the first in English. Dampier describes strange animals and plants with a pioneer's patience. Masefield adds the supplement and the remaining voyages to complete the set. The volume shows why scientists, not only sailors, honored Dampier's name.
devereux-volume-06:
Book six of Lytton's Devereux fills this sixth volume, named The Retreat. The hero reaches St Petersburg as the Czar's death shakes the court. The Czarina, whose faith to her husband was more than suspected, bears the loss with fair calm, the tale dryly notes.

Jealousy between the English king and Russia makes the hero's wish to quit the imperial service look natural. His pardon from King George had come three years before. Catherine grants his dismissal in flattering terms, with a high order in honour of her famed feat. Montreuil's hidden plot, and a letter writ at his dictation on the uncle's altered plans, blacken the close. This file holds book six only.
doe-osti-17011135-vitrification-of-hanfo:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory issued this September 2026 report on turning Hanford tank waste into glass, a process called vitrification. Derek Dixon and seven coauthors studied waste from tank 241-AW-106, plus a matching fake waste, called a simulant. The work supports the plant being built to treat Hanford tank waste for disposal.

Actual waste was diluted with Columbia River water to a set sodium level, filtered, and treated by ion exchange to remove cesium. Glass forming chemicals and waste loading were set from published glass models. Small melter runs then tested how the feed melted, so odd behavior can be spotted before full plant runs begin.
doe-osti-3563284-final-technical-report-:
University of Delaware final report, by Kevin Solomon, covers genetic tools for anaerobic fungi that break down plant biomass, under award DE-SC0022206. The project ran from September 1, 2021 to January 31, 2026. Plant cell walls resist breakdown, which raises biofuel costs.

Anaerobic fungi carry strong natural enzymes for this job. One project strand paired the fungi with engineered yeast to make fragrances and fuels from farm residues. Multiomics studies mapped how the fungi control their breakdown genes. Talks at national meetings spread the results. Better fungal tools could cut pretreatment costs for biomass plants.
dreyer-history-planetary-systems-1906:
J. L. E. Dreyer published his History of the Planetary Systems in 1906. The subtitle carries the story from Thales to Kepler in one volume. Dreyer was a Danish astronomer and a leading historian of astronomy.

Greek spheres and epicycles give way slowly to medieval refinements here. Ptolemy's system receives full treatment as ancient astronomy's summit. Copernicus, Tycho, and Kepler then rebuild the heavens in the final chapters. Dreyer edited Tycho Brahe's complete works, which deepens his later chapters. The book became the classic history of ancient and medieval astronomy. Two thousand years of cosmology unfold in his single, lucid volume for students.
dunsany-time-and-the-gods-1906:
Dunsany's gods met their master in Time and the Gods, the sequel of 1906. Time stalks the deities of Pegana in these tales, and one by one they learn they can die. The cycle deepens the myth world of his first book.

Kings pray, gods war and fade, and a green slave god rises as old faiths fall. Dunsany writes of the death of gods with a poet's calm and awe. The book taught later fantasy how to let its gods end in beauty and in sorrow. It is the sadder and greater of the two Pegana books.
ehrlich-collected-studies-immunity-vol1-:
Paul Ehrlich was a German doctor and chemist who studied how the body defends itself against disease. Charles Bolduan translated his research papers into English. This first volume of the collected studies was published in 1906.

The papers present Ehrlich's side-chain theory, his picture of how cells make antibodies to fight toxins. With his co-workers he studied hemolysins, substances in blood that break down red blood cells. The contents list experiments on receptors, immune sera, and the chemical basis of immunity. This research laid groundwork for immunology, the science of body defense, and for modern drug design as well.
ernest-maltravers-volume-06:
Volume Six of Ernest Maltravers opens Book the Sixth of Edward Bulwer Lytton's novel on a fine July morning in London. A gentleman returned after years abroad walks from Regent's Park toward St. James's, counting his wasted youth. His old cronies have all done well: Tom Stevens is under-secretary of state, Pearson heads a school, and Ernest Maltravers has made a name.

The climber measures himself worth them all put together, and has done nothing. Meanwhile Cesarini woos Florence for her birth and wealth, as the text coldly notes, and Lumley Ferrers converses with eloquent lips while his cold heart plans every word. Two Euripides mottoes frame the book: gold the arch-exceller, and no yielding the path to knaves.
essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volume-06:
Friendship opens Volume 6 of Michel de Montaigne's Essays in Charles Cotton's translation, and the chapter still anchors the set. Montaigne (1533-1592) wrote it for Etienne de La Boetie, his dead friend and fellow judge. Their bond, he says, joined two souls into one. Few essays in French match its warmth or fame.

Sonnets by La Boetie follow, printed as a memorial to the young poet. Later chapters treat moderation, sober judgment about God's plans, and pleasures worth refusing even when they cost life itself. Cannibals, his famous study of Brazilians brought to France, asks why Europeans call others savage while staging cruel wars at home. Pieces on clothes, chance, government faults, Cato, mixed tears and laughter, and solitude round out the run. Start here for range: love, travel, politics, and private retreat share one questioning voice.
europmc-pmc10037406:
Kim, Kim, and Chung review how DNA escapes from mitochondria and switches on an immune alarm pathway, in a 2023 paper. DNA normally stays inside the cell nucleus and its mitochondria, the cell's powerhouses. DNA found loose in the cell is read as a danger sign, much like the DNA of an invading germ.

The authors trace the routes by which mitochondrial DNA leaks out. They explain how a sensor called cGAS then triggers the STING pathway and an immune response. The review links this alarm to infection defense, aging, and disease.
europmc-pmc10322706:
Kim and a large team reported a new drug in 2023 that blocks KRAS, a protein often changed in cancer. KRAS acts like a switch that tells cells to grow. When the switch sticks on, tumours can form. Past drugs could block just one form of the switch, called G12C.

The new drug from Kim binds KRAS when the switch is off, and it spares two close kin proteins. It stopped the switch from turning on in tests on many changed forms. Growth slowed only in cancer cells that held a changed KRAS. In mice, the drug shrank tumours with no loss of body weight.
europmc-pmc10860306:
Khan, Fatima, Aisha, and Malik review why cancer drugs stop working in this 2024 paper. Resistance is a core hurdle in cancer care. Some tumours resist from the start, while others learn to resist over time. Changes in genes, gene use, proteins, energy use, and the tumour's surroundings can all drive it.
