Binding is the art of fastening book leaves together. Covers of parchment, leather, or board complete it. The writer once bound his own book. Scrolls were joined by bands and wrapped in mantles. The oldest covers come from the Cairo Genizah. They overlap, with a pointed flap and straps. Yemenite Jews still use that style.

After printing, rich owners ornamented their books. Clasps and mountings came in gold and silver. Brides received prayer-books so adorned. Whole bindings of silver served as gifts in Italy. Pressed leather bore flowers and garlands. Jewish binders worked at Prague and in many ghettos.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-blois-3406:
Blois is a French town in Loir-et-Cher. In 1171 it became a scene of horror. A mayor's servant accused the Jews of murder. He claimed they crucified a Christian child at Passover. Count Theobald imprisoned the whole congregation. Ransom talks failed when a priest intervened.

The witness then faced a water test. He did not sink, so people believed him guilty. The Jews were condemned to death by fire. On May 26, 1171, they died singing "'Alenu." Pulcelina, once favored by the count, died too. R. Tam decreed the anniversary a fast-day. Four dirges kept the memory alive.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bonavoglio-hefe: Hefez Moses Bonavoglio of Messina was a Sicilian physician born at the end of the fourteenth century. He died in 1447. In 1428 seventeen Jewish communities of Sicily sent him to King Alfonso V. His task was to win repeal of anti-Jewish laws passed that year. He succeeded and won the king's favor. Alfonso made him his physician and counselor. Later he was chosen chief rabbi of Sicily.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bridle-3706:
Bridle in English Bibles renders three Hebrew words, used also for bit. The entry warns that those words seldom mean full horse head-gear. In many passages halter, a simple rope or leather strap, fits better.

No account of head-harness appears in the Hebrew Bible. Horses came late and served luxury more than work among Hebrews. Ox, ass, and mule did the daily labor, guided by a goad. Camels were led by a rope through a ring in the nostril. Simple bridles of twine and wooden bits were known, though. One Psalm word is better rendered muzzle, the entry argues at its close.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-capito-kopfel-w: Wolfgang Fabricius Capito, called Köpfel, was a German Hebrew scholar born at Hagenau, in Alsace, in 1478. He died in November, 1541. In 1515 he became professor of theology at Basel. Eight years later he was made provost of St. Thomas at Strasburg. He wrote a Hebrew grammar and several theological works. The notice is only three sentences long. It names no single work and gives no detail on his teaching or his role among the reformers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-casluhim-4106: Casluhim, in Genesis x. 14 and I Chronicles i. 12, are sons of Mizraim, hence part of the Egyptians. Scholars offered rival placements for them. Bochart linked them to the Colchians at the east end of the Black Sea, on an old claim that those people were Egyptians who had moved away. Knobel proposed the Casiotis, a desert coast tract by Lake Sirbonis. Ebers backed that view with a Coptic word origin. The entry finds that origin impossible and ends openly: nothing sure can be said about the name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cherkassy-polis: Cherkassy, in Polish Czerkasy, is a district town in the government of Kiev, in Russia. It stands on the right bank of the Dnieper, about 126 miles from Kiev. The town was a chief Cossack center from the early sixteenth century. Few Jews, mostly leaseholders, seem to have lived there early. The census of 1765 counts one Jew. By 1797 the town held 783 Jewish inhabitants. In 1898, out of 26,165 people in the town, 5,884 were Jews. Most were small traders, artisans, and day laborers. Many followed the local Ḥasidic rabbi.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-clavering-rober: Robert Clavering, bishop of Peterborough and a Christian Hebraist, was born in 1671 and died on July 21, 1747. From 1715 until his death he held the post of regius professor of Hebrew at Oxford. The entry records one publication. At Oxford in 1705 he brought out a rendering of two parts of Maimonides' Yad, the sections on Torah study and on repentance. Three reference works are named as the sources for these few facts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-council-of-jewi:
Council of Jewish Women grew out of the Congress of Jewish Women in Chicago in 1893. That congress sat within the World's Parliament of Religions at the Columbian Exposition. Sadie American urged the women to band together in a lasting union. Her resolution passed at the final session. The new National Council pledged work in religion, charity, and education for Judaism and humanity at large.

The article sets out the council's aims in full. Members would study Jewish history, literature, and customs. They would improve Sabbath schools and join social reform. Local sections, meetings, and study circles carried the plan out. The entry stresses that no single form of Judaism was imposed on members.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cup-of-benedict: Cup of Benediction is the cup of wine taken right after grace at the end of a meal. The Mishnah first states the rule for it. Wine after a meal is blessed by one person for the whole company. At Passover the third of the four cups fills this role. Later custom urged a man with only a little wine to save it for this cup. The one saying grace held the cup in his right hand. In northern lands, beer, mead, or spirits took wine's place.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-darmesteter-jam:
James Darmesteter was a French Orientalist born March 28, 1849, at Château-Salins in Lorraine, and he died October 19, 1894, at Paris. His family had been booksellers and bookbinders in Lorraine. After strong schooling in Paris, he won the Prix d'Honneur in 1867 and turned to Eastern languages and literature.

Darmesteter held the chair of Iranian languages at the Collège de France. In February 1886 he left for Bombay and spent thirteen months in India studying with Parsee scholars. His translation of the Avesta, the sacred books of Zoroastrianism, won the French Academy's Prix Biennal of twenty thousand francs in 1893. He also wrote widely on English literature, including work on Shakespeare.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dax-5006: Dax is a town in the department of Landes, France, with a population of 11,000, and this entry is short. It says the Jews living there were too few to form a congregation. On November 20, 1684, the Conseil d'Etat decreed the expulsion of the Jews from Dax. The list attached to that decree names only three Portuguese families: Fernandes, Flores, and Léon. The entry gives no earlier history of Jews in the town and names no other families or events.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dernburg-heinri:
Heinrich Dernburg was a German jurist born at Mayence on March 3, 1829, brother of Friedrich Dernburg. His family ties to the French Derenbourgs, the entry notes. He studied at Giessen and Berlin, graduating in 1851. That year he began teaching law at Heidelberg. Zurich called him in 1852, and Halle in 1862.

From 1873 Dernburg was professor of Roman and Prussian law at Berlin, and he sat in the Prussian upper house. His books cover the law of pledges, guardianship, and mortgages. His textbook of Prussian private law ran from 1871 to 1880. His "Pandekten" reached a sixth edition in 1900-01. The entry closes by noting that his father and the whole family became Christians.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dinhabah-5206: Dinhabah appears in the Old Testament as a city of Idumea. The entry calls it the capital of Idumea and the probable birthplace of Bela, son of Beor, king of Edom. It cites Genesis xxxvi. 32 and First Chronicles i. 43 for that link. The entry is only a few lines long. It adds that efforts to locate the Dinhabah of Scripture have so far been unsuccessful, so no site is named.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-drama-5306: Drama is a city of European Turkey, in the vilayet of Salonica, twenty-five miles from Serrès. The entry identifies it with the ancient Drabescus. Its small Jewish community was founded in 1860 by immigrants from Serrès and Monastir. The community keeps a synagogue and a boys' school with fifty pupils. The entry counts sixty-two Jewish families in a total population of 9,000. Most of those Jews, apart from a few well-to-do families, live by pedling in nearby villages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eber-5406:
Eber is named as the ancestor who gave the Hebrews their name. He was a grandson of Arphaxad and great-grandson of Shem. His sons were Joktan, ancestor of the Arabs, and Peleg. From Peleg's line, five generations on, came Abram.

The word Eber means the region beyond. The entry argues it first named a district, not a man. Kindred names in Shem's list, like Arphaxad and Serug, are place names too. That reading explains why Abraham is tied so closely to Eber. Eber the land lay beyond the Euphrates, near Assyria, held longest by Shem's peoples.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eladah-r-v-elea: Eladah, also spelled Eleadah, appears in a family list for the tribe of Ephraim. The entry gives only a few facts about him. He was a son of Tahath and the father of a later Tahath. His name stands in the list in First Chronicles. A second list, in Numbers, does not name him. The entry adds one event from his life. Eladah died during a raid on the town of Gath. No dates, deeds, or words of his are given beyond that short record.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elon-5706: Elon is a name tied to three men in the Bible. The chief Elon was the tenth judge of Israel. He judged Israel for ten years in all. He died and was buried at Aijalon in Zebulun. The entry gives a second, critical view of the man. Elon may be no man at all, it says. He may be a clan of Zebulun dressed as a person. Two more Elons are a Hittite father-in-law of Esau and a son of Zebulun.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ephraim-ben-sam: France was home to Ephraim ben Samson, a Bible commentator who lived in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. His Perush al ha-Torah rests mostly on gematria and notarikon. Those are methods that read words by letter values and letter patterns. He followed Eleazar of Worms closely. The entry notes that he wrote the Genesis part before 1220. His commentary was printed at Leghorn in 1800. Azulai later used parts of it in Nahal Kedumim.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-euphemism-5906:
Euphemism is the swap of a harsh or blunt phrase for a softer, indirect one, and the entry gathers its Jewish uses. Bible and Talmud both use such swaps often. The rabbis praised fitting speech, saying a person should always use clean terms. Fear played a part too: an ill-omened word, they held, could bring the harm it named.

For dying, the Bible says a man rested with his fathers, or was gathered to his people. Blunt body terms are veiled, and cursing is at times written as blessing. The entry lists Talmudic names for the device, meaning pure expression or expression of honor. Later writing called it an expression of much light. Examples run through the long entry in groups.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-foa-foi-or-foy-:
Foa, also spelled Foi or Foy, is a French family that came from Italy in the eighteenth century. One branch was allowed to take the name Margfoy. Solomon Foa was the first of the line to settle at Bordeaux. His son David Ḥayyim Foy was a privileged mercer. In 1787 the parliament of Navarre let him settle at Pau. His son Israel bought the Jewish cemetery for that town. It was laid out in 1822.

At Bayonne and Bordeaux the name is spelled Foy. At Marseilles the form Foa has been kept. The Marseilles branch counts an explorer, Edmond Foa, among its members. Captains, commanders, and an engineer are also named from that side of the family. A long list of town records and histories closes this short family entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-folk-songs-2406:
Folk-songs are songs and ballads born among the common people and picturing common life. Jewish folk-songs exist in many tongues besides Hebrew and Judæo-German. Ladino is one of them. Traces of Hebrew folk-songs appear in the Talmud. It tells of girls dancing in the vineyards on set days and singing of good breeding over beauty. A scrap of a bridal song praises a bride with no paint and no curls.

A hymn for the close of the Sabbath tells of a poor pious man made rich by Elijah. Judæo-German songs lived in Germany and among Yiddish speakers in Russia and Poland. Some are reworkings of German or Slavonic songs, but their spirit is Jewish. One girl's song laments that all girls marry while she stays alone. One named collection holds 375 Yiddish folk-songs.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-frankfort-on-th:
Frankfort-on-the-Main is a city in the Prussian province of Hesse-Nassau. The start of its Jewish community is uncertain. Probably no Jews lived there during the first two Crusades, since the city is not named among places of persecution. A Frankfort Jew is mentioned in a house sale at Cologne between 1175 and 1191. The first firm news dates from 1241. On May 24 of that year 180 Hebrews were killed in a riot, and many fled.

The Jews owed money duties to emperor, archbishop, and city alike. During the Black Death of 1349 they were persecuted again. The long entry follows the Judengasse, its cemetery of more than five acres, and its hospitals. A new age began at the end of the eighteenth century. In 1796 Jews got leave to live among Christians. Full civic equality came in 1811, was cut back in 1816, and was made complete in 1864.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-frug-semion-gri:
Semion Grigoryevich Frug, a Russian writer and poet born in 1860, came from the Jewish farm colony of Bobrovy-Kut in Kherson. His first poem appeared in Razsvyet in 1880 and drew public notice. In 1881 he moved to St. Petersburg. He wrote for many Jewish journals, often under false names such as Ben-Zvi.

His first book of poems came out in 1885, with a second in 1887. Critics prized the lyric force of his verse. He also wrote Yiddish poems, sketches of people he had met, and Zionist songs printed in 1902. By 1903 he lived in St. Petersburg and wrote for the weekly Budushchnost.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ghiron-6606:
Ghiron is an old family first from Gerona in Spain, known in Hebrew as the Geronim. It has bred many rabbis. Jacob Yakkir Ghiron, born at Adrianople in 1813, died at Jerusalem in February 1874. A strong Talmudist, he became rabbi at Adrianople in 1835. In 1863 he was chosen chief rabbi of Constantinople.

In that post he brought in reforms and drew up a charter for the communities. The sultan approved it and gave him honors. He had the Adrianople synagogue rebuilt after it burned in 1846. In 1872 he gave up office to end his days in Jerusalem. There he founded a house of study. His book Abir Yaakob came out at Salonica in 1838.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-goodman-tobias-:
Tobias Goodman was an English preacher and author. He died after 1824. He ranks among the earliest English preachers of London's Jewish community. He was reader and minister at the Denmark Court Synagogue. That house was the first synagogue in London's West End. There, as early as 1817, he preached in English on Princess Charlotte's death. It is the earliest English sermon on record from a London synagogue.

Later he preached on George III's death in 1820. By about 1824 he preached English sermons each Sabbath at Rosemary Lane. He also worked outside London. At Liverpool's Seel Street Synagogue he gave his discourse "The Faith of Israel" in 1819. That text grew into a book in 1834. He had earlier translated a work by Jedaiah Bedersi in 1806.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-grunfeld-heinri:
Heinrich Grünfeld was an Austrian violoncellist. He was born at Prague on April 21, 1855. He was a brother of Alfred Grünfeld, the pianist. The Prague Conservatorium trained him. In 1876 he went to Berlin and taught eight years at the Neue Akademie der Tonkunst.

With Xaver Scharwenka and Gustav Holländer he ran trio evenings that grew very popular. The entry then gives an odd date for his next honor. It says he was made court violoncellist to King William of Prussia in 1866. That date sits oddly with his Berlin move of 1876, but it is the date the entry prints.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hadassi-judah-b:
Judah ben Elijah Hadassi was a Karaite scholar, controversialist, and liturgist who worked at Constantinople in the middle of the twelfth century. His byname "ha-Abel" means "mourner for Zion." Little of his life is known beyond his schooling under his elder brother Nathan. He knew Hebrew grammar, Masorah, theology, and philosophy, and read Arabic and Greek well.

His fame rests on "Eshkol ha-Kofer," begun on Oct. 9, 1148. Written in rimed prose, it treats the commandments under the heads of the Ten Words, arguing that all law grows out of the Decalogue. Its first section swells into a survey of the science of his day, from astronomy to folk-lore. Later parts attack Christians, Rabbinites, and other sects, and set out his own rules of grammar and reading of Scripture.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hanina-hananiah: Hanina (Hananiah) b. Antigonus was a tanna of priestly descent, a contemporary of Akiba and Ishmael. He may have seen the Temple service, since he knew the fluters before the altar, and many laws of the priests and Temple precedents survive in his name. He is also cited on marital questions. Only one haggadah is his, on the precept of the fringes and the promise that ten men will take hold of a Jew's skirt, saying, "We will go with you."
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hasdai-ben-solo: Hasdai ben Solomon was a Spanish rabbi, probably born in Tudela. He studied at Barcelona under Nissim Gerondi. A friend called him the Spanish worthy. He served as rabbi until 1379, when plague struck Tudela. Still single, he moved to Valencia and took a rabbinic post there. In strict piety he fought ritual changes made by a rabbi in Pamplona. He also opposed reading the Esther scroll in Spanish. At Fraga he tried, and failed, to change a local prayer custom.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-heliopolis-on-1:
Heliopolis, also called On, was an Egyptian city. Joseph's father-in-law came from there, as Genesis tells. The entry calls it perhaps the oldest of all Egyptian cities, and the most sacred around 3000 before the common era. Its god was a form of the sun-god, and its name means house of the sun.

Its temples were famed for size and beauty, its priests for learning. Herodotus praised that learning. In politics the city counted for little, though trade on the Syria road mattered. Jewish settlements stood in and around it. By the Arab age it lay deserted, with one obelisk left among its ruins.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-herodias-7606:
Herodias was a daughter of Aristobulus and Berenice, and a granddaughter of Herod I. She first married her uncle Herod and lived with him in Rome. Their daughter was Salome. Herod Antipas later fell in love with her during a visit to Rome.

Antipas divorced his first wife and married Herodias, against Jewish law as the entry states. That marriage led to war with Aretas and later to Antipas seeking a royal title, which caused his fall. Herodias chose exile with him over comfort with her brother. The Gospels blame her for John the Baptist's death, a point Josephus does not confirm.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hillel-b-samuel: Hillel, son of Samuel and grandson of Naḥman in the entry's naming, was a Palestinian haggadist of the fourth century. His father may have been his teacher, the entry suggests. He also learned from others, among them Levi, son of Ḥama. One saying of his gives a teacher's merit as five times a pupil's in heaven's sight. He proves it from a verse in Canticles about a thousand and two hundred. Elsewhere he uses Nehemiah to argue that present authorities deserve the same respect once shown to ancients.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hofmann-isaak-l:
Isaak Löw, Edler von Hofmannsthal, born June 10, 1759, at Prostiebor in Bohemia, was an Austrian merchant. Born to poor parents who had fled famine, he studied at Prague from age thirteen. He then taught in the house of a rich tobacco farmer.

Hofmann kept his employer's books and followed him to Vienna in 1788. By 1794 he was sole head of the firm. From 1796 he built a silk business and farmed Hungary's silk monopoly from 1802. The house held that right nearly fifty years. He led Vienna's Jewish community for decades and founded its poor institute in 1822. The emperor knighted him in 1835. He died at Vienna on Dec. 12, 1849.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-host-desecratio:
Desecration of the host was a charge often laid against Jews in the Middle Ages. The host is the sacred wafer of the mass. Jews were said to steal it, pierce it, and make it bleed. On weak testimony or confessions won by torture, accused Jews were tried and burned, sometimes with their whole community.

The charge arose after the doctrine of transubstantiation was recognized in 1215. The first firm case came at Belitz in 1243, where the Jews were burned. Long lists of later cases follow across Europe. A few rulers and Luther rejected the charge. A lecture of 1848 explained red growths on old wafers as the likely source of bleeding-host tales.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ibn-migas-josep:
Joseph ben Meir ha-Levi ibn Migas was a Spanish rabbi who headed the school at Lucena. Born in 1077, he died at Lucena in 1141. He went to Lucena at twelve and studied fourteen years under Isaac Alfasi. On his deathbed in 1103 Alfasi passed over his own son and named Joseph, then twenty-six, to lead the academy.

Joseph held that post for thirty-eight quiet years. Judah ha-Levi marked his accession and his wedding with poems. Two hundred and fourteen of his responsa were later gathered and printed. His Talmud notes survive in scraps quoted by others. Maimonides praised his learning as unmatched. The old claim that he taught Maimonides is an error, since the boy was six when Joseph died.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-israelitische-a:
The Israelitische Allianz zu Wien was a society for the advancement of Jewish interests, founded at Vienna in 1872 by Joseph Ritter von Wertheimer. It was patterned on the Alliance Israélite Universelle of Paris. Oppression of the Jews in Rumania and attacks in Asiatic Turkey moved its founding. Its organizers, among them Ignatz Kuranda and Leopold Kompert, set two aims: better Jewish schooling in Austria and Galicia, and real relief for Jews still suffering for their race.

Relief soon took the larger share. The society spent about 862,000 crowns on persecuted Russian Jews in 1881-83 and about 367,000 crowns on Rumanian emigrants in 1900-02. A Vienna conference in 1882 put it in charge of the Russian relief work for all of western Europe. It raised about 220,000 crowns for the Kishinef massacre victims. In Galicia its school work ran through the Baron de Hirsch Fund from 1892.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacob-ben-morde: Jacob ben Mordecai, called Jacob of Fulda, was a German scholar of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Banished from his native Fulda, he settled at Schwerin. He wrote "Tikkun Sheloshah Mishmarot" (1691), prayers for the three watches of the night, drawn mainly from the Zohar. His wife Laza translated it into Judaeo-German and added a preface; Benjacob gives the authorship to her. His second work, "Shoshannat Ya'akob" (Amsterdam, 1706), treats palm-reading, face-reading, and astrology.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jeschurun-8606: Jeschurun was a periodical published first at Frankfort-on-the-Main and later at Hanover. Samson Raphael Hirsch founded it in October 1854 and issued it as a monthly until 1870. From 1882 to 1886 his son Isaac Hirsch brought it out as a weekly. It was then merged into Der Israelit, another paper. The short entry ends with its religious stance: the journal stood for an ultra-Orthodox position. No writers, debates, or sample contents are named.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joel-b-judah-se: Joel ben Judah Selki ha-Levi, whose surname Lämmel may be a later addition, wrote a book called Dibre ha-Iggeret. It tells, in the verse style of its day, of the suffering of the Jews of Glogau when Prussian forces besieged that town in the winter of 1740-41. The book came out in 1741 at an unknown place and grew so rare that many book men never saw it. It was reprinted at Cracow in 1895 with a better known tale of woe.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseph-8806:
Joseph was a leading Jewish family that settled in Canada near the end of the eighteenth century. The family traced back to Naphtali Joseph, of an Anglo-Jewish line from the Netherlands. Henry Joseph, born in London in 1775, reached Canada in 1790 and built trading posts from Hudson's Bay to Quebec.

The entry profiles seven members across three generations. Henry's sons and grandsons led banks, steamship lines, railways, and telegraph firms. Abraham Joseph served on the Quebec city council and in its light infantry. Gershom Joseph became the first Canadian Israelite named a queen's counsel, in 1892. Jesse Joseph set up a direct ship line between Antwerp and Montreal. Several men also led Montreal's Spanish and Portuguese synagogue.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joshua-jehoshua:
Joshua, in Hebrew Yehoshua, was the son of Nun and the servant and successor of Moses. An Ephraimite first named Hoshea, he was renamed by Moses. He first stands out leading picked troops against the Amalekites in the desert. He guarded the Tabernacle and stood by Moses when Eldad and Medad prophesied in the camp.

As one of the spies sent into Canaan, he and Caleb alone urged trust and faced down a frightened crowd. For that faith the two alone of their age group were promised entry into the land. The long entry traces his life in Bible data and in rabbinic legend, then turns to other men of the same name, down to the high priest of the return from exile.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judah-ha-levi-b: Judan, or Judah ha-Levi ben Shalom, was a Palestinian amora of the fourth generation, in the second half of the fourth century. Few of his legal rulings stand in the Jerusalem Talmud, and he lost recorded clashes with Hananiah and Mattaniah. His name appears far more often in tales and teachings. One saying of his holds that God rewards good deeds, but blesses even those with none to their credit, out of sheer love. Another retells how Joseph, tempted, saw his father's face and held firm.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ka-b-al-ashraf-:
Ka'b al-Ashraf was a Jewish poet of Medina and a fierce enemy of Mohammed. His father was an Arab of the family of Nabhan, while his mother was a Jewess of the Banu al-Naḍir. Raised in his mother's family and faith after his father's early death, he is said by tradition to have once professed Islam before turning against it.

After the battle of Badr, Ka'b wrote poems that mourned the Meccan defeat and urged the Ḳuraish to take revenge. Mohammed ordered him killed, and Mohammed b. Maslamah entered his house on a pretext and murdered him. The entry weighs the charges made against him by Moslem writers and notes that their truth is open to doubt.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-khaibar-4206:
Khaibar was a fortified town of Arabia, in the district of Hejaz. It lay four days' journey northwest of Medina. In Mohammed's time the name covered a whole province. Various Jewish tribes lived there. Tales tie their coming to the days of Moses, of Saul, or of David. One sober guess makes them heirs of Jonadab b. Rechab.

The Jews of Khaibar held seven fortresses against Bedouin raids. In 628 Mohammed invaded the district. The Jews fell back to their strongholds and fought hard. The fort of Ḳamuṣ held out for two months. At last they gave up, but stayed on by paying tribute. About 640 the calif Omar broke the pact and drove them out. Later reports of a great Jewish city there are doubted by the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-krauss-samuel-9: Samuel Krauss, a Hungarian philologist and historian born at Ukk on Feb. 18, 1866, studied in Talmud schools before teaching in small villages. He entered the Budapest rabbinical seminary in 1884 and graduated in 1889. Study at Berlin and Giessen brought a doctorate in 1893. In 1894 he became professor of Hebrew at the Budapest teachers' seminary and was ordained rabbi. His chief work treats Greek and Latin loan words in Talmud, Midrash, and Targum, in two volumes dated 1898-99. A life of Jesus from Jewish sources followed in 1902.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lee-sidney-9706: Sidney Lee, an English editor born in London on Dec. 5, 1859, was schooled at the City of London School and Balliol College, Oxford. He joined the Dictionary of National Biography as assistant editor for its first twenty-one volumes, dated 1881-90. Joint editor and then sole editor followed; he closed the whole work in 1903. An honorary doctorate came in 1900. His lives of William Shakespeare in 1898 and Queen Victoria in 1902 stand as standard works. He toured America lecturing in 1903.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-leontopolis-gre:
Leontopolis, Greek for Lion City, was a place in the nome of Heliopolis in Egypt, 180 stadia from Memphis. It held a Jewish sanctuary. The entry calls it the only one outside Jerusalem where sacrifices were offered. Only Josephus gives a full account of this temple; the Talmudic reports are confused.

Josephus tells two tales of its founding. One names Onias III as builder. The other, which the entry finds more likely, names his son, who fled to Alexandria after his father's murder in 171 B.C. King Ptolemy VI let the youth build a shrine like Jerusalem's, with priests and Levites of his own race. Onias pointed to a prophecy in Isaiah as his warrant.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levi-ben-abraha:
Levi ben Abraham ben Hayyim was a French encyclopedist of Provence. He was born at Villefranche-de-Confluent between 1240 and 1250. He died near Arles soon after 1315. He came from a learned family. His father was a synagogue poet and rabbi at Narbonne.

Levi led the liberal side in the Provence fight over the study of secular sciences. He taught tongues and lectured at Montpellier from 1276 to earn a scant living. Hosts in Narbonne and Beziers sheltered him, then bowed to pressure from the orthodox party. He was banned by that party. When the fight ended in 1315, he found rest at Arles. He was the grandfather, on the mother's side, of Levi ben Gershon.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levy-nathan-990:
Nathan Levy founded the first Jewish cemetery in Philadelphia. He was born in February 1704 and died in Philadelphia on Dec. 23, 1753. He likely came from New York, where a merchant of his name belonged to Shearith Israel in 1730. In Philadelphia he ran a general commission business with David Franks.

On Sept. 25, 1740, Levy got a grant of thirty feet square for a burying place. In 1752 he added the lot next to it. He meant the ground for the Jews of the city, not for his family alone. Shots fired at the ground led him to wall it in brick in 1751. He was buried there himself, and the plot now belongs to Congregation Mickvé Israel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lipman-clara-10: Clara Lipman was an American actress born in Chicago. She made her stage debut with Modjeska in 1888 and then played young lead roles in other companies. She created the main role in Incog in 1891 and played Julie Bon Bon in The Girl from Paris in 1898. With her husband, Louis Mann, she starred for five years in several plays. She left the stage during the 1902-3 season after an injury to one of her arms. She also wrote a play called Pepi in 1898.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lying-hebr-shak:
Lying, defined as telling a falsehood with intent to deceive, is treated in a Jewish Encyclopedia article of 1906 by Kaufmann Kohler. The entry works through four Hebrew words for falsehood. It gathers what Jewish sources say about the sin across many centuries. The tone throughout is one of strong condemnation.

The article first draws on the Bible. The Law commands keeping far from a false matter and forbids dealing falsely with one another. False witness stands among the crimes named in the Ten Commandments. Psalms and prophets call lying an offense against a God who does not lie. Rabbinic teaching then sharpens the point. Ben Sira warns that the habit of lying is worse than theft, since it brings ruin and disgrace. The Rabbis taught that God's seal is truth, and that liars cannot behold God's majesty. The entry serves as a compact survey of Jewish ethics on speech.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-maison-karl-103:
Karl Maison, a Bavarian merchant and deputy, receives an entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Oberdorf, Wurttemberg, on September 18, 1840, he was trained for business at Offenbach. At twenty-four he became a partner in the Munich firm of A. Maison. He died at Munich on September 29, 1896.

The article records his rise in Bavarian commercial life. In 1871 he was appointed a commercial councilor. Four years later he joined the Upper Bavarian Chamber of Commerce and Manufacture. He later directed that body and served as consul for Denmark and for Sweden-Norway. From 1887 to 1896 he represented Munich in the Chamber of Deputies. The short entry preserves a Jewish businessman who moved from a family firm into diplomacy and parliament.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-margolis-isaac-:
Isaac ben Eliah Margolis, a Russo-Polish rabbi and author, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born in Kalvariya, Russian Poland, in 1842, he descended from Yom-Tob Lipmann Heller of Prague. His youth went to Talmud study. Business reverses and zealots made his life at Meretz unpleasant. He died in New York in 1887.

The article follows him from tutoring to the pulpit. At Kovno he taught in the house of Ezekiel Jaffe. Later he became rabbi of Druskeniki in the Grodno government. In 1884 he emigrated to the United States and led New York's Congregation Anshe-Kalvariya. His books defend the Talmud against its critics. One answers Lilienblum's attacks by name. Another gathers Talmudic and Midrashic legends in elegant Hebrew. He also wrote widely for the Hebrew periodicals of his day. The entry preserves a defender of tradition who carried the fight to America.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-may-lewis-10506:
Cyrus Adler and Joseph Silverman profile Lewis May, an American merchant and banker, in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in Worms on September 23, 1823. He came to the United States in 1840 and set up his own business at Shreveport, Louisiana, in 1845. A partnership formed in 1850 carried his trade to San Francisco and Portland, Oregon, and then to New York, where he settled in 1856. He died at Dobbs Ferry, New York, on July 22, 1897.

In 1869 May left trade and founded the banking firm of May and King. The entry gives equal space to his communal record. He served nineteen years as treasurer and director of Mount Sinai Hospital and was first president of the Young Men's Hebrew Association. He was also trustee and president of Temple Emanu-El for thirty-three years. The temple honored him with a testimonial in 1888 and a memorial window after his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-melo-david-aben:
David Abenatar Melo, a Spanish rabbi and poet broken and remade by the Inquisition, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Richard Gottheil and William Milwitzky. Born in Spain about 1550, he translated some of the Psalms into Spanish verse, and the work itself drew the Inquisition's suspicion. He was imprisoned and tortured for several years before his acquittal in 1611, whereupon he left Spain for Amsterdam.

In Amsterdam his gifts found their public. He won a reputation as a stylist and scholar, joined the literary academy "De los Pintos," and was appointed rabbi of the Portuguese synagogue Bet Yisrael. The entry notes that his verses keep returning to the tortures he endured in prison, so that his poetry doubles as testimony. Short as it is, the notice preserves one of the starkest literary biographies of the Sephardic diaspora.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-midrash-haggada:
Midrash Haggadah is the great body of rabbinic storytelling and moral teaching built around the Bible's non-legal passages. Isidore Singer and J. Theodor map the whole field in a long Jewish Encyclopedia article of 1906. It opens with a general statement, then sorts the works by age and kind, from the tannaitic collections onward.

The survey moves through the earliest verse-by-verse works such as Bereshit Rabbah, then the homiletic midrashim preached around the holidays, from the Pesikta to Tanhuma. Separate sections treat the midrashim on Canticles, Ruth, Ecclesiastes, and Esther, and special books like Pirke Rabbi Eliezer. It closes with the medieval anthologies, Yalkut Shimoni and Midrash ha-Gadol, that preserved so much of the rest.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-miedzyrzecz-mes:
Miedzyrzecz, also called Meseritz, was a town in Russian Poland near Warsaw where Jews formed two-thirds of the people: 9,000 of 13,681 residents in 1904. Herman Rosenthal and Judah David Eisenstein wrote its Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. Jewish settlement probably began in the sixteenth century, with families arriving from Germany, especially Frankfurt.

The article says Jews controlled the town's business, and its signature industry was making bristles for export to Germany, work introduced by Moses Michel Migdal. A stone synagogue seating about 3,000 rose around 1800 with help from Count Potocki, and the town supported a Talmud Torah and a yeshivah. Its emigrants founded the Yesod ha-Ma'alah colony near Safed in 1885, every settler a Miedzyrzecz Jew.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mirror-10106:
The mirror of the ancient world was polished metal, not glass. Joseph Jacobs explains it in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Egypt's mirrors were brass. Exodus mentions them at the tabernacle. Job compares the sky to a molten mirror. Isaiah lists hand-mirrors among the ornaments of the daughters of Zion. That identification is somewhat doubtful, though.

The rabbis regulated the object they knew. On the Sabbath one might look only into a mirror fixed to a wall. Men were discouraged from mirror-gazing altogether as effeminate. The patriarch's household, close to the government, was excused, though. The article closes with the mirror superstitions of eastern European Jews. The covering of mirrors is among them. Their origins, it finds, are hard to trace.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-modena-10906:
Modena, the Italian family, is a companion entry by Richard Gottheil and Ismar Elbogen in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It gathers the name-bearers the city produced. Its most shadowy member is David ben Abraham Modena. He is the supposed author of a Hebrew-Italian school dictionary, Dabar Ṭob. It was printed at Venice in three parallel columns: Hebrew, Italian, and German. Even his existence is doubted.

Its most solid member is David Zacuto Modena, a popular preacher and teacher of the nineteenth century. He wrote on circumcision customs and made a catechism of religion for children, with an Italian translation. He also wrote responsa and a prayer-book commentary for the Italian rite. He added notes on the Pentateuch and three hundred sermons. Only the first three works reached print, the entry notes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mordecai-ben-na:
Mordecai ben Nathan ben Eliakim ben Isaac of Strasburg was a French commentator. The full name matters, there being so many Mordecais. He lived at Corbeil at the end of the thirteenth century. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and J. S. Raisin give him three lines in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Those lines rest on Gross's Gallia Judaica.

His one recorded work is a commentary on the Sefer Miẓwot ha-Ḳaṭon, the SeMaḲ. That book is the popular digest of the commandments. His commentary was printed in the Constantinople edition of that book. Nothing else is told: no dates, no teachers, no other writings. The entry stands as a marker that a commentary existed and a man wrote it, in Corbeil, seven centuries ago.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-ben-josep:
Moses ben Joseph ha-Kohen was a liturgical poet of the late twelfth century. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach give him a short Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He may be the Moses ben Joseph who aided the oppressed Jews of the Rhineland in 1196.

One poem of his is described: a selihah, a prayer for forgiveness, called Arba'ah Abot Nezikin. In it the four kingdoms that oppressed Israel appear as four animals: the bear, the lion, the panther, and the swine. The image turns the history of exile into a beast fable inside a prayer. The entry is brief, but it fixes the poem and its striking picture.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mulberry-11206:
The mulberry, the fruit of the black mulberry tree, is the subject of a short Jewish Encyclopedia article by Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger. Surprisingly, the tree is not named in the Hebrew Old Testament. The mulberry trees some readers find in Second Samuel rest on a mistaken reading, the article says.

The blood of the mulberry, its dark red juice, does appear in First Maccabees. In post-biblical Hebrew the tree is called tut, a name kept in modern Arabic. The article describes the black, juicy berry, eaten fresh and made into a popular wine. The white mulberry, it notes, reached Palestine only long after the common era began.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nancy-hebr-1130:
Nancy, the old capital of Lorraine, had a Jewish community whose first settlement date is unknown. Richard Gottheil and S. Kahn wrote the Jewish Encyclopedia article on it. Expelled in the late fourteenth century, the Jews returned in the seventeenth. In 1721 Duke Leopold allowed one hundred eighty Jewish families to live and trade in Lorraine.

Later decrees squeezed them: a special quarter in 1736, with confiscation for Jews who stayed in their own houses. King Stanislaus eased the rules but kept the cap of one hundred eighty families. By 1789 the community was prosperous, and its own bishop admitted its services before the National Assembly. Berr Isaac Berr spoke there for full citizens' rights.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nebraska-11406:
Nebraska's Jews are traced from trail crossings to settled towns. Cyrus Adler and Abram Simon wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews crossed the state in the gold rush years. No record shows settlement before 1856. That year two men floated a house downriver to Omaha.

After the Civil War, settlement grew fast and sure. Germans and Hungarians came first, then Russians and Rumanians. By 1904 the state held about 3,800 Jews in all. Omaha alone held about 3,200 of them. Temple Israel there began in 1868. Orthodox congregations followed, plus hospitals and charity groups. Lincoln added a Reform congregation and its own cemetery.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-newcastle-upon-:
Newcastle-upon-Tyne is England's great coal-trading seaport. Joseph Jacobs and Isidore Harris wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The city held 214,803 people in all. About five hundred Jewish families lived among them. Jews are named there even before the expulsion.

The present community dates back only to about 1830. Seven residents then agreed to fund a burial ground. David Cohen's house hosted a service in 1832. The congregation was formally established that October. Its first regular synagogue rose in Temple street in 1838. Growth forced a second congregation by 1868. The two merged again in 1873, after long division. Their United Synagogue was consecrated in 1880. It counts 220 seat-holders at present.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-noveira-menahem:
Menahem Noveira was a rabbi and poet of Verona. The entry was written by the Editorial Board's Executive Committee and Peter Wiernik for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived in the eighteenth century in Italy. Hezekiah Mordecai Basan was his grandfather. Three responsa of his survive in print.

Those answers ride with his grandfather's Pene Yiẓḥaḳ. Noveira himself published that book at Mantua in 1744. His Yeme Temimim holds funeral sermons for two rabbis. Both men were Verona rabbis named Pincherle. Verse of his own clothes those sad occasions. He also ruled the founding of a free school. Another work marks a new Spanish synagogue's dedication. Death took him suddenly in Verona's synagogue. He fell on a Friday evening, chanting Lekah Dodi.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ottingen-11806:
Öttingen was a small realm and county in Germany. Isidore Singer and Schulim Ochser wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It spread to about one hundred square units of land. Two noble houses held the land in joint rule. Its towns held a string of small Jewish groups.

The first date for Jews of Öttingen is 1298. That year saw the Rindfleisch riots and deaths of Jews. In 1331 Emperor Ludwig gave a count a right there. He could use and hold his Jews with all rights. In 1342 a decree set a tax on each Jew. Each Jew past twelve paid gold at Christmas each year. In 1552 a count cast all Jews out of the land. They went to Esslingen and would not come back.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pardo-11906:
Pardo is a family that took its name from Prado, Castile. M. Franco, A. Porter, Schulim Ochser, and others wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Joseph Jacobs, Gotthard Deutsch, and E. Slijper helped as well. Most of its men won fame in the Levant, the east lands.

David Pardo stands first among the men of this line. He wrote notes on texts and hymns for prayer. He was born at Venice on March 29, 1719. He died at Jerusalem in the year 1792. His father Jacob was a rabbi in Venice town. When his studies were done, David left Venice for Ragusa. He lived some years at Sarajevo, in Bosnia, as a teacher. From there he went to Spalato, in Dalmatia. He was made chief rabbi of that town in time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-penitential-day:
The Penitential Days are the first ten days of Tishri. They run from New Year to the Day of Atonement. Cyrus Adler and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The season joins judgment with a chance to repent.

The Mishnah calls the first day a day of judgment. All creatures pass before God's throne like sheep. Yet the verdict is not sealed at once. Prayer and repentance can still change the outcome. Prayer books mark the days with special lines. One asks God to write the faithful in the book of life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-philipson-david:
David Philipson was an American Reform rabbi of Cincinnati. He was born at Wabash, Indiana, in 1862. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He trained at Hebrew Union College and Johns Hopkins.

Philipson first served a Baltimore pulpit for four years. In 1888 he moved to B'ne Israel in Cincinnati. He also taught preaching at the college there. Civic and Jewish boards filled his calendar for decades. His many books include The Jew in English Fiction. He helped edit the memoirs of Isaac Wise.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pleiades-12206:
The Pleiades hide in the Bible under the name Kimah. Kaufmann Kohler and Ludwig Blau wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Kimah appears three times, always beside Orion. The Greek version renders it Pleiades once. Job and Amos are the books that name it.

Aquila and the other translators follow that rendering. The Targum keeps the Hebrew word unchanged. Its root may mean to heap up, or to bind. The Talmud counts about a hundred stars there. The cluster shines in the northern sky. Its tail points west of the Milky Way.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-posner-david-be:
David ben Naphtali Herz Posner was a Polish compiler of sermons. The Editorial Board and Israel Berlin wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived in the mid seventeenth century. He stayed first at Posen and later at Krotoschin. His father was Naphtali Herz Spitz, a known scholar.

Posner's one book is called Yalkut Dawid, the Gatherings of David. It came out at Dyhernfurth in 1691. His father saw the book through the press. It gathers sermon matter on the Pentateuch. The matter comes from Talmud, Midrash, and later authors. One scholar linked him to a second David Posner. The entry says that link seems to be a mistake.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pruzhany-12406:
Pruzhany is a Russian town in the government of Grodno. Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews lived there by the end of the sixteenth century. Joel Sirkes held his first rabbinate in the town. Russian papers name the community first in 1583.

In 1628 the Council of Lithuania made a firm choice. Pruzhany was to be its fixed meeting place from then on. The choice seems not to have been kept, though. In 1817 the town held just 824 souls in all. It grew fast under Russian rule after that. The entry gives its rabbis, schools, and counts of souls.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabina-ii-b-hun:
Rabina the Second, son of Huna, was a Babylonian teacher of the seventh set. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He never knew his father, who died in his childhood. His mother told him his father's views in later years. The Talmud names those talks with his mother more than once.

After his father's death, his uncle took charge of him. That uncle was Rabina the First, his namesake. Rabina the Second sat as judge at Sura in time. He took that seat soon after the death of Ashi. The entry places him at the very end of an age. His set closed the line of the amoraim.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-raziel-book-of-:
The Book of Raziel is a collection of secret writings. Crawford Howell Toy and Ludwig Blau wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Its parts were not all written by one author. One hand likely compiled and edited them later.

The article notes that the book contradicts itself. One part says Raziel gave its contents to Adam. Another part says they were given to Noah. The book was said to be cut on sapphire stone. It passed down the generations until Solomon held it. Scholars divide it into three main parts. Later sections add creation lore and amulet formulas. The entry treats a famous magic book with care and doubt.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reuben-ben-stro:
Reuben ben Strobilus was a Jewish scholar of the second century. Isidore Singer and Samuel Krauss wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He took part in the public affairs of his time. His fame rests on a mission to Rome.

The article sets his work under Hadrian's persecutions. Rome had banned Sabbath observance, circumcision, and ritual baths. Reuben dressed his hair in Roman fashion to hide his identity. He argued that Jewish law would shrink Jewish numbers. Sabbath rest made Jews poor, he told officials. The bans were lifted on that sly reasoning. When his identity emerged, Rome restored the bans. The entry also records his sayings on sin. It shows wit used as a political tool.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rofe-daniel-b-s:
Daniel b. Solomon Rofe was an Italian physician and scholar of the fifteenth century. Isidore Singer and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Fano. Records mention him in 1430, 1448, and 1470.

The article lists several works from his pen. He wrote a super commentary on Ibn Ezra. He glossed Kimhi's commentaries on Amos, Micah, and Isaiah. Those copies were once held by Luzzatto and De Rossi. He made a synopsis of Ibn Ezra on Genesis with notes. Its title is Ha-Gersa ha-Aheret. He also wrote an account of his journey to Crete in 1473. Five sources support the entry. Readers meet a doctor who also explained Scripture closely.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rothenburg-1290:
Rothenburg is a town of Middle Franconia, in Bavaria, set on the river Tauber. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote its entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Jews had settled there by the early twelfth century at the latest.

A Würzburg document of 1119 already names a Jew of Rothenburg. In 1251 King Conrad IV mortgaged the town, Jews included, for 3,000 marks of silver. A century later Charles IV handed Rothenburg to the bishop of Würzburg. The gift covered the Jewish school, cemetery, and houses as property. It also freed the town's rulers from their duty to protect the Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-saint-petersbur:
Saint Petersburg, capital of Russia, long barred Jews from living there legally. Herman Rosenthal and J. G. Lipman wrote its entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. A few Jews reached it anyway under Elizabeth and Catherine II.

One early resident was Antonio Sanchez, a Spanish Jew of the Academy of Sciences. Under Catherine only three or four Jews lived in the capital. Numbers grew slowly until a substantial group stood there by 1800. By 1802 the Jews had formed a communal organization of their own. Lacking a cemetery, they shared ground with a Lutheran congregation by agreement.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-isaac-13:
Joseph Jacobs and Meldola de Sola wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Isaac Samuel. He was an English ḥazzan, the singer who leads synagogue prayer. Samuel was born in London on March 9, 1833. In 1860 he became minister of the Bristol congregation. In 1864 he became senior ḥazzan of the Bayswater Synagogue.

For forty-one years Samuel served as honorary secretary of the Jews' Deaf and Dumb Home. He helped put up its present building and later enlarge it. In 1888 he began teaching ḥazzanut, the cantor's art, at Jews' College. In 1892 the London County Council named him Jewish chaplain to the Colney Hatch Asylum. He was the only Jewish minister in England paid for such work in a non-sectarian institution.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sarmad-mohammed:
Isidore Singer and Louis H. Gray wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Mohammed Sa'id Sarmad. He was a Persian poet of Jewish birth. Sarmad flourished in the first half of the seventeenth century. He was born at Kashan, into a rabbinical family. Later he embraced Islam and went to India as a merchant.

At Tatta, Sarmad fell in love with a young Hindu named Abhichand. He converted the youth to a blend of Judaism and Islam. In 1647 he met Moshan Fani, author of the Dabistan, a survey of religions. Sarmad fed him material for a thin chapter on the Jews. His views mixed Hindu and Muslim ideas. Under Shah Jehan he was left alone. Aurangzeb, after taking the throne in 1658, charged him with heresy. Sarmad was put to death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schorr-joshua-h:
Wilhelm Bacher and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Joshua Heschel Schorr. He is commonly known as Osias Schorr. Schorr was a Galician Hebrew scholar, critic, and communal worker. He was born at Brody on May 22, 1814. He died there on September 2, 1895. His rich parents gave him only a scanty ḥeder schooling.

Schorr educated himself with fierce drive. Isaac Erter guided his study of Hebrew, Talmud, and languages. From Erter he took his fine style and his sarcasm. Luzzatto also shaped his critical bent. Schorr founded and ran the journal He-Ḥaluẓ. In it he attacked Ḥasidism and obscurantism with a pungent pen. He went further than his allies. He charged that the Gemara's rabbis often misread the Mishnah. About 1865 his wife and only son died. He lost most of his fortune too.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-seligsohn-max-1:
Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Max Seligsohn. He was a Russian-American Orientalist. Seligsohn was born in Russia on April 13, 1865. He trained for the rabbinate at Slutsk, in the government of Minsk. In 1888 he went to New York. He studied modern languages there until 1894.

At Paris, Seligsohn turned to Oriental languages, above all Semitics. He earned diplomas in 1897 and 1900. In 1898 the Alliance sent him toward Abyssinia to study the Falashas. Difficulties stopped him at Cairo, where he taught for eighteen months. In 1902 he joined the office editors of The Jewish Encyclopedia in New York. His Diwan of Tarafah renders an Arabic poet into French. He also translated an Arabic book on geomancy. His articles treat Judæo-Persian literature.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shapiro-aryeh-l:
Aryeh Löb ben Isaac Shapiro was a Polish rabbi and grammarian born in 1701. Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He came to Wilna as a child and married into a leading family there. His Talmud knowledge was wide, and he studied mathematics and logic too.

As a young man Shapiro wrote to a Karaite scholar at Troki. Later he served Wilna as judge and communal scribe. He wrote a double commentary on the tract Soferim, printed in 1732. A Hebrew grammar by him followed in 1741. One responsum of his, from 1754, survives in another rabbi's book. He died at Wilna in 1761, and the entry keeps his work in view.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-slouschz-david-:
David Solomon Slouschz was a Russian rabbi and preacher born at Odessa in 1852. Isidore Singer and M Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He studied at the yeshivah of Minsk from age fourteen. He then studied at the famed yeshivah of Volozhin. At nineteen he was ordained by Naphtali Hirsch Berlin.

In 1879 Slouschz became a preacher in an Odessa synagogue. Two years later he was made rabbi of Moldovanka. That was a Jewish district of Odessa itself. He was also a political Zionist for many years. He sat on the central committee of the Chovevei Zion. His Reshit Dawid, with responsa and sermons, appeared in 1881.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-soloveichik-jos:
Joseph Baer Soloveichik was a Russian Talmudist and rabbi born in 1820. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Julius Gottlieb wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Nieswish in Russia that year. At an early age he was sent to Volozhin to study. He later led the yeshivah at Minsk as Gershon's successor.

A family quarrel forced him to divorce his first wife. Bittered, he left Russia to study under Kluger at Brody. He traveled there as a hired carrier's assistant in hardship. He later served as rabbi at Slutzk, Warsaw, and Brisk. At Brisk in 1890 he founded a Palestine colonization society. His responsa, Bet ha-Levi, appeared in three parts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stein-am-anger-:
Stein-am-Anger, in Hungarian Szombathely, is a town in Hungary. Isidore Singer and Bela Bernstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Though now large, its Jewish community is of recent origin. In 1567 the town won a rule barring all but Catholics. Jews could rent shops but stay only by day.

Down to 1800 only three or four Jewish families lived there. The rest dwelt in outlying districts near the town. In 1830 they split from Rechnitz and formed their own community. The emancipation law of 1840 opened the city doors at last. In 1848 Jews there were attacked and plundered badly. A large, handsome temple was built in 1880.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sultansky-morde:
Mordecai Sultansky was a Karaite scholar born at Lutzk in 1785. Kaufmann Kohler and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He ranked among the leading Karaite scholars of his century. He served as hakam of Lutzk after his father. He later held the same office at Eupatoria in Crimea.

Sultansky wrote a Hebrew grammar printed at Eupatoria in 1857. A second book appeared there a year later. It argues against rabbinical philosophy and Hasidic mysticism. It also seeks to explain biblical teaching on angels. He died at Eupatoria before 1878, the entry notes. The brief record preserves a Karaite voice in print. Readers meet a sect leader who defended his tradition in Hebrew.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tal-tobias-1420:
Tobias Tal was a Dutch rabbi born at Amsterdam in 1847. Isidore Singer and E. Slijper wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He studied at Dünner's seminary and at Utrecht. He earned his doctorate there in 1874. He died at The Hague on October 24, 1898.

Tal served briefly as rabbi in Amsterdam first. In 1880 he became chief rabbi of Gelderland. He settled at Arnhem the next year. In 1895 The Hague called him as its chief rabbi. He defended the Talmud's ethics against a Leyden professor. Their printed dispute ran through 1880 and 1881. In 1898 he published a history of Dutch Jews. Queen Wilhelmina's private archives fed that work. The entry joins pulpit service with national history.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tishbi-judah-be:
Judah ben Elijah Tishbi was a Karaite scholar and liturgical poet at Belgrade. Kaufmann Kohler and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He worked in the first half of the sixteenth century. His grandfather was Abraham ben Judah, a Bible exegete.

Judah copied and completed his grandfather's work, Yesod Mikra. That book explains Scripture in the Karaite tradition. He also composed liturgical poems of his own. Several entered the printed Karaite prayer-book. Its second and third volumes carry his pieces. He further copied the Yehi Me'orot, a work on precepts. That text was ascribed to Tobiah ben Moses. Pinsker and Fürst supply the entry's main sources.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-uriel-14606:
Uriel is one of the four chief archangels in Jewish tradition. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Blau wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Michael, Gabriel, Raphael, and Uriel guard the globe's four quarters. Uriel is usually named last among the four. Sometimes another angel takes his place in the list.

He also ranks among the seven archangels in Enoch. There he is prince of angels and of Tartarus. His name means the fire of God, scholars argue. He is thus angel of thunder, earthquake, and flame. Enoch has him warn Noah's family of the world's end. In Second Esdras he poses three hard problems to Ezra. Weigh the fire's weight is the first of them. Medieval mysticism made him Sunday's princely angel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-viol-lit-skin-1:
The viol was a stringed instrument of ancient Israel. Emil G. Hirsch and Wilhelm Nowack wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Next to the kinnor, it was the instrument Israelites used most. The Bible gives no clear picture of it. Scholars must therefore guess from other evidence.

Most identify the viol with the Arab santir. That instrument is a low, oblong box. Strings stretch over a slightly curved sounding board. The player sits low and holds it in the lap. A palace picture at Kuyunjik shows a like instrument. A band there greets the returning king Assurbanipal. The Hebrew name may point to its skin covered board.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-we-al-kullom-14:
We Al Kullom is a brief prayer in the Yom Kippur service. Cyrus Adler and Francis L. Cohen wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The prayer breaks up the long confession of sins. That confession lists sins in alphabetical order. We Al Kullom divides it into three sections.

Its melody varies from place to place. Polish and German versions both appear in Baer's prayer book. All versions rest on one plaintive phrase. That phrase carries the wailing tone of the Selihah prayers. The entry points readers to the article on the Al Het confession. It shows how a short prayer paces a long one.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wiener-neustadt:
Wiener Neustadt is an Austrian city south of Vienna. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Alexander Büchler wrote this entry. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews settled there soon after its twelfth century founding. A 1239 order barred them from certain offices. Their rights rested on Austrian laws of 1244 and 1277.

The oldest tombstone found there dates to 1285. It marks the grave of Guta, wife of Shalom. During the Black Death the Jews were protected. Under Maximilian they were expelled instead. Their synagogue became a Catholic church in 1497. Jews returned in 1848 but lacked a cemetery. They gained one only in 1889.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-woman-rights-of:
Rights of woman in Jewish law is the theme of a long legal study. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote it for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The study sorts the theme into five parts. Each part treats one side of a woman's place in law.

First comes the power of a father over his girl. Next comes her right to share in an estate. Third come the rights and debts of a husband. Fourth come her chances to learn and to work. Last comes her place as a mother of a house. The study starts with the tale of Rebekah in Genesis. Her kin asked if she would go with the man. Yet the law let a father sell his girl in old times. That clash sets the tone for the whole piece.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yizhak-bar-redi:
Yizhak bar Redifa was a scholar of Palestine in the fourth century. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He passed on the tale lore of Rabbi Ammi to men. His name stands at the head of such tales in three books.

He once asked the scholar Jeremiah to rule on a point. He got a vague reply and no firm rule then. His own work treats the tales of Samson at length. One note of his treats a verse in Isaiah on dress. He says pert girls put scent in their shoes in those days. They stamped their feet to wake base lust in young men. He likened that lust to the bite of a snake in heat. More notes treat the tribe of Benjamin and its fate.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zechariah-ben-s:
Zechariah ben Solomon Ashkenazi was a German Talmud man of the 1500s. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He served as rabbi of the north rite Jews at Jerusalem. He died in that town at the end of his life.

He was the father-in-law of Joseph Caro, the great codifier. Caro speaks of him as a man deep in the law books. His name stands with that of David ben Zimra on a writ. In 1565 a case of the rite of halizah split the town. A man had wed the widow of his dead brother then. That act broke the north rite rule of that land. Zechariah and his peers cast that man out at once. David ben Zimra held that the ban had no right base.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zutra-mar-i-153:
Mar Zutra the First was exilarch, the head of Babylon's Jews, from 401 to 409. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He followed Mar Kahana in the office and lived in the days of R. Ashi. Though his rank was higher, he had to follow Ashi's enactments.

Zutra left Nehardea and made his home at Sura. There he held a yearly reception at the opening of the harvest season. Delegates from all the Babylonian communities came to it, and the gatherings were called rigli. Other delegations also visited him at Sura. The entry admits that nothing further is known about his career.
jonson-volpone-1606:
Ben Jonson wrote Volpone in 1606, and many call it his masterpiece. Jonson set the comedy in Venice and named his characters after animals: Volpone is the fox, his servant Mosca the fly. The play mixes sharp satire with a plot built like a trap.

Volpone, a rich old magnifico, pretends to be dying so that hopeful legacy hunters shower him with gifts. Mosca helps each visitor believe he will inherit everything. The game grows crueler until Volpone tries one trick too many. Jonson ends with unusually harsh punishments for a comedy. The play remains a fierce, funny study of greed eating itself.
journal-of-discourses-vol-06:
Volume Six, from 1859, finds the Saints home again in their valley. A federal army camps in their midst, a daily test of patience. Young turns the discourses toward the hard work of consolidation.

Building the kingdom's farms, shops, and institutions fills the sermons' plans. Speakers urge self-reliance in food, cloth, and tools of every kind. Faith becomes statecraft, preached in the Tabernacle week by week here. The tone cools from war heat toward patient, daily construction. Readers watch a refuge turn into a lasting commonwealth in Utah's valleys. Patience, in these talks, counts as a form of warfare by other means.
kenelm-chillingly-volume-06:
Volume six of Kenelm Chillingly opens Book Six with Sir Peter leaving for London. News that Kenelm has left town without a word appalls him. The journey's real purpose is a resettlement: twenty thousand pounds for Chillingly Gordon, his cousin's son. That business done, Sir Peter breakfasts with his cousin Mivers.

Mivers, a bachelor, delivers a set speech at the omelette against marriage. Bachelorhood, he insists, is the only safe protection of a man's positive happiness. His statistics on marriage's dangers amuse and irritate the widowed baronet in equal parts. This volume turns the novel's marriage debate onto the older generation. Sir Peter must weigh family duty against Kenelm's stubborn freedom.
kipling-puck-of-pooks-hill-1906:
Rudyard Kipling wrote Puck of Pook's Hill in 1906 for children, including his own. Kipling had settled in Sussex, in the south of England, and set the stories in the fields near his house. Two children, Dan and Una, perform a bit of Shakespeare in a meadow on Midsummer's Eve.

Their play summons Puck himself, the last of the old People of the Hills. Puck brings figures out of England's past to tell their stories: a Roman soldier on Hadrian's Wall, Norman knights, and others. Each tale ties the land to the people who held it. Kipling turned history into living memory for young readers.
kore-kosmou-mead-1906:
The Kore Kosmou, the Virgin of the World, is the longest Hermetic piece that survives, kept by the anthologist Stobaeus. In it the goddess Isis teaches her son Horus how the world and mankind were made. G. R. S. Mead turned it into English in 1906, within his study Thrice-Greatest Hermes, and the piece is given here on its own.

Isis tells of the souls sent down into bodies, their forgetting, and their long road back to the stars. The tale mixes Egyptian myth with Greek thought on fate and the elements. Mead, a theosophist, read Hermes as a sage of a single ancient wisdom. His version made the Kore Kosmou a favorite of English readers of the Hermetic books.
kropotkin-conquest-bread-1906:
Peter Kropotkin published The Conquest of Bread in 1906, in its English form, as the classic program of anarchist communism. Kropotkin wrote for workers who made everything and owned little. He argued that food, housing, and goods already produced could meet everyone's needs if shared by free agreement.

Chapters plan how a free society would take over bakeries, farms, and workshops and run them without wages or bosses. Kropotkin attacked the wage system as the root of poverty amid plenty. He answered fears of laziness with examples of willing work. The book shaped anarchist movements worldwide and still serves as their clearest statement of the world they want.
lagerlof-wonderful-adventures-nils-1906:
Selma Lagerlof published The Wonderful Adventures of Nils in 1906, a children's book written to teach Swedish geography. Nils is a lazy boy who torments animals on his farm. A magic spell shrinks him to tiny size. He flies off on the back of a goose, joining a flock of wild geese.

The flock travels the length of Sweden, from south to far north. Nils learns kindness, courage, and the ways of animals on the way. Folk tales and natural facts fill each stop. Swedish schools used the book for years. It remains a beloved classic, read far beyond Sweden for its charm and wonder.
lea-inquisition-spain-vol-1-1906:
In 1906 Henry Charles Lea turned from the medieval Inquisition to its most famous child: the Spanish Inquisition. This first volume of his History of the Inquisition of Spain tells how Ferdinand and Isabella founded the Holy Office in 1478. Lea wrote from the Spanish archives with his usual cold precision.

The converso crisis drives the tale: Jews who had taken baptism, watched by neighbors and hunted by the new tribunal. Lea lays out the founding, the first inquisitors, the burnings at Seville, and the expulsion of the Jews in 1492. He shows how crown and church built the machine together. The volume opens the standard history of the Spanish tribunal.
lea-inquisition-spain-vol-2-1906:
The second volume of Henry Charles Lea's History of the Inquisition of Spain, from 1906, opens the machine and shows its gears. Jurisprudence and procedure are the subjects: how a case began, how it was tried, and how it ended at the auto de fe. Lea draws the picture from the tribunal's own papers.

Secret denunciations, endless prison waits, torture within set rules, and sentences read in public theater fill his chapters. He explains the edicts of faith, the familiars, and the censors of books. The auto de fe, part sermon and part spectacle, gets its full anatomy. Lea's dry account of legal horror is the standard one in English.
lockyer-stonehenge-astronomically-consid:
Astronomer Norman Lockyer argued that Stonehenge was built as a star and sun temple. His 1906 book extends that claim to stone sites across Britain. Lockyer founded a famed science journal and led solar studies.

He measures the alignment of stones against solstice sunrise lines. Temple avenues, he says, point to key stars and seasons. His method helped birth the field now called archaeoastronomy. Critics dispute many of his dates and links. Yet his core claim, that builders watched the sky, won wide support. The book is a bold thesis, fully worked out.
london-white-fang-1906:
Jack London published White Fang in 1906, a wolfdog's passage from the Yukon wild to domestication. The companion mirror of The Call of the Wild reverses Buck's road: tame blood calls this hero toward the fire. London answered critics who charged him with faking nature by building the tale on careful Klondike observation.

White Fang, three parts wolf, learns the wild's law from his mother Kiche and the famine winters of the Mackenzie country. Gray Beaver, Beauty Smith, and a San Francisco dog pit teach him man's cruelty. Weedon Scott, a mining engineer, tames him with patience and kindness, a method no hand had tried on the fighting wolf. In California White Fang saves Judge Scott from a convict and earns his rest at Sierra Vista. The book's study of heredity and environment made it a school classic.
lowell-mars-and-its-canals-1906:
Percival Lowell set out his canal scheme in full grown form in this book of 1906. It rests on eleven more years of watch at his Flagstaff lens since his first Mars book. The lines on Mars had grown in his maps to a vast web of works.

Lowell gives charts, plates, and counts to show the canals are too straight to be a trick of nature. He reads them as the last great work of a race on a world that dries year by year. The book is the high case for a lived in Mars, made by its chief voice.
lucretia-volume-06:
Volume 6 of Lucretia pauses for a retrospect on its heroine's lost years. The narrator looks back between the death of Dalibard and her return. Lucretia arrives unannounced at William Mainwaring's house, dressed in widow's weeds. Susan welcomes her with tender warmth and quick forgiveness.

Mainwaring has risen as the active partner in a bank. His house is prosperous, and Lucretia seems gentle, frank, and changed. Yet the reader knows her training in darkness too well. Lytton asks whether such a nature can truly be reformed. The volume sets fair seeming against a poisoned past. It prepares the final acts of the tragedy.
machen-house-of-souls-1906:
Machen's tales of awe and dread stand gathered in The House of Souls of 1906. Its crown is The White People, a girl's diary of rites learned in the Welsh hills. Lovecraft took that tale as his model for the folk horror story.

A Fragment of Life tells of a clerk who wakes to wonder in a dull London life. The Red Hand hunts a killer by signs cut in stone and chalk. Hill, street, and suburb all hide old gods in Machen's world. The book is his gift at its peak, in one strong volume.
mandeville-fable-bees-1806:
Bernard Mandeville, a Dutch doctor settled in London, published The Fable of the Bees under the motto Private Vices, Publick Benefits. The edition of 1806 given here holds the poem, the complete Remarks, and the second part. His scandalous claim was simple: the greed, vanity, and luxury that preachers damned were the very springs of trade and wealth.

A hive of bees thrives while its members cheat and spend, then falls poor when all turn honest. Mandeville pressed that paradox until churchmen and moralists cried out. Hutcheson, Berkeley, and Adam Smith all felt bound to answer him. The Fable remains the great provocation of early economics, cheeky, shrewd, and impossible to ignore.
margery-gred-a-tale-of-old-nuremberg-vol:
Volume six of Margery tells how the hunted Herdegen was found. Ann and Margery seek him in the Lorenzer Wald, the city forest. He hides in a simple beekeeper's hut where no horseman can pass. Even in peasant's weeds, Margery finds her brother a goodly man.

Herdegen clasps his sweetheart Ann as ardently as on his homecoming. Then he sees Margery in mourning dress and takes her to his heart. One dear to him has died while he was hidden away. His eye is steadier now, and his voice graver and calmer. Ebers mixes flight, love, and grief in these forest scenes.
mark-twain-s-letters-volume-5-1901-1906:
Volume five of Mark Twain's Letters covers 1901 to 1906. Many letters go to Twichell, his pastor and oldest friend. Paine heads the year 'Mark Twain as a Reformer.' A Louisville paper marveled at the humorist's transformation.

The genial joker had become a knight errant with a lance. He broke it against Church or State when they blocked mankind's road. Summers at Saranac and the McKinley assassination mark these pages. Protest letters against empire and cruelty pour from his pen. Grief for his wife shadows the public honors. The sage writes on, witty, wrathful, and tender.
mctaggart-dogmas-religion-1906:
Some Dogmas of Religion, published in 1906, is McTaggart's fearless examination of what religious belief can survive reason. He takes up dogmas one by one, God, freedom, survival, and the soul, and weighs each from an idealist standpoint.

His results startled readers: he argues against a personal, all-powerful God while defending survival after death and the primacy of love. McTaggart was an atheist who thought religion's emotions truer than its creeds. The book's candor and calm made it notorious in Edwardian Cambridge. It remains one of the most honest works of its kind in English.
mead-thrice-greatest-hermes-vol-2-1906:
G. R. S. Mead, a scholar close to the Theosophical movement, published Thrice-Greatest Hermes in 1906. Volume two translates the surviving sermons and fragments of the Hermetic literature. The Corpus Hermeticum tracts and the Perfect Sermon appear here.

Mead renders Hermes as a living teacher rather than a museum piece. Flowing commentary surrounds the translations and explains their spiritual teaching. Generations of seekers met Hermes through Mead before any other writer. His warm style contrasts with Walter Scott's drier academic edition. For the occult revival of the early twentieth century, Mead's Hermes was the standard doorway.
mead-thrice-greatest-hermes-vol1-1906:
G. R. S. Mead opens his great English Hermetica in Thrice-Greatest Hermes, Volume One, from 1906. Prolegomena come first: the history and meaning of the Hermetic writings. Mead, a Theosophical scholar, traces Hermes Trismegistus through Greek, Egyptian, and early Christian worlds with patient and loving erudition.
