Saliva carries a natural antiviral protein called SLPI. At normal levels in saliva, it blocks HIV-1. How it shields cells was unclear. Bénédicte Py and colleagues found its landing sites in PLOS ONE in 2009. They identified two cell-surface proteins as its receptors. They are the phospholipid scramblases 1 and 4.

The scramblases sit in the cell membrane. They also interact with CD4, the doorway HIV uses to enter cells. SLPI docking there may explain its antiviral punch. The study maps a natural defense in fine detail. It could inspire new ways to block HIV at the cell surface.
plos-pone-0005106:
The tongue's sweet sensor also lives in the pancreas. There it may taste sugar in the blood. Yuko Nakagawa and colleagues studied it in PLOS ONE in 2009. They worked in MIN6 cells and mouse islets. The receptor's expression was checked first. Then its function was tested in insulin-making beta cells.

The sweet taste receptor activated calcium signaling. It also activated cyclic AMP signaling. Together those systems stimulated insulin secretion. The pancreas can, in effect, taste sweetness. That adds a sensor to blood-sugar control. It may respond to sweeteners as well as sugar. The finding links taste machinery to metabolism. It opens questions about artificial sweeteners and insulin.
plos-pone-0005206:
Spotting one marked protein in a single cell is routine, but reading many marks at once is hard. Fluorescent tags have broad, overlapping colors, which limits how many can be read together. Shachaf and colleagues offered a new tag system in PLOS ONE in 2009 based on Raman scattering.

Their composite nanoparticles boost a scattered light signal that carries a sharp fingerprint. The method detects protein phosphorylation, a key on-off tag, inside single cells. Narrow fingerprints could let labs read far more cell marks at once than fluorescence allows. Tags like these could one day let a lab read a whole panel of cell marks from a single drop of sample at once.
plos-pone-0005306:
Ribosomal protein L22 helps build the large subunit of the ribosome, the cell's protein factory. It also binds RNA and gathers in the nucleolus, the factory's workshop inside the nucleus. Houmani and Ruf mapped what drives both traits in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Clusters of basic amino acids, the positively charged building blocks, contribute to L22's RNA binding. The same clusters help send the protein to the nucleolus. Shared targeting codes like this show how one small protein region can serve two jobs at once. Small marks of this kind, just a few charged parts in a row. Turn up again and again in cell life as address tags that send proteins to the right room.
plos-pone-0005406:
Angiotensin II drives damaging changes in the kidney, but a shorter relative, angiotensin-(1-7), may counter it. That peptide acts through a receptor called Mas. Esteban and colleagues studied the pair's role in renal inflammation in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Kidneys deficient in Mas showed diminished damage in models of renal insufficiency, placing the axis among the key players in kidney inflammation. The counter-regulatory arm of the angiotensin system is a drug target in its own right. Balancing the system may protect kidneys better than blocking one side alone. Kidney harm creeps up on many men and women with high blood pressure. Diabetes, so a built-in brake in the same system that drives the harm is a lead of great worth for new drugs.
plos-pone-0005506:
Morgan Goulding traced cell fates in a snail embryo for a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Snails and their kin divide in a spiral pattern, and each early cell is fated to form set parts of the body. In the mud snail Ilyanassa, that map was known only for the first day of divisions.

Goulding extended the map much further, cell by cell. The fuller map shows that some body regions form faster than in related animals. Comparing maps across species shows how development speeds up or slows down as animals evolve new forms.
plos-pone-0005606:
Francisco Álvarez-Blasco and co-authors studied a blood protein gene in women with polycystic ovary syndrome in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. The syndrome affects hormone balance, weight, and blood sugar in women before menopause. The protein haptoglobin mops up free haemoglobin, and its forms differ in how well they fight oxidation.

The team asked whether the weaker form of the gene adds to the oxidation and inflammation seen in the syndrome. They compared women with the syndrome across gene forms and measures of sugar control. A gene effect would help sort patients by risk.
plos-pone-0005706:
Chenyu Zhang and Adam Kuspa watched in 2009 how a bacterial invader rewires the power plants of a soil amoeba. The amoeba Dictyostelium serves as a stand-in host for Legionella, the germ behind Legionnaires' disease. The germ survives inside cells that would normally digest it.

During infection, the amoeba's mitochondria cut back on gene activity and even chop up their own ribosomal RNA. Those changes may help the germ feed or hide. Studying them in a simple host reveals tricks the germ likely uses in human lung cells too. Each trick is a possible weak point for future drugs.
plos-pone-0005806:
Carla Ribeiro and co-authors studied in 2009 how a common antibiotic resets gene activity in human airway cells. Azithromycin, taken long-term at low doses, helps patients with certain chronic lung diseases. The benefit seems to come from calming inflammation, not just killing germs.

The team profiled gene changes in well-differentiated airway epithelia after treatment. Pathways for inflammation, fat metabolism, and cell cycling all shifted. Those shifts sketch how the drug soothes airways over months. Knowing the pathways may let doctors mimic the benefit with fewer antibiotic side effects, like resistance.
plos-pone-0005906:
Maria Swanberg and co-authors narrowed in 2009 the gene regions that decide how much nerve damage a strain suffers. When axons are cut, some animals lose far more neurons than others, and genes set that susceptibility. Two regions, Vra1 and Vra2, were known to be involved.

Fine mapping shrank those regions toward the actual causal genes. Knowing them could explain why neurodegeneration varies so much between patients. It also offers targets for protecting axons in diseases from glaucoma to multiple sclerosis. The study is patient genetics: each narrowed interval makes the final gene hunt cheaper.
plos-pone-0006006:
A memory chemical in the brain also answers to immune signals. Virginie Labrousse, Laurence Costes, Agnès Aubert and colleagues explored that link in 2009 in mice lacking the P2X7 receptor, a sensor on immune and brain cells. Their PLOS ONE paper looks at the hippocampus, a brain area vital for place memory, and at two molecules tied to learning.

Mice without the receptor showed weaker spatial memory, matched by low levels of both IL-1beta and c-Fos in the hippocampus. An immune signal thus seems required for normal remembering. The work ties inflammation's tools to memory's machinery and hints that some memory loss may start in the immune system, not in neurons alone.
plos-pone-0006106:
A protein that rises in asthma patients' blood may be written in their genes. Camilla Rathcke, Johan Holmkvist, Lise Husmoen and colleagues checked that link in a large Danish group in 2009. Their PLOS ONE study tests polymorphisms in CHI3L1, the gene for the protein YKL-40, against asthma and atopy in six thousand five hundred fourteen adults.

YKL-40 levels already serve as a marker for asthma and poor lung function. If common variants in its gene also track the disease, the marker gains a causal hint, not just a correlation. A population study of this size can settle modest effects, and its results feed the search for asthma's inherited share.
plos-pone-0006206:
Glioblastoma is among the most common and worst-treated primary brain tumors. Francesca Pistollato and colleagues studied cells grown from such tumors in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. They examined a factor called HIF-1 alpha, which responds to low oxygen. They also studied BMP2, a signal that can push tumor cells toward a star-like brain cell fate.

Oxygen levels and BMP2 together reshape how HIF-1 alpha is tuned in these cells. Low oxygen had earlier cast doubt on using BMP signals as therapy. Understanding the tug of war helps judge when such treatment might work. The work adds detail to the search for better brain tumor care.
plos-pone-0006306:
Tuberculosis urgently needs new drugs as resistant strains spread worldwide. Alistair Brown and colleagues tested platensimycin, an antibiotic from soil bacteria, against TB enzymes in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The enzymes, called beta-ketoacyl-ACP synthases, build the fatty acids of the bacterium's waxy cell wall.

Blocking wall building is a proven strategy against Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The study measures how well platensimycin hits those mycobacterial targets. A natural compound with a fresh target profile is valuable against multi-drug resistant strains. The work is an early step, from enzyme tests toward possible treatments.
plos-pone-0006406:
Electronic noses try to copy animal smell, but they rarely match the original. Amalia Berna, Alisha Anderson, and Stephen Trowell benchmarked e-nose sensors against biology in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The instruments have had limited utility because their discriminating power lags behind living noses and antennae.

The manner in which odour space is sampled explains part of that gap. Bio-benchmarking sets the biological original as the standard to beat. Honest benchmarks steer engineers toward designs that close the gap. Applications from food quality to security depend on better artificial smell.
plos-pone-0006506:
Zuben Sauna, Chinyere Okunji, Ryan Hunt, and colleagues characterized antibodies against a clotting enzyme in PLOS ONE in 2009. ADAMTS13 is a zinc metalloprotease that cleaves von Willebrand Factor, a protein that helps blood clot. Problems with ADAMTS13 are implicated in thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, a serious clotting disorder. The team studied antibodies that are sensitive to the enzyme's conformation, its folded shape.

Shape-sensitive antibodies can reveal when the enzyme changes form. They can also become diagnostic tools for the disorder. Characterizing them is a step toward better tests for patients. The work sits where protein structure meets clinical medicine.
plos-pone-0006606:
Tandis Vazin and co-authors combined factors to grow dopamine nerve cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. One strong way to make these cells from embryonic stem cells uses signals from stromal cells. But defined factors are safer and more clean for medical use. The team present a new mix of factors, which they term SPIE. It drives stem cells toward the dopamine nerve cell fate.

Their title says SPIE promotes this cell fate from human embryonic stem cells. Steady, safe growth of dopamine cells is a key goal for Parkinson's disease cell therapy. People with that disease lose just these cells. A defined mix is a step toward cells that clinics could one day use.
plos-pone-0006706:
Sasan R. Fereidouni and colleagues infected mallard ducks with bird flu viruses in PLOS ONE in 2009. Wild birds may carry the dangerous H5N1 form of avian influenza. Whether they spread it widely is still debated. Ducks commonly catch milder flu subtypes, sometimes several at once. Earlier mild infections might change how a later dangerous infection plays out.

The team gave mallards immunity from low-pathogenic viruses first. Some immunity matched the later virus, and some came from other subtypes. They then exposed the ducks to highly pathogenic avian influenza. Comparing groups showed how prior immunity blunted or failed to blunt disease. The results inform how outbreaks may move through wild duck populations.
plos-pone-0006806:
Suja S. Rajan and David C. Sokal checked old HIV forecasts against what truly hit Malawi in PLOS ONE in 2009. In 1992, a team had charted the epidemic for the years ahead. They used data from the past decade and the standard models of the day. High and low paths framed the forecast. This report sets those paths next to real counts through the year 2000.

Such checks are rare, and they teach a lot. Where the forecast missed, the miss shows modelers what to fix. Malawi's epidemic was watched as closely as any in Africa. Which path came close tells planners how much to trust the next forecast. The check closes the loop on ten years of plans.
plos-pone-0006906:
Tiago F. Outeiro and his team watched dopamine bend the shape of a Parkinson's protein in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein is alpha-synuclein. When its units clump, nerve cells sicken and die in Parkinson's disease. Clumps had most often been caught by round-about means in cells. Soap-based pulls can warp the very thing they aim to gauge.

Dopamine changed the protein's shape on its own. A bent shape may seed the bad clumps. The cells that die first in Parkinson's are the ones that make dopamine. A straight hit of dopamine on the protein could help solve that riddle. The find ties brain chemistry to the disease's mark protein.
plos-pone-0007006:
Roberto Danovaro, Serena Fonda Umani, and Antonio Pusceddu warned about warming seas in PLOS ONE in 2009. All oceans carry marine snow, small clumps of organic matter. Warming surface water can make the water column more stable. That stability can let marine snow merge into huge mucilage aggregates.

The authors link that process to the spread of microbial pathogens. Their focus was the Mediterranean Sea. Mucilage events foul beaches, nets, and marine life. If warming makes them more common, coastal health and tourism both suffer. The paper frames mucilage as a climate change problem, not just a nuisance.
plos-pone-0007106:
Lauren Solomon, Jennifer Li, Nathalie Bérubé, and colleagues tested a chromatin protein in mouse cartilage in PLOS ONE in 2009. Mutations in the human ATRX gene cause developmental defects. These include skeletal deformities and dwarfism. ATRX remodels chromatin, the packaging of DNA. Its actual job in building skeletons was unknown.

The team deleted Atrx in mouse cartilage using a targeted genetic switch. Skeletal development was barely disturbed, as their title reports. A minimal effect is still an answer. It suggests other tissues or partners carry ATRX's developmental weight, steering future work elsewhere.
plos-pone-0007206:
Anette P. Gjesing, Thomas Sparsø, Knut Borch-Johnsen, and colleagues tested gene links to obesity and blood pressure in 2009. Their PLOS ONE study covers 6,514 adult Danes, named in the title in words as more than six thousand adults. Earlier evidence on the ADRB2 gene was unusually unclear and mixed.

ADRB2 makes the beta-2 adrenergic receptor, which affects body fat and blood pressure. Some reports linked single variants to real effects, while others found none. The authors test haplotypes, or inherited variant groups. They find no consistent effect on obesity, hypertension, or related body measures.
plos-pone-0007306:
Masato Abe, Yuka Setoguchi, Tsubasa Tanaka, and colleagues studied membrane traffic control in fruit fly wing cells in 2009. A lipid-making enzyme called class III PI3K regulates vesicular transport at many steps. It produces a lipid signal that marks membranes for sorting inside cells as cargo moves through.

Protein location at distinct membrane domains needs tight regulation. The authors examine a partner protein, Rabenosyn-5, alongside PI3K. They report location-dependent regulation of membrane proteins in Drosophila wing cells. Their work shows the same transport machinery can act differently depending on where a protein sits.
plos-pone-0007406:
Aoife T. Heaslip, Stephanie C. Ems-McClung, and Ke Hu characterized a microtubule-binding protein in a parasite in 2009. The microtubule cytoskeleton gives essential structural support to all eukaryotic cells. These assemblies are built in a spatially and temporally controlled manner to perform very different functions, from cell division to maintaining cell shape.

The parasite is Toxoplasma gondii, which infects many animals and some humans. The authors identify a novel microtubule binding protein, TgICMAP1, in this parasite. Their PLOS ONE characterization adds a part to the parasite's internal skeleton. Such parasite-specific parts can become drug targets.
plos-pone-0007506:
Kevin Gobeske and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on why exercise sharpens the mind. Running and enriched surroundings are known to grow new neurons in the adult hippocampus, the brain's memory hub. They also improve some kinds of learning. The signals that connect exercise to new neurons were unclear. The team tested one pathway, called BMP signaling, in mice.

BMP signaling mediated the effects of exercise on both new neuron birth and cognition. When the pathway's influence changed, the benefits of exercise changed with it. That places a defined molecular chain between behavior and brain growth. A known pathway is something medicine can work with. The study moves the exercise-brain link from folklore toward mechanism. It also suggests new ways to mimic exercise's gains for people who cannot run.
plos-pone-0007606:
Jordi Viñas and Sergi Tudela published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on identifying tuna by their genes. Tunas of the genus Thunnus include the bluefins, among the most valuable and most endangered trade fish in the world. Once a fish is cut into steaks or sushi, sight identification fails. That gap lets protected species slip into trade. The authors set out to validate a genetic identification method for these species.

A validated DNA method gives regulators a firm tool. Samples taken at markets or ports can be assigned to species with confidence. Enforcement of protections for threatened tunas depends on exactly that confidence. Without it, quotas and bans are hard to police. The study is methodological, but its stakes are conservation stakes. Naming the fish correctly is the first step to saving it.
plos-pone-0007706:
Gentaro Kumagai and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It tests stem cell transplants as a treatment for spinal cord injury. Grafts of neural stem cells after injury have improved movement in rodents. Which cell types help most was still unclear.

The team derived gliogenic stem cells from embryonic stem cells. These cells are primed to become glia, the support cells of the nervous system. After transplant, the cells aided functional recovery in injured animals. The study helps sort which graft cells suit spinal repair, a step toward future human trials.
plos-pone-0007806:
Gangwei Ou and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It studies a toxin made by the cholera bacterium, Vibrio cholerae. Cholera causes severe diarrhea through the gut. One of its weapons is cytolysin, which attacks intestinal cells.

The authors show that cytolysin provokes an inflammatory response in human intestinal cells. A second bacterial product, the protease PrtV, modulates that response. PrtV normally shields the bacterium from tiny predators in water. Inside the gut, it also dials the toxin-driven alarm up or down. The interplay helps explain how cholera symptoms unfold.
plos-pone-0007906:
Yevgeniy Grigoryev and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It maps how immune activation reshapes gene splicing in human T and B cells. Alternative splicing lets one gene yield several proteins. Parts called exons are included or skipped during processing.

Splicing shifts were known to occur when lymphocytes activate. Which genes change, and in what classes, was little known. The genome-wide analysis found distinct classes of alternatively spliced genes. The catalogue helps immunologists see activation as a splicing program, not just a volume change. It may expose new control points in immune responses.
plos-pone-0008006:
Ney Leite and colleagues solved the shape of a mosquito scent carrier in PLOS ONE in 2009. Aedes aegypti spreads yellow fever and dengue by finding people to bite. Carrier proteins in its antennae grab scent molecules and ferry them to sensors.

The shape showed a pocket where scents sit, capped by a lid that opens or shuts with acidity. That lid may time the grab and release of each scent. A lid that can be jammed is a tempting target for sprays or traps that blind the mosquito to its hosts.
plos-pone-0008106:
Kara Bischoff and colleagues solved the case of a fly wing mutant in PLOS ONE in 2009. The mutant, called xenicid, grows blistered wings. Wing building needs many gene systems in step: pattern, cell fate, cell size, and cell grip all play a part.

The fault lay in a gene called Additional sex combs, cut short at its tail end. Cloned patches of mutant tissue in otherwise normal wings proved the link. That gene is a chromatin regulator, a shaper of gene access, so the case ties wing form to how DNA is packed.
plos-pone-0008206:
Jian Huang and colleagues cataloged small RNAs in a parasite in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Schistosoma japonicum causes schistosomiasis, a serious parasitic disease found worldwide. MicroRNAs are tiny RNAs that do not code for proteins. They help control gene activity in many living things. Little was known about them in this parasite.

Using deep sequencing, the team searched the whole genome for these microRNAs. A full catalog shows which regulators the parasite carries. Those regulators may shape its growth and its life inside hosts. The list gives future studies a starting point for new control ideas.
plos-pone-0008306:
Koen Nelissen and colleagues mapped shape perception in the monkey brain in PLOS ONE in 2009. The brain extracts three-dimensional shape from flat images. Shading and texture are two monocular cues to depth. The team used contrast-enhanced fMRI in alert monkeys. They mapped which cortical regions respond to each cue.

A parallel human imaging study allowed direct cross-species comparison of the results. Shared regions would point to a common primate system for shape. Knowing where depth structure is computed guides models of vision. The work links single-cue processing to the wider visual system.
plos-pone-0008406:
Rajaie Namas and colleagues studied trauma and shock responses in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Trauma with hemorrhagic shock triggers cytokine-driven acute inflammation. That inflammation is generally considered detrimental to patients. Paradoxically, blood levels of the early cytokine TNF-alpha were elevated in survivors. Other signals such as IL-6 and IL-10 did not show the same pattern.

An adequately robust early TNF-alpha response proved a hallmark of survival. The first hours after admission carried the key signal. A strong early response may organize later healing rather than harm. That flips a common assumption in trauma care.
plos-pone-0008506:
Joao Cordeiro and co-authors study how vaccinia virus spreads in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Vaccinia is a virus related to smallpox. To exit an infected cell, it must cross the actin cortex. That cortex is a mesh under the cell membrane that acts as a barrier. Past work hinted the virus boosts its own spread. A viral protein called F11 plays a part in that process.

F11 blocks RhoA signaling, a system that tightens the actin mesh. Blocking it loosens the barrier and enhances viral spread. The team show this both in lab cells and in a mouse nasal infection. The find clarifies a key exit step for the virus.
plos-pone-0008606:
Mathias Kolliker and co-authors examine parent-offspring conflict in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Across many species, offspring have means to influence parental investment. Young can beg, signal, or compete for food and care. Parental investment thus evolves as an interacting trait. Indirect genetic effects may strongly affect how offspring and parent behaviors coevolve. Theory had focused mainly on offspring demands or parent supply alone.

The authors model antagonistic parent-offspring co-adaptation. Each side adapts in ways that oppose the other's interests. Their dynamics differ from models where only one side evolves. The work refines evolutionary theory of family conflict and care.
plos-pone-0008706:
Prabhakar Putheti, Amit Awasthi, Joyce Popoola, and colleagues showed that human memory T cells can change jobs. Their immunology study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. IL-9 is a growth signal for T cells and mast cells. In mice, certain signals push helper T cells to make IL-9. Whether adult human memory cells could do the same was open.

The team cultured human CD4 memory cells under guiding conditions. The cells began making IL-9, a new identity for them. Flexible memory cells could feed allergies or fight parasites, depending on setting. The finding adds a branch to how doctors picture immune memory.
plos-pone-0008806:
Christopher Williams and Eric Kramer used physics to prize the tapered shape of whiskers. Their analysis appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Whiskers help land mammals feel their way in the dark. Each whisker carries touch forces down to sensors at its base. Real whiskers thin toward the tip rather than staying uniform. Whether that taper improves sensing was the question.

Their mechanical analysis compared tapered and straight shafts. A taper spreads signals in ways that sharpen touch information. The geometry acts like a built-in signal processor. Engineers designing artificial touch sensors can borrow the same trick.
plos-pone-0008906:
Karan Mangla, David Dill, and Mark Horowitz stress-tested computer models of the yeast cell cycle. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Living cells must keep division timing steady despite noise. Modelers often update every signal in a model at once. That tidy choice hides real timing variation between steps. Asynchronous updating, where steps fire at varied times, is more realistic. Budding and fission yeasts offered two classic models to compare.

Both cycles kept working under sloppy, varied timing in their tests. Robust timing may be a built-in feature of cell cycle design. Modelers can trust these models further than feared. The result also suggests real cells tolerate noisy clocks well.
plos-pone-0009006:
Michael Suits and co-authors took the portrait of a sugar-cutting enzyme from a strep bacterium, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The bacterium, Streptococcus pyogenes, causes strep throat and worse infections. Its enzyme, an alpha-mannosidase, snips mannose sugars off larger molecules. The enzyme belongs to the GH38 family, versions of which work in human cells too.

The team solved the enzyme's three-dimensional structure. They also measured how fast it cuts its sugar targets. The structure shows the shape of the cutting site in fine detail. Comparing bacterial and human versions may help design drugs that hit only the germ's copy.
plos-pone-0009106:
Robert Friesen and co-authors tested a new class of antibodies against severe flu in ferrets, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Circulating H1N1 viruses had grown resistant to oseltamivir, the leading flu drug of the time. Highly dangerous bird flu strains added a second, pandemic threat. Fresh ways to control influenza were urgently needed by health officials.

The antibodies were given before infection and again after it had started. Ferrets were protected by the dose given ahead and helped by treatment after. Antibodies that can both prevent and treat flu are rare and valuable. They could be stockpiled as backup for a pandemic when vaccines lag behind.
plos-pone-0009206:
Ian Stevenson and Konrad Körding published this neuroscience methods study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Neuroscientists want maps of how neurons influence each other. Different recording tools capture that activity at very different speeds. Spike records resolve far less than a millisecond, while other methods blur time much more.

The authors asked whether maps built at one time scale agree with maps built at another. If the maps match, results from slow and fast tools can be compared fairly. If they differ, each method may be telling a different story. Their analysis of functional connectivity across time scales helps researchers know how much trust to place in each kind of map.
plos-pone-0009306:
Guillaume Calmettes and co-authors published this heart study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Low oxygen, or hypoxia, strains the heart and underlies many common diseases. Bodies can adapt to long-term low oxygen, gaining a measure of resistance. Understanding that adaptation could help doctors protect hearts during sudden oxygen loss.

The team studied mice kept in chronic low oxygen. Their hearts regulated energy supply better than unadapted hearts. That improved control countered the disturbed energy balance that hypoxia usually causes. The work shows adaptation is not just endurance; it rewires how the heart manages fuel.
plos-pone-0009406:
Jeffrey Brown and C. James McKnight published this cell structure study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The brush border lines the gut's absorbing surface. It is built from microvilli, finger-like projections about one micrometer long. Thousands of them stand in neat hexagonal arrays on each cell.

The authors present a molecular model of the skeleton inside those fingers. The model also explains how the whole border is organized. A working model of this tiny machinery clarifies how the gut maximizes its absorbing area. It also helps explain what fails in diseases where the brush border breaks down.
plos-pone-0009506:
Nisha Yadav and co-authors applied statistics to an ancient script in PLOS ONE in 2010. The Indus script comes from a Bronze Age culture in South Asia. No one has yet read it. Some scholars doubt the signs form true writing at all. The team used n-gram methods, which count how often symbol pairs and chains occur.

Patterns in those counts can be compared with known writing systems and with non writing sign sets. Their analysis probes whether the Indus signs behave like language. Results of this kind cannot yet translate the script. They can, though, test claims about its basic nature with numbers instead of opinion.
plos-pone-0009606:
Ronnaug Solberg and co-authors profiled blood chemistry in pigs in PLOS ONE in 2010. When the body is starved of oxygen, doctors have few good tests to track the damage. That gap matters most for newborns after a hard birth. The team used pigs, whose bodies respond much like ours. They measured hundreds of small molecules in blood during oxygen loss and revival.

The pattern of molecules shifted in clear ways as oxygen fell and returned. Some molecules tracked cell injury and recovery closely. Those are candidates for early warning tests. Better tests could guide the first critical minutes of resuscitation, in pig studies now and perhaps in care later.
plos-pone-0009706:
Fragile X syndrome is a genetic condition tied to autism and social difficulties. Marjelo Mines and colleagues studied a mouse model of the syndrome for PLOS ONE in 2010. They focused on GSK3, an enzyme that acts like a switch inside cells.

The enzyme shaped how the mice behaved with other mice. It influenced which companions they preferred and how anxious they acted during meetings. Social symptoms are central to both fragile X and autism. Tying one enzyme to those behaviors offers a target for future treatments. The work adds a molecular clue to a behavioral puzzle.
plos-pone-0009806:
Kimberly R Drake and colleagues explore, in PLOS ONE in 2010, where a popular cell marker sits inside living cells. The marker is LC3 joined to a glowing tag, used to track autophagy, the process where cells break down worn parts. Pictures often show the marker pooled in the nucleus, the cell control center.

Careful microscopy in two common cell lines confirmed more loose marker in the nucleus than outside it. Blocking active export from the nucleus did not change that pattern. Starting autophagy also changed it only a little. Instead, the marker seems trapped in large protein groups in both places, which slows its movement and keeps the pools apart.
plos-pone-0009906:
A protein that helps cells take in fats also shapes how cholesterol leaves the body. Pin Yue and colleagues studied mice that lack that protein entirely. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The missing protein is CD36, and the mice are called CD36 null. Without it, the liver secreted more apoA-I, a building block of good cholesterol particles. ApoA-I is the main protein in HDL, the good cholesterol carrier. The mice also showed enhanced peripheral efflux of cholesterol and phospholipid. The findings redraw the map of how cholesterol exits tissues.
plos-pone-0010006:
Kylie Swisher and Roy Parker studied yeast cell structures in a PLOS ONE paper from 2010. When cells face stress, they gather loose RNA and proteins into clumps called stress granules and P-bodies. These clumps help control which messages get translated into protein and which get broken down.

The authors located five proteins, Pbp1, Pbp4, Lsm12, Dhh1, and Pab1, in the common yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae. They tested where each protein sits and what each one does to stress granules. One of them, Pbp1, links to a human protein tied to nerve disease, so yeast findings may carry wider lessons.
plos-pone-0010106:
Nancy Crum-Cianflone leads a 2010 PLOS ONE study of weight trends among people living with HIV in the United States military. Early in the epidemic, wasting was the main worry. As treatment improved and patients lived longer, weight gain was largely unmeasured.

Records for over sixteen hundred patients from nineteen eighty-five to two thousand and four show about nine percent obese at diagnosis, and more in recent years. Most patients gained weight during infection, more so when virus levels were low and immune counts high. The authors read the gain as better health plus wider population trends, and urge weight care as part of HIV care.
plos-pone-0010206:
The authors were Burkhard Poeggeler, Kumar Sambamurti, Sandra Siedlak, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study tested a natural compound against aging damage. Aging has many drivers, but reactive oxygen species are widely seen as major contributors. Mitochondria, the cell's power plants, make most of those harsh molecules, so they sit at the center of aging theories.

The team found a novel endogenous indole, a compound the body itself makes. It protected rodent mitochondria from damage in their tests. It also extended lifespan in rotifers, tiny aquatic animals used in aging research.
plos-pone-0010306:
Jian-Yi Xu and co-authors study cannabis-like signals in rat memory circuits in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The hippocampus, a brain area vital for memory, receives two input routes onto the same nerve cells. Body-made cannabis-like chemicals, called endocannabinoids, tune the strength of such connections through a receptor named CB1.

Recording from single cells, the team found long-term weakening of connections differed between the two input routes. Blocking CB1 erased the difference, pointing to the receptor as the cause. Short-term weakening and a drug's effect also differed by route. Route-specific tuning, they suggest, shapes how these memory cells add up their inputs.
plos-pone-0010406:
Cees van den Wijngaard and colleagues asked whether symptom tracking can spot local outbreaks, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Health agencies increasingly watch patterns of illness reports to catch unusual events early. Critics doubt such watching helps at the small, local scale. The team tested it on outbreaks of lower airway infections. They checked whether alarms fired for real outbreaks without drowning staff in false ones.

A system that cries wolf loses trust fast in practice. Balancing early warning against noise is the core design problem. Their evaluation speaks to towns deciding whether to invest in such systems. It also clarifies what syndromic data can and cannot do. Watching symptoms is cheap, but only useful if the signal beats the noise.
plos-pone-0010506:
Swaminathan Sethu, Peter Pushparaj and Alirio Melendez linked an enzyme to inflammation in a mouse model of peritonitis in PLOS ONE in 2010. The signal TNF-alpha drives many inflammatory diseases. The team had shown in dishes that TNF-alpha uses an enzyme, PLD1, to switch on an inflammatory master control. They now tested that link in living mice. The model inflamed the abdominal lining, mimicking a serious human condition.

PLD1 proved necessary for the full inflammatory response in the animals. Confirming a dish result in a body is a key step toward drug development. Enzymes like PLD1 are druggable, unlike some signaling proteins. This study supports PLD1 as a target in TNF-driven diseases. It also maps one route from signal to inflammation.
plos-pone-0010606:
Brigitte Bollag and colleagues studied a small protein made by JC virus, in PLOS ONE in 2010. JC virus lives quietly in many people and rarely causes harm. Its small t protein was known to matter, but its role in copying viral DNA was vague.

The team showed the small protein grabs two host control systems, PP2A and the Rb family. Viruses missing a working small t copied their DNA poorly. Those grabs push infected cells toward a state that favors virus growth. The details help explain how a mostly silent virus can turn dangerous when immunity fails.
plos-pone-0010706:
Steven Jackson and colleagues mapped the brief windows when stem cells heed growth signals, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Embryonic stem cells can be guided toward gut and other inner tissues by timed doses of signals. Three signal families, BMP, Wnt, and activin, do much of that guiding in the early embryo.

Each signal worked only during its own time window in the dish. Too early or too late, and the same dose did little. The windows overlapped in a set order. Recipes for growing replacement tissues depend on such timing charts, since the right signal at the wrong hour makes the wrong cell type.
plos-pone-0010806:
Olga Alekseyenko, Carol Lee, and Edward Kravitz manipulated serotonin neurons in fighting fruit flies, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Male flies fight over food and mates, and their fights escalate in set patterns. Serotonin, a brain chemical tied to mood in people, shapes aggression across many species. Older drug studies in flies could not target serotonin cells precisely.

Genetic tools switched specific serotonin neurons up or down during fights. The changes altered how fast aggression escalated. Fly fights are simple, but their control circuits can be taken apart gene by gene. What those circuits teach may explain why the same chemical steadies some tempers and not others.
plos-pone-0010906:
Birgit Fogal, Carolyn McClaskey, Sha Yan and co-authors published this brain study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Premature babies can suffer white matter injury, where the cells that coat nerve fibers with insulation, called oligodendrocytes, are lost or fail to mature. No drug existed to push those cells to grow and wrap fibers, so the team tested diazoxide, a drug that opens potassium channels.

Because calming a cell's electric state seems to favor these cells' growth, diazoxide was a logical candidate. In rat precursor cell cultures and in brain slice cultures, the drug encouraged the precursor cells to multiply and supported the formation of insulation. Fogal and colleagues offer early evidence that a known, approved drug might be repurposed to help repair the injured preterm brain.
plos-pone-0011006:
Sarah Bennett, John Mercer and Mohamed Noor published this fruit fly genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The human BRCA2 gene guards against breast cancer, and its fly counterpart carries a repeating array of segments that bind a DNA repair partner. Their group had found that array apparently expanded in the ancestor of one fly species, Drosophila yakuba, and now examined variation within that species and its relatives.

They found short, typical arrays also circulating in the very species thought to carry the expansion, alongside the long form. Those short forms do not look inherited from a single common source, suggesting independent contractions produced look-alike arrays, a phenomenon called homoplasy. Bennett and colleagues caution that repeat counts can mislead family trees, since the same number can evolve twice. The lesson applies wherever repetitive DNA is used to trace evolution.
plos-pone-0011106:
Rotman, Amado and Kuzminov described a viral stowaway in PLOS ONE in 2010. A bacterial virus called Lula can live quietly inside gut bacteria grown in labs. The authors found it could also spread sideways between cultures without anyone moving it on purpose.

The study details the tactics the virus uses to travel and persist in the lab setting. Unnoticed spread can spoil experiments and confuse results in many labs. Knowing how Lula moves helps labs guard their cultures against it. The work is a practical warning for anyone who grows bacteria for research.
plos-pone-0011206:
Melo, Reyes-Lecca, Vitor-Silva and colleagues studied schoolchildren with two infections in PLOS ONE in 2010. In their study area, many children carry both gut worms and a relapsing form of malaria. Anemia, a shortage of red blood cells, is a common harm of malaria in children.

Children carrying both infections suffered less anemia than expected. That odd partnership complicates policy, since removing worms is normally a clear good. Programs must weigh competing harms before changing deworming plans in malaria zones. The finding urges joined up thinking about children who rarely carry just one infection.
plos-pone-0011306:
Boye, Boye, Pang and colleagues restored vision in mice by gene therapy for PLOS ONE in 2010. The mice lacked an enzyme needed in the retina's light sensing cells, causing blindness from birth. The team delivered a working copy of the gene to the eye and then tested sight in several ways.

Both functional measures and behavior showed vision was restored in the treated mice. That proof of concept supports gene therapy for inherited blindness of this type. Eye doctors gain a model showing what success should look like before human trials. The work moves inherited retinal disease care toward actual cures.
plos-pone-0011406:
José Nájera and co-authors tested in 2010 whether adding one viral gene could strengthen an experimental HIV vaccine. The vaccine uses a harmless carrier virus, NYVAC-B, to deliver HIV pieces that train the immune system. The team inserted a host-range gene from a related virus, hoping the carrier would persist longer and teach more strongly.

In animal tests, the modified carrier raised stronger immune responses against the HIV pieces than the original carrier did. A small genetic tweak improving the carrier itself is a practical path forward, since the HIV pieces need not change. The result matters for the long search for an HIV vaccine, where many candidates fail for being too weak. Strengthening trusted carriers may be as important as choosing which viral pieces to deliver.
plos-pone-0011506:
Xiaowei Zhang and co-authors mapped in 2010 how brain wiring changes in mice born without the dopamine transporter. The transporter normally mops up dopamine after it signals, so without it dopamine lingers and floods the gaps between brain cells from birth. Such mice are used to model conditions involving dopamine excess, including aspects of ADHD and addiction.

The team found altered neurocircuitry across the knockout mouse brain, showing that lifelong dopamine excess reshapes the wiring itself, not just moment-to-moment signaling. Structure and chemistry thus grow up together, each bending the other. The altered circuits caution model users: behavior in these mice reflects a differently built brain. They also show what sustained dopamine imbalance can do during development, a lesson for any condition or drug that raises dopamine for years.
plos-pone-0011606:
Timothy Sweeney and co-authors studied sepsis in mice in PLOS ONE in 2010. Sepsis is a severe whole-body reaction to infection, here caused by Staphylococcus aureus bacteria. The team focused on the PGC gene family, which switches on production of mitochondria, the cell's energy factories, and responds when those factories are damaged.

They tracked how each of the three family members behaved during infection. The members were not regulated alike, moving in different directions rather than as one unit. That split response matters because restoring energy supply is a hoped-for route to helping patients survive sepsis.
plos-pone-0011706:
Mohsin Yakub and Mohammad Iqbal surveyed adults in Karachi, Pakistan, for PLOS ONE in 2010. Both high blood lead and high levels of homocysteine, a blood amino acid, have been tied to cardiovascular disease. Average levels of both have been reported as high in the Pakistani population.

The survey measured blood lead and plasma homocysteine in the same people and tested how the two relate. Their cross-sectional results examine whether lead exposure travels with this heart-risk marker. The link, if confirmed, would flag a double burden for communities already exposed to lead pollution.
plos-pone-0011806:
Inna Ovsyannikova and co-authors studied genetic influences on rubella vaccine response, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Recent work suggested HLA genes help determine how strongly people respond to the vaccine. The class III region of that complex holds several immune genes, including those for lymphotoxin alpha, tumour necrosis factor and a leukocyte transcript.

The team examined extended gene combinations, or haplotypes, spanning these genes and their association with vaccine-induced immunity. Their results help explain why the same shot protects people unequally. Genetic prediction of weak responders could guide booster policy for rubella.
plos-pone-0011906:
Clive Rosenthal, Christopher Kennard, and David Soto asked in 2010 whether people can learn a visual sequence without seeing its parts properly. Learning links between items that sit near each other in space and time is a basic feature of memory. Higher-order patterns, where items are separated, can be picked up with or without awareness.

Their study concerns visuospatial sequence learning when the visual input itself is unavailable to awareness. If the brain still registers the pattern, then sequence learning runs deeper than conscious sight. Findings of this kind speak to patients with damaged vision, whose brains may keep learning from material they cannot report seeing.
plos-pone-0012006:
Phillip Gienapp and Juha Merilä tested in 2010 whether Siberian jays are as faithful as their reputation claims. Extra-pair paternity, chicks fathered outside the pair, is common in birds and varies with ecology and social life. Group-living species often show high rates, which made the group-living jays an interesting case.

Genetic testing found no evidence of extra-pair paternity in the Siberian jays studied. A species that truly keeps pair bonds, with fathers investing in their own young, is a valuable exception for testing theories about why cheating evolves elsewhere. The jays' fidelity also fits their cooperative family life, where trust inside the group is the working currency.
plos-pone-0012106:
Sarah Pendergrass, Everett Hayes, Giuseppina Farina, and colleagues studied blood markers in people with a limited form of scleroderma, in PLOS ONE in 2010. In this illness the skin and organs slowly harden, and some patients go on to develop dangerous high pressure in the lung arteries. Checking for that lung problem now needs invasive tests, so a blood signal would be a real advance.

Patients who had the lung complication carried blood signs of inflammation and blood vessel injury that set them apart. Markers like these could lead to simple screening tests that flag risk early. They also hint at how the lung damage starts, which may guide future treatment.
plos-pone-0012206:
Wai-Kin Mat, Hong Xue, and J Tze-Fei Wong reported changes in the genetic code itself, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The code that translates DNA into proteins has kept the same set of building blocks for roughly three billion years, in every known organism. That frozen pattern makes the rare exceptions, where a lab-made or unusual code assigns a new building block, scientifically precious.

The authors describe code mutations in which a bacterium encodes a fluorine-bearing variant in place of a standard one. Each such case tests which parts of the code are truly fixed by chemistry and which are historical accident. That question touches the origin of life and the design of engineered organisms with expanded chemistry.
plos-pone-0012306:
Julia Lee, Puthigae Sathish, Daniel Donaghy, and co-authors studied how pasture grass survives running out of carbon, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A plant cannot move to better conditions, so when drought or cold cuts its photosynthesis, it must ration the sugars it has stored. Using ryegrass, the backbone of temperate pasture farming, they tracked which biological processes the plant adjusts first when carbon runs short.

The grass actively remodels its metabolism to stretch its reserves rather than simply starving. Knowing the survival program helps breeders select grasses that bounce back after drought or hard grazing. For livestock regions, that resilience is the difference between a paddock recovering and a farm buying feed.
plos-pone-0012406:
Jason Noel, Nabil Arrach, Ali Alagely and colleagues tracked how Salmonella bacteria respond to tomatoes, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Outbreaks traced to raw vegetables showed that gut germs can live on and in plants for long stretches before infecting people. The team used a gene-fishing method to see which Salmonella genes switch on inside tomato fruit.

The bacteria answered differently depending on tomato variety and on how ripe the fruit was. Ripeness and breed thus shape how well the germ persists on produce. Food safety rules that treat all tomatoes alike may miss real risk differences, and growers could use variety choice as one more defense.
plos-pone-0012506:
Shengli Zhao, Yang Zhou, Jimmy Gross and colleagues created a mouse line that lights up newborn brain cells, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Adult brains grow new neurons in the hippocampus, a region for memory, and those newborns may help learning and mood. Studying them has been hard because they blend into mature neighbors.

In the GAD67-GFP mice, young dentate granule cells glow green, so researchers can find and follow them live. A reliable label turns guesswork into direct observation. The tool should speed studies of how exercise, stress, and drugs change adult brain growth, with relevance to depression and memory loss.
plos-pone-0012606:
Raz and co-authors studied brain damage after a stroke-like event in rats. After blood flow to the brain is cut and restored, harmful oxygen radicals surge and kill nerve cells. An enzyme called NADPH oxidase helps make those radicals, yet what switches it on in the brain was poorly known.

Their 2010 paper points to Rac1, a small switch protein, as a key controller of that enzyme after ischemia. When Rac1's role was blocked, damage and memory problems were reduced in their tests. The finding names a possible drug target for limiting harm after stroke.
plos-pone-0012706:
Wu, Zhou, Lan and co-authors followed the signals that let a goat egg cell finish dividing. When an egg divides, a ring of actin and myosin squeezes it into two unequal parts. Their 2010 study used a chemical trigger to start this division in goat oocytes outside the body.

They show the master factor MPF turns on two partners, RhoA and MAPK, to build and tighten the ring. Egg division underpins fertility in farm animals and people alike. Mapping its controls helps explain failed fertilisation and guides breeding work.  Timing of each signal was measured during the division.
plos-pone-0012806:
Wang, Huang and Hsu asked whether stunted growth explains the lasting brain effects of a steroid given to newborns. Dexamethasone is used to help the lungs of babies born too early. Worry has grown that it also harms the hippocampus, the brain's memory centre, over the long term.

Their 2010 rat study separated the drug's growth-slowing effect from its direct effect on synapses, the links between neurons. Untangling the two matters for judging how risky the drug really is. Neonatal care needs that balance to be evidence based.  Synapse strength was measured in brain slices from treated pups.
plos-pone-0335006:
Oluwasegun Akinyemi and co-authors asked what happened to hospital bills for women treated for major depression after Medicaid expanded under the Affordable Care Act. They compared Maryland and New Jersey, two states that expanded coverage, with Florida, which did not. The records covered more than a decade of inpatient stays by women with depression as the main diagnosis.

The two expanding states moved in opposite directions. In Maryland, charges fell compared with Florida, and the drop reached every racial group and insurance type, with the biggest falls for uninsured and Medicaid patients. In New Jersey, charges rose instead. The split suggests that how a state pays hospitals can matter as much as whether it expands coverage at all.
plos-pone-0342806:
Tatiana Maroilley and co-authors describe a Calgary course that gives health science undergraduates real research instead of canned laboratory exercises. Bioinformatics needs fluency in both biology and computing, and few degrees teach the blend. Their 2026 report covers a course-based research experience run across three winter terms at the Cumming School of Medicine.

Student teams investigated how large genetic rearrangements change gene activity in a tiny roundworm, a standard model animal. Students detected the variants, traced their effects in expression data, and presented findings like working researchers. Maroilley and colleagues argue the format scales research training beyond the few students who win laboratory placements, while teaching applied computing on a live question.
plos-pone-0343606:
Iqramul Haq, Md Yusuf Hossain Ador, and Diego Nobrega test whether machine learning can flag unsafe drinking water in Bangladesh, in this 2026 study. The bacterium E. coli signals fecal contamination, but lab testing every household supply is slow and costly. The team used a national survey covering more than six thousand household water samples and trained ten different algorithms to predict contamination from survey information.

About two in five households had contaminated drinking water, with one hill district standing out as the worst hotspot. After the data were balanced to handle the uneven classes, ensemble methods performed best; one boosting model edged out the rest on overall accuracy and caught nearly all contaminated samples. The authors argue such models could let authorities target scarce lab testing where risk is highest.
plos-pone-0344506:
Chongchao Zhang and colleagues propose a login method for electric car charging that keeps checking who is plugged in, rather than checking once at the start. Their scheme, PufCB-Auth, builds a fingerprint from two sources: the unique electrical quirks of the charger's hardware, which cannot be cloned, and the driver's own charging habits. Together these factors guard against stolen passwords and copied credentials.

Habits drift and hardware signals wobble, so an enhanced version refreshes the stored fingerprint over time instead of locking users out. Simulations showed the method verified users accurately with little computing cost, suiting busy public chargers with modest hardware. The authors tested the design against a modern fast-charging standard and present it as ready for real-world trials.
plos-pone-0346606:
Osman Darici, Chanel Cabak, and Jeremy D Wong built a low cost camera system in 2026 that grades walking function without body markers. Standard gait labs are dear and slow, so formal walking assessments happen rarely for older adults.

Three ordinary cameras feed open source tracking software and custom analysis. Against a laboratory marker system in a small test group, step length, step width, and head speed matched very closely. Reports on older volunteers resembled published norms, with room to add extra gait measures. A cheap, automatic setup could bring regular walking checks into ordinary clinics and homes.
plos-pone-0347206:
Seth M. Gibbons and a team of colleagues tested whether DNA floating in river water can track river herring, once-abundant fish now in decline in North Carolina. The murky Neuse and Tar-Pamlico rivers defeat easy counting. Weekly water samples at eight sites during spawning season were checked for herring genetic traces, alongside traditional electric-shock fishing counts at two places.

DNA levels and fish counts rose together during the first three weeks of spawning. Later, DNA stayed high even as adult fish left, likely lingering from eggs, young fish, and the water itself. Upriver sites gave the most consistent signals. The authors say the method suits long-term monitoring of these hard-to-watch rivers.
plos-pone-0347606:
Hanane Abbou and her team read eleven genes in one hundred nine people from Morocco. The genes run the body's own cannabis-like signal web. This web steers pain, mood, and more. The team found one hundred seventy gene forms never seen in print. They then zoomed in on one shift in the chief gene of the web.

In cell models, that shift shook the build of the web's key lock. The lock lost some of its twist and sat less snug. It took a higher-energy, less firm shape. The team says such shifts may change how folk react to drugs based on this plant.
plos-pone-0348206:
Courtney Bir, Jinho Jung, and Nicole Olynk Widmar asked American workers not whether they like remote work, but why. Using a nationally representative survey from late 2021, during the pandemic, respondents repeatedly picked their most and least valued reasons for working from home. The 2026 study then grouped workers by what they prized most.

Balancing the job with caregiving topped the list, followed by saving commute time and money, avoiding illness, and simply liking home. Four camps emerged, centred variously on caregiving, productivity and comfort, multitasking and safety, or no single motive. Remote workers also changed grooming and dress habits. The authors warn employers that one flexibility policy will not fit all.
plos-pone-0348506:
Yuanxiang Peng surveyed five hundred visitors at a major international music festival to test whether going green wins loyalty. The study separates festival green efforts into environmental, social, and economic practices. Then it traces how those practices shape whether visitors praise, return to, and support an event. It looks for the mental steps in between.

All three kinds of practice directly strengthened visitors' supportive intentions, with environmental action carrying the strongest pull. The effect also travelled along chains: green practices raised environmental awareness, awareness raised the value visitors felt they got. That sense of value fed satisfaction, which in turn fed loyalty. Peng advises organisers to treat these practices as a strategic asset that improves the experience itself, not a compliance chore to hide backstage.
plos-pone-0348606:
Qian Yang, Yun Wang, and Mingjun Wu evaluated a staffing change in their hospital's sterile supply department, the unit that cleans and packs surgical instruments. Under the new model, supply staff are posted forward in the operating suite itself rather than serving it from a distance. The team compared a year of the new model against the previous year under the traditional setup.

Instruments needing a second cleaning fell by about two-thirds, packing quality rose, and clinical staff reported higher satisfaction. The first scheduled surgery of the day also started on time far more often. Small logistics changes rarely make headlines, yet in surgery a missing or dirty instrument delays care, so a forward-posted team shows measurable value.
plos-pone-0348806:
Qin Lai and co-workers rate the front faces of old Catholic churches in China's Sichuan and Chongqing region. Built between eighteen forty and nineteen forty-nine, these churches blend Chinese and Western building traditions. Their 2026 study scores sixty-two surviving churches on how their fronts meet their surroundings, their outlines, styles, decoration, and religious expression.

About a fifth of the churches are mainly Chinese in style. Chinese-style fronts still borrowed Western vertical layouts, while Western fronts often added Chinese touches and plain folk decoration. Style, decoration, and religious expression rose and fell together closely. Grading heritage fronts with numbers gives protectors a shared language for deciding what to save and how.
plos-pone-0348906:
Ying Lu and co-authors built a system that watches and listens to miners, then judges whether their emotions have turned unsafe. Tired, angry, or frightened miners judge risks poorly, and mistakes underground can kill. Their model reads two channels at once: the sound of speech, handled by networks that catch both tone patterns and how they unfold over time. It also reads facial expressions, using a compact vision network.

Trained on recordings sorted into five unsafe emotional states, the combined system recognised them with accuracy in the mid-eighties percent range. Small field trials in a working mine suggested the approach can function outside the lab. The authors offer the system as an early warning layer, flagging struggling miners before a poor decision becomes an accident.
plos-pone-0349106:
Palanisamy Angappan and co-workers tackle a shop-floor problem: a tough heat-proof metal alloy that is hard to cut cleanly. The alloy is used in hot settings but hardens fast while being cut and holds heat poorly. In their 2026 study, they test cutting tools marked with tiny laser-made grooves, paired with a semi-solid lubricant, on a computer-run lathe.

Tools with grooves running in straight parallel lines did the best cutting work. They left the smoothest surface, needed the least force, and stayed the coolest of the four tool types tried. The grooves shortened contact with flying metal chips and helped the lubricant work better. Wear checks under a microscope showed rubbing and material spread as the main damage.
plos-pone-0349206:
Antonina Kaczorowska and colleagues asked more than eleven hundred people aged sixty to ninety in southwestern Poland how good their lives feel, using a standard World Health Organization quality of life questionnaire. Scores cover body, mind, relationships, and surroundings. The team then looked for the social traits that separate people thriving in old age from those merely getting by.

Just over half the group rated their quality of life as good. Men scored higher than women on mental and environmental measures, people in relationships scored higher across most areas, and more schooling lifted nearly every score. Good self-rated health and fewer chronic illnesses mattered most of all. The authors urge policy that widens access to education and protects health across the whole lifespan, not only in old age.
plos-pone-0349406:
Mariam Ahmed, Sharon Owino, and co-authors studied a little-known brain receptor, GPR37, to see whether dialing it down changes body weight and blood sugar control. With obesity affecting about forty percent of American adults, fresh drug targets are in demand, and this receptor family supplies many existing medicines. Their 2026 study used mice carrying only one working copy of the gene and measured weight, glucose tolerance, and insulin response.

Male mice with reduced gene dosage weighed less, handled fasting better, and responded more sensitively to insulin than normal males. The effect was sex-biased, showing clearly in males. The authors read this as a previously unrecognized role for the receptor in whole-body energy balance and nominate it for deeper, tissue-specific follow-up as a possible metabolic drug target.
plos-pone-0349506:
Damilola Onietan and colleagues lay out a protocol for mapping research on psychosocial help for teenagers uprooted by war and persecution. Adolescents make up forty percent of the world's forcibly displaced people and carry heavy mental health burdens, yet support programs for them are scattered and unevenly studied. A scoping review will chart what exists before anyone judges what works.

The review will gather studies of refugees, asylum seekers, and internally displaced youth aged ten to nineteen. It will span qualitative, quantitative, and mixed designs, where the intervention aims at psychological well-being or social functioning. The finished map is meant to steer policy and practice toward the gaps, showing which groups and which kinds of help researchers have ignored.
plos-pone-0349606:
Lotte J S Fleurkens-Ewals and co-authors ran a reader study in 2026 on scoring cancer spread inside the abdomen from CT scans. The score guides treatment for cancers that seed the belly lining, and pre-drawn region outlines might help readers agree.

Eighty-two clinicians from nineteen countries scored nine scans, with and without colour overlays marking the regions. Agreement, closeness to the surgical score, confidence, and user experience were compared. The overlays did not significantly improve agreement, the headline the authors report plainly. Negative results like this save hospitals from buying decision aids that feel helpful but do not measurably help.
plos-pone-0350006:
Karina Patasova, Marie Holmqvist, and co-authors hunted for hidden genetic links between systemic sclerosis, a rare autoimmune disease, and the cancers its patients develop at elevated rates. Whole-genome comparisons had found no overall relationship, but averaging can hide local links where effects point in opposite directions. Their 2026 study applied finer methods that test genetic correlation region by region against breast and lung cancers and blood malignancies.

Again, no overall genetic correlation appeared. Zooming in, though, they found twenty-three local regions where the diseases' genetics correlated significantly, some positively and some negatively, exactly the pattern global methods miss. Follow-up analyses probed genes in those regions for shared biology. The authors argue the sclerosis-cancer connection may live in specific genomic neighborhoods rather than across the whole genome.
plos-pone-0350106:
Hye Young Hong and Young Ae Kang led a review of lung patients in Korea. The illness is a slow lung infection from a germ kin to the TB germ. Care takes a year or more of drugs. Many patients quit too soon. The team followed four hundred twenty patients treated from 2010 to 2023. They split those who quit early from those who finished.

Thirty in a hundred quit early. Bad drug side effects raised the odds of quitting a lot. Poor diet did too. Quitters then died at near three times the rate of finishers. Low diet scores also tracked with death. The team urges close watch for side effects and food support from day one.
plos-pone-0350506:
Donrawee Waeyeng and Soisungwan Satarug led a study of diet and kidney health in southern Thailand. People there face long-term contact with two toxic metals, cadmium and lead. Both metals can harm the kidneys. The team asked if eating more plant foods might help. They signed up ninety-six adults aged fifty and over in late 2024.

People who ate more plant foods showed less of a urine sign of kidney cell harm. Those who ate more nuts and seeds did best of all. High metal contact, by contrast, came with signs of kidney stress. The team says plant-rich diets may soften metal harm. They also back the urine test as an early warning tool.
plos-pone-0350806:
Felix A Andong and colleagues studied breeding male village weaver birds in Amurum Forest Reserve, Nigeria, during the costly season when males breed, moult, and fight infection at once. One hundred and forty eight males were grouped by worm infection and moult status. Blood stress balance, blood sugar, and feather colour quality were measured within minutes of capture.

About half the males carried the worms. Infected birds showed strained stress chemistry. Males facing both infection and moult scored worst on sugar control and feather quality by far, beyond either burden alone in direct contrasts. Bright honest signals, the work shows, collapse first when body budgets are doubly drained.
plos-pone-0351106:
Akram Hasanov and four colleagues study the wildest days in energy stock markets — the rare crashes and spikes that standard risk models handle badly, in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. Using two decades of daily data to early 2025, they estimated how quickly the chance of extreme returns decays for renewable and conventional energy share indices. The method asks, in effect, how many statistical moments of the return distribution even exist.

Both kinds of index showed heavy tails following a power law. Average returns and volatility appear finite and usable, but higher shape measures may be mathematically infinite, which quietly breaks tools built on them. A rolling analysis showed tail risk swelling around major market stresses. Investors in green energy, the authors warn, should plan for extremes that history understates.
plos-pone-0351306:
Markku Kallio and colleagues pooled data on close to sixteen hundred children with confirmed bacterial meningitis in six countries across Latin America, Angola, and Finland. Simple spinal fluid tests at admission, sugar, protein, and white cell counts, were checked against death in hospital and brain outcome at discharge. Such cheap tests could help triage where intensive care is scarce.

Death rose step by step as spinal fluid sugar fell and as protein rose. Children with both very low sugar and very high protein died at a rate near twenty seven percent, versus one percent when both values looked normal. Low white cell counts also warned of danger. Two routine numbers together, the authors show, flag high risk children early.
plos-pone-0351406:
Bian and colleagues audited urine leakage prevention for intensive care patients with catheters in a Chinese hospital in a 2026 study. The team first built audit standards from the best available evidence, then checked real practice with dozens of nurses and patients. Gaps between standards and bedside care were then analyzed for causes.

Audits of this kind sort which failures come from knowledge, staffing, supplies, or habit. That sorting shapes training and workflow fixes in the next phase of the project. Catheter leakage harms skin, comfort, and infection risk, so even small compliance gains matter in units where patients stay for weeks. The baseline review gives the unit a clear starting measure.
plos-pone-0351506:
Long COVID symptoms vary wildly between people, so Su-jin Kim and Jinhee Kim sorted Korean adults with lasting symptoms into natural groups. Their 2026 PLOS One survey covered about six hundred thirty adults whose symptoms had run at least twelve weeks, scoring twenty-six complaints and overall quality of life.

Four profiles fit best. About a quarter had light symptoms overall; the largest group, over two fifths, had moderate problems across many body systems; another group centered on exhaustion that worsens after effort. Quality of life fell as symptom load rose. The authors say clinics should treat these profiles differently rather than handing everyone the same plan.
plos-pone-0351606:
Editorial Note: PLOS One flags an overlap concern between a published study of DNA sequences in ice from Antarctica's subglacial Lake Vostok and a companion paper by the same group. This 2026 note explains that both articles analyze the same two ice cores, which the authors had declared before publication.

The authors say the papers differ in focus: one on the lake's likely living conditions, the other on which species and body processes the sequences suggest. An independent editorial board member reviewed the overlap question. Readers should keep the shared dataset in mind when weighing the two papers' conclusions about life beneath the Antarctic ice.
plos-pone-0351706:
Dinh Thi Nguyen and Loan Thi Ho catalogued the leaf beetles of Cat Ba Island, a limestone island off northern Vietnam, pairing old-fashioned specimen work with DNA barcoding. Shelf islands in Southeast Asia are biological crossroads and among the least surveyed places for insects. Field collecting found thirty-six species-level units across thirty genera, dominated by one large subfamily.

Barcoding sorted the catch into thirty-one genetic clusters, most of them new to the global barcode library, proof of how much diversity sits undocumented on one island. Clock estimates place the main lineages' origins in the Miocene, before the island itself took shape, so the beetles are heirs of mainland forests later stranded by rising seas. For conservation, Cat Ba is not a depauperate offshoot but an archive, and its beetles deserve the archive's protection.
plos-pone-0352206:
Lismaryin Muñoz-Requene, Pedro Sánchez-Zamora, and Rosa Gallardo-Cobos measured how exposed Nicaragua's North Caribbean Coast is to tropical cyclones, town by town. The region is among the country's most storm-hit and poorest, and climate change is loading the dice further. They built a vulnerability index from twelve indicators covering exposure, the fragility of people and housing, and each municipality's capacity to adapt.

The map that emerged is uneven. Bonanza combined high exposure and fragility with weak adaptive capacity, while Waslala showed sturdier structure. Three clusters of towns shared similar risk profiles. A single regional plan would fit none of them well. For disaster agencies, the index names where shelters, drainage, and income support buy the most safety before the next storm season, not after the damage is photographed.
plos-pone-0352506:
Isabel von Känel-Cordoba and seven colleagues gather everything known about the half-distance Ironman triathlon, in this 2026 PLOS ONE systematic review. The event — a swim, a long bike ride, and a half marathon — has boomed worldwide, yet research has trailed the full-distance race. Searching five databases, the team assembled eighty-six studies covering training, nutrition, body measures, weather, and medical issues.

Cycling emerged as the strongest single predictor of finish time. Professional men peaked around age twenty-eight, women around thirty-two, and participation is growing fastest among women and older athletes. Racing temporarily dents immunity and muscles, then recovers. The authors note the field's blind spots: small samples and too few women studied.
plos-pone-0352906:
Rafael Flores and co-authors designed a family of lipoic-acid-derived molecules aimed at a brain receptor tied to neurodegeneration. The sigma-1 receptor is implicated in Alzheimer's disease and related disorders, and diverse, easy-to-make activators are wanted. Their 2026 design follows a three-part recipe: a sulphur-bearing hydrophobic head, a flexible amide linker, and a greasy tail.

Twenty-one molecules were designed, docked in the computer, synthesised, and tested for binding at both sigma receptor types. Three stood out for selective sigma-1 binding in the nanomolar range, though a standard comparison ligand bound far tighter still. Flores and colleagues keep the three as starting leads for a follow-up round of structure tuning.
plos-pone-0353106:
Yinchun Wang and four co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One language study of Chinese scholars speaking academic English. Their focus is hedging, the words speakers use to soften claims. Hedging is a known stumbling block at conferences and defenses. The team built a large corpus of Chinese scholars' spoken English. They compared it with an American academic speech corpus. Verb-based hedges were the focus.

Chinese scholars used far fewer personal stance markers like 'I think.' They used far more shared markers like 'we see.' The authors read this as a strategy that favors group harmony and shared duty. The study does not stop at diagnosis. It builds a classroom module with worksheets to train these forms. The aim is fewer communication failures in high-stakes settings.
plos-pone-0353206:
Limin Tang and seven colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One experiment on licorice stem and leaf silage as cattle feed, tested in laboratory rumen fluid rather than live animals. The team prepared silage at four dry matter levels and followed fermentation over seventy-two hours, measuring gas output, acidity, nutrient breakdown, and the microbes involved. A licorice feed additive was included in the silage.

The batch at fifty-five percent dry matter performed best overall, producing the most gas and microbial protein, breaking down nutrients fastest, and supporting the richest microbial community. Helpful fermentation products also peaked earlier in that batch. Statistical rankings placed it first among the four, and the authors recommend that moisture level for turning licorice stems and leaves into useful dairy feed.
plos-pone-0353306:
Wieland and colleagues compared two advanced methods for fitting random epidemic models in a 2026 study. Epidemic models that include chance events help forecast outbreaks, but working out their settings from data is mathematically hard. The team tested both methods on three standard disease models of rising complexity.

Each method had to recover known settings from data produced by the models themselves. Their strengths differed by model and data richness, giving modelers a practical guide on which to pick. Fast, reliable fitting matters during real outbreaks, when officials need quick forecasts that honestly reflect uncertainty. The comparison saves future teams from choosing a fitting tool blind.
plos-pone-0353506:
Sabah and Alaa presented a self-tuning method for grouping texts by topic in a 2026 study. Modern language models turn text into rich numeric codes, but each model shines in different fields. Older blending methods fix how much each model counts ahead of time, wasting their complementary strengths.

Their framework lets a search algorithm adjust the blend weights as grouping proceeds, with no labels needed. Better blends should give cleaner clusters for tasks like news sorting and routing technical questions. The work targets a quiet but costly step in text systems, where poor grouping early on degrades every later answer. Dynamic weighting offers a path to clusters that fit each collection's own character.
plos-pone-0353606:
Hattan Abutarboush and colleagues report in 2026 on a thin microwave absorber built from printed rings. Their design uses two nested rings on a common circuit board material, with four small stubs placed evenly around the outer ring and a solid metal backing. Keeping the build to one layer was the central aim.

Tests of a made sample matched computer models and showed strong uptake in six separate frequency bands, each above nine tenths of the incoming energy. Lower bands linked mainly to magnetic responses, while higher bands mixed electric effects as well. A simple flat design that handles several bands at once could help with shielding, sensing, and reducing unwanted radar reflections.
plos-pone-0353706:
Natthapon Inta, Annmarie Grealish, and Mary Leamy explore what recovery from mental illness means in Thailand, in this 2026 PLOS ONE interview study. Recovery is a guiding idea in modern mental health care, but its meaning shifts between cultures.
