They spoke with service users, family carers, and health professionals in primary and community services, then tested the themes in feedback workshops.

Participants described recovery as moving from symptom relief toward hope, meaning, and social connection. Family backing, community acceptance, and trusting relationships with staff were central, while obstacles appeared at personal, family, service, and community levels. From this, the authors propose a recovery support model fitted to Thai culture.
plos-pone-0353906:
Niu and colleagues, in a 2026 study, ask whether immune system genes raise the risk of clogged heart arteries in people from Northeast China. The HLA genes help the immune system tell self from invader, and they vary a lot between people. The team compared two HLA genes in about two hundred people, split between those prone to artery clogging and controls.

Dozens of gene variants were counted. Two single variants appeared more often in the disease-prone group, but neither survived strict correction for the many tests run. A paired combination of the two variants, inherited together, was more than twice as common in the disease-prone group. That signal also faded under the strictest correction, though its size was too large, the authors argue, to dismiss as pure noise. They label the pair a candidate risk marker and call for much larger studies to confirm or refute it.
plos-pone-0354206:
Lyu and colleagues, in a 2026 review, work out how much exercise helps depression among middle-aged and older people with Parkinson's disease, and which kinds help most. Earlier trials tested exercise one dose at a time, which hid the shape of the benefit. The team pooled twenty-five trials and modeled dose on a continuous scale, counting weekly energy spent.

Benefit followed a curve, not a straight climb. Gains held across a broad middle band of weekly dose and peaked near its center; at the highest doses the effect turned unstable. Two kinds of exercise stood out: exercise paired with mental training, and mind-body exercise such as tai chi styles, both peaking at the same middle dose. Walking helped only at higher doses, and several other types showed no dependable range. The authors say dose and kind must be prescribed together, like a drug and its amount.
plos-pone-0354606:
Nnaemeka Iriemenam and co-authors tested front-line health staff at seven Nigerian sites for coronavirus antibodies late in the pandemic. Health staff faced the worst exposure, and counts of past infection guide safety plans. Their 2026 study enrolled more than twelve hundred nurses, lab staff, doctors, and pharmacists for blood tests and a habits survey.

Antibodies were near universal: about ninety-eight in one hundred staff tested as past-exposed. Most hits bore the mark of the virus's inner protein, a sign of true past infection, not shots alone. Nurses were three times as apt to test as past-exposed as lab staff. Half the staff still lacked shots at the time. The team urges stronger shots and ward safety for front-line staff.
plos-pone-0354706:
Fei Chen and co-authors propose in 2026 a better way to estimate the health of lithium ion batteries from electrical response tests. Single response measures miss how ageing parts of a battery interact, giving weak predictions. Their method picks several response features that track capacity loss, then feeds them to a neural network tuned by three search methods borrowed from nature.

Across test conditions with plenty of data and with noisy, scarce data, tuned networks kept errors low and stable. Two of the tuning methods stood out in the hardest cases. Reliable health estimates matter for safe use of batteries in vehicles and portable devices.
plos-pone-0355106:
Issiaka Sare and co-authors tested a locally isolated fungus as a malaria mosquito killer and traced its effects across generations. Fungi offer an eco-friendlier alternative to chemical insecticides, but their full life-history costs to mosquitoes were unclear. Their 2026 study exposed a major malaria vector to two strains of the fungus at larval and adult stages.

Larvae were reared in spore-dosed water, and survivors were followed for lifespan, wing size, egg laying, and blood feeding. Separately, sprayed adult females were followed through their offspring's survival. Survival analysis used standard hazard models, with other traits compared across treatments. Sare and colleagues frame the results for biocontrol planners weighing fungal sprays against resistance-prone chemicals.
plos-pone-0355406:
Amit Hasan and co-authors report in 2026 the first known case in Bangladesh of a fungus causing leaf spot on quinoa, a nutritious grain like crop with growing local promise. Sick plants at a university farm in Dhaka yielded one fungus again and again from spotted leaves. Shape study, gene sequencing, and family tree analysis named the culprit, and infection tests on healthy plants reproduced the spots.

The fungus was reisolated from the newly sick plants, completing the classic proof of cause. Colonies grew grey to black with curved, thick walled spores. The authors warn growers to watch for this emerging threat and urge resistance screening and joined up disease control.
plos-pone-0355506:
Benedicto Mgala and colleagues explore in 2026 daily life for patients in Tanzania who must take warfarin for life after receiving an artificial heart valve. The drug prevents dangerous clots but needs tight dose control, a strict diet, and regular blood checks. Twelve patients at the national heart institute gave in depth interviews about their routines.

Many felt better after surgery, yet diet limits, side effects, low mood, and lost work weighed heavily. Keeping blood levels in range was hard amid money strain, uneven drug use, mixed advice, and scarce testing away from the centre. The authors call for a clearer, joined up path of care.
plos-pone-0355606:
Qiuhong Deng leads a 2026 PLOS ONE study of why cervical cancer resists immunotherapy, treatment that frees the immune system to attack tumors. A protein called IGF2BP1 reads a chemical tag on gene messages, named m6A, and was suspected of helping tumors dodge immune attack. Its control was unknown.

Across datasets and four cancer cell lines, IGF2BP1 ran high and tracked with poor survival. Silencing it slowed growth and made tumors respond better to a checkpoint drug, with more killer T cells entering and firing. Another protein, HDAC2, normally keeps IGF2BP1 repressed by cleaning tags off its gene switch. Losing HDAC2 frees it. Targeting the axis partly restored drug effect.
plos-pone-0356006:
Vicente Lopez-Chavarrias, Irene Aldea, and Jovita Fernández-Pinero published a 2026 software paper in PLOS ONE introducing PePApipe, a tool that automates genome analysis for African swine fever virus. The virus devastates pig farming and triggers trade bans, and tracing outbreaks needs full genomes, yet the analysis steps were scattered across separate programs. The pipeline chains thirteen tools into one workflow, from raw sequencing reads through quality checks, genome assembly, and variant listing.

PePApipe was built for laboratory professionals with little computing background, needing only basic command-line skills, and it can run on a single machine or a computing cluster for batches. Outputs arrive in structured folders: a consensus genome plus a file of differences from a chosen reference, with intermediate files kept and steps switchable. The authors say one automated path cuts user error and makes results reproducible, easing the step from sequencer to outbreak report.
plos-pone-0356206:
Daisuke Sudo and Daisuke Toyoda ran a pilot trial testing whether eye exercise training adds anything to leg strengthening for thirty community-dwelling older adults. The bid was to cut falls by sharpening vision. Their 2026 randomized study trained both groups' legs for eight weeks. Half also drilled six visual skills on a dedicated training system. The skills ran from eye-hand coordination to peripheral perception.

No clear advantage appeared. Adjusted comparisons showed no confirmed differences in visual or physical outcomes. Several estimates leaned toward the vision group on exactly the skills practiced, though with wide uncertainty. The authors are candid: thirty people cannot settle the question. The pilot's real product is a blueprint for a properly powered trial with fairer controls and meaningful endpoints.
plos-pone-0356806:
Irina Elena Ionescu and colleagues compared two standard recipes for growing dendritic cells, the immune system's teaching cells, from mouse bone marrow, because the recipe quietly changes what the cells become. Their 2026 laboratory study grew cells with one growth factor alone or with a second added, then compared surface markers, cytokine output, and the ability to coach naive T cells.

Cells grown with the single factor looked mature yet still answered bacterial stimuli with cytokines and primed T cells in an antigen-specific way. Adding the second factor kept cells less mature but introduced nonspecific T cell signaling that could muddy experiments. The message for immunologists is to choose, and re-check, the recipe against the exact question being asked.
plos-pone-0356906:
Guillaume Bouguéon and colleagues test how long prepared bags of idarubicin, a workhorse drug against blood cancers, stay safe to use. Hospital pharmacies would like to prepare doses ahead, but shelf life in modern plastic bags lacked solid data. The team filled bags at two strengths in two common fluids. Some bags were stored cold. Others sat at room temperature. Samples were assayed across a full month, alongside checks for particles, acidity, and salt balance.

Drug levels stayed above ninety-five percent of the starting strength through day thirty in every condition, with no breakdown products detected. Bags showed no color change or precipitate, particle counts stayed within limits, and acidity and salt balance did not drift. Bouguéon and colleagues say pharmacies can safely prepare a month ahead under either storage style.
plos-pone-0357006:
Nayana Gunathilaka, Deshaka Jayakody, and Iranga Dilshan mapped fifteen years of rickettsioses in Sri Lanka. These are tick- and mite-borne fevers that are often missed. Their 2026 analysis used weekly national case reports from all twenty-five districts between 2009 and 2023. Satellite weather data was paired with the reports. The aim was to find where and when the diseases strike, and which climate conditions travel with them.

More than eighteen thousand cases were reported. They were heavily concentrated in Jaffna in the north, with the central highlands next. The modeling linked incidence patterns to local climate and geography. Knowing the hotspots and seasons lets health officials aim fever testing, public warnings, and vector control. They can target the districts and months where these under-recognized illnesses actually cluster.
plos-pone-0357106:
Julia Ruß and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article in veterinary medicine. It measures serum reverse triiodothyronine, a thyroid-related hormone in blood, in three groups of dogs: those with hypothyroidism, those whose illness is not thyroidal, and healthy dogs. Thyroid tests in dogs are notoriously muddied by other illnesses.

Nonthyroidal illness can make a healthy thyroid look underactive, leading to wrong treatment. Comparing this hormone across the three groups tests whether it separates true thyroid failure from the shadow of other disease. Veterinarians diagnosing sluggish, gaining dogs are the readers who need cleaner thyroid markers.
plos-pone-0357206:
Ruy Felipe Melo Viegas led a team of eight authors who compared blood and saliva tests in heart failure patients, in a PLOS ONE study from 2026. Checking a failing heart now means drawing blood to measure stress and injury markers. The team asked whether saliva could carry the same signals in useful amounts.

Viegas and his co-authors measured three markers in both fluids: one linked to heart strain, one to heart muscle injury, and one to inflammation. Setting the saliva values beside the blood values shows how close a spit test could come to the standard. A simple saliva check would make repeat testing easier for patients who need close tracking.
plos-pone-0357406:
Huawei Wang led a team of five authors improving crane scheduling in railway freight yards, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Rail-mounted gantry cranes move containers between trains and trucks, and poor scheduling jams the whole yard. The team built a flexible scheduling method that balances several goals at once.

Wang's model weighs speed against energy use and fairness across jobs, instead of chasing one target. Yards must make that trade-off daily as trains arrive off schedule. A model that bends without breaking helps dispatchers keep freight moving. Faster, steadier yards lower the cost of rail freight, which matters for shifting goods off roads and cutting transport emissions at the same time.
plos-pone-0357706:
Aysegul Erinc and colleagues ask whether a simple blood score predicts survival in people with scarring lung disease who do not have diabetes. The score combines fasting sugar and blood fat values and is often read as a sign of insulin resistance. Records covered well over a hundred patients on anti-scarring therapy, followed for close to three years on median, with lung tests and survival tracked.

The abstract reports the cohort's profile and the study design in detail, linking the score with lung function and death from any cause. Because patients here stayed within the non-diabetic range, the work tests whether small shifts in the score still carry meaning. Erinc and colleagues frame the score as a cheap add-on to scans and lung tests when judging outlook.
plos-pone-0357806:
Katie L Kowalski led a team of eight authors measuring rehabilitation science across Canada, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. They asked who produces rehabilitation research, how much they publish, and what impact it has. Their data mixed public records with a survey of faculty across the country.

Kowalski's faculty-wide picture shows where the field is strong, where it is thin, and who shapes its future. Universities and funders can use that picture to spot gaps, such as regions or topics with few active researchers. Rehabilitation serves an aging population with growing needs, so the health of its research base matters beyond academia. The study offers a baseline for judging future growth.
plos-pone-0357906:
J. Richard T. Korecki and coauthors published a 2026 protocol in PLOS ONE for project FIERCE, a trial testing a meditation program built for stressed doctors. Most healthcare providers report burnout, poor sleep, and low mood from workplace strain, and mindfulness courses help but rarely target positive emotion. Their six-week program, BEST, delivered online, adapts the Buddhist Four Immeasurables practice to cultivate loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity.

Ninety full-time doctors will be randomized to the program or a waitlist, completing surveys and giving blood samples at the start, middle, and end. Perceived stress is the main outcome, with burnout, depression, well-being, and sleep also tracked, with blood inflammation markers adding a hard-data layer. The design also tests what carries any benefit, measuring compassion, positive affect, equanimity, and mindfulness as candidate carriers. A positive-emotion focus, they hope, proves stronger medicine than attention training alone.
plos-pone-0359206:
Kathryn Date and eight colleagues published this study protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026. It describes the CONIFAS2 study, a feasibility test of a nature-based intervention for children with ADHD. The intervention was co-produced, designed together with the people who would use it.

A feasibility study asks whether a bigger trial can work at all: will families join, stay, and accept the activities? Nature-based activities are a low-drug option many families welcome, but they still need proper testing. Researchers planning the full trial, and clinicians who advise families with ADHD, are the readers for this groundwork.
plos-pone-0359306:
Monique Bussmann, Marieke Groot, Chris Kuiper, and Mieke Cardol published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It is an ethnographic multi-case study of musical encounters in healthcare, moments when music is brought to patients. The authors call these encounters precarious, valuable yet fragile, and explore why.

Perspectives come from both care professionals and the musicians themselves, whose views of the same visit can differ sharply. Ethnographic observation across several cases shows how setting, timing, and expectations make or break a musical visit. Arts-in-health organizers and hospital staff hosting musicians are the readers for this account.
pmc-10656306:
Joseph Spear, Jesse M Ehrenfeld, and Brian J Miller wrote a 2023 viewpoint arguing that artificial intelligence can cut the waste in American health care delivery. Care now eats nearly a fifth of the national economy, and past reforms have mostly added paperwork for patients and doctors alike. The authors cast AI as a thresher that can strip that burden away.

They map three zones of opportunity: automating administrative work, augmenting clinical practice, and a third zone of system-level gains. In each, they argue, AI can lower cost, improve care, and give time back to both sides of the clinic door. The piece is a policy argument, not a trial report.
pmc-10671806:
Fatima Alam and co-authors review how sex and gender shape e-cigarette use and its health effects. E-cigarettes deliver nicotine, flavorings, and other substances, and studies link them to lung harm, worse respiratory disease, and behavioral effects. Much of that research ignores sex as a variable. The review gathers studies from 2018 to 2023 that did report sex differences.

The search finds 115 relevant studies. Reported differences cover reasons for starting, smoking history, device and flavor choices, and use of other substances. They also cover body responses to nicotine and toxicants in e-liquids, flare-ups of lung disease, and behavior such as anxiety, depression, sexuality, and bullying. The authors conclude that sex and gender influence susceptibility to the harms of vaping. They urge future studies to build these variables into their designs from the start.
pmc-10675406:
Othmane Atanane and colleagues built a tiny learning system in 2023 to catch water leaks. Cities face rising water stress and shortages. Leaks in building pipes waste large amounts silently. Sensors plus on-device learning can spot leaks locally. Local decisions cut delay and central system costs. The team used an existing sound dataset for plastic pipes. Sound clips became image-like patterns for analysis. Five image network designs were adapted through transfer learning. The best model was then shrunk for a small board.

All networks learned to detect leak sounds well. One efficient design scored highest on every measure. Its test accuracy came close to ninety-eight percent. After compression, it ran on an Arduino-class edge device. Inference took about two seconds per check. Memory and storage needs stayed very small. The authors present a near hands-off leak watcher. Real buildings could host such devices widely, they argue.
pmc-10694906:
Wang and ten co-authors build tiny particles that attack breast tumors two ways at once. Their 2023 paper pairs heat therapy with flooding the cell's power units with calcium. Past calcium carriers could not hold the dose high enough for long. The new carrier packs a plant drug and a dye inside chalk-like shells.

Once inside tumor cells, the shells break down in acid and free calcium. The flood drops the cells' energy output. Near-infrared light heats the cells and speeds the breakdown. Cell and animal tests showed the paired attack slowed tumors. The team frames the work as a step toward combined nano-therapy.
pmc-10696706:
Han Zhang and six co-authors pool evidence on whether human herpesvirus infection raises cervical cancer risk, in a systematic review from twenty twenty-three. Human papillomavirus is the established cause of cervical cancer. What other viruses add remains unclear. The team searched major databases and appraised study quality with a standard tool.

Sixty-seven studies that fit, covering seven herpesviruses, entered the meta-analysis. Overall, herpesvirus infection was linked to higher odds of cervical cancer and of lesions that come before cancer. Herpes simplex virus type 2 and Epstein-Barr virus each showed positive correlations with both outcomes. Herpes simplex type 1 and cytomegalovirus showed no such link. The roles of three rarer herpesviruses stayed unclear in the data. The review suggests some herpesviruses may act as cofactors alongside papillomavirus.
pmc-10699306:
Malcolm Lim and seven colleagues deliver chemotherapy to breast cancer that has spread to the brain using antibody-guided nanoparticles. Brain metastases resist standard chemotherapy because effective doses are toxic and little drug crosses into the brain. Their hyperbranched polymer carrier targets the HER3 receptor, common on these metastases, and releases doxorubicin faster in acidic compartments inside cells.

In cell tests the targeted carrier killed breast cancer cells selectively. In a mouse model it slowed tumor growth, shrank tumors, and extended survival, with fourteen times more carrier reaching the brain than an untargeted version. Heart and ovary toxicity were lower than with free drug. The authors see a path to treating brain metastases more safely.
pmc-10704106:
Sprengholz, Henkel, Böhm, and Betsch warn in twenty twenty-three that distorted memories of the pandemic could hamper preparation for the next crisis. Studies in Germany asked people in twenty twenty and again in late twenty twenty-two about their past risk views, behaviour, and trust in science and government. Recalled answers were then checked against what people had actually said earlier.

Recall bent systematically with vaccination status. Vaccinated people overrated their past caution and trust, while unvaccinated people underrated theirs, above all when vaccination was core to identity. Paying for correct recall shrank the bias, so it was not mere forgetting. Stronger bias tracked harsher judgments of past policy. The authors fear rival stories of the crisis will deepen division.
pmc-10707406:
Tianlong Ding and six co-authors test if the cell shear ADAM17 marks fate and immune mix in liver cancer. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-three. This cancer is the most death-dealt tumor kind, and ADAM17 had been tied to tumor birth. Gene use in big cancer banks, life-span curves, cell runs, and mouse runs were all brought to bear.

High ADAM17 use tied to short life, late stage, and high blood marks. Paths lit near it span shape shift, flare, and growth chains. Its use also tracked immune cell mix and brake marks in tumors. Cell and mouse work showed it drives growth and spread. The team read it as a fate mark.
pmc-10708606:
Bartosz Musznicki and co-authors model city sensor networks from open data, in a 2023 paper from Poland. Wireless sensors need well planned links to move data well. Real maps of devices can give truer models than made up layouts.

The team wrote a set of methods that turn device location data into graph models of links. They built both snapshots and time spanning models for four large Polish cities. Tests then probed how the modeled networks behave and where they are weak. The authors close with paths for more work. City staff and network designers can use the approach to plan sensor rollouts on real streets.
pmc-10708806:
Madiha Khan and co-authors report a new material for sensing ethanol gas, in a 2023 study. Good gas sensors must be stable, picky, and quick, and finding materials that do all three is hard. The team combined two metal oxides, zirconium oxide and cobalt oxide, into tiny hybrid structures. They tested the mix as the active layer of a sensor at 200 degrees Celsius.

The sensor picked out ethanol clearly at low levels and answered a test pulse in under a minute. Its slow recovery, about six minutes, is a drawback the authors note. They credit the porous shape, which lets gas reach active sites, and an inner electric field where the two oxides meet. The results mark the pairing as a strong candidate for ethanol detection.
pmc-10709906:
False teeth collect slime films that threaten the mouth beneath, and the plastic they are made from decides how much film sticks. Salma Fathy and co-authors compare two denture plastics in a 2023 study, each made by hand packing and by computer milling. Discs of each kind were soaked in a bath carrying tiny particles of a common antiseptic.

The milled acetal discs came out roughest, before the soak and after. Every group grew far less film once coated, and the effect held for nineteen days as the antiseptic leaked out slowly. Before coating, roughness predicted film; after coating, it stopped mattering.
pmc-10711006:
Moving DNA or RNA into cells is a daily lab task, but the fatty carriers used often kill many of the cells. Tatsushi Yoshida, Kenta Yamasaki, and Kenjiro Tadagaki show in a 2023 study that the deaths follow the cell's own suicide program, called apoptosis. When they added a drug that blocks the enzymes driving that program, far more cells survived the procedure.

The drug also raised the share of cells that took up the new genetic material. The authors propose the blocker as a simple add-on that makes this common lab method gentler and more reliable, with possible uses in gene therapy and vaccines.
pmc-10716106:
Zhou and coauthors review tiny implanted sensors that track body signals in animals. Live tracking alerts vets to illness in animals early. It also helps probe how human illness works. Implanted chemical sensors meet that need with little harm.

Such sensors work without blood draws and cause little pain. They can track glucose, ions, and other body marks nonstop. The review traces how the field grew over years. It sums up sensor designs, coatings, and power needs. It also maps uses in farm and lab animals. Gaps hold long-term stability and safe removal.
pmc-10716406:
Rebecka Steffen Johansson and three co-authors checked whether heart attacks with clean arteries leave a flow flaw years later, in a study published in 2023. Such attacks have many roots; one is small vessel disease, which early scans can miss. A quarter of cases receive no diagnosis from the first scan. Their group held 15 such patients with clean first scans, plus 15 matched peers.

Five years on, a stress scan read blood flow through the heart wall. The former patients ran lower flow than the peers, with no gap in other scan marks or risk facts. Pill use split the groups on one drug type. The authors read the low flow as small vessel disease at work, late if not at first. They urge flow readings in the follow-up of such cases.
pmc-10720806:
Dongyao Xu, Youbao Huang, and Wei Wang published a letter in 2023 commenting on a trial of pain control after keyhole gallbladder surgery. The trial found that adding surgical pain techniques to drugs beat drugs alone, for pain at rest, pain on coughing, and sleep on the first night. The letter writers praise the work, then raise points they see as gaps.

One concern is that the trial did not state which gallbladder diseases its patients had. People with long-standing gallbladder inflammation hurt more after surgery than those with simple polyps, so the mix matters for reading the results. The letter goes on with further comments in the same spirit. Such exchanges help readers weigh how far a trial's findings can travel.
pmc-10729006:
Steven Lynn and co-authors report a 2023 study of a scale for ego loss. Ego loss, a fading sense of self, is a hallmark of psychedelic drug use. The team built a ten-item scale to rate it in daily life. Here they check the scale again in a fresh group. Student volunteers, 527 in all, filled in the scale and related measures online.

The check found the same two-part shape as before. One part covers ego loss and one covers unity with others and the world. Scores held steady and linked well with traits such as mindfulness and dissociation. Sleep and mood measures also fit the expected pattern. Drug researchers get a tested tool for a state that is hard to pin down. A sound scale lets studies compare ego loss across drugs, doses, and settings. The sample is students, not patients, so clinic use needs its own checks.
pmc-10734206:
Petrova and colleagues test how long stays in a new tongue land reshape sound picks in this twenty twenty-three study. Tongues weigh pitch and length in unlike ways when speech sounds are sorted. Grown learners may or may not pick up the new weights with time abroad.

Inside, Mandarin-born folks with long UK stays weighed length more like UK-born folks in speech tests. Newer guests still leaned on pitch far more in those same speech tests. In music beat tests, both guest groups leaned on pitch more than UK-born folks did. Both guest groups also fought to shut out pitch when a task asked for loud-based picks. Time abroad retunes speech picks in set spots, the team says, not all at once.
pmc-10736406:
Jourdyn Lawrence and Ichiro Kawachi ask whether racial discrimination in institutional settings harms cognitive function. Black adults in the United States face the lasting legacy of structural racism plus everyday social stress, and gaps in cognitive aging persist. Inflammation has been proposed as one path by which discrimination gets under the skin. The team drew on the CARDIA study, which follows Black and white adults over time.

To guard against measurement error and hidden confounding, the authors used an instrumental variable analysis. That design aims at an unbiased, causal estimate rather than a simple correlation. They linked reports of discrimination in settings like work and housing to a battery of standard thinking tests. More reported discrimination went with worse cognitive function. The authors argue that the results point to institutions and policy as places where action could protect brain health, rather than placing the burden on individuals alone.
pmc-10737306:
Marguerite DeLiema and Kathleen Wilber published a 2023 symposium summary on making research partnerships work in the study of adult maltreatment. Protecting abused or neglected adults takes many professions at once: health care, social services, police, and courts. Researchers who build screening tools or test interventions must team up with the agencies that do that protection work.

The piece collects lessons from early career researchers who have done so. One team describes joint projects with a large Texas health system and protection agencies in Oklahoma, including how they adapted when the pandemic disrupted data collection. Another analyzed interviews with state agencies in Montana for themes about collaboration. The lead author adds guidance on administrative barriers, such as contracts and legal agreements between sectors. The aim is practical: help the next studies start with trust and shared systems already in place.
pmc-10738206:
Rafael de Cabo and Mustapha Bouhrara review new scanning methods for aging research in a paper from 2023. The methods use magnetic resonance, the same base idea as hospital MRI scans. New versions can probe tissue structure and chemistry without cutting or harming the sample. The review centers on lab animals used as models of human aging.

The authors explain how water in tissue reacts to magnetic fields in ways that reveal density, acidity, and fine structure. They survey tools such as diffusion imaging and chemical exchange methods. These scans could track aging over time and test treatments in the same animal. The pair urge wider use of the methods in aging trials.
pmc-10740806:
König and co-authors model how much heart risk stays behind after cholesterol lowering, and how age shapes it. Strong evidence backs the view that LDL cholesterol drives cardiovascular disease. Patients still need clear numbers on what a given drop buys them. Even at best cholesterol levels, a real residue of risk remains. The team built math models from trial data for relative and total risk cuts.

Age stood out as a clear driver of starting risk. Its odds ratio was 1.02 per year in their checks. Data from the Whickham cohort matched that pattern. The models help doctors explain both the gain from treatment and the risk that persists.
pmc-10741206:
Aleksandra Dajnowska and co-authors map, in a 2023 study, where a hormone-like peptide called spexin shows up in the cow gut. Spexin influences feeding and metabolism in small animals, but large farm mammals were a blank. The team sampled three gut segments from Holstein-Friesian cattle, the true stomach, the small intestine's middle stretch, and the colon, and stained them for the peptide and its receptor's gene.

The receptor gene spoke loudest in the small intestine segment. Staining patterns differed by region in a telling way. In stomach and small intestine, the peptide sat mostly in the lower nerve web of the gut wall. In the colon it concentrated in the deeper nerve web that drives movement. The authors read this geography as a clue to segment-specific jobs, from secretion to motility, and offer the map as a first reference for ruminant gut regulation.
pmc-10742806:
Mamiko Sato and co-authors studied drinking among Japanese women in fertility treatment in a 2023 paper. The study sits inside a wider project on work and mental health during assisted reproduction. Alcohol use during treatment can affect outcomes, so the team asked which social factors track with continued drinking.

Participants answered surveys on habits, work, and mental state after starting treatment. The analysis weighed factors such as job strain and distress against drinking risk. Knowing which women are most likely to keep drinking lets clinics offer support where it counts, without blanket lectures. The findings feed counseling that respects the heavy emotional load of fertility care.
pmc-10743006:
Wu and co-authors build a phone-linked sensor that detects a potent food toxin at the point of need, in a research paper from 2023. The toxin, aflatoxin B1, contaminates crops like peanuts and corn and harms health at tiny doses. Lab tests are accurate but slow and place-bound.

Their sensor stands its capture probes on tiny DNA pyramids, which space the probes evenly and keep them upright. That order boosts binding and speeds electron flow, sharpening the signal. Paired with a phone app and a pocket workstation, the sensor found the toxin down to 3 picograms per milliliter. Tests in peanut, soybean, corn, and lake water gave sound recoveries. Results matched a gold-standard lab method.
pmc-10743706:
Tanveer Alam Khan and co-authors review how a plant hormone family helps crops bear harsh conditions, in work from 2023. Drought, heat, and salt may cut food yields by a quarter by 2050 if left unchecked. The hormones, called brassinosteroids, steer seed sprouting, vein growth, and breeding in plants.

Their signal chain lets plants answer stress through tuned gene work and harm cleanup. Two decades of study still leave gaps in how the chain acts under each stress. The review sums up that proof and argues that tuning the chain, its making, or its sensing could breed tougher crops for a warming world.
pmc-10744206:
Sappington and Spencer review how adult western corn rootworms move, and what that means for pest control. Movement shapes the beetle's spread, its gene flow, and how fast it beats control tools. Past data conflict: some show short trips, others imply long-range spread.

That clash echoes two known puzzles, Reid's paradox and Slatkin's paradox. The authors propose that the species is partly migratory, with two behavior types. Some beetles stay local as residents, while others migrate over long distances. That split model could improve forecasts of range growth and resistance spread in cornfields.
pmc-10745906:
Constanze Gummelt and six co-authors published a microbiology study in twenty twenty-three on how an anthrax-like bacterium manages to form spores despite a genetic oddity. Bacillus cereus biovar anthracis causes fatal disease in African rainforest wildlife. Every strain carries a large insertion inside sigK, a gene spores cannot form without.

During sporulation the insertion is cut out, restoring the gene, and the team asked whether that extra step slows or blocks the process. Gene expression tracking and electron microscopy showed it did neither. Two mutant strains did fail, but because of damage in other regulator genes. The work explains how this unusual pathogen keeps a life stage it needs to spread.
pmc-10746006:
Huiting Xu, Xinxin Xiang, Weizhe Ding, Wei Dong, and Yihong Hu review ways to make human B cells live and divide forever in the lab, in work from 2023. B cells make antibodies, and immortal lines keep making the same antibody endlessly. Such lines speed drug antibody work and diagnostic products.

Routes include infection with a herpes virus, infection with a monkey virus, direct gene edits, and switching on a surface signal. The review weighs how each route works and what it yields. Human antibodies from these lines dodge the rejection that animal antibodies can trigger. Over one hundred antibody drugs are now approved. The authors close with open problems and next steps.
pmc-10747106:
Steven Gameiro and five co-authors map variants of human papillomavirus type sixteen in North American head and neck cancers, in a two thousand twenty-three virology paper. In cervical cancer, these intratypic variants clearly differ in risk and outcome; in head and neck cancer they were barely charted.

Combining a Southwestern Ontario cohort with Cancer Genome Atlas cases gave one hundred forty-nine HPV16-positive tumors. Nearly all belonged to lineage A, and about half carried the T350G change in the E6 gene. That variant tracked with differences in tumor staging and disease-free survival in simple analyses, though not after adjustment. Immune response measures also differed, hinting the variant may carry prognostic value.
pmc-10747506:
Norphanphoun and Hyde report new fungus species on mangrove trees in Thailand. The fungus genus holds major plant pathogens worldwide. Four species were detailed from mangrove ecosystems in the study. Two species proved new to science in Thailand.

A known species was found on a new host there. A fourth species from Taiwan mangroves set a host record too. Gene analysis plus form traits backed each identification. The host tree was a common mangrove type in both sites. New data expand the known diversity of the genus. Mangrove links of these fungi are now clearer.
pmc-10748306:
Natasha Samsunder and colleagues reviewed how well COVID tests performed in South African studies during the first years of the pandemic. Their scoping review, published in twenty twenty-three, gathered peer-reviewed work from March twenty twenty to August twenty twenty-two. Some studies tested gene or antigen detection, which finds the virus itself, while more studies tested antibody detection, which finds the body response after infection. The team compared sensitivity, meaning how often each test correctly flagged an infected person.

Sensitivity ranged widely for both test families, from poor to perfect depending on the study. Timing explained much of the spread. Gene and antigen tests worked best when samples came early in infection, while antibody tests worked better later, once the response had developed. The authors conclude that no single assay was both sensitive and specific enough on its own, so timing and test choice must be matched carefully.
pmc-10748506:
Amir Elalouf, Hadas Elalouf, and Ariel Rosenfeld review how the immune system and fungal infections interact in people who receive organ transplants. Transplant surgery gives hope to patients with failing organs, and drugs that calm the immune system have raised survival. Those same drugs leave recipients open to fungal infections, which often cause vague symptoms and are hard to spot. The review seeks a balance between keeping the new organ safe and fighting infection.

The authors cover the basic immune response to fungi, new findings on how that response changes, and ways to adjust treatment. They stress early diagnosis and note that a stronger innate immune response might let doctors lower the calming drugs safely. The review also points to gene effects on immune and fungal interaction, and to single-cell tools paired with machine learning as a route to new markers. It closes with open questions and research directions.
pmc-10749306:
Daniel Runco and seven colleagues published a pilot study in two thousand twenty-three on a stress protein in children with cancer. The protein, GDF15, drives nausea and appetite loss in adults with cancer. Nothing was known about its levels in children just diagnosed.

Thirty children with new cancer and twenty-seven matched healthy children took part. Blood levels of the protein were about twice as high in the cancer group at diagnosis. The children also gave body measures and answered quality of life surveys, repeated three months later. Early follow-up data showed no clear change in levels over that span. The authors frame the protein as a possible target against cancer-related malnutrition in children.
pmc-10751906:
Jun Wang and co-authors print custom radiation shields for women's reconstructed chests, shaped to each body by 3D printing, in a 2023 study. After mastectomy and reconstruction, radiotherapy needs a bolus, a layer that pulls the dose up to the skin. Flat sheets gap and fold on rebuilt contours, scattering the dose. Thirty patients treated between 2019 and 2021 wore printed, individualised boluses instead.

Dose coverage of the target volume stayed strong and even, with a good homogeneity index, and the printed shells hugged the chest wall, dosing organs at risk within limits. Skin toxicity was graded by a standard scale. The authors conclude the custom bolus delivers precise treatment where one-size sheets fail. The work is part of radiotherapy's wider turn toward printing the interface between machine and patient.
pmc-10753906:
Michele Valsecchi, Amparo Galindo, and George Jackson present a 2023 modeling study of plastics. Polyethylene is a half-crystal plastic used in films and pipes. Hydrocarbon fluids soak into it, and that uptake matters for packaging and plant safety. The team joins a fluid model with a structure model of the half-crystal form. Chains that tie crystals together are counted by the structure model.

Each sample gets one parameter set fitted to past lab data. With that single set, the model predicts uptake curves for many pure fluids. The match shows that fluid forces and sample structure split cleanly. Engineers can then predict uptake for new fluids from one calibration. Plastic makers get a tool that cuts soak testing. The split also clarifies which traits belong to the polymer grade and which belong to the fluid, a distinction that guides material choice.
pmc-10801106:
Eti Muharremi and Gentian Vyshka look at the health of the three leaders who met at Yalta in nineteen forty-five. Their twenty twenty-three article covers Franklin Roosevelt, Joseph Stalin, and Winston Churchill, who all suffered strokes after the conference. Their failing health played out behind a veil of secrecy.

The authors review each leader's state during and after Yalta, the role of high blood pressure, and other risk factors that could have been changed. Roosevelt died before the war ended, which forced a leadership handover at a key moment. The deaths of Churchill and Stalin shaped the early Cold War. The piece argues that hidden illness in top leaders is a world-shaping force.
pmc-10801906:
Lin Wang and three colleagues published a combined analysis in two thousand twenty-three on a gut-related chemical and stroke. The chemical, TMAO, is made when gut microbes process certain foods. Whether its blood level predicts brain infarction and recovery was disputed.

Fifteen studies with over forty thousand patients, all from China or Germany, were pooled. Higher TMAO linked to worse disability scores three months after stroke. It also linked to first strokes, to repeat strokes, and to greater severity at onset. No clear link with death after stroke appeared. The authors rate TMAO as a marker of risk and outcome rather than a proven cause. They note all data came from just two countries.
pmc-10822906:
Haijun Han and co-authors test a probiotic against allergic rhinitis in adults, in a study published in 2023. The strain, a Lactobacillus plantarum called GUANKE, was known to balance immune replies. Adults with a past of the allergy took the probiotic for four weeks. Scores for nose and other symptoms were logged before and after, as were blood marks.

Symptom scores fell a great deal, and control scores rose in step. Sub-scores for runny nose, itch, sneeze, and tears each improved. Blood levels of the allergy antibody IgE dropped in a marked way. Twenty immune signal proteins shifted, six up and fourteen down. Those proteins cluster in cytokine and chemokine paths, which fits the balance claim.
pmc-10826606:
Hongmei Deng and ten co-authors study how COVID-19 vaccination fared in over a thousand pregnant women infected with the Omicron variant in Shanghai, in this 2023 study. Large pregnancy samples had not been reported from China. Seven hundred and seven women had received one to three doses of an inactivated vaccine, and 317 unvaccinated women served as comparison.

Women with three doses left hospital sooner than unvaccinated women, about nine days against eleven. Antibody rates rose with vaccination, and antibody positive patients also recovered faster. Mild side effects, mostly fatigue, appeared in about twelve percent of vaccinated women. Delivery choices and newborn health scores were unaffected, and all 120 newborns tested negative for the virus and its antibodies. The authors judge the vaccine safe and helpful in pregnancy.
pmc-10834706:
Ana João Santos, Irina Kislaya, Carlos Matias-Dias, and Ausenda Machado examine why people in Portugal do or do not take flu and COVID-19 vaccines. Their study's journal record is dated 2023. The team surveyed 1,050 adults by phone or online and read their answers through the Health Belief Model. That frame weighs how at risk people feel, how bad the illness seems, and what blocks action.

Only about three in ten people had taken the flu vaccine. Feeling unlikely to catch flu was the main reason for skipping it, followed by blocks such as supply shortages and fear of side effects. COVID-19 vaccine uptake was far higher, above eight in ten, helped by a strong sense of how severe that disease could be. People who took the flu shot also rated the COVID-19 vaccine as more useful, a link the authors discuss for future campaigns.
pmc-10835806:
Ting Zhu, Yaoyao Feng, Xiaoxuan Dong, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2024. It streamlines the official variety test for wintersweet, a beloved Chinese flower with a tangle of named varieties, using machine vision and a genetic algorithm to pick the traits that matter.

Variety certification checks distinctness, uniformity, and stability, normally by hand. The team measured forty-two flower traits automatically with pattern recognition, including fourteen new ones. Eight classifiers competed; random forest won, and the outer petals alone carried the strongest signal. A genetic search then trimmed the list to twenty-two core traits, lifting accuracy to just over ninety-nine percent. Clustering on those traits drew a family tree of twenty-three varieties. The authors say the trimmed test is faster and sharper for breeders registering new wintersweets.
pmc-10864506:
Mwaba Sifanu and co-authors analyze, in a study whose journal version is dated 2023, dust exposure records from a Zambian copper mine. Breathing fine mine dust can scar lungs for good, so mines must measure and control it. The team reviewed measurements taken from 2017 to 2022 across two shafts and a processing plant, and judged the mine's own monitoring plan as well.

The file held 253 measurements. About six percent ran above the South African limit used for comparison. Plant areas such as screening and crushing rooms showed the highest peaks, up to eighteen units in one tipping area. Average levels stayed modest. The bigger finding was method: the mine sampled too few spots each year to support firm judgments. The authors urge a standard sampling plan, such as the European EN689, across Zambia.
pmc-10896906:
Heimann, Weiss, and Muller study brain stimulation and language in aging, in work dated twenty twenty-three. Language skill and its brain side balance decline with age. Word fluency also drops and can signal early dementia related change.

Their study gave mild direct current stimulation over a left frontal language area, paired with word fluency training. Ultrasound Doppler measured blood flow shifts that show language lateralization during tasks. Groups held younger healthy elders, older healthy elders, and patients with mild cognitive impairment. The test asks whether stimulation can soften age related language change, a low cost idea worth careful proof.
pmc-10909106:
Siwaporn Thanasan and co-authors present a 2023 journal article testing whether a cheap stain test alone can certify HER2-positive breast cancer. Full guidelines pair the stain test with a gene probe test, but the stain is cheaper and easier where budgets are thin. The Bangkok team ran both on 510 tumors, then judged the stain against gene amplification for borderline and strong-positive cases.

Agreement proved strong: sensitivity near eighty-eight percent, specificity near ninety-four, and accuracy near ninety percent. Strong-positive stains almost always meant true amplification. The authors suggest a firm 3+ stain could stand alone to start anti-HER2 treatment without waiting for the gene test.
pmc-11037506:
Ashish Subedi and co-authors published this summary article in 2023 on the British Thoracic Society's updated guidance for pleural disease. The pleura is the lining around the lungs, and its diseases include fluid build-up, infection, and collapsed lung. The society's 2023 guideline replaced a 2010 version and covers how to investigate and manage these conditions, backed by a companion statement on procedures.

The article walks through the main changes. For a collapsed lung, care now follows symptoms: quiet cases can be watched or managed outside hospital, while risky cases still need drainage. It explains needle aspiration versus chest drains, and notes that graded talc remains the agent of choice for sealing the pleural space. Procedure details cover chest tubes, long-term catheters, biopsy, and thoracoscopy, along with handling complications. Mesothelioma and rare pleural diseases sit outside this guideline's scope.
pmc-11525906:
Deb Nag and five co-authors update the account of what causes obstructive sleep apnea, in a 2024 review. Apnea, where breathing repeatedly stalls in sleep, is tied to obesity and lifestyle and carries wide effects across body systems. Anatomy, function, and habits have long been studied as causes. The review focuses on newer evidence that inflammation and immune mechanisms help drive the disease itself, not just suffer from it.

Understanding causes precisely is the path to prevention rather than lifelong machines. The authors gather the validating studies for immune pathways and discuss what they open up: targeted drugs and preventive steps for people at risk. The piece serves clinicians who manage apnea and researchers hunting its roots.
pmc-11532506:
Guoou Xie, Tiezheng Qi, Yiyan Yao, Dongcai Feng, and Weimin Zhou report a 2024 study on a gene that may sort bladder cancer patients by likely course and best care. Bladder cancer is the tenth most common cancer round the world, and its mixed nature blunts current tests and drugs. The tissue around a tumour shapes its growth, so genes that track that setting could guide care.

The team focused on one such gene and first read its immune profile across cancers. In bladder cancer alone, high gene levels linked to a friendly set of traits: better outlook, a calmer subtype, and low immune cell entry. Low levels linked to poor outlook, a harsher subtype, and high immune entry, but also to more gain from radiation and immune drugs. The gene may help split patients for the right treatment.
pmc-11538206:
Haque and co-authors train an AI model to outline rare hormone tumors on whole-body scans, in a research paper from 2024. The tumors, pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas, can spread and grow hard to count by hand. A tracer-based PET and CT scan is the standard way to picture them.

The team trained a 3D nnUNet model on scans from patients with spread, inoperable disease. On held-out scans, the model matched expert outlines well for the main tumor group. It also worked, less strongly, on two other tumor cohorts used as extra tests. Small, faint lesions were the ones most often missed, and the liver caused most false calls due to its high background signal. The authors say the tool could speed tumor burden checks during care.
pmc-11546606:
Ioannis Liampas and co-authors review blood markers for frontotemporal dementia. Their 2024 review sorts which tests help and which do not. This dementia attacks behavior and language, and can mimic mental illness. Blood tests would be cheaper and kinder than scans or spinal taps.

One marker, neurofilament light chain, stands out. It helps separate the disease from psychiatric look-alikes and tracks decline. Its heavy-chain cousin may flag the turn into full dementia. A marker called progranulin can spot carriers of one gene fault. Total tau disappoints, though its altered form may help against Alzheimer's confusion. A protein named TDP-43 looks promising for diagnosis. The review maps a fast-moving test menu.
pmc-11548506:
Meng Li and co-authors forecast how climate change will move the homelands of two magnolia subspecies in East Asia. The tree, Magnolia sieboldii, is a prized ornamental whose wild stands are already struggling. Using a habitat model fed with sightings and climate data, the team mapped where each subspecies can live now and under future climate paths.

Warm-season rain shaped both ranges most, but the two parted ways on other factors: one answers mainly to temperature swings and yearly warmth, the other to altitude and dry-season warmth. The first subspecies, now spread wide across northeast China, Korea, and Japan, should push north and grow. The second, scattered in Japan and southern Chinese mountains, should shrink southward. The authors urge priority protection for the shrinking one, mixing wild protection, cultivation, and cross-breeding.
pmc-11565706:
Moritz Krebs and Ferdi Schüth made nitrite and nitrate directly from liquid ammonia with electrochemical craft, in a study published in 2024. The two salts feed farms and chemical plants, and a small local production could cut truck and plant load. Earlier electrochemical methods worked in water with weak ammonia. Theirs works in the pure liquid, a first.

Oxygen, activated at the negative pole, does the oxidation. The pair of salts came out with a joint charge yield past forty in a hundred. That rate makes the route worth a scale-up look. The authors frame it as green power put to work: when wind and sun spill surplus, store it as salt. Cold liquid handling is the price of the craft.
pmc-11575006:
A liver cancer protein called DDX20 helps tumor cells move, unless DAPK restrains it. Yan Ye and co-authors trace how DAPK protects DDX20 from destruction. The cell tags DDX20 for the proteasome with ubiquitin. The tagger is an enzyme named TRIM25, which binds the protein's first 244 building blocks. DAPK interacts with that same segment. By sitting there, DAPK blocks the tagging and steadies DDX20 levels.

The three proteins form a joint complex in cells. Removing TRIM25 weakens the DAPK-DDX20 pair, so TRIM25 also acts as a bridge. Silencing TRIM25 slowed liver cancer cell migration and invasion. The authors cast TRIM25 as the cancer-promoting partner in the trio.
pmc-11577906:
Shahrul and five co-authors surveyed young adults in Malaysia in twenty twenty-four about braces fitted by non-dentists. Cheap, easily reached treatment from unlicensed providers is growing and can harm patients. The team asked what young people know and think about this practice.

An online survey drew four hundred twenty-six replies, with an average age near twenty-three. About seventy-six percent knew non-dentists fit braces, mostly learning of it through social media. Low cost was the top reason for choosing them, followed by no waiting list. Most respondents knew the practice is illegal and can cause harm. Legal enforcement was the favored fix. Job type, more than gender or schooling, shaped legal awareness in the results.
pmc-11580006:
Ipek Cicekli and Raika Durusoy wrote a 2024 paper on whether parents who smoke raise a child's risk of type 1 diabetes. In this disease the immune system destroys the cells that make insulin, usually in childhood. Genes explain part of the risk, but smoke in the home has been raised as a possible trigger.

The team compared two hundred forty-eight children aged four to fourteen. One group had the disease and the other was healthy, and parents answered a survey face to face about smoking at home and during pregnancy. Mothers' smoking in pregnancy did not differ between groups. Parents of children with the disease did smoke more cigarettes per day at home. Studies of this kind cannot prove cause, but they mark where deeper work should look.
pmc-11580306:
Eyaya Habtie Dagnaw and colleagues measured late abortion care in Ethiopia in 2024. Five hospitals in the South Gondar district took part. Women of reproductive age seeking induced abortion were interviewed. Just under four hundred women joined through systematic sampling. Late presentation meant arriving after the early safe window. Interviews at the clinic captured personal and pregnancy factors. Models tested which factors tracked with late arrival.

About one woman in five presented late. Living in a rural area raised the odds. Irregular menstrual cycles raised them far more strongly. Slow decisions about ending the pregnancy raised them most. Pregnancies from incest also linked to late arrival. Past contraceptive use lowered the odds of lateness. The authors urge awareness drives in rural communities. Teaching should cover late-care risks and complications. Faster decisions could cut illness and death, they argue.
pmc-11584706:
Ludovico Lami and Bartosz Regula solve exactly how much entanglement can be distilled under a broad family of forbidden operations. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-four. The distillation rate for noisy quantum states is among quantum information's oldest open questions.

Their operation class, dually non-entangling channels, preserves both separable states and separable measurements. Under it, the distillable entanglement equals a tweaked version of the regularised relative entropy, measured separably. Only one such exact formula existed before, for a narrower class. A bonus falls out: under these rules, every entangled state yields some distillable entanglement. Their upper bound also settles a question posed by Li and Winter about entropy variants. Dilution costs match the wider theory, proving a strong irreversibility.
pmc-11587106:
Fumiko Yamamoto, Takeshi Yokoyama, Yan Su, and Masataka Suzuki test how sex differences arise in the silkworm in this 2024 study. Classic theory says insect sex is set inside each cell, with no sex hormones involved. Yet some traits seem shaped by outside signals, so the team checked which force dominates in one tissue.

They studied the fat body of mixed-sex silkworm larvae, where male and female cells sit side by side. Comparing gene activity between normal males and females found over two hundred sex-linked genes. A math model predicted each gene's activity from the mix of cells present. For most genes, the predictions matched the real readings closely. The result supports cell-by-cell control for this tissue.
pmc-11587806:
Yixin Chen and co-authors review how organophosphate pesticides harm the nervous system in a 2024 paper. These compounds are used worldwide in farming and pest control. Exposure can cause nausea, tremors, and convulsions, and severe cases can end in breathing failure or death. The review sums up the toxic mechanisms and how they interlock.

The compounds block a key enzyme and also act through receptors and other targets beyond that enzyme. The authors outline links between poisoning and later disorders such as dementia, developmental conditions, and Parkinson's disease. They also explore treatment ideas that might soften the damage. Readers get a broad map of harm pathways and their ties to chronic brain disease.
pmc-11590406:
Gaku Yamamichi and colleagues fish prostate cancer's secretions for a blood signal that bone spread has begun, in this study from twenty twenty-four. Bone metastasis is castration-resistant prostate cancer's fatal turn, and PSA watches it poorly. Screening the broth of four cancer cell lines found twenty-seven hundred proteins; the team pursued the GDF15 propeptide, a precursor fragment also secreted by bone cells.

The fragment proved an accomplice: it sped cancer cell growth, invasion, and migration, and in mice worsened bone metastasis. It also stoked both bone-building and bone-eating cells, remodelling the neighborhood tumors exploit. In four hundred sixteen patients it diagnosed bone spread far better than PSA, and its ups and downs tracked bone scan changes during treatment while PSA wandered. The authors propose it as an early-warning biomarker for intervention.
pmc-11592306:
Christopher Berlin and co-authors compare, in 2024, long-term outcomes for bowel cancer that has spread to both liver and lungs. Surgery to remove both sets of spread tumors is debated, since proof of lasting benefit is thin. The team reviewed one hundred ninety-two patients treated at a large academic center.

One hundred patients had both tumor sets removed, while the rest had non-surgical care. Even after matching the groups for baseline differences, the surgery group lived much longer, with median survival more than double. The authors argue for an aggressive surgical approach in carefully chosen patients. Selection remains key, since not every patient can bear such surgery.
pmc-11594106:
Savelyev and co-authors build a soft material that can carry electric signals and suit use in tissue repair. Healing nerve or heart tissue needs scaffolds that pass the body's own signals. Their gel mixes bovine serum albumin, gelatin, a light-sensitive dye, and carbon nanotubes. A laser shaped the gel into fine structures through two-photon polymerization. The team reports a strong light response, with a cross section of 580 GM.

The mix was thick enough to hold shape across the full pattern area. Light bending inside the gel helped the shaping process along. Tests confirmed the finished structures conduct electricity. The authors see uses in neural interfaces and in scaffolds for tissues that rely on signals.
pmc-11594406:
Nikola Lenar and colleagues published a sensor study in 2024. They compared two conducting plastics used in chemical sensors. The sensors measure potassium and similar ions in solution. A thin transducer layer sits inside each electrode. Its material affects stability, lifetime, and signal quality. One plastic is known as POT. The other is a PEDOT blend. The team compared both materials directly.

First they checked structure, wetting, heat, and electrical traits. Then they built potassium sensors with each plastic. The POT layer repelled water very strongly. That trait pointed to a longer sensor lifetime. The PEDOT blend gave higher electrical capacitance instead. Higher capacitance steadied the sensor signal over time. Both materials performed well in tests. Designers can choose based on which strength matters most.
pmc-11597106:
Gerard Pérez-Pi and co-authors built a free-standing carbon nanofiber film studded with cobalt phosphide particles to make hydrogen in a microbe-assisted cell, in this 2024 study. The films come off a scalable spinning process plus a heat treatment. They are porous, with surface area up to about five hundred square meters per gram.

As catalysts for splitting hydrogen out of water, the films needed under 140 millivolts of extra push at working current. Wired directly as the cathode of a microbial electrolysis cell, the film ran at just 0.75 volts. Hydrogen came out at under thirty kilowatt-hours per kilogram, a strong efficiency mark. The authors pitch the film as a cheap, sturdy electrode.
pmc-11597606:
Joseph Blondeau and co-authors compare antibiotics against two swine lung bacteria in a 2024 study. One drug, a newer fluoroquinolone, was recently approved for swine respiratory disease. Hard lab data on its strength against field isolates remained scarce.

The team measured two thresholds for the new drug and seven rivals. The first threshold stops bacterial growth, and the second blocks resistant mutants. Farm isolates of both bacterial species went through the tests. The new drug posted the lowest values on nearly every measure. For one species, half the strains stopped at the smallest tested dose. Such lab rankings help veterinarians pick drugs that work now and resist failure later.
pmc-11598906:
Annika Bartel and co-authors tested a stain for a mutated cancer protein in dog carcinomas in two thousand twenty-four. Changes in the BRAF gene are part of cancer profiling in both humans and dogs. The team asked if two commercial antibodies could reliably detect the dog form of the mutation in tissue samples.

They tested two hundred twenty-seven tumors from eleven body sites and confirmed results with a sensitive DNA test. Mutated cases appeared in prostate, bladder, and mouth cancers, while other types tested negative. Both antibodies gave consistent cell staining and matched the DNA results. The authors say biopsy staining could help guide targeted drug treatment for those three cancer types in dogs.
pmc-11599506:
Zhuo Zhang, Hetian Du, Weijie Gao, and Donghui Zhang review engineered immune cells for heart repair in a 2024 article. Macrophages are immune cells that rush to heart injury, clear dead cells, and guide repair. Their behavior shifts over time, from driving inflammation early to calming it later.

The review covers the roles of both resident and recruited macrophages in heart disease. It then turns to engineering: cells can be tuned or loaded to home to injured heart tissue, cut inflammation, limit scarring, and support regrowth. Recent studies of such engineered cells are summed up. The authors see them as a promising living therapy, though much testing remains before routine use.
pmc-11599706:
Biao Yin, Liping Mo, Wei Min, Shan Li, and Cunwei Yu published an algorithms study in twenty twenty-four improving the beetle antennae search method and applying it to wireless sensor coverage. The original algorithm, modeled on how beetles sniff toward food, converges imprecisely and gets stuck in local optima. Three fixes were combined into a new version.

A dynamic step size sharpened accuracy, a golden sine update diversified the search, and a criss-cross disturbance helped escape traps. On twelve benchmark functions the new method beat the original and several rivals. Applied to networks of thirty and fifty sensor nodes, it achieved better coverage than seven competing algorithms.
pmc-11599906:
Jakub Smoleń and co-authors develop, in 2024, a light building material that turns waste into part of green design. They made porous ceramic granules from waste and used them as filler in an epoxy-based concrete. Two granule sizes were tested, and soaking them in resin first proved useful, since resin in the pores grips better.

Concrete made with only the finer granules was strongest, reaching high values in both crushing and bending tests. The material let heat pass about half as fast as standard concrete and absorbed very little water, which suggests good frost resistance. The authors present it as a candidate for sustainable building parts.
pmc-11600906:
Šimun Naletilić and Ema Gagović lead a team dissecting wild carnivores across Croatia for heartworm, a mosquito-borne parasite of dogs that also threatens people. Their study appeared in two thousand twenty-four. Golden jackals are expanding across Europe, raising reservoir questions. Foxes and badgers share the same landscapes.

Hearts from hundreds of animals collected in rabies surveillance were examined. A small share of jackals carried the worms, confirmed by shape and gene tests. Loads ran from a couple of worms to several per animal. No fox and no badger carried the parasite. Infected jackals were all adults, some hosting a breeding pair. The authors identify jackals as a wildlife reservoir worth watching. Dog protection in jackal country gains an argument. Continued surveillance can track whether prevalence climbs.
pmc-11601206:
Liu and eleven co-authors shape a jellyfish bot whose body is its own fuel tank in this twenty twenty-four study. Sea bots most haul a stiff pack that just feeds their gear and brains. A soft tank could spread that weight and shrink the bot's drag in the sea.

Inside, two flow-cell builds were cast in the soft bell shape of a jellyfish. Each build runs on zinc pairs, one built to charge back and one mixed type. The bot swam on flow cells alone, with most of its weight as fuel broth. Charge per bulk and per face both beat stiff pack norms by wide shares. Swim time on one fill ran past an hour in the team's tests.
pmc-11603906:
Jinkyeong Lee and five colleagues compare the genes of Vibrio vulnificus bacteria from patients and from nature in South Korea. People catch this germ from raw seafood or seawater. It can cause blood poisoning and wound infections. The team studied fifteen strains from patients and eleven from the environment.

They found twenty sequence types, and eight were new. Both groups often carried a gene linked to drug resistance. Worryingly, both groups also failed to respond to third-generation cephalosporins, drugs used to treat the infection. Patient strains resisted more drugs overall. Yet counts of harm-causing genes, and traits like sticking to cells and swimming, were much the same in both groups. The authors say strains from nature are just as risky, and drug resistance checks must go on.
pmc-11604706:
Noura El-Naggar, Ragaa Hamouda, and Naglaa Elshafey use artificial intelligence to boost production of a cancer drug enzyme in a 2024 study. The enzyme, L-asparaginase, is a cornerstone of treatment for childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia. The catch is that many bacterial versions also carry a sister activity that causes side effects. A soil microbe they isolated makes the enzyme without that sister activity.

The microbe, a Streptomyces strain, grows on solid beds of mixed soybean and wheat bran. The team varied four inputs, the bran mix, sugar, the enzyme's raw material, and a nitrogen salt, under a designed experiment plan. A neural network then learned the response surface, predicted the best mix, and was checked against real runs. Smarter tuning of a cheap fermentation could widen the supply of a front-line drug.
pmc-11607306:
Rukhsar Sabir and Tahir Mehmood race three neural networks at spotting melanoma in skin images in a 2024 paper. Melanoma is the deadliest skin cancer, and early catches save lives. The team trained a plain convolutional network, a ResNet-18, and an EfficientNet-B0 on the same image set. Their pipeline normalized and augmented images, then segmented, extracted features, and classified.

EfficientNet-B0 won clearly, at ninety-seven percent accuracy. The runner-up reached eighty-seven, and the basic model eighty. The winner also led on sensitivity, specificity, and the other reported scores, with a three percent error rate. The authors say the result shows compact modern networks can classify skin lesions with near-expert polish in this setup. They present the comparison as guidance for groups building screening tools, while the task's stakes demand care.
pmc-11607806:
Jasper Zhao Zhen Wu, Olga Zayts-Spence, and Zoë Fortune published this conceptual paper in 2024 on mental health stigma at work. Research on how stigma operates through language in organizations is thin, and models are lacking. Building on classic ideas about stigma as a language of relationships, the authors propose a model of how workplaces produce and reinforce it. The model draws on in-depth interviews with 23 professional services employees in Hong Kong.

In their model, the workplace is a discursive space where stigma moves across three layers: face-to-face encounters, organizational practices, and wider social beliefs. Everyday talk, including how employees manage what others know about them, carries stigma between those layers. The authors say the model shows how stigma can quietly govern relationships and even career prospects. They offer it as a tool for analyzing stigma in other organizations.
pmc-11608306:
Priscilla Gomes da Silva and co-authors sample outdoor air in a Spanish city for traces of the COVID virus, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Most air studies had focused indoors, leaving open-air spread unclear. Air was drawn at nine spots in Valladolid's center during winter two thousand twenty-one, in both crowded and empty settings.

Six of twenty samples tested positive for viral RNA. Every positive came from a crowded spot, none from empty ones. Amounts were small next to indoor finds. The authors tie presence to crowd size and relaxed safety habits. Outdoor air can carry the virus, they conclude, mainly where people pack in.
pmc-11611106:
Mega Hasanul Huda and a large team combine past trials to judge whether technology helps tuberculosis patients finish treatment, in a 2024 paper. TB care takes months of daily medicine, and many patients stop early, which breeds drug resistance. Phone reminders, video checks, and other digital tools have been proposed to keep patients on track. The team searched six databases for randomized trials published from 2018 to early 2023.

Two reviewers checked each trial's quality with a standard bias tool. Results were pooled with a random-effects model, and the team also checked for publication bias. The analysis weighs adherence, treatment completion, and overall success together. Its findings can help health programs choose which digital support is worth paying for.
pmc-11611906:
Ara Monadjem and co-authors published this data paper in 2024, the African bat database. Where each species lives is the bedrock of conservation, yet bat ranges are poorly mapped, above all in Africa. Museum specimens sit mostly overseas, and new species keep splitting from old ones. The team gathered 17,285 checked locality records for all 266 bat species of sub-Saharan Africa.

Each record is backed by a specimen or gene proof and matched to current names. From the points they built range models and computed the standard area measures used on the Red List of threatened species. An online viewer makes the data open to all. The authors offer the set as a base for ecology and for guarding bats, a group that pollinates, hunts pests, and seeds forests.
pmc-11612206:
Yuanchao Luo and co-authors present a 2024 study on whether high blood sugar on arrival predicts pneumonia after hip fracture surgery. Hip fractures strike older adults, and pneumonia is a feared complication of the repair operation. The team mined records for 1,267 older patients admitted with hip fractures.

Patients were split by admission glucose into normal and high groups. Matching methods paired similar patients across the groups to strip out other differences. The analysis then estimated the pneumonia odds tied to high sugar alone. It also traced how risk climbs as glucose rises, dose by dose. Separate checks compared patients with and without diabetes. The work aims to flag a cheap, early warning sign that wards can act on.
pmc-11613406:
Vladimir Resanovic, Aleksandar Resanovic, and Zlatibor Loncar published a case report in 2024 on a rare hernia that traps bowel in elderly patients. An obturator hernia pushes tissue through a small canal in the pelvis. It strikes mainly frail older women, hides from routine examination, and kills when diagnosis comes late.

Their patient was an eighty-three-year-old woman with cramping pain, vomiting, and constipation in the right lower belly. A CT scan revealed the trapped hernia, and emergency surgery confirmed a loop of small bowel caught in the canal. Because of her asthma the surgeons chose an open operation. The authors weigh open against keyhole repair and argue the choice should fit each patient, with early scanning and fast surgery as the constants.
pmc-11614606:
Qi Xie and colleagues build a bone scaffold that also fights germs, in this materials study from twenty twenty-four. Bone defects need a filler that invites new bone and resists infection after surgery. Their scaffold starts from collagen, the protein of bone's frame, spiked with graphene oxide sheets loaded with curcumin, the active part of turmeric.

The mix was freeze-dried and cross-linked into a sponge. The team measured its pores, water handling, breakdown rate, and how slowly it let curcumin seep out. One recipe, with a low share of the loaded sheets, hit the sweet spot: friendly to cells and steady in release. In dish tests, cells stuck, lived, and multiplied better on it than on plainer scaffolds, bone-forming activity rose, and bacteria fared worse. The authors say the bone-friendly, germ-hostile mix is a sound base for smarter bone repair materials.
pmc-11615306:
Ridhwan Lye and co-authors test whether a computer model can judge sex from skull scans better than a person. Forensic experts often judge sex by eye from bones, but eye judgments can carry bias. They can also lose accuracy when used on groups far from the ones they were built on. The team trained deep learning models on two hundred head scans of Indonesian people.

The best model learned sex and skull traits at the same time. It reached ninety-seven percent accuracy, well above the human judge at eighty-two percent. Maps of the model's focus showed it used both known skull traits and overall size and shape. The authors see such tools as aids that can cut bias in forensic work.
pmc-11616306:
Yu Xiong and co-authors survey a decade of growth in radiopharmaceuticals, drugs labeled with radioisotopes for imaging or therapy. Their 2024 letter focuses on radionuclide drug conjugates, precision drugs that carry a radioactive payload to a target. Two approved products showed the approach can work well in patients.

The authors counted trials of such conjugates over ten years using an industry database. A few hundred trials were found, yet barely half remain active, and most finished trials sit in early phases. The letter frames this as steady, incremental progress rather than a breakthrough wave. It argues the field's promise is real but young, with many candidates still proving safety and benefit.
