The survey gives clinicians and investors a grounded map of where the area stands.
pmc-11617306:
Mathieson and fourteen colleagues test whether EEG monitoring is feasible for newborns with encephalopathy in Uganda, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Birth-related brain injury is a leading cause of childhood death and disability. Continuous EEG is the gold standard for neonatal brain monitoring, but low-income country data are lacking. The cohort was recruited at a Kampala referral hospital.

Diagnostic-quality EEGs were recorded for fifty of fifty-one recruited babies, showing feasibility. Background activity was graded over the first three days, and seizures were annotated remotely by experts. Clinical presentation was tracked with standard scoring systems. Of thirty-nine children followed to eighteen to twenty-four months, thirteen had died and seven had neurodevelopmental impairment. The study links EEG patterns to early childhood outcomes in a low-resource setting.
pmc-11619706:
Maryann Mason and co-authors describe a door-to-door overdose prevention pilot in Illinois, in a 2024 case study. Many people who use drugs never reach the vans or centers where harm reduction supplies are usually handed out. The Block-by-Block program, running since 2022 at five sites in four counties, brings naloxone training and test strips to homes and neutral neighborhood spots.

Local partners host the visits, reaching users plus their friends, family, and neighbors in areas hit hardest by fatal overdoses. The paper reports how the model was put into practice and how feasible and acceptable it proved, as a template for reaching hidden populations.
pmc-11622206:
Ming Han and nine co-authors search for blood signs of a dangerous clot in the liver's portal vein among patients with advanced cirrhosis, in this 2024 study. The clot lacks a sensitive early marker. The team focused on webs of DNA that white blood cells cast out, called NETs, and on the enzyme that chews them up.

Blood from 145 patients in one study and 33 in a second was checked for the web markers and enzyme activity. Patients with clots showed more web debris and weaker enzyme activity, with or without liver cancer. One debris marker alone sorted patients well, and combining all three measures sorted better. The authors propose the imbalance as a diagnostic lead for a complication that now hides until late.
pmc-11622606:
Shinya Tanaka and colleagues compare hip fracture care in older Japanese patients before and after the COVID-19 pandemic began. Their 2024 retrospective multicentre study spans three hospitals.

Nearly nineteen hundred patients aged sixty-five and older who had hip fracture surgery were grouped by injury year, from twenty nineteen through twenty twenty-one. Patient numbers fell by roughly seven percent in both pandemic groups. Waiting time for surgery, hospital stay, and in-hospital death or complication rates did not change significantly. Infection did increase in the early pandemic group. The study shows how major societal disruption affected fracture numbers more than perioperative management.
pmc-11624606:
Chen Ranran and co-authors present a 2024 study on forecasting a full day of eye pressure swings from daytime readings alone. Pressure inside the eye rises and falls over 24 hours, and big swings worsen glaucoma. Round-the-clock monitoring is cumbersome, so the team trained machine learning models to infer the swing class from routine measures.

Records from monitored patients supplied 22 features. Statistical screens sorted them into four subsets of rising strictness. Five classification algorithms were trained and compared on accuracy, sensitivity, and curve scores. The winning model was unpacked with an explanation method that ranks each feature's push on the prediction. A reliable forecast could spare patients overnight stays in pressure labs. It could also flag hidden swingers for closer care.
pmc-11625706:
Yang and seven colleagues use polarized light to grade healing of the Achilles tendon in twenty twenty-four. The tendon at the heel is often torn, and doctors lack a clean way to score how well it heals. Their method shines light that vibrates in set planes and reads how tissue bends it. No dyes or labels are needed.

Hurt tendons bent light less and in a more jumbled way than healed ones. Computer models of the tissue tied those shifts to thicker fibers, straighter fiber lay, and more collagen. The team built a single score from the light data. It draws a map that shows injury and grades how well each treatment worked.
pmc-11627506:
Juliana Amaral Prata and co-authors examine how nurse-midwives cared for women in labor during the COVID-19 pandemic, through the lens of Jean Watson's theory of human caring. Pandemic rules pushed care toward cold, procedural routines. The team interviewed forty nurse-midwives in 2021 and sorted their accounts against the ten elements of Watson's Clinical Caritas process.

The care they described touched all ten elements, grouped into five dimensions. A creative dimension showed in the workarounds staff invented to keep care human under restrictions. Humanistic and cultural dimensions shaped the manner of care itself. Those in turn fed an educational dimension and a spiritual one. The authors conclude that the midwives managed a transpersonal quality of care, keeping person-to-person connection alive in spite of rules that nearly always pushed the other way.
pmc-11629206:
One-time gene therapy promises to free people with hemophilia from endless factor infusions. Saarang Deshpande and co-authors pool the trial evidence in this 2024 review, covering twenty trials and nearly four hundred men with severe forms of hemophilia A or B.

Both therapies cut yearly bleeding and infusion counts sharply. Factor levels for type B held near their peak after two years, while type A levels faded to about half, showing weaker staying power. About one patient in five had a serious side effect, but no clots or immune blockers appeared. The authors weigh lasting benefit against durability as the field's open question.
pmc-11630606:
Hasibul Hassain Emon and colleagues published a public health study in twenty twenty-four on overweight and obesity among university students in Bangladesh. The team wanted to know how common excess weight is and how it connects with grades and self-esteem. Data came from a structured questionnaire given to six hundred students at Jahangirnagar University.

Nearly four in ten students were overweight or obese, with rates higher among males. Obese students showed the lowest academic performance across disciplines. Body mass index correlated negatively with self-esteem, and physical activity measures were also recorded. The findings link heavier weight with both weaker grades and poorer psychological well-being in this student group.
pmc-11630706:
Guillermo Ceniza-Bordallo and co-authors review low back pain during and after spaceflight, in a review paper from 2024. Spaceflight changes the spine and can trigger acute or lasting pain in astronauts. Animal studies add data, yet no full synthesis covered spine changes and pain rates together across humans and animals.

The review follows standard reporting rules and a registered protocol. Eleven studies passed screening from more than one hundred abstracts. Evidence shows astronauts lose muscle and face spine changes in flight. Pain rates during and after flight are reported across studies. Quality and evidence strength are graded. The synthesis guides countermeasures for crew spine health.
pmc-11631406:
Laura Kemppainen and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-four register study of death rates among older migrants in Finland. Migrants often outlive native-born peers, a pattern called the mortality advantage. Whether it holds into old age, by cause of death, was unproven there.

All deaths over nearly two decades were analyzed for people aged seventy and over. Standardized rates compared migrants with Finnish-born residents. Breakdowns by cause and region of origin followed. Regression adjusted for age, sex, income, and residence. Evidence of a migrant advantage appeared across various causes, adding old-age data to a debated field.
pmc-11631606:
Changqin Luo, Qingmin He, and Xiaocui Yang present a 2024 case report on gallbladder stones that were not truly stones. A 54-year-old woman had belly pain and swelling for a month, yet her first ultrasound was clear. After she took the antibiotic ceftriaxone for a chest infection, she felt pain under her right ribs.

A CT scan then showed what looked like gallbladder stones. Six weeks after she stopped the drug, a follow-up exam showed the stones were gone. That vanishing act confirmed drug-induced pseudolithiasis, a sludge that mimics stones. The authors also review how the drug causes this effect, how it shows up, and how to spot it. Their summary helps doctors avoid needless surgery.
pmc-11633006:
Andreas Ekholm and four co-authors published an imaging study in twenty twenty-four on predicting breast cancer growth-rate scores from microscope slides instead of gene tests. Proliferation signatures help personalize treatment, but sequencing is not always available. The team trained deep learning models on whole slide images paired with RNA data from eight hundred nineteen patients.

Two convolutional networks learned to estimate an eleven-gene proliferation score and the MKI67 marker gene. On unseen internal cases the predictions correlated strongly with the true values, and moderately on a fully independent external set of nearly a thousand tumors. Survival modeling confirmed the image-based scores still carried prognostic weight. Slides, in short, leak molecular information a network can read.
pmc-11633206:
Haipeng Chen and six co-authors read how a sea berry breed meets drought in growth and gene use. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. The shrub is a prime tree for dry lands, prized for world and purse worth. Year-old plants sat in three water grades for one hundred twenty days, and root gene and protein reads were run.

Drought cut height, stem width, root mass, and a shield rate, while main roots grew long. Thousands of genes and hundreds of proteins split by grade. Plant call paths lit in both dry grades, and fat shield cells joined in the hard grade. The shrub shifts shield spends as dry deepens.
pmc-11635206:
Meng Chen and colleagues review whether exercise helps people recover after pulmonary embolism. Their systematic review and meta-analysis appeared in twenty twenty-four. Survivors often keep shortness of breath and a lower quality of life. Exercise helps in heart disease and chronic lung disease, but its value after embolism was unclear.

The team searched seven databases for trials in these patients. Only two studies with a few hundred participants qualified. Pooled results showed no clear gain in walking test scores. Quality of life scores also showed no clear gain. The authors present a thin evidence base, so readers should treat exercise advice for these patients as still unsettled.
pmc-11639006:
Kathy Liu and seven co-authors published a 2024 population study of health care use and cost during COVID-19 in Alberta, Canada. Covering 255,037 adults with confirmed infection from March 2020 to December 2021, the team tracked community and hospital care across the first four waves. Hospital care dwarfed other costs, at a marginal cost near 21,700 Canadian dollars per hospitalized patient.

Emergency department costs peaked in wave 2, while outpatient costs fell after wave 1. ICU care in wave 2 cost notably less than in wave 1, a drop of about 24,000 dollars per admission. The authors stress that severe infections drive spending. They call for studies of the social factors behind shifting use, to plan better for the next pandemic.
pmc-11640106:
A sharp lemon-scent oil from an Asian tree could lift foods and scents, if its mixes held. The head of this report is dated 2024 (the catalog says 2025). Naiwen Xing and five co-authors steadied the mixes by tying fish-skin gelatin to a starch sugar through dry heat. Four sugar sizes were tried. A mid-large one lifted the steadiness score by more than one and a half times over plain gelatin.

The tied films wrapped oil drops at near half the old size. Their surfaces turned more water-shy, and their charge neared the mark for a stable mix. The tied gelatin also fought rust-like decay harder in two bench tests. The team pitch the dressed gelatin as a green emulsifier for food use.
pmc-11640406:
Turker Tuncer and six co-authors coined a word-like language for heart trace readings, in a paper published in 2024. Heart traces sort hearts well, but their decisions are hard to explain. Their language, Cardioish, turns each trace lead into marks and builds a phrase from the lead transitions. A four-step framework pulls features, picks the best, classifies, then speaks the phrase as the reason.

On two public sets, one for mental illness and one for heart attacks, the framework topped 99 in a hundred on classification accuracy. The phrases let a reader see which lead transitions drove the decision. The authors tie the phrases to heart map theory as well. They present the language as a bridge: strong scores that a doctor can read.
pmc-11640506:
Shi and co-authors build a season-aware model to assess Japanese sardine stocks in the Northwest Pacific. Stock checks often miss how fish move with seasons and place. Their model folds migration patterns into seasonal abundance indexes for assessment.

Results show sardine numbers rising steadily over the study window. The stock's center of gravity shifted clearly toward the northeast. The stock looked sustainable, with a 94.8 to 99 percent recovery chance. The authors still urge careful management, given the species' wild swings in the past. They frame the method as a tool for distant-water fishery science.
pmc-11640906:
Zhao and co-authors test a natural antibiotic, azalomycin F, against eczema-like skin disease in mice. The compound also fights fungi and tumors and calms inflammation. Mice with chemically induced skin lesions got the drug on their backs for 12 days. Doses ran from 10 to 30 mg per kg. The team scored lesions, counted scratching, and read skin tissue. Blood levels of IgE and several alarm cytokines were measured too.

Mid doses cut lesion scores and scratching the most. Skin thickening and mast cell entry also fell. Blood IgE and four inflammatory signals dropped with treatment. Gene reads probed the pathways behind the gains.
pmc-11641306:
Zorana Mutavski and her team pack elderberry waste extracts with pressed carbon dioxide. Their study from twenty twenty-four gives worth to a juice trade scrap. The scrap is rich in rutin, a plant compound that guards cells. A packed shell should hold its strength for use in foods or health pills.

Five extraction paths gave the first extracts for the work. Plain paths and paths with ultrasound, microwave, and boosted steps were set side by side. A gas-based PGSS step then formed the shells. Two food-grade carriers went in at a set ratio. Yield, catch rate, and grain traits told of success. The waste stream turns into a source of food stuff this way. Waste-to-worth work gains one more case in point here.
pmc-11641606:
Katarzyna Potyka and Józefa Dąbek track an inflammation signal across the stages of coronary artery disease. The signal is tumor necrosis factor alpha, a protein that helps drive vessel damage. The team measured how actively its gene and its two receptor genes were read in blood cells from 240 people: healthy controls and patients with early, stable, and acute disease.

As the disease stage worsened, the main gene's activity rose significantly, while the receptor genes' activity fell. Neither the number of blocked arteries nor the heart's pumping fraction changed that pattern. The authors read the opposing drift as a fingerprint of the disease's advance. They suggest it could serve as a marker for early, noninvasive diagnosis, catching artery disease before it declares itself in a crisis.
pmc-11641706:
Lazarros Chavalala, Rachel Tsakani Lebese, and Lufuno Makhado interview nurses about why men in a South African province avoid health care, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Men's reluctance to seek care tracks with worse outcomes and shorter lives, and norms of masculinity are suspected drivers. Fourteen professional nurses spoke in semi-structured interviews.

Nurses pointed to self-medication, distrust of Western medicine, and reliance on traditional healers. Men, they said, tend to seek care only when illness turns severe, feel uncomfortable with female nurses, and prize respectful treatment. Cultural norms remain a barrier, especially around intimate examinations by female clinicians. The authors call for services that take those norms seriously.
pmc-11642006:
Tomasz Gasior reviews new tools for finding and grading heart muscle disease, in an update from two thousand twenty-four. These diseases change the shape and work of the heart for reasons other than blocked heart arteries. Gasior covers scans of the heart and gene tests, and how the two fit together.

Heart scans can show wall size, scars, and weak spots, while gene tests can show risk passed through families. Used together, they help doctors judge the risk of sudden death and choose who needs a shock device. New tools such as smart software and strain scans may sharpen care further.
pmc-11642206:
Yuqi Hong and colleagues published a 2024 review of ribosomal proteins in reproduction. Ribosomes build all cell proteins. Their component proteins do more than that. Evidence ties them to egg and embryo development. Several stress pathways run through them.

The review covers cell stress, oxidation, growth, and recycling pathways. Each pathway links these proteins to fertility. Diagnostic marker potential is discussed. Drug targeting possibilities are also raised. Mechanisms remain partly unclear, the authors admit. Reproductive medicine could gain new tools from this biology. The paper maps a fast-growing research front.
pmc-11642306:
Natalia Wronska and co-authors test films made from chitosan that fight fungi, as a way to keep food fresh for longer. Their 2024 study checks plain chitosan and types mixed with zinc oxide or graphene, for use on fungi that spoil food.

The team put the films to Aspergillus flavus and Penicillium expansum. The zinc oxide mix stopped spores from sprouting in both strains, and time on the films cut how many spores stayed alive. The films also changed how well fungal cell walls let things pass, most of all in Aspergillus flavus. Tests on human skin cells found no harm to genes in fibroblasts. But keratinocytes did show DNA harm with the zinc oxide mix. The team says such films could cut the use of man-made fungicides.
pmc-11643206:
Rozenn Langlet and colleagues worked on seed coatings that leave out microplastics, in a study published in twenty twenty-four. Film coatings protect seeds during treatment and planting, but many contain plastic that rules now push growers to replace. The team tested several stand-ins, including starch-based syrups, plant gums, cellulose, and other polymers, with and without a thickener. Using a light scattering method, they watched how particles settled, how clear liquid formed on top, and how well settled particles could be mixed back in.

Each stand-in changed settling behavior, generally slowing how fast particles sank while making remixing harder. The thickener helped some mixes and hurt others, depending on the polymer. One gum-based mix remixed especially well. The authors offer remixing ability as a practical test when judging plastic-free coating recipes.
pmc-11644306:
Wu and colleagues coat cotton fabric in twenty twenty-four with silver particles that conduct electricity and kill bacteria, using plant compounds as helpers. The plant compounds, drawn from natural sources, drive a classic silver mirror reaction that lays the particles down evenly. The result is a durable hybrid coating with two useful traits at once.

The team compared plant compounds of different sizes. Smaller ones gave a tighter, denser coating, while a well-known plant acid gave the most stable coating, keeping strong conductivity after repeated washing. Electric tests confirmed the plant compounds shield the silver from dissolving. The coated fabrics also showed clear germ-killing power. The route offers a greener swap for synthetic chemicals.
pmc-11644406:
Joaquín Marzano-Felisatti, Rafael Martínez-Gallego, José Pino-Ortega, and six colleagues track young beach volleyball players in this two thousand twenty-four study. Young players often split time between indoor and beach volleyball, and their physical demands were unknown. Thirty-two young male players, grouped by age, under fifteen or under nineteen, and by specialization, were tracked across forty matches with wearable electronic performance systems recording distances, set duration, and acceleration profiles.

Older players and beach-focused players covered more distance per set, about seven hundred nineteen meters against roughly six hundred, and hit higher maximum accelerations and decelerations. Indoor players, oddly, performed more total acceleration and deceleration actions per set. Set outcome, winning or losing, showed no clear physical differences. The authors conclude age and focus, more than match result, shape the physical profile of youth beach volleyball, informing age-matched training loads.
pmc-11644506:
Spinelli and co-authors test epoxy blends filled with carbon tubes and graphene flakes. Blends with two fillers can beat blends with just one filler type. The team used two load levels, 0.1 and 0.5 weight percent of mixed filler. Those loads sit below and above the point where charge starts to flow. The tube-to-flake mix changed from run to run by plan. Hardness, depth of press, and stiffness came from fine press tests.

A planned test grid showed how each filler share moved the scores. A curved fit then linked filler shares to the traits they sought. Shape scans backed up the press test scores. The best and worst blends went to full sim runs for a closer look. Matched sim scores gave more clues on how the blends bend and bear load.
pmc-11644906:
Saud Sattar and co-authors watch battery fluid change color during use as a sign of wear, in this 2024 study. Lithium-ion cells lose capacity as their electrolyte breaks down, faster at high temperature. State of health checks usually need the cell opened or rested. This team placed optical sensors on working cells to track the fluid's color in real time.

Cells cycled at high temperature showed clear color shifts as they aged. Those shifts tracked the fade in capacity across the tests. Heat sped both the color change and the degradation. The authors frame color as a live, visible marker of electrolyte breakdown. They aim to turn this qualitative link into a measured health gauge in later work.
pmc-11649906:
Baddouri and Hannig weigh probiotics as an add-on cure for periodontitis in a 2024 clinical perspective. The gum disease is common, and many types of microbes play a part in it. Probiotics might help standard care by bringing oral microbes back into balance, but hope for them may run ahead of the proof.

The review looks at forty clinical studies. The results were mixed, since the studies used distinct designs, types of probiotic, and outcome measures. Gains looked stronger in severe cases. With longer follow-up, gains varied and in some cases faded. The authors urge care, and call the case so far promising but not yet settled, let alone proven.
pmc-11653606:
Splitting water and alcohol with light to release hydrogen needs catalysts that catch photons well. Asier Agrelo-Lestón and co-authors build hybrid catalysts that pair gold compounds with titanium dioxide. A coumarin-based part acts as the light catcher, thanks to its strong color.

The team compared gold complexes and gold particles at two loading levels under ultraviolet and visible light. Adding gold boosted hydrogen output up to 2.7 times over a standard gold reference. Detailed imaging and spectroscopy showed tiny gold particles forming in the best samples. One sample partly converted during use, and that change explained its top production rate. The authors credit the mix of light-catching dye, gold helpers, and light-amplifying particles for the gains.
pmc-11653806:
Yuta Katsumi and co-authors ask whether brain shrinkage seen on a first scan can forecast how fast a rare dementia will worsen, in work from 2024. The illness harms the back of the brain first, so sight and space skills fade early. How fast it moves varies a lot from person to person.

The team studied thirty-four patients and twenty-four healthy adults of like age. Patients showed the most shrinkage in back brain areas, above all in the sight network. Shrinkage in a network that guides focused looking best forecast faster decline in daily function. The authors say such a scan measure could help doctors plan care for each patient. They note the finding needs to be checked in new groups.
pmc-11655306:
Zhiyong Wang and colleagues build a gene score to forecast how liver cancer will behave, in this study from twenty twenty-four. The genes all involve lysosomes, the cell's recycling sacs, which tumors can bend to their growth and spread. The team mined large public cancer databases for gene and outcome data on liver tumors.

From many candidates, machine learning picked four lysosome genes that, combined, form their index. Patients with high scores fared worse and had more immune cells crowding their tumors. The score also tracked with how tumors might answer drug and immune therapy, tested in the data. To check the biology, the team silenced one gene, CTSV, in liver cancer cells, and the cells grew and moved less. The authors offer the index as a tool to sort patients by risk and to guide treatment choices, pending checks in the clinic.
pmc-11656206:
Ozgen and coauthors check a fast lab test for a joint compound in creams. The compound belongs to a family used in skin and joint goods. Past tests were slow and needed long prep steps. The new test aims for plain, quick checks in routine labs.

The method pulls the compound straight from gel or cream. Samples then go right into the test device for reading. Checks proved the test is straight, exact, and stable. Global guide rules set the bars those checks had to meet. Both gel and cream forms passed with high scores. Labs can now assay such goods with far less prep.
pmc-11656506:
Mohammed and co-authors compare two ways to treat an abscess that forms around the appendix. Antibiotics alone are one option; adding a drain placed through the skin is the other. No agreement exists on which works best, and some surgeons favor removing the appendix.

The team searched PubMed, EMBASE, Scopus, and trial registers for matching studies. Duplicates were removed and papers were screened for fit. Pooled results compared hospital stay length and treatment success between the two groups. Mean differences came with 95 percent confidence ranges. The findings aim to guide care for this common surgical emergency.
pmc-11656706:
Florian Schunck and co-authors report a 2024 study that ties gene activity data into a model of chemical harm in zebrafish embryos. Risk testing for the chemical industry needs sound predictions with less animal testing. Gene data gathered over time may link cell events after exposure to effects on the whole animal.

The team built a model around nrf2, a gene that acts as a stress regulator in cells. Its activity level stands in for damage, which then drives detox steps and death in the model. Fitting the model to rich data sets took tools from molecular biology, dynamic modeling, and Bayesian statistics. The test case asked whether nrf2 activity can predict death in zebrafish embryos. The authors present the method as a template for using molecular markers in survival forecasts.
pmc-11657106:
Alan Barnicle and a large team of co-authors analyze in 2024 genomic instability in more than two thousand ovarian cancer patients across six trials of the drug olaparib. Drugs of this class changed ovarian cancer care. The team asked what patterns of DNA repair failure appear across tumor samples from those trials.

Repair deficiency was tested in 2,147 tumors. About half carried BRCA mutations, and those tumors scored far higher for genomic instability. Tumors with other repair gene mutations showed mixed scores. The analysis maps how instability scores vary by mutation type, aiding patient selection for this drug class.
pmc-11657206:
Nura Yousef and eleven colleagues published a 2024 nationwide survey on awareness of consanguinity and genetic disease in Saudi Arabia. Consanguinity means marriage between close relatives. More than half of marriages in Saudi Arabia are between first cousins, which raises the prevalence of inherited diseases and the cost of long-term care.

Earlier studies found limited awareness of this link, even among educated Arabs. The national study gauged public understanding of how cousin marriage relates to genetic disease in children. It also explored the challenges of raising awareness without offending cultural norms. The authors discuss potential solutions to reduce the national healthcare burden, such as premarital screening and genetic counseling services.
pmc-11658306:
Chuanfan Zhong and co-authors linked a DNA repair pathway's activity to how advanced prostate cancer answers hormone-blocking drugs, in a 2024 study. These cancers often respond at first, then resist. Using a per-sample enrichment method, the team found the repair pathway running higher in poor responders.

They built a gene score from the pathway that split patients into risk groups; the high group answered the drugs worse. Mutation maps and pathway analyses fleshed out the groups' differences. Lab and animal tests then checked the pathway's effect on drug sensitivity and DNA repair directly. The authors propose the score as both a forecast tool and a target lead.
pmc-11659606:
Alexandra DeLone and four co-authors trace how childhood hardship shapes young adults with chronic illness in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Early adversity is known to blunt emotion control and worsen mental health. Their group carried an extra load: long-term medical conditions. The authors tested a chain of links between the past and present adjustment. Illness-related thoughts sat in the middle of the chain.

Five hundred fifty-seven college students with chronic conditions answered surveys. Worry about the illness and feeling intruded upon by it carried the effect forward, joined by poor emotion regulation. Each link suggests a support target. Counselors might ease illness worry before tackling mood. Psychologists of chronic illness are the readers.
pmc-11662906:
Robinson and seven co-authors discuss ethics in psychedelic pain research, in work from twenty twenty-four. Psychedelics have a long history of cultural and medical use. Interest has surged again, most of all in psychiatry, with early promise for hard to treat depression.

Chronic pain is a major burden with few non opioid options, so psychedelics are being explored there too. National funding has resumed after decades of little support. The authors warn that pain patients with limited autonomy are vulnerable. Consent, risk, benefit, and complex drug rules all need careful handling before trials expand.
pmc-11663706:
Anne Marmagne, Fabien Chardon, and Celine Masclaux-Daubresse present a study whose head gives the year as 2024. The catalog lists it under 2025. Autophagy is a cell recycling system that moves nitrogen from aging leaves to seeds. Arabidopsis mutants without autophagy age early, stay small, and yield few seeds. Their seeds also carry skewed nitrogen and carbon levels. The open question is where the fault lies: in the leaves that send, or the seeds that receive.

The team restored one key autophagy gene in only one tissue at a time. A leaf-aged promoter drove the rescue in source leaves. A seed promoter drove it in seeds alone. Comparing the two rescues splits local roles cleanly. Plant scientists get a tissue-level answer to a whole-plant puzzle. Seed quality in crops may one day be tuned by guarding recycling in the right tissue only.
pmc-11666306:
Jean-Claude Tardif and Simon Kouz put a large heart-attack trial in perspective, in a 2024 article. After a heart attack, two drug ideas compete for a place in routine care. One is low-dose colchicine, an old anti-inflammatory that cut repeat events in earlier trials. The other is spironolactone, which blocks the hormone aldosterone and helps failing hearts, though its routine use after every major heart attack was unproven.

The trial they discuss enrolled patients whose heart attacks were treated with stents. It asked whether colchicine reduces repeat artery events and whether spironolactone reduces heart failure plus artery events. The authors walk through the evidence before the trial, including the odd fact that one colchicine study ran during the pandemic, and frame what the new results should change in practice.
pmc-11666906:
Wangzhao Tian, Wenwen Yang, Xiaorui Wang, and Yanjiang Yang present a 2024 study of how food choices may affect a common bowel condition. The condition forms small pouches in the wall of the colon. Diet is thought to play a role, but cause and effect are hard to prove from surveys alone.

The team used gene variants as natural experiments to test twenty diet factors. Case data came from a Finnish biobank with more than thirty thousand patients, and diet data came from the UK Biobank. Pork intake and two kinds of fish intake linked to higher risk in the checks. Dried fruit intake linked to lower risk.
pmc-11667706:
Alexandra Balola, Sofia Ferreira, and Isabel Rocha published a review in two thousand twenty-four on turning plastic waste into bacterial feedstock. PET plastic can be enzymatically broken down, yielding ethylene glycol, a two-carbon molecule mostly discarded today. Escherichia coli might eat it and make valuable chemicals instead.

The review surveys natural and engineered pathways that let this workhorse bacterium grow on ethylene glycol. Protein and metabolic engineering strategies for converting it into target products are assessed. Closing the loop from waste plastic to biochemicals is the prize. Hurdles include slow growth on the substrate and pathway balance. The authors offer routes to make the approach industrially real.
pmc-11668806:
Jinsong Yang and eight co-authors test whether a fused strain of helpful bacteria makes better silage from king grass. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. Silage is fermented fodder, and its quality hinges on which bacteria drive the ferment.

The team compared three mixes: two parent strains on their own blend, and a hybrid strain made by fusing parent cells. The hybrid batch had the lowest propionic acid yet more total organic acids. Some batches held less crude fiber and more soluble sugars than others. Over time the hybrid batch changed in a steady way, and gene reads showed Lactobacillus taking over as the lead strain. The work suggests hybrid strains can lift feed quality for livestock farmers.
pmc-11669006:
Emma Bassan and seven co-authors use text mining to survey the whole literature on assistance dogs. Their overview was published in twenty twenty-four. Trained dogs help people with many physical and mental conditions, and the research pile grows fast and wide.

A keyword search on one database yielded four hundred and fifty articles. The team charted them by year, place, and outlet. Automated mining then picked out the most telling words. A topic model split the set into themes. The exercise showed the shape of the field across all its angles at once. The authors argue that such machine reading can support scholars facing topics too large to review by hand in reasonable time.
pmc-11669806:
Katie Harron and eleven colleagues published a policy paper in two thousand twenty-four on research into England's health visiting service. Health visitors support every family with children under five. Yet evidence on what the service achieves is thin, and stakeholders disagree on what to study first.

The team consulted parents, policymakers, and service leads, and reviewed the literature. Parents wanted research on care that feels responsive and easy to reach. Officials wanted clear descriptions and ratings of current and ideal services. The authors warn that studies using routine data alone will likely miss real effects. They call for planned prospective and experimental studies on outcomes from bonding to school readiness.
pmc-11672706:
Coch Tanguy Floyde Tanga and nine co-authors published a review in twenty twenty-four on antimicrobial resistance in African great apes. Resistant bacteria are a global health threat, driven mainly by antibiotic overuse in people, livestock, and farming. Because apes share many pathogens with humans, they may reveal how resistance spreads into wild environments.

The review covered sixteen studies, most on wild apes living near people to different degrees. A few compared wild and captive animals or tested captive apes alone. The authors map what is known about resistant genes in apes and point out the gaps. Apes, they argue, can serve as sentinels for human-driven resistance.
pmc-11673106:
Martin Kovařík and co-authors studied how electron beam exposure changes nanotube devices in two thousand twenty-four. Making nanoscale devices often involves electron beams, and a standard transistor setup is used to measure new materials. The team watched tungsten disulfide nanotubes while the beam hit them inside a microscope.

Exposure changed each nanotube's resistance by a factor of two to fourteen, and the change did not reverse over hours to days. Surface potential scans pointed to charging of the supporting oxide as the main cause, not damage to the tube itself. The authors warn that care is needed when measuring nanostructures on insulating oxides that face electron exposure during or after fabrication.
pmc-11674006:
Miriam Kaňuchová, Veronika Brindza Lachová, Kateřina Bogdanová, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2024. It tests a wound-healing pair: an extract of agrimony, a plant long used on wounds, and a lab-made antibacterial compound, given together.

Agrimony extract is rich in polyphenols and fights oxidation. The partner compound kills bacteria in dishes while sparing the skin cells that rebuild tissue. The team checked the pair against staphylococcus, a common wound germ. They watched skin cells turn into the contractile cells that close wounds, lay down matrix, and multiply. They also tracked two growth signals in skin and vessel cells, and followed healing in rats day by day. The aim is a treatment that closes wounds faster without losing its germ-fighting edge, bridging herbal medicine and synthetic chemistry.
pmc-11674806:
Tassilo Dege and co-authors report a rare sweat gland cancer on a finger that was first taken for a wart, in work from 2024. The cancer grows slowly, mostly on hands and toes, and mostly in men. Telling it from benign sweat gland tumors is hard on sight alone.

Their patient was a man aged fifty-two with a growing finger tumor. Under the microscope, the growth showed the tube and spike forms of this cancer, with a telling stain pattern. Tests found the virus type HPV-42, which is strongly tied to this cancer, and ruled out a common mutation. The authors say these checks help sort look-alike tumors and guide care, since the cancer can return or spread.
pmc-11674906:
Christopher Sennett and colleagues studied a protein best known from Parkinson disease for its role in blood platelets. Platelets release stored granules when they clump to stop bleeding, and that release depends on a molecular clasp that fuses granules with the cell surface. The protein, alpha-synuclein, helps assemble similar clasps in other cells, but its platelet role was unclear. Writing in twenty twenty-four, the team studied mice that lack the protein and examined platelets in the lab and bleeding in living animals.

Mice without the protein showed weaker platelet clumping, secretion, and sticking, and they bled longer. When platelets switch on, the protein gains a phosphate tag and moves to the cell membrane, where it partners more with clasp parts. That tagging depends on calcium and a known signaling pair, and a natural platelet brake blocks it. The authors conclude the protein helps build the fusion clasp.
pmc-11675006:
Meera Elmasri and colleagues review why a bladder cancer treatment often causes urinary symptoms, in a twenty twenty-four article. The treatment, called BCG, places a weakened germ into the bladder to wake the immune system against the tumor. It works well, yet many patients get urgency, frequent urination, and pelvic pain. Some quit treatment because of these effects, which can hurt their cancer outcome.

The review argues the symptoms grow from swelling, a leakier bladder lining, and changed signaling in the bladder wall. These shifts likely disturb both the nerves that sense fullness and the muscle that squeezes. The authors draw on proof from other bladder disorders and from trials in cancer patients. They call for more work to pin down the exact chain of events.
pmc-11675106:
Ariella Levisohn and co-authors surveyed Black mothers in Boston about care after birth in a 2024 paper. Black birthing people attend postpartum visits at lower rates, a gap tied to worse outcomes. The team surveyed 121 people who had delivered within two years, using validated stress and empowerment scales plus demographic questions.

One third never attended their postpartum appointment. Public insurance, less than a college degree, and working outside the home each predicted missing the visit. Those who attended reported lower stress and higher empowerment scores. The commonest barriers were no time off work, COVID concerns, and no childcare. The authors call for institutional and policy support built around those concrete obstacles.
pmc-11675606:
María Elena Soto and five co-authors reported three cases of a heart valve infection marked by oxidative stress, in twenty twenty-four. In this illness, infective endocarditis, germs infect the heart valves and the body's redox balance is lost. The team took valve tissue from three patients who had valve replacement surgery and whose course was tangled by the infection, and set it against tissue from patients without the infection.

The infected tissue showed raised activity of several defense enzymes that fight oxidative damage. At the same time, a key protective compound fell, while two damage markers rose. The authors say the infection tips the valves into oxidative stress, and that the stress feeds on itself in a loop. That loop harms the heart further and may help drive the fatal course the illness can take.
pmc-11675906:
Dmitry Vishnevetskii, Elizaveta Polyakova, Yana Andrianova, and seven colleagues create light-responsive gels in this two thousand twenty-four materials paper. Their system combines a cysteine-silver sol with iodate anions. In darkness, weak, snot-like gels form, but only within a narrow iodate range. The team probed self-assembly with many techniques, from thickness and light measures to electron microscopy and X-ray methods.

Visible light raised gel thickness sharply and changed their color in a striking way. Microscopy showed the network transform: many round and oval particles appeared and the gel fibers thickened. Analysis revealed a redox reaction producing silver iodide and silver oxide particles in and on the sol particles. The base sol responded only to iodate over many other common ions. The authors present a new low-weight gel maker with light-sensitive traits, of possible use for sensing.
pmc-11676506:
Nobutake Tamai and colleagues published a biophysics study in 2024. They studied how sugars affect model cell membranes. The membrane lipid is called DMPC for short. Four single sugars were tested in water solutions. Two were common sugars, glucose and fructose. Two were rare sugars, allose and psicose. Heat scanning measured membrane phase changes precisely. Some samples had equal sugar inside and outside vesicles. Others deliberately had unequal sugar concentrations.

Sugar amount barely changed transition temperatures overall. Transition heat also stayed largely stable across sugars. Unequal sugar split the main transition peak clearly. That splitting happened for every sugar tested. Most sugar likely stays outside the membrane interior. Such results inform food and cell preservation science. Rare sugars behaved much like common ones here.
pmc-11677006:
Clara Lopes and co-authors present a 2024 review of how the physical environment rewrites the chemistry of brown algae, the large seaweeds that structure many coasts. These algae answer stress with a rich brew of compounds that defend them and interest industry, from medicines to cosmetics and food. What a batch contains depends heavily on where and when it grew.

The review covers studies from 2014 to 2024 on six drivers: water motion, temperature, light, nutrients, season, and saltiness. For each, the authors weigh how the compound profile shifts and what that means for the ecosystem. The synthesis doubles as a prospecting guide for harvesting bioactive compounds reliably.
pmc-11677206:
Asimina Ganotopoulou and co-authors test whether a blood enzyme linked to artery disease also tracks a stiffening of the heart in people with type 2 diabetes, in a 2024 paper. The enzyme, ADAMTS-7, helps remodel tissues and blood vessels and is known to play a part in atherosclerosis, the clogging of arteries. Its tie to heart function was barely studied. The team measured the enzyme in patients' blood and examined their hearts with ultrasound.

The heart problem in view is diastolic dysfunction, where the heart relaxes poorly between beats. That problem rose strongly with age but showed no clear link to enzyme levels. Looking at single ultrasound measures, the enzyme leaned positive only with one timing measure, deceleration time, while age explained most of the rest. The authors say the enzyme's role in this heart problem, and in heart failure among diabetics, needs more study before any verdict.
pmc-11677806:
Daniel Ricardo Delgado and four co-authors published a pharmaceutical chemistry study in twenty twenty-four measuring how the antibiotic sulfamethazine dissolves in mixtures of two solvents across nine temperatures. Solubility decides whether a drug can be formulated, and blending solvents is a standard trick to raise it. The shaking-flask method produced the data.

Solubility was lowest in pure propanol at the coldest temperature and highest in pure acetonitrile at the warmest, rising in a smooth logarithmic pattern between. The effect tracked the mixture's acid-base character rather than its solubility parameter. Dissolving absorbed heat and was driven forward by entropy, with strong compensation between the two. Such maps help formulators pick solvent blends rationally instead of by trial.
pmc-11678106:
Hao Wen and colleagues catalog a master gene family across the sugarcane genome, in this study from twenty twenty-four. GRAS transcription factors steer plant growth, development, and stress response. The hybrid cultivar ZZ1, a commercial Saccharum, had never been surveyed. The haul was enormous: seven hundred forty-seven complete GRAS genes, sorted into eleven subfamilies.

The family proved structurally diverse yet motif-conserved, with promoters crowded by signal-responsive elements, hinting at complex environmental control. Predicted protein structures showed conserved cores with flexible disordered tails. Network analysis tied one member, ShGRAS21A, to the response against smut, a major cane disease. The authors deliver the census as groundwork: breeders and engineers now have addresses for the genes that may govern cane stature, stress tolerance, and disease resistance.
pmc-11678706:
Andreea Herascu and co-authors wrote this 2024 review on insulin resistance in people with type 1 diabetes. Insulin resistance is best known as the core fault in type 2 diabetes, yet it can also develop in type 1. When it does, blood sugar targets grow harder to reach and the outlook worsens.

The review explains how the resistance arises and what it travels with, such as excess weight and a sedentary life. It also covers the harm that follows, above all a higher risk to the heart and blood vessels. Since these patients already take insulin, resistance must be gauged by stand-in measures like an estimated glucose disposal rate. The authors survey the main fixes, from diet and exercise to drugs such as metformin.
pmc-11678806:
Jessica Patricia Wiseman and Divya Maitreyi Chari wrote a lab study in two thousand twenty-four on materials that might help heal brain injury. For deep wounds in the brain, no therapy now helps tissue regrow. Bridges made of biomaterials are one hopeful route, and materials already approved for surgery could reach patients faster.

Testing such materials needs models that mimic real injury without heavy cost or animal use. The authors used thin slices of living brain tissue, kept alive in the lab, with a simulated injury. Into that setting they placed a surgical-grade biomaterial. Then they watched how nerve cells reacted to and grew with the material.
pmc-11678906:
Céline Damiani and a team of co-authors test new malaria drug parts in the lab, in a paper dated twenty twenty-four. The compounds are arylamino alcohols, kin to the partner drug mefloquine. The team checked how well each one blocks the forming of beta-hematin, a stand-in for the waste crystals malaria germs make.

They compared three pairs of mirror-image forms against two strains of the malaria germ. Chloroquine, mefloquine, and enpiroline served as reference drugs. Some new forms killed germs well, blocked crystal growth strongly, and harmed liver cells little. The results help explain how this drug family works and which forms merit more study.
pmc-11679706:
Jerome Dinga, Victor Titanji, and nine co-authors linked malaria and body nutrient levels in young children in Cameroon, in work from twenty twenty-four. In Buea Health District, malaria and poor diet both hit children under five hard. Germs can also drain the very nutrients a child needs. The team drew blood from eighty children in early twenty twenty-four and measured a panel of nutrient markers.

Levels shifted between sick and well children. Ferritin, a marker tied to iron stores, ran higher in children with malaria. The team reads such shifts with care, since illness itself can move these markers. Still, the data help clinics judge when low nutrients and malaria feed each other.
pmc-11680006:
Wenxiang Zeng and co-authors show that microplastic feeding worsens joint inflammation in lupus-prone mice, in a 2024 study. Microplastics enter bodies through air and food, and their health effects are only beginning to be mapped. Lupus frequently inflames joints, yet no work had asked what the particles do to lupus arthritis. Female mice of a lupus-like strain received oral microplastics at two doses from eight weeks of age.

Exposed mice showed more synovial damage, worse knee structure and function, and higher oxidative stress and cell death. Two signaling pathways were activated in the joint tissue, as the title names. For an autoimmune disease with joint pain as a daily burden, a common pollutant acting as an aggravator deserves attention.
pmc-11680106:
Edward Mocarski, writing alone in two thousand twenty-four, reviews cytomegalovirus biology through the lens of cell death suppression. These betaherpesviruses persist for life in their hosts by outmaneuvering the immune system.

Programmed cell death is a host defense that can kill infected cells before the virus finishes replicating. Over two decades, studies of virus-encoded death suppressors have mapped how cytomegaloviruses block apoptosis, necroptosis, pyroptosis, and a newer mitochondrial protease pathway. Those inhibitors also calm inflammation, helping the virus balance persistence against clearance. Mocarski argues the suppression machinery explains both the virus's success and its danger when host immunity fails.
pmc-11680206:
An eight-year-old beagle kept swallowing pieces of his cotton toys, and months later he arrived at the clinic off his food, vomiting, with a sore belly and dark stools. Andrada Negoescu and co-authors report what surgeons found: a tumor growing in the wall of his small intestine. The removed mass proved to be an osteosarcoma, a bone cancer growing far from any bone, with cotton fibers embedded inside it.

The tumor cells carried the markers pathologists expected for that diagnosis. Seven months later, nodules appeared in the dog's liver. He died ten months after the surgery. The authors present the case as the first documented one of its kind, possibly seeded by the swallowed fibers.
pmc-11689706:
Dana Ketcher and seven co-authors share lessons, in twenty twenty-four, from an Indigenous dementia project. Their work is community-based, meaning the community helps guide the study. Yet at the data analysis stage, community voices are often left out. That gap matters most for groups that have faced bias and loss. The team built a way to include community members in reading and coding talks and texts.

Their frame brings in community researchers and advisors, even those new to such work. It aims to check scholar bias and center local values and world views. The paper walks through their step-by-step method, built by trial over many rounds.
pmc-11689806:
Pamela Elfenbein describes a campus program that brings caregivers of all ages into one monthly circle. Most caregivers of older adults are over 45, yet a 2020 national study found that 11 percent are also in school, full or part time. Her 2024 presentation shares the plan of a group run by Adult Children of Aging Parents in Hall County. Students, staff, faculty, and community caregivers meet side by side.

Each meeting offers information, resources, and peer support, aiming at a better life for caregivers and the older adults they serve. Learning flows both ways: young and old trade skills and views. The plan rests on a named principle for age-friendly universities, the fourth such principle, which promotes shared learning across ages. Elfenbein gives the steps in full so other campuses can build a similar program.
pmc-11689906:
Kina White and Paulita Edwards-Childs tell how the health department in Mississippi built an age-friendly public health system. The state is not known for public health spending. While the state's total population falls, its population aged 65 and older grew a lot from 2010 to 2021. The health of older residents called for a planned reply.

With national aging and health groups as partners, the department took up a six-part frame for age-friendly public health systems. It earned exemplar status. It formed an advisory committee from many sectors and a statewide action plan. It made a healthy aging data report and county profiles with over 120 indicators. Staff gave them by hand to mayors in all 82 counties. With partners, it also built a champion program of older volunteers.
pmc-11690006:
Kina White and Paulita Edwards-Childs describe, in twenty twenty-four, Mississippi's public health plan for dementia. The state has the highest death rate from Alzheimer's disease and related illness in the nation. Risk is higher in rural areas, and all of the state's counties lack enough doctors. Black residents and tribal groups bear a large share of the burden.

The plan, part of a national BOLD effort, stresses joint work across groups. Steps include town teaching, aid for caregivers, early checks, and dementia-friendly services. It also works with tribal nations and weaves in their healing ways. Churches and towns that welcome people with dementia are early examples.
pmc-11690406:
Katherine McGilton, Karen Spilsbury, and Carl Thompson lead a symposium, in twenty twenty-four, on fixing long-term care world-wide. Years of study have not moved many care home rules, they note. Staff face poor terms and shaky jobs. Homes struggle to hire and keep good staff, and to give care that fits each resident. The session brings work from several countries to one stage.

Talks cover how to draw and keep staff, and the right mix of skills on a team. One talk shares a nurse-led change to breakfast time in care homes. Others review steps taken by states in Europe, both before and during COVID-19.
pmc-11690606:
Joseph Gaugler and co-authors test, in a 2024 study, a coaching program for one of caregiving's hardest transitions: moving a relative with dementia into residential care. The Residential Care Transition Module offers six telehealth sessions of psychosocial support and education. Two hundred forty family caregivers were randomized to the program or usual care and surveyed over twelve months on stress, depressive symptoms, competence, and confidence.

On the headline measures, the program group did no better than the control group. Two subgroups told a different story. Caregivers whose relatives had moved within the prior three months showed falling depressive symptoms early on. Employed caregivers in the program grew in self-efficacy across the year. The authors read the mixed result as a lesson in heterogeneity: dementia caregiving is not one situation, and support lands where timing and circumstance fit. Measuring what caregivers themselves value may show benefits the standard scales missed.
pmc-11690706:
Ginger Williams and six co-authors describe how Colorado State Extension adapted a healthy aging course. Their twenty twenty-four report covers the Aging Mastery Program, a ten-session course in English and Spanish. The team took it to Native American, Spanish-speaking immigrant, and East African refugee groups in Colorado. These groups face high rates of poor health and isolation, in part due to language gaps.

Staff used state data to pick sites, then held listening sessions to build trust. They trained and paid local champions to teach the course. Champions later helped write grants and plan new sessions. Work is now set to grow to eight more towns.
pmc-11691206:
Jennifer Crook and co-authors studied extreme heat and food insecurity among low-income older adults in a 2024 paper. Heat strains health, and older people with little money already struggle to eat well. The team interviewed 45 adults in Central Florida communities and measured food security with a standard federal questionnaire.

Thirteen participants were food insecure and 32 were secure. The insecure group reported stronger heat effects on their health, daily activities, and sleep than the secure group. No clear difference appeared for food access or hydration itself. The authors argue that heat and hunger compound each other in this group, so aid programs should plan for both at once.
pmc-11691506:
Yi-Hsiu Lin and Tsuann Kuo published a study in 2024 on a life review program in Taiwan, seen from the perspective of the leaders who run it. In life review groups, older adults meet weekly to reflect on their life events, guided by set themes. The program has been implemented in Taiwan for more than ten years.

More than eighty program leaders participated in a survey and interviews. Most were women, and most held at least a college degree. Leaders reported that the groups helped older adults communicate with family members and strengthened family bonding. The groups also gave participants the courage to face difficult past events. Participants integrated their past into a coherent whole and looked to the future with more hope. The findings link the program to less depression, less loneliness, and greater self-confidence among older adults.
pmc-11691706:
Gerald Liao, Jackson Wezeman, and Warren Ladiges gave a symposium talk in two thousand twenty-four proposing the house cricket as a model for aging research. Aging studies use many animal models, each with trade-offs in lifespan, cost, and access to organs. No model captures all of human aging, so fresh candidates are worth testing.

The domestic cricket offers a short life, simple but well-defined organs, cheap upkeep, and new nerve growth in a brain region like the hippocampus. In a pilot, adult crickets fed chow mixed with flax oil lived significantly longer than controls. The authors stress how fast and cheap such dietary tests can run.
pmc-11692006:
Lenora Smith and Charles O'Brien present a 2024 paper on Neurospective, a phone app platform built to catch cognitive decline early. No cure exists for Alzheimer disease, so spotting decline early matters: lifestyle steps may slow the slide from mild impairment. The app aims to make screening cheap, engaging, and available anywhere.

Its tests are mini-games modelled on standard clinic screens, probing language, memory, reasoning, and problem solving. The platform also gathers broader user data and plans machine learning on top, to sharpen the screening over time. The authors present the design as a route to dementia checks that reach people long before a clinic visit would.
pmc-11692206:
Lillian Hung and five co-authors published a study in 2024 on families using telepresence robots with relatives who live in long-term care homes. A telepresence robot lets family members visit by screen. When a loved one moves into care, family caregivers shift from being the main caregiver to being visitors, a transition many find difficult. The COVID-19 pandemic made it harder, with strict protocols and long periods apart.

The study ran from May 2021 to August 2023 in five urban care homes in British Columbia, Canada. Twenty family care partners used the robots and shared their experiences in interviews. Four themes stood out. The robots reduced the burden on care partners and helped them work with staff. They also gave care partners more control over their own role and expanded what visits could accomplish. The authors say more research is needed on how sustainable such use is over time.
pmc-11692306:
Thinh Huynh and co-authors report early results, in a 2024 conference paper, on how a single bout of exercise shifts brain-support factors and stress hormone levels in middle-aged and older adults. Such shifts may explain part of how regular activity guards the brain. The team asked whether long exercise history or current daily activity better predicts the response.

Fifty-four healthy adults took a fitness test, wore activity trackers for a week, then exercised once for blood checks. Long-term history did not predict either response. People who moved more day to day showed a stronger brain-factor rise and a smaller stress hormone rise. The brain-factor link faded with age, which hints that timing of activity matters.
pmc-11692406:
Makenna Green, Jamie Mayer, Laura White, and Gail Kouame review service learning as a pipeline into dementia care jobs, in a 2024 paper. Dementia cases climb as the population ages, and the care workforce gap widens with education cited as a barrier. Service learning puts students to work with patients while they study.

The review searched seven databases and kept thirty-two studies of health majors whose courses included community work with adults with dementia. Clinical rotations were excluded to isolate the teaching model. Most programs leaned on preparatory training plus direct contact and reflection. The authors extract student traits, program parts, and outcomes across the set. Their aim is a recipe for courses that both teach and recruit the next dementia workforce.
pmc-11692506:
Katherine Luci and co-authors pilot a video-group program for veterans living with mild cognitive impairment, in a 2024 study. The nine-session program, MiND-MCI, mixes peer support with lessons on memory, coping, and healthy habits. Sixteen veterans aged 61 to 79, all testing in the impaired range, joined from home. Attendance and retention were tracked, along with usability and acceptability questionnaires.

Eighty-eight percent stayed the course, attending seven of nine sessions on average. Eleven veterans joined at least three quarters of the sessions. Satisfaction scores ran high across three separate measures. Facilitators flagged tech troubles and wide variation in impairment as the main hurdles, and prized the peer support. The authors judge the format feasible and worth a fuller trial.
pmc-11692706:
Angela Perone and three co-authors set out a framework that puts power at the heart of fair aging, in a report published in 2024. Loneliness and social isolation in old age are well-recorded harms, but most work is set in the United States and skips power. Their framework joins power theory with the social and political drivers of health. It maps five kinds of power and how they shape who receives what care.

Three cases show the framework at work. One reads loneliness among rural Indigenous elders in Taiwan. One reads isolation among city elders in mainland China. One reads both among nursing home residents in Spain. Each case maps how power shapes the drivers and where fair action can step in. The authors aim the framework at researchers, government staff, and hands-on workers alike.
pmc-11700606:
Livestock farming has long reacted to problems after animals fall sick or fall behind. Caleb Grohmann and Jared Decker argue in a 2025 overview that sensors and artificial intelligence flip that order, letting managers act before trouble lands.

Cameras, wearables, and production records now stream in automatically around the clock. Learning models fold those streams into daily forecasts of health, well-being, and output for each animal or herd. Managers can plan interventions from those forecasts instead of from yesterday's losses. The new measurements also give breeders better traits to select for, targeting the real drivers of sustainable production rather than rough stand-ins. The authors frame the shift as farm-wide, not a single gadget.
pmc-11710006:
Hsiao-Tien Chien Hagar and Min-Hao Kuo studied how abnormal tau protein harms brain cells, in work published in twenty twenty-five on Alzheimer disease. Tau that carries too many phosphate groups is a hallmark of the disease, but how it kills cells is still unclear. The team made this altered tau in the lab and applied it to a human nerve-like cell line. They tracked cell shape and survival, and used mass spectrometry to see which proteins changed within hours of treatment.

The altered tau caused strong shape changes and cell death within about a day. One protein, heme oxygenase one, dropped more sharply than any other early on. The authors then tested whether restoring that protein protects cells, and whether the two proteins bind directly. Their results point to a harmful tug of war between altered tau and a normally protective enzyme.
pmc-11710506:
Benjamin Chapin and co-authors present a 2025 study on sight based focus before surgery. Older adults can face delirium after an operation, a state of confusion that raises harm. The team asked if simple focus tests done before surgery could flag who was at risk.

They studied adults aged sixty five and older who had planned bone surgery. Each person did line and cue tasks that test how focus shifts. After surgery, most had no delirium, while a small share had mild or full signs. Two focus scores tracked with later delirium scores, while age and a broad test did not. The authors urge more work on these cheap tests.
pmc-11712106:
Feyikemi Mary Akinyelure and co-authors set out a proposed training project for carers in Lagos, Nigeria, in a 2025 plan. Older people in Nigeria often face neglect or abuse, with the poor hit hardest, the authors write. Their project trains carers in cognitive therapy: guided table activities, memory exercises, and problem solving games.

The plan is to train one hundred twenty health care assistants each year. Training covers dementia knowledge in theory and dementia screening in practice. Results will be judged with a standard mental state exam and a clock drawing test. The team hopes trained carers will extend life and cut the impact of dementia. The plan also tests whether such training can run well in Lagos.
pmc-11712206:
Ríona Mc Ardle and co-authors pilot a home activity tracking plan for older couples in a 2025 study. Walking supports healthy ageing, but researchers need honest records of how partners and neighborhoods shape it. Twenty-one couples took part for seven days.

Each person wore a motion sensor on the lower back, carried a phone with a GPS app when out, and kept a nightly activity diary. Nearly all wore the sensor for the full week and all finished their diaries. The GPS app captured about three quarters of the days, with most gaps blamed on tech faults. Couples found the kit acceptable overall. The authors say the plan is ready for larger studies of walking and ageing.
pmc-11712806:
Ismael Luis Calandri and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on running a dementia prevention trial across twelve Latin American countries. The trial, LatAm-FINGERS, tests lifestyle change rather than drugs, the first of its kind on that scale in the region. Its people share a language yet differ widely in wealth, culture, and care access.

The team describes how each site helped design the work, so plans fit local life. Shared training and local champions kept sign-up and follow-through on track. The paper also notes a second goal: teaching the public that dementia can often be held off. Their playbook may guide prevention trials in other mixed regions.
pmc-11712906:
Yu Mi Choi, Hyun-Ju Seo, and Seong Min Kim present a 2025 methods paper that checks whether a short quality-of-life tool works well for family caregivers of people with dementia. The tool, called HINT-8, has eight items. It had not been tested in this group in Korea before.

The team gave the tool, along with two longer standard tools, to 340 caregivers reached through dementia centres and home nursing services. Their plan compares scores across the tools and repeats the tool to test stability over time. A short tool that proves sound would help services spot caregiver needs quickly and plan support.
pmc-11713106:
Tavia E Evans and co-authors present a 2025 study of genes, sex, and shrinkage of the hippocampus, a brain area central to memory. The team asked whether a person's inherited risk for Alzheimer's disease speeds up that shrinkage, and whether the effect differs between women and men and across disease stages.

They followed 1,051 people in the ADNI cohort with gene data and repeat scans over up to eight years. Risk scores were built with and without the APOE gene region, which is known to raise risk. The study tests how much of the gene effect on brain change runs through that one region alone.
pmc-11713406:
Ravinder Singh and Aditya Sunkaria study genes for proteins that cells release, using a lab model of Alzheimer's disease, in this 2025 paper. Released proteins can show up in blood or spinal fluid, so they may serve as early signs of the disease. The team hunted for such genes in brain cells.

They filtered a human protein atlas for released proteins, then matched those against brain cell proteins and known disease genes. Twenty-four candidate genes stood out. The team then treated nerve cells in dishes with forms of amyloid to mimic early disease. They measured which candidate genes changed their activity, a step toward new early markers.
pmc-11713906:
Wen Liu, Heather Suh, and Kyuri Lee review ways to improve mealtimes for people with dementia in a 2025 paper. Eating well keeps up strength, social contact, and pleasure in food. Dementia makes meals hard for patients and tiring for caregivers. The review gathers tested programs that aim to make meals safer and calmer.

The team searched five health databases for studies from 2012 to 2023. Each study was sorted by the kind of program it tested and rated for quality. Where several studies tested the same kind of help, the results were pooled. The review shows which approaches raise food intake or ease caregiver strain. Care homes can use it to pick programs with real proof behind them.
pmc-11714006:
Sampada Tamhankar and three co-authors test whether drugs that switch on a fat control switch can help rebuild myelin in Alzheimer's disease, in a 2025 conference paper. Myelin is the fatty coat that speeds nerve signals, and it thins as the disease grows. The coat is rebuilt by cells called oligodendrocytes.

The switch, named LXR, steers cholesterol, a chief part of myelin. The team gave a strong switch on drug to mice bred for the disease and to a human cell line that acts like the coat building cells. Lab tests then read the cell proteins. Diseased mice showed lower levels of young and mature coat cells than normal mice. The work checks whether the drug can push those cells to recoat bare fibers.
pmc-11714306:
Chad Guilliams and Erin Abner test whether a parent's history of dementia skews the known link between low mood and thinking loss, in a 2025 conference paper. Family history can pull certain people into studies, which may bend results. Many teams now swap it for gene marks instead.

The team sorted nearly twenty-one thousand adults without dementia by mood and thinking state at their first visit. People with low mood had more than twice the odds of mild thinking loss. Adding a parent's history to the model barely moved that link, though it did shift it a touch upward. The authors also tracked who slid to worse states over time, using death as a rival outcome in the models.
pmc-11714506:
Darlingtina Esiaka and four co-authors test whether schooling links to memory area size in older Black Americans, and whether the link splits by sex, in a 2025 conference paper. Schooling is thought to build a reserve that guards thinking in old age. The memory area in question is the hippocampus, which shrinks as Alzheimer's disease nears.

The team used 38 adults from a Kentucky aging center cohort, with a mean age near 73. School years ran from ten to twenty-one. Each person had health checks, thinking tests, and a brain scan. In men, more schooling went strongly with a larger left hippocampus. The authors report no such link in women in this small group. They urge bigger studies of how schooling shapes the brain in Black adults.
pmc-11715306:
Wei-Ju Lee and co-authors hunted a better scan mark for thought skills in a rare passed-down vessel disease. The disease, called CADASIL, stems from a flaw in one gene and harms small brain vessels. White spots on scans are its classic sign, yet they track thought skills poorly. A newer mark reads how wide the spread of water flow is in white matter tracts.

The team scanned gene carriers with no past stroke or dementia and a matched set of non-carriers. All took tests of memory, speed, planning, and space skills. Carriers showed worse white spots and a wider spread mark than non-carriers. The spread mark lined up with slower speed and weaker space skills once age and schooling were weighed. The white spot load showed no such link, which puts the new mark ahead.
pmc-11715606:
Jennifer Frontera and co-authors ask whether blood biomarkers of brain harm match brain volumes two years after COVID-19. Many people who had the virus report lasting brain fog and slow thinking, yet the cause stays unclear. Their 2025 study scanned and tested 90 adults. Most had laboratory proof of past infection, and a small group had never had the virus.

In the group that had the virus, high blood markers of neurodegeneration, blood-brain barrier leakage, and inflammation went with smaller volumes in mood and memory regions. The pattern was sharp in those with poor cognitive test scores and absent in those with sound scores. It also did not appear in the group that never had the virus. The team reads the blood-and-scan match as a clue to how the virus may mark the brain. More work must prove cause, not just a link.
pmc-11715706:
Zlatomira Georgieva Ilchovska, Akram A Hosseini, and JeYoung Jung test whether two brain chemicals explain the language losses of frontotemporal dementia, in this 2025 study. The disease erodes the frontal and temporal lobes, seats of word knowledge. A standing hypothesis blames disturbed balance between glutamate, an excitatory signal, and GABA, an inhibitory one.

Brain scans that read chemistry without surgery measured both chemicals in frontal and temporal cortex. Seven patients with the disease were compared with two Alzheimer's patients and twenty-three healthy peers. The dementia group scored worse on language, memory, and executive tasks, and handled a word knowledge task less well than both other groups. The excitation inhibition balance dropped in the temporal lobe. The authors present the pattern as early support for the chemical hypothesis, gathered from a small sample.
pmc-11716006:
Haiyun Chen and six co-authors check how stable a widely used brain scan program's readings are when the same person is scanned twice, in this 2025 study. The program, FreeSurfer, measures brain regions that shrink in Alzheimer's disease, and trials rely on it to track change. If readings jump between scans for no real reason, small true changes get lost.

One hundred adults aged sixty and older at a New York center had two scans about five weeks apart on the same machine. Measures of memory regions, cortex thickness, and total head size matched closely between the two scans. Gaps between readings did not track with age, sex, schooling, or thinking scores. The results back the program's use for following brain change over time.
pmc-11716206:
Yuancheng Li and co-authors build a lab-made molecule that can fish a key Alzheimer's marker out of blood or spinal fluid, in a 2025 paper. Tests for the disease often rely on antibodies to grab amyloid beta, a protein fragment tied to the illness. Antibodies vary between batches and spoil in storage. The team offers a synthetic stand-in built from a chain of modified amino acid units.

The researchers made a large library of these synthetic chains and screened it for ones that grip a form of amyloid called Aβ40. They mapped the winning chains with lab instruments, then fixed them to magnetic beads. The beads can pull the target protein out of a sample for measurement. A stable, factory-made gripper like this could make fluid tests for the disease cheaper and more steady.
pmc-11716906:
Carlos Cordeiro Junior and co-authors study, in a 2025 paper, how swelling pathways act in the brains of mice bred to develop Alzheimer's-like disease. Plaques and tangles in the disease are tied to poor clearing of two proteins and to an overactive immune response in the brain.

Forty-eight mice were treated with lithium for three months at two dose levels, with an untreated group for comparison. Tissue from the hippocampus, a memory region, was screened for its full protein set. The team traced how sensor proteins that spark swelling connect with the disease proteins. They also asked how lithium, a long-used drug, shifts that network.
pmc-11726106:
