Marcio Nucci and nine co-authors issue consensus guidance in two thousand twenty-four on fever during low white cell counts. Febrile neutropenia is a dangerous side effect of treating blood diseases. Resistant bacteria are making it harder to manage, and the pattern varies by region.

Ten experts from a Brazilian hematology association built the recommendations by a structured Delphi process. The document covers the first workup of a febrile patient and preventive treatment. It sets out starting antibiotic and antifungal choices, when to change them, and when therapy can stop. The guidance is tuned to local infection patterns rather than copied from abroad. The authors present it as a shared standard for Brazilian centers.
pmc-11728106:
Grzegorz Wryk and co-authors run, in a 2024 study, a broad contest of methods that fill in missing values in protein measurement data. Such data sets can lose up to half their entries, which blurs results. Ten filling methods were tested, from simple floor values to global pattern methods, on data from two protein search tools.

Fake gaps were cut into complete data at varied rates and patterns, so each method's error could be scored fairly. The team also checked whether a log step before filling helped or hurt. Results were judged by error size and by how well true and false finds were sorted. The study gives labs a grounded pick of method by gap type.
pmc-11728706:
Arturs Medvids and co-authors present an optical method to size tiny nanostructures in this 2024 paper. The method reads the color of light a structure emits when excited. That emission shifts toward blue as the structure shrinks. Two test objects were used, carbon nanocones and a sharp microscope tip.

For the carbon cones, the shifted spectrum gave a top size of 2.0 nanometers. For the atomic force microscope tip, green emission sat right at its apex. The spectrum gave a tip size of 1.5 nanometers, matching electron microscope measures. Time resolved readings showed how the excited state lifetime changes along the cone. The method needs no special sample preparation or costly sizing equipment.
pmc-11731306:
Rajkumar Kundavaram and colleagues reported a heart study in 2024 on children treated for acute lymphoblastic leukemia. A key drug in their treatment can harm the heart, sometimes soon after dosing and sometimes much later. The team used ultrasound heart scans before treatment and again three days after the first treatment dose in a small group of children. They compared many measures of how well both sides of the heart pumped and relaxed.

After the dose, both the right and left sides of the heart showed weaker pumping and slower relaxation. Several standard scan measures moved in the direction of early damage, even though the changes were modest. The authors argue that routine heart scans should be part of care from the start of treatment. Early spotting of quiet heart changes, they say, lets doctors act before the damage grows into plain heart failure.
pmc-11783306:
Saul Pierotti, Tomas Fitzgerald, and Ewan Birney present a software paper published in 2024 on a pipeline for genome-wide association studies. Linear mixed models handle population structure in such studies, but the usual way of setting significance by shuffling outcomes breaks down when samples are related or covariates matter.

Their tool, FlexLMM, runs inside the Nextflow workflow system. It first regresses the population structure out of the data, then shuffles only the leftover residuals, which keeps the procedure valid. The exact model can be defined flexibly by the user. The authors aim it at researchers crossing inbred lines of model organisms, farm animals, and plants, where structure is unavoidable. Code and documentation are freely available.
pmc-11786206:
Zahra Taghinejad, Mohammad Asgharzadeh, and Ali Akbar Pourfathollah raise an urgent alert about dengue spreading through blood transfusion in Iran in a 2024 paper. Dengue is an emerging problem in the country, with close to one hundred fifty new confirmed cases noted. The virus spreads mainly by Aedes mosquitoes, which are expanding their range fast.

Donated blood is another route: a donor with silent infection can pass the virus to a patient. The authors argue for screening and vigilance in blood services as case counts climb. Their warning is brief but pointed, aimed at transfusion policy before a preventable route opens. It also flags hospital routes of spread that infection control teams should review.
pmc-11805206:
Anand Tripathi and colleagues tested bracket bonding under different curing lights in 2024. Orthodontic brackets must stick firmly to teeth. Light curing sets the bonding glue. Sixty extracted premolar teeth were used. Three lamp types formed the groups. Two curing times were compared within groups.

Twenty seconds beat ten seconds clearly. Bond strength rose with longer curing. Lamp type also changed the results. Plasma arc and other lamps differed measurably. Both factors reached statistical significance here. Stronger bonds support successful treatment overall. Clinic choices should weigh lamp and time. Quick cures may cost holding strength.
pmc-11839406:
Asma Afzal and co-authors pool studies on two non-invasive tests for bowel polyps, in work published in 2024. Polyps can turn into bowel cancer, so finding them early matters. A stool test that detects hidden blood is standard for cancer screening, but its use for polyps is less settled. Breath and stool gas compounds have also been tested.

The review gathered studies that reported accuracy for either test against advanced polyps. Twenty-two stool test papers and twelve gas compound papers entered the review, with most feeding the pooled analysis. The team checked study quality with a standard tool and computed combined sensitivity and specificity for the tests. The work aims to show whether either method, or both together, can sort patients toward timely scope exams.
pmc-11888606:
Sornamalar M and five co-authors build a scaffold meant to regrow the inside of a damaged tooth, in a 2024 laboratory study. The pulp-dentin complex, the tooth's living core, does not repair itself well after deep decay. Their scaffold blends a nano phosphorylated form of pullulan, a natural sugar polymer, into carboxymethyl chitosan gel. Five mixing ratios were made, freeze-dried, and examined with standard materials tools.

Human dental pulp stem cells were then grown on the scaffolds to check survival and growth. The best ratio was compared against plain chitosan and a bone-forming medium. A scaffold that pulp stem cells accept is a step toward regenerative fillings that rebuild living tooth tissue instead of inert plugs.
pmc-11928306:
Gisèle Mukeya Mvumbi and co-authors published a 2024 study of two liver viruses, hepatitis B and C, in women who sell sex in Bamako, Mali. Both viruses are a health problem in poor countries. How often they strike this at-risk group, with or without HIV, was thin in past data. The team set out to count them.

Four hundred women took part in one year, half with HIV and half without it. Questionnaires, blood samples, and swabs were taken. Marks of the first virus ran at over six in a hundred in the HIV group, and over four in a hundred without HIV. Marks of the second virus ran higher in both. Paid sex before eighteen tied strongly to the first virus, as did the marks of the second. The team calls for a targeted prevention plan for this group.
pmc-12169106:
Atharva S Kulkarni is first author on a 2025 review of mass spectrometry methods for studying host and microbiome chemistry. The microbiome is the community of microbes living in and on a body. Host and microbes trade chemical signals, including natural products, small molecules microbes make, but these are scarce amid host and food chemicals.

Covering work from twenty fifteen to twenty twenty-five, the review explains how mass spectrometers, instruments that sort molecules by weight, plus new lab and computer methods, find those signals. Examples come from human and mouse systems, with parallels from other ecosystems. The findings help researchers decode how microbes shape health and disease.
pmc-12331206:
Anna L Alves Fernandes and co-authors published a research paper in 2024 on whether slight, harmless facial asymmetry in women comes with differences in bite and chewing muscles. Subtle asymmetry is common and usually counted as normal, yet it might still track functional imbalances. Forty-two women aged eighteen to thirty were sorted by 3D face scans into symmetric and slightly asymmetric groups.

Bite force at the molars and contact patterns were measured, and ultrasound gauged two chewing muscles. No measure differed significantly between groups. The main chewing muscle was thicker than the temple muscle in both groups, and slightly thicker in the asymmetric group, but not beyond chance. The authors read slight asymmetry as functionally benign.
pmc-12663306:
Mashael Maashi and seven co-authors build a deep learning model that segments lungs and screens for tuberculosis in chest X-rays, with shape aware feature blending. Tuberculosis is a chronic bacterial lung illness and a major killer. The study came out in twenty twenty-five.

Chest X-rays are the main first check, and deep learning now aids spotting suspect marks. The model stacks features in layers and fuses them with shape sense, to sharpen both lung outlines and disease calls. The aim is early, exact screening that helps radiologists flag lesions and nodes. The authors frame it as a low cost aid for busy clinics.
pmc-12663406:
Véronique Gaudreault, Benoit Marchand, Raphaëlle Larcher, and seven colleagues map the neighborhoods of trafficking proteins in this two thousand twenty-five cell biology paper. RAB GTPases are the largest small GTPase family and direct membrane trafficking: cargo sorting, vesicle budding, transport, docking, and fusion. Their protein partners interact transiently, making them hard to catch. Proximity labeling solves this by chemically tagging whatever sits near a target protein inside living cells.

Using APEX2 labeling on twenty-three human RAB proteins, the team catalogued each one's neighboring proteome. Bioinformatics surfaced new connections, including a novel RAB25 partnership with DENND6A, where extra RAB25 pulled DENND6A onto recycling endosomes. Functional links also emerged between RAB14 and the EARP complex, and between SHIP164 and its relative UHRF1BP1, in endosomal recruitment. The authors offer the dataset as a resource for discovering how RAB proteins organize cellular logistics.
pmc-12671106:
Jinming Liu and co-authors published a study in 2025 on the safety of guided cancer drugs for bladder cancer. These drugs link an antibody to a poison payload, homing in on tumor cells. Their real-world harm profiles are still being mapped.

The team mined a United States harm-report system from 2004 to 2024. Of 494 reports on four such drugs, one drug made up over ninety percent. Each drug showed a distinct harm pattern: skin and metabolism ills for the main one, gut events for another. Kidney signals emerged for one drug, and bleeding and lung signals for a fourth. One mouth infection tied to the main drug was missing from its label. The authors urge drug-specific watch plans in the clinic.
pmc-12686406:
Xiaokun Hong and co-authors built a database and a deep learning predictor for how protein modifications steer phase separation in a 2025 paper. Liquid-liquid phase separation forms the membraneless droplets that organize cell chemistry, and it goes wrong in several diseases. Chemical tags added to proteins after they are built, called post-translational modifications, strongly tune that separation.

No dedicated resource gathered those effects before. The team curated a database of modification-regulated cases, then trained a model to predict new ones. Predictions can guide experiments on droplet control, a possible drug strategy for diseases of faulty droplets. The work pairs a data resource with a tool, a combination that tends to speed a young field.
pmc-12687906:
Myriam Jaam and co-authors audit heart-protective prescribing for diabetic patients with artery disease in Qatar primary care. Guidelines urge a bundle of drug classes for this high-risk group. Records from twenty-nine clinics covered 2,870 patients through 2021. Only about ten percent got high-intensity statins as advised.

About twelve percent received the newer sugar-lowering heart drugs. Blood pressure drugs of the ACE or ARB family reached fifty-six percent. Male sex, worse sugar control, and a lipid diagnosis each raised guideline use. Together such traits explained only sixteen percent of the variation. The authors call the gap wide and press for fixes against clinical inertia.
pmc-12692306:
Kornieieva and co-authors review whether molecular hydrogen gas could help treat heart failure. The condition, where the heart cannot pump enough blood, grows more common and still kills many patients within five years. Current drugs do not cover all its tangled causes.

Hydrogen seems to protect the heart by fighting oxidation, calming inflammation, and slowing cell death. Studies in several failure models show it easing stress on heart cells, supporting their energy factories, and limiting scarring and thickening. The reviewers call this the first summary of the field. They stress the work is young, and human value remains unproven.
pmc-12696306:
Dimitrios Katsaros and Dimitrios Mougiakakos reviewed engineered T cells as a treatment for immune disorders of the nerves and brain, in a paper published in 2025. The cells carry a made receptor that aims them at one target type. In blood cancers they wipe the target out deeply and for long. Cell design now chases safer, cheaper, faster cells.

The same wipe-out can serve autoimmune disorders of the nerves. Early trials cover a muscle weakness illness, a cord illness, and a stiff person illness, with promising early marks. Broad B cell depletion leads; finer depletion of just the harmful B cells is in development. The pair sorts who fits the treatment, how to prepare them, and the harm watch afterward. They call nerve use a strong new front.
pmc-12696906:
Likai Pang and co-authors test a treatment for spinal cord injury based on cell packets loaded with a small RNA strand, in a research paper from 2025. Cord injury harms feeling and movement, and many new cases occur each year. Small RNA strands guide gene activity, and shifts in them shape stress, swelling, and cell death after injury.

Packets from stem cells carried the strand into tests in cells and in mice. Treated cells grew better, and stress after injury eased. Mice showed better recovery of movement. Gene data helped pick the strand and its targets. The work points to a new path for cord repair.
pmc-12699206:
Jianping Yang and co-authors published this grassland study in 2025. Shrubs are spreading across the alpine meadows of the Tibetan Plateau as the climate warms and grazing pressure grows. Tibetan herders have fought the spread for centuries by uprooting shrubs, burning patches in the dormant season, and rotating herds. The team measured encroachment across the Zoige Plateau at heights from 3,400 to 3,900 meters. They also ran experiments removing shrubs, restricting canopies, and excluding roots.

Elevation strongly limited how fast shrubs spread in the short term. The experiments showed that shade from shrub canopies does most of the damage, explaining about sixty percent of the change. Roots mattered far less, at under three percent. Canopy shade starves the grasses beneath, letting shrubs tighten their hold. Traditional herding methods strike exactly at that canopy advantage. By cutting the shade, they free the understory grasses to recover.
pmc-12701306:
Xue-Yao Guo and co-authors present a 2025 review of Parkinson's disease. The disease is a progressive brain disorder with a growing global burden. Current drugs ease symptoms but do not stop the disease. Faulty clumping of one protein sits near the core of the process. The review spans spread, risk factors, molecular causes, prevention, and therapy. Newer risks include gut germ imbalance and environmental toxins.

Body-wide routes, such as gut-brain and kidney-brain axes, join the classic brain story. Molecular faults range from protein cleanup failure to iron imbalance. Prevention and therapy sections weigh what can be done now. Clinicians and students get one integrated map of a complex disease. The body-wide framing is the review's fresh angle: Parkinson's may start far from the brain, which changes where early detection should look.
pmc-12701606:
Nosair and four colleagues test a plant pigment packed in tiny bubbles against a hardy hospital germ in twenty twenty-five. The germ forms slimy layers, called biofilms, that shrug off drug care. It also talks to its kin with chemical signals to build those layers. The pigment, from a related germ, was packed into fat bubbles to help it work.

Packed pigment killed drug resistant strains in lab tests and cut biofilm growth by a wide margin. It also cut movement, iron grabbing, and the signal gene the germ uses to coordinate. In mice with lung infection, it cut germ counts and raised survival. The team sees it as a new path against stubborn infections.
pmc-12703006: Mohamed Azmi, Nur 'Aini Eddy Warman, Fatimah Mohamed Shah, and a wider team wrote this case report, published in 2025. It describes muscle breakdown caused by an underactive thyroid alone, with none of the usual triggers such as trauma or drugs. Rhabdomyolysis from hypothyroidism is rare but dangerous, since debris from dying muscle can wreck the kidneys. The authors stress it can appear without classic thyroid symptoms. They urge creatine kinase screening in puzzling presentations, so treatment starts before kidney injury sets in.
pmc-12703206:
Silas Fischer and co-authors present a 2025 natural history study of microscopic algae riding on migrating songbirds. Protists turn up in odd far-flung places, and how they travel is a standing puzzle. Waterbirds are known microbe carriers, but land birds that migrate long distances were barely checked.

The team sampled tail feathers from four thrush species with different migration styles. Every one of the seven samples held diatoms, the glass-shelled algae: 224 individuals from 25 genera in all. Most were freshwater bottom-dwellers, and some still held their green chloroplasts, a sign they might be alive. The authors suggest songbirds are overlooked ferries for these microbes. That route could help explain how pond species cross dry land between wetlands.
pmc-12706206:
Nick Mamo and five co-authors improve a Dutch care network for persistent symptoms in a 2025 paper. Conditions like functional disorders need joined-up care from many professionals, yet fragmented systems leave patients and staff frustrated. Their participatory study sat inside a regional network for a year, led by an action group of patients-by-experience and local professionals. The group picked goals and ran concrete actions to improve how the network works.

The paper reports which change processes proved realistic inside such a network. It also draws lessons on the conditions that make change stick, such as shared ownership and a facilitator embedded in the group. The focus is practical know-how for other networks.
pmc-12706906:
Anderson, Tsuyuki, Fernandez DeSoto, and Stockman study medical mistrust among women who have lived through sexual violence. Their study is from two thousand twenty-five and is set in the United States. Survivors face worse health yet may shun care for fear of fresh trauma, stigma, or cost. Such mistrust has been less studied in this group.

The THRIVE study tracked women who had faced recent forced sex, and compared them with women who had not. Mistrust was scored with a group-based scale and its sub-scales. Women with past or recent rape showed higher mistrust than others, with recent cases the highest. Black women scored higher than non-Black women. The authors call for care that is trauma-aware and for routine screening for violence.
pmc-12709006:
Christopher Ahmad and co-authors studied whether pre-surgery survey scores predict recovery after elbow ligament surgery in a 2025 paper. The operation, common in baseball pitchers, repairs the ligament that steadies the elbow when throwing. Return-to-sport rates are good, but each player's timeline and risk of setbacks vary.

The team drew on a multi-center registry of baseball players treated between 2019 and 2023. Of 506 screened patients, 146 had at least two years of follow-up and full survey data. The authors tested whether baseline scores and surgical details forecast recovery milestones and adverse events. Sound forecasts would help players and teams plan seasons around surgery more honestly.
pmc-12709706:
Adriana Toro and co-authors defend, in twenty twenty-five, a new surgical technique for acute cholecystitis, inflamed gallbladder, in a point-by-point response to critics. A commentary in the same journal had attacked their method. Their earlier paper presented the technique as a way to avoid subtotal cholecystectomy, a partial gallbladder removal used when full removal is unsafe. The critics questioned that claim. This manuscript answers each criticism in turn.

The authors explain why the technique deserves a place in the surgeon's toolkit for very severe cases. The title itself urges care: a new technique to use carefully. The exchange shows scientific debate in print, with the original team clarifying scope and intent.
pmc-12714706:
Yu Liu, Yong Wan, Weimin Huang, and Zihao Zhan present a 2025 paper on spotting storage tanks in satellite and aerial images. Tanks at oil and gas sites matter for tracking methane leaks, a strong greenhouse gas. Older feature-based methods raise many false alarms, and standard deep learning detectors miss small tanks or confuse them with the background.

Their method draws circular boxes, matching the round top view of most tanks, and adds a large selective kernel that adjusts how wide the model looks. Round boxes keep the overlap score steady for small objects. The authors report fewer missed tanks and fewer false hits than the common detectors they compare against.
pmc-12715206:
Li wrote a solo study in twenty twenty-five on a smart plan to run food supply chains in a green way. Farms and food firms face waste, poor tracking, and shocks like storms or late trucks. Old plans adapt poorly when trade shifts fast.

His plan pairs a two-way memory net with a search rule drawn from sea rescue work. Sensors and market trends feed the net to forecast make and store needs. The search rule then picks plans that fit room, stock, and demand caps. In tests it cut waste by about a third and raised gains. It beat five rival tools on key scores.
pmc-12716506:
People with multiple sclerosis who take B-cell depleting drugs face higher risk from COVID-19, and it was unclear how well vaccines protect them. The authors followed 226 people with the disease through three doses of messenger RNA vaccine. They measured antibodies that block the virus, testing the ancestral strain and several variants from the pandemic years.

Before the third dose, people on B-cell depleting therapy had far lower blocking antibodies than healthy adults or patients on other treatments. The third dose did not lift them much. Patients whose B cells were intact matched healthy adults and gained strong boosts from the third dose. After that dose, the gap between the two patient groups widened further. No one in the study was hospitalized or died from COVID-19. The findings point to weaker vaccine protection for the depleted group.
pmc-12716706:
Nikesh Gyawali and three co-authors present a 2025 study of how vaccine talk on social media changed across a decade. The team collected English posts about vaccines from a major platform, spanning seven calm years and the three pandemic years. Public feeling toward vaccines seemed to harden in that window, but the narrative shift needed measuring.

Their data set curates 18.7 million posts from an initial 129 million, spanning 2013 to 2022. Drawing on a psychology model of how groups judge warmth and competence, they coded how speakers portray vaccines and the people tied to them. The analysis traces which story lines rose after COVID-19 arrived and which faded.
pmc-12717706:
Baranya Suprabha and colleagues examine whether stressed parents have children who cope worse, fear more, and behave worse during dental treatment. Parenting stress is known to affect children's coping strategies and behavior in non-dental settings. The cross-sectional study enrolled one hundred sixty-eight children aged eight to twelve who required dental treatment under local anaesthesia.

Parents completed a stress scale; children completed coping and fear questionnaires; behavior was rated on Frankl's scale. Contrary to expectation, no significant correlation emerged between parenting stress scores and children's use of destructive, external, or internal coping strategies. Parenting stress scores also did not differ significantly by children's clinical dental fear status. The null results caution dentists against assuming a stressed parent means a difficult child.
pmc-12717806:
Jingyi Zhao, Xinwei Wang, and Baolong Li review how uric acid levels link to Alzheimer's disease, in two thousand twenty-five. Uric acid is a waste product in the blood. Studies have found a U-shaped link, where both low and high levels go with higher risk.

At normal levels, the acid may protect the brain by fighting cell damage and swelling. It may also help clear the harmful proteins that build up in the disease. At abnormal levels, it may do the opposite and speed harm. The review also covers current drugs for the disease, and plant and standard drugs that affect the acid, to guide future work.
pmc-12719206:
Jiangfei Li and co-authors pack cannabidiol oil into porous starch to make it dissolve and absorb better, in a study from 2025. The full-spectrum oil has many noted health uses, but it mixes poorly with water and little of it reaches the body. Porous starch, full of tiny holes, can carry such oils.

The team tuned the mix and reached a packing rate near 81 percent under the best settings. The oil sat in the starch in a loose, non-crystal form and withstood more heat than free oil. The packed form dissolved about 18 times better in water and released far faster in fluids that mimic the stomach and gut. Its defense against oxidation rose by over 20 percent as well.
pmc-12719506:
Yong Wu and nine co-authors present a 2025 study on combining moxibustion with chemotherapy against stomach cancer. Moxibustion is a traditional treatment that warms acupuncture points with burning herbs. Tumors often shield themselves with an immune-suppressing environment, which blunts therapy. The team paired data analysis with mouse experiments to test whether the combined treatment reshapes that shield.

Two immune signals tied to suppression ran high in stomach tumors and linked to worse outlooks. In mice, the combination slowed tumor growth most, cutting it by nearly half. It also lowered suppressor cells and their signals in the blood while raising killer T cells inside tumors. The authors describe a two-way effect: less suppression and stronger attack at once. They present the pairing as a model for joining traditional and Western cancer care.
pmc-12721106:
Zoe Djajadikarta and co-authors report secondary results from a trial of home step training in multiple sclerosis, in work published in 2025. The main trial tested a computerised stepping game played at home. This analysis asked whether the training also improved ankle position sense and calf muscle performance.

Sixty-six people with the disease were split between six months of the game system and usual care. Tests measured how small an ankle movement people could detect, their reaction time, and calf strength and endurance before and after. No measure differed between the groups, and recovery after a sustained contraction was alike too. The authors conclude the step system did not improve position sense or muscle performance, even though it targets falls through other routes.
pmc-12722306:
Nastaran Salehi, Olle Eriksson, Johan Hellsvik, and Manuel Pereiro model magnetism at two scales at once in a 2025 study. Some magnetic behavior needs atom-level detail, while device-scale patterns need a coarser view. Their three-dimensional hybrid simulation joins both, letting engineered defects sit inside a larger magnetic body.

They built two test defects: a double slit that splits spin waves, and a small tetrahedral cluster whose properties can be tuned. The slit produced interference patterns like those of light waves, a hint for wave-based computing. The cluster bent domain walls and could destroy or reshape skyrmions, the tiny swirls eyed for future memory. Defect design thus steers magnetic behavior.
pmc-12723306:
Ryan Jonathan Sitanggang and a large team of co-authors published this commentary in 2025. It tells how HTAsiaLink, a network that links health technology assessment groups across Asia and the Pacific, wrote its first strategic plan. Such assessments weigh the value of new health tools so governments can spend wisely.

The network began in 2011 and now counts more than fifty members from twenty economies. In 2024 it ran a planning process that mixed a review of other networks' plans with wide input from members. The work produced five priorities, each with actions and signs of success. The authors share the process so other networks, above all in lower-income settings, can copy what worked. They stress that member voices shaped the plan from the start.
pmc-12729306:
Laura Menabò and co-authors let Italian students define bullying in their own words. Their 2025 study used focus groups rather than surveys, since much bullying research leans on numbers alone. They asked how youth define bullying, what roles people play, and how victims cope.

Sixteen focus groups brought together more than two hundred students. Seven domains emerged from the talks. Power imbalance was the most shared mark of bullying, while intent and repetition were less agreed. Physical and verbal forms were widely named, and relational forms less so. Students named defender as a rare role beside bullies and bystanders. Coping ideas ranged from seeking support to nonchalance. The study gives schools a picture of bullying as students actually see it.
pmc-12729806:
Aneesha VijayaKumar and a team of co-authors reviewed crop biofortification as a fix for hidden hunger in South Asia. Their review, from twenty twenty-five, deals with micronutrient malnutrition. Lack of key vitamins and minerals stunts growth, clouds thought, and opens the door to disease. India and its neighbors bear a heavy share. The team sums the scale of the lack by age group and the traits that feed it.

They then map the ways to breed or treat crops so food holds more of the lacked nutrients. Such crops can reach far homes at low cost once in the seed line. State schemes round the plan out. Readers in food policy get a green path to a deep health gap.
pmc-12730806:
Francesco Tona faulted modern cardiology culture in two thousand twenty-five. Technology in the field has never been stronger. Yet he sees the urge to ask why, and judgment, fading. Hands-on work often comes before thinking now. Whether a body fits the tool now outweighs whether treatment truly fits the patient. Sales pressure and set formulas reinforce that reflex.

Industry pressure shapes training settings as well. Rules can make tool-first habits seem normal. Research favors stand-in results over ones that matter. Checking current devices often beats asking new questions. Tona calls for bringing back the question why. Reforms in culture, schooling, and the system itself are needed. Technology should serve reasoning, not replace it. Values that put patients first must lead again.
pmc-12732806:
Dzakovich and co-authors study how spinach flavonoids change during digestion and how genes shape that change. Spinach holds a wide set of these plant compounds, which may drive its health gains. Little was known about their range, uptake, or heritability.

The team grew thirty spinach types, both hybrids and open-pollinated, under set conditions twice. They measured thirty-nine flavonoids and found the levels were shaped more by the setting than by genes. Two branches in flavonoid making may exist. How much reached the body after digestion showed stronger gene control than raw leaf content, a useful trait for breeders.
pmc-12734306:
Bassam Bin-Abbas and Mosleh Jabari compare weekly long-acting growth hormone against daily shots in children. Their systematic review and meta-analysis was published in twenty twenty-five. Daily injections work, but the burden wears families down and doses get missed.

The weekly form is chemically padded to linger in the body. The team searched three databases to late twenty twenty-five under standard review rules. Growth speed, height scores, and side effects were pooled across trials. Dose strength within the weekly arm was also compared, higher against lower. The question is practical: can one shot a week match seven without new harms? The synthesis gives prescribers a single evidence base for that choice.
pmc-12734806:
Turner leads a large team surveying harmful algae around the Isles of Scilly, in work from twenty twenty-five. The islands lie off the far southwest of the United Kingdom. Wild shellfish beds there are gathered for local food, but algae toxins had never been checked.

The team tested seawater and shellfish with field microscopes, lab tests, gene sequencing, and toxin kits. Local citizen scientists helped with sampling across the isolated islands. The survey design had to adapt during the national COVID period. Results give the first clear picture of which harmful species and toxins occur there. That baseline helps protect people who harvest and eat local shellfish.
pmc-12736006:
Dariusz Dziki and co-authors tested pasta made with flour from unroasted coffee beans in a 2025 food study. They added the green coffee flour at levels from two to eight percent of the mix. Two drying methods were compared: warm air drying and a microwave method under low pressure.

Both the added flour and the drying choice changed the pasta's texture, chemistry, and health-linked compounds. The microwave method cracked the pasta and left an uneven inner structure even at the lowest addition, while air drying showed no visible change. Cooking time also shifted between methods. Food makers get guidance on how much novelty the pasta can take before quality suffers.
pmc-12736206:
Milan Senćanski, writing alone in 2025, screens drug candidates for disordered proteins. Such proteins, like the Alzheimer's-linked tau, lack a fixed shape for drugs to grip. Standard discovery struggles with them. Senćanski applies a spectrum-based computing method that reads molecules by their electron interaction patterns.

Marker patterns came from known tau ligands and from tau sequences shared across mammals. He screened an approved-drug library and a natural product trove. The screen surfaced drugs already tied to tau or Alzheimer's paths. It also flagged Bryostatin-14, a natural product that tunes enzymes acting on tau. The method offers a cheap first pass to pair with other discovery tools.
pmc-12736306:
Mariateresa Giglio and colleagues followed back-pain patients given a botanical supplement alongside their usual care. Chronic low back pain with nerve involvement resists standard drugs and tolerates them poorly. Extracts of Acmella oleracea and Boswellia serrata have anti-inflammatory and pain-relieving properties. The prospective, multicentre, real-world study enrolled 103 such patients across Italian centers. The standardized extract was added to ongoing therapy for eight weeks.

Neuropathic pain questionnaires tracked burning, tingling, and related symptoms. General pain intensity, disability, and quality of life were also scored. Painkiller use and side effects were monitored for safety. Real-world cohorts cannot prove cause like trials can, but they show how a supplement performs in ordinary practice. The twenty twenty-five study explores a gentler adjunct for a stubborn pain population.
pmc-12736606:
David Castro and co-authors tune the charge balance in films made from chitosan and a modified cassava starch, in work from twenty twenty-five. Such plant based films could shield food with less plastic waste. Plain mixes are weak and soak up water, which limits use.

Pairing the two oppositely charged polymers forms a tighter complex with smoother structure. Films were cast at a mild acidity and checked by microscopy, spectra, heat tests, and stretch tests. The complex films proved two to four times stronger than plain mixes and stretched a bit farther. They also dissolved far less in water, gut like fluid, and salt buffer. The best mix sat near a charge ratio of one.
pmc-12736806:
Guan and co-authors tailor steering feel to each driver's style. Standard steering cannot adapt to split driver tastes. Their system first reads the driver's style from motion data. A closed loop then steers the wheel feel to a target. Tests ran on a driving simulator across conditions.

The method held up across the range of trials run. Drivers reported a comfy and pleasing wheel feel. The loop kept the target feel steady as conditions changed. The authors say style-aware steering lifts the driving experience. Carmakers could use such tuning as tastes shift from volume to quality.
pmc-12736906:
Shuvo and co-authors published a 2025 study of a gut bacterium, Flavonifractor plautii, as a candidate next-generation probiotic. Standard probiotics rely on a small set of well-worn strains, so new candidates are in demand. The team isolated the strain from human feces, read its full genome, and named it PMC93. They then dosed a lab system that mimics the human gut ecosystem, daily for one week.

The strain did not disturb the overall mix of gut microbes, a good safety sign. It raised the ratio of one large bacterial group to another, a score the team tracks, beyond what standard probiotics achieved. Helpful groups that make short-chain fatty acids grew, while harmful groups shrank. The strain also passed safety tests in animals. The authors present it as a promising candidate for gut health products.
pmc-12737206:
Guillem Monrós-Andreu and co-authors assess probes for bubbly flows in a 2025 paper. Four-sensor probes measure local traits of gas-liquid flows, but their accuracy depends on probe shape and on how bubbles strike them. Classic analyses assume round bubbles and straight paths.

Their Monte Carlo framework drops those assumptions. Bubbles can be ellipsoids arriving at varied angles, and many probe shapes are tested. From synthetic signals they recover area, speeds, and chord lengths in one scheme. They distill compact correction laws and design maps for other probes. Safe ranges for probe spacing and size are given.
pmc-12738606:
Liuyun Cai and four co-authors test whether ultrasound scans can help predict survival in cervical cancer. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Doctors know a lot about what drives this cancer, but the value of scan findings for outlook was still unclear.

The team drew records for four hundred twenty-eight patients from a hospital in Chongqing, China, covering twenty nineteen to twenty twenty-four. Most records trained the model, and the rest checked it. Older age and late stage raised the risk of early death. So did having no surgery, rich blood flow on the scan, and spread into nearby tissue. The authors built these factors into a chart that estimates survival at one, two, and three years.
pmc-12742106:
Yadi Li and co-authors set out a plan to compare brain stimulation and acupuncture for depression across all trials at once, in a 2025 protocol paper. Depression burdens more than 300 million people, and standard antidepressants help many but leave others with weak relief or heavy side effects. Gentle electric or magnetic stimulation of the scalp and needle therapy both promise drug-free help. Direct head-to-head trials, though, are rare, and protocols vary widely.

The team will search fourteen databases for trials of these treatments and merge the results in a network meta-analysis. That method compares treatments that never met in one trial by chaining shared comparisons. The outcomes are benefit and acceptability: how much symptoms ease, and how often patients quit. The paper argues the ranking will guide choices only as far as the underlying evidence is firm.
pmc-12742306:
Gao, Li, Hu, Hu, and Su study a placental enzyme in colorectal cancer spread, in work from twenty twenty-five. Colorectal cancer is prevalent worldwide, and metastasis drives its high mortality. A process called epithelial mesenchymal transition lets cancer cells detach and spread.

The enzyme ALPP was compared between metastatic and non metastatic tumor samples from a cancer genome atlas. Cell experiments then tested its role. ALPP induced the transition by activating the Wnt beta catenin signaling pathway, a known growth route. A driver of spread that can be measured in tumors may serve as both a risk marker and a drug target.
pmc-12743406:
Çınar, Demir, and Güven compared 3D-printed dental models with traditional stone models in twenty twenty-five. Accurate models matter for implant work, and printers now make them from resins of differing thickness, or viscosity. The question was whether resin choice shifts the printed positions of implant analogs.

From a reference model with eight implants, the team made stone models and printed models in low- and high-viscosity resin, eight of each. High-resolution scans fed metrology software measuring overall trueness and the three-dimensional and angular deviations of analogs. Printed models beat stone on overall trueness, ranked low-viscosity first. For analog positions, low-viscosity prints matched stone, while high-viscosity prints deviated significantly most often. Abutment-level scan bodies proved more accurate than implant-level ones in all groups. Resin viscosity, they conclude, affects positional accuracy.
pmc-12747106:
Ruemu Birhiray and three co-authors report a striking pancreatic cancer case in a 2025 paper. Pancreatic cancer kills about fifty thousand Americans a year and rarely allows long survival. A small subgroup carries inherited DNA repair defects that open a drug door.

The patient, a seventy-two-year-old woman, carried inherited mutations in two repair genes. Those defects leave tumors unable to fix certain DNA damage. After strong chemotherapy she reached complete remission. A maintenance pill that blocks DNA repair in cancer cells has kept her in remission for over forty months. That drug is approved for a related mutation group, not hers. The case argues for widening access to repair-targeted therapy in pancreatic cancer.
pmc-12748306:
Wai Miu Emma Liu and co-authors review whether surgical robot skills learned on one machine carry to another. Their review appeared in 2025. With several platforms now approved, training might not need to restart per machine. The team searched five databases to January 2025 and kept five studies that trained people on simulators across at least two platforms, scoring them with objective metrics or rating scales.

Beginners and experts performed consistently across machines, including the leading Da Vinci family and two newer rivals. Mid-level trainees dipped when switching. Prior robot experience, more than machine choice, predicted baseline skill and progress. The authors conclude core robotic skills do transfer, which supports shared training curricula, though evidence for early trainees stays thin.
pmc-12749406:
Shuang Han and colleagues read the full genome of a rare Tibetan medicine plant to help keep it alive, in this study from twenty twenty-five. Swertia przewalskii is one source of the Tibetan remedy called Zangyinchen. In Qinghai province it sits on the first list of plants with extremely small populations, a formal danger flag.

Using three sequencing methods together, the team built a chromosome-level genome of about two billion letters, anchored to twelve chromosomes. They catalogued some thirty-five thousand protein-coding genes, plus thousands of small RNA genes. Nearly nine in ten genes could be matched to known functions in public databases. The authors offer the genome as a base for conservation biology. It can guide breeding, reveal how the plant copes with its harsh home, and help managers judge which wild patches matter most for survival.
pmc-12749606:
Fatty liver disease turns dangerous when scarring joins the fat, and catching that turn without a biopsy is a standing goal. Fei Xia and co-authors trained a deep learning model on rats with diet-induced liver disease. Three versions competed: one reading ordinary ultrasound, one reading stiffness maps from elastography, and one combining both image types with clinical data.

The combined model won clearly, with the best discrimination score of the three. Decision analysis showed it would help clinicians across most risk thresholds. Calibration checks said its probabilities meant what they said. The authors present the multimodal recipe as the way forward for spotting fibrotic fatty liver early.
pmc-12749706:
Hyun-Joo Kim and co-authors present a 2025 food science study on zapping wheat with reactive air plasma to squeeze out more, and better, oil. Plasma treatment is a cold, chemical-free way to roughen plant surfaces. The team tested whether it could raise lipid yield and the anti-aging activity of wheat lipids for cosmetics.

Ten minutes of plasma gave the best extraction, lifting yield from about 1.8 to about 3.0 percent. The treated oil also blocked two skin-aging enzymes far more strongly and moisturized better at the tested dose. Two prized fatty acids rose five-fold and eight-fold. Microscopy showed the grain surface disrupted and smoothed, easing the oil's escape. The authors propose plasma-treated wheat lipids as cosmetic ingredients, pending animal and scale-up tests.
pmc-12750006:
Hui Zhang and co-authors compare the cost-effectiveness of two radiation schedules for advanced lung cancer that cannot be operated on. Their 2025 study weighs a moderately shortened schedule against the conventional longer one, both given with chemotherapy. The shorter schedule has shown better local control and survival hints in earlier studies, without clearly worse side effects.

The team built a three-stage model that follows patients over five years. It counts life years, quality-adjusted life years, and total costs for each schedule. Prior trials supplied the clinical inputs on control and toxicity. Economic value for this exact use had been largely unstudied, despite wide interest in shorter treatment. A clear cost picture helps hospitals and payers decide whether fewer, larger doses are worth adopting as standard care.
pmc-12750706:
Audrey Faveyrial and eleven colleagues published a 2025 protocol and study report on telemonitoring during injectable anticancer treatment in France. Before each treatment cycle, staff must check blood tests and call patients to confirm they are fit for therapy. Structured call programs at two French cancer centers already improved prescription accuracy and cut waiting times.

The OPTIMACURE study, a multicenter randomized prospective trial, tests whether adding the Cureety Techcare telemonitoring platform to usual care improves matters further. Patients report symptoms and results remotely between visits, so problems surface before the treatment day. The study weighs clinical benefit, safety, and workflow against standard follow-up. Its results will inform whether telemonitoring should become routine in chemotherapy services.
pmc-12751606:
Alisson Silva and co-authors upgraded a protein prediction tool in a 2025 paper. Proteins work in pairs and teams inside cells, and mapping those links helps explain life and design drugs. Lab mapping is slow and costly, so computer forecasts fill the gap. Their tool, GenPPi, builds such maps from bacterial genomes but leaned too much on plain sequence likeness.

The new form, GenPPi 1.5, adds a forest learning model trained on sixty traits drawn from amino acid profiles. A fresh sampling step keeps the shape of the link web intact while it trains. The gains aim for maps that catch more true links without warping the web's form.
pmc-12751806:
Yuting Li and co-authors uncover, in a 2025 study, a self-protection program inside the degenerating retina, and how to amplify it. Retinitis pigmentosa kills the eye's light sensors over time, and inflammation lit by the retina's own immune cells hurries the loss. Estrogen's role had looked contradictory. The team names its alpha receptor, Esr1, as a central brake on that inflammation, rising as degeneration proceeds.

In two mouse models, plain estrogen helped one and harmed the other, but a drug that switches on Esr1 alone protected both, saving light sensors and vision responses. The mechanism runs through the microglia: receptor activation cuts their output of a toxic signal and breaks a self-feeding recruitment loop. Blocking that signal's main receiver protected even better than broad blockers. The authors frame Esr1 activation as turning up a defense the retina already owns.
pmc-12752706:
Milena Hesse, Gregor Linden, and Holger Frey studied how heat and solvent shape a common plastic blend in a 2025 paper. The blend joins two oxide chains and is used widely in labs and in industry. Though it has been made for decades, how heat and the liquid it forms in sway the chain mix was not well mapped.

The team made the blend in three solvents and at heats from 25 to 60 degrees Celsius. They tracked how fast each part joins the chain, then checked the heat traits and dissolving traits of each batch. Their map links the pot settings to the traits of the end product. Makers can use it to tune the blend for a set use.
pmc-12753006:
Auden Balouch and co-authors shine multiphoton light into rat skull defects to count how many implanted stem cells survive, and where they go, in a 2024 study. Stem cell therapy for bone repair has an embarrassing secret: under five percent of injected cells remain at the site within days. The team instead delivered mesenchymal stem cells inside granular gel scaffolds, the cells tagged with fluorescent dots, into skull defects in rats.

At three and seven days, microscopy mapped the tagged cells through the scaffold at micron detail, while also counting invading host cells and identifying macrophage types. About three quarters of a million cells went in per defect. The imaging method itself is a contribution: a way to audit cell therapy honestly, quantifying survival and spread instead of assuming the dose delivered is the dose that stayed.
pmc-12753106:
Marina Medel-Plaza and co-authors present a 2025 study on a steel surface designed to resist bacterial films. Infections around bone implants are a major problem in orthopedic surgery. The team tested a treated stainless steel, anodized to change its surface, against the plain steel used as a reference.

Six bacterial species common in implant infections were grown on both surfaces. Sticking was checked after ninety minutes with a microscope, and films were grown for one to two days in a fluid like joint fluid. The treated steel cut bacterial sticking and surface coverage for every species. Film growth also fell sharply on the treated surface. Images confirmed fewer bacteria and less of the slime matrix they build.
pmc-12753406:
Wanyu Shu, Liang Chen, Jiadong Qiu, and Sung Min Kim pool the evidence on aerobic exercise for older adults with mild cognitive impairment in a 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis. Exercise is a drug-free candidate for protecting the aging brain, and trials have measured its effect on thinking skills many times. Sleep quality and overall quality of life, equally important to patients, are usually reported piecemeal.

Combining the trials statistically gives a clearer verdict on all three outcomes at once. A firm evidence base helps clinicians prescribe exercise with the same confidence they bring to medication for early cognitive decline.
pmc-12753706:
Long Qinhong and colleagues separate gravity field sources to characterise deep and shallow tectonics at the northwestern margin of the Sichuan-Yunnan block in China. Their 2025 study addresses a region with intense seismic activity.

The team refined a gravity model using measured data and a global crust model as control. Wavelet analysis separated field sources at different scales, and power spectrum analysis estimated source depths for each level. The regional gravity anomaly ran low in the north and high in the south. Several named major faults were all identified as deep, large faults at tens of kilometres depth. Results offer physical insight into crustal structure.
pmc-12758106:
Jessica Abrams and a large team of co-authors report a 2025 study of teaching tools used inside a heart screening program in Brazil. Rheumatic heart disease can be prevented, yet it still kills young people early in poorer countries. Teaching is a key way to cut that burden, above all where reading skills are low.

The team built four flipcharts with simple text and pictures over three years. The charts were taught during screening visits in high-burden areas over three years of field work. The study checks whether patients, families, school children, and community members found the charts welcome and clear. It also measures how much knowledge people gained from the lessons. The results can help other programs teach heart health in plain, visual ways.
pmc-12758806:
Jorge Escudero and three colleagues published an insect study in two thousand twenty-five on what keeps young insects young. In flies, a protein called Chinmo holds larvae in their young state. The team studied the same protein in the German cockroach, which grows through nymph stages instead.

They tracked the chinmo gene across the cockroach's nymph stages and found it stayed active until the final stage, then dropped. Silencing the gene made nymphs change into adults two moults early. A second protein, Abrupt, acted in the opposite direction on partner genes. Together the results show both proteins help hold the young state in two very different kinds of insects. The findings inform how complete metamorphosis may have evolved.
pmc-12765706:
Lichun Han and ten co-authors hunt for gene marks that can tell who will gain from TNF blocker drugs in bowel disease. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. New work ties a cell mark called lactylation and germ-eater cell states to this ill. Whether those genes flag drug gain was still unclear.

Gene web and learning tools sifted past patient data for marks split by gain or no gain. Four genes split the groups before care, and a model built on them scored well in train and check sets. Five more genes split groups weeks in. Mouse gut tests backed the marks, and extra lactate boosted drug gain in mice. The team calls the marks ripe for more checks.
pmc-12775706:
Kosuke Hashimoto and co-authors test a scan measure as a warning sign for patients on a targeted lung cancer drug in a 2025 study. The drug, osimertinib, treats non-small cell lung cancer carrying a sensitive mutation in a growth gene. PET scans show how much sugar the tumor burns, and one measure, the total volume of active tumor, may reflect disease burden better than peak uptake alone.

Sixty-eight patients had scans before starting the drug. Spread to bone and liver tracked with high volume values. Response rates and side effects did not differ by scan uptake level. In adjusted analysis, the volume measure stood out as a predictor of how long patients lived without the cancer growing. The authors call it a significant marker for this treatment.
pmc-12777806:
Sofia Aragones, Ana Maria Jimenez-Garcia, and Natalia Arias pool studies on sex splits in trauma signs among refugees. Their review appeared in twenty twenty-five. War and hunt force vast folks to flee, with hard stress at each leg. The team searched four bases to late twenty twenty-four for work on trauma, worry, and low mood by sex.

Twenty-five studies fit, with most in the pooled counts. Women showed high odds and rates of trauma signs, plus more worry and low mood. Harm kinds split by sex too, with sex force high for women and kidnap high for men. Signs ran long for both sexes. The team urges sex-fit help and rules.
pmc-12785406:
Chen Wu and Lixiong Yang study how sharing outpatient costs with rural families affects children's health and household budgets in China, in a 2025 paper. Rural children face thin medical resources and insurance designs not built for them. Cost-sharing rules decide whether parents seek clinic care early or wait. Using a 2018 national household income survey, the authors matched comparable families to isolate the policy's association.

Children under the policy showed better health scores and a higher chance of reimbursement. The links seemed to run through more outpatient visits, healthier mothers, and greater spending on school food and lodging. Unlike adults, children showed no swapping of clinic visits for hospital stays, which fits care parents dare not postpone. The authors read the policy as a lever that nudges rural families toward timely care.
pmc-12785606:
Pasquale Padalino and co-authors report a fatal case of West Nile virus infection in a 2025 medical paper. The patient was a woman of forty-five with two long-term health problems. One problem left her short of a hormone from glands in the neck. The other, Sjögren's syndrome, is an immune disorder. Her illness grew into severe swelling of the brain and spinal cord.

Doctors traced damage in the thalamus, the cerebellum, and motor pathways of the cord. Stains of tissue samples showed immune cells along those motor routes, which supports spread along nerve links. Lung problems followed, and the patient died. The authors ask how her two conditions may have helped the virus invade the nervous system.
pmc-12787806:
Asiye Yavşan and Recep Türken present a 2025 lab study on how strongly dental crown materials stick to titanium implant posts, depending on how they are made and prepared. One hundred twenty samples of four computer-aided materials, half milled and half 3D printed, were bonded to titanium disks with resin cement. Three surface preparations were compared: primer alone, acid etching plus primer, and sandblasting plus primer.

Both material and preparation mattered greatly, and they interacted. Printed materials bonded more strongly than milled ones. Sandblasting with primer topped the table for the best material, while primer alone on another material gave the weakest bond. Microscope images confirmed rougher surfaces after sandblasting, and failures there tore through material rather than peeling cleanly. The authors advise matching the surface protocol to each material in implant dentistry.
pmc-12795806:
Aguida Mohammed Echarif and co-authors build, in twenty twenty-five, a resource-light machine learning framework for real-time load monitoring in solar-powered aviation. Non-intrusive load monitoring infers which devices draw power from one aggregate signal. Aircraft impose strict limits on weight, latency, and compute. The team evaluated six learning models on high-rate power data, sampled two hundred thousand times per second. The data captured transients and steady states across all flight phases. Smoothing and downsampling cut noise while keeping key features.

A nearest neighbor model gave the best balance of accuracy and cost, with a score near zero point nine four and a run time of a fifth of a second. A hybrid neural model had the lowest error but took over four minutes, suiting offline analysis.
pmc-12801706:
Alessandro Costa, Sharanjeet Sidhu, and Thomas Hardy present a 2025 case report on a rare bleeding emergency during eye anesthesia. Bleeding behind the eyeball can crush the eye's blood supply and blind it if pressure is not relieved fast. It usually follows trauma or surgery, and only rarely an anesthetic injection. Their patient was a seventy-five-year-old man having a routine sub-Tenon's block, an injection around the eye, before a minor eye procedure.

He had no known bleeding risk, yet bleeding began at once. He felt severe pain, his lids swelled tight, his eye stopped moving, and pressure inside the eye spiked. An emergency cut at the eye's corner released the pressure and saved his sight. The authors stress that teams must watch for this rare event even in low-risk patients. Speed, they note, is what preserves vision.
pmc-12804806:
Hui Xue and a large consortium team report a genome-wide study of brainstem structures, published in 2025. The brainstem contains nuclei and tracts serving vital functions, but earlier genetic work drew mainly on European participants.

The team ran cross-ancestry meta-analyses in more than one hundred thousand individuals for brainstem volume, and in a smaller group for eight substructure volumes. They report hundreds of locus-trait associations, most of them new, and prioritize many genes linked to these traits. Some effects differed between ancestries, while many were similar. Results show shared and distinct genetic patterns for the midbrain, pons, and medulla.
pmc-12815906:
Chavarin Amarase and four colleagues test a new orthopedic plate that reports bone healing through vibration, in a study published in two thousand twenty-five. Judging whether a fracture has united usually means imaging and guesswork. Their plate design listens to the bone's natural frequency instead.

The physics is simple: a fractured bone strains more under load, raising frequency, while a healed bone strains less. Eight human cadaveric tibias were fitted with the plate. Fracture gaps and united states were tested under loads up to four hundred newtons. Frequency stayed flat across loads in the healed condition but behaved differently with a fracture gap. The authors argue frequency monitoring could one day track healing continuously.
pmc-12816106:
Stienstra and coauthors adapt network mapping from mass spectra to NMR spectra. NMR is a top tool to solve chemical structures. Auto workflows for NMR lag far behind mass methods, though. The team ports key network ideas to a two-axis NMR test.

That test maps carbon and hydrogen signals in one grid. A tuned distance score matches peaks across spectra. Library lookup with that score found most true kin hits. Bigger libraries did not lift that hit rate much. Full networking then links spectra into kin groups. Group links spread name tags across unknown compounds.
pmc-12817806:
Gut microbes live in neighborhoods, and who sits next to whom shapes what the community does. Gurdip Uppal and co-authors present MCSPACE, a probabilistic AI tool that reads microbe co-location data and infers those neighborhoods over time. New lab methods can now sample such location data at huge scale, but the data are noisy and tangled.

To test the tool, the team built the largest data set of its kind: mouse guts tracked through diet changes over 76 days. MCSPACE also ran on two human data sets and beat existing methods in benchmarks. It found microbial groups that persist for months in the human gut, and groups that reshuffle when diet changes in mice. The authors release the software openly. They argue place, not just presence, is a missing layer in microbiome science.
pmc-12820506:
Ha Ngo and co-authors examine how often family doctors prescribe anti-vertigo drugs, and for how long, in this 2025 study. Evidence that these drugs help dizziness is thin. One of them, betahistine, is still among the most prescribed off-label drugs. Doctors in primary care likely write much of that volume. The team mined records from hundreds of Dutch practices. More than a million patients' data covered the years 2018 to 2021.

They counted new and long-term prescriptions for patients with balance symptoms. Traits linked to long-term use were also sought. Long courses are the worry when benefit is unproven. The study is records-based, with identities removed. Its findings can feed prescribing guidance and review campaigns. Dizzy patients are common in primary care, so even small rates mean many people.
pmc-12822006:
Sherif Eid and co-authors build a sensor that tracks copper ions in water as they change, moment by moment. Their paper appeared in 2025. Copper ions are toxic and widely used in industry, yet standard tests are slow and cannot follow fast changes. The sensor is a printed electrode coated with a thin film that responds to copper alone. A layer of tiny plastic grains carries the signal.

The sensor answered within ten seconds and worked across a wide range of copper levels. The team used it to watch copper grains form in a flask, step by step. From the readings they worked out the energy terms of that process. The sensor also suited checks of water samples from the field. Fast, cheap copper checks could help both factories and water safety work.
pmc-12824206:
Lv Zhang, Kai Xu, and Heng Fan study a puzzle in quantum physics in this twenty twenty-five paper. Some disordered materials can hold energy in place instead of letting it spread, a state called many-body localization. Rare hot spots can break that state and spread heat to nearby regions, like an avalanche.

The authors model a chain of linked particles that keeps a basic symmetry while its parts interact. They find an in-between phase where energy does spread, set between two unlike frozen phases. By tracking the slowest rate at which the system heats up when linked to a large outside bath, they show how the hot-spot effect shifts the point where the frozen state fails.
pmc-12831306:
Zeynab Yousefi and co-authors test in 2025 a drug combination against liver fibrosis in rats, pairing the diabetes drug liraglutide with the antifibrotic pirfenidone. Each drug alone had shown promise, but their joint effect on cell cleanup and a key inflammatory complex was unexplored. Fifty male rats were split into five groups, including sham and bile-duct-ligated disease groups.

After twenty days, the combination cut liver injury markers more than either drug alone. Scar tissue deposition fell and tissue structure improved. Inflammatory signals dropped while a protective signal rose. Cell cleanup markers shifted favorably, and the inflammatory complex was suppressed more strongly.
pmc-12835006:
Hadiza Ado Suleiman and colleagues turn coconut shell waste into a filter for toxic metals, in this study from twenty twenty-five. Factory wastewater, such as tannery waste, often carries cadmium, lead, and other heavy metals. The team made activated carbon from the shells and treated it with potassium hydroxide to open its pores and add gripping sites.

In lab-made solutions, the carbon pulled out more than eighty percent of five metals: cadmium, lead, manganese, nickel, and copper. In real tannery wastewater its grip fell below half at first. After the team tuned the mix of contact time, dose, acidity, and warmth, removal climbed above ninety-five percent. Tests pointed to chemical bonding as the way metals stick. The carbon could also be stripped clean with acid and used again, which adds to its appeal as a cheap, local filter.
pmc-12838406:
Catrin Jones and co-authors count the hours of care that starting kidney replacement therapy demands in a 2025 study. For patients whose kidneys have failed, the switch to dialysis or a transplant is an intense stretch: frequent clinic visits, procedures, hospital stays, and dialysis sessions fill the week. Cancer research calls this burden time toxicity, and the team borrows the idea for kidney care.

Their retrospective study follows all adults who began replacement therapy in their service, by any of the three routes. They add up the time-based workload of the transition from records. They also test which patient traits go with a heavier load. Counting time as a cost in its own right can change how services schedule the handover and support the patients who carry most.
pmc-12840806:
Yiting Yang and eleven co-authors map gene activity in pig testes before and after sexual maturity. Male fertility rests on a web of gene switches that turn sperm making on. The team used a long-read sequencing method that captures full gene messages, not just fragments. They compared young boars with mature ones and found more than eleven thousand genes whose activity changed.

Thousands of message variants and long non-coding RNAs also shifted. The changed genes clustered in sperm making and in key growth pathways. A few core genes moved in step across all levels read. The paper gives breeders and biologists a deep map of how the pig testis matures.
pmc-12846306:
Junshu Zhu and eight co-authors test the lethal and sublethal effects of a new insecticide, cycloxaprid, on the green peach aphid, a global pest with high proofing to old sprays. The new drug keeps effect on proofed pests. The study came out in twenty twenty-five.

The drug killed lab and field proofed aphids more strongly than a standard rival. In fields, the rival fell short of needed control, while the new drug cleared a far higher bar. At a low dose that does not kill outright, life table work showed shorter life and fewer young in the next adult brood for both drugs, with growth rates also cut.
pmc-12846706:
Vinícius Menezes Braga and co-authors study liver bile duct cancer driven by aflatoxin mixtures in rats, in a research paper from 2025. Aflatoxins are potent mold toxins that target the liver. Their power to cause this bile duct cancer type was underexplored, though one member toxin is well studied for liver cell cancer.

Male rats got a toxin mixture dominated by the main aflatoxin, or a control, by daily feeding tube for ninety days. After twelve months, twelve tumors were analyzed by microscopy and protein staining. Tumors showed gland-like structure and high growth rates. A tumor suppressor protein piled up in most tumors, and cell cycle control was disturbed. Wnt pathway activation was rare.
pmc-12848306:
Sofija Markovic and colleagues present the first math model of how a toxin and antitoxin pair inside bacteria can create dormant persister cells that survive antibiotics. Persisters cause infections that return after treatment, and their origin has puzzled researchers for nearly a century. In the system modeled, the antitoxin is a small RNA that keeps the toxin in check, and feedback loops link the pair. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team analyzes the equations and runs simulations to map when the circuit settles in one state or flips between two.

Two steady states appear: low toxin with normal growth, and high toxin with dormancy, with random switching between them. Stress such as antibiotics or starvation can push the system into the two-state regime. The authors chart which feedback features control the switch, offering testable guidance for experiments.
pmc-12856506:
Priyanka Verma and co-authors test whether two ultrasound measures can predict trouble for babies in pregnancies that look low-risk, in a 2025 study. The measures are the amniotic fluid index, a gauge of the fluid around the baby, and the cerebroplacental ratio, which compares blood flow in the baby's brain and cord. Both are used to judge fetal well-being, but their combined power in normal-sized, full-term pregnancies was unclear.

The study followed 236 such pregnancies between 37 and 40 weeks. One group was checked with fluid alone and the other with both measures, and outcomes were compared after birth. Delivery patterns and newborn health were much the same in both groups. Curve analysis showed both measures, alone or combined, discriminated poorly for low newborn scores, intensive care admission, and surgical delivery. The authors report the limits plainly.
pmc-12859906:
He Li and co-authors set side by side ways, in statistics, to model an outcome from multi-omics data joined as one set. Their 2025 piece asks how best to shrink more than one large set of biological data into scores that can be used as a whole.

The team sets out one univariate method, like polygenic scores, and two multivariate methods. Their test runs used data sets that were linked and spread in a normal way. They also used a mix of normal data and data in fixed groups. The multivariate ways did well in most cases. They did best with a few more parts in the score, and beat the univariate way for two normal data sets. In real data on metabolomics and genes, used to model body mass index, all ways did much the same. The piece helps staff pick a way to join data sets.
pmc-12860006:
Hendrianus Hendrianus and nine co-authors pool the evidence on a fast blood-thinning drug for the sickest heart patients, in a 2025 review. Cangrelor is given by vein and blocks platelets within minutes, unlike pills that absorb slowly in a shocked body. The patients in question have cardiogenic shock or have just been resuscitated, and all undergo stenting. Evidence for this group was extremely thin. The authors searched three databases for studies comparing the drug against standard oral therapy.

Outcomes pooled include death from any cause, heart death, stent clots, heart attack, stroke, and blood flow grades. The synthesis, registered in advance, gives intensive care and cath lab teams a firmer basis for a drug choice they currently make on habit and hope.
pmc-12866506:
Keshavarz and co-authors ask whether protein fragments in dairy foods link to lower risk of muscle loss in older adults. Sarcopenia, the steady loss of muscle mass and strength, raises risks of fracture, poor mobility, and death. Some dairy peptides survive digestion and stay active in the body. The team compared 80 older adults in Shiraz, Iran who had sarcopenia with 80 who did not. Diet data came from a larger survey at local health centers.

The team estimated how much of these peptides each person ate from dairy products. They then compared intake between the two groups. Sarcopenia was judged by standard diagnostic rules. The study tests whether a common food group quietly guards aging muscle.
pmc-12870006:
Hyun Jin Oh, Chung Ho Kim, Hyun-Wook Park, and Bomi Park present a study from two thousand twenty-five on the path from a stomach infection to stomach cancer. The infection is caused by Helicobacter pylori, a common stomach bacterium. The Correa pathway describes the steps: chronic inflammation, thinning of the stomach lining, cell change, growths, and then cancer.

The team used national insurance data for about six point eight million Koreans screened in two thousand eighteen. They estimated how much clearing the infection lowers cancer risk. They also measured how much of that effect flows through the middle steps of the pathway, using causal methods built for the question.
pmc-12881406:
Junghyun Sung and eleven co-authors achieve polariton condensation in a thick tungsten disulfide structure far from the usual exciton resonance, in a two thousand twenty-five photonics paper. Bulk layered semiconductors were long written off for polariton work because their excitons are weak and indirect.

The team built bound-state-in-the-continuum cavities from fifty-nanometer WS2 and saw a large Rabi splitting near two hundred ninety-four millielectronvolts. Condensation was driven by indirect excitons feeding photons straight into the cavity modes. Even with excitons making up only about six percent of the hybrid particles, shrinking the pump spot tuned, with light, how tightly the condensate was held. The result opens polariton physics to indirect-gap solids.
pmc-12892206:

pmc-12903506:

pmc-12920706:

pmc-12932506:
Lin Zhu and a large team of co-authors test a herbal formula paired with an antibiotic in gut infection. The text is dated 2025, though the catalog lists 2026. pmc-12977306:

pmc-13087006:
Gui-Min Yin and three co-authors review duckweeds as a tool for green biotechnology in this two thousand twenty-six paper. Duckweeds are the smallest and fastest-growing flowering plants. The paper makes the case for duckweed as a clean factory for future products.
pmc-13099706:

pmc-13124606:
Qian Zhao and four co-authors report a woman whose only first sign of hidden breast cancer was a spread to a lymph node between the chest muscles, in this 2026 case report. pmc-13135506:

pmc-13135606:

pmc-13136206:

pmc-13136506:
Marzie Reisi, Ashraf Kazemi, and Nafisehsadat Nekuei dig into how man-and-wife pairs cope as one with a lack of young borne. Their 2026 work is based on talks. It hears from thirty-six folk in Iran, with ten pairs heard as pairs.

They took in life side by side with the lack, a find of ease for the heart, and a firm build of the pair's bond. pmc-13142006:
Rixt van der Veen, Marian Joëls, and Aniko Korosi published a 2026 methods essay on early-life adversity research. Hardship early in life raises later mental illness risk. pmc-13143506:

pmc-13146506:

pmc-13148706:

pmc-13157306:

pmc-13158506:

pmc-13158606:

pmc-13167006:

pmc-13171306:

pmc-13176806:

pmc-13183006:

pmc-13183106:

pmc-13184306:

pmc-13185006:

pmc-13186006:

pmc-13186906:

pmc-13189206:

pmc-13191506:

pmc-13194106:

pmc-13194306:

pmc-13194606:

pmc-13195806:

pmc-13197106:

pmc-13197706:

pmc-13198506:

pmc-13198606:

pmc-13200306:

pmc-13200806:

pmc-13202206:

pmc-13202606:

pmc-13204206:

pmc-13204306:

pmc-13206606:

pmc-13209506:

pmc-13210106:

pmc-13210906:
