pmc-13212806:
Ken Batai and colleagues study in 2026 how body fat and muscle, measured on medical scans, relate to kidney cancer features. Body composition differs across racial and ethnic groups and may shape how aggressive a tumour proves to be.

Scans from 268 patients taken before surgery supplied measures of fat under the skin, fat around organs, fat inside muscle, and muscle itself. Fat patterns varied by group, with Hispanic patients showing higher values on two measures. Fat inside muscle linked strongly to one tumour subtype, while other fat measures tied to higher grade or later stage. A low-fat, low-muscle pattern also carried higher odds of high-grade disease.
pmc-13213006:
Falconer and co-authors argue that school absence in England should be treated as a public health problem, in a paper from 2026. Lasting absence harms learning, social growth, and health at once. The authors bring in a new framework from the United States that frames absence in health terms. They ask how that frame could fit English schools and services.

The piece lays out workable steps for health services and local councils. It casts absence not as a fault of families but as a sign of unmet need. Health partners would join schools in spotting and easing the drivers of absence. Those drivers span illness, mental strain, and hardship at home. The authors say the shift in view could unlock joint action. The United States frame offers a tested start point for the change.
pmc-13213606:
Sin Yee Lim and colleagues report in 2026 a woman whose skin sarcoma seemed to explode after repeated procedures that never fully removed it. Complete removal is the cornerstone of cure for solid cancers, yet leftover tumour is common, and its response to surgical trauma is poorly charted in humans.

The seventy-year-old patient's tumour regrew rapidly after each intervention that left visible disease behind, then spread aggressively through the body. Measuring growth rates showed marked acceleration after those incomplete procedures, a pattern the authors call hyperprogression. Inflammation from tissue injury may feed leftover cancer, they suggest. The case adds human evidence to animal data and argues for caution when clearance cannot be achieved.
pmc-13214106:
Debao Yi and colleagues published a 2026 study of sulfate transporter genes in tomato. Selenium is a nutrient people need in small amounts. Plants absorb it through sulfate pathways by chemical similarity. Adding selenium to crops could improve human diets. Tomato transporter genes were poorly mapped.

The team found twelve transporter genes in the tomato genome. Most share a common structural core. Their control regions respond to plant hormones. Selenium treatment switched on different genes in roots and leaves. Stress tests showed further response patterns. These genes are candidates for breeding selenium-rich tomatoes.
pmc-13217206:
Patil, Khan, and Mahyavanshi chart infections of the brain and spinal cord in children from rural western India. Such infections remain a leading cause of death and disability for children in poorer countries. Local patterns shift with vaccine uptake, environment, and how easily families can reach care, yet rural data from this region were scarce.

The study tracks which infections appeared, how their frequency changed, and what neurological outcomes children were left with. Findings like these help hospitals plan beds, tests, and follow-up for survivors with lasting damage. They also show where prevention, above all vaccination and earlier referral, could cut the toll most.
pmc-13217906:
Alice Vanneste and co-authors present a 2026 qualitative study on patient experience data: what patients report about outcomes, experiences, and preferences. The study asks why such data still struggles to enter healthcare decision-making in Europe despite wide agreement that it should.

Thirty-eight stakeholders were interviewed, drawn from industry, academia, nonprofits, regulators, reimbursement agencies, and patient groups. Three barriers recurred: no clear Europe-wide policy framework or quality bar for such data, too few proven collection tools, and little openness about how agencies weigh the data they receive. Suggested ways forward include shared guidelines, training in patient involvement, and better methods research. Views split on who should lead, which the authors say makes continued coordination across groups vital.
pmc-13218006:
Sena Gizem Arslan and Birgul Dingirdan Gultekinler test a low-cost force plate for jump and balance checks. Force plates give sound data, but their price and size keep them out of many clinics and gyms. The team tested the Meloq EasyBase plate in seventy-eight healthy young adults. Each person stood on one leg and did a jump test, then came back a week or so later to repeat the tests.

Jump height scores were highly steady across visits, and balance scores were fair to good. The plate's balance scores also matched a simple clinic balance test. The authors see it as a handy tool for field use.
pmc-13218306:
Qi Wang and co-authors test a teaching model that blends AI, case-based learning, and a flipped classroom for reproductive medicine residents, in a 2026 randomized controlled trial. Lecture teaching often fails to build clinical decision-making during residency rotations, a problem as infertility care grows more complex. The trial ran at the First Hospital of Jilin University.

Fifty obstetrics and gynecology residents were randomized to the blended model or to traditional lectures. The blended group worked through cases with virtual patients before class on one platform, reviewed cases on another, and then debated them in class. After the course, the blended group scored higher on theory tests, on observed clinical evaluations, and on structured clinical exams. They also reported stronger motivation, better clinical thinking, and more self-guided learning than the lecture group. The authors recommend the model as an effective, transferable way to train reproductive medicine doctors.
pmc-13218606:
Louise-Helene Gagnon, Humara Edell, and Patricia E. Lee review the diagnosis and management of urinary incontinence in women in a 2026 article. Incontinence is common and undertreated, because patients stay silent: many assume leaking is normal with aging or feel embarrassed to raise it. Earlier work suggests a majority of women never seek care, and it costs Canada an estimated 2.6 billion dollars a year.

The first step is classifying the problem, because treatment follows the type. Stress incontinence leaks urine when abdominal pressure rises, as with coughing or exercise, while urge incontinence follows a need to urinate, usually with frequency and night-time trips. First-line care is conservative: behavioural therapy, pelvic floor and bladder training, noninvasive options, and attention to contributing conditions. Surgery is the second-line answer for stress incontinence, and medication for urge incontinence. Matching the plan to the type is what makes treatment work.
pmc-13219706:
Amir Hossein Alipour, Fatemeh Hoda Fallah, and Bahman Abedi Kiasari build blood tests for two widespread polyomaviruses in a 2026 study. BK and JC viruses infect most people in childhood, then persist, becoming dangerous when immunity is suppressed, as in transplant patients. Reliable antibody tests are the backbone of tracking who carries them.

The team produced the viruses' VP1 shell proteins in insect cells and used them to build ELISA assays, then ran sixty-seven serum samples. Antibodies to BK virus appeared in 77.6 percent of samples and to JC virus in 34.3 percent, with both rising with age, as expected for infections acquired. Competition experiments showed the two tests did not confuse one virus's antibodies for the other's, confirming specificity. Antigens made in the insect-cell system gave stronger signals than alternatives. The authors offer the assays for population surveys and for watching at-risk patients such as transplant recipients.
pmc-13222006:
Ni Luh Lany Christina and co-authors review how endometriosis affects ovarian reserve, in a 2026 systematic review of studies published between 2015 and 2024. Endometriosis causes chronic pelvic pain and infertility, and cysts on the ovaries can erode the egg supply. Ten studies met the quality and reporting standards the team applied.

Women with endometriosis showed lower hormone markers and fewer visible follicles than healthy comparison groups. Chronic inflammation and oxidative stress were identified as damaging routes. Surgery to remove cysts can ease symptoms and may aid fertility, yet it can also remove healthy tissue and deepen reserve loss. Early diagnosis and personalized planning are the authors' main prescriptions.
pmc-13222306:
Hidekazu Tanaka and co-authors present updated guidance in 2026 on heart ultrasound for patients on cancer therapy. Cancer drugs can damage the heart, and longer survival makes spotting that damage early ever more important. The Japanese Society of Echocardiography first issued guidance in 2020, and this focused update reflects new evidence and imaging advances.

Two measures anchor the guidance: ejection fraction, the share of blood the heart pumps out, and global longitudinal strain, a finer gauge of muscle shortening. The document sets standard protocols before, during, and after drug therapy, plus long-term checks after chest radiation. It also covers heart inflammation linked to immune checkpoint drugs and stresses measurement quality, three-dimensional imaging, and AI support.
pmc-13223606:
Yiheng Chi, Li Ke, Tanghai Cheng, and Xinrui Ma reviewed work on motor imagery for children with developmental coordination disorder in two thousand twenty-six. Children with the disorder struggle with movement skills. Motor imagery means picturing an action in the mind without moving.

The review pulls together theory, brain studies, and trials of training. Many children with the disorder also picture actions poorly, which may reflect weak inner models for planning moves. Training that pairs imagery with watching actions showed early promise for daily skills. The authors say proof is still early, and they call for larger trials, shared methods, and care plans shaped to each child.
pmc-13225306:
Severi Santavirta and four co-authors model how people watch social scenes in films in a 2026 paper. Viewers constantly sample features from raw brightness up to the emotional tone of interactions. Over a hundred participants watched full films and clips while eye trackers recorded gaze position, pupil size, and blinking. Dozens of stimulus features were extracted, from motion and faces to pleasantness ratings.

Faces and eyes drew gaze above other content, and pupils answered brightness, scene cuts, and arousal. Blinking dropped during engaging stretches. The authors conclude social vision is steered mainly by raw and mid-level features, while high-level social signals act mostly through the pupil.
pmc-13225506:
Xiang Zhang, Miaomiao Liu, Kang Liu, and Yigang He published this 2026 study mapping blood groups in Gansu Province, in northwest China. Safe transfusion depends on knowing which ABO and RhD types the donors of a region hold versus what its patients need. The rich ethnic mix of Gansu suggested a distinctive pattern worth charting.

Records covered 71,363 donors from 2014 to 2023 and 188,827 patients from 2018 to 2023. The two groups differed clearly: type O positive was scarcer among patients than donors, while A and B positive ran higher. The rarest slot, AB negative, appeared twice as often in patients as in donors. Donation volumes also trended downward over the decade. The authors draw supply lessons for planners balancing stock against demand.
pmc-13227206:
Rogério Aires and colleagues check a 2026 mouse study of whether cyclophosphamide, a drug widely used to suppress the immune system in experiments, quietly disturbs the brain. If it did, countless neuroimmune studies could be confounded. Male mice received weekly injections for three or four weeks, then underwent behaviour batteries, brain tissue checks, and gene-expression measurement.

Immune suppression clearly took hold in the body, with slower weight gain and altered white-cell counts. Behaviour, though, barely moved, showing only mild, passing changes in strength and sickness-like signs. Brain tissue showed no structural damage and no activation of star-shaped support cells. One gene, Lgals3, rose significantly in the brain, a molecular footnote in an otherwise reassuring picture of central resilience.
pmc-13227806:
Abdulelah K Alqawlaq and colleagues report a 2026 Saudi case of a teenager with an ultra-rare skeletal disorder who went from wheelchair use to walking with support after staged joint surgery. Whole-genome sequencing confirmed spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia with joint laxity type 3, caused by a fault in the EXOC6B gene. The disorder loosens joints, invites repeated dislocations, and had severely damaged both hips and knees since early childhood.

Surgeons replaced both hips first, then both knees, tailoring the plan to her anatomy. Pain fell markedly and mobility returned step by step until she could walk with assistance. The team presents the case as the first surgically managed report of this condition in Saudi Arabia, arguing rare-disease patients deserve individualised operative planning.
pmc-13229406:
Kuang Ma and colleagues present MultiVTP in 2026, a computer method for finding human proteins that viruses target. A single host protein can serve several viruses, so the task is framed as multilabel prediction. The work uses only information inside host proteins themselves.

MultiVTP samples small graphs around each query protein and combines several kinds of protein features. A graph transformer then looks for patterns shared across viruses and patterns tied to one virus. Tests against other models showed stronger accuracy, even when training data were limited. Applied across the human proteome, the method points to new candidate targets for single viruses and for several viruses at once.
pmc-13230506:
Simon Hefner and colleagues test in 2026 whether photos of fingernails and eyelids can estimate hemoglobin without a blood draw. Their HeMonitor study enrolled three hundred sixty-seven patients with blood cancers plus healthy donors for comparison. Machine learning models learned to predict lab hemoglobin values from the images alone.

The best model landed close to lab values, with spread near one unit on the reported scale. A second exploratory layer combined each estimate with patient reports of overall health and fatigue. Lower estimates generally matched worse quality of life, which fits the known burden of anemia. Agreement with clinician judgment looked encouraging in borderline ranges. Home monitoring built this way still needs testing in planned follow-up studies.
pmc-13233006:
Charles Amoatey Odonkor and colleagues published a 2026 pilot study testing whether shoe-mounted sensors can measure walking as accurately as laboratory cameras. Twenty people took part, half with knee osteoarthritis and half healthy. Each person walked at a self-chosen pace, a fast pace, and an endurance pace while sensors and a motion capture system recorded more than 5,000 strides.

Sensor estimates of walking speed matched the camera system almost exactly, and stride length and cadence also agreed closely. Everyone finished the protocol with minimal problems. Participants who reported more physical activity tended to walk faster with longer strides, though the small sample makes that pattern tentative. The authors see the sensors as a practical way to track walking outside the lab.
pmc-13233806:
Miguel Castro and colleagues published a 2026 environmental study of peatland restoration in Kalimantan, Indonesia. Drained tropical peat burns readily, and Indonesia's peat fires rank among the country's largest greenhouse gas sources. After catastrophic fires in 2015, the government and partners blocked drainage canals to rewet peatlands. The team used statistical counterfactual methods to estimate what would have burned without the rewetting between 2017 and 2022.

Effects varied by place, and canal blocks whose rewetted zones overlapped performed best at preventing fire. If every block worked at that level, rewetting could avoid up to 6.4 percent of the burnt area and deliver economic returns above one hundred percent within a decade at the best sites. The authors argue restoration pays, provided blocks are placed to overlap.
pmc-13234106:
Zhixiang Jiang and colleagues published a 2026 materials study on parking helpful bacteria on biochar, charcoal made from heated plant waste. Anchored microbes survive harsh conditions better, a boon for cleaning salty or polluted soils. The team made biochars from several feedstocks at two temperatures and measured how well each loaded the soil bacterium Bacillus subtilis.

Biochars cooked at seven hundred degrees carried far more bacteria than those made at four hundred, by roughly fourteen to sixty percent. Loading changed the char surface, adding carbon and nitrogen, enriching chemical groups, and flipping it from water-repelling to water-loving. Modeling pointed to chemical, single-layer attachment driven by charge pull, hydrogen bonds, and water-shy forces together. Bacteria settled in two stages, sticking and filling pores first, then locking in with their own glue-like coatings. Anchored bacteria also tolerated salt far better.
pmc-13235406:
Ariyawan Tantipongpiradet and colleagues tested in 2026 whether an olive-derived compound can protect rats against chronic stress. Hydroxytyrosol, produced through biotechnology, was given daily in an oral jelly before and during a period of unpredictable restraint stress. Rats of both sexes underwent tests of anxiety, mood, memory, and social behaviour. Brain tissue from the hippocampus was also sequenced cell by cell.

Stress alone produced anxiety-like behaviour, reduced pleasure response, memory problems, and social withdrawal in the animals. Treatment prevented those behavioural changes across the tests reported. Stress-related drops in dopamine and serotonin were also prevented, while a stress hormone rise was blunted. Thousands of gene changes across neurons and support cells were largely normalized by treatment. The authors identify hydroxytyrosol as a dietary candidate for building stress resilience.
pmc-13235706:
Perin and colleagues estimate what killed newborns and young children worldwide between 2000 and 2024. Their secondary analysis covers 195 countries. It uses a Bayesian statistical model to split deaths by cause, drawing on journal studies, health surveys, and World Health Organization mortality records, among many other sources.

Cause splits matter because the big killers of the first month differ from those of ages one to four. Fresh estimates show where past gains came from and where deaths still cluster. Governments and aid groups use such numbers to aim vaccines, newborn care, and nutrition money. The authors update an earlier round of estimates with data through the pandemic years.
pmc-13235906:
Reginato and Brandl build a new tool for naming the small, hidden fishes of coral reefs. Reefs hold more than a third of all marine species, yet many reef fishes are tiny, shy, and easy to confuse. Specialists who can tell them apart are few, so much reef life goes unrecorded in surveys.

Their tool joins deep learning with the branching structure of biological classification and very detailed images. Teaching the model the family tree, not just the final name, helps it sort look-alike species. Better identification from photos could widen reef monitoring sharply, letting cameras and computers do work that now waits on a handful of experts.
pmc-13236106:
Taro Higuchi, Hiro Nakao, and Yoshitsugu Fukuda described in 2026 a bone infection in a four-month-old girl that looked like a paralysed leg. She had stopped extending her left leg for six days and resisted during nappy changes. Early hip imaging at a community clinic had shown nothing abnormal. She had no fever, redness, swelling, or loss of appetite on presentation.

Examination in infants localizes pain poorly, so the authors stress imaging the whole affected limb early. Prompt recognition matters because acute bone infection can settle into chronic disease and form enclosed abscesses. Such abscesses near the growth plate can disturb later bone growth, requiring long follow-up. Serious disease can hide behind quiet presentations without fever or general symptoms in this age group. A systematic workup for limb disuse in infants forms the article's central practical message.
pmc-13236506:
Javier Cifuentes-Quin and co-authors compared in 2026 side effects of two shortened radiotherapy schedules for prostate cancer in Colombia. More than two hundred men treated at one oncology centre between 2018 and 2025 entered the comparison. One schedule spread dose over moderately fewer sessions, while the other compressed treatment into very few sessions. Toxicity was graded with standard criteria for both early and later effects.

Early side effects occurred in about a quarter of the moderately compressed group, notably above the ultra-compressed group. Later side effects also appeared far more often under the moderate schedule in the records. Erectile dysfunction was the single most common late problem recorded in follow-up. Adjusted analysis confirmed lower odds of early toxicity with the ultra-compressed schedule independently. The authors argue the shorter course suits middle-income settings by improving efficiency and access without worse safety.
pmc-13237406:
Howard Sofen, Ranga Gogineni, Tushar Nishandar, and Jerry Bagel published a study in twenty twenty-six on whether body weight blunts a psoriasis drug's effect on the scalp. The drug blocks a single immune signal and is dosed the same for all. The team re-cut data from a blind trial of scalp disease over a full year.

Patients were split by whether their body mass index sat at or above the obesity line. Scores tracked clear skin on the scalp, itch relief, and how much scalp was clear of flakes. Near half of each arm met the weight bar. The check was a side look, not the trial's main aim, so its power is thin by design. The authors frame the read as a guide for doctors whose patients ask if weight will dull their drug.
pmc-13238106:
Zhao and co-authors interview families of disabled older adults living at home in Zhengzhou, China. Families are the main setting for guarding these elders' health. Both elders and caregivers face body, mind, and social strain as disability reshapes daily life.

The study used existence-relatedness-growth theory to frame family health needs. Twelve pairs, each an elder plus their main caregiver, took part in long interviews. Pairs were found by purposive and snowball sampling from December 2024 to February 2025. Themes were sorted with a guided analysis. Findings aim to ground family support programs in real stated needs.
pmc-13238806:
Maryam Zamani, Maryam Farhadian, Nasrin Piran, and Shiva Borzouei build a model that predicts several diabetes complications at once. Their 2026 paper notes that type 2 diabetes damages small and large vessels together, yet older models predict one outcome at a time. Joint prediction matches how the disease actually harms patients.

The team studied just under a thousand patients in retrospect. They grouped complications into small-vessel types, such as eye, kidney, and nerve damage, and large-vessel types, such as heart and brain events. Their stacked model layers three learning methods under a final combiner, in two multi-label arrangements. One arrangement clearly led on standard scores. An explanation method then surfaced the strongest risk factors, keeping the model readable for clinicians.
pmc-13239106:
Sodergren and colleagues test whether an adult quality-of-life form works for teens with cancer, in a study from twenty twenty-six. The form is the EORTC QLQ-C30, the most used cancer-specific measure in adult trials. Teens, with distinct growth needs, are often left out of trials. Lowering trial entry ages makes the question urgent.

Two hundred teens aged twelve to seventeen completed the adult form alongside a teen one. They also fed back on fit, ease, and the format they liked best, paper or screen. Filling it in took about twelve minutes on average. The teens found it acceptable and easy to finish. Score testing confirmed the subscale structure, with acceptable-to-good match. The study spans many tongues and cultures. Its verdict supports using the adult form with teenage patients.
pmc-13239306:
Samuel Gonçalves Encarnação and colleagues pooled twenty-three observational studies in 2026 on device-measured activity, sitting time, and frailty in older adults. Wearable accelerometers supplied the movement data, avoiding the rosy bias of self-report. Fourteen studies fed the activity meta-analysis and eleven the sedentary-time one.

Spontaneous physical activity correlated moderately and inversely with frailty: more movement, less frailty. Sedentary time correlated positively, with most analyzed studies agreeing. Both pools varied a lot between studies, and removing single studies shifted the numbers noticeably, so the authors keep the claims at association level. Even so, the direction is consistent enough to back programs that get older adults moving and sitting less. Frailty prevention, they argue, is partly a daily-steps problem.
pmc-13239706: A 2026 correction notice in the journal Food Science and Nutrition amends the funding statement of a study by Noreen and co-authors on bioactive compounds from jujube fruit. The notice is a correction only, with no new results or changed conclusions. It adds two omitted funding sources, a Hallym University research fund award from 2023 and a Korean National Research Foundation programme grant, and the authors apologise for the omission.
pmc-13240406:
Abdisalam Ahmed Sandeyl and colleagues describe lungs wrecked by earlier tuberculosis in a 2026 Ugandan case report. A 60-year-old man with six years of poorly completed tuberculosis treatment arrived with three weeks of worsening cough, foul yellow sputum sometimes streaked with blood, breathlessness, and chest pain.

Scans showed extensive damage, with widened distorted airways, large air blisters, and scarring worst in the left lung. Sputum grew two bacteria, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Streptococcus pneumoniae, confirming an infective flare on top of the structural damage. Intravenous antibiotics, later matched to the culture results, plus supportive care eased his symptoms. The case underlines the cost of incomplete tuberculosis treatment.
pmc-13240906:
Nguyen at Vietnam's National Economics University weighed land use efficiency and urban form across three Indochina capitals. Hanoi, Vientiane, and Phnom Penh were tracked from 2017 to 2024. The assessment paired the UN land-consumption indicator with spatial clustering statistics. A shape index gauged how compact each capital's footprint stayed.

Land expansion outran population growth in all three cities. Phnom Penh showed the most compact, strongly grouped growth despite the fastest land uptake. Hanoi sprawled with weaker clustering, while Vientiane expanded in loose, fragmented patches. Nguyen urges tighter spatial planning before these trajectories harden.
pmc-13241206:
Singh and colleagues at Royal Darwin Hospital charted chronic melioidosis across Australia's Northern Territory over thirty-four years. Cases with symptoms lasting two months or more came to one hundred twenty-six. That was under a tenth of all melioidosis recorded since 1989. Chronic cases were set head-to-head with acute presentations.

Pneumonia and skin infections dominated, and scans were often first read as cancer or tuberculosis. Chronic patients carried fewer classic risk factors like diabetes. Their blood tests turned positive far less often, and death was much rarer. Antibody tests, notably, flagged eighty-seven percent of chronic cases at diagnosis.
pmc-13241506:
Galectins, a family of proteins that bind sugar chains on other molecules, take center stage in a review by Popatia and colleagues at the University of Ottawa. The authors map how these proteins steer signaling inside and outside cells. Sixteen mammalian galectins fall into three structural types, each with its own binding habits. Their influence reaches growth, blood vessel formation, and immune control.

Across diseases, the review links galectins to cancer spread, heart and vessel damage, brain degeneration, metabolic problems, and autoimmunity. Some family members push in opposite directions depending on tissue, which complicates drug design. Trials already test blockers ranging from modified carbohydrates and pectins to antibodies. New tools such as single-cell glyco-RNA sequencing and CRISPR glycoengineering may sharpen future galectin drugs.
pmc-13241606:
Phimha and colleagues at Khon Kaen University measured what a denture visit really costs elderly Thai patients and their caretakers. The team surveyed three hundred forty-six patient-caretaker pairs at three tertiary hospitals. Data came from structured questionnaires collected over six months. Costs were split into direct payments and lost income.

Each visit drained about one hundred forty-eight purchasing-power-adjusted dollars from the household. Patients carried the largest share through medical payments and their own lost earnings. Caretakers absorbed well over a third of the burden, almost entirely as forgone wages. Visits averaged more than six hours, and the authors urge policies that cut both household costs and clinic time.
pmc-13241706:
Draidi's team in Doha chased a bleeding source that hid from every camera and scan. Their patient, 69, kept returning with black stools and severe anemia needing transfusions. His blood pressure swung wildly between spells. Standard upper and lower scope exams found nothing at all. CT vessel scans also failed to find the elusive leak.

A swallowed camera capsule hinted at far small-bowel bleeding without pinpointing it. Sepsis tangled the transfusion-dependent course. Keyhole surgery finally exposed two jejunal pouches with engorged vessels. Cutting out that bowel segment stopped the bleeding for good.
pmc-13242106:
Güner's team at Hacettepe fix a naming slip in their 2023 study of swallowing problems and frailty in Alzheimer's disease. The Methods named the thinking test the Mini-Mental State Examination. The team in fact used the test's standard form. Rights and trademark claims forced the fix. The study first appeared in BMC Geriatrics.

Every mention now reads Standardized Mini-Mental State Examination, shortened to SMMSE. The mark rests with the test's creator and its licensed seller. The authors state plainly that the data, results, and takeaways stand untouched. The journal amended the article in full.
pmc-13242206:
Hesti Witasari Jos Erry and a large team publish a 2026 systematic review of stem cell exosomes from 3D spheroid cultures for tooth pulp regeneration. Tiny vesicles released by stem cells carry healing signals without using live cells. Growing the parent cells as spheres may strengthen those signals compared with flat dish culture.

Ten early lab studies met the review standards. Vesicles from sphere cultures encouraged blood vessel growth, tooth-forming cell development, and calmer immune responses. Several studies reported stronger repair markers than vesicles from flat cultures. Few studies, however, tested tooth pulp outcomes directly; others offered indirect evidence from different tissues. The authors call the approach promising but preliminary, and they ask for standardized studies before clinical use.
pmc-13242506:
Mahmoud Abdel-Nasser and colleagues studied how to protect a badly decayed old manuscript without harsh chemicals. Their paper appeared in Scientific Reports in 2026. The eleventh-century manuscript, paper pages and leather binding alike, suffered stains, acidity, weakened fibers, and missing pieces. Imaging and chemical tests documented the damage, and the team cultured the fungi living on it, finding thirteen strains, led by Aspergillus species that secrete fiber-eating enzymes.

Their proposed remedy pairs an extract from bacterial probiotics with nanoparticles made by green methods. The goal is a treatment that suppresses the manuscript's own fungi while sparing the artifact, the conservator, and the environment. Traditional synthetic fungicides can endanger all three. The study first proves how much of the decay is biological, driven by enzymes the fungi release. It then argues this gentler mix deserves a place in museum practice.
pmc-13242806:
Yanchi Wang and co-authors publish a 2026 questionnaire study of nursing students at one Chinese university, linking childhood trauma to early psychotic-like symptoms. Such prodromal symptoms can precede psychosis and cause real distress. The study tested whether depression and anxiety carry part of the trauma effect.

About a quarter of the students reported prodromal symptoms. Overall, trauma scores and distress scores both rose alongside symptom scores. Pathway analysis found significant mediation only for physical abuse and sexual abuse. For each, depression and anxiety together carried about half of the association with symptoms. The authors note the one-time design cannot prove cause. They suggest support for affected students should target mood and anxiety symptoms directly.
pmc-13242906:
Deepika Beereddy and co-authors describe a severe immune complication of cancer immunotherapy that resisted standard treatment. Their case report appeared in Cureus in 2026. A seventy-seven-year-old woman with advanced endometrial cancer developed weakness, drooping eyelids, double vision, and breathing trouble twenty-four days after one combined dose of chemotherapy and pembrolizumab. Tests showed inflammation of heart muscle, skeletal muscle, and the nerve-muscle junction, plus an overactive thyroid.

This overlap syndrome can be fatal, and her case proved stubborn. Pulse steroids and plasma exchange helped too little, so rituximab was added, and continuing heart inflammation later forced two further immune drugs, abatacept and ruxolitinib. Under the escalated regimen her symptoms and blood markers finally improved, and she went home on a tapering plan. The authors urge doctors who spot one part of the triad to screen for the others.
pmc-13243106:
Ying Lei and colleagues wrote this 2026 review on Crohn's disease, a long-term gut illness that often leads to disability. Watching the disease closely matters, but common checks can be invasive, slow to show change, or unable to see through the full bowel wall.

The review centres on blood fats and on creeping fat, a layer of belly fat that wraps around the inflamed bowel in this disease. During active illness, patients show a typical pattern of disturbed blood fats tied to body-wide inflammation. Creeping fat itself feeds inflammation and scarring, and scans can use it to predict surgery risk and return of disease after an operation.
pmc-13243406:
Søren Esben Rytter Heilskov and colleagues revisit an old idea about acts that seem to make no sense in a 2026 essay on criminal insanity. Courts lean on delusions, stated in words, when judging whether psychosis drove a crime. Yet some disturbed acts are never explained by the person who did them.

The essay returns to psychiatrist Klaus Conrad and his notion of senseless actions in early schizophrenia. A historical case from Karl Wilmanns shows how such acts can mark the slide into open psychosis. The authors argue that these acts reflect a broad break in how a person finds meaning in the world. Judging them fairly needs the person's life story as context, they conclude.
pmc-13244506:
Muhammed Hassan Nasr and co-authors ran a placebo-controlled trial of high-dose vitamin D in men with type 2 diabetes. Their study appeared in the Journal of Pharmaceutical Policy and Practice in 2026. Sixty men at Taibah University in Saudi Arabia took either fifty thousand units of vitamin D3 weekly or a dummy pill for twenty-four weeks. Blood tests tracked vitamin levels, insulin resistance, fasting sugar, and glucose control.

The supplement did its first job well: vitamin D levels climbed in the treated group and deficiency was corrected, while the placebo group barely moved. But the hoped-for metabolic payoff never came. Insulin resistance, fasting glucose, and glycated hemoglobin all failed to improve beyond placebo. Weight and lipids likewise showed no shift. The authors conclude vitamin D should be prescribed to fix deficiency, not marketed as a glucose treatment. Their negative result matters because hopes were high.
pmc-13246506:
Nguyen and colleagues measured what marine plastic costs small-scale fishers in Viet Nam, in this 2026 Communications Earth and Environment study. Working in the Mekong and Red River deltas, the team interviewed nearly two hundred nearshore fishers, ran follow-up verification interviews, and audited the debris hauled up in hundreds of fishing nets.

Plastic cost each vessel roughly thirty-four hundred dollars a year, about an eighth of vessel revenue and a quarter of the owner's income, through lost time, damaged gear, and reduced catches. Fishers also reported injuries, and even deaths, from entanglement incidents at sea. The burden fell hardest on lower-income Mekong fishers. Paying fishers to collect plastic at priority spots, the authors suggest, could cut pollution and support livelihoods together.
pmc-13246706:
Dana Baron Shahaf and colleagues test a one-channel brain wave marker during heart surgery in 2026 work. Thinking often dips after surgery in older patients, sometimes for good. A live marker of brain trouble during the operation could open a window to act.

The team studied EEG and test data from 100 adults having cardiac surgery. Their Brain Reactivity Index tracked with thinking change in patients aged 65 and over. The link showed within the first half hour of anesthesia. It held strongest for patients whose starting scores sat in a middle band. Younger patients showed no such link. The marker may flag risk while care can still adjust.
pmc-13246806:
Jander, Bergner, Schönwald, and co-authors examined whether a newer Parkinson's infusion therapy also eases non-motor symptoms, in this 2026 Journal of Neurology study. Foslevodopa/foscarbidopa delivers Parkinson's medication continuously under the skin and is approved for motor swings in advanced disease, but its effects on sleep, pain, mood, and gut problems were poorly documented. The team followed twenty-one day-clinic patients for nine weeks.

Standard non-motor scores improved by roughly a third, a change past the threshold patients can feel, with the largest gains in sleep disturbance, pain, and constipation. Questionnaire scores for gut symptoms, sleep quality, and depression also improved early on. Four patients developed psychotic symptoms, a known risk. The authors call the results encouraging but exploratory, needing controlled trials.
pmc-13247206:
Yunjun Wang and co-authors traced how two keratin proteins help thyroid cancer resist a key drug in a 2026 study. The drug, lenvatinib, is a main option when papillary thyroid cancer stops responding to iodine treatment. Resistance to it is a major clinical block with no clear fix yet.

The team compared tumor and normal tissue and ran cell and animal studies on the protein KRT15. Together with its partner KRT81, it raises the activity of a lipid-handling enzyme called DGKB. That shift in fat metabolism helps cancer cells survive the drug. Blocking the keratin pair or the enzyme could restore drug power. The work gives drug developers a concrete chain to target in resistant tumors.
pmc-13247306:
Liu and co-authors tested a plant extract against hair graying in this 2026 Dermatology Research and Practice study. Graying is driven largely by oxidative stress killing or disabling the melanocytes that pigment hair, and no effective treatment exists. The team tested Gynostemma pentaphyllum extract, from a vine used in Asian herbal medicine, on pigment cells and mice stressed with hydrogen peroxide.

In cell culture the extract kept melanocytes alive, cut their death rate and internal reactive oxygen, and raised melanin production and the activity of two protective enzymes. In mice it visibly protected hair follicles from peroxide damage. The authors link the effect partly to the Wnt/beta-catenin signaling pathway and propose the extract as a candidate anti-graying treatment, pending human testing.
pmc-13248106:
Okura and co-authors report a genetic kidney-tubule disorder hiding until old age, in this 2026 Case Reports in Endocrinology article. Bartter syndrome type 3, a defect in salt handling in the kidney's loop of Henle, normally declares itself in childhood. Their patient was a sixty-six-year-old woman whose only clue was severe, stubborn low blood potassium found without symptoms, alongside the syndrome's typical alkaline blood and overactive hormone signals.

Ordinary potassium replacement, even at high doses, failed to fix her levels. Careful diuretic challenge tests separated Bartter physiology from its mimic, Gitelman syndrome, and gene sequencing confirmed a homozygous stop variant in the CLCNKB gene. A low-dose combination of an ACE inhibitor and spironolactone then normalized her potassium safely. The authors urge keeping Bartter syndrome in mind for unexplained low potassium at any age.
pmc-13248306:
Hao and a large team searched eye scans for warning signs of abnormal blood vessel growth, in a 2026 study. Their patients had chronic central serous chorioretinopathy, a fluid disorder under the retina that sometimes develops a harmful vessel membrane. Using widefield dye imaging, they compared eyes with and without that complication.

The study covered two hundred ninety-three eyes from two hundred twelve patients, and about a third had the vessel growth. A dominant drainage vein in one corner, vessel links near the macula, and pale scattered spots each stood out in the affected group. The authors propose these features as markers that flag eyes needing closer watching.
pmc-13248906:
Belongia and a large Vaccine Safety Datalink team checked whether COVID-19 vaccines ever made the disease worse, reported in 2026. Enhanced disease after vaccination was a theoretical worry when the shots were authorized. The team estimated vaccine protection against hospitalization and severe illness across variant waves from 2021 to 2023, watching for any negative protection.

Two original doses protected against hospitalization at over ninety percent during the pre-Delta and Delta periods. Protection dipped under Omicron but stayed clearly positive, and booster or bivalent doses restored much of it. At no point, for any dose or variant, did the numbers suggest enhanced disease. The authors close a long-standing safety question with real-world data.
pmc-13249606:
Srivastava and an Indian team profiled immune signals in spinal fluid from patients with autoimmune encephalitis, in a 2026 study. In this condition the immune system attacks the brain, and antibody tests are slow or sometimes come back negative. The researchers measured six signaling proteins in fluid from forty-three patients and thirty-four comparison patients.

Every measured signal ran higher in the encephalitis group. Two attractant proteins, CXCL10 and CXCL13, stood out and rose together with a third, interleukin-6. Patients without detectable antibodies showed the same pattern as those with them. The authors propose the panel as a supporting test that can speed recognition, while stressing it cannot diagnose the condition alone.
pmc-13249706:
Huizenga and colleagues asked teenagers directly how they cope with mental health struggles, in a 2026 pair of Dutch studies. An online tool let adolescents describe, in their own words, what they do about attention problems, behavior problems, or emotional problems, and rate how much each tactic helps. The first study ran during the pandemic with two hundred eighteen participants.

Fifty-one distinct strategies surfaced, some familiar from coping research and others invented by teenagers themselves, and tactics differed by symptom type. The strategies used most were also rated most helpful. A second study after the pandemic, with one hundred eighteen fresh participants, reproduced the picture closely. Helpfulness did not depend on whether a tactic aimed at solving the problem or avoiding it.
pmc-13250506:
Maria L. White and a large team report 2026 findings on how a bacterium recovers when food returns after starvation. Working with Caulobacter crescentus, a microbe common in fresh water, they searched for genes needed to restart growth. The study centers on polyphosphate, a chain of phosphate units that many cells store for later use.

The team found that a gene called ppk1, which builds polyphosphate, is required for recovery after phosphate starvation. When phosphate floods back, normal cells use polyphosphate production to pull the extra phosphate out of their interior. Cells that cannot make polyphosphate build up too much of the energy-carrying molecule ATP and stay stuck, unable to grow. The work shows that storing phosphate is not just saving for later. It also protects the cell during the sudden shift from scarcity to plenty.
pmc-13251306:
Qianwen Ding and a large team test a gut bacteria protein against fatty liver in fish in this 2026 study. The protein, Amuc_1100, comes from a gut microbe linked to metabolic health, and earlier work showed it eases fat build-up in the liver on a fatty diet.

Zebrafish fed the protein with a high-fat diet gained less weight and stored less liver fat than fish on the diet alone. Moving gut microbes from treated fish into germ-free fish copied the benefit, while wiping microbes out with antibiotics erased it. The protein was found to bind a partner in the gut wall, and blocking that partner stopped the effect.
pmc-13251506:
Sanaz Ahmadi Ghezeldasht and colleagues review the hunt for drugs against HTLV-1, a leukemia-causing retrovirus, in 2026. Between five and twenty million people carry the virus worldwide, yet no direct antiviral therapy exists for it. The review centers on the viral protease, a scissor-like enzyme the virus needs to mature and become infectious.

Borrowing HIV protease blockers has largely failed, and the review explains why. The HTLV-1 enzyme grips its targets in a narrower, differently shaped pocket than its HIV cousin, so drugs fitted to one do not fit the other. The authors assess design strategies built around the enzyme's own structure, including computer screening of candidate molecules and combination chemistry. They argue that progress needs chemical starting points drawn for this protease alone. The piece closes with research directions meant to speed the first effective drug.
pmc-13251706:
Tomoki Teramoto and colleagues review intravenous amikacin as opening therapy for cavitary Mycobacterium avium complex lung disease in a 2026 retrospective study. This slow-growing infection is rising in Japan, and guidelines advise adding the injected antibiotic for severe, cavity-forming cases. Evidence for starting with it, especially in older patients, has been thin.

The study covered twenty-one patients treated at Kurashiki Central Hospital between 2021 and 2024, with doses tuned by blood-level monitoring for every patient. By six months, just over half had cleared the bacterium from sputum, and chest imaging improved in most patients by one year. Patients aged seventy-five and older fared no worse than younger ones, and nearly all older patients completed at least three months of injections. Only two patients stopped treatment early. The authors judge the drug-monitored regimen effective and tolerable.
pmc-13252706:
JunYoung Seo and co-authors simplify patient leaflets with a chatbot in this 2026 study. Digital therapeutics are software treatments with real evidence behind them, but their explanation sheets are often too hard to read, which holds back uptake.

The team built a rewriting tool on GPT-4o and tested it in two online experiments with 500 people each, covering insomnia and nicotine dependence treatments. Readers were picked for relevance, such as smokers or poor sleepers. Those given the simplified sheets improved their felt understanding more than readers of the originals, and rated the text easier and clearer. Effects were small to moderate, the authors note.
pmc-13252806:
Adanze Cynthia and colleagues map health care access for Sub-Saharan African migrants in Europe in this 2026 scoping review. This growing population faces heavy barriers to care, and the review gathers what is known as these communities age.

Fourteen studies met the bar across five databases. Three themes stood out. Structural blocks included insurance gaps, legal insecurity, and tangled administration. Undocumented migrants, women, and people with HIV faced sharper vulnerability. Language and culture often clashed with health systems. Only one study looked at ageing and long-term care choices. The authors urge migrant-sensitive services and long-term research following people across their lives.
pmc-13252906:
Loai Albinsaad and colleagues describe a one-sided thyroid in this 2026 case report. A 34-year-old Saudi man came in with swelling on the right side of his neck that pressed on his throat, causing trouble swallowing and breathing.

Examination confirmed an enlarged right thyroid lobe, while hormone levels stayed normal. Ultrasound found several solid lumps inside it, and a needle sample raised suspicion of a follicular growth. Surgeons removed the right half of the gland and confirmed a non-invasive growth of that type. The surprise was the left side: he had been born with no left thyroid lobe at all, a rare defect usually found only by chance.
pmc-13253706:
Ashok Aspatwar reviews carbonic anhydrase VIII, called CA VIII, in a 2026 paper on cell signaling. Most proteins in this family help balance acid in the body, but CA VIII lacks a key part and cannot do that job. Yet it is kept across species and is rich in nerve tissue, hinting at a new role.

Evidence cited shows CA VIII binds a channel that releases calcium inside cells, shaping nerve firing and brain growth. Gene faults in families from Iraq and Saudi Arabia link its loss to ataxia, meaning poor balance, and slow brain growth. The author casts CA VIII as a repurposed signal regulator.
pmc-13254206:
Mona Nabil and colleagues set out greener lab methods to measure a cold and flu medicine in a 2026 study. The product mixes phenylephrine, chlorpheniramine, and ibuprofen to ease congestion, allergy, and fever. Two chromatography methods, which separate and measure ingredients, were built with ecology in mind.

One method used thin-layer plates and the other a liquid system that finished in about six minutes. Both separated the three drugs cleanly and hit very low detection limits, as stated in the paper. The liquid method could also track how fast tablets dissolve, and both passed standard validation checks.
pmc-13254506:
Jeng-Wen Chen and colleagues mine a national assessment platform for patterns in how medical residents earn trust in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Taiwan's ear, nose, and throat residency programs all record competency decisions on one digital platform, built around entrustable professional activities, units of work a trainee may perform at a given supervision level. The team analyzed 3,504 committee decisions covering 292 residents and twelve activities.

Residents' median supervision levels rose with training year but often stalled below the expected target in the senior years. Overall, seventy-three percent of decisions met their target, with shortfalls concentrated in the fourth and fifth years. Two system factors predicted underattainment: starting an activity's sequence late, and committees meeting less often to review progress. The authors argue that these are fixable system constraints rather than trainee failings. National learning analytics, they say, exposes where assessment machinery itself slows doctors down.
pmc-13254906:
Kristine Wiborg Høgsbjerg and a large Danish team report radiotherapy quality assurance results from the DBCG RT Natural trial in 2026. The trial explores gentler treatment, including partial breast irradiation, for lower-risk breast cancer after conserving surgery. Before de-escalation can be trusted, the radiation actually delivered across many centers must match the plan.

The audit included every trial patient who received partial breast irradiation, using prospectively collected treatment data shared in standard imaging format across centers. Protocol adherence ran high. Target coverage was consistently achieved while keeping high-dose volumes minimal, and doses to heart and lungs stayed within protocol limits in every treated patient. The authors say the comprehensive, multicenter checking was possible because complete digital treatment records were gathered as the trial ran rather than reconstructed later. In their reading, the results support safe rollout of partial breast irradiation in routine practice.
pmc-13255206:
Somayeh Momenyan and co-authors trace PTSD paths after road crashes in a 2026 cohort study. They followed 1,042 survivors recruited from Canadian emergency departments between 2018 and 2020. Symptoms were checked at 2, 4, 6, and 12 months, along with life quality and return to work and daily activities.

Three paths emerged: Chronic, Delayed-Recovery, and Resilient. The first two groups started with high life quality, then fell sharply and stayed low on full recovery and return to work. They were more often female and had more pain and distress before injury. The authors urge early care that treats PTSD and pain together.
pmc-13255706:
Grazia Palomba and a large Sardinian team report a 2026 study of how driver gene changes affect survival in metastatic colorectal cancer. Sardinia's people are genetically uniform, which sharpens such work. The team looked back at 208 patients, checking their tumors for KRAS, NRAS, and BRAF mutations plus microsatellite instability.

Mutations were found in two-thirds of patients, most often in KRAS, and never in pairs within the same tumor. Patients with no driver mutation lived a median of 38 months, versus 26 months for RAS-mutated cases and just 14 months for BRAF-mutated cases. Microsatellite status and the mutated share of tumor DNA did not split survival. With other factors weighed in, BRAF mutation and older age at first treatment predicted poorer outcomes. The authors say mutation testing stays vital for an honest outlook in this disease.
pmc-13256206:
Huy Le Ngoc and colleagues present a 2026 cross-sectional study of mobile health engagement among patients with multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, a long and demanding treatment. Phones can deliver education and provider contact during such therapy, yet whether engagement tracks with what patients know and do was unclear. The team built a twelve-item engagement score and checked its quality first.

The score proved internally consistent, and one weak item was dropped to improve it. Patients with stronger engagement scored significantly higher on knowledge, attitudes, and the combined measure, in a stepwise pattern across engagement levels. Day-to-day practice scores, however, did not follow engagement. The authors read the gap as a reminder that knowing and approving are easier to move than habits, and that mHealth programs should target behavior directly.
pmc-13257306:
Teona Turashvili and colleagues examine a puzzling lining change in womb tissue samples in a 2026 staining study. Ciliated change, where surface cells grow hair-like fringes, appears in benign and malignant lesions alike. Three hundred fifteen specimens from 2019 to 2024 were split evenly across seven diagnoses.

Digital analysis compared lesions with and without the ciliated change for three marker proteins. In benign categories, ciliated lesions showed less E-cadherin and more beta-catenin, often inside the nucleus. Cancers broke that pattern, showing opposite or weaker shifts. Vimentin fell consistently wherever ciliated change appeared. Two other markers gave mixed, less useful signals. Pathologists gain a caution: marker meaning depends on context, so a single stain cannot label these lesions as harmless or dangerous by itself.
pmc-13257406:
Lihua Chen and co-authors published a formal correction in 2026 to their earlier study of a fungal gene. The original work examined VdPT1, which codes for a neutral trehalase in Verticillium dahliae. That plant pathogen study linked the gene to fungal growth and disease-causing ability.

The notice replaces faulty images tied to two experiments shown in Figures 7 and 8. Corrected versions of both figures appear in the notice itself. Chen and colleagues state that the fix leaves their scientific conclusions unchanged. An academic editor approved the correction, and the original publication has also been updated.
pmc-13257506:
Jiaxi Xia and colleagues develop a long-lasting antibacterial spray based on a zinc framework material in a 2026 study. Common sprays evaporate fast, irritate skin, or wash off surfaces quickly. The new formula suspends ZIF-8 particles in ethanol with a binder that anchors coatings to gauze and glass.

The material releases zinc ions in response to acidity and generates reactive oxygen inside bacteria. Near-total killing was reached for staph, E. coli, and drug-resistant staph at the tested strength. Coatings kept most of their power after five washes and a week outdoors. Rat skin showed no irritation in safety checks. Infection control teams gain a durable option for surfaces and dressings. Human skin testing and virus data would complete the picture.
pmc-13258906:
Hui Yang and colleagues test if coumarin shields citrus seedlings from aluminum harm in a 2026 plant study. Aluminum in sour soils stalls roots and cuts leaf food making. Seedlings grew for weeks with aluminum, coumarin, both, or none of them.

Coumarin eased growth loss and kept the food making parts in good shape. Treated plants held less aluminum in their stems and leaves. Food and salt balance plus guard traits also held up well under stress. Plants with no coumarin raised their own guards, with more sugars and plant phenols. Farms on sour soils gain a shield choice with a clear path of action.
pmc-13259206:
Yingbing Hu and colleagues profile scent chemistry across magnolia flower organs and stages in a 2026 study. A newly registered variety smells stronger as blooms open fully. Stamens, pistils, and petals were sampled at bud, half open, and full bloom stages.

Nearly fourteen hundred metabolites were catalogued, with terpenoids the largest group. Early stage scent leaned green and herbal, while full bloom turned fruity and sweet, mainly in petals. Gene activity showed petals preparing scent ingredients early, then switching pathways at full bloom. Each organ followed its own metabolic pattern. Perfume and breeding researchers gain the first full scent resource for this variety.
pmc-13260106:
Zhangfan Ding and colleagues publish a recipe for imaging whole organs in three dimensions within about two days. Seeing cells and molecules across an intact organ beats slicing it thin, but antibody staining of big tissues is slow. Their 2026 protocol compresses every stage.

Steps run from bleaching and antigen retrieval through enzyme digestion that lets antibodies soak deep. The team then details whole-tissue labeling, dehydration, and optical clearing for light-sheet microscopy. Human tissues and soft organs both fit the workflow. Labs chasing tumor and tissue microenvironments get a fast, start-to-finish playbook, building on the group's earlier method paper.
pmc-13260206:
Tahra ElObeid and co-authors turn beet sugar waste into an ice cream ingredient. Factories extracting red beet pigment discard a sugary liquid that still holds value. Their 2026 study cleans and concentrates that stream to stand in for glucose syrup.

Ion-exchange and adsorber resins clarified and decolored the liquid before evaporation thickened it. Fourteen ice cream mixes, planned by statistical design, swapped the upcycled syrup against glucose syrup and salep stabilizer. Color, texture, melting, and flow all modeled predictably across recipes.Usable ice cream resulted, proving colorant waste can rejoin the food chain under a circular economy.
pmc-13261606:
Guozhen Chen and co-authors developed in 2026 an enzyme-free electrochemical sensor for hydrogen peroxide built on a copper porphyrin and graphene composite. Hydrogen peroxide matters in medicine, food safety, and industry, yet enzyme sensors decay quickly. Their composite spreads copper TCPP evenly across reduced graphene oxide sheets through flat molecular stacking.

Electrodes coated with the material reduced peroxide in proportion to its concentration across a wide range. The detection limit reached a low level suitable for trace checks, with clear signal at three times the noise. Trials on store-bought disinfectant samples returned values very close to the known amounts. The authors describe the platform as a stable, sensitive option for environmental monitoring. The design avoids fragile biological parts entirely, which should extend working life.
pmc-13261806:
Xian-Xing Yu and colleagues built in 2026 a prediction model for bleeding growth after a spontaneous brain hemorrhage in older patients. Expansion of the bleed drives early decline, so spotting risk fast matters. Their study enrolled 194 patients aged sixty and over, each scanned again within two days.

Fifty-six patients, close to three in ten, saw their hematoma expand. Seven factors independently raised the odds, including older age, worse stroke scale scores, and higher neutrophil counts. Scan signs mattered too: a black hole sign and an irregular bleed shape both flagged danger. Higher blood sodium, by contrast, lowered the odds. The combined model sorted patients sharply, keeping strong accuracy after internal correction for optimism. The authors offer it for early bedside sorting of elderly hemorrhage patients.
pmc-13263506:
Weili Bao and co-authors present a 2026 case report of two elderly patients who developed a serious eye infection after cataract surgery. The infection, endophthalmitis, is inflammation inside the eye that can destroy vision. Both patients, aged 69 and 87, received emergency surgery to remove the eye's gel, washing of the front chamber, and vancomycin injected into the eye.

Cultures from the eye gel confirmed Enterococcus faecalis, a gut bacterium, which was sensitive to several antibiotics including vancomycin. Both patients needed repeat washing because cloudiness persisted. Vision later improved clearly in both cases. The authors suggest early gel-removal surgery plus vancomycin works well, while warning that two cases are a small base for conclusions.
pmc-13264306:
Ugur Yener and a large team survey pain medicine fellowship training in the United States in a 2026 cross-sectional study. The specialty has widened since formal recognition in the early nineteen nineties, drawing trainees from many primary fields and adding new treatment methods. Surveys went separately to current trainees, program directors and employers through societies and direct outreach, gathering five hundred eighteen responses across the three groups with differing expectations about skills and leadership preparation.

Directors answered at a strong rate, while overall response share could not be calculated without known totals. Findings highlight where the groups agree and where their priorities diverge on curriculum content and career readiness. The authors aim to guide how fellowships shape future leaders rather than only technicians.
pmc-13264406:
Huizhen Wu and colleagues test cheek acupuncture for bladder discomfort from catheters after kidney stone surgery in a 2026 randomized trial. One hundred eighteen patients having ureteroscopic stone removal were assigned to true or sham treatment in the recovery room for thirty minutes after waking. True treatment placed needles at defined cheek points linked in that system to the pelvis; sham used identical tubes without skin penetration, keeping patients and assessors unaware of group.

Moderate to severe discomfort at one hour was far less common with true treatment, and the advantage held at two hours but faded later. Fewer treated patients needed rescue medication. Pain and sleep scores were similar between groups. A brief facial technique may ease the earliest, worst catheter discomfort window.
pmc-13265006:
Dandan Sun and a large team wrote a 2026 study on whether end-stage kidney disease changes how the sedative ciprofol works. The drug is used in general anesthesia, and failing kidneys can alter drug handling, so dosing for transplant patients needs proof. They compared kidney transplant patients on dialysis with matched patients whose kidneys worked normally.

Using a dose step-up and step-down method, they found the dose needed to stop response to airway device placement was the same in both groups. Drug use during surgery, waking times, and blood pressure and heart stability also matched. Side effects like low blood pressure, slow heart rate, and slowed breathing occurred at like rates. The authors conclude that kidney failure does not meaningfully change this drug's sedative effect or safety.
pmc-13265206:
Lihong Guo and colleagues create prediction charts for cervical cancer that has spread to the liver, in a 2026 registry study. This spread pattern carries a very poor outlook. No dedicated tool existed for individual forecasts. Registry cases diagnosed from 2010 to 2020 were analysed.

A total of 704 patients were split into training and validation cohorts. Survival at two years was under one in ten. Chemotherapy and radiotherapy each linked to better survival, while spread to the lungs worsened it. Tissue type also mattered for cancer-specific survival. Charts built from these factors support personalised counselling and care planning.
pmc-13265706:
Allison J Nielsen and colleagues measure hidden and unlocked gun storage among Colorado owners, in a 2026 survey study. Hiding a gun does not lock it against children or others. A 2023 state-representative survey asked owners about storage. The analysis kept 432 respondents who owned at least one firearm.

Nearly half kept at least one firearm hidden and unlocked. Handguns were stored that way more often than long guns. In homes with children, about a third still used hidden unlocked storage. The authors warn that prevention efforts must stress the limits of hiding alone for blocking unauthorised access.
pmc-13265906:
Wenjie Hua and the team uncover a signalling chain that protects scar-forming cells in lung fibrosis, in a 2026 study. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis pairs alveolar injury with runaway fibroblast growth. Single-cell data suggested faulty talk between lung lining cells and fibroblasts. Lab and mouse tests verified the chain.

Injured lining cells release a signal called midkine. It activates a receptor on aggressive fibroblasts, blocking an iron-driven death process. Downstream, a stabilising protein protects a key defence compound. Changing signal levels in models confirmed each step. The pathway offers new targets for diagnosis or intervention.
pmc-13266006:
Pu Pu and co-authors (2026) test a three-target antibody against triple-negative breast cancer in lab models. This cancer lacks the usual drug targets and needs new options. Many of its tumors run on three signals: EGFR, cMet, and VEGF. The antibody, TAVO412, grabs all three at once, touching EGFR at two spots. In cell tests it blocked growth signals from the first two targets. It also recruited immune killing and choked off blood vessel growth.

The two-spot grip beat a marketed two-target antibody on tumor cells with low EGFR levels. The drug then shrank tumors in several mouse models grown from patient-like cell lines. The authors present TAVO412 as a strong preclinical candidate. One molecule doing three jobs could simplify treatment if the safety holds in people. They note that human trials are the next step; all evidence so far comes from cells and animals.
pmc-13266406: A 2026 correction notice fixes the author list of a 2025 paper on a green method for measuring calcium in medicines using curcumin, a plant pigment. Dipak Paudel had been left off the author list. The notice records his contributions: he ran the HPLC analysis of samples and standards, processed the data, and curated the study data set. The corrected list names Nim Bahadur Dangi, Hemraj Sharma, Dipak Paudel, and Hari Prasad Sapkota, with their Nepali university affiliations. The notice closes with an apology for the error.
pmc-13267506:
Valentin Flaudias and co-authors published this psychiatry study in 2026 on eating disorders. Such disorders are increasingly viewed as having an addictive side, and food addiction is well documented in bulimia and binge-eating disorder but murkier in anorexia. The authors test a three-part model of addiction, covering a thinking system, a feeling system, and a body-sensing system, in 115 patients across the three diagnoses.

Patients completed questionnaires on emotional appetite, body awareness, thinking flexibility, and food addiction symptoms. Taken one at a time, trouble in each of the three systems went with stronger food addiction. In a joint model, only body-sensing trouble and negative emotions held up; thinking flexibility dropped out. The pattern looked similar across diagnoses. The authors conclude that body sense and feelings may drive the addictive side of eating disorders, and they call for sharper tools to measure the thinking system.
pmc-13267806:
Xiaohan Wang and Zhiping Wang wrote a 2026 letter about a trial of the sedative remimazolam during painless colonoscopy. The trial found that a higher dose and a slower injection both cut hiccups, a side effect that can disturb the procedure. The letter writers praise the finding but raise three points for the trial team to clarify.

First, with about 40 patients per subgroup, the trial may have been too small to rule out an interaction between dose and injection speed. Second, the higher dose also deepened sedation, which alone could suppress hiccups, so dose and depth are hard to separate. Third, slower injection cut how often hiccups started but seemed to lengthen them when they did. The writers suggest added monitoring in future work.
pmc-13268706:
Charles Matthews and colleagues present a 2026 study comparing two factory systems for making a bone-growth protein used in surgery. The approved product is grown in hamster ovary cells; growing it in E. coli bacteria could be cheaper. The team screened four bacterial-made versions in cell tests, picked the strongest, and compared it with the hamster-cell product in 15 rats. Sponges carrying the protein were placed in muscle pouches for four weeks.

The winning bacterial version beat the standard in cell tests and formed roughly ten times more bone in rats, with more mature structure under the microscope. But the four bacterial versions varied widely among themselves. The authors warn that potency cannot be assumed from protein weight alone: each supplier's product needs its own testing before clinical trust.
pmc-13269206:
Zaiyu Tang and co-authors mine in 2026 more than thirty-six thousand Reddit posts to learn how the public talks about artificial intelligence in health care. Posts and comments from 2020 to 2025 were sorted by a topic model and scored for sentiment. Fourteen topics grouped into six domains, from human-centered care and medical services to regulation and cultural views.

Positive posts slightly outweighed negative ones, with a large neutral middle. Worries clustered around immature technology, commercial motives, privacy and safety risks, and fear of doctors being displaced. Sentiment shifted over time, notably after generative AI tools spread widely. The authors advise transparent communication, clearer rules, and workforce planning so that public trust can keep pace with medical AI's rollout.
pmc-13269606:
Dingpin Huang and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 building a model that predicts a key immune marker, PD-L1, in non-small cell lung cancer. The model fuses CT scan features with features from stained tissue slides. High marker levels help doctors choose immune therapy for this common lung cancer.

Records from 328 patients were split into training, checking, and test sets, and 55.5 percent of patients were marker positive. The fused model beat either single-source model, with accuracy scores of 0.90, 0.80, and 0.73 across the sets. In a separate group on immune therapy, patients with high model scores lived longer without disease growth. The score stayed predictive when combined with clinical factors.
pmc-13269806:
Aileen M Barnes and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on a mouse model of a rare brittle bone disease with unusually heavy bones. A fault blocks the cutting of a tail piece from collagen, the main bone protein. The team examined bones and bone-forming cells from the engineered mice.

Mouse thigh bones were extremely brittle, with thin walls and lower bone volume despite the heavy label. Their mineral content was higher, but the mineral particles were thinner and more disorganized, and collagen fibers looked like barbed wire. Bone-forming cells from mice and humans switched on bone-making genes five to 25 times more strongly. Pathways for cell sticking and movement fell. The authors say faulty processing changes cell behavior itself.
pmc-13270106:

pmc-13271906:

pmc-13272506:

pmc-13272806:

pmc-13273606:

pmc-13273906:

pmc-13275506:

pmc-13275806:

pmc-13276306:

pmc-13276606:

pmc-13276706:

pmc-13276806:

pmc-13277106:

pmc-13277406:

pmc-13278406:

pmc-13279006:

pmc-13279206:

pmc-13282406:

pmc-13284206:

pmc-13285906:

pmc-13286406:

pmc-13286706:

pmc-13286806:

pmc-13286906:

pmc-13287106:

Some faulty networks forbid the classic version yet allow this one, and results until now came piecemeal.
