Semi-open decision sets and semi-continuous maps, tools dating to 1963, turn out to be exactly the right lens, since they let a connected space map onto a split one. Weak and strong validity versions prove equivalent, and every known solvability result in the area gets a unified topological explanation.
pmc-13288206:
Clair Davison and co-authors review what the Attention Training Technique changes in the brain, in a 2026 synthesis. The technique is a short listening exercise from metacognitive therapy for emotional disorders. Patients practice shifting attention among sounds to loosen rigid threat focus. The review gathered studies that measured thinking tasks or brain activity after the training. Searches covered five databases for work from 1990 to late 2025.

Twenty studies with 1,230 participants met the rules for inclusion. Only four used clinical samples, while most tested healthy volunteers or students. Across fourteen thinking tasks, effects ranged from small to large, and the emotional dot-probe task showed the most steady gains. Brain measures from three methods pointed the same way, toward stronger control networks and quieter self-focused activity. The authors note uneven study quality and call for better protocol reporting.
pmc-13288606:
Joanna L Harris and co-authors assemble the first species-level picture of manta and devil rays around the Mascarene islands in a 2026 synthesis. Combining diver reports and citizen-science sightings from 2014 to 2026 for Reunion, Mauritius, and Rodrigues, they logged 107 sightings across 75 separate events.

Thurston's devil rays and oceanic mantas dominated the records, reef mantas and sicklefin devil rays appeared rarely, and many animals stayed unidentified, while Rodrigues produced no records at all. Sightings clustered off Reunion's west and southwest coasts, peaked from late spring into early summer, and included rare courtship and one manta seen again almost four years later. With all mobulids now under strict trade protection, the baseline should guide monitoring.
pmc-13288706:
Florian Bernhardt and a large team study end-of-life care access in Germany in 2026. The work deals with Muslim migrants and their children. Talks ran from August 2021 to December 2022. Six centers in North Rhine-Westphalia took part. The set held 53 adults from 14 nations.

Four groups fed the talks. They were patients in such care and patients outside it. Kin and boundary staff also joined. The core idea was same same but different. Formal equality still felt blocked day to day. Six forces fed delays in a loop. They spanned othering, poor facts, and family roles. Stigma, language, and death views counted too. Native-language help was named as a lever.
pmc-13289006:
Gonzalo Romero-Martinez and colleagues study daily habits and mood in Colombia. Their 2026 survey covers students at one public university. It holds 1,125 students in all. Most were women, at 56.7 percent. Surveys tapped exercise, sitting, and sleep.

Only 15.5 percent met all three daily guides. Meeting more guides linked to lower mood symptoms. Students who met all three had far lower odds of worry. Their odds of low mood were also lower. Enough exercise and sleep each helped alone. Long sitting linked to worse symptoms. The design cannot prove cause and effect.
pmc-13289506:
Ayman Azhary and co-authors measure blood-borne viruses among dialysis patients in war-torn Khartoum State, Sudan, in a 2026 study. Dialysis patients face high infection risk because their blood passes through shared machines for years. The study drew test results from the state public health laboratory for 940 patients across fifteen facilities, covering mid to late 2025. Three viruses were tracked: hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV.

Hepatitis C was the most common, at 12.2 percent of patients, ahead of hepatitis B at 7.1 percent, while HIV was rare at 0.6 percent. Rates for hepatitis C varied widely between facilities, a pattern the authors highlight. The work was done in a conflict-affected region where services are strained. Its numbers give health officials a current map of where infection control in dialysis units needs the most help.
pmc-13289606:
Zhao and six co-authors pair shape optimization with a mineral coating to help titanium scaffolds grow bone, in a study from twenty twenty-six. Printed porous titanium is strong but its surface is inert, which invites scar tissue. The team shapes the pore lattice with fluid simulations for good flow. They then coat it evenly with a thin bone-like mineral layer.

The coating boosts stem cell sticking, growth, and bone differentiation. In dog muscle tests, one lattice shape spurs bone formation best. Its deep fluid flow and even shear stress explain the edge. In rabbit thigh bone defects, the tuned scaffold bonds tightly to bone and fills with new bone. The design may improve clinical implants.
pmc-13289906:
Emmanuel O Osayi and colleagues present a 2026 surveillance cohort on mother-to-child HIV transmission outcomes in Plateau State, Nigeria. Most child HIV comes from perinatal spread, and how fast illness appears shapes outlook. Records covered HIV-exposed infants with confirmed positive tests who started therapy between October 2018 and September 2022 at fifteen facilities across three districts.

A total of 57 infants entered, with a near even sex split and a mean starting age of 0.7 years for therapy. Follow-up ran from six months to five years after starting drugs. By the end, 70 percent had favorable outcomes, and most of those suppressed the virus fully as reported. The rest died, transferred, stopped, or interrupted care.
pmc-13290106:
A phone-based questionnaire system that writes patient answers straight into the medical record is described by Eunjoung Choi and colleagues in 2026. Their platform, Miri-Alimi, sends previsit questionnaires through a social networking service and transfers structured replies into the electronic record automatically.

In a cardiology clinic study run from August to November 2024, 751 outpatients received the questionnaire link before their visits. The response rate was 38.5%, with first-visit patients answering more often than heart failure follow-up patients, and responders were younger on average. Among follow-up patients, record completeness on breathlessness, swelling, and medication adherence was far higher for responders. Satisfaction among patients and providers ran high, supporting wider use of messaging-based data collection.
pmc-13290706:
A missing immune protein produced a family puzzle and a treatment dilemma in a 2026 report by Mattia Moratti and colleagues on GIMAP5 deficiency. The first Italian pediatric case anchors the study, set beside a review of twenty published patients with this rare disorder of immunity, lymphoproliferation, and progressive liver disease.

The 11-year-old boy carried two faulty copies of the gene, made no detectable protein, and suffered autoimmune cytopenias, severe viral infections, and early liver abnormalities. His T cells looked exhausted and his memory B-cell pool was unusually expanded. His twin carried one faulty copy, made less protein, and showed only a localized vascular anomaly without immune defects. Sirolimus, an mTOR inhibitor, brought the boy's cytopenias into lasting remission. The authors argue such precision treatment can stabilize patients while families weigh a stem cell transplant.
pmc-13291106:
Erhan Hüseyin Cömert leads a 2026 study of pregnancy odds after ICSI treatment. The work centers on the day of embryo transfer. Records from 2020 to 2025 were screened. Three hundred transfers, one per couple, were kept.

Only 37 pregnancies occurred in the set. The main model thus used just four factors. Woman’s age and AMH level were two of them. Sperm source and embryo stage made up the rest. Checks for optimism and calibration were built in. The team calls the work exploratory by design. It should frame counseling talks, not drive choices. A sac on ultrasound defined pregnancy here.
pmc-13291206:
Tiny packets shed by nerve support cells carry stage-linked cargo. Manju Sharma leads a 2026 lab study of these packets from Schwann cells. Such cells switch from wrapping nerves to repair mode after injury. Their shed packets pass signals between cells.

Rat Schwann cells were grown at three life stages. Packet contents were mapped for proteins and small RNA strands. Repair-stage packets held a distinct RNA mix. Adding them to young cells switched on a repair gene. Tweaking one small RNA changed cell growth and movement. Some long RNA strands may sponge up small RNAs in turn. The work maps how packets may steer nerve repair.
pmc-13291306:
Aimed radiation to the prostate may help spread cancer last longer. Christian Trapp leads a 2026 review of patient records. Such cancer is often treated with body-wide drugs alone. Adding prostate radiation is called primary directed therapy.

Records covered 24 men treated from 2011 to 2023. Most had few spread spots and modern scan staging. Nearly all also got hormone blocking drugs. Most had aimed radiation to spread spots too. Half the men stayed free of progress for years. Survival passed the follow-up span for the group. Side effects were tracked as a safety check. Small numbers call for larger trials to confirm.
pmc-13292206:
Markel G Ibarluzea and a large team model a fat-lengthening enzyme to guide drug design, in a 2026 computational study. ELOVL6 stretches sixteen-carbon fatty acids into eighteen-carbon ones in liver and fat tissue. The enzyme is tied to metabolic and brain diseases, making it an attractive drug target. No crystal structure exists, which blocks the usual design route. The team combined predicted structures, molecular dynamics, and free energy calculations instead.

Simulations traced the most favorable path a fatty acid takes into the enzyme's tunnel. They also captured shape changes that come with ligand binding. Known inhibitors were tested in silico and preferred the active site, matching measured binding strengths. Comparing cousin enzymes pinpointed residues likely to grant selectivity for ELOVL6 over its relatives. The authors offer their framework as a starting scaffold for inhibitor programs. Experimental structures can later refine the model.
pmc-13292306:
Or Segal, Hadas Hevron, and Noam Weinbach compare a 2026 study of teenagers living through the same war from different homes. Two hundred Israeli adolescents aged 14 to 18 were assessed four to eight months after the Israel-Hamas war began. Half had been internally displaced from high-risk areas, and half had stayed put, with similar backgrounds otherwise.

Displaced teens reported heavier emotional distress, driven mainly by stress and depression rather than anxiety alone. They also struggled more with regulating emotions and tolerated uncertainty less well. Those two difficulties statistically carried much of the link between displacement and distress. The authors, calling theirs the first such comparison during active war, urge targeted support for displaced adolescents that builds emotion skills and steadiness under uncertainty.
pmc-13292506:
Caren Kamau and co-authors listen to a 2026 qualitative study of mothers and health workers in Kajiado County, Kenya, on what shapes mental health around pregnancy and birth. Perinatal depression may affect up to 30 percent of Kenyan women. Focus groups at five facilities, two urban and three rural, gathered 51 mothers and 39 health workers in March 2025.

Three themes emerged. First, mothers lacked control over money and decisions while carrying most household burdens, with early marriage and female genital mutilation leaving girls unready for motherhood. Second, distance, cost, and low expectations thinned care, and women feared traumatic births and caesarean sections. Third, communities often read mental illness as irrationality or spirit possession, delaying help, with stigma also shadowing caesareans and HIV. The authors tie maternal wellbeing tightly to gender norms.
pmc-13292606: A 2026 notice retracts a 2019 International Journal of Molecular Sciences article by Jin-Woo Jeong and co-authors on fermented oyster extract and bone cells. An editorial investigation confirmed inappropriate image editing and duplication with figures from an earlier paper by a similar group. The authors cooperated, but their explanations and materials could not resolve the problems. The editorial board lost confidence in the findings and retracted the article under MDPI policy, with the editor-in-chief's approval. The authors were informed and stated their disagreement with the decision.
pmc-13294106:
Ana Karen Villa-Merlan and colleagues dissect what makes the scorpion venom peptide Uy234 kill bacteria in a 2026 study. Native peptide from Urodacus yaschenkoi was tested against Staphylococcus aureus and a drug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii isolate. Two altered versions removed single features: one swapped proline at position 9, the other lost the capped tail end.

Only the native peptide stopped growth and killed both pathogens. Fluorescent viability tests showed membrane damage in staph cells only with the native form. Microscopy and artificial membrane work showed thinning, spreading, and dose-dependent leaking. Simulations backed the bench results. Both altered features are essential, a useful rule for peptide drug design.
pmc-13294206:
Huixin Zhang and coauthors study motoric cognitive risk syndrome in brain small vessel disease for a 2026 cross-sectional analysis. The syndrome pairs slow walking with memory complaints and predicts poor outcomes, yet its drivers inside vessel disease were murky. Registry patients aged 55 and older without likely dementia gave clinic data, activity reports, and brain imaging markers, totaling 225 people.

Prevalence was 16.4%, with mean age 65.4 years and 54.2% men. The syndrome tied to lower average systolic pressure and higher total vessel disease burden. Memory complaints alone tied to white matter damage near the cortex, while slow gait tied to lipid problems and worse daily function. Inactivity links stayed imprecise from sparse data.
pmc-13294306:
Maria Shilova and burns colleagues survey laser practice for thick burn scars in a 2026 questionnaire study. Laser care is spreading fast, but protocols vary widely. A team-built survey, translated into Spanish, Chinese, and German, reached burns clinicians worldwide between December 2021 and June 2023, drawing 43 responses.

Nearly everyone used carbon dioxide fractional lasers, a third used pulsed dye lasers, and about half mixed lasers in one session. Most treated both fresh and mature scars, set power by scar thickness judged mostly by eye, and paired steroids or other add-ons. Anesthesia, pain relief, and dressings differed sharply. Shared mapping can seed common standards and trials.
pmc-13294806: A 2026 correction by Guanmin Zhang, Qiuju Hu, and Haiyang Zou repairs the reference list of their article on the endocannabinoid system, exercise, and depression. Several sources had been pasted into the main text as full references and left out of the reference list itself. The notice adds those missing entries, covering work on stress, fear conditioning, brain-derived neurotrophic factor, and exercise effects, and reformats the in-text citations to match. No findings or arguments in the article are touched by the change.
pmc-13295006:
Changhong Jiang and colleagues review nanomedicine for kidney injury after blood flow returns in a 2026 article. Restored flow can itself damage kidneys through oxidative stress, inflammation, cell death, and poor microcirculation. Current diagnosis and treatment lack precision, leaving room for targeted nanoscale tools.

Carriers surveyed include mineral and polymer particles, enzyme-like nanomaterials, cell vesicles, camouflaged particles, and injectable gels. Such systems promise earlier detection, delivery straight to injured tissue, and longer drug action with less body-wide toxicity. The authors stress that safety, body handling, and movement into clinics remain open problems needing urgent work before routine use.
pmc-13295106:
Barbara Strasser and colleagues review how food and drink choices change the sense of effort during endurance exercise in a 2026 article. How hard exercise feels helps decide how long people can keep going, in sport and in daily life alike. Anything that softens that feeling may therefore lift performance.

Proven aids such as caffeine, beta-alanine, and carbohydrate mouth rinsing are examined alongside less settled options like certain amino acids and probiotics. Routes include slower fatigue build-up, better motor signal flow, and changed brain network activity tied to effort. The authors call for work on best doses and mixtures for each sport and person.
pmc-13295806:
Junli Feng and colleagues map where a plant pathogen could live worldwide in a 2026 study. Phytopythium litorale may threaten plant health and wild ecosystems as climates shift. Records numbering 150 from around the globe and 36 environmental factors fed a habitat model.

Suitable ground now covers a vast area across North America, Europe, Asia, and Oceania. Coldest-season temperature, seasonal temperature swing, and cold-season rain controlled the pattern most strongly. Future climates expand the suitable zone and push it toward higher latitudes, with the centre moving far northeast. The maps give officials a head start for watching borders and forests.
pmc-13296706:
In a 2026 review, Yaliang Huang and co-authors cover light- and electricity-based sensors for amyloid-beta oligomers, a toxic clump tied to Alzheimer's disease. Standard tests are costly and slow, while these sensors promise sensitivity in small, portable devices.

The review covers direct and sandwich-style designs and the catchers they use, from antibodies and aptamers to printed plastic moulds. Nanomaterials and signal boosting tricks that sharpen accuracy and stability get special focus. Remaining hurdles and next steps are laid out, aiming to guide sensor design for early Alzheimer's diagnosis and related precision medicine work.
pmc-13296806:
Junmei Chen and colleagues reconstruct, in 2026, how climate shrank the range of dawn redwood, a famous relict tree now confined to a small corner of China. Using 755 fossil records with deep-time niche modelling, they trace where the genus could live across past eras.

The tree spread widely across mid-to-high latitudes in the earlier era, then retreated toward lower latitudes as the world dried and cooled. Yearly rainfall was the key driver across both eras. Ice ages of the recent period then crushed its range. The authors say the story guides conservation of relict plants under future warming.
pmc-13297506:
Claudia Moriello and colleagues test whether tomato extracts can shield human red blood cells from mercury harm, in a 2026 laboratory study. Mercury drives oxidative stress, an overload of reactive oxygen that damages cells, and red cells are exposed around the clock with few repair tools. Extracts came from two tomato types, Piccadilly and Piennolo, and cells were stressed with mercury chloride.

One extract held more protective plant compounds, yet both shielded cells about equally well. Treated cells made fewer reactive oxygen species, kept their fat layers and sulfur groups intact, and held onto their internal antioxidant store. A danger signal that normally flips to the cell surface stayed hidden, keeping the blood less prone to clotting. Diet-derived compounds may thus guard blood cells directly.
pmc-13297606:
Faizaan Fazal Khan and Goo-Rak Kwon ask whether carrying more copies of a risk gene variant speeds the slide from mild memory trouble to Alzheimer's dementia, in a 2026 study. The variant, APOE ε4, is often treated as a simple yes-or-no factor. Records from a large imaging initiative covered 1,115 people with mild impairment, grouped by whether they held zero, one, or two copies.

Just over a third worsened to dementia during follow-up. Typical time without worsening fell sharply with each added copy. It ran from over eighteen years with no copy to under three and a half years with two copies. The no-copy figure rests on late follow-up, though. Each copy raised the hazard even after brain size and test scores were counted. Larger memory-centre volume, by contrast, protected.
pmc-13298206:
Diagnostic PCR fails when stray chemicals from patient samples stall the enzyme that copies RNA, and Inês F Costa with colleagues worked out why some engineered enzymes resist in a 2026 study. They tested five variants of a retroviral reverse transcriptase against eleven clinically relevant inhibitors across temperatures from 40 to 70 °C.

A recurring set of mutations, including E69K and W313F, marked the toughest enzymes, apparently by gripping the nucleic acid target more firmly. Tolerance peaked near 40 °C, where binding stayed productive; the unmodified enzyme was shut down by several inhibitors outright. The authors offer design rules for sturdier enzymes in sensitive RNA tests.
pmc-13299506:
Two caterpillar fungi from different mountains run different ecological strategies, suggests a 2026 preliminary multi-omics study by Yanpeng Ding and colleagues. They compared Chinese cordyceps from Nagqu, Tibet, with Xinjiang cordyceps from the Altai Mountains across microbes, metabolites, and genomes.

The Tibetan fungus paired with specialized, host-adapted bacteria geared to nutrient capture. The Altai species instead hosted diverse decomposer fungi and a soil-like bacterial community rich in defense and biofilm genes, which may explain why its fruiting bodies persist three to five years. Its genome had shed many gene families. The authors stress single-site sampling and frame the work as hypothesis generation.
pmc-13299606:
COVID in pregnancy, caught or blocked by a shot, wakes a clear immune stir in the afterbirth, yet leaves its flesh near whole. Nils Hoymann and his team show that in a 2026 study of 118 afterbirths born in weeks 37 to 40 of pregnancy.

Gene and protein reads split the groups. Afterbirths from shot or past-ill moms showed shifts in S100B, IL6, and CCL5. Sharp live ill trimmed two more marks, p38 MAPK and Bcl-2. Cells grown from the births let out more immune calls, G-CSF and IL-8 among them. Yet the flesh, seen through the scope, split by group in scant ways. The team read the stir as real but short of true harm.
pmc-13300206:
Are fillings and extractions spread evenly across the mouth? Bojana Milekić and colleagues answer with 30,063 treatment records from 2,738 patients at one private practice, covering 1999 to 2025, in a 2026 retrospective study. They sorted restorations, extractions, root-canal work, and prosthetics by tooth position, jaw, age, and sex.

Left and right sides matched closely overall, supporting symmetry as a working assumption in diagnosis. One finding survived strict correction: extra work on the right first premolar, driven by the lower jaw. The upper jaw drew 56.3 percent of interventions against 43.7 percent for the lower. Weaker hints in younger adults faded after correction, so the authors urge care in generalizing.
pmc-13300806:
S S Popescu and co-authors report early German experience with same-day discharge after electrophysiology procedures in a 2026 prospective study. Sending ablation patients home the same day could free hospital capacity as fibrillation cases climb, yet overnight stays remain the European norm. One hundred patients discharged under a strict eligibility protocol were matched against one hundred who stayed overnight, with a next day check for groin problems and fluid around the heart.

Median discharge time in the early group was about five and a half hours after the procedure. Early complications ran lower in the discharge group, though not significantly, and seven percent showed an issue at the day one visit without anyone needing admission. Emergency visits, unplanned clinic calls, and readmissions over thirty days were comparable. Because the discharge group was younger and healthier, the authors frame the result as proof of feasibility for carefully chosen patients.
pmc-13301006:
Mohammed A Alqawasma and co-authors describe a pulmonary vein clot found by chance during endobronchial ultrasound in a 2026 case report with literature review. A forty-seven-year-old woman was having robotic bronchoscopy biopsy and ultrasound guided node sampling for a lung mass. A filling defect was spotted inside a branch of her right lower pulmonary vein. CT angiography confirmed the thrombosis, and blood thinning treatment worked.

Pulmonary vein thrombosis is rare, easily missed, and usually tied to lung surgery, transplantation, cancer, or ablation procedures. The authors' search found earlier ultrasound finds of this kind were exceedingly rare and mostly malignant clots. That makes this bland incidental clot, in their account, a first of its type in print. They argue the case shows ultrasound bronchoscopy can surface serious vascular findings beyond its lymph node brief, with real consequences for management.
pmc-13301106:
R Rademaker and co-authors compare how often mapping catheters themselves provoke dangerous rhythms during scar related tachycardia ablation, in a 2026 prospective two-center study. Thirty heart attack survivors underwent functional substrate mapping with both a multi-spline catheter and a single tip catheter in random order, under set pacing protocols, with strict safety stop rules.

The multi-spline tools mapped far faster and gathered double the points. They also caused far more mechanical mischief. Over half the patients had at least one catheter triggered tachycardia, against seventeen percent with the single tip. Every emergency shock for a triggered rhythm happened during multi-spline mapping. The protocol had to be abandoned early in twenty-seven percent of patients, always while the multi-spline catheter was in use. The authors urge a careful risk benefit calculation before choosing speed over gentleness in fragile ventricles.
pmc-13301406:
A Giomi and co-authors probe whether fragmented signals truly mark nerve clusters worth ablating in a 2026 mapping study. Ganglionated plexi, knots of the heart's nerve network, are targets for fainting treatment, yet the jagged electrograms used to find them may reflect passing nerve traffic rather than fixed anatomy. Thirteen patients without structural heart disease had right atrial maps drawn before and after a two milligram dose of atropine, a drug that silences that traffic.

Baseline maps showed a pattern on the back septal wall: three zones, each with a heavily fragmented core wrapped in lighter fragmentation. Atropine shrank the fragmented territory in all three zones. The outer rings melted away under the drug, marking them functional, while the cores resisted, marking them structural. The authors warn that standard fragmentation criteria overshoot the plexus area, and suggest aiming ablation at the resistant core could cut risk while keeping the benefit.
pmc-13301706:
When a heart attack patient has several blocked arteries, should doctors fix them all, and when? Trials over the past decade moved practice away from treating only the culprit lesion in stable patients.

Angiography-guided complete treatment holds the firmest evidence, while physiology-guided selection trims procedures without beating it head-to-head. Imaging inside the artery adds plaque detail, though outcome trials in this setting stay scarce. Early treatment of extra lesions suits selected stable patients, but no universal immediate rule exists, and shock cases remain the hardest call, the authors conclude.
pmc-13301806:
Adnan Ismaiel, Jackson Maul, and Patricia Millner compare the genomes of two closely related Trichoderma fungi in a 2026 study. Both species are hard to tell apart, yet each shows promise for protecting crops from disease and boosting plant growth. The authors searched both genomes for genes tied to those farm uses.

Each species carries seven chromosomes, though one holds roughly a thousand extra genes overall. Genes for enzymes that attack fungal cell walls and break down plant material were slightly more numerous in Trichoderma asperellum. That species also carried extra genes for making protective compounds and fifteen copies of a ribosomal marker region, against seven in its relative. The authors note that one genome lacked annotation, so follow-up work on gene activity is still needed.
pmc-13301906:
I Bozzi and co-authors ask, in a 2026 population study, how abnormalities on a standard ECG shift the heart age that artificial intelligence reads from the trace. This ECG-age, and its gap from real age, predicts future cardiovascular trouble. Which trace faults push the estimate upward was not well mapped.

The team analysed just over two million ECGs from a large telehealth network, keeping only each person's first clean recording. Traces were classed as normal or carrying minor or major faults under a standard coding system. Both fault classes were linked to a higher age gap, with major faults showing roughly double the effect of minor ones. Men also showed larger gaps than women, which may sharpen how this biomarker is interpreted.
pmc-13303006:
Tara Srinivasan and Afshan Khan wrote a paper from 2026 that sets out a dance-based plan to support teen mental health. Teen mental health problems are rising around the world. Yet cost, distance, staff shortages, and shame keep many teens from the usual care. The authors argue for low-cost, easy-to-reach options that sit next to clinic care rather than in place of it.

Their plan joins movement, feeling, social contact, and calm focus in short dance sessions. A session led by a guide takes ten to fifteen minutes, and a self-led one takes less than five. No special training is needed, and the sessions can run online. A trial workshop with twelve adults showed how the plan works in practice. A web site built on the plan now reaches more than five hundred students, which hints at how far it could spread.
pmc-13303906:
Durga Prasanna Misra and co-authors edit a 2026 collection on Takayasu arteritis, a rare inflammation of large arteries. Topics span inherited risk, immune drug therapy, artery wall change, heart involvement, surgery, and a new ultrasound method.

One study links a gene variant tied to steroid resistance with more steroid side effects and blocked-artery events in 81 patients. Another follows a young woman whose narrowed arch arteries reopened over seven years on an interleukin-6 blocking drug. Testing for steroid risk and starting biologic drugs earlier in high-risk patients are raised as practical steps.
pmc-13304606:
Silvia Dimova leads a 2026 study of paper sheets coated with a conducting polymer and carbon nanotubes that clean dye from water under light. Cheap, flexible hybrids could treat colored wastewater without costly powders.

A carboxyl-bearing polyaniline wrap was grown around nanotubes in acid, forming stable inks that soaked evenly into filter paper fibers. Two starter chemicals were compared for coating quality. Layer checks confirmed tight contact between polymer and tubes and even coverage. Under ultraviolet light the sheets broke down a test blue dye, showing promise for low-cost water cleanup tools.
pmc-13306406:
Calin Romulus Fodor reported outcomes for a canine bypass implant method in severe upper jaw bone loss in a 2026 case series. Thirteen patients missing back upper teeth lacked height for standard upright implants and faced large grafting as the alternative.

Nineteen long one-piece implants were angled beside the canine root to grip distant hard bone near the nose or palate. Scan checks showed nasal grip in 84.2% and palatal grip in 73.7% of implants in reported figures, with average follow-up of 26.1 months. The series presents early survival and placement results for this graft-sparing route.
pmc-13306606:
Hyung-Ju Seo mapped how a kidney drug, atrasentan, breaks down in human liver material in a 2026 study. Knowing activation routes matters because liver harm is a known risk for this endothelin-blocking candidate.

High-resolution mass checks combined with feature networking found eighteen breakdown products from phase one and phase two changes in reported results. Named routes included demethylenation, dealkylation and hydroxylation, plus sugar tagging for removal. Enzyme typing with single human enzymes showed which liver proteins drive each step, sharpening the safety picture for later trials. The map may help drug makers spot liver risk at an early stage.
pmc-13306806:
Roksana Aftab moved a salt-handling gene from a salt-loving grass into a laboratory plant in a 2026 study. The gene SvNHX2, from Sporobolus virginicus, codes a vacuole pump that locks sodium away from sensitive cell parts.

Salt switched the gene on strongly, mainly in shoots of the source grass. Engineered Arabidopsis grew better at 100 and 125 mM salt on plates and at 100 mM in water culture in reported trials. Roots stored more sodium while potassium held steady, pointing to safe compartment storage as the protective route. The gene may be of use in crops grown on salty ground near the sea.
pmc-13307106:
Marwah Albeladi proposed an energy-aware control frame for dense 6G internet-of-things networks in a 2026 study. Future networks promise 1 Tbps peaks and latency under 0.1 ms, yet device crowds swell control chatter and power use.

The EASE-6G design installs flow rules ahead of need, forecasts traffic with a memory network, and trims signalling through a learning controller. Simulations in OMNeT++ with Simu5G compared the design against two rival smart network schemes. Energy fell while performance held in reported runs, supporting predictive control for very dense device fields.
pmc-13307606:
Federica Loi and co-authors analyze a cattle disease epidemic in Sardinia in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Lumpy skin disease, a viral illness spread by biting insects, returned to Italy in June two thousand twenty-five after six years away from Europe. Sardinia had never had it before.

Seventy-nine outbreaks were confirmed in the first season, most from local spread. The epidemic doubled in under two weeks early on, and spread moved at a median pace of several kilometers a day. One tight cluster in the center-east held about a quarter of outbreaks. Vaccination cut farm-level outbreak risk by roughly eighty-two percent. The authors assess how fast control measures worked under field conditions.
pmc-13308206:
Nikhil Benroy Noronha and co-authors survey in 2026 researchers and ethics board members across India on how ethics review works for trials run at many sites. Replies came from 106 researchers and 136 board members with such trial experience, gathered from August to October 2024 through network sampling.

Only a fifth of researchers and under a third of board members backed the current site by site model as it stands. Few called the process both effective and fast, and views split on joint, named, or national review as the fix. Shared blocks spanned clashing rulings, slow timelines, thin resources, and poor talk between boards. All sides agreed the system needs reform.
pmc-13308906:
Agnik Saha and co-authors grade in 2026 large language models that write about breast and cervical cancers for the public, on word skill, safety, and ease of grasp. They tested five broad models and three medical models on real world questions drawn from public medical data sets.

Broad models, led by Llama 3 and Gemma, wrote with the best flow and warmth in expert and metric checks. Their prose often ran too hard for wide crowds to grasp at a glance. Medical models wrote in simpler words yet scored worse on safety, with more made up claims, bias, and harsh tone. Mixed designs that join both strengths are the path the authors favour.
pmc-13309506:
Heta Mattila and colleagues compare how two seaweeds handle harsh light in a 2026 study. Green macroalgae differ in whether they can switch on a fast safety valve that sheds excess light energy as heat. One alga here lacks that fast valve, while a look-alike relative has it.

Both algae faced steady and flickering strong light, and damage to their light-harvesting system was tracked. Damage rates matched between light patterns and between the two algae. The alga without the fast valve recovered more slowly and moved energy along more slowly under strong light, while its relative sped up. A drug that blocks the safety valve changed the picture further. The authors read the slower recovery as control, not extra harm.
pmc-13310206:
Pau González and co-authors test a designer Wnt signal booster after spinal cord injury in rats in a 2026 study. The Wnt pathway can aid repair, but natural Wnt proteins are hard to make and hit many targets at once. A fused surrogate called scFv-Dkk1c switches the pathway on more cleanly.

Rats with spinal cord injury received the surrogate during recovery, and movement recovery was the headline measure. Treated rats regained movement better than untreated injured rats in the reported results. Myelin sparing, nerve cell counts, immune cell behavior, blood vessel growth, and serotonin fiber return were also checked. The authors present the surrogate as a cleaner route to Wnt-based spinal repair.
pmc-13310506:
Congfeng Li and co-authors test a blood ratio for judging pneumonia severity in older adults in a 2026 study. Community-acquired pneumonia hits older patients hard, and simple admission markers help sort who needs intensive care. A ratio joining a cell enzyme, lactate dehydrogenase, to the protein albumin was the candidate.

Records covered 423 patients aged 60 and older at six Chinese hospitals between 2022 and 2025, with severe pneumonia in 102 cases, or 24.1 percent of the cohort in the report. Higher transformed ratio values on admission linked strongly to severe disease in first analyses. Group splits by age, sex, and other diseases checked whether the link held broadly. The authors propose the ratio as a cheap severity flag.
pmc-13310606:
Christine Yu and co-authors survey two foodborne viruses in farm irrigation water across the United States in a 2026 study. Norovirus and hepatitis A virus can reach crops through tainted water and spark outbreaks. How often they occur in farm water, and which trapping method finds them best, guided the work.

Monthly samples over two growing seasons came from 36 sites on 21 farms in Georgia and Ohio. Two trapping methods concentrated viruses from ten-liter samples for gene testing. Detection hit 8.4 percent for one norovirus group and 9.4 percent for hepatitis A across the sampling in the study, spread over 24 sites on 15 farms. Spiked-water tests then compared method recovery head to head.
pmc-13310706:
Agnieszka Kamińska led a 2026 nationwide survey on eye health supplements among adults in Poland. Many people take vitamins or oils for vision, yet public knowledge of diet and eye health is unclear. The survey asked what people know, what they take, and why they take it.

Answers came from 1,090 adults in March 2026 through an online poll. Only a small share rated their own knowledge as good, yet more than one quarter used eye supplements. Prevention and doctor advice were the top reasons, with antioxidant vitamins and omega-3 oils most common. Use was higher among people who wore glasses or had an eye diagnosis.
pmc-13310806:
Stéphane Legleye and co-authors study alcohol, tobacco, and cannabis use among second generation immigrants in France in a 2026 survey. First generation immigrants often use less than the majority group, but the second generation path is less clear. Keeping the heritage language at home may guard against higher use.

A national sample focused on 2,736 people from Maghreb and southern Europe roots, compared with 19,185 majority peers. First generation use was lowest. Second generation peers who spoke the heritage language at age 15 used less than peers who spoke only French. Mixed parentage also shaped use. Prevention that honors culture may help most.
pmc-13310906:
Ping Wu and co-authors compare mental and social state in COVID-19 patients with and without chronic illness in a 2026 study. Long term illness may deepen anxiety and low mood during infection and weaken coping and support. The team used standard scales plus blood markers at a Fujian hospital.

Sixty patients were enrolled in early 2023, with 46 who had chronic illness and 14 who did not. Patients with chronic illness scored higher on anxiety and depression and differed on coping, support, and a blood ratio marker. A shy, stressed personality type linked to combined anxiety and low mood. Joint medical and mental care may help this group.
pmc-13311006:
Jarosław Garski and Dariusz Walkowiak study doubt about smart tools among Polish health workers in a 2026 mixed methods paper. Hospitals often blame slow uptake on staff skill gaps. Role alone, whether doctor or manager, poorly foretold resistance in their data.

Four outlook groups emerged instead, from skeptics to optimists, split by cost focus and practical stance. Stated skill gaps masked deeper defenses such as work exhaustion, legal fear, and tight budgets. Leaders should drop generic role based training and craft change plans per outlook group. Trust repair, not just teaching, drives uptake.
pmc-13311206:
Yi-San Lee and co-authors test in 2026 a plant-based feed mix for calves, blending extract of the herb Bidens pilosa with bentonite clay into a formulation called BPB. Calf diarrhoea drives antibiotic use, medical costs, and deaths in young herds, and resistance concerns push farmers toward options. Gut health drives growth, since the calf gut handles food breakdown, nutrient uptake, and mucosal defence.

The study tests BPB as an option aimed at diarrhoea control and gut microbe balance. Its aim is to raise gut germs linked with helpful effects while cutting germs tied to harm. Feed use sits among the results under study, tying microbial shifts to growth. Probiotics have given mixed results in calves because strains vary and stay is short. A stable phytogenic powder avoids some of those problems, which is the appeal behind testing this mix in livestock farming.
pmc-13311306:
Giulia M. Stella and co-authors set out the plan for the ATHENA study in 2026, testing a sport-based program after lung cancer surgery. Surgery saves lives but weakens breathing muscles and quality of life.

Patients who had lung removal for early-stage cancer and scored best on fitness review will train at a university sports medicine center in Pavia. The plan runs three sessions a week for six months in training blocks. Breathing tests, exercise capacity, energy use, and quality of life are checked at start, three months, and six months. The pilot design will show whether the program is workable.
pmc-13311906:
Yuanxin Cao and colleagues describe their 2026 project building a web-based mindfulness platform for families of organ donors. Donor families face sudden decisions and social stigma, and support for them is scarce.

The team first rated existing mindfulness apps with a standard scale and studied the best ones' features. Guided by an information-motivation-skills model, they built a platform with seven sections, from lessons and practice rooms to quizzes and community exchange. A before-and-after test in users showed easing of trauma, depression, and anxiety signs. The platform gives hospitals a ready tool for donor family care.
pmc-13312006:
Srikanth Nalla, Pravin Sudhakar Patil, and Sireesha TV report a 2026 case of a giant ovarian cyst that proved benign despite its size. Big adnexal masses usually raise strong cancer fears.

The patient, a 53-year-old woman, had four months of belly swelling and missed periods. Ultrasound showed a 27 cm cystic mass. Contrast CT found a smooth cyst with near-water density readings of 0 to 4 units, no enhancement, and no solid parts, fluid spread, or gland swelling. Tumor markers sat near normal. Staging surgery followed, and tissue study confirmed a benign mucinous cystadenoma. Water-like density, they argue, predicts benignity better than size.
pmc-13312106:
Marina Bogiatzis and co-authors present a 2026 scoping review of education programs for patients having colorectal surgery that leaves them with a stoma. Living with a stoma brings physical, psychological, and social challenges, and teaching around the time of surgery is meant to ease the adjustment.

Searching four databases through mid-November 2024, the team gathered 35 articles from 18 countries. Most programs relied on face-to-face teaching by nurses, backed by written material or tools such as telehealth and mobile apps, and a few involved peers or patients in designing the teaching. Education improved knowledge, self-care, and quality of life, while teaching both before and after surgery was linked to shorter hospital stays and fewer complications. The authors favor combined, personal approaches across the whole pathway.
pmc-13312706:
Chiara Terzo, David C. Burr, Xin-Yu Xie, and Maria Concetta Morrone report a 2026 study on how the brain carries visual detail across eye movements. Each quick jump of the eyes forces the visual system to join new views with what came just before. The team studied a bias called serial dependence, where a past view pulls the current one toward it.

Volunteers viewed a brief striped patch at set angles, then reported its angle from memory while brain signals were recorded. Rhythms in the alpha band, timed to each eye movement, tracked how strong the memory trace was. Stronger alpha signals meant a weaker bias effect. The results suggest these rhythms help hold detail steady across eye movements.
pmc-13312806:
Paulina Sindrewicz-Goral and co-authors review, in a 2026 article, how drug designers might attack galectin-3, a sugar-binding protein implicated in cancer, inflammation, and fibrosis. Inhibitors exist and some have done well in early trials, but every one of them aims at the same canonical binding pocket on the protein's recognition domain, the so-called S-face.

The review maps galectin-3's three-part construction and the distinct jobs of each segment, then argues the target is bigger than one pocket. The opposite F-face of the recognition domain can also bind sugars through a non-canonical interface. The flexible N-terminal tail, unique to galectin-3 among its family, offers a spot rivals cannot cross-react with. Drugs touching several segments at once, or combinations aimed at different segments, could beat single-site blockers, the authors propose.
pmc-13313006:
Bassem A Almalki presents a 2026 systematic review of MeltDose extended-release tacrolimus, the backbone anti-rejection drug for organ transplants, whose narrow safety window makes its delivery form matter. The MeltDose formulation, sold as Envarsus XR, was engineered to dissolve better, absorb more fully, and swing less between doses than the standard immediate-release version.

Searching two databases through October 2025, the review gathered 351 records and kept six studies across kidney, heart, and conversion settings, combining them narratively because designs differed too much for pooling. Rejection rates matched the standard drug closely, with graft survival and mortality also comparable. The consistent edge was dose: patients held therapeutic blood levels on roughly 20 to 30 percent less drug per day. Almalki concludes the pharmacokinetic gain is real, while proof of better long-term outcomes is still pending.
pmc-13313206:
Bryan D. Lakey and co-workers study the gut microbe Akkermansia muciniphila in a 2026 paper on how sugars from mucus control when it starts to grow. The microbe lives on mucus sugars in the colon and supports host metabolism, yet the gut mix of foods and sugars shifts by host, gut region, and state of health.

The team compared a human strain and a mouse strain of the microbe. Food sugars acted on the two strains in unlike ways, hinting at tuning to each host. In contrast, several sugars taken from mucin delayed the start of growth in both strains, in a dose-linked way. Gene suppressor tests pointed to sugar kinases and a part of a sugar uptake system as brakes. The lag before growth thus acts as a key checkpoint for settling in the gut.
pmc-13314406:
Rongrong Song and a large team set out a trial plan, published in 2026, to test whether a neck nerve block can cut delirium after gut cancer surgery in older patients. Delirium after surgery is common and grave in this group, bringing longer stays, more illness and death, and high costs.

The stellate ganglion block calms the sympathetic nerves and may ease inflammation, but firm trial proof in this setting is lacking. Their single-center trial will enroll 174 patients aged 60 years or more set for radical gut cancer surgery. Patients will split evenly between the real block and a sham one, as planned in the protocol. Neither patients nor outcome judges will know who got what. The study aims to give a clear verdict on a cheap, simple guard against a feared complication.
pmc-13314806:
Tess Allegra Forest, Margaret L. Schlichting, and Amy S. Finn study how learning speed shapes memory in children and adults, in a paper from 2026. Young learners must weigh keeping fine detail of each event against drawing broad lessons from many events.

Their preregistered study scanned the brains of 35 children aged 9 to 10 years and 35 adults, as counted in the report, during a pattern learning task. A decoding method told whether each brain caught the hidden structure early or late. Adults who caught it early formed only general memories, while late catchers kept both detail and gist. In children the pattern flipped into a trade-off of its own, by the results reported. The work links the pace of learning to how memory types split as we grow.
pmc-13315006:
Hyun Jung Park, Hyeri Kim, Sanghoon Byun, and Chongsuk Ryou build a 3D brain cell ball that can catch prion disease, in a 2026 study. Prion diseases are fatal and catching, marked by misfolded prion protein piling in the brain, and flat cell cultures miss the brain web of cell ties.

Their spheroids grow from mouse neural stem cells into mixed balls of neurons and astrocytes. Dosed with a lab prion strain, the balls showed cell death and astrocyte flare, echoes of real disease. They also bred more prions and stayed infectious, and they kept their traits after freezing, as the authors report. The model lets labs watch prion spread over time and screen drugs in a brain-like setting, short of animal work.
pmc-13315806:
Jimpei Hitsuwari tested in 2026, in a preregistered study, how comfort with ambiguity relates to resting brain connectivity in a Japanese sample. A prior study had linked higher tolerance with stronger links in integration and control networks, and lower tolerance with stronger threat and error monitoring circuits.

Thirty-nine participants had resting MRI scans and completed a three-part ambiguity scale covering discomfort, absolutism, and need for complexity. Targeted region-to-region tests, adjusted for age, sex, and head motion, found no clear link for any dimension. Effects were negligible, though need for complexity showed a small simple correlation with one parietal to frontal link. The flat result still helps guide the next round of work.
pmc-13315906:
Haoyue Zhang and co-authors studied in 2026 how rock and tectonic forces shape how fast mountain vegetation bounces back after disturbance. Plant type and temperature ruled the global pattern, with trees most resilient, then herbs and shrubs, together explaining 86 percent of spatial variation across mountain datasets.

After climate and human effects were removed, rock pathways still mattered strongly. Tree resilience peaked on steep, actively cut ground over hard plutonic and metamorphic rock and over carbonate rock. Herb resilience tied to soil carbon on mafic and metamorphic rock, while shrubs stayed mostly temperature driven and warmed less on poor soils.
pmc-13316206:
Tae Joung Ha and Jin Hwan Lee profiled green perilla seeds in 2026 at three ripening stages, unripe, mid-ripe, and fully ripe, for metabolites and antioxidant strength. Green perilla serves as food and medicine in East Asia, and advanced mass spectrometry identified twelve plant chemicals with stage-linked patterns.

Six isolated phenolics peaked at mid-ripe, reaching 28,697.8 micrograms per gram in the reported totals, while protein and oil rose steadily toward full ripe and oil share climbed from 13.5 to 46.1 percent across stages. Antioxidant tests were also strongest at mid-ripe, guiding the best harvest point for functional use.
pmc-13316306:
Katarzyna M Luda and colleagues, in a 2026 mouse study, ask whether a long-lasting viral infection makes fat tissue and liver disease worse in obesity. White fat normally buffers lipids for the whole body. That buffering fails in obesity and during chronic infection, allowing fat to build up in the liver.

Obese mice were infected with a chronic strain of lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus. Infection caused lasting loss of white fat, steady weight loss and fewer resident macrophages in visceral fat, alongside worse fatty liver disease. Removing CD8 T cells helped only slightly. Blocking tumour necrosis factor or controlling blood sugar with metformin also failed to reverse the changes, pointing to distinct virus-driven metabolic harm in obesity.
pmc-13316606:
Gabriel Hooper and co-authors, reporting in 2026, chart how treatment unfolds for advanced prostate cancer that no longer responds to hormone therapy. Many drugs now exist, from chemotherapy and hormone pathway blockers to targeted and radioligand treatments. Whether patients actually reach later lines of therapy is less clear.

The cohort held 5,096 patients who began first-line treatment between January 2021 and June 2025. Just over half reached a second line, and about a quarter reached a third. Hormone pathway inhibitors dominated early lines, while taxane chemotherapy became most common later. The authors call for better sequencing, stronger first treatments and improved access so fewer patients drop out between lines.
pmc-13317806:
Marwa H Elajami reports, in 2026, a single case of recurrent vaginal atrophy treated with rose stem cell exosomes plus hyaluronic acid. Low oestrogen thins the vaginal lining and causes dryness, irritation and raised acidity. Long-term hormone treatment worries many patients, prompting interest in non-hormonal options.

The patient was a 41-year-old woman approaching menopause whose discomfort, dryness, itching and discharge had resisted repeated antimicrobial treatment. Examination showed pale thin tissue with reduced lactobacilli and no infection. She received three intravaginal sessions, spaced about a month apart, using freeze-dried exosomes mixed with hyaluronic acid and delivered by electroporation. Follow-up biopsy showed a thicker lining and symptoms eased, with no short-term local side effects. The author stresses that one uncontrolled case cannot prove safety or benefit.
pmc-13318606:
Weiping Lu and co-workers present a 2026 modelling study using MRI scans. The scans were taken before surgery for perianal abscess. The model predicts whether Escherichia coli or another germ is the cause. That distinction guides antibiotic choice. Records came from 215 patients with confirmed abscess cultures.

Image features came from three scan types. Clinical details such as sex and diabetes joined them. Both details were strong predictors in the analysis. A combined score was drawn as a nomogram for bedside use. It reached an AUC of 0.885 in the testing set. Imaging alone scored 0.860 on that measure in the same testing. Calibration and decision checks also looked good. The authors propose a noninvasive step toward matching antibiotics to the likely germ.
pmc-13319006:
Kaipeng Fan and colleagues present a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis comparing magnetic seizure therapy with electroconvulsive therapy for major depression. Searches ran across six databases to November 2025. Thirteen studies with 607 participants were included. Response and remission were the main outcomes, with thinking effects tracked closely.

Response rates were comparable, with a relative risk of 1.10 for magnetic therapy in the pooled result. Remission also matched between treatments. One sensitivity check favoured electroconvulsive therapy on score change, so the authors urge caution. Magnetic therapy preserved thinking far better, with a large effect size of 1.19 in their analysis. Patients reoriented about seventeen minutes faster and had fewer side effects overall. The authors back it where memory concerns dominate.
pmc-13319506:
Marta Toledano-Fonseca and co-authors study blood tests for bowel cancer that has spread in a 2026 article on tumor side. Bowel tumors on the right and left sides act in unlike ways and respond to drugs in unlike ways too. Blood tests that track tumor gene bits can guide care, but side may change what those tests mean.

Blood from 232 patients was checked for tumor gene changes, the share of changed bits, and total loose DNA levels. On the left side, changed genes, high loose DNA, and a high tumor marker each tracked with worse outcomes. On the right side, only the share of changed bits carried clear weight. Side should be read alongside any such test.
pmc-13319706:
Nouf AlMuhanna and co-authors report, in 2026, successful use of baricitinib for a stubborn inflammatory skin disease in a twelve-year-old boy. The condition, abbreviated PLEVA, causes recurrent crops of red spots that can blister, die and crust, leaving pitted scars. Evidence points to misdirected T-cell activity, and standard treatments from antibiotics to immune suppressants often help only partly or briefly.

The boy had a generalised itchy eruption for two years, with a history of repeated tonsillitis and many antibiotic courses. Baricitinib blocks Janus kinase signalling, a pathway implicated in several T-cell skin diseases, and is approved for eczema and hair loss. His disease improved on the drug, the authors report, suggesting Janus kinase inhibition deserves study as an option for treatment-resistant cases.
pmc-13320006: A retraction notice issued in 2026 by the JMIR Publications Editorial Office withdraws a population study on stomach and food pipe cancers in China. The study had covered trends from 1990 to 2019 and forecasts to 2044 for cancers tied to food borne agents. The notice itself is the whole item here. It states that an author faked a peer review by posing as an assigned reviewer. All authors back the withdrawal. The case has gone to the home institute for more checks.
pmc-13320506:
Daigo Iwasaki and co-authors set out a 2026 lab method for checking active plant compounds in black ginger extract, a food ingredient widely used in Japan. Testing six related compounds normally needs six pure reference samples, which are hard to obtain. The new method uses just one reference sample plus a magnetic resonance technique that measures amounts directly.

Fast liquid separation on a special column reached a lowest measurable level of 2.00 units per litre for the set. Checks against a second mass based method confirmed the right compounds were being read. Accuracy and repeat results met AOAC rules for such tests. Fewer reference samples should lower cost and ease quality checks for makers in other places too.
pmc-13320706:
Zineb Bentounsi and co-authors survey, in 2026, young European family doctors and trainees about sustainable healthcare. Health services emit substantial greenhouse gases, and family doctors are well placed to cut that footprint if training prepares them. The survey circulated through a young family doctors network.

One hundred thirty respondents from fifteen countries took part, though most came from just three countries. About two thirds said they had never worked with sustainable healthcare before, and most of those answering said training had included no teaching on the topic. Knowledge scores centred on three of five questions, with younger respondents, women and trainees scoring higher. Nearly everyone answering supported adding planetary health to the family medicine curriculum. The authors call the findings exploratory and urge validated teaching tools.
pmc-13321206:
Vaibhav P. Mhaindarkar and colleagues probe, in 2026, how the two halves of an unusual DNA enzyme cooperate. Reverse gyrase, found in heat-loving microbes, winds DNA into positive supercoils using energy from ATP. One domain resembles a helicase and the other a topoisomerase, and they must move together for the reaction to work.

The team used hydrogen-deuterium exchange, a method that reveals which protein regions become exposed, to watch the enzyme from Thermotoga maritima bind DNA and a nucleotide analogue. DNA binding opened a region at the domain interface where two charged side chains interact. Removing those charges slightly boosted activity, while locking them together with a chemical bridge killed it. The results support a model where interface rearrangement is essential, and they sketch the first structural picture of the enzyme on DNA.
pmc-13321806:
Sadat Shafi and colleagues target the sugar supply of malaria parasites in a 2026 study. Drug resistant Plasmodium falciparum needs new attack routes. Parasites growing in red blood cells depend on steady glucose, brought in by a carrier called PfHT. Blocking that carrier could starve the parasite.

Computer docking over a drug database flagged the plant compound ginsenoside Rg1 as a candidate blocker, and yeast tests confirmed it targets PfHT. The carrier was more abundant in drug resistant parasites. Rg1 curbed growth in culture and boosted a standard partner drug in joint tests, which supports the starvation plan.
pmc-13322006:
Li and co-authors report a new recombinant strain of avian leukosis virus found in Chinese native chickens. These viruses cause tumors and weaken immunity, and they pose a real threat to poultry farms. The strain, named GD24LHB130, came from Qingyuan Partridge chickens in Guangdong Province in 2024. Full genome reads showed it is a type K virus carrying parts from type J. The swapped parts include the LTR, pol gene, and tail region.

In lab tests, the new strain copied itself much faster than classic type K strains. The type J LTR seemed to drive much of that gain. Tests in birds confirmed stronger disease effects. The findings warn that mixing between virus types can yield more harmful strains.
pmc-13322706:
Melville and co-authors test whether some early medical abortions in Australia can safely skip ultrasound in this 2026 study. Ultrasound normally confirms how far a pregnancy has advanced and where it sits. A history based checklist could spare women the scan, which is hard to reach in rural areas. Patients at several clinics completed the checklist, then had their usual scan anyway.

Of 705 patients, about two thirds were sure of their last period or conception date. The tool cleared 214 patients, roughly three in ten, for care without ultrasound. Every one of them proved to have a pregnancy inside the uterus, and only one was further along than the 63 day limit. Melville concludes the checklist identifies a group who can safely forgo routine scanning.
pmc-13322806:
Yue Sun and Zhenghao Hou study mobile internet use and depression in China in a 2026 article. Panel data from the China Family Panel Studies for 2020 to 2022 were analysed with fixed effects models. Mental health now sits high on national health agendas, and phone based internet shapes daily life for most residents.

Mobile internet use went with clearly lower depressive symptoms, and the result held after checks for reverse causation. Exercise frequency acted as one pathway, since heavier mobile use may support more activity, which in turn eases mood. Gains were stronger in vulnerable groups, including people with abnormal body mass and workers without pension cover. Fair digital access is urged.
pmc-13323706:
Zhishu Sun, Ruijing Geng, and Ge Zhang published a paper in 2026 on classifying items in hypergraphs while admitting the labels are fuzzy. A hypergraph links groups, not just pairs, and suits tangled real relationships. Most learning methods force each item into one crisp summary, yet attributes like a paper's keywords arrive noisy or incomplete, so the meaning is genuinely uncertain.

Their network first splits the hypergraph into two augmented views. Fuzzy encoders then learn representations that keep degrees of belonging rather than hard assignments. Contrast steps align the views at the level of single items, group links, and memberships, while decoders rebuild the structure to keep it honest. Across several datasets the fuzzy approach classified nodes better than crisp rivals, evidence that modeling uncertainty beats pretending it away.
pmc-13323806:
Brett M. Montelaro and team checked why proven heart failure drugs still go underused, by listening to real clinic conversations. Their 2026 paper is a secondary analysis of recorded visits from the POCKET-COST-HF trial, in which a checklist tool focused on prescription price transparency was used at two academic health centers. The team coded the transcripts to find what blocked tuning of guideline-directed therapy and where decision support could be improved.

Medical comorbidities were the most common barrier, but clinical inertia and drug cost also blocked tuning in a large share of visits. Many outpatient visits never addressed drug tuning at all. The authors conclude that refining activation and choice-support tools still has value at scale. This holds especially for tools that confront inertia and cost head-on, rather than assuming clinicians and patients will raise dosing on their own.
pmc-13324306:
Nina A M Houben leads a European study counting blood lost to lab tests in extremely preterm babies, published in 2026. Sixty-four neonatal units in 22 countries recorded diagnostic blood draws during the first 28 days for 320 babies born below 28 weeks, over six weeks per centre in 2022 to 2023.

Median birth weight sat near 800 grams in the cohort. Cumulative test losses by day 28 reached about half of calculated blood volume for babies born at 24 weeks, falling with each added week of gestation in the reported medians. Anaemia of prematurity is fed partly by this steady drain. The authors argue that test volumes deserve the same care as transfusion thresholds in tiny infants.
pmc-13325306:
Roderick C. Peul and team tested whether measured fluorescence imaging can track by the numbers sigmoid colon perfusion during open aortic aneurysm repair. Their 2026 study looked back at near-infrared glow tapes with green dye from 25 patients at a single center. Time-brightness curves from the sigmoid colon and small gut were rated as adequate, questionable, or poor, using four curve-derived blood-flow measures.

Blood flow deteriorated significantly after reconstruction on all four parameters, yet none of the 24 patients followed for gut damage developed colon ischemia. The authors read this as support for heightened awareness rather than immediate bowel resection when malperfusion is suspected, since a blood-flow dip alone did not predict tissue loss. The take-home message is practical: glow imaging gives the surgical team a real-time, objective blood-flow readout to guide decisions during repair.
pmc-13326306:
Jiao Yao and co-authors build a tool that flags spread of thyroid cancer beyond the gland, in work published in 2026. Spread of this kind shapes how wide surgery should be. The team drew on sound scans and cell images from near four hundred patients at five centers, spanning seven years.

They pulled traits from both image types and kept twenty-one for the joint model. The model beat models built on either image type alone, in training and in two test groups. It also raised the exactness of human readers by a wide margin. Trait weights showed sound traits led, with cell traits adding support. The authors offer the tool as a pre-surgery aid.
pmc-13327806:
Ellis Slotman and a large Dutch team chart radiotherapy patterns for bone metastases around the COVID-19 years in a 2026 study. Short courses of one or two large doses ease pain about as well as longer courses, yet uptake varied for years. Data came from eleven Dutch departments for 2018 to 2022.

In total 17,336 patients received 31,677 treatment courses, and 81.4 percent were short courses, though department shares ranged from 33.6 percent to 98.9 percent across centers. Short-course use rose clearly once the pandemic began in 2020, likely to cut hospital visits. A smaller group of 278 patients gave pain scores over three months for comparing outcomes between course lengths.
pmc-13327906:
Roland van den Tillaar compares two throwing wind-ups in elite handball in a 2026 study. Twenty-five top players made running overhead throws with either a circular or a whip-like wind-up while a camera system tracked ball speed, joint angles, and shoulder forces at 250 frames per second. Coaches debate which style loads the shoulder more.

Ball speed and peak outward shoulder rotation speed ran higher with the circular style, and key force peaks landed closer to release, while the whip style opened a wider rotation angle earlier. Peak shoulder torque and force, though, did not differ clearly between styles, only their timing did. Van den Tillaar cautions that the small sample cannot prove equal stress, so both throws should be coached with shoulder load in mind.
pmc-13332406:
Ibrahim Güler and co-authors tested whether large AI models that read images can judge cosmetic Botox results, in a 2026 observational study. Grading wrinkle change from photographs is subjective even for experts, so an automated judge would be valuable if it were trustworthy.

Four current multimodal models each judged 23 paired before-and-after facial cases five times, giving 460 evaluations in total. Every model picked the post-treatment photo correctly in all cases. Yet spotting which facial region improved often failed to beat simply guessing the most common answer, and no model beat the baseline around the eyes. The models claimed improvement far more often than raters had recorded it, with positive errors swamping missed ones, and repeat runs disagreed widely. The authors conclude the models grasp the general look of change but miss clinical nuance, and need specialist training and expert benchmarks before use.
pmc-13332506:
Sachin Singh and colleagues report a 2026 case in which leukemia immunotherapy briefly caused severe leaking of the mitral valve in a woman whose valve was already quietly vulnerable. She had taken the diet drug fenfluramine ten years earlier, a fact she disclosed only late.

The 48-year-old had B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia and only a trace of valve leakage at baseline. After her second blinatumomab cycle she developed acute heart failure. A repeat scan showed severe leakage with a restricted rear leaflet, without the body-wide inflammation or organ damage that drug reactions usually bring. The team held the drug, treated the heart failure, and the leak improved enough to restart therapy safely. They argue the drug's pressure shifts unmasked a fenfluramine-weakened valve, and that careful, non-judgmental history taking plus hemodynamic care can keep lifesaving treatment going.
pmc-13332606:
Antonello Cocchieri and colleagues examined whether hospital payment groups hide big differences in nursing work, in a 2026 retrospective study from a large Rome hospital. Diagnosis-related groups set standard payments, but two patients in the same group may need vastly different amounts of nursing care.

The study covered 14,169 adult stays discharged in 2022 across the 20 most frequent groups. Nursing diagnoses per stay ranged from 1 to 17 and nursing actions from 1 to 770, with wide spread even inside single groups.
