Sheean and colleagues present in 2026, as conference poster 11, a randomized trial of blood flow restriction therapy during the first twelve weeks of rehabilitation after knee ligament reconstruction. The therapy trains muscles with a cuff that partly limits blood flow, aiming to build muscle at low loads. Weak thigh muscles dog recovery, and the technique promised a shortcut.

Patients receiving a quadriceps tendon graft were randomized after surgery to identical work-matched exercise programs with or without the cuff for twelve weeks. Strength plus MRI-measured thigh muscle volume were then compared. Forty-five patients were randomized and thirty-eight completed the program. There were no differences between the groups in isometric or isokinetic thigh strength, and none in quadriceps or hamstring muscle volume at twelve weeks. The authors call it the largest such trial with a standardized surgical approach.
pmc-13531806:
Yingying Shen, Peiqing Zheng, and Jiaxu Zheng test in 2026 whether two gene variants raise lung cancer risk in a Chinese population. A case-control study genotyped 500 patients with non-small cell lung cancer and 500 matched controls on a mass-spectrometry platform. Smoking, sex, and age were handled in adjusted models.

One variant in TP63, a damage-response gene, and one in CIR1, tied to a growth pathway, each raised the odds of lung adenocarcinoma by roughly 40 percent after strict correction. The TP63 signal looked stronger in people who had smoked, though the interaction itself stayed unproven. Larger groups must confirm the findings.
pmc-13531906:
Hong-cheng Xing leads a 2026 mouse study uncovering a brake that protects jawbone from inflammatory breakdown in gum disease. A receptor called ROR2 in jaw stem cells normally traps a signaling partner and mutes production of an inflammatory messenger. Without that brake, mice lost more bone as bone-eating cells multiplied.

Removing the trapped partner gene rescued the bone balance in deficient mice. The team then built a temperature-sensitive gel carrying antibodies that neutralize the messenger. The gel eased gum disease bone loss in living animals, preserving bone-building capacity while trimming bone-eating coverage.
pmc-13532006:
Guanghui Shen and co-authors study in 2026 how mismatched distress between parents and teenagers relates to self-injury without suicidal intent. A total of 147 parent-teen pairs joined, with teens treated for depression or bipolar disorder. Both sides completed a standard distress scale, while teens reported self-injury frequency for surface-style analysis.

Teen distress alone tracked more self-injury across depression, anxiety, and stress measures. Mismatch itself predicted higher self-injury for all three dimensions, whichever side felt worse. For anxiety the harm curved upward at extremes in either direction. Family work on shared emotional understanding is the authors prescription.
pmc-13536706:
Can Wang and co-authors investigate a gene regulator called ATAD2 in womb lining cancer in a 2026 laboratory study. High levels of the regulator track with worse survival and faster cancer growth, so the team raised and lowered its levels in cancer cells and tested its partners. Animal tests also checked whether blocking the regulator slows tumors. The work links cell aging, immune escape, and tumor growth in one pathway.

ATAD2 was found to stabilize a second protein, SIRT7, which quiets a tumor guard pathway involving p53 and p21. With aging signals suppressed, cancer cells avoided an aged state and released fewer warning signals, while the tumor surroundings became less hostile to growth. Blocking ATAD2 restored those signals and slowed tumor growth and spread in animals. The authors propose ATAD2 as a drug target worth further testing.
pmc-13536906:
Geir Erland Tjønnfjord and co-authors report three patients with a rare inherited anemia caused by a new gene variant. Their 2026 paper covers congenital dyserythropoietic anemia type II, the most common form of a group where red cell making is faulty. The bone marrow overgrows with young red cells, many with two nuclei.

The three patients, from Somalia, were diagnosed in early adulthood. Each had mild anemia, with signs of red cell breakdown or raised young red cell counts. A binding test showed reduced binding in all three, fitting the disease. Gene tests found the same new variant in both copies of the SEC23B gene in each patient. Adding new variants to the catalog helps labs confirm this rare diagnosis in future patients.
pmc-13537106:
Ostermeier and colleagues reported that people with HIV on antiretroviral therapy carry many platelet-natural killer cell complexes in their blood, in a 2026 study. These are pairings of clotting fragments with antiviral immune cells. Natural killer cells are central to controlling HIV, yet they malfunction during infection. Platelets are activated under treatment, sticking to immune cells through a protein called P-selectin.

Ostermeier found the complexes more frequent in treated HIV patients than in uninfected controls. The killer cells inside complexes looked different: more activation markers and interferon production, but less of an activating receptor. Growing killer cells alongside platelets in the laboratory pushed them toward the activated profile. In macaques, complex levels tracked viral loads in blood and spinal fluid, and the link weakened after treatment with an antibody that blocks the platelet-gluing interaction. The authors propose platelet activation gluing to killer cells contributes to their dysfunction.
pmc-13537606:
Some ovarian cancers answer PARP-blocking drugs even without the classic BRCA faults, and a DNA repair protein may explain why. Ou Deng and co-authors compared drug-sensitive and drug-resistant cancer cell lines with normal BRCA genes. Chemical fishing with the drug pulled out different protein teams. One protein, MSH6, clustered more in the sensitive cells' drug complex. Tagging studies showed distinct signaling patterns between the groups as well.

Removing MSH6 made sensitive cells resist the drug. A growth pathway also answered the drug in opposite directions across the groups. The findings nominate MSH6 as a marker for who may benefit beyond the BRCA rule. Protein-team reading, the authors argue, beats gene lists alone for such calls.
pmc-13537906:
Serin Lee, Eunju Jang, and Jun Chang compare two flu vaccine targets for lung-resident killer T cells in a 2026 mouse study. Universal flu vaccines aim for lasting T cells in the lungs that attack shared viral parts. Nose-delivered virus carriers carrying either nucleoprotein or polymerase basic protein 1 produced similar cell counts in airways. Survival after a lethal flu dose and cell quality measures then separated the two vaccines sharply.

Only the nucleoprotein vaccine gave full survival. Its cells favored a surface pattern linked to stronger killing, showed far higher sensitivity to tiny viral signals, and killed more strongly inside lungs. Polymerase cells favored a different surface pattern with weaker performance. The authors argue that target choice should prize cell quality over cell count alone.
pmc-13538706:
Wenlai Cui and colleagues compare warm-up priming plans for tennis serve play in a 2026 test. Players primed upper limbs, lower limbs, or the full body with either ballistic or heavy work, then served at set gaps up to fifteen minutes later. Serve speed and accuracy were tracked across every setup and time point.

Serve speed rose after priming in all setups. Ballistic work beat heavy work overall, with its edge focused in the first nine minutes and strongest for upper limb and full body routines. Accuracy shifted over time but never differed clearly between setups at matching times. The authors advise ballistic upper or full body priming shortly before serving.
pmc-13539806:
Yuxiang He and four colleagues describe, in a 2026 case report, a stroke that followed stent placement in a neck artery. The patient, a 51-year-old man, had severe narrowing with a tear in the left vertebral artery and received a stent to hold it open.

After the procedure he became confused and lost memory, signs pointing to damage in the thalamus on both sides. Scans confirmed that pattern, caused by blockage of a variant vessel called the artery of Percheron, which feeds that region in some people. He recovered well with supportive care and rehabilitation. The authors warn intervention teams to watch for this rare clot complication.
pmc-13539906:
Ender Eren Ozcelik and seven colleagues map, in a 2026 bibliometric study, how research on immune treatment for solid tumors grew over twenty-five years. Their source was a title-based search of the Web of Science collection, checked against a high-impact subset from Scopus.

More than fifty thousand documents appeared between 2000 and 2025, with output climbing steeply after the first checkpoint drug approval in 2011. China now publishes more than the United States, though American papers gather more citations and wider collaboration. Topic maps shift from an early cytokine period to checkpoint drugs, then toward the tumor surroundings and treatment given before surgery.
pmc-13540206:
Fatemeh Navab and six colleagues examine, in a 2026 cross-sectional study, how swapping one protein food for another relates to the acid load of the diet in people on haemodialysis. Failing kidneys handle acid poorly, and protein choice is one lever patients can adjust.

Across several centres, 307 patients completed a long food frequency questionnaire, and blood albumin gauged nutritional state. Statistical swaps that kept calories equal produced counterintuitive results: replacing red or processed meat with dairy, legume, or nut protein tracked with higher odds of a heavy acid load. Directions reversed for several meat-for-plant swaps. Albumin levels strongly modified these patterns, the authors report.
pmc-13540406:
Kılınç Oktay and colleagues published a 2026 letter on a new gene fault behind low platelets from birth. A gene called MPIG6B helps build platelets, the blood bits that stop bleeding. Faults in it cause low platelets plus slow spleen and marrow changes. Their patient, a nine-year-old boy in Türkiye, carried a variant never reported before.

His platelet counts stayed low from his third day of life onward. At age four, anemia and a swollen spleen joined the picture. His sister and cousin also carried low platelet counts in the family. The same fault played out unevenly across the children in the family. The case widens the known range of this rare disorder. His parents were first cousins, a pattern tied to recessive inheritance.
pmc-13541806:
Catarina Coelho, René Bobe, and Susana Carvalho review wild neighbours in 2026. Their subject is primates and hoofed animals living side by side. Ecologists long noticed this pairing. Few studies treated it head-on. Sharing space and food raises basic questions. How do species persist together over time?

The authors gathered the published evidence on these pairs. They mapped where associations occur. They also mapped which species pair up. Gains and losses for each side were weighed. African studies dominate the record. Baboons beside small to medium antelope lead the list. Help with foraging is a common gain. Early warning against predators is another.
pmc-13542106:
Elham Bagheri and Yalda Mohsenzadeh model image memory in a 2026 study. They asked what makes some images stick after one viewing. Their tool is an autoencoder. That network squeezes an image into a compact code. It then rebuilds the image from the code. Memorability is a measurable property of images.

Images the network rebuilt badly tended to be memorable. The distinctiveness of each code also tracked memorability. A small prediction network read the codes. It forecast memorability scores robustly. Heat maps highlighted the visual features behind the forecasts. The authors argue this learned space mirrors human memory. Hard-to-rebuild images linger, much as odd scenes linger for people.
pmc-13542706:
Two patients in Nicaragua burned from the same rare drug reaction, and only one lived, in a 2026 case pair by Marvin Alfaro, Virgilio Blandón, and Miguel Borge. Both had the overlap form of Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, where skin and mucous membranes blister and peel.

The healthy 18 year old, with a low risk score, recovered fully on steroids. The 32 year old woman had advanced kidney failure; her skin improved, but her kidneys and then her organs failed, and she died on day 28 after refusing dialysis. The authors warn that the standard score misses deaths driven by sick organs.
pmc-13542806:
Yan Lin and co-authors test a digital diabetes program with behavioral nudges in this 2026 trial. Adults with type 2 diabetes need steady self-care, and online programs often lose users or show patchy results. Four Chinese hospitals randomized 293 adults to the nudge-rich program or to standard digital education. Scores were checked at the start and after twelve weeks.

The nudge group improved more on nearly every measure: blood sugar control, fasting glucose, weight, blood pressure, and cholesterol. Self-management behavior, confidence, and habit strength also rose more. Nearly all participants finished the study. The authors say pairing structured lessons with small behavioral prompts strengthens both body outcomes and the habits behind them.
pmc-13543306:
Ting Zhang and co-authors wrote a 2026 review of a gut germ that may support healthy aging. The germ, which lives in the gut lining, drops in many age linked diseases. Yet it is rich in very old people who stay healthy, which hints at a guard role.

The review sums proof that the germ and its products help the gut wall, calm long term swelling, and tune immune work. Gains in trials and lab work span brain, muscle, bone, vessel, and sugar health. Early human trials show promise for muscle loss and metabolic faults. The authors also flag hard points for clinic use, such as strain gaps, safety checks, and stable production. Large trials in old adults are still needed.
pmc-13543506:
Yusaku Yokotani and colleagues published a 2026 case report of a small gallbladder polyp that slowly grew into a precancerous tumour called intracholecystic papillary neoplasm. Such growths are rare, and small polyps are usually watched rather than removed. A 56-year-old woman's polyp measured 7.6 millimetres at discovery and reached 11.2 millimetres over two years and eight months. Enhanced scans showed a papillary lesion that took up contrast dye, and the gallbladder was removed by keyhole surgery.

Under the microscope the lesion proved to be the pyloric gland type of the neoplasm, with low-grade dysplasia and no invasive cancer. Staining for mucin proteins supported a gastric-type identity. No recurrence appeared during follow-up. Steady growth, a frond-like shape, and enhancement, the authors argue, can mark a neoplasm even below the usual ten-millimetre action threshold, so watchful waiting should not become neglect.
pmc-13543606:
Ha Thu Dinh's team validated a short questionnaire in 2026 for borderline personality features in Vietnamese adolescents, traits of emotional, relationship, and identity instability that connect to maltreatment and depression. No locally checked tool existed in Vietnam. The eleven-item scale was given, in Vietnamese, to 2,326 grade seven and nine students from eight randomly chosen northern schools. It sat alongside measures of maltreatment and depressive symptoms, and its structure was tested on split halves of the sample.

The scale proved consistent and single-factor, and it scored boys and girls on the same footing. Girls scored clearly higher than boys. Scores tracked closely with both maltreatment and depression, exactly as theory predicts. Schools and clinics in Vietnam now have a brief, locally checked screen for a high-risk trait pattern, the authors conclude, suitable for spotting teenagers who need fuller review.
pmc-13544206:
Hao Shen and co-authors published a research paper in 2026 on a skin patch sensor that measures sweat rate across its full range, from vapor to liquid flow. Sweat carries clues about stress, skin health, and dehydration, but older sensors read only one form. The patch pairs a microfluidic channel that senses liquid with a humidity element that senses vapor.

A water-repelling splitter membrane keeps the two modes from interfering and shields the humidity element from corrosion. The device reads continuously across a wide span of rates with fast response. The authors demonstrate uses in psychology testing, skin assessment, and dehydration checks, aiming at wearables that track body state through the day.
pmc-13545406: Cao and a large group of co-authors set out general requirements for a lab test that hunts leftover stem cells in cell products grown for therapy. Even tiny traces of undifferentiated stem cells can pose a safety risk, so makers need sensitive checks. The document frames the probe-based PCR assay as an ultra-trace measurement, where the detection limit supports a yes-or-no judgment. It calls for markers specific to stem cells and proper reference controls. The requirements adapt to products grown from many stem cell sources.
pmc-13546706:
Mohammed Babatunde Sadiq and colleagues ran a 2026 pilot study on whether routine hoof trimming stresses dairy cows that are not lame. Twenty healthy cows with normal gait and no hoof lesions were split into a group trimmed by the standard five-step Dutch method. A control group was only restrained as if trimmed. Blood cortisol, walking scores, time spent lying, feeding, and standing, plus milk yield, were tracked over two days.

Cortisol rose in both groups right after handling, showing restraint alone is stressful, yet trimmed cows kept higher cortisol and lay down more on the following two days. Walking scores and milk yield did not differ. The authors conclude that preventive trimming itself can cause short-term stress, and that letting cows rest matters for recovery.
pmc-13547206:
Xue Zhang and colleagues reported in 2026 a rare eye infection caused by Nocardia brasiliensis, a soil bacterium, that was first mistaken for ordinary eye inflammation. A 67-year-old man had two months of recurring pain and redness in his right eye before his vision collapsed quickly and pus appeared inside the eye. He had no known immune weakness, though testing found previously unrecognized diabetes.

Fluid from the eye plus gene sequencing identified the bacterium. Antibiotics given into the eye and by vein, followed by surgery to remove the eye's gel and fill the space with silicone oil, still could not stop the damage. The cornea clouded and his final vision in that eye was only light perception. The authors urge early microbe testing in stubborn eye inflammation.
pmc-13547706:
A large team of co-authors reports a study dated two thousand twenty-six on gene silencing inside a crop pathogen. The pathogen causes clubroot, a disease that swells the roots of cabbage-family crops. It belongs to the rhizarians, a major branch of life where gene silencing by RNA interference was barely studied and might even be lost.

Sequencing small RNAs across five life stages found many silencing RNAs of a characteristic size and pattern. The genome held two working copies of a key silencing protein but no copy of the usual cutting partner. A stand-in protein with a related part seems to fill that role, making the pathway unusual.
pmc-13548206:
Ana Maria Sandoval Barrantes and co-authors study an online course that teaches Peruvian health workers about diabetes and insulin, in this 2026 paper. Weak training limits insulin use across the country. The state launched the course in late 2021 for staff in public clinics.

The mixed study surveyed all enrollees, then interviewed a sample in depth. Five hundred thirty-six workers joined nationwide, and about sixty-three percent finished. Acceptability answers and completion patterns were read together. The authors judge whether flexible, cheap online training can close a national skills gap, and what keeps workers from finishing their modules.
pmc-13548706:
Stanslas Avaga and colleagues measure how often chemotherapy damages the nerves of cancer patients at a Ugandan regional center, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Nerve injury from platinum drugs, vinca alkaloids, and taxanes can progress to weakness and disability. Over two months, the team enrolled 235 adults on chemotherapy at Mbarara Regional Cancer Centre, interviewing patients, reviewing files, and scoring symptoms with a standard twenty-item tool.

Nearly a third of patients had chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy. Odds rose with age past sixty, with a past episode of nerve trouble that had resolved before chemotherapy, and with taking other nerve-toxic medicines alongside. Only about thirty percent of affected patients received any treatment, usually nerve pain drugs or vitamins, while guidelines recommend a specific antidepressant the center rarely used. The authors urge closer monitoring of high-risk patients so treatment starts promptly.
pmc-13549706:
Ryota Kitano and his seven co-authors report, in a 2026 case study, a young man's rare brain tumor that spread through the fluid around his spine. It then answered, for a while, to targeted drugs. The tumor type often carries a mutation called BRAF V600E. His also carried a second mutation linked to spread and poor outcomes. After three operations, radiation, and chemotherapy, the disease seeded his spine.

Spinal radiation came first. Then the team started a paired drug treatment that blocks the mutated pathway at two points. Scans showed the spread shrinking, and his symptoms eased. The reprieve lasted ten months before regrowth. He was still alive when the report was written. The authors present the pairing as a real option where no standard treatment exists, and they flag the second mutation as a possible marker for spread risk.
pmc-13550006:
Yunhee Kang and co-authors present a 2026 study of new mothers' sleep in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam. Sleep in the first month after birth is shaped by feeding and night care demands. Past work relied on mothers' own reports. This team used a wrist device to measure sleep and asked how sleep varies with feeding style.

Mothers at one month after birth slept about 5.5 hours a day, well under adult norms. Just under half fed only breast milk. Mothers fed about seven times by day and three times by night on average. After the team weighed social and care factors, feeding style showed no clear link to sleep length. Night feeding counts also showed no firm link. The results suggest new mothers' short sleep is near universal, not a feeding-style effect.
pmc-13550306:
Guang Zhang and colleagues dissect how the oyster mushroom defends itself against heat, in a 2026 molecular study. Heat waves bottleneck commercial production of Pleurotus ostreatus, ruining yield and quality. The team studied a gene for glutathione peroxidase, an antioxidant enzyme, and found it quiet during mushroom formation but switched on by stresses, heat above all.

Silencing the gene produced a surprise: the fungus grew faster, branched more, and suffered less heat damage, with lower chemical scarring from oxidation and a muted heat shock protein response. The silenced strains stockpiled more trehalose, a protective sugar, and a scavenger that mops up reactive oxygen erased that buildup, tying the effect to oxygen signaling. Blocking trehalose production restored heat sensitivity. The authors name the gene a breeding target for heat-hardy mushrooms.
pmc-13550406:
Ilaria Stanisci and colleagues gather the recent European evidence on air pollution and death from specific causes, in a 2026 review combining meta-analysis and meta-regression. Thirty-one studies from 2020 to 2025, including two large Italian projects, were screened, with pooled analysis possible for the fine particle studies. The team graded bias risk with an international tool.

Fine particles showed the clearest toll. Each added increment raised overall mortality by about a tenth in pooled terms. Cardiovascular and respiratory deaths also rose. Long-term exposure hurt more than brief spikes. Nitrogen dioxide tracked with the same three outcomes under long exposure, while coarse particles looked weaker and ozone evidence was mixed. Heavy differences between studies temper the numbers. The authors back tighter standards aligned with world health guidance.
pmc-13551306:
Bíró and colleagues present a 2026 longitudinal case study of how dreams changed during one year of psychotherapy with a 28-year-old patient. The patient had anxiety and depressive symptoms alongside ulcerative colitis, a chronic bowel inflammation. Five dreams judged clinically important were analyzed together with session notes and the patient's own associations.

Three themes ran through the dreams: vulnerability and loss of control, threat perception with emotional overwhelm, and emerging control and agency. Early dreams showed helplessness and sharp sensitivity to danger. Later dreams cast the dreamer as able to notice danger and respond in a more adaptive way. The authors suggest dream content can act as a sensitive window on improving emotion regulation during therapy, especially in psychosomatic care.
pmc-13551606:
Ashleigh Bull and co-authors test, in 2026, whether an unfunded network of burn centers can jointly study older burn patients. Older adults are a growing share of burn cases and need special care, yet single centers are too small to answer key questions. Twelve North American centers agreed to pool standardized data on patients aged sixty and older.

The shared database holds more than sixteen hundred patients treated over three years. Typical burns were small, yet one in ten patients died in hospital and healing took a median of forty days. Most had one operation within days. The pilot shows volunteer collaboration can produce useful shared data without grant money.
pmc-13551706:
Liyuan Zhang, leading six colleagues, published a 2026 retrospective study linking a simple insulin resistance marker to death after bleeding in the basal ganglia, a deep brain region. The triglyceride-glucose index had no established relation to prognosis in this stroke type. The single-center study followed 282 patients for one year, confirming deaths by standardized phone follow-up and modeling risk with survival methods.

Forty-nine patients, about one in six, died within the year. Each standard deviation rise in the index carried a notably higher mortality risk in the reported model, with risk climbing roughly linearly past a cutoff value the authors identified. Adding the index to a basic model improved some accuracy measures but not others, a mixed result the authors report plainly alongside robustness checks.
pmc-13551906:
Pengfei Zhang, Wanning Huang, Qiang Li, and Xiuyun Wu published a 2026 study of men's curling at the 2022 Beijing Winter Olympics. The team compared China with the medal-winning teams across 34 matches. They logged shot types and takeout moves. They compared tactical range and success rates. They then modeled which signs predicted a win.

China leaned on attacking shots such as draws and hit-and-rolls. Medal teams mixed attack and defense with wider range. Medalists also landed key shots more often. One takeout type predicted winning strongly in the models. Sweeping success predicted losing, oddly. The team reads sweeping as a rescue move used under pressure, not a cause of defeat.
pmc-13553506:
Dan Qi and six colleagues target nucleolin-driven cancer stemness in high-risk neuroblastoma. Neuroblastoma is the most common solid tumor outside the brain in children, arising from developing nerve-lineage cells. High-risk disease makes up about half of cases and drives most deaths. Event-free survival for high-risk disease stays near 40 to 50 percent, and relapse is typically fatal.

Cancer stem cells in neuroblastoma renew themselves, seed tumors, and fuel spread, treatment resistance, and return of disease. The team's earlier work tied nucleolin to upkeep of CD34-positive stem cells. Their 2027 paper reports that targeting nucleolin-driven stemness suppresses high-risk neuroblastoma in living models. The work points to nucleolin as a lever against relapse and resistance.
pmc-13555606:
Sen Yan, Xiaohong Wang, Cai Li, and Rong Wang review smart gel systems for stroke treatment in a paper from 2026. Ischemic stroke unfolds in fast-changing phases, from oxygen burst to inflammation to repair. Single-dose protectants match that timeline poorly. The review examines hydrogels loaded with nanozymes, tiny catalytic particles, that switch on under local cues. Cues include acidity, low oxygen, clotting enzymes, and inflammatory signals.

Designs vary in how particles are trapped, anchored, or assembled in place. The goal is phase-matched care of the vessel and brain tissue together. Direct evidence for full systems in stroke remains thin, the authors admit. They propose benchmarks for testing before any clinical claims. The piece is a design framework, not a readiness report.
pmc-13555906:
Abdirezak Mawlid Abdi and three colleagues analyse what Somalia needs to fold chronic disease and mental health care into basic clinics in a 2026 review. Somalia's coverage index sits very low, and clinicians number barely a tenth per thousand people. Chronic diseases already drive about two fifths of deaths. The team drew on national plans, disease burden estimates, and health accounts, then costed expansion toward eighty percent coverage by 2030.

Households pay nearly half of health costs from their own pockets, above the danger line for catastrophic spending. Medicines and supplies form the largest cost driver in the expansion model, reflecting years of chronic care. Gaps in financing and service delivery remain structural. The authors judge integration workable and frame it as the route toward universal coverage.
pmc-13556006:
Pelin Kiyat and Melis Palamar studied 524 healthy volunteers in 2026 to see how eye dominance lines up with hand dominance and eye structure. Participants aged 20 to 60 took a hole-in-card test for eye dominance and a standard handedness inventory. Detailed scans measured the cornea, retina, and choroid, while a separate device measured the length of each eye.

About six in ten volunteers were right-eye dominant. A striking crossed pattern appeared: people with a dominant left eye were far more often right-handed than people with a dominant right eye. Dominant eyes also showed a thicker central cornea once strict statistical corrections were applied, with some retinal measures trending the same way. Choroid measures did not differ. The findings matter for clinicians who plan surgery or interpret scans one eye at a time.
pmc-13556106:
Xiaoyong Xiao and thirteen colleagues identified in 2026 a protein, tenascin C, that helps drive abdominal aortic aneurysm, the dangerous ballooning of the body's main artery. A burst aneurysm kills most patients, and disordered artery wall muscle cells sit at the disease's core. The team combined single-cell sequencing of patient tissue, public data, clinical samples, and mouse experiments to trace the protein's role.

Tenascin C signals ran high in aneurysm tissue, and blood levels of the protein predicted the condition in patients. Mice engineered to lack the protein only in artery muscle cells formed fewer aneurysms under chemical provocation, with calmer muscle cell behaviour. Mechanistic work showed the protein pushes an inflammatory switch into the cell nucleus through a surface receptor. The pathway gives drug developers a defined target chain to interrupt.
pmc-13556306:
Guang-Pei Chen, Douglas Prah, and Eric Paulson report a shared-duty roster for medical physicists across a four-site radiation oncology network, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Site-only coverage had bred uneven workloads and missed quality checks. A physicist-of-the-day model, backed by a live dashboard, pooled the routine work.

Two matched twenty-one-month spans were compared. Task ratios between main and satellite sites evened out sharply. Claim times for chart closing fell from about thirty-seven minutes to six at the main campus. Weekly checks neared perfect completion, and charge capture rose. Staff surveys praised the clarity and balance, the authors report.
pmc-13558306:
Asha K. Rajan and twelve colleagues reviewed in 2026 how to dose the last-resort antibiotic polymyxin B in patients whose kidneys are failing. Drug-resistant Gram-negative infections leave few options, and this drug's behaviour in damaged kidneys, with or without dialysis-like support, is hard to predict. The systematic review gathered population pharmacokinetic studies of adults with renal impairment published up to May 2025 and appraised their quality with a validated tool.

Eleven studies covering 603 patients qualified. Clearance and distribution volume varied widely between individuals. Kidney function, the type of continuous replacement therapy, and illness severity were the main forces moving drug exposure, with flow-driven replacement methods clearing the drug faster. The authors advise against dosing by kidney numbers alone and outline a loading approach plus individual adjustment built on all three factors.
pmc-13558506:
Augustin and colleagues report in 2026 early results from AD-REAL, a multinational study of adults with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis. The study follows them as they start oral systemic treatments in routine care for this chronic itchy skin disease. How long patients stay on these drugs was poorly documented.

The cohort began with 313 patients starting either older conventional drugs, the drug baricitinib, or other drugs from the same Janus kinase inhibitor family. By week 24, about half of the conventional group had stopped their first treatment. Under a third of the baricitinib group and under a fifth of the other inhibitor group had stopped. Ineffectiveness was the main reason for stopping the newer drugs. Far more patients on the newer drugs also reached mild disease levels on a standard eczema severity score.
pmc-13559106:
Ting Zhou and Feng Xiong published a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis on how childhood weight status relates to the timing of puberty. Heavier children have been reported to enter puberty earlier, especially girls, though findings vary between studies. The pair searched five databases, including Chinese sources, for observational work using weight or body mass index as the exposure.

Forty-one studies covering 416,789 participants from 18 countries or regions entered the review. Pooled estimates put the risk of early puberty about 56 percent higher in overweight or obese children than in normal-weight peers. The risk climbed step by step from overweight through obesity to severe obesity, showing a dose-response pattern. Effects were strongest for menarche timing among the markers examined. The authors call for shared definitions of exposure and outcome so future studies compare more cleanly.
pmc-13559206:
Shunsuke Eguchi and co-authors tested whether a heart strain measure still predicts short-term death in intermediate-risk lung clots at a second hospital, in a 2026 study. Their group had earlier found that right ventricle strain below a set cutoff flagged danger. This external check used records from an independent center, for patients treated from 2019 to 2022.

Of 119 patients, six died within thirty days, and strain could be measured in 92 percent. Those who died showed lower strain values than survivors. The measure stayed linked to death in single-variable analysis. The authors weigh how much trust the earlier cutoff deserves in present-day practice.
pmc-13560206:
Hayat Topçu and eight colleagues dissect drought responses in two contrasting strawberry cultivars. Drought limits strawberry yields worldwide, yet cultivar tolerance mechanisms stay poorly understood. Their 2026 study compares drought-tolerant Kara with drought-sensitive E22 under water deficit and PEG-induced osmotic stress. It joins body, chemical, and gene analyses.

E22 lost chlorophyll and photosystem power while Kara held or raised chlorophyll and kept higher power. Proline, a key stress shield, rose much higher in Kara at peak stress. E22 rewrote over 22,500 transcripts under PEG, shutting photosynthesis paths and firing stress signals, while Kara changed under 900 transcripts per stress. Osmotic sensing thus drives large-scale gene control under drought.
pmc-13560706:
Baodi Shang and colleagues report the complete genome of an Acinetobacter strain taken from a sick hybrid sturgeon at a fish farm in Guizhou Province, China. Their 2026 genome announcement describes strain BZX-2, cultured from mucus on ulcerated skin of the hybrid fish in April 2024. Relatives of this bacterium have already sickened farmed sturgeon, disturbing organs and gut communities.

Hybrid long- and short-read sequencing assembled one chromosome of about 3.82 million bases carrying 3,566 predicted protein-coding genes. The team catalogued the strain's antibiotic resistance genes as part of the characterization. The isolate now rests in a national culture collection for other researchers. The authors frame the genome as groundwork for preventing and controlling sturgeon disease in aquaculture, where Acinetobacter outbreaks threaten a valuable farmed fish.
pmc-13561606:
Haodong Guo and colleagues map twenty-five years of research on imaging-guided localization in breast cancer surgery, the techniques that help surgeons find tumors that cannot be felt. Their 2026 bibliometric analysis searches the Web of Science in November 2025 and keeps 366 publications from 2000 to 2025. Network and keyword tools chart who publishes, who cites, and how themes move.

Output climbed steadily after 2011, signaling growing interest, while average citations per article drifted downward in recent years. The United States dominates output, citation impact, and international collaboration in the country analysis. Themes shifted visibly from wire-guided localization and basic imaging toward precision approaches tied to chemotherapy before surgery. The most cited work is clinical, showing guidance improving surgical precision and margin control. The authors call for rigorous comparative trials and wider collaboration to standardize the new methods.
pmc-13561706:
Ling Du and Lei Wang present this 2026 case report on a rare kidney cancer, primary renal squamous cell carcinoma. It makes up under one percent of kidney tumors and has no standard treatment path. Their patient was a fifty-six year old man whose cancer returned soon after kidney removal.

The recurrence appeared one month after surgery for a large, locally advanced tumor. Doctors treated it with sunitinib, a targeted drug that blocks tumor blood vessel signals, combined with precise radiotherapy aimed at the returning mass. The tumor shrank in a partial response, his strength score rose sharply, he gained weight, and his anemia cleared. No spread appeared during follow-up. The authors suggest this pairing deserves study for similar relapses.
pmc-13562506:
Ahmad Sulaiman, writing alone, develops a volcanic rock into a copper filter for polluted water, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Copper from industrial effluent is toxic. It never biodegrades once it is in the ground or the streams. Adsorption can clean it up. But commercial adsorbents for the task are expensive to buy.

Pumice is porous, abundant, and cheap. Yet raw pumice adsorbs in a weak way on its own. Sulaiman prepared and characterized an ion exchanger based on Syrian pumice specifically. The review of past work shows chemical activation can raise capacity in such a stock. Local materials count for a lot in lands where imported resins strain budgets. The study sets Syrian deposits in place as a remediation resource for the land. Affordable water treatment often hinges on geology. It hinges on what rock a region has in the ground as it stands.
pmc-13562606:
Kun Yang and co-authors test, in a 2026 study, whether secondary-type mutations darken the outlook in a leukemia subtype usually considered favorable. NPM1-mutated acute myeloid leukemia often responds well, yet patients vary widely, and these extra mutations were suspected culprits.

The team reviewed 179 patients, weighing age, common partner mutations, and the secondary-type set together. Only age sixty or more and the FLT3-ITD mutation independently predicted worse survival. Patients carrying NPM1, FLT3-ITD, and DNMT3A together fared worst. Secondary-type mutations showed no survival link in the whole group or in risk and age subgroups, though few carriers limits certainty.
pmc-13562806:
Jianwei Wang and co-authors decode what drives people to pay for cancer screening in a 2026 study from China. Willingness to pay is a common lens on why screening uptake lags: if people will not pay, cost or perceived value may be the block. The team joins two classic behavior models, one built on health beliefs and one on planned action, into a single frame.

A staged survey in a cancer screening demonstration zone enrolled more than forty-five hundred residents, most around seventy years old. Questionnaires covered background, both models' measures, and willingness to pay. Layered models picked out the correlates, and a path analysis tested how the beliefs and intentions link in a chain. The map shows where health messages and pricing could move uptake together.
pmc-13563206:
Rashmi Neginhal and Rebecca Rejo George review how the lack of gravity wears the whole body down, read as a web of systems. Their short review, from two thousand twenty-six, draws on flights, ground tests, and cell work.

No weight lifts the load that sets fluid spread, force sense, balance, and blood calm. The shifts do not come organ by organ; they spring from fouled talk across organs. Muscle waste starts in days, with strength lost first. Bone thins at a set pace each month at load sites, and does not fully come back. The heart reshapes, blood bulk shrinks, and stance calm fails on return.
pmc-13563906:
Sheng Zhang and co-authors tested a protective enzyme in retinal pigment cells under low-oxygen stress in two thousand twenty-six. These cells support the retina and are prone to damage from poor oxygen and oxidative stress. A chemical, cobalt chloride, is often used to mimic low oxygen in the lab.

They exposed a cell line to rising doses and tracked wound recovery and metabolic activity. A mid dose gave clear injury without the worst damage, so they used it for deeper tests. Stress markers rose and the enzyme's level fell. A drug that activates the enzyme improved recovery and restored its level, while a blocking drug made injury worse. The enzyme's detox role looks protective.
pmc-13564106:
Rodrigues and colleagues published in twenty twenty-six a genomics study of a burrowing bug damaging peanut crops in the United States. Knowing a pest's identity, diet, and movement usually takes slow field work. New threats, though, demand fast answers. The team combined gut-content DNA tests with population gene sequencing. They examined bugs caught in light traps near peanut fields. Two look-alike species turned up, not the single expected pest.

One species had never been counted a peanut pest before. Gut tests showed both species eat many plants, with somewhat different menus. Peanut itself was a rare item in either diet. Gene data showed weak spread over distance for both species. The authors frame the problem as a pest complex, not a lone species. Genomic shortcuts can speed responses to emerging pests.
pmc-13564506:
Eun Ha Kim, Jung Jun Park, Chang-Moon Lee, Hyeon Jin Kim, and Jung Sick Lee describe a sand dollar's feeding apparatus in this two thousand twenty-six paper. Aristotle's lantern is the jaw-like structure sea urchins use to eat; in Scaphechinus mirabilis its fine structure was unmapped. The team combined light microscopy, scanning electron microscopy, and three-dimensional X-ray microscopy.

The lantern is a star-shaped calcareous assembly of pyramids, joints, and teeth on the shell. Each pyramid splits into two demi-pyramids with an epiphysis and a bump; joints combine ligaments and a rotula. A tooth is an elongated trapezoid, about four millimeters long, with an embedded part tied to ligament and muscle and a projecting part meeting the food. Its fifteen to twenty calcareous layers end in a worn tip. The authors read the tooth as specialized for crushing sediment and food particles internally.
pmc-13565106:
Tara Coreanu and nine colleagues published a 2026 study on a blood score that may foretell outcomes in skin cancer care. The cancer is cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, a common skin malignancy. A drug called cemiplimab has changed its treatment, but doctors lack a good test to sort patients by risk before therapy.

Their score, called GINI, blends immune strength, nutrition, and inflammation into one number. The team checked whether the score, taken before treatment, tracks how patients fare on the drug. Patients across all disease stages were included. A cheap blood-based score could help teams choose who needs closer watch or stronger care. The study tests GINI as that sorting tool.
pmc-13565506:
Sándor Pál, Margit Solymár, and Hussain Alizadeh published a 2026 study of the long-term health of children whose parents took tyrosine kinase inhibitors for chronic myeloid leukemia. These drugs transformed the outlook for this blood cancer, but evidence about offspring exposed before conception or during pregnancy has been limited. Nervous parents need follow-up measured in decades, not months.

The single-centre study followed patients with chronic-phase disease who had a pregnancy, or whose partner did, in association with drug exposure. Offspring health was tracked through adolescence and early adulthood, with follow-up reaching 24.6 years. The authors describe pregnancy outcomes and later health in this cohort. Long-term data of this kind directly inform counseling for patients who want children during treatment.
pmc-13566506:
Osman Görkem Muratoğlu and co-authors examine in 2026 whether flexible nailing restores the natural bow of the radius bone in children's forearm fractures. Union alone is not enough; the bow's size and peak location both shape forearm rotation. They reviewed sixty-one children treated with elastic nails, measuring bow size and position on X-rays taken after surgery.

Average bow size sat near the low end of the reference range. Bow position fell inside its range in about eighty-five percent of cases. Both measures were in range together in about half the children. Regression hunted factors tied to that combined result. Most patients were boys around eleven years old.
pmc-13566706:
Robert Balan and co-authors report early experience with an automated suturing device in heart valve surgery in a 2026 study. Minimally invasive valve replacement offers patients real gains, but stitching the new valve's ring in place through small openings is demanding. The device aims to place those stitches in a standard way.

The team reviewed the first 43 patients treated with the device from 2021 to 2025, covering mitral and aortic valve jobs. Every case was completed with the device, with no mechanical failures or stitch line breaks during surgery. Two patients died within thirty days from medical problems not tied to the device, in a group with high baseline risk. The report judges the tool feasible and safe in early use.
pmc-13566906:
Lingling Xing and twelve co-authors present a 2026 study of a prenatal screening failure flag and its link to poor fetal growth. The screen reads free DNA in the mother's blood. In about 0.2 percent of cases it fails because the mother's own DNA level runs too high, even after a second extraction.

From more than seventy three thousand pregnancies at a large center in China, the team found 102 single pregnancies with that failure flag. They matched them with 396 controls whose DNA level was normal. The main outcome was fetal growth restriction, where the baby grows too slowly. The study weighs whether the flag should prompt closer growth checks.
pmc-13567806:
Zhuwen Yan and co-authors published a research paper in 2026 on keeping steel strip flat when a rolling mill squeezes it with extreme force. Under very high force, flatness control on a six-stand cold mill breaks down and wavy edges appear. The team replaced slow physics simulations with two fast learned stand-ins, trained on sampled process settings.

A combined search then tuned the bending forces on two roller pairs at once, balancing thickness spread, crown shapes, flatness error, and pressure balance. At the highest force tested, thickness spread fell from eighteen to six micrometers and pressure unevenness dropped by three quarters. Edge waves nearly vanished. The recipe offers mills a fast fix under crushing loads.
pmc-13568006:
When a power plant's sensors cry wolf, operators must guess fast: is the process broken, or is the data lying? Fuliang Ma and co-authors build a triage framework for that fork in a 2026 paper on energy systems.

A fixed detector first flags anomalies. Nine consistency checks, grounded in physics, then sort physical faults from measurement-integrity problems. On a chemical process benchmark and a wind farm simulator, cause attribution scored well above chance. Weighing the cost of each wrong response, the framework cut expected losses by up to about twenty-nine percent against blanket reactions. Matched pairs designed to be indistinguishable stayed at chance, an honest boundary: some causes cannot be told apart from data alone, and those cases go to human review.
pmc-13569106:
Geovana Rocha Marzochi and colleagues test, in a 2026 study, whether essential oils from orange and citronella can act as natural weed killers, as herbicide-resistant weeds push farmers to seek alternatives. Oils made by two extraction methods were applied at several doses to seeds of four major weeds, and sprouting and early growth were measured.

Citronella oils nearly stopped seedlings from the middle dose upward, driven by compounds such as citronellol and geraniol. Orange oils weakened germination more gently and unevenly across weed species. The contrast positions citronella oil as a strong bioherbicide candidate and orange oil as a supporting tool in greener weed control.
pmc-13569206:
Javier Caviedes-Bucheli and colleagues review a little-studied brake on tooth pain: neuropeptide Y, a signalling molecule inside the dental pulp. The pulp is a densely wired, rigid tissue where inflammation can quickly raise pressure, choke blood flow, and cause pain. While two excitatory messengers, substance P and CGRP, are well known drivers of that spiral, neuropeptide Y's counterbalancing role has been underexplored. Their 2026 review synthesised 92 studies.

Across models, neuropeptide Y emerged as a master regulator that damps excitation, constricts vessels, and quiets pain-sensing nerves, partly by suppressing CGRP release. In decayed teeth its levels shift with disease stage, hinting at an early protective program that fails as damage advances. The authors frame pulp outcomes as a balance between excitatory and inhibitory signals, with neuropeptide Y as a potential therapeutic lever.
pmc-13569606:
Xiao Wu, Duo Jiang, and Bin Li build, in a 2026 retrospective study, prediction models for complete tumor disappearance after immune therapy given before lung cancer surgery. Two established markers, a tumor protein level and the number of tumor mutations, were combined with clinical features in 232 surgical patients, then checked in 115 later patients at the same hospital.

Combined immune therapy with chemotherapy strongly raised the odds of complete response, as did higher marker levels, while nodal spread lowered them. A paper chart and a machine-learning model were both built and graded for accuracy and calibration. Such tools could help surgeons and patients judge who gains most from pre-surgery immune treatment.
pmc-13571206:
Wei Dong, Xin Zhao, and Qiuxia Gao examine patients receiving continuous blood purification, a demanding dialysis-related treatment. Their cross-sectional study, published in 2026, asks how depressive mood relates to treatment compliance through sleep quality and family resilience.

The authors surveyed one hundred ninety-five patients using scales for depression, sleep quality, family resilience, and dialysis adherence. Depressive mood was linked to poorer sleep and lower family resilience, and both were linked to lower adherence. The chain path from depression through sleep and resilience to adherence contributed a small share of the total effect. The findings point to sleep and family support as possible routes to better compliance.
pmc-13571506:
Yasha Taimuri and Riaz Ahmad review low-oxygen signals in liver scarring in a 2026 paper. Scarred livers form when injury keeps laying down stiff matrix until the organ's shape is lost. Damaged tissue also runs short of oxygen. Proteins that sense low oxygen then switch on genes that drive more scarring, swelling, and abnormal blood vessel growth.

One lead protein in that sensing system activates the liver's scar-making cells. The review also covers fresh links to a form of cell damage driven by iron and rust-like chemistry. Drugs that block the oxygen-sensing path are weighed as future treatments. The authors map where proof is strong and where it is still thin.
pmc-13571806:
Patrik Šimják and colleagues report, in a 2026 prenatal case, blocked nasal passages on both sides spotted in the first trimester. The finding was the first sign of a severe new syndrome in one twin. The pregnancy was a naturally conceived twin pair. Screening at thirteen weeks was normal for both, yet one fetus showed a gap at the upper jaw that prompted a closer look.

Three-dimensional imaging showed both nasal cavities symmetrically widened with clean bony edges and a prominent central bone, suggesting choanal atresia, a blockage never before reported this early. Genetic testing later found a new harmful variant in the KMT2D gene, giving the first prenatal diagnosis of BCAHH syndrome. Early nasal imaging may flag this condition before birth.
pmc-13572206:
Xiaoyu Zhao and co-authors test, in a 2026 study, whether curcumin, the yellow compound in turmeric, protects chick livers against a common plasticizer called DEHP that leaks from plastics into the environment. Cell experiments and live chick exposures traced damage through oxidative stress, energy production, and a mixed cell-death program.

In cells, curcumin restored mitochondrial power, calmed calcium imbalance, and eased internal stress while suppressing a sugar-burning pathway that the plasticizer switched on. Blocking that pathway lowered death markers too. In live chicks, the plasticizer shrank body weight and swelled and scarred the liver, while curcumin feeding largely reversed those changes. The findings support turmeric compounds as a feed defense where plastic contamination reaches poultry.
pmc-13572306:
Four surgeons survey Dutch specialists on elbow nerve surgery in a paper from 2026. The condition, ulnar neuropathy at the elbow, pinches the nerve that serves the hand. Several operations exist, and no single one is agreed best. Follow-up care also varies. The team sent a questionnaire to Dutch plastic, neuro, and orthopedic surgeons with hand expertise.

One hundred sixty-three surgeons replied. Open decompression was the clear favorite for first operations. For repeat operations, moving the nerve under the skin was most chosen. First check-ups usually came four to eight weeks after surgery. Hand therapy was advised by two thirds of surgeons. The authors call for standard, evidence-based protocols.
pmc-13572406:
Somayeh BeyranvandRaad, with two colleagues, presents a 2026 computer study of a nano sheet that might carry the gut drug mesalazine. The drug calms swelling in the bowel, but poor delivery can blunt its effect and raise side effects. The carrier in focus is graphitic carbon nitride, a flat sheet of carbon and nitrogen.

Quantum chemistry calculations compared the drug on the sheet in gas and in water. Binding was favourable in both, at about minus 19.68 and minus 21.50 kilocalories per mole for the most stable pose. Weak forces, not strong bonds, held the pair, which should let the drug come off at the target. Charge flowed from the drug to the sheet. Light absorption peaks shifted in each medium. The authors rate the sheet as a strong carrier prospect.
pmc-13572506:
Maryam Malekpour and four co-authors published a review in twenty twenty-six on copper ferrite, a magnetic speck of matter with real range in medicine. One tiny grain can heat up in a magnetic field, carry drugs, sharpen scan images, and kill germs. The review asks how the way these grains are made steers what they can do.

The authors sort the levers: how the grains are cooked, what atoms are swapped in, how the coat is built, and how they are joined with other stuff. Each choice shifts size, pull, and safety in the body. They then map those traits onto uses, from cancer care to germ control. Gaps in proof of safety get plain words. The piece reads as a builder's guide, not a mere list.
pmc-13573606:
Miles Martinati and co-authors watch salt steer the self-assembly of a dye molecule in water, in a research paper from 2026. The dye, a perylene bisimide, is a prized building block for layered molecular structures. Its clumping is fast and its glow blinds normal probes.

Two light methods, one tracking glow changes and one using Raman scattering, followed the process. Pairs of molecules formed quickly regardless of salt. Chain growth, though, leaned hard on salt: chloride ions slowed the escape of single units, steadying the chains. Raman signals tied these steps to structural shifts inside the stacks. The findings clarify how electrolytes sculpt molecular assembly.
pmc-13574206:
R Elilarassi and co-authors review AI for magnetism in a 2026 paper on spintronics, electronics that use electron spin. New devices need magnetic materials with exact traits: strong spin alignment, large moments, and stability under heat. The search space of mixtures and structures is vast, which is where learning models come in.

The review covers models that predict magnetic traits from data, fed by quantum calculations and lab databases. It explains how features are built from composition, structure, and electron behavior. Graph-based networks and physics-guided learning get special attention. Alloy families, topological systems, and atom-thin magnets are surveyed as hunting grounds. The authors look ahead to self-driving discovery loops that mix prediction with testing.
pmc-13574306:
Marshall and co-authors draw up design guidelines for online health forums, grounded in user experience. Such forums are widely used, yet proof of their benefit is mixed. Better design, tied to theory and lived experience, could improve results. The team ran 54 interviews, with 36 forum users and 18 forum staff. Four design workshops with staff added more input.

Ideas also came from past design research and from self-determination theory. A structured analysis sorted the material into a well-being support frame. The output is a set of guidelines for safe forums that support well-being. The authors hope builders will test the guidelines in live services.
pmc-13574506:
Paolo Compagnucci and fifteen co-authors pool evidence on a heart procedure in a 2026 review. Pulsed field ablation zaps faulty heart tissue with electric pulses. It is well studied in upper heart chambers, less so in the lower ones. Faulty rhythms there can be deadly and hard to treat.

The team gathered seventy five studies, split between lab and clinic work. Just over three hundred fifty patients appeared in the clinical set. Lab lesions reached about six millimeters deep on average. Depth held up even in scarred heart muscle. Full wall penetration varied, running higher inside scar. The review maps how lab measures line up with patient outcomes. It also flags where proof remains thin for wider use.
pmc-13575106:
Nate Christensen sets out a 2026 physics paper linking stability boundaries across fields, from quantum systems to the expanding universe. His organising idea is a damping ratio, a unit-free number that marks where a system's behaviour changes class. At a value of one, the system reaches a special boundary called an exceptional point.

Christensen shows an exact algebraic link between the start of cosmic acceleration and a critical damping point for the growth of structure. He is clear that the link restates known equations rather than adding a new law. Its value, he argues, lies in a testable forecast: models beyond the standard flat cosmology should show a small offset that the standard model lacks. Particle lifetimes are also sorted into stability bands under his scheme.
pmc-13576006:
Albaladejo-Carrasco and co-authors review models of hormone effects in type one diabetes in a paper from two thousand twenty-six. Women with this condition often find blood sugar harder to control at certain points in the monthly cycle. Hormones from the ovaries seem to affect not just insulin sensitivity but several control processes at once.

The review surveys math models that try to link hormone cycles with glucose and insulin control. It finds only a few that join the two systems in an explicit way. The authors say this gap matters as automatic insulin systems grow more common. Better models could lead to tools and dosing methods designed for women.
pmc-13576106:
Mia L Barron leads a 2026 scoping review of communication between clinicians and African American adults living with lupus. Lupus is an autoimmune disease that damages many organs, and outcomes run worse for African American patients. Weak communication and missed screening for changeable risks add to that gap.

Searches of four databases covering 2012 to mid-2025 yielded 214 papers, of which 20 met the review's rules. Helpful habits included involving family, speaking more slowly, and showing empathy. Several papers pushed for decision aids with communication built in. None tested a communication tool aimed at cutting changeable risks or improving outcomes in this group. The authors flag that absence as the key gap for future work.
pmc-13576206:
Chang-Zhu He and five colleagues test whether combining structural and blood flow eye scans improves spotting normal-tension glaucoma in very short-sighted eyes, in a 2026 diagnostic study. High myopia and this glaucoma type can look alike, making diagnosis tricky. Structural scans map tissue layers, while a related scan maps tiny vessels.

The study enrolled 87 patients, 42 with high myopia alone and 45 with glaucoma added. Structural measures beat vessel measures overall. One layer measure at the lower macula scored best, at 0.85 on the ranking accuracy scale, while the best vessel measure sat lower. Machine learning and standard regression models were built from the chosen features and checked with resampling and calibration tests. Explanation tools showed how each feature pushed individual predictions. The authors see combined data as useful support for a hard distinction.
pmc-13576306:
Giuseppe Migliaretti and Paolo Giacomo Arduino test whether entrance exam scores forecast success in dental school, in a 2026 study from the University of Turin. Italy long admitted dental students by national exam, and a recent reform scrapped that route. The team looked back at 431 students enrolled between 2009 and 2018.

Higher admission scores tracked with earning credits on schedule and graduating on time. The test predicted first-year performance with a ranking score of 0.71, and degree completion at 0.70 in the same units. A cut-off of 40 out of 90 separated strugglers: students below it had five times the odds of falling behind on first-year credits. The authors argue the findings should inform the debate on removing the exam, given the risks for dropout rates and wasted resources.
pmc-13576606:
Chiu and colleagues published a 2026 trial on a magnetic tracer for breast cancer surgery. Surgeons check the first lymph node, the sentinel node, to stage early breast cancer. The standard method pairs a radioactive tracer with a blue dye. The trial tested iron oxide particles that a magnet probe can find instead.

Nearly 300 patients were split between the magnetic tracer and the standard pair. The magnetic method found the sentinel node in over 99 percent of cases. The standard pair scored a perfect rate, a gap within the set limit. One failure occurred in the magnetic group across 153 procedures. The authors back the magnetic tracer as a sound stand-in option. The trial ran from 2021 to 2024 across several hospital centers.
pmc-13578506:
Konsta Kukkonen and six co-authors compare how male hormone signals reshape DNA access in healthy and cancerous prostate cells, in this twenty twenty-six study. The hormone switch, the androgen receptor, opens and closes stretches of DNA. Its effect in healthy prostate cells was poorly known, for lack of good cell models.

The team used lab cell lines of both types, with and without the hormone. Even before the hormone, the two cell types differed widely in which DNA lay open. The hormone widened the gap, opening distinct sets of sites in each type. The maps show why the same hormone can drive growth in cancer yet act calmly in healthy tissue.
pmc-13579306:
Flavio Miura and eight co-authors published an education research study in twenty twenty-six on how well exams actually measure doctors' retained ethics training. Residents took interactive courses on practical ethics and professional conduct, then sat twenty-question retention tests. The team subjected both exams to classical psychometric analysis.

The first exam was easy and weakly reliable; nearly everyone answered nearly everything correctly, leaving little spread to measure. The second improved markedly on reliability and discrimination. The authors argue easy items after good teaching can signal genuine short-term retention, not just a bad test. Still, ceiling effects limit what such exams can prove. The paper presses medical schools to design ethics assessment as carefully as ethics teaching.
pmc-13580006:
Yuteng Wang and a large team of co-authors link social isolation and loneliness to early menopause and death in women, in a 2026 study of the UK Biobank. Nearly eighty thousand women were classed by when menopause came, early at forty to forty five or in the normal band after that. Isolation was scored from living setup, contact, and group life; loneliness from felt loneliness and having someone to confide in.

Both hardships tied to higher odds of early menopause, modestly but steadily. The survival penalty hit far harder in the early group: high isolation raised death risk by over half there, against a far smaller lift in the normal group. Survival curves split wider as hardship rose. The authors urge menopause care to screen for social strain.
pmc-13580606:
Arif Ahmed and a team of co-authors test trust in AI health answers, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. Two randomized experiments asked whether habit-like reliance on AI skews how people judge its output. Highlight cues in the text were tested as a counterweight.

The first run used 338 college students; the second, 563 online workers. Each split people by answer accuracy and by whether key text was highlighted. Trust was scored on a multi-item scale. The design separates blind trust from earned trust and checks whether simple cues can curb overreliance on wrong answers.
pmc-13583806:
Susan Phillips and Han Han review whether machine learning risk scores truly improve on the classic Framingham heart risk score. New algorithms promise sharper forecasts of cardiovascular disease. Twenty-nine studies that compared the two head-on passed the screen. Twenty-three claimed better prediction than the old score.

Most wins rode on adding social and demographic inputs the old score never used. Some gains leaned on pricey scans added to cheap screening data. Outcome labels often drifted from the classic score's own definitions. Statistical wins were read as clinical wins without proof. Over-counting risk and its overdiagnosis shadow went largely undiscussed.
pmc-13584006:
Huidi Li, Nikolaos Chrysanthidis, Scott L Brincat, Jonas Rose, and Earl K Miller study how the brain reshapes its code once a choice is made. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. Value-based choice means a subject holds two options in mind and picks the one worth more. How the brain's code for those options changes after the pick was not clear.

They record from a front brain zone in primates who hold two option-value pairs in memory. Before the pick, the code is sorted by the order in which options came. Once a pick can be made, the chosen and the passed options turn into split code zones. The chosen code grows and lines up with the act to come.
pmc-13585106:
Simran Desai and four co-authors published a 2026 study of a sleep breathing problem in children with misaligned teeth and jaws. Upper airway resistance syndrome makes breathing harder during sleep, causing broken sleep and daytime tiredness without obvious drops in oxygen. Mouth breathing in childhood can also push teeth into poor positions.

The study compared 25 children with malocclusion against 25 controls in Bengaluru, India, all aged 8 to 14. The breathing problem was clearly more common in the malocclusion group. Class II bite patterns, narrow upper jaws, and set-back lower jaws were all linked to it. The authors recommend early orthodontic screening and teamwork between dentists, child doctors, and ear, nose, and throat specialists.
pmc-13585606:
Ma, Chen, Guo, and Han reported a hard-to-classify lung cancer case in twenty twenty-six. Small cell lung cancer has subtypes; one, marked by the protein POU2F3, makes few of the usual neuroendocrine markers, so small biopsies can mislead. Their patient was a sixty-one-year-old man with a high-grade tumor in the left upper lung lobe.

Two biopsies from different sites both suggested small cell carcinoma, but marker patterns varied between samples and reviews. POU2F3 staining supported the subtype assignment. While classification stayed unresolved, the team used a chemotherapy plus immunotherapy bridge. After four cycles the tumor shrank markedly, and a multidisciplinary decision led to surgery. The removed tissue showed a complete pathological response. Later cycles followed, and surveillance imaging in twenty twenty-six showed no recurrence, with no tumor DNA in blood. The authors stress one case sets no standard.
pmc-13587006:
Panning Wang and four co-authors review protein chip tools for stomach cancer research in a paper from 2026. Stomach cancer kills many people worldwide, in part because it is found late and varies a lot between patients. Gene studies miss shifts in the proteins that run cells, so chips that measure hundreds to thousands of proteins at once fill a gap.

The review covers chip types and their use in finding early markers, sorting tumors into subtypes, and judging drug response. Panels of many markers beat single-marker tests, and chip data expose pathways behind growth and drug resistance. Cost and clinic readiness remain open issues.
pmc-13587106:
Adelie YS Tan and a large team map decay in the striatum, a deep brain hub for movement, in X-linked dystonia parkinsonism. The inherited disease, first described in 1976 and rooted on the Philippine island of Panay, mixes twisting movements with Parkinson-like slowness. Its brain signature stayed murky because so few cases have been studied. The team stained post-mortem tissue from 18 patients and 10 people without brain disease.

Decay ran in a gradient from top to bottom of the striatum, and one inner compartment, the matrix, wore away faster than its partner patches. The pattern tracked how long the disease had run more than the length of the gene repeat that causes it, though that repeat did set the age when symptoms began. The authors read the damage as the slow breakup of a wider movement circuit over the course of the illness.
pmc-13587806:
Houria Ech-Cherif and co-authors show that the two molecular subgroups of a rare human nerve sheath cancer also appear in dogs, in a 2026 study. These aggressive tumors grow from Schwann-lineage cells and carry poor outlooks in both species, while arising more often in dogs. Human tumors split into two groups with different pathways and prognoses, raising the question of a canine match.

pmc-13595506:

pmc-13617106:

Most cited the set only once, usually in the introduction or methods. About a third reported using the recommended measures in their own work. The team also coded written feedback and tracked attention scores and reader saves. The audit shows where the guideline landed and where the revision should push harder.
pmc-13618906:
Ioannis Vasilikos and seventeen colleagues test borrowed eye surgery chemistry on the dura mater, the tough membrane wrapping the brain and spinal cord, whose defects challenge neurosurgeons. Riboflavin plus ultraviolet-A light crosslinks collagen in the cornea. Here the team applied it to forty specimens of cow dura outside the body, varying vitamin concentration and light intensity. They measured stiffness with an atomic force microscope before and after in matched spots.

Ultraviolet light alone stiffened the tissue modestly, two to three fold. Adding riboflavin produced a dramatic, concentration-dependent effect: the strongest recipe raised the elastic modulus about one hundred fifty fold. Post-treatment stiffness rose in a nearly perfect straight line with riboflavin dose, making the effect precisely adjustable. The authors call it proof of concept for biochemical reinforcement of dural tissue, with human tissue testing, macroscopic strength checks, penetration depth, and safety work still to come.
pmc-13619006:
Milena Marie Santo and nine colleagues compare the microbial chemistry along the gut under four feeding regimes. The options were round-the-clock pasture, hay freely available, or hay plus oats at two starch doses. After feeding, the horses were dissected and digesta sampled from successive sections, analyzed for dry matter, acidity, short-chain fatty acids, ammonia, and lactate, the fingerprints of microbial fermentation.

Gut section dominated: each measure differed between sections, with a clean divide between foregut and hindgut, and within the hindgut. Diet still mattered. Pasture-fed horses showed the highest fatty acid levels, signaling vigorous fermentation. In the far hindgut, pasture raised markers of amino acid breakdown, suggesting microbes there fermented more protein. Oat supplementation changed chemistry in the stomach, pointing to higher protein-splitting activity upstream. The map explains how feeding shifts where fermentation happens in the horse gut, relevant to gut health and disorder risk.
pmc-13619206:
Guang-Hua Liang, Talante Juma, and Heng Liu measure germ contamination on surgical tools during joint replacement, in this 2026 study. Germs that land on tools mid-surgery might seed later infection, but how often this happens was unclear. The team cultured samples from blades, suction tips, and antiseptic drapes in 127 first-time joint operations. Patients were then followed for two to three years.

About ten percent of patients had at least one positive culture. The skin-cutting blade showed the highest rate, near six percent, though no tool differed clearly from the unused control blade. Rates did differ across tool types overall. No patient developed a surgical infection during follow-up. The authors stress that lab contamination and real infection are different things.
pmc-13619706:
Niklas Amann and thirteen colleagues reviewed how often women with breast cancer and an inherited BRCA mutation chose preventive removal of the ovaries and fallopian tubes. Such surgery is the only proven way to cut the raised ovarian cancer risk these mutations bring. The team studied 148 patients treated at a German university center between 2012 and 2024.

About sixty percent carried a BRCA1 change and the rest a BRCA2 change. Just over two thirds of the group went on to have the preventive surgery, and most of those operations happened within two years of the breast cancer diagnosis. Hidden ovarian cancer turned up in three women at the time of surgery, while four women without the surgery later developed ovarian cancer. The authors argue the operation should keep being offered and discussed under current guidelines.
pmc-13621806:
Cécile De Cat and five co-authors ask how much exposure multilingual children need before their school language skills match those of monolingual classmates. Children who grow up with several languages are often judged against one-language norms, which can hide real support needs. The study covers children aged five to nine learning English, French, or Dutch as the language of school.

The team tested sentence repetition and word knowledge, then used statistical models that allow for turning points instead of fixed cut-offs. For grammar, group scores entered the monolingual range after roughly fifty-nine months of added-up exposure, with gains levelling off near that point. Word knowledge showed no clear threshold, and thinking skills plus rich language experience mattered more than exposure alone. The authors advise steady language support through primary school rather than early withdrawal.
pmc-13623606:
Zidong Zhou, Hongqiu Wu, and Xifeng Qiao present a 2026 study on food-specific IgG antibodies and symptoms in children. IgG testing for food intolerance is popular but its links to symptoms are murky. The team reviewed one hundred children in Zhuhai, China, testing blood antibodies against fourteen common foods. Egg, milk, and wheat topped the list, positive in most children.

The more often a food tested positive, the larger its share of strong reactions. Boys and girls differed in how reaction strength tracked positivity, and responses tended to weaken with age. Cough, nasal complaints, and tic disorders were the commonest symptoms. A pattern-mining method found four strong rules; the strongest tied a traditional symptom pattern to combined egg and milk positivity. The authors say the links may guide diets for intolerant children, while stressing that prospective studies must confirm them.
pmc-13623906:
Xian and three co-authors review smart materials that react to signals inside organ-on-a-chip devices. These chips grow human tissue in tiny channels to mimic organs for testing. Standard chip materials, though, stay static while real tissues change over time.

Responsive materials shift their structure, flow, or sensing behavior when they meet heat, chemistry, or biological cues. The review sorts recent advances by the material's job in the chip: shaping the tissue's surroundings, joining tissues, or reading out results. Most cited work comes from the last three years. The authors map material choices to measured biological performance. They offer the survey as a design guide for the next chips.
pmc-13624706:
Suguru Miida and colleagues chart how thigh-level muscle, measured at the third lumbar level on CT scans, wastes away over five years in people with cirrhosis.
